But the virtual and as it were radical denomination he takes not from the intellect but from his own nature, because by its own nature and entity anything whatever is intelligible; wherefore according to this denomination it does not depend on the intellect, but is prior to it. The testimony of Aristotle, on the other hand, touches on the manner of defining one relative through the other; wherefore it cannot be conveniently explained before we reach the category of relation.

> Sed licèt distinctio obiecti in esse rei, & in esse scibilis à Caie. tradita necessaria sit, non est tamen sufficiens ad explicandam vnitatem specificam, quam in Logica ponimus, nisi ampliùs explicetur, & ostendatur, à quonam sit sumenda vnitas obiecti, in esse scibilis: nam illud tantùm erit ratio formalis à qua eandem vnitatem accipiet scientia. Explicandã verò est per aliam distinctionem, ita habentem. In quocumque obiecto scientiæ, potentiæ, vel habitus, duo reperimus, nempe rem, quã per scientiam, aut potentiam percipimus: & hæc vocatur ratio Quæ, hoc est ratio Quæ percipitur: reperitur etiam ratio Sub qua potentia versatur circa illam, aut eam percipit: & hæc dicitur ratio, Sub qua, obiecti, per quam determinatur: & ex vtraque ratione, Quæ, & Sub qua, constituitur vnum obiectum completum atque totale: ex ratione, Quæ, tanquam ex materiali, & ex ratione, Sub qua, tanquam ex formali: vnde contingere potest, quod eadem ratio. Quæ, sit obiectum diuersorum habituum, aut potentiarũ, propter diuersas rationes, sub quibus percipitur: & propterea verum est, à ratione, sub qua, tanquam à formali, & vltima, sumere suam vnitatem, potentias, habitus, & scientias Hoc exemplo fiet res manifesta. In obiecto visus, reperimus id, quod videtur, & hoc est color, aut lumen, & vocatur [p. 15] ratio, Quæ obiectiua: reperimus etiam visibilitatem, quę non est aliud, quàm colorem, aut lumen ex propria natura posse mouere potentiam visiuam, & ab ea videri: & ex vtraque ratione, nempe colore, & visibilitate, constituitur obiectum completum potentiæ visiuæ, ex colore quidem, vt materia, ex visibilitate verò, vt forma, à qua vnitatem accipit eadem potentia: & eodem modo ad obiecta scientiarum applicanda est distinctio hæc: dicendúmque rationem, Sub qua, esse rationem scibilis, à qua vnitas specifica earum sumenda est.

But although the distinction of the object in its being as a thing and in its being as knowable, handed down by Cajetan, is necessary, it is not, however, sufficient to explain the specific unity that we posit in Logic, unless it is explained further and it is shown from what the unity of the object in its being as knowable is to be taken; for that alone will be the formal ratio from which the science will receive the same unity. It is to be explained, then, by another distinction, which runs thus. In any object of a science, power or habit we find two things: namely the thing which we perceive through the science or power, and this is called the ratio Quae, that is, the ratio Which is perceived; and there is also found the ratio Sub qua, under which the power is concerned with it or perceives it; and this is called the ratio Sub qua of the object, by which it is determined. And from both rationes, the Quae and the Sub qua, one complete and total object is constituted: from the ratio Quae as from the material, and from the ratio Sub qua as from the formal. Whence it can happen that the same ratio Quae is the object of different habits or powers, on account of the different rationes under which it is perceived; and therefore it is true that powers, habits and sciences take their unity from the ratio Sub qua, as from the formal and ultimate one. By this example the matter will become manifest. In the object of sight we find that which is seen, and this is color or light, and it is called [p. 15] the objective ratio Quae; we also find visibility, which is nothing other than that color or light can, from its own nature, move the visual power and be seen by it; and from both rationes, namely color and visibility, the complete object of the visual power is constituted: from color, as matter, and from visibility, as form, from which the same power receives its unity. And in the same way this distinction is to be applied to the objects of the sciences; and it is to be said that the ratio Sub qua is the ratio of knowability, from which their specific unity is to be taken.

> Sed restat explicandum, id quod in hac re difficillimum est, nempe ratio, Sub qua, in obiectis sciẽtiarum: nam ratio, Quæ, satis est manifesta: est nâmque materia circa quam versatur scientia, vt ens rationis, in Logica: & ens reale, in Metaphysic. Caiet. & Ferra. vbi suprà, rationẽ scibilis, in obiecto cuiuslibet scientiæ, ex tali modo abstrahẽdi à materia accipienda esse docent, vt ratio, Sub qua, in obiecto Metaph. sit omnimoda abstractio eius à materia, hoc est abstractio à materia, non solùm sensibili, sed etiam intelligibili: in Philosophia naturali, abstractio à materia singulari, non tamen à materia sensibili.

But it remains to explain what is most difficult in this matter, namely the ratio Sub qua in the objects of the sciences; for the ratio Quae is quite manifest: for it is the matter about which the science is concerned, as being of reason in Logic, and real being in Metaphysics. Cajetan and Ferrara, in the places cited above, teach that the ratio of knowability in the object of any science is to be taken from such and such a mode of abstracting from matter: so that the ratio Sub qua in the object of Metaphysics is its total abstraction from matter, that is, abstraction from matter not only sensible but also intelligible; in natural Philosophy, abstraction from singular matter, but not from sensible matter.

> Hanc tamen sententiam falsam reputo, quia abstractio à materia nimis vniuersalis est: & propterea non potest esse ratio, Sub qua, tribuens scientię specificam vnitatem, aut distinctionem: nam sub eadem abstractione continentur plures, ac diuersę scientię, vt sub abstractione à materia singulari, & non sensibili, vtraque Philosophia, Naturalis, & Moralis: sub abstractione à materia sensibili, vtraque, Mathematica, videlicet, Geometria, & Arithmetica.

This opinion, however, I consider false, because abstraction from matter is too universal; and therefore it cannot be the ratio Sub qua conferring specific unity or distinction on a science: for under the same abstraction several and different sciences are contained: as under abstraction from singular matter and not from sensible matter, both Philosophies, Natural and Moral; under abstraction from sensible matter, both Mathematical sciences, namely Geometry and Arithmetic.

> Veram ergo sententiam ex doctrina D. Th. colligo, nempe rationem, Sub qua, in obiectis scientiarum, desumendam esse, ex tali medio assentiendi conclusionibus, sicut in fide sumitur ex testimonio dicentis, medium verò assentiendi conclusionibus, sunt principia disposita in demonstratione, ex quibus colligitur conclusio: v. g. medium assentiendi huic conclusioni, homo est risibilis, sunt illa principia, omne animal rationale est risibile, omnis homo est animal rationale sic disposita, vt ex eis colligatur, hominem esse risibilem: nam propter illa assentimus conclusioni. Materia igitur, circa quam versatur scientia, in quantum sumitur sub talibus principiis eiusdem scientiæ in demonstratione dispositis, propter quæ assentitur intellectus conclusionibus de eo demonstratis, est obiectum completum: sed principia sic disposita est ratio formalis, Sub qua, obiectiua, à qua scientia sumit suam vnitatem specificam. Et colligitur etiam ex doctrina, quam tradit Arist. [p. 16] de vnitate, ac distinctione scientiarum 1. li. de posteriori resolutione c. 23. vbi *principia scientiarum duobus modis se habere docet*: nam vel sic sunt diuersa, vt nec ex aliis fiant, nec ex alterutris, hoc est, nec ex aliis communibus dependeant, nec necessariam dependentiam inter se habeant: & hæc diuersas scientias constituunt: sic se habent principia Philosophię, & mathematicæ, & propterea diuersę sunt tales scientię. Sed principia Philosophiæ naturalis, ex communibus principiis Physicis, pertinentia ad materiam & formam, fiunt, & intrinsecam dependentiam inter se habent, in quantum principia librorum de cœlo, & mundo præsupponuntur necessariò ad principia librorum de Generatione, & corruptione, & hæc ad libros de anima: propterea eandem scientiam secundùm speciem constituunt omnes istę partes. Et ita etiam se habent principia Logicæ: quia principia particularia omnium partium, præsupponunt communia principia entis rationis, aut modi sciendi, ex quibus fieri dicuntur: & eadem principia partium Logicę se præsupponunt: & posteriora habent necessariam connexionem & dependentiam ex prioribus, vt principium enuntiationis, quod est definitio eius, præsupponit necessariò principia prædicabilium & prædicamentorum, quæ sunt definitiones eorum: ac tandem principia syllogisticę artis, præsupponunt, atque dependent ex principiis enuntiationis: & hoc est ex alterutris fieri, hoc est posteriora ex prioribus, propter necessariam dependentiam, quàm ab eis habent: & principia quæ ita se habent, dicuntur eadem formaliter, propter intrinsecam connexionem, ac dependentiam: & solùm materialiter diuersa, quia diuersam continent materiam, simplicem quidem, aut compositam, & compositam quoque diuersam, vnde sequitur, rationem, Sub qua, in obiecto Dialecticæ, ex iisdem principiis desumptam, eandem esse, ideò vnitatem specificam scientię tribuere.

The true opinion, then, I gather from the doctrine of St. Thomas: namely that the ratio Sub qua in the objects of the sciences is to be taken from such and such a middle for assenting to the conclusions, just as in faith it is taken from the testimony of the one speaking. Now the middle for assenting to the conclusions is the principles disposed in a demonstration, from which the conclusion is gathered: for example, the middle for assenting to this conclusion, Man is risible, is those principles, Every rational animal is risible, Every man is a rational animal, so disposed that from them it is gathered that man is risible: for on account of them we assent to the conclusion. The matter, therefore, about which a science is concerned, inasmuch as it is taken under such principles of the same science disposed in a demonstration, on account of which the intellect assents to the conclusions demonstrated of it, is the complete object; but the principles so disposed are the formal objective ratio Sub qua, from which the science takes its specific unity. And it is gathered also from the doctrine that Aristotle hands down [p. 16] on the unity and distinction of the sciences, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 23, where he teaches that the principles of the sciences stand in two ways: for either they are so different that they neither come from others nor from one another, that is, they neither depend on other, common principles, nor have a necessary dependence among themselves; and these constitute different sciences: thus stand the principles of Philosophy and of Mathematics, and therefore such sciences are different. But the principles of natural Philosophy come from the common principles of Physics, pertaining to matter and form, and have an intrinsic dependence among themselves, inasmuch as the principles of the books On the Heavens and the World are necessarily presupposed to the principles of the books On Generation and Corruption, and these to the books On the Soul; therefore all these parts constitute the same science according to species. And so too stand the principles of Logic: because the particular principles of all the parts presuppose the common principles of being of reason, or of mode of knowing, from which they are said to come; and the same principles of the parts of Logic presuppose one another, and the posterior ones have a necessary connection with and dependence on the prior ones: as the principle of the enunciation, which is its definition, necessarily presupposes the principles of the predicables and categories, which are their definitions; and finally the principles of the syllogistic art presuppose and depend on the principles of the enunciation; and this is to come from one another, that is, the posterior from the prior, on account of the necessary dependence they have on them. And principles that stand thus are called the same formally, on account of their intrinsic connection and dependence, and different only materially, because they contain different matter, simple or composite, and composite matter of different kinds too. Whence it follows that the ratio Sub qua in the object of Dialectic, taken from those same principles, is the same, and therefore confers specific unity on the science.

> 11 Ad primum argumentum primæ opinionis respondetur partes Logicæ materialiter quidem, aut in esse rei, diuersas esse: sed formaliter, aut in esse scribili, habere vnitatem specificam: Sicut colores specie differunt, vt albedo, & nigredo in esse rei, cùm sint res, aut qualitates diuersæ speciei: at verò sub ratione formali visibilis eiusdem sunt speciei: quod efficaciter probatur, quia eundem habent modum mouendi visum: vnde visio albi, & nigri, non sunt diuersę speciei, sed eiusdem: eadem ergo ratione partes Logicæ, vt prædicabilia, prædicamenta, enuntiatio, ac syllogismus, vt sunt res quædam, diuersaque instrumenta, specie distinguuntur: ac sub ratione scribilis, [p. 17] nẽpe, vt sub eiusdem principiis, & per easdem demonstrationes probantur conclusiones earum, eiusdem rationis sunt, quia eundem modum habet Logica eas cognoscendi, hoc est, per eadẽ principia. Et quod in argumento additur; Principia esse diuersa eodem modo soluendum est. Esse quidem diuersas veritates; sed propter intrinsecam connexionem, ac dependentiam, quam habent ex principiis communibus entis rationis, & inter sese; in quantum posteriora præsupponunt necessariò priora, vt principia syllogismi, & principia enuntiationis, principia simplicium, ex quibus enuntiatio componitur, hoc est prædicabilium, & prædicamẽtorum, eadem principia formaliter reputantur, vt Arist. docuit vbi suprà, & propter formalem principiorum identitatem, demonstrationes cuiuslibet partis Logicæ, eiusdem etiam rationis sunt, atque etiam omnes conclusiones, & obiectum quoque idem, propter formalem identitatem principiorum.

11 To the first argument of the first opinion the reply is that the parts of Logic are indeed different materially, or in their being as things, but formally, or in their being as knowable, they have specific unity. Just as colors differ in species, as whiteness and blackness, in their being as things, since they are things or qualities of different species; but under the formal ratio of the visible they are of the same species: which is efficaciously proved, because they have the same mode of moving sight; whence the vision of white and of black are not of different species but of the same. By the same reasoning, then, the parts of Logic, such as the predicables, the categories, the enunciation and the syllogism, as they are certain things and different instruments, are distinguished in species; but under the ratio of the knowable, [p. 17] namely as their conclusions are proved under the same principles and through the same demonstrations, they are of the same ratio, because Logic has the same mode of knowing them, that is, through the same principles. And what is added in the argument, that the principles are different, is to be resolved in the same way: that they are indeed different truths; but on account of the intrinsic connection and dependence that they have on the common principles of being of reason, and among themselves, inasmuch as the posterior necessarily presuppose the prior (as the principles of the syllogism and the principles of the enunciation presuppose the principles of the simple terms of which the enunciation is composed, that is, of the predicables and categories), they are reputed formally the same principles, as Aristotle taught in the place above; and on account of the formal identity of the principles, the demonstrations of any part of Logic are also of the same ratio, and so too are all the conclusions, and the object is likewise the same, on account of the formal identity of the principles.

> Ad secundum respõdeo, quòd dum intellectus acquisiuit habitum Logicæ per demonstrationem vnius partis, & postea se exercet circa alias partes per nouas demonstrationes, quasdam alias facilitates acquirit, non tamen alios habitus: quia facilitates istæ, eiusdem rationis sunt, propter vnitatem specificam principiorum, & conclusionum, per quas acquiruntur, & solùm distinguuntur materialiter, tanquam partes integrantes eiusdem habitus: qui licèt sit qualitas spiritualis, & ideo non habeat partes integrantes quantitatiuas, atque corporeas, sic vt habent corpora: habet tamen spirituales, iuxta propriam naturam, quæ dicuntur partes extensionis: sicut certum est habere partes intensionis, vt suo loco explicabitur, nec propter tales partes desinit esse qualitas simplex, quemadmodum desineret esse, si essent distincti habitus, vt asserit opposita sententia: quia esse simplicem qualitatem, hoc tantùm significat, quòd non sit composita ex multis qualitatibus aut habitibus formaliter, aut specie diuersis: nam talis compositio tolleret vnitatem specificam eius, quam certum est non tollere partes integrantes, solùm materialiter diuersas: sicut non tollit quin albedo Petri sit simplex qualitas, quod habeat partes integrantes in capite, & pede. Hanc autem compositionem partium integrantium, ac materialium, tribuit scientiæ D. Tho. 17. quæst. 12. art. 2. etiam si expressè doceat esse simplicem habitum, & qualitatem, vt vidimus: quare non credit repugnare simplicitati eius.

To the second I reply that when the intellect has acquired the habit of Logic through the demonstration of one part, and afterwards exercises itself about other parts through new demonstrations, it acquires certain other facilities, yet not other habits: because these facilities are of the same ratio, on account of the specific unity of the principles and conclusions through which they are acquired, and are distinguished only materially, as integral parts of the same habit. And although this habit is a spiritual quality, and therefore does not have quantitative and bodily integral parts, as bodies have, it has nevertheless spiritual ones, according to its own nature, which are called parts of extension; just as it is certain that it has parts of intension, as will be explained in its place. Nor on account of such parts does it cease to be a simple quality, as it would cease to be if there were distinct habits, as the opposite opinion asserts: because to be a simple quality signifies only that it is not composed of many qualities or habits formally or specifically different; for such a composition would take away its specific unity, which it is certain integral parts, different only materially, do not take away: just as the fact that Peter’s whiteness has integral parts in the head and in the foot does not prevent it from being a simple quality. And this composition of integral and material parts St. Thomas attributes to science, 17, q. 12, a. 2, even though he expressly teaches that it is a simple habit and quality, as we have seen; wherefore he does not believe that it is repugnant to its simplicity. B

[p. 18]

> QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

### Quæst. 5. Vtrum Logica sit scientia practica, & speculatiua — Whether Dialectic is a practical or a speculative science.

> Vtrùm Dialectica sit scientia practica, vel speculatiua.

[…]

> 12 Præsupponit titulus quæstionis quasdam esse scientias practicas, & alias speculatiuas: quod docet expressè Arist. 2. lib. Meta. & est cõmunis sententia totius scholę; probaturque hoc argumento. Practicum est quod sua natura ordinatur ad opus: sed quædam sunt scientiæ de operabilibus à nobis, & quæ ad finem operandi earum cognitionem ordinant; vt Philosophia moralis agens de virtutibus, & medicina de corpore humano sanabili; aliæ verò quæ circa res purè speculatiuas versantur: ergo necesse est admittere practicas, & speculatiuas scientias. Quo supposito, quærimus, an Dialectica pertineat ad practicas, vel ad speculatiuas Sed vt quæstio meliùs intelligatur, adnotandum est, quid sit praxis, & quid practicum. Praxis idem est quod operatio, & practicum idem, quod operatiuum, vel principium operationis, vel directiuum eiusdem operationis: sed principium operationis duplex est, proximum, & remotum: proximum est illud, à quo operatio procedit, vel dirigitur, remotum verò, quod considerat operationem in communi, tradens præcepta eam faciendi, aut dirigẽdi: ex quibus sequitur, vt eam in singulari faciat, aut dirigat. Exemplum primi habemus in artibus. Nam ars fabrilis proximum principium est operationis. Exemplum secundi in scientiis practicis. Nam cùm scientia non sit de singularibus, sed de vniuersalibus, & operatio nõ fiat nisi in singulari: non possunt scientiæ esse proximum principium operationis, sed remotum tantùm; ex eo quòd præcepta in communi tradunt, docentes quonam modo efficienda sit, aut dirigenda in singulari. Vnde sequitur, practicum, priùs ad principalius dici de artibus quàm de scientiis: sed ad veram rationem scientiæ practicæ satis est, esse principium remotum operationis modo explicato, quia impossibile est esse principium proximum operationis, cùm non in singulari, sed in communi eam consideret. Vtraque acceptio practici continetur in Doctrina Aristo. prima quidem, & propria 6. Ethic. c. 5. vsque ad 8. vbi solùm enumerat duos habitus practicos; nempe prudentiam, & artem: quia solùm isti sunt principia proxima factiua, aut directiua operationis. Secunda verò & minùs propria 2. li. Met. cap. 1. tex. 1. lib. 6. cap 1. tex. 2. & 3. & lib. 11 c. 1. quibus locis practicũ, attribuit scientiis, diuidens eas in speculatiuas, & practicas [p. 19] sed scientiis non potest conuenire primo ac propriissimo modo sumpto, sed solùm secundo modo, & minùs proprio, sufficienti tamen, vt verè & propriè dicantur scientię practicę. ex quibus intelligitur, quòd dum quærimus An Logica sit scientia speculatiua vel practica, non de practico propriissimo loquimur, sed de minùs proprio quod potest conuenire scientiis.

12 The title of the question presupposes that some sciences are practical and others speculative: which Aristotle teaches expressly, Metaph. 2, and it is the common opinion of the whole school; and it is proved by this argument. That is practical which by its own nature is ordered to a work; but some sciences are about things operable by us, and order their cognition to the end of operating, as moral Philosophy, which treats of the virtues, and medicine, of the human body as able to be healed; others, however, are concerned with purely speculative things; therefore it is necessary to admit practical and speculative sciences. This supposed, we ask whether Dialectic belongs to the practical or to the speculative sciences. But in order that the question may be better understood, it should be noted what praxis is, and what the practical is. Praxis is the same as operation, and the practical the same as the operative, or the principle of the operation, or what is directive of the same operation. But the principle of an operation is twofold, proximate and remote. The proximate is that from which the operation proceeds or by which it is directed; the remote, on the other hand, is that which considers the operation in general, handing down precepts for making or directing it; from which it follows that it makes or directs it in the singular. We have an example of the first in the arts: for the smith’s art is the proximate principle of the operation. An example of the second in the practical sciences: for since science is not of singulars but of universals, and an operation does not take place except in the singular, the sciences cannot be the proximate principle of operation, but only the remote one, from the fact that they hand down precepts in general, teaching in what way things are to be made or directed in the singular. Whence it follows that “practical” is said first and more principally of the arts than of the sciences; but for the true ratio of a practical science it is enough to be the remote principle of an operation in the manner explained, because it is impossible for it to be the proximate principle of an operation, since it considers it not in the singular but in general. Both acceptations of “practical” are contained in the doctrine of Aristotle: the first and proper one in Ethics 6, ch. 5 through 8, where he enumerates only two practical habits, namely prudence and art, because only these are proximate principles, productive or directive, of an operation; the second and less proper one in Metaph. 2, ch. 1, text 1; bk. 6, ch. 1, text 2 and 3; and bk. 11, ch. 1, in which places he attributes “practical” to the sciences, dividing them into speculative and practical [p. 19] but it cannot belong to the sciences taken in the first and most proper mode, but only in the second and less proper mode, which is nevertheless sufficient for them to be truly and properly called practical sciences. From which it is understood that when we ask whether Logic is a speculative or a practical science, we are not speaking of the most proper “practical,” but of the less proper, which can belong to the sciences.

> 13 Circa quæstionem igitur sic explicatã quatuor sunt opiniones. Prima tenet, Logicam esse scientiam speculatiuam, & non practicam, quam sequuntur Scotus quæst. 1. prol. Duran. quæst. 6. Sotus, & Tolet. quæst. 5. proœmiali. Soncinas 6. Meta. quæst. 6. Capreolus quæst. 1. prol. art 2. Niphus 1. Meta. quæst. 1. Canariensis in scriptis primæ partis, quæst. 5. art. 1. & eiusdem sententiæ videtur esse D. Tho. opusculo 10. fol. 128. pag. 1. & 12. quæst. 57. art. 1. ad 2. probaturque duobus argum. Primo, quia ex fine colligitur, An scientia sit practica, vel speculatiua, vt docet Arist. 2. Meta. tex. 3. sed finis Logicæ non est componere syllogismum, aut quodlibet aliud instrumentum, sed naturam eius & proprietates quærere atque speculari: ergo non est scientia practica, sed speculatiua. Probatur antecedens, quia non dicetur aliquis acquisisse Logicam, ex eo quòd syllogismos efficiat, sed quia naturam eius cognoscit per demonstrationem: ergo Logica non operatiua syllogismi, sed naturam eius speculatur: quare nec erit practica sed speculatiua.

13 On the question so explained, then, there are four opinions. The first holds that Logic is a speculative science and not a practical one. It is followed by Scotus, q. 1 of the prologue; Durandus, q. 6; Soto and Toledo, proemial q. 5; Soncinas, Metaph. 6, q. 6; Capreolus, q. 1 of the prologue, a. 2; Nifo, Metaph. 1, q. 1; Canariensis in his writings on the first part, q. 5, a. 1; and of the same opinion St. Thomas seems to be, opusculum 10, fol. 128, p. 1, and 1-2, q. 57, a. 1, ad 2. And it is proved by two arguments. First, because whether a science is practical or speculative is gathered from its end, as Aristotle teaches, Metaph. 2, text 3; but the end of Logic is not to compose a syllogism or any other instrument whatever, but to inquire into and speculate on its nature and properties; therefore it is not a practical science but a speculative one. The antecedent is proved: because someone will not be said to have acquired Logic from the fact that he produces syllogisms, but because he knows its nature through demonstration; therefore Logic is not productive of the syllogism but speculates on its nature; wherefore it will not be practical but speculative.

> Secundò probatur, ex modo procedendi: nam scientia practica procedit modo compositorio, quia compositio, operatio quædam est: speculatiua verò modo resolutorio, resoluendo, aut reducendo proprias conclusiones vsque ad prima principia: sed Logica non procedit modo compositorio; sed resolutorio, inquirendo naturam, & proprietates syllogismorum, & aliorum instrumentorum: ergo erit speculatiua. Probatur minor; quia etiam si aliquis nullum componeret syllogismum, Logicus verè diceretur; ex eo quòd cognosceret naturam, & proprietates eius per demonstrationem; ergo Logica non procedit modo compositorio sed resolutorio.

Second, it is proved from the mode of proceeding: for a practical science proceeds in the compositive mode, because composition is a certain operation; but a speculative one in the resolutive mode, resolving or reducing its own conclusions back to the first principles; but Logic does not proceed in the compositive mode but in the resolutive, inquiring into the nature and properties of syllogisms and of the other instruments; therefore it will be speculative. The minor is proved: because even if someone composed no syllogism, he would truly be called a logician from the fact that he knew its nature and properties through demonstration; therefore Logic does not proceed in the compositive mode but in the resolutive.

> Secunda opinio, affirmat Logicam esse scientiam practicam: quam tenent Gabriel 13. quæst. prol. Ocham in 3. d. 2. quęst. 6. Venetus in principio suæ Logicæ. Albertus Magnus 2. lib. de Anima, c. 1. 12. Iandunus 6. Meta. quęst. 1. & 5. Fonseca Meta. cap. 3 quæst 2. sect. 4 & probatur 1. nam illa est scientia practica. quę operatiua est, aut directiua operationum: sed Logica est directiua operationum intellectus, ergo est practica. Probatur minor. 1. ex Aristot. 1. Rheto. cap. 1. vbi docet, *Dialecticam [p. 20] inuentam esse ad dirigendas operationes, quæ bene & male fieri poterant*. Deinde ratione, quia operationes intellectus secundùm propriam naturam consideratæ, non pertinent ad Logicam, sed ad Philosophiam naturalem: solùm ergo considerantur in Logica, quatenus diriguntur, & ordinantur, vt sine errore fiant, & constituatur ex eis syllogismus, aut aliud instrumentum: ergo Logica est directiua earum quod est esse practicam. Exemplum huius veritatis habemus in arte fabrili perfectè practica, quæ circa ligna versatur: non secundùm eorum naturam: nam hoc modo considerata ad Philosophiam potiùs pertinent, sed disponendo, ac præparando, vt fiat ex eis cathedra: ergo Logica, quæ versatur circa opera intellectus sic ordinando, vt ex eis possit fieri syllogismus, practica scientia erit.

The second opinion affirms that Logic is a practical science. It is held by Gabriel, q. 13 of the prologue; Ockham on bk. 3, d. 2, q. 6; Paul of Venice at the beginning of his Logic; Albert the Great, On the Soul 2, ch. 1, 2; Jandun, Metaph. 6, q. 1 and 5; Fonseca, Metaph., ch. 3, q. 2, sect. 4. And it is proved, first: for that science is practical which is operative or directive of operations; but Logic is directive of the operations of the intellect; therefore it is practical. The minor is proved, first, from Aristotle, Rhetoric 1, ch. 1, where he teaches that Dialectic B ij [p. 20] was invented to direct operations which could be done well and badly. Next, by reason: because the operations of the intellect, considered according to their own nature, do not pertain to Logic but to natural Philosophy; therefore they are considered in Logic only insofar as they are directed and ordered, so that they may take place without error and a syllogism or another instrument may be constructed out of them; therefore Logic is directive of them, which is to be practical. We have an example of this truth in the art of the carpenter, which is perfectly practical, and which is concerned with pieces of wood: not according to their nature (for considered in this way they pertain rather to Philosophy), but by disposing and preparing them so that a chair may be made out of them; therefore Logic, which is concerned with the works of the intellect by so ordering them that a syllogism can be made out of them, will be a practical science.

> Secundò. Scientiæ speculatiuæ quæruntur propter seipsas, vt per eas cognitionem suorum obiectorum consequamur: practicæ verò non propter se, sed propter operationes dirigendas: sed Logicam, non propter seipsam quærimus, sed propter alias scientias, ad quas consequendas ordinatur, tanquam instrumentum earum: ergo non est speculatiua sed practica.

Second, speculative sciences are sought for their own sake, so that through them we may attain the cognition of their objects; practical ones, however, not for their own sake but for the sake of directing operations; but we seek Logic not for its own sake but for the sake of the other sciences, to the attaining of which it is ordered as their instrument; therefore it is not speculative but practical.

> Tertia sententia cùm videret vtramqne rationem, practicam videlicet & speculatiuam, habere Dialecticam, & vtramque rationem non posse conuenire eidem habitui, duplicem habitum in ea distinguit: vnum speculatiuum, quo consideramus naturam syllogismorum & aliorum instrumentorum: alterum practicum, quo eos componimus & primum habitum vocat Dialecticam Theoricam, hoc est, cognoscitiuam obiecti: secundum Dialecticam practicam, hoc est, directiuam: & vtitur exemplo medicinę, in qua duplex etiam ponendus est habitus, vnus quo consideratur natura corporis sanabilis, & Medicamentorum, & vocatur Theorica medicina: alter quo applicantur mendicamenta ad curandum corpus, & vocatur practica medicina.

The third opinion, seeing that Dialectic has both rationes, namely the practical and the speculative, and that both rationes cannot belong to the same habit, distinguishes a twofold habit in it: one speculative, by which we consider the nature of syllogisms and of the other instruments; the other practical, by which we compose them. And the first habit it calls Theoretical Dialectic, that is, cognitive of the object; the second, practical Dialectic, that is, directive. And it uses the example of medicine, in which a twofold habit must also be posited: one by which the nature of the healable body and of medicines is considered, and it is called Theoretical medicine; the other by which medicines are applied to curing the body, and it is called practical medicine.

> Postrema sententia asserit, Dialecticã nec esse speculatiuam, nec practicam per se, sed instrumentum potiùs ordinatum ad consequendas speculatiuas scientias, & practicas: & propter vtramque rationem speculatiuam, & practicam, modo quodam accidentali ei conuenire. Ita tenet Petrus Niger quęst. 14. sui clyp. & Græci omnes, asserentes. *Dialecticam non esse Philosophiæ vniuersaliter acceptæ partem, sed instrumentum.* Probatur hæc sententia, quodam testimonio Arist. 1. lib. Topicorum c. 9. vbi problemata, quæ sunt propositiones in vtramque partem probabiles, in contemplatiua, actiua, & instrumentaria diuidit: [p. 21] & hæc postrema vocat problemata Dialectica: ergo sentit Dialecticam non esse speculatiuam, nec practicam, sed instrumentariam. Deinde ratione, quia Logica dirigit opera intellectus: sed intellectus non est speculatiuus nec practicus: sed vniuersalior quædam potentia, cui vtraque ratio conuenit accidentaliter: idem ergo dicendum erit de Dialectica.

The last opinion asserts that Dialectic is neither speculative nor practical per se, but rather an instrument ordered to attaining the speculative and the practical sciences; and that on account of this both rationes, the speculative and the practical, belong to it in a certain accidental manner. So holds Peter Nigri, q. 14 of his Clypeus, and all the Greeks, who assert that Dialectic is not a part of Philosophy taken universally, but an instrument. This opinion is proved by a certain testimony of Aristotle, Topics 1, ch. 9, where he divides problems, which are propositions probable on either side, into contemplative, active and instrumental [p. 21] and these last he calls dialectical problems: therefore he holds that Dialectic is neither speculative nor practical, but instrumental. Next, by reason: because Logic directs the works of the intellect; but the intellect is neither speculative nor practical, but a certain more universal power, to which each ratio belongs accidentally: the same, therefore, must be said of Dialectic.

> 14 Pro solutione quæstionis, notandũ est 1. Logicã duo præstare. Primũ namque præcepta tradit conficiendi syllogismos & cætera instrumenta, explicans partes, ex quibus componi debent. Probatur hoc ex definitione syllogismi, quæ asserit, *Esse orationem, in qua quibusdam positis, aliud necessariò sequitur, per ea quæ posita sunt*, id est, virtute præmissarum: Præmissæ igitur, quæ sunt maior, & minor, dispositæ in modo, & figura, sunt partes quasi materiales syllogismi: dispositio verò in modo & figura quasi forma eius est. Aristot. etiam in libris de posteriori resolutione, præcipuè cap. 2. 1. lib. definit demonstrationem, dicens *esse syllogismum constantem ex primis*, hoc est principiis, & veris quidem, nam ex falso non sequitur vera conclusio, & ex causis conclusionis: quia præmissæ causæ conclusionis sunt. Hæc igitur sunt præcepta efficiendi syllogismũ, ac demonstrationem. Secundum quod præstat, est probare eadem præcepta per demonstrationem, resoluendo conclusiones, vsque ad prima principia, quod fecit Aristoteles ibidẽ, docens *non posse aliquam habere scientiam conclusionis, nisi sciat pretermissas demonstrare, easque reducere vsque ad prima principia per se nota, atque indemonstrabilia.*

14 For the solution of the question, it should be noted, first, that Logic performs two things. For first it delivers the precepts for constructing syllogisms and the other instruments, explaining the parts of which they ought to be composed. This is proved from the definition of the syllogism, which asserts that it is an expression in which, certain things being posited, something else follows of necessity because these are posited, that is, by virtue of the premises. The premises, therefore, which are the major and the minor, disposed in mood and figure, are as it were the material parts of the syllogism; while the disposition in mood and figure is as it were its form. Aristotle also, in the books Posterior Analytics, especially bk. 1, ch. 2, defines demonstration, saying that it is a syllogism consisting of first things, that is, of principles, and of true ones indeed, for from the false a true conclusion does not follow, and of the causes of the conclusion: because the premises are the causes of the conclusion. These, then, are the precepts for making a syllogism and a demonstration. The second thing it performs is to prove these same precepts through demonstration, resolving the conclusions all the way to the first principles, which Aristotle did in the same place, teaching that one cannot have science of any conclusion unless one knows how to demonstrate the premises and to reduce them all the way to the first principles, known per se and indemonstrable.

> Secundò notandũ est idem esse præcepta tradere componẽdi syllogismum & demonstrationem, quod docere modum, quo componi debeat, vt possit esse instrumentum acquirendi scientiam: & hoc est etiam procedere modo compositorio: quemadmodum ars domificatoria, ideo procedere dicitur modo compositorio, quia docet, ex lapidibus, & lignis, hoc, vel illo modo dispositis, domum esse componendam. Idem est etiã docere per demonstrationem componere syllogismum, resoluendo aut reducendo conclusiones vsque ad prima principia, quod est procedere modo resolutorio: vnde sequitur euidens esse, quòd vtrumque modum procedendi habeat Logica, & intrinsecum quidem: quia non posset perfectam cognitionem modi sciendi tradere, nisi vtroque modo procederet.

It should be noted, second, that to deliver the precepts for composing a syllogism and a demonstration is the same as to teach the mode in which it ought to be composed so that it can be an instrument for acquiring science; and this is also to proceed in the compositive mode: just as the art of house-building is said to proceed in the compositive mode because it teaches that a house is to be composed of stones and timbers disposed in this or that way. To teach through demonstration how to compose a syllogism, resolving or reducing the conclusions all the way to the first principles, is likewise the same as to proceed in the resolutive mode: whence it follows that it is evident that Logic has each mode of proceeding, and intrinsically indeed: because it could not deliver a perfect cognition of the mode of knowing unless it proceeded in both modes.

> Tertio notandum est: non solùm habere Logicam vtrumque modum procedendi, sed etiam vtrumque finem, nempe operandi, & speculandi, & componendi syllogismum quod sic probo, Modus compositorius sua natura ordinatur ad bene [p. 22] componendum syllogismum: & bene componere syllogismũ, est ordinare, aut dirigere operationes intellectus, ex quibus componitur: ergo Logica habet pro fine dirigere operationes, qui est finis practicus. De fine verò speculationis patet, nam modus procedendi resolutorius ordinatur ex se ad speculandam naturam obiecti, de quo probantur passiones per demonstrationes, quarum conclusiones reducuntur ad prima principia ergo ex modo resolutorio colligitur euidenter, finis speculandi naturam obiecti.

It should be noted, third, that Logic has not only each mode of proceeding but also each end, namely of operating and of speculating, and of composing a syllogism, which I prove thus. The compositive mode is by its nature ordered to correctly B iij [p. 22] composing a syllogism; and to compose a syllogism well is to order or direct the operations of the intellect of which it is composed: therefore Logic has for its end to direct operations, which is a practical end. As for the end of speculation, it is plain: for the resolutive mode of proceeding is of itself ordered to speculating the nature of the object, of which attributes are proved through demonstrations whose conclusions are reduced to the first principles; therefore from the resolutive mode the end of speculating the nature of the object is evidently gathered.

> 15 Postremò notandũ hos modos procedendi, resolutorium, & compositorium, atque etiam hos fines dirigendi operationes intellectus, & speculandi naturam modi sciendi, quasi partiales, & inadæquatos esse respectu Logicę, & cõtineri sub adæquato, & totali fine eiusdem scientiæ, qui est perfectè cognoscere naturam modi sciendi. Probatur hoc argumento: nam ad perfectam cognitionem modi sciendi non sufficit scire modum componendi syllogismum, & alia instrumenta, sed requiritur, quòd per demonstrationem cognoscatur, demonstratio verò vt perfecta sit, petit resolutionem præmissarum vsque ad prima principia, quod est naturam eiusdem modi speculari: ergo perfecta cognitio modi sciendi qui est obiectũ Logicę & finis eius adæquatus atque totalis, vtrumque finem quasi partialem continet, & respectu vtriusque superior est. Sed sub eo mutuò sibi correspondent partiales & inadæquati fines, atque modi procedendi, & vnus ordinatur ad alterum, atque è conuerso quia Logica docet componere syllogismum, vt per eum tanquam per instrumentum speculetur naturam eius, & naturam eius speculatur, vt perfectè sciat eum componere quia perfecta compositio petit perfectam cognitionem totius compositi & partium eius, & sic modus correspondet modo, & finis correspondet fini, & ex vtroque resultat perfecta cognitio modi sciendi, qui est finis adæquatus Logicæ, altior vtroque, & vtrumque continens eminenter.

15 Finally it should be noted that these modes of proceeding, the resolutive and the compositive, and also these ends of directing the operations of the intellect and of speculating the nature of the mode of knowing, are as it were partial and inadequate with respect to Logic, and are contained under the adequate and total end of the same science, which is to know perfectly the nature of the mode of knowing. This is proved by this argument: for a perfect cognition of the mode of knowing it is not enough to know the mode of composing a syllogism and the other instruments, but it is required that it be known through demonstration; and demonstration, in order to be perfect, demands the resolution of the premises all the way to the first principles, which is to speculate the nature of that same mode: therefore the perfect cognition of the mode of knowing, which is the object of Logic and its adequate and total end, contains each end as a partial one, as it were, and is superior with respect to both. But under it the partial and inadequate ends, and the modes of proceeding, correspond mutually to each other, and one is ordered to the other and conversely: because Logic teaches how to compose a syllogism so that through it, as through an instrument, it may speculate its nature; and it speculates its nature so that it may know perfectly how to compose it, because perfect composition demands perfect cognition of the whole composite and of its parts; and thus mode corresponds to mode, and end corresponds to end, and from both there results the perfect cognition of the mode of knowing, which is the adequate end of Logic, higher than both and containing both eminently.

> His suppositis, nostra sentẽtia est Logicã simul esse practicã & speculatiuam scienti; quam pręter alios sequuntur, pater Suarius tom. 1. suę Meta. disp 44. circa finem, & pater Gabriel. Vasquez in. part. D Tho. disp. 9. cap 1. num. 1. quam efficaciter probat hoc arg. ex doctrina tradita sic colligendo. Scientia practica est illa quę non solùm est de re operabili, aut dirigibili, sed procedit modo operabili, & in finem operandi, aut dirigẽdi operationes ordinatur: sed Logica habet has tres conditiones ergo est verè practica. Probatur minor, nam in primis de re operabili, aut dirigibili agit, nempe de operationibus [p. 23] intellectus, & modo quidem operabili, hoc est, compositorio, & tandem in finem dirigendi easdem operationes ordinatur, quod & facit, dum eas ordinat in syllogismum aut aliud instrumentum. Quòd verò sit etiam speculatiua probo. Nam speculatiua scientia est, quæ de re speculabili agit, modóque resolutorio procedit, & in finem speculandi naturam eius ordinatur: sed talis est Logica, ergo est speculatiua. Minor ita probatur. Modus sciendi, aut ens rationis, quod est obiectum Logicæ est, res speculabilis habens passiones, quæ de illo demonstrari possunt, & verè demonstrantur in Logica docente, resoluente easdem demonstrationes vsque ad prima principia: quod est resolutorio modo procedere: & modus iste resolutorius ordinatur ex se ad speculandam naturam rei, ergo habet etiam pro fine speculationem sui obiecti. Et hoc arg. satis declarat, quàm sit falsum id, quod quidem ex his, qui sequuntur primam opinionem, asserunt, nempe, Dialecticam procedere modo practico, sed hunc modum procedendi ordinari ad speculationem: & ideo non efficere scientiam practicam, sed speculatiuam. Non enim minùs ordinatur modus procedendi resolutorius ad praxim, cùm ordinetur ad perfectè componendum syllogismum, & nihilominus constituit Dialecticam speculatiuam: ergo etiam si modus compositorius ordinetur ad speculationem, constituet scientiam practicam. Præterea, cùm modus compositorius sit de essentia scientiæ practicæ, non potest reperiri in aliqua scientia, quin eam constituat practicam, siue ordinetur ad speculationem, vel non ordinetur. Ordinatio enim potiùs ostendit talem scientiam habere vtramque rationem practicæ, & speculatiuæ.

These things supposed, our view is that Logic is at once a practical and a speculative science; which, besides others, Father Suárez follows, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 44, near the end, and Father Gabriel Vázquez on 1 p. of St. Thomas, disp. 9, ch. 1, no. 1, who proves it effectively by this argument, gathering it thus from the doctrine delivered. A practical science is one that is not only about a thing that is operable or directible, but proceeds in an operable mode and is ordered to the end of operating or of directing operations: but Logic has these three conditions; therefore it is truly practical. The minor is proved: for in the first place it deals with a thing that is operable or directible, namely with the operations [p. 23] of the intellect; and indeed in an operable mode, that is, the compositive; and finally it is ordered to the end of directing those same operations, which it also does when it orders them into a syllogism or another instrument. That it is also speculative I prove. For a speculative science is one that deals with a speculable thing, proceeds in the resolutive mode, and is ordered to the end of speculating its nature; but such is Logic; therefore it is speculative. The minor is proved thus. The mode of knowing, or being of reason, which is the object of Logic, is a speculable thing having attributes which can be demonstrated of it, and are truly demonstrated in logica docens, which resolves those demonstrations all the way to the first principles: which is to proceed in the resolutive mode; and that resolutive mode is of itself ordered to speculating the nature of the thing; therefore it also has for its end the speculation of its object. And this argument shows clearly enough how false is what certain of those who follow the first opinion assert, namely, that Dialectic proceeds in a practical mode, but that this mode of proceeding is ordered to speculation, and therefore does not make a practical science but a speculative one. For the resolutive mode of proceeding is no less ordered to praxis, since it is ordered to composing a syllogism perfectly, and nonetheless it constitutes Dialectic speculative: therefore, even if the compositive mode is ordered to speculation, it will constitute a practical science. Moreover, since the compositive mode is of the essence of practical science, it cannot be found in any science without constituting it practical, whether it is ordered to speculation or not. For the ordering rather shows that such a science has each ratio, the practical and the speculative.

> Probatur secundò, quia Logica est ianua, per quam ad reliquas scientias ingredimur, & quasi organum, & instrumentum ad eas acquirendas, præbetque modum sciendi omnibus: sed inter alias scientias quædam sunt speculatiuæ, aliæ practicæ: ergo necesse est Dialecticam habere vtramque conditionem: quia si practica non sit, non potest esse ianua per quam ad practicas scientias ingrediamur, nec poterit eis tribuere modum sciendi, ac procedendi practicum: & eadem ratione non poterit hæc tribuere speculatiuis, nisi speculatiua sit. Necesse est ergo vtramque conditionem ei concedere.

This is proved, second, because Logic is the gate through which we enter the other sciences, and as it were the organ and instrument for acquiring them, and it furnishes the mode of knowing to all of them; but among the other sciences some are speculative, others practical: therefore Dialectic must have each condition: because if it is not practical, it cannot be the gate through which we enter the practical sciences, nor will it be able to give them the mode of knowing and of proceeding practically; and by the same reasoning it could not give this to the speculative ones unless it were speculative. It is necessary, therefore, to grant it each condition.

> Sed restat quoddam arg. aduersus nostram sententiam priùs soluendũ, quàm ad soluenda argumenta aliarum opinionum procedamus, & est huiusmodi. Practicum & speculatiuum, sunt differentiæ, per quas scientiæ distinguuntur specie: ergo non possunt eidem scientiæ conuenire. Probatur consequentia, [p. 24] quia ex duabus speciebus non potest componi tertia: ergo nec ex practico, & speculatiuo Dialectica. Sequeretur enim in duabus speciebus collocari, & quasi monstrum esse.

But there remains a certain argument against our view, which must be solved before we proceed to solve the arguments of the other opinions; and it is of this kind. Practical and speculative are differences by which sciences are distinguished in species; therefore they cannot belong to the same science. The consequence is proved B iiij [p. 24] because from two species a third cannot be composed: therefore neither can Dialectic be composed of the practical and the speculative. For it would follow that it is placed in two species, and is as it were a monster.

> Pro solutione huius arg. adnotandum est, quòd sicut in causis efficientibus vniuersalibus, possunt esse vnitate virtutes diuersæ speciei, ita vt vna, & simplex virtus causæ superioris vtramque contineat eminenter, & respectu illius quælibet sit quasi inadæquata, & in causis formalibus, sub vna forma superiori, contineri possunt rationes essentiales inferiorum formarum, ita vt vna & simplex cùm sit forma superior, tribuere possit vnum & aliud esse, quod ab vtraque forma inferiori tribuitur: eodem modo vna scientia superior, quæ habet modum formæ, continere potest rationes, aut modos essentiales diuersos inferiorum sciẽtiarum. Exempla horum trium habere possumus satis manifesta. Nam sol per vnam ac simplicem virtutem, efficere potest plures effectus specie diuersos, qui non nisi à causis particularibus specie diuersis procedere possunt: quia in vna illa forma continentur eminenter virtutes inferiores specie diuersæ: in formis quoq; anima rationalis tribuit corpori esse vegetatiuum, & sensitiuum, quos gradus essendi, tribuunt formæ inferiores specie diuersæ, vt forma plantæ, & equi: ita vt verum sit animã rationalem simul esse vegetatiuã, & sensitiuam, & in ea reperiri vnitas perfectiones formarũ specie diuersarum, quas continere dicitur, non solùm eminenter, sed etiam formaliter sub gradu quodam superiori. Et tandem in scientiis docet D. Th. 1 part. q 1. att. 4. sacram Theologiam, simul esse practicam, & speculatiuam, ita vt vtrãque perfectionem sub gradu superiori complectatur, propter eminentiam sui obiecti, quod est Deus, tanquam veritas speculabilis, & vltimus finis nostrarũ operationum. Idem ergo nos concedimus Dialecticæ, non propter eminentiam sui obiecti: sed propter vniuersalitatem: quia modus sciendi est respectu omnium scientiarum, & modum sciendi tribuit practicis, atque speculatiuis: & ideo necesse est vtrumq; modum continere, eminenter quidem, quia quantum ad hoc superior est aliis scientiis, & etiam formaliter, quia formaliter continet vtrumque modum procedendi, resolutorium, & compositorium: & ad vtrumque finem dirigendi operationes intellectus, & speculandi naturam modi sciendi ordinatur. Sed rationes practicæ, & speculatiuæ, inadæquatæ sunt respectu ipsius, sub adæquata & superiori ratione perfectè cognoscendi naturam modi sciendi contentæ.

For the solution of this argument it should be noted that, just as in universal efficient causes virtues of diverse species can exist in unity, so that one simple virtue of the superior cause contains both eminently, and with respect to it each is as it were inadequate; and as in formal causes the essential rationes of inferior forms can be contained under one superior form, so that, since the superior form is one and simple, it can give the one and the other being that is given by each of the inferior forms: in the same way one superior science, which has the mode of a form, can contain diverse essential rationes or modes of inferior sciences. We can have sufficiently manifest examples of these three. For the sun, by one simple virtue, can produce several effects diverse in species, which cannot proceed except from particular causes diverse in species: because in that one form the inferior virtues diverse in species are contained eminently. In forms, too, the rational soul gives the body vegetative and sensitive being, which grades of being are given by inferior forms diverse in species, such as the form of a plant and that of a horse: so that it is true that the rational soul is at once vegetative and sensitive, and that there is found in it, in unity, the perfections of forms diverse in species, which it is said to contain not only eminently but also formally, under a certain superior grade. And finally, in the sciences, St. Thomas teaches, 1 p., q. 1, a. 4, that sacred Theology is at once practical and speculative, so that it embraces each perfection under a superior grade, on account of the eminence of its object, which is God, as speculable truth and as the ultimate end of our operations. The same, therefore, we grant to Dialectic, not on account of the eminence of its object, but on account of its universality: because the mode of knowing bears on all the sciences, and it gives the mode of knowing to the practical and to the speculative ones; and therefore it must contain each mode, eminently indeed, because as to this it is superior to the other sciences, and also formally, because it formally contains each mode of proceeding, the resolutive and the compositive, and it is ordered to each end, that of directing the operations of the intellect and that of speculating the nature of the mode of knowing. But the practical and speculative rationes are inadequate with respect to it, being contained under the adequate and superior ratio of knowing perfectly the nature of the mode of knowing.

> Ex his respondeo ad formam arg. nam dum dicitur, practicum, & speculatiuum esse rationes specie diuersas, concedendum est: [p. 25] & ideo non posse eidem scientię particulari conuenire: sed bene vniuersali, habẽti superiorem quandam rationem eminenter, atque formaliter continentem vtramque perfectionem. Quemadmodum vegetatiuum, & sensitiuum, non possunt conuenire eidem formæ particulari, sed bene vniuersali, qualis est anima rationalis: nec propterea talis scientia vniuersalis erit in duplici specie, sed habebit vnam quandam eminentiorem speciem, vtramque rationem continentem, respectu cuius quælibet est quasi partialis, & inadæquata.

From these things I reply to the form of the argument: for when it is said that the practical and the speculative are rationes diverse in species, it must be granted [p. 25] and therefore they cannot belong to the same particular science, but they can well belong to a universal one, having a certain superior ratio that contains each perfection eminently and formally. Just as vegetative and sensitive cannot belong to the same particular form, but can well belong to a universal one, such as the rational soul is; nor on that account will such a universal science be in a twofold species, but it will have one more eminent species, containing each ratio, with respect to which each is as it were partial and inadequate.

> Arg. primæ & secundæ opinionis. probant quidẽ Dialecticã esse practicã, & esse speculatiuã, non tamen, quòd alterã tãtum rationẽ habeat, ita vt vel solũ sit practica, vel solũ speculatiua.

The arguments of the first and second opinions do indeed prove that Dialectic is practical and that it is speculative, but not that it has only one ratio, so that it is either only practical or only speculative.

> Vltima autẽ sententia falsa est, quia esse Dialecticam instrumentum omnium scientiarum, non tollit ab ea veram rationem scientiæ, & ideo nec veram rationem practicæ, & speculatiuæ: sed probat esse sciẽtiam vniuersalem, ex quo habet, quòd vtramque simul rationem cõplectatur eminẽter simul, & formaliter: quia sub ratione formali superiori, atque eminẽtiori.

The last opinion, however, is false, because Dialectic’s being the instrument of all the sciences does not take away from it the true ratio of science, and therefore not the true ratio of practical and speculative either; but it proves that it is a universal science, from which it has it that it embraces both rationes at once, eminently and at the same time formally: because it does so under a superior and more eminent formal ratio.

> Testimonium verò Aristo de problemate instrumentario, quod Dialecticæ tribuit, difficultate caret: quia sensus illius est, non esse actiuum solum, vel solum contemplatiuum, sed sub ratione superiori vtrumque continere. De intellectu verò alia est ratio, ac de scientiis: quia cũ sit potentia vniuersalis, abstrahit ab vtraq; ratione practici, & speculatiui, quæ respectu sciẽtiarũ sunt quasi essentiales modi, per quos specie distinguũtur.

The testimony of Aristotle about the instrumental problem, which he attributes to Dialectic, is free of difficulty; for its sense is that it is not only active, or only contemplative, but contains both under a superior ratio. With the intellect, however, the case is different from that of the sciences: because, since it is a universal power, it abstracts from each ratio, the practical and the speculative, which with respect to the sciences are as it were essential modes by which they are distinguished in species.

## QUESTION VI

> *Quod sit obiectum Dialecticæ, vtrùm modus sciendi realis, vel ens rationis.*

What the object of Dialectic is: whether the real mode of knowing, or a being of reason.

> 17 Obiectum, subiectũ, & materia, vocari solet res illa, circa quam versatur scientia: nam hæc tria nomina eandem ferè significationem habẽt. Obiectum dicitur per ordinem ad habitum, quia quasi scopus est, in quem tendit: Subiectum, per ordinem ad passiones, quæ de illo probantur in scientia: Materia verò per respectum ad rationem formalem, Sub qua, à scientia ipsa consideratur. Idem est ergo quærere, quodnam sit obiectum Logicæ, & quæ sit materia circa quam versatur, aut quod sit subiectũ, de quo demonstrat passiones, & cuius cognitionem assequi intendit: & his explicatur titulus quæstionis.

17 Object, subject, and matter are the names customarily given to the thing about which a science is concerned: for these three names have almost the same signification. It is called object by order to the habit, because it is as it were the target at which the habit aims; subject, by order to the attributes which are proved of it in the science; matter, by relation to the formal ratio under which it is considered by the science itself. It is the same, therefore, to ask what the object of Logic is, and what the matter is about which it is concerned, or what the subject is of which it demonstrates attributes and whose cognition it intends to attain: and with this the title of the question is explained.

> Sed conditiones, quas habere debet obiectum, proponendę sunt, vt intelligatur illud esse obiectum huius scientiæ, potiùs quàm aliud, cui meliùs conueniunt. Est autem prima conditio, [p. 26] vt sit in rerum natura, vel certè possibile sit: non enim requiritur actualis eius existentia: nam de rosa in hyeme, quando non est, datur scientia, quia saltem est possibilis: de re enim impossibili, vt de chimæra, non potest dari scientia. Secunda conditio est, quòd cognitio eius intendatur in scientia. Tertia, vt sub se comprehendat omnia, quæ tractantur in scientia. Postrema quòd sit vnum aliquo modo, vt vnitatem possit tribuere scientiæ.

But the conditions which the object ought to have must be proposed, so that it may be understood that this is the object of this science rather than something else, to which they belong better. Now the first condition [p. 26] is that it exist in the nature of things, or at least be possible: for its actual existence is not required; for of the rose in winter, when it does not exist, there is science, because it is at least possible; but of an impossible thing, such as a chimera, there cannot be science. The second condition is that its cognition be intended in the science. The third, that it comprehend under itself all the things that are treated in the science. The last, that it be one in some way, so that it can give unity to the science.

> His expositis, præsupponenda sunt tanquam certa illa, in quibus omnes conueniunt, vt ad difficultatem quæstionis perueniamus. *Est autem certum primò*, Dialecticam habere aliquam materiam determinatam, circa quam proximè versetur, tanquam circa proprium obiectum. Cuius ratio est, quia quælibet determinata scientia, determinatam cognitionem alicuius rei intendere debet: sed Logica est determinata scientia, & distincta à cæteris: ergo habebit determinatam materiam, seu obiectum, cuius cognitionem intendat, & per quod ab aliis scientiis distinguatur: quia sicut potentia sumit suam vnitatem specificam ab obiecto, sic etiam scientia, vt Arist. docet 2. lib. de anima, ca 4. Et licèt hoc videatur contrarium doctrinæ Arist. asserentis, *Dialecticam non esse vnius generis obiecti, aut circa omnia obiecta scientiarum versari.* 1. li. Post. c. 12. & tex. 24. & 4. li. Met. tex. 5 verè tamen contrarium non est, quia de materia remota Dialecticæ loquitur, & hæc non est determinata, cùm circa omnes res mundi, enuntiationes, & syllogismos efficiat: proxima verò materia eius determinata est, de qua inquirit quæstio præsens, an sit hæc, vel illa.

These things set out, the points on which all agree must be presupposed as certain, so that we may arrive at the difficulty of the question. Now it is certain, first, that Dialectic has some determinate matter about which it is proximately concerned, as about its proper object. The reason for this is that every determinate science must intend the determinate cognition of some thing; but Logic is a determinate science, and distinct from the others: therefore it will have a determinate matter, or object, whose cognition it intends, and by which it is distinguished from the other sciences: because just as a power takes its specific unity from its object, so also does a science, as Aristotle teaches, On the Soul 2, ch. 4. And although this seems contrary to the doctrine of Aristotle, who asserts that Dialectic is not of an object of one genus, or that it is concerned with all the objects of the sciences, Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 12, and text 24, and Metaph. 4, text 5, yet in truth it is not contrary, because he speaks of the remote matter of Dialectic, and this is not determinate, since it makes enunciations and syllogisms about all the things in the world; but its proximate matter is determinate, and about it the present question inquires whether it is this or that.

> Secundò certum est, hanc materiam proximam Dialecticæ non esse voces, aut nomina, vt antiqui Dialectici asserebant, ex quo Nominales in schola vocati sunt: quia licet vocibus vtatur ad significandas res: de iis tamen principaliter disputat, vt docuit expressè Arist. 4. li. Met. tex. 5. & probat experientia: quia syllogismos, & cætera instrumenta in rebus constituit.

It is certain, second, that this proximate matter of Dialectic is not words or names, as the ancient Dialecticians asserted, from which they came to be called Nominalists in the school: because, although it uses words to signify things, it nevertheless disputes principally about the things, as Aristotle expressly taught, Metaph. 4, text 5, and as experience proves: because it constitutes syllogisms and the other instruments in things.

> Certum est tertiò, materiam proximam, aut obiectum Dialecticæ esse ens rationis: nam ex hoc Rationalis vocatur: sed ens rationis duplex est, vnum directè & per se factum à ratione aut intellectu, quales sunt operationes eius, vt apprehensio simplicium, compositio & diuisio, ac syllogismus: aliud est ens rationis, non directè factum ab intellectu, sed quasi indirectè, & per accidens: & est proprietas consequens easdem operationes, vt ordinatas ab eo, hoc est, vt constitutas in propositione, aut syllogismo: & proprietas hæc non est realis, quia non conuenit eisdem operationibus ex propria natura, sed tribuitur eis [p. 27] ab intellectu, dum sic ab eo ordinatur: vt dum ordinat tres propositiones, maiorem, minorem, & conclusionem, iuxta regulas syllogisticas, talem earum ordinationem consequitur proprietas, seu denominatio syllogismi, quam eis tribuit intellectus: & proprietas hæc vocatur ens rationis, non directè, sed indirectè factum ab intellectu, & quod non habet aliud esse, quàm cognosci ab illo.

It is certain, third, that the proximate matter, or object, of Dialectic is a being of reason: for from this it is called Rational. But being of reason is twofold: one is made directly and per se by reason or the intellect, such as are its operations, like the apprehension of simples, composition and division, and the syllogism; the other is a being of reason not made directly by the intellect, but as it were indirectly and per accidens; and it is a property following those same operations as ordered by it, that is, as constituted in a proposition or a syllogism; and this property is not real, because it does not belong to those operations from their own nature, but is attributed to them [p. 27] by the intellect while they are thus ordered by it: as when it orders three propositions, the major, the minor, and the conclusion, according to the syllogistic rules, there follows on such an ordering of them the property or denomination of syllogism, which the intellect attributes to them; and this property is called a being of reason made not directly but indirectly by the intellect, and one which has no other being than to be known by it.

> 18 Iuxta hęc duo entia rationis, duę in primis sunt opiniones de obiecto Dialecticę. Prima, quam moderni plures defendunt, tenet, primũ ens rationis esse obiectũ eius, nẽpe operationes ipsas reales intellectus, vt dirigibiles ab intellectu, vel vt actu diriguntur, hoc est, vt cõstitui possunt in syllogismũ, vel vt actu constituuntur: & vtrumque horum dicunt esse quid reale, hoc est, tã operationes ipsas, quàm dirigibilitatẽ (vt sic loquamur) hoc est, aptitudinẽ, vt ex eis fieri possit syllogismus, atque etiã ordinationem actualem. Duobus enim modis defenditur hæc sententia à modernis: quidã operationes reales dicunt esse obiectum non vt actu ordinantur, quia ordinatio actualis nihil intrinsecum potest in eis ponere, sed solam denominationẽ extrinsecam, ab operatione quasi reflexa intellectus, eas ordinante, sed secundùm aptitudinem quam habent, vt ordinari possint & hanc aptitudinem vocant ordinabilitatem, aut dirigibilitatem: & realem quidem, cùm eis ex propria natura conueniat, & antequam ordinẽtur. Alij verò easdem operationes, vt actu ordinantur, dicunt esse obiectum, ita vt aliquis modus realis, in eis sit actualis ordinatio: nam cùm ordinentur per verum ac reale iudicium intellectus, aut certè non sint aliud operationes ipsæ, quàm iudicia quædam intellectus ordinata, non potest nõ esse aliquid in eis ordinatio. Conueniũt tamen vtriq; opinantes in eo, quòd operationes istæ secundùm aliquẽ modum, aut proprietatem realem sint obiectum: & ideo obiectum formale Dialecticę, dicunt omnes, esse modum sciendi realem.

18 Corresponding to these two beings of reason, there are in the first place two opinions about the object of Dialectic. The first, which several moderns defend, holds that the first being of reason is its object, namely the real operations of the intellect themselves, as directible by the intellect, or as they are actually directed, that is, as they can be constituted in a syllogism, or as they are actually constituted; and they say that each of these is something real, that is, both the operations themselves and their directibility (so to speak), that is, the aptitude for a syllogism to be made from them, and also their actual ordering. For this opinion is defended in two ways by the moderns: some say that the real operations are the object, not as they are actually ordered, because the actual ordering can posit nothing intrinsic in them, but only an extrinsic denomination from an as it were reflex operation of the intellect ordering them, but according to the aptitude they have to be capable of being ordered; and this aptitude they call ordinability or directibility, and a real one indeed, since it belongs to them from their own nature, even before they are ordered. Others say that those same operations as actually ordered are the object, so that the actual ordering is some real mode in them: for since they are ordered through a true and real judgment of the intellect, or at least the operations themselves are nothing other than certain ordered judgments of the intellect, the ordering cannot fail to be something in them. Those holding either view agree, however, in this, that these operations are the object according to some real mode or property; and therefore all of them say that the formal object of Dialectic is the real mode of knowing.

> Probant 1. auctores huius sententiæ, quòd ens rationis secundùm, nõ sit obiectum hoc arg. Obiectum scientię duo habere debet primũ: passiones quę de illo demonstrantur in sciẽtia secundũ, quod per se consideretur ab ipsa scientia: sed neutrum habet ens rationis, ergo non potest esse obiectum. Non primum, nã ens rationis nihil est in rebus, sed solùm habet esse obiectiuè in intellectu, tãquam aliquid ab eo confictum, ergo nec habet naturam, cuius cognitionem intendat, nec passiones quæ de illo probentur: nã si passiones haberet, vel essent reales, & hoc non: vel entia rationis, & tunc de illis prædicaretur formaliter, quod repugnat: sicut repugnat hominẽ prædicari formaliter [p. 28] de risibilitate aut de risibili. Secundò probatur, quia cũ nõ sit directè factũ ab intellectu, nec est directè aut per se cognitũ ab eo: sed indirectè & per accidens: ergo nec erit directè aut per se cognitũ per sciẽtiam quæ habitus intellectualis est.

The authors of this opinion prove that the second being of reason is not the object by this argument. The object of a science must have two things: first, attributes which are demonstrated of it in the science; second, that it be considered per se by the science itself; but a being of reason has neither: therefore it cannot be the object. Not the first, for a being of reason is nothing in things, but has only objective being in the intellect, as something fashioned by it; therefore it neither has a nature whose cognition the science might intend, nor attributes which might be proved of it: for if it had attributes, they would be either real, and this is not so; or beings of reason, and then they would be predicated of them formally, which is repugnant; just as it is repugnant for man to be predicated formally [p. 28] of risibility or of the risible. Second, it is proved: because, since it is not made directly by the intellect, neither is it known directly or per se by it, but indirectly and per accidens: therefore neither will it be known directly or per se by science, which is an intellectual habit.

> Deinde probant secundò, quòd ens rationis primũ, aut modus sciendi realis, sit obiectum Logicæ, alio argumento. Syllogismus, vel demonstratio continet operationes intellectus ordinatas, & est instrumentum reale: ergo est modus sciendi realis: quare tanquam aliquid reale consideratur in Dialectica: & eadem est ratio de aliis instrumentis: ergo modus sciendi realis, tanquam quid cõmune omnibus, erit obiectum Logicæ. Antecedens ita probant: Demonstratio habet effectum realem, nempe scientiam quam generat: ergo est causa realis eius, quare non potest esse ens rationis, sed reale. Et confirmant, quia Dialectica est scientia practica, vt vidimus ergo habet praxim, hoc est, operationem factam à se vel ordinatam, pro obiecto: sed operatio, vt facta vel ordinata, est quid reale: quia nihil potest per se fieri, aut per se ordinari, nisi sit reale: ergo obiectum Logicæ reale debet esse.

Next they prove, second, that the first being of reason, or the real mode of knowing, is the object of Logic, by another argument. A syllogism or demonstration contains ordered operations of the intellect, and is a real instrument: therefore it is a real mode of knowing; wherefore it is considered in Dialectic as something real; and the same reasoning holds of the other instruments: therefore the real mode of knowing, as something common to all of them, will be the object of Logic. The antecedent they prove thus: Demonstration has a real effect, namely the science which it generates: therefore it is its real cause; wherefore it cannot be a being of reason, but is real. And they confirm it: because Dialectic is a practical science, as we have seen; therefore it has a praxis, that is, an operation made or ordered by it, for its object; but an operation, as made or ordered, is something real: because nothing can be per se made or per se ordered unless it is real: therefore the object of Logic must be real.

> Secundo. Operationes intellectus, quatenus dirigibiles sunt ab eodem intellectu, pertinent ad aliquam scientiam, vel artem, à qua dirigi possunt & non ad aliam quàm ad Dialecticã, quia nec per aliam diriguntur: ergo vt dirigibiles, sunt obiectũ huius scientiæ, & dirigibilitas est proprietas realis earum: sicut intelligibilitas est proprietas realis entis realis, & numerabilitas numeri, & visibilitas coloris: ergo sub ratione realis sunt obiectum Dialecticæ, quod ex consequenti erit aliquid reale.

Second. The operations of the intellect, insofar as they are directible by that same intellect, pertain to some science or art by which they can be directed, and to no other than Dialectic, because they are not directed by any other: therefore, as directible, they are the object of this science; and directibility is a real property of them, just as intelligibility is a real property of real being, and numerability of number, and visibility of color: therefore under a real ratio they are the object of Dialectic, which consequently will be something real.

> 19 Secunda opinio asserit, Ens rationis, quod indirectè fit ab intellectu, esse obiectum Dialecticæ. Quam sequuntur D. Th. 4. M lect. 4. & opusc. 4. de natura generis, c. 4. Cai. sup de genere. Flãdria 4. M. q. 5. art. 2. Sotus q. 5. proœ. & ex antiquioribus Ca. in Ep. præd. c. vlt. & 4. Me tex. cõment. 2. Auicena 1. Me. c. 2 & ex modernis nõ pauci, habetque fundamẽta in doctrina Arist. 9 Me. tex. 5. vbi asserit, *Dialecticũ sicut & Philosophũ agere de ente vniuersali*: sed nõ agit de ente vniuersali reali, de quo agũt Metaphysicus atque Philosophus: ergo intelligit Arist. agere de alio ente vniuersali nõ habẽte esse reale in rerũ natura, sed solũ obiectiuè in intellectu, quod est ens rationis.

19 The second opinion asserts that the being of reason which is made indirectly by the intellect is the object of Dialectic. It is followed by St. Thomas, Metaph. 4, lect. 4, and opusc. 4, On the Nature of Genus, ch. 4; Cajetan on the chapter on genus; Dominic of Flanders, Metaph. 4, q. 5, a. 2; Soto, proem. q. 5; and among the more ancient, the Commentator in the Epitome of the Predicables, last ch., and Metaph. 4, text, comment 2; Avicenna, Metaph. 1, ch. 2; and not a few of the moderns; and it has foundations in the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 5, where he asserts that Dialectic, like Philosophy, deals with universal being; but it does not deal with real universal being, with which the Metaphysician and the Philosopher deal: therefore Aristotle means that it deals with another universal being, which has no real being in the nature of things, but only objectively in the intellect, and this is a being of reason.

> 20 Probatur deinde hoc vnico arg. Logica agit per se de genere & specie, quatenus prædicabilia sunt, de subiecto etiam, & prædicato, vt alia sunt, & propositionem componũt: sed hæc omnia sunt entia rationis: nam à parte rei, aut ante operationem intellectus, nec dantur genus, & species, nec subiectũ, & [p. 29] prędicatũ: ergo ens rationis, vt cõprehẽdit hæc, & alia, erit obiectũ Logicę, & confirmari potest. Quia ea quæ tractantur in Logica secundũ rationẽ materialem entia realia sunt, prędicamentũ, propositio, & syllogismus, formaliter verò sunt entia rationis: sicut formæ, à quibus dominatur, quæ sunt relationes rationis, aut secundæ intentionis: ergo formale obiectũ huius scientiæ, ens rationis est, quamuis materiale sit ens reale.

20 It is then proved by this single argument.
