Albedinem etiam sentimus, per visum, & calorem, per tactum: ergo euidenter probatur, quòd hæc accidentia, & similia, non sint extrinsecæ attributiones, aut denominationes: sed veræ entitates reales: quia sola denominatio extrinseca, non sentitur, nec potest esse per se, obiectum sensus.

But some reply, for the first opinion, that accident is not a being but of a being, that is, that it is something of substance, as Aristotle often asserts; and this is to have no other entity than attribution to substance, consisting in a certain denomination extrinsic to substance but intrinsic and essential to itself. But this cannot be true, as is gathered first of all from the same solution. For if accident is of a being, then it is of the being of substance; it has, therefore, a true entity, through which it affects substance. Which seems to be evidently proved by these experiences. Quantity in the Eucharist does not inhere in substance, but is separated from it; and yet it is a true entity, which we see and touch. Whiteness too we perceive by sight, and heat by touch. Therefore it is evidently proved that these accidents and the like are not extrinsic attributions or denominations, but true real entities: because an extrinsic denomination alone is not perceived, nor can it be a per se object of sense.

> 25 Et confirmari potest: Quia accidentia hæc, habent suos effectus formales, in subiectis, in quibus sunt: nec solùm formales, sed reales, & physicos: vt albedo, facit parietem, realiter, & formaliter album: & calor, facit aquam realiter, & formaliter calidam: sed effectus isti, non possunt procedere à causis in sola denominatione extrinseca consistentibus, sed ab his, quæ veram, & intrinsecam habent entitatem realem: per cuius realem virtutem eos producunt: ergo accidentia, veram & intrinsecam habent entitatem: alioqui, intellectus, & voluntas, quæ sunt accidentia, superaddita substantiæ animæ rationalis, ad operandum, non erunt nisi denominationes extrinsecæ, ei superadditæ. Quod patet esse falsum: cùm sint potentiæ reales, per quas tanquam per virtutes reales, elicit anima veras & reales operationes.

25 And it can be confirmed: because these accidents have their formal effects in the subjects in which they are; and not only formal but real and physical ones: as whiteness makes the wall really and formally white, and heat makes water really and formally hot. But these effects cannot proceed from causes consisting in extrinsic denomination alone, but from those which have a true and intrinsic real entity, by whose real power they produce them; therefore accidents have a true and intrinsic entity. Otherwise the intellect and will, which are accidents superadded to the substance of the rational soul for operating, will be nothing but extrinsic denominations superadded to it. Which is plainly false, since they are real powers, through which, as through real powers, the soul elicits true and real operations.

> Ad argumentum verò, Neganda est consequentia: quia licèt solùm in principali analogato, reperiatur prima & per se ratio significata per analogum, in cæteris verò, solùm per attributionem ad illud, intrinsecè tamen, & formaliter reperiri potest: quia attributio, hoc non tollit, vt probatum est.

To the argument, the consequence is to be denied: because, although the ratio signified by the analogous term is found first and per se only in the principal analogate, and in the others only by attribution to it, yet it can be found in them intrinsically and formally, because attribution does not take this away, as has been proved. O ij

[p. 212]

### An conceptus formalis analogorum sit vnus, & abstractus ab analogatis, vel multiplex, & ab eis an abstrahi possit — Whether the formal concept of analogous terms is one and abstracted from the analogates, or manifold; and whether it can be abstracted from them.

> 26 COnceptus, quem format intellectus de aliquo: duplex est, vt cap. de differentia notauimus: formalis, & obiectiuus. Conceptus formalis, est qualitas mentis, quam intellectus producit, vbi sibi faciat obiectum actu præsens, & illud intelligat: nam per hanc qualitatem, sibi perfectè repræsentatur. Conceptus verò obiectiuus, est obiectum, quod intelligitur, in quantum per formalem repræsentatur. Et de vtroque procedit quæstio: & ideo habebit duplicem partem. In prima disputabimus, de vnitate conceptus formalis. In secunda, de vnitate conceptus obiectiui.

26 The concept that the intellect forms of something is twofold, as we noted in the chapter on difference: formal and objective. The formal concept is a quality of the mind which the intellect produces when it makes the object actually present to itself and understands it: for through this quality it is perfectly represented to it. The objective concept is the object that is understood, inasmuch as it is represented through the formal one. And the question proceeds concerning both, and therefore it will have two parts. In the first we shall dispute about the unity of the formal concept; in the second, about the unity of the objective concept.

> Sed conceptus formalis, etiam est duplex: Vnus est, conceptus vocis significantis, Alter, conceptus rei significatæ. Et de primò certum est, quòd sit vnus: quia nomen analogum, est vna vox simplex: ergo per vnum simplicem conceptum, à nobis intelligitur. De conceptu verò formali rei significatæ, per nomen analogum, procedit quæstio, *An sit vnus*.

But the formal concept is also twofold: one is the concept of the signifying word, the other the concept of the thing signified. And concerning the first it is certain that it is one, because the analogous name is one simple word; therefore it is understood by us through one simple concept. But concerning the formal concept of the thing signified by the analogous name, the question proceeds whether it is one.

> Prima opinio tenet, Dari vnum conceptum formalem rei significatæ, per analogum, ita Scotus, loco inferiùs citando. Herueus quodlib. 2. q. 7. Sotus cap. præsenti. Fonseca 4. Meta. cap 2. q. 12. sect. 5. P. Franciscus Suarius, tomo. 1. suæ Met. dist. 2. sect. 1. sed diuerso modo procedunt: nam Scotus vnum conceptum formalem ponit: quia tenet, ens esse vniuocum: Vniuoca verò, vnico conceptu formali medio, sua vniuocata significant. P. Suarius, ideo ponit vnum conceptum formalem: quia vnum etiam ponit obiectiuum, abstractum ab analogatis. Herueus & Sotus, licèt non ponant eundem conceptum obiectiuum, asserunt tamen formalem esse vnum. Et tandem Fonseca ponit vnum formalem, non distinctum, sed confusum: quia non repræsentat distinctè analogata, sed confusè.

The first opinion holds that there is given one formal concept of the thing signified by the analogous term. So Scotus, in the place to be cited below; Hervaeus, Quodlibet 2, q. 7; Soto, on the present chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 12, sect. 5; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 2, sect. 1. But they proceed in different ways. For Scotus posits one formal concept because he holds that being is univocal, and univocals signify their univocates by means of a single formal concept. Father Suárez posits one formal concept because he also posits one objective concept abstracted from the analogates. Hervaeus and Soto, although they do not posit the same objective concept, nevertheless assert that the formal one is one. And finally Fonseca posits one formal concept, not distinct but confused, because it represents the analogates not distinctly but confusedly.

> 27 Probatur duplici arg. Primò, quia analogum, non solùm est vna vox simplex, & non æquiuoca, sed vnam habens significationem, ex sua impositione: sed voces significant mediis conceptibus: ergo significabit, medio vnico conceptu formali. Quod experientia videtur probari: nam audito nomine Entis, aut alterius analogi, non concipit intellectus analogata, sub determinato conceptu, vt substantiam, vel accidens, sed vnum quid, nempe entitatem: ergo non format plures conceptus formales eorum, sed vnum eiusdem entitatis.

27 It is proved by a twofold argument. First, because the analogous term is not only one simple word, and not equivocal, but one having one signification from its imposition; but words signify by means of concepts; therefore it will signify by means of a single formal concept. Which seems to be proved by experience: for when the name being, or of another analogous term, is heard, the intellect does not conceive the analogates under a determinate concept, as substance or accident, but one something, namely entity; therefore it does not form several formal concepts of them, but one of that same entity.

> Secundò, Quia si conceptus formalis analogi, non est vnus, [p. 213] sed plures: ergo tot formabit conceptus intellectus, audito nomine, quod analogata habet: vnde si hæc fuerint decem, vt cõtingit in ente, significante omnia prædicamenta, vel etiam si fuerint vigenti, tot cõceptus simul formabit intellectus: quod videtur impossibile. Probatur consequentia, quia si plures format non est maior ratio, quare duos tantùm, & non plures. Nec etiam, quare formet conceptum potiùs horum, quàm aliorum: ergo vel tot, quot sunt analogata: vel tantùm vnum.

Second, because if the formal concept of the analogous term is not one, [p. 213] but several, then the intellect, on hearing the name, will form as many concepts as the analogates it has; hence if these are ten, as happens in being, which signifies all the categories, or even if they are twenty, the intellect will form that many concepts at once, which seems impossible. The consequence is proved: because if it forms several, there is no greater reason why it should form two only and not more; nor, again, why it should form a concept of these rather than of others; therefore either as many as there are analogates, or only one.

> 28 Secunda opinio: Negat conceptũ formalem analogi, esse vnum: quam sequitur Ferra. 1. cõtra gent. c. 34. & cum eo plures moderni: Et hæc videtur nobis probabilior.

28 The second opinion denies that the formal concept of the analogous term is one. Ferrara follows it, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 34, and with him many moderns; and this seems to us more probable.

> Et probatur primò: Quia analogum conuenit cum æquiuoco, in eo, quòd significat multa simpliciter, diuersa: non tamen omnino diuersa, sed secundùm quid eadem: & in hoc distinguitur: sed audito nomine æquiuoco, format intellectus diuersos conceptus formales, propter diuersitatem significatorum: ergo audito nomine analogo, formabit etiam plures simpliciter: licet non omnino diuersos, sed aliqualem similitudinem habentes.

And it is proved, first: because the analogous term agrees with the equivocal in this, that it signifies many things simply different, yet not altogether different, but the same in a certain respect; and in this it is distinguished. But on hearing an equivocal name the intellect forms different formal concepts, on account of the diversity of the significates; therefore on hearing an analogous name it will also form several, simply, although not altogether different, but having some similarity.

> Secundò: Vnitas conceptus formalis, sumitur ex vnitate cõceptus obiectiui, per illum repræsentati: sicut vnitas imaginis, ex vnitate rei repræsentatæ: sed conceptus obiectiuus analogi, non est vnus, vt in 2. parte questionis probabitur: ergo nec erit vnus formalis. Errant enim satis apertè illi, qui non ponentes vnum conceptum obiectiuum analogatorum, sed plures, admittunt nihilominus vnitatem conceptus formalis: contra quos euidenter concludit, ad hominem, hoc argumentum quia nullam potest habere vnitatem conceptus formalis, quam non accipiat ab obiectiuo.

Second: the unity of the formal concept is taken from the unity of the objective concept represented by it, as the unity of an image from the unity of the thing represented; but the objective concept of the analogous term is not one, as will be proved in the second part of the question; therefore neither will the formal one be one. For those err quite plainly who, positing not one objective concept of the analogates but several, nevertheless admit a unity of the formal concept: against whom this argument concludes evidently, ad hominem, because it can have no unity of the formal concept which it does not receive from the objective one.

> Ad primum arg. Concedendum est antecedens, ex ea parte, qua dicit, analogum esse vnam vocem simplicem: & ideo, vnus datur cõceptus eius: sed negandum, quòd vnam habeat significationem: sicut nõ habet vnam rem significatam, sed plures, atque diuersas simpliciter, ad quas significandas, vnica impositione fuit imposita: quia licet plures sint res, omnes tamen habent attributionem ad vnam: & ideo vnica voce, & vnica impositione, ad eas significandas, possunt designari.

To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted in the part where it says that the analogous term is one simple word, and therefore there is given one concept of it; but it is to be denied that it has one signification: just as it does not have one thing signified, but several, and simply different, to signify which it was imposed by a single imposition: because, although the things are several, yet all have attribution to one; and therefore they can be designated by a single word and by a single imposition to signify them.

> 29 Ad experientiam verò, in eodem argumento adductam, Cõcedimus, quòd audito nomine analogo, non cõcipit intellectus analogata sub expresso, aut distincto conceptu, bene tamen sub confuso actuali: vt in secunda parte dicetur. Nec tamen concipit vnum quid, eis commune, sed plura simpliciter [p. 214] diuersa, sub ratione tamen communi, solùm secundùm quid propter attributionem, quam habent ad vnum.

29 To the experience adduced in the same argument, we grant that on hearing an analogous name the intellect does not conceive the analogates under an express or distinct concept, but it does conceive them under a confused actual one, as will be said in the second part. Yet it does not conceive one something common to them, but several things simply O iij [p. 214] different, yet under a common ratio, the same only in a certain respect, on account of the attribution which they have to one.

> Ad secundum: Concedendum est totum, quod assumit, & negandum, esse impossibile quòd decem conceptus formet intellectus, si decem sint significata analogi: vt cõtingit in ente, vel etiam plures, si plura habeat significata. Non est enim impossibile, intellectum tot simul formare conceptus, sub vnitate eiusdem vocis, tot res significantis: quot satis est manifestum, in æquiuoco: quo audito, nullus negat, tot formare conceptus intellectum, quot sunt significata eius, plura vel pauciora: & in analogo, est alia ratio particularis: quia non solùm plures conceptus, habent ordinem ad vnam vocem: sed etiam ad vnam rem, principaliter significatam, ad cuius conceptum ordinantur omnes alij.

To the second: everything it assumes is to be granted, and it is to be denied that it is impossible that the intellect form ten concepts if there are ten significates of the analogous term, as happens in being, or even more, if it has more significates. For it is not impossible for the intellect to form so many concepts at once under the unity of the same word signifying so many things, which is quite manifest in the equivocal: on hearing which no one denies that the intellect forms as many concepts as there are significates of it, more or fewer. And in the analogous term there is another particular reason: because the several concepts have an order not only to one word, but also to one thing principally signified, to whose concept all the others are ordered.

> Et ex hoc intelligitur, non dari conceptum formalem, analogis communem, atque distinctum, à conceptibus analogatorum, sed plures tantùm eorundem. Vnde nullus datur conceptus formalis entis, præter conceptus prædicamentorum.

And from this it is understood that there is given no formal concept common to the analogous terms and distinct from the concepts of the analogates, but only several concepts of them. Hence there is given no formal concept of being besides the concepts of the categories.

### Secunda pars quæstionis, de vnitate conceptus obiectiui analogorum — Second part of the question, on the unity of the objective concept of analogous terms.

> 30 DVplicia sunt analoga, vt dubio præcedenti insinuauimus. Quædam sunt: quorum significatum non reperitur formaliter, & intrinsecè, nisi in principali analogato, in cæteris veró, per Denominationem extrinsecam: vt sanum, quod sanitatem significat, sicut album, significat albedinem: & tamen sanitas, non reperitur formaliter, nisi in solo animali: in vrina veró, & medicina solùm per denominationem extrinsecam, signi, vel causæ. Alia sunt analoga, quorum significatum reperitur formaliter, in omnibus analogatis: sed per se primò & principaliter, in vno tantùm, in reliquis verò, per intrinsecam dependentiam, & attributionem ad illud: & de vtrisque procedit quæstio, An habeat vnum conceptum communem, & abstrahibilem ab analogatis. Sed de primis primò dicendum est, deinde de aliis.

30 Analogous terms are of two kinds, as we intimated in the preceding doubt. Some are those whose significate is not found formally and intrinsically except in the principal analogate, and in the others by extrinsic denomination: as healthy, which signifies health as white signifies whiteness; and yet health is not found formally except in the animal alone, but in urine and medicine only by the extrinsic denomination of sign or of cause. Others are analogous terms whose significate is found formally in all the analogates, but per se first and principally in one only, and in the rest through an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it. And concerning both the question proceeds whether they have one common concept, abstractable from the analogates. But we must speak first of the first, then of the others.

> Est igitur prima opinio modernorum: Quòd hæc analoga, significent vnum conceptum obiectiuum: quem intellectus abstrahit ab analogatis. Probatur primò: quia hęc analoga, nõ sunt æquiuoca: ergo non habent solam vocem cõmunem, sed aliquid etiam, per illam significatum: sed quæcunque ratio cõmunis potest abstrahi à particularibus, quæ in ea conueniunt: ergo datur conceptus horum analogorum, abstrahibilis ab eis

The first opinion, then, is that of moderns: that these analogous terms signify one objective concept, which the intellect abstracts from the analogates. It is proved, first: because these analogous terms are not equivocal; therefore they have not only a common word, but also something signified by it; but any common ratio can be abstracted from the particulars that agree in it; therefore there is given a concept of these analogous terms abstractable from them

[p. 215]

> Secundò: Quia audito nomine, sanum: potest aliquis concipere, aliquam rationem communem sanitatis, non considerando rationes particulares, aut distinguendo diuersas, quas habet, in animali, vrina, & medicina: & conceptus iste communis est eis; ergo est vnus, & abstractus ab eisdem, secundùm particulares rationes consideratis.

Second: because on hearing the name healthy someone can conceive some common ratio of health, not considering the particular ratios, or distinguishing the different ones which it has in the animal, urine, and medicine; and this concept is common to them; therefore it is one, and abstracted from them considered according to their particular ratios.

> Secunda opinio est communis, & vera: quòd ab his analogis, non possit abstrahi conceptus communis, sed ea proximè significare rationes particulares analogatorum, aliquo modo similes, vel proportionatas: in ordine ad vnum principale. Ita Caiet. opus. de analogia nominum cap. 5. Sotus cap. præsenti, q 1. art. 2. Corol. 3. Fonseca 4. Meta. cap 2. quæst. 1. sect. 6. vers. 3. discrimen.

The second opinion is the common and true one: that from these analogous terms a common concept cannot be abstracted, but that they proximately signify the particular ratios of the analogates, in some way similar or proportioned in order to one principal. So Cajetan, opusc. On the Analogy of Names, ch. 5; Soto, on the present chapter, q. 1, a. 2, corol. 3; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 1, sect. 6, at the verse “3. Discrimen.”

> 31 Et probatur ratione: Quia hæc analogata significant vnam formam, solùm existentem in principali analogato, non in aliis, in quibus solum est, per extrinsecam denominationem, vt sanum, significat formam sanitatis in solo animali inhærentem non in vrina, & medecina, quæ solùm dicuntur sana per extrinsecum respectum, causæ, vel signi ad sanitatem animali: sed à re, formaliter significata, & per solam extrinsecam denominationem, non est abstrahibilis vna ratio, vel conceptus communis: quia forma, & signum, vel causa, se habent, tanquam causa, & effectus: quorum rationes diuersę sunt, licèt ordinem dependentiæ, vel attributionis habeant, & ideo non datur conceptus eis communis: ergo nec dabitur conceptus communis, horum analogatorum.

31 And it is proved by reason: because these analogates signify one form, existing only in the principal analogate, not in the others, in which it is only by extrinsic denomination: as healthy signifies the form of health inhering in the animal alone, not in urine and medicine, which are called healthy only by an extrinsic respect of cause or sign to the health of the animal. But from a thing signified formally and by extrinsic denomination alone, one ratio or common concept is not abstractable, because the form and the sign or cause stand as cause and effect, whose ratios are different, although they have an order of dependence or attribution; and therefore there is not given a concept common to them. Therefore neither will there be given a common concept of these analogates.

> Secundò: Quia conceptus vnus, & communis multis, formaliter debet in eis reperiri: sed conceptus horum analogorum, solùm reperitur formaliter in principali analogato, vt patet de conceptu sanitatis; ergo non est vnus omnibus eis communis.

Second: because one concept, common to many, must be found in them formally; but the concept of these analogates is found formally only in the principal analogate, as is plain of the concept of health; therefore it is not one, common to all of them.

> Sed respondent aliqui pro prima sententia, Conceptum horum analogatorum, non esse soliùs formæ, sed abstrahere ab inclusione formæ, aut ratione signi, vel causæ: ita vt vniuersalior sit, solùm dicens vniuersalitatem rationem sanitatis: & non particularem sanitatis formalis: & hunc conceptum abstractum, formaliter, reperiri in omnibus: nam esse causam sanitatis, formaliter, & intrinsecè, reperitur in medicina; & esse signum, formaliter conuenit vrinæ, sicut sanitas actualis: formaliter conuenit animali.

But some reply, for the first opinion, that the concept of these analogates is not of the form alone, but abstracts from the inclusion of the form, or of the ratio of sign or of cause, so that it is more general, expressing only universally the ratio of health and not the particular ratio of formal health; and that this abstracted concept is found formally in all: for to be a cause of health is found formally and intrinsically in medicine, and to be a sign belongs formally to urine, just as actual health belongs formally to the animal.

> 32 Hæc tamẽ solutio falsum supponit: Quia nomen sanum, impositum est ad significandam, veram, & actualem sanitatem, vnde in communi modo loquendi, & concipiendi, illud solum [p. 216] vocatur sanum, quod formalem habet sanitatem: sicut nomen risus, impositum est ad significandum *verum risum* hominis: quem solum intelligimus, audito hoc nomine: ergo non significant huiusmodi analoga, vniuersaliorem illam rationem, sed ex eo, significant minus principalia analogata, quia intrinsecam habent attributionem, ad formam existentem in principali analogato, per nomen primario significatam. Nec vera est illa ratio communis, vniuersalior, & abstrahens à formali, & intrinseca sanitate, quam obijcit argumentum, sed ficta: quia formæ, signo, & causæ, nihil datur commune, sed solùm hæc appellatur sana, per attributionem ad illam propter quam ei aliquo modo assimilantur: sed similitudo non est intelligibilis, sine rationibus particularibus eorum: & ideo, nec est ab eis abstrahibilis: imò, nec intelligibilia sunt particularia significata, nisi actu intellectis rationibus particularibus: non quidem distinctè, & expressè, vt significantur propriis nominibus, sed confusè tantùm: & hoc modo significantur nomine communi, & analogo: cuius ideo, non potest dari conceptus obiectus, communis, abstractus ab analogatis.

32 This solution, however, supposes something false: because the name healthy was imposed to signify true and actual health; hence in the common manner of speaking and conceiving, that alone O iiij [p. 216] is called healthy which has formal health; just as the name laughter was imposed to signify the true laughter of man, which alone we understand on hearing this name. Therefore analogous terms of this kind do not signify that more universal ratio, but from the fact that they signify it they signify the less principal analogates, because these have an intrinsic attribution to the form existing in the principal analogate, primarily signified by the name. Nor is that common, more universal ratio, abstracting from formal and intrinsic health, which the argument objects, a true one, but a fictitious one: because to the form, the sign, and the cause nothing common is given, but these are only called healthy by attribution to that form, on account of which they are in some way assimilated to it. But the similarity is not intelligible without their particular ratios, and therefore it is not abstractable from them; indeed, the particular significates are not even intelligible except when the particular ratios are actually understood, not distinctly and expressly, as they are signified by their proper names, but only confusedly; and in this way they are signified by the common and analogous name, of which, therefore, there cannot be given an objective concept that is common and abstracted from the analogates.

> 33 Ad primum arg. Concedendum est antecedens, cum prima consequentia: minor verò distinguenda: nam ratio communis, duplex est: Communis, simpliciter, aut secundùm quid: illa reperitur in vniuocis, hęc in analogis: & illa solùm, abstrahibilis est, à particularibus rationibus vniuocatorum: hæc verò, nullo modo potest abstrahi, à particularibus rationibus analogatorum: sed necessariò debet eas actu confuso includere. Ratio huius discriminis est: quia ratio communis simpliciter, est ratio naturæ, aut modi, in inferioribus existentis, communis verò secundùm quid, nihil est præter proportionem, aut attributionem, inter rationes particulares: & ideo, non est intelligibilis, sine inclusione actuali particularium, saltem confusa: & ex consequenti, nisi intellectis particularibus, actu confuso, hoc est, non distinctè nec expressè: vt significantur propriis nominibus: & hoc est, non esse abstrahibilem conceptum communem ab eis: quia conceptus, qui à particularibus abstrahitur, non includit ea actu, sed solùm in potentia.

33 To the first argument, the antecedent is to be granted, with the first consequence; but the minor is to be distinguished. For a common ratio is twofold: common simply, or in a certain respect. The former is found in univocals, the latter in analogous terms; and the former alone is abstractable from the particular ratios of the univocates, whereas the latter can in no way be abstracted from the particular ratios of the analogates, but must necessarily include them by a confused act. The reason for this difference is that a ratio common simply is the ratio of a nature or mode existing in the inferiors, while one common in a certain respect is nothing besides the proportion or attribution among the particular ratios; and therefore it is not intelligible without an actual inclusion of the particulars, at least a confused one; and consequently not unless the particulars are understood by a confused act, that is, not distinctly nor expressly, as they are signified by their proper names. And this is for there not to be a common concept abstractable from them: because a concept that is abstracted from particulars does not include them in act, but only in potency.

> 34 Ad secundum, Distinguendum est antecedens: quia dupliciter contingit, concipere rationem communem, audito nomine analogo: non conceptis particularibus. Distinctè, & expressè: aut solùm confusè. Actu igitur expresso, & primo modo, concipi nequit ratio communis, secundùm quid, non conceptis particularibus, sed secundo modo: quia communis illa ratio, non *est aliud, præter* particulares proportionatas: & ideo, necessariò [p. 217] conceptas actu, eodem conceptu: non actu expresso, aut explicito, sed confuso, & quasi implicito.

34 To the second, the antecedent is to be distinguished: because it happens in two ways that a common ratio is conceived on hearing an analogous name without the particulars being conceived: distinctly and expressly, or only confusedly. By an express act, then, and in the first way, a ratio common in a certain respect cannot be conceived without the particulars being conceived; but in the second way it can: because that common ratio is nothing other than the proportioned particulars; and therefore they are necessarily [p. 217] conceived in act by the same concept: not by an express or explicit act, but by a confused and as it were implicit one.

> Maior est difficultas, de aliis analogis, quorum ratio, vel forma significata formaliter, & intrinsecè, reperitur in omnibus analogatis: licèt primò, & per se in vno, in aliis verò, per intrinsecam dependentiam, & attributionem, ad illud & tale analogum, est ens, secundùm communem, & veram sententiam: & ideo in illo placet exemplum ponere. Cùm enim forma significata, quę est entitas, formaliter reperiatur, in substantia, & accidentibus, videtur, abstrahi posse rationem communem entitatis, à particularibus rationibus prædicamentorum, quam participabunt omnia, tanquam formam intrinsecam.

The difficulty is greater concerning the other analogous terms, whose ratio or form signified is found formally and intrinsically in all the analogates, although first and per se in one, and in the others through an intrinsic dependence on and attribution to it. And such an analogous term is being, according to the common and true opinion; and therefore it is fitting to take the example in it. For since the form signified, which is entity, is found formally in substance and in accidents, it seems that a common ratio of entity can be abstracted from the particular ratios of the categories, which all will participate as an intrinsic form.

> 35 Et est prima opinio, quæ asserit, Conceptum analogi, vnum simpliciter esse, & abstractum, à particularibus rationibus analogorum: & ideò ratione distinctum ab eis. Ita Iauellus 4. Met. quæ. 1. Sotus vbi suprà. Probatur testimoniis Arist. & D. Tho. deinde rationibus. Arist. 4. Meta. tex. 7. asserit, Metaphysicam considerare ens, in quantum ens; quasi dicat, non vt substantiam, vel accidens, sed sub ratione vniuersaliori, entitas realis: datur ergo ratio vniuersalior, Substantia, & Accidente, quam necesse est, esse abstractam ab eis, vnam atque communem. Probatur consequentia: quia Vniuersale, est quid abstractum à particularibus, eisque commune.

35 And the first opinion is that which asserts that the concept of the analogous term is simply one, and abstracted from the particular ratios of the analogous terms, and therefore distinct in ratio from them. So Javelli, Metaph. 4, q. 1; Soto in the place cited above. It is proved by testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas, then by arguments. Aristotle, Metaph. 4, text 7, asserts that Metaphysics considers being inasmuch as it is being: as if to say, not as substance or accident, but under the more universal ratio of real entity. There is given, therefore, a ratio more universal than substance and accident, which must be abstracted from them, one and common. The consequence is proved: because the universal is something abstracted from particulars and common to them.

> 36 Et D. Tho. 1 par. quæst. 5. art. 3. ad primum, ait, *Substantiam, quantitatem, & qualitatem contrahere ens applicando illud ad aliquam quidditatem, seu naturam: sed contractio non potest intelligi nisi respectu alicuius communis, quod determinatur ad particularia*, ergo sentit ens, & quodcunque ex his analogis significare conceptum communem, & abstractum ab analogatis.

36 And St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 5, a. 3, ad 1, says that substance, quantity, and quality contract being by applying it to some quiddity or nature; but contraction cannot be understood except with respect to something common which is determined to particulars. Therefore he thinks that being, and any one of these analogous terms, signifies a common concept abstracted from the analogates.

> Probatur etiam ratione, Primò: quia entitas formaliter, & intrinsecè est in substantia, & accidente: ergo in eo conueniunt, vel assimilantur, quòd vtrumque formaliter est ens, sed cuiuscunque conuenientiæ abstrahi potest conceptus communis eis, quæ eam habent, ergo abstrahibilis est conceptus communis entitatis, in qua assimilantur substantia, & accidens, & iste erit vnus atque ratione distinctus ab eis.

It is also proved by reason. First: because entity is formally and intrinsically in substance and in accident; therefore they agree, or are assimilated, in this, that each is formally a being. But from any agreement whatever a concept common to the things that have it can be abstracted; therefore a common concept of entity is abstractable, in which substance and accident are assimilated; and this will be one, and distinct in ratio from them.

> Secundò: Quia concipere possumus de re aliqua, quòd sit ens, & dubitare an sit substantia, vel accidens: ergo in conceptu entis, neutrum includitur secundùm particularem rationem, aut modum intrinsecum. Probatur consequentia, Quia si includerentur speciales rationes, certò cognosceremus, quænam ei conueniret, eo ipso quod concipimus esse ens, & ideo non haberet locum dubitatio. Sed si non includuntur speciales [p. 218] rationes in eo conceptu, erit abstaactus, & vnus: cùm nihil includat diuersitatis, sed solam conuenientiam: ergo datur vnus conceptus analogi abstractus ab analogatis.

Second: because we can conceive of some thing that it is a being, and doubt whether it is a substance or an accident; therefore in the concept of being neither is included according to its particular ratio or intrinsic mode. The consequence is proved: because if the special ratios were included, we would know with certainty which of them belonged to it by the very fact that we conceive it to be a being, and therefore doubt would have no place. But if the special [p. 218] ratios are not included in that concept, it will be abstracted and one, since it includes nothing of diversity, but only agreement; therefore there is given one concept of the analogous term abstracted from the analogates.

> 37 Probatur tertiò, quia si non datur conceptus, abstractus, & cõmunis entis, erit quasi aggregatus ex omnibus rationibus specialibus prædicamentorum. Ita vt qui dicit ens, dicat substantiam, quantitatem, qualitatem, & cætera prædicamenta: sed talis conceptus de nullo analogato potest prædicari, ergo falsæ erunt omnes istæ prędicationes, Substãtia est ens, Quantitas est ens, Qualitas est ens, quod est absurdum. Probatur consequentia, quia sensus earum erit, Substantia est substantia, quantitas & qualitas, & sic de cæteris, qui est manifestè falsus.

37 It is proved third: because if there is not given an abstracted and common concept of being, it will be as it were an aggregate of all the special ratios of the categories, so that whoever says being says substance, quantity, quality, and the other categories. But such a concept can be predicated of no analogate; therefore all these predications will be false: Substance is a being, Quantity is a being, Quality is a being; which is absurd. The consequence is proved: because their sense will be Substance is substance, quantity, and quality, and so of the rest, which is manifestly false.

> Hanc sententiam defendit P. Franciscus Suarius 1. tom. suæ Meta. disp. 2. sect. 1. additque tria Primum, hunc conceptum obiectiuum entis sic esse præcisum ab inferioribus, vt in eo non includantur actu distincto, vel confuso modi intrinseci eorum, videlicet per se, & in alio. Secundum, ens non significare immediatè substantiam, & accidens, sed illum conceptum communem, & abstractum, quo medio descẽdit ens ad vtrumque. Tertium, hunc conceptum communem non solùm esse vnum, vt abstractum ab inferioribus, sed etiam, vt ad illa comparatur: & hoc addidit propter quandam opinionem aliorum modernorum, qui dicunt, vt abstractum esse vnum, non tamen vt comparatum ad inferiora: quia in illis, vt expressè conceptis diuersificatur, quam sententiam specialiter referre necessarium non puto. In his autem tribus, satis consequenter loquitur doctissimus pater.

This opinion is defended by Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 1 of his Metaph., disp. 2, sect. 1, and he adds three things. First, that this objective concept of being is so prescinded from the inferiors that their intrinsic modes, namely per se and in another, are not included in it by a distinct or confused act. Second, that being does not immediately signify substance and accident, but that common and abstracted concept, by means of which being descends to both. Third, that this common concept is one not only as abstracted from the inferiors, but also as it is compared to them. And he added this on account of a certain opinion of other moderns, who say that it is one as abstracted, yet not as compared to the inferiors, because in them, as expressly conceived, it is diversified; which opinion I do not think it necessary to report specially. In these three things, however, the most learned Father speaks quite consistently.

> 38 Secunda opinio est aliorum modernorum, qui concedunt conceptum entis abstrahi posse à particularibus substantiæ, & accidentis, & vt sic abstractum ab eis esse vnum simpliciter, sed comparatum, cum eisdem, vel consideratum in eis expressè conceptis, hoc est, vt propriis nominibus significantur, non esse vnum, sed fieri in eis diuersum. Quod probari potest, quia communis ratio entitatis, vt est in substantia, & accidenti, non distinguitur ab eis, licèt in abstractione distinguatur, sed conceptus expressi eorum sunt diuersi, ergo ratio entis, vt in eis existens, non potest esse vna, sed debet esse diuersa.

38 The second opinion is that of other moderns, who grant that the concept of being can be abstracted from the particulars of substance and accident, and that, thus abstracted from them, it is one simply; but that compared with them, or considered in them as expressly conceived, that is, as they are signified by their proper names, it is not one, but becomes diverse in them. Which can be proved: because the common ratio of entity, as it is in substance and accident, is not distinguished from them, although it is distinguished in abstraction; but their express concepts are diverse; therefore the ratio of being, as existing in them, cannot be one, but must be diverse.

> 39 Tertia opinio, negat omnino dari vnum conceptum obiectiuum simpliciter abstractum ab analogatis, quam sequuntur Cap. in 2. d. 2. quæst. 1. & apud ipsum Aureol Ferra. 1. cont. gent. cap 30. Deca Hispalens. in 1. d. 2 quæst. Caiet. in opusc. de ente & essentia, ca. 1. q. 2. & tract. de nom. analog c 5. & 6. Sot. 4. Metaph. q. 2. Pere. 2. lib. Phys. c. 2. in fine, Fland. 4. Meta. q 5. [p. 219] art. 6 Fons. 4. Met. c. 2. q. 2. P. Gabr. Vazquez 1 p. d. 22. c. 5. & d. 114. c. 2 & plures alij, & hæc est probabilior sententia

39 The third opinion altogether denies that there is given one objective concept simply abstracted from the analogates. It is followed by Capreolus, In 2, d. 2, q. 1, and, as reported by him, Auriol; Ferrara, on Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 30; Deza of Seville, In 1, d. 2, q.; Cajetan in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 1, q. 2, and in the treatise On the Analogy of Names, ch. 5 and 6; Soto, Metaph. 4, q. 2; Pereira, Phys. bk. 2, ch. 2, at the end; Dominic of Flanders, Metaph. 4, q. 5; [p. 219] a. 6; Fonseca, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, q. 2; Father Gabriel Vázquez, 1 p., d. 22, ch. 5, and d. 114, ch. 2; and many others. And this is the more probable opinion.

> Probatur aduersus primam, & secundam, testimonis Arist. & D. Thom. Arist. enim 4 Met. ca. 2. duo asserit, nempe. *Quòd ens multipliciter dicitur, & quòd dicitur ad vnum, vel ad vnam naturam*: ex vtroque autem colligitur, quòd non detur vnus conceptus eius abstractus ab analogatis, quod sic probo: Nam si multipliciter dicitur, ergo non vno modo, nec per vnum conceptum, sed per plures: & si dicitur in ordine ad vnum: ergo in suo conceptu includit multa. Probatur consequentia, quia vbi datur vnum, vel multa ad vnum ordinata, vbi est multiplicitas; sed si multa includit in suo conceptu, non potest talis conceptus esse vnus, quia multa diuersa sunt: ergo, nòn datur vnus conceptus obiectiuus entis. Et 8. Meta. cap. 6. tex. 16 asserit, *Ens statim esse substantiam, quantitatem, & qualitatem*, hoc est, immediatè ad illa descendere, & non vt vniuocũ, quod non nisi medio vnico conceptu eis communi, descendit ad vniuocata, vt animal ad hominem, & equum, ergo sentit non habere conceptum communem: nam eo mediante, descenderet ab substantiam, & accidens.

It is proved against the first and second by testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, Metaph. 4, ch. 2, asserts two things, namely that being is said in many ways, and that it is said with reference to one, or to one nature. And from both it is gathered that there is not given one concept of it abstracted from the analogates, which I prove thus. For if it is said in many ways, then not in one way, nor through one concept, but through several; and if it is said in order to one, then in its concept it includes many. The consequence is proved: because where there is given one, or many ordered to one, there is multiplicity; but if it includes many in its concept, such a concept cannot be one, because the many are different; therefore there is not given one objective concept of being. And in Metaph. 8, ch. 6, text 16, he asserts that being is straightway substance, quantity, and quality, that is, that it descends to them immediately, and not as a univocal term, which descends to the univocates only by means of a single concept common to them, as animal to man and horse. Therefore he thinks that it does not have a common concept: for by means of it, it would descend to substance and accident.

> Et D. Tho. 1. p. q 13 art. 5. ita ait: *Neque enim in his, quæ analogicè dicuntur, est vna ratio sicut in vniuocis, nec totaliter diuersa sicut in æquiuocis, sed nomen, quod sic multipliciter dicitur, significat diuersas proportiones in ordine ad vnum*, &c.

And St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 5, says thus: For in those things which are said analogically there is neither one ratio, as in univocals, nor a totally different one, as in equivocals; but the name which is thus said in many ways signifies different proportions in order to one, etc.

> Ex quibus verbis hoc arg. colligitur: Conceptus entis, apud D. Thom. significat diuersas proportiones in ordine ad vnum: sed non potest significare diuersas proportiones in ordine ad vnum, nisi diuersa illa, quæ tales habent proportiones simul significet, & hæc sunt analogata: ergo non potest abstrahi conceptus eius ab analogatis, nec esse vnus simpliciter.

From these words this argument is gathered. The concept of being, according to St. Thomas, signifies different proportions in order to one; but it cannot signify different proportions in order to one unless it signifies at once those different things which have such proportions, and these are the analogates; therefore its concept cannot be abstracted from the analogates, nor be one simply.

> Probatur deinde ratione aduersus primam sententiam, desumpta ex definitione analogorum, quam admittunt omnes. Analoga sunt, quorum nomen est cõmune, ratio verò substantię nomini accommodata, nec omnino eadem: neque omnino diuersa: sed ratio substantiæ est conceptus obiectiuus, ergo iste non est omnino idem, nec omnino diuersus, sed diuersus simpliciter, & idem secundùm quid, ratione attributionis, quare sequitur, non esse abstrahibilem ab analogatis, inter quę attributio, & diuersitas reperitur, nec potest esse vnus simpliciter.

It is proved next by an argument against the first opinion, taken from the definition of analogous terms, which all admit. Analogous terms are those whose name is common, but the ratio of substance accommodated to the name is neither altogether the same nor altogether different; but the ratio of substance is the objective concept; therefore this is neither altogether the same nor altogether different, but different simply and the same in a certain respect, by reason of attribution. Wherefore it follows that it is not abstractable from the analogates, among which attribution and diversity are found, nor can it be one simply.

> Secundò: Si conceptus entis abstrahitur, aut præscinditur à substantia, & accidenti: ergo distinguitur ratione ab illis: sed quæ distinguuntur aliqua distinctione, vt sic distincta, non se includunt; ergo conceptus entis, vt sic præcisus à modis [p. 220] intrinsecis substantiæ, & accidentis, nec eos potest includere, nec in eis includi. Primum probatum est falsum: sed probatur etiam falsum esse secundum, quia conceptus entis est transcedens, ergo includitur in quacunque entitate, siue sit completa, siue incompleta, siue sit natura, vel modus: alioqui, si nõ includat ens erit nihil.

Second: if the concept of being is abstracted or prescinded from substance and accident, then it is distinguished in ratio from them; but things that are distinguished by some distinction, as thus distinct, do not include each other; therefore the concept of being, as thus prescinded from the modes [p. 220] intrinsic to substance and accident, can neither include them nor be included in them. The first has been proved false; but the second is also proved to be false, because the concept of being is transcendental; therefore it is included in any entity whatever, whether complete or incomplete, whether a nature or a mode; otherwise, if being were not included, it would be nothing.

> 41 Probatur tertiò: Quia si conceptus entis est abstractus simpliciter à modis intrinsecis, & eos non includit actu, vt fatetur prima sententia, sequitur sic esse vnum, vt nullam includat diuersitatem. Probatur consequentia, quia tota aduersitas substantiæ & accidentis, est per modos intrinsecos per se, & in alio, si ergo hos nõ includit actu, sicut genus non includit actu differentias, erit vnus simpliciter, & consequenter vniuocus.

41 It is proved third: because if the concept of being is simply abstracted from the intrinsic modes and does not include them in act, as the first opinion admits, it follows that it is one in such a way that it includes no diversity. The consequence is proved: because the whole diversity of substance and accident is through the intrinsic modes per se and in another; if, then, it does not include these in act, as genus does not include the differences in act, it will be one simply, and consequently univocal.

> Respondet prima sententia: Quòd licèt non includat actu modos, & in hoc conueniat cum vniuoco, differt tamen ab eo, quòd conceptus vniuocè eodem modo, aut æqualiter participabilis est ab vniuocatis: conceptus verò analogi, vt entis ex propria natura, est diuerso modo participabilis ab analogatis secundùm attributionem vnius, vel multorum ad vnum, & hoc satis est, vt nõ sit vniuocus, sed analogus. Sed hæc solutio sic impugnatur: Cõceptus entis non potest esse diuerso modo participabilis: nec potest vllam habere diuersitatem, nisi per diuersos modos intrinsecos per se, & in alio, per quos determinatur ad esse substantiæ, & accidentium, ergo repugnat vllam habere diuersitatem, aut diuerso modo esse participabilem, nisi per ipsos modos: sed dum ab eis abstrahitur, eos non includit, ergo non potest esse diuerso modo participabilis.

The first opinion replies that, although it does not include the modes in act, and in this agrees with the univocal, yet it differs from it in that a univocal concept is participable by the univocates in the same way, or equally, whereas the concept of the analogous term, such as that of being, is of its own nature participable in different ways by the analogates, according to the attribution of one, or of many, to one; and this is enough for it not to be univocal but analogous. But this solution is attacked thus: the concept of being cannot be participable in different ways, nor can it have any diversity, except through the different intrinsic modes per se and in another, by which it is determined to the being of substance and of accidents; therefore it is repugnant that it have any diversity, or be participable in different ways, except through those very modes; but while it is abstracted from them it does not include them; therefore it cannot be participable in different ways.

> 42 Et confirmari efficaciter potest hoc modo: Conceptum communem abstrahi à particularibus, non est aliud, quàm rationem communem cognosci sine particularibus, aut eis non cognitis, ergo Conceptum entis abstrahi à modis per se, & in alio, est cognosci rationem entis, non consideratis modis, neque ordine ad illos: nam eo ipso, quòd consideraretur ordo ad illos, non esset conceptus abstractus: sed nullam potest habere diuersitatem ratio entis sine modis, aut sine ordine ad illos: ergo si ab eis abstrahatur, erit conceptus omnino vnus & idem, non minùs, quàm conceptus vniuocus, & ens ipsum non erit analogum, sed vniuocum.

42 And it can be effectively confirmed in this way: for a common concept to be abstracted from particulars is nothing other than for the common ratio to be known without the particulars, or with them not known; therefore for the concept of being to be abstracted from the modes per se and in another is for the ratio of being to be known without the modes being considered, or the order to them: for by the very fact that the order to them were considered, it would not be an abstracted concept. But the ratio of being can have no diversity without the modes, or without the order to them; therefore if it is abstracted from them, it will be a concept altogether one and the same, no less than a univocal concept, and being itself will not be analogous but univocal.

> Probatur deinde aduersus secundam opinionem. Primò: Quia si semel admittitur conceptus entis abstractus à particularibus substantiæ, & accidentis, & esse vnum, sequitur ens esse vniuocum. Probatur consequentia: quia illum conceptum abstractum, & vnum, significat primò ens, ergo ratio significata [p. 221] per nomen est eadem, & nomen commune, vt dicitur in definitione vniuocorum. Secundò, quia repugnat conceptum in abstractione esse vnum, & non inferioribus expressis: ergo semper est vnus. Probatur antecedens: quia si semel abstrahitur ab eis: ergo distinguitur ratione abstractus ab eisdem vt expressis: sed comparatus ad eos est idem conceptus, qui consideratur in abstractione, & non alius: ergo erit etiam ratione distinctus: & ideo eandem habebit vnitatem quam ei tribuunt in abstractione.

It is proved next against the second opinion. First: because if once a concept of being abstracted from the particulars of substance and accident is admitted, and that it is one, it follows that being is univocal. The consequence is proved: because being signifies first that abstracted and one concept; therefore the ratio signified [p. 221] by the name is the same, and the name common, as is said in the definition of univocals. Second, because it is repugnant that the concept be one in abstraction and not one when the inferiors are expressed: therefore it is always one. The antecedent is proved: because if once it is abstracted from them, then, as abstracted, it is distinguished by reason from the same taken as expressed; but compared to them it is the same concept which is considered in abstraction, and not another: therefore it will also be distinguished by reason; and therefore it will have the same unity that they attribute to it in abstraction.

### Quonam modo conceptus analogi contineat analogata — In what way the concept of the analogous term contains the analogates.

> NOstra igitur sententia tenet, Conceptum obiectiuum entis, & cuiuscunque analogi, non esse simpliciter abstrahibilem ab analogatis, sed eos necessariò includere. Circa modum verò, quo ea includat, non cõueniunt omnes, qui eam sequuntur. Duo tamen sunt apud eos recepta. Primum, quòd ea includat actu, & non solùm in potentia, quia hoc vltimum nec tollit vnitatem conceptus, nec vniuocationem nominis. Secundum, quòd non includat eos actu explicito, distincto, vel expresso, quod est dicere, non includere eos, vt significantur propriis nominibus, sed in quantum sub nomine communi significantur, vt sub nomine entitatis, vt de ente loquatur. Et ratio huius est quia ens significat substantiam, & accidens, in quantum habent attributionem: sed sub propriis nominibus eam non habent, sed sub nomine communi entis significata, & confusè contenta: ergo hoc tantùm modo significantur nomine analogo, & continentur in conceptu eius, & non sub expressis conceptibus, aut nominibus.

Our view, then, holds that the objective concept of being, and of any analogous term whatever, is not simply abstractable from the analogates, but necessarily includes them. But concerning the way in which it includes them, not all who follow it agree. Two things, however, are received among them. The first, that it includes them in act, and not only in potency, because this last takes away neither the unity of the concept nor the univocation of the name. The second, that it does not include them in explicit, distinct, or express act, which is to say, that it does not include them as they are signified by their proper names, but inasmuch as they are signified under the common name, as under the name of entity, if we are speaking of being. And the reason for this is that being signifies substance and accident inasmuch as they have attribution; but under their proper names they do not have it, but signified under the common name of being, and confusedly contained: therefore only in this way are they signified by the analogous name and contained in its concept, and not under express concepts or names.

> Differunt igitur, quantum ad modum eos includendi. Nam Soncinas & Herueus vbi supra, asserunt conceptum, quem immediatè significat ens, esse hoc disiunctum, substantiam, vel accidens. Hoc tamen ab omnibus, ferè reiicitur. Primò, quia conceptus per determinatam vocem significatus debet esse determinatus, disiunctũ verò illud, nec determinatè dicit substantiam, neq; accidens. Secũdò, quia ens significat multa per attributionem ad vnum, ergo significat omnia simpliciter, hoc est, sine disiunctione. Probatur consequentia: quia attributio non versatur inter multa disiunctiuè significata, sed absolutè.

They differ, then, as to the way of including them. For Soncinas and Hervaeus, in the places cited above, assert that the concept which being immediately signifies is this disjunctive one, substance or accident. This, however, is rejected by almost all. First, because a concept signified by a determinate word must be determinate, whereas that disjunctive one says determinately neither substance nor accident. Second, because being signifies many things by attribution to one; therefore it signifies all of them simply, that is, without disjunction. The consequence is proved: because attribution does not hold among many things signified disjunctively, but absolutely.

> Nec etiam significat analogum sua analogata copulatiuè, ita vt conceptus entis sit substantia, & accidens, quia ex eo sequeretur omnes propositiones, in quibus prædicatur, de quolibet eorum esse falsas: vt substantia est ens: accidens est ens, quia sensus earum esset, substantia, est substantia, vel accidens: [p. 222] accidens est substantia, vel accidens.

Nor again does the analogous term signify its analogates copulatively, so that the concept of being is substance and accident: because from this it would follow that all propositions in which it is predicated of any one of them are false, as Substance is a being, Accident is a being, because their sense would be: Substance is substance and accident: [p. 222] Accident is substance and accident.

> Propterea, est secunda opinio aliorum, Quòd ens primaria significatione, significet ens per se, quod est substantia & ens simpliciter: secundariò verò accidentia, tanquam aliquid eiusdem substantiæ. Sed hoc etiam videtur falsum: quia analogum per se primò significat multa cum attributione: ergo non significat primò solum analogatum principale, sed omnia, quamuis principale significatum sit dignitate primum.

Therefore there is a second opinion, that of others: that being, in its primary signification, signifies being per se, which is substance and being simply; but secondarily accidents, as something of the same substance. But this too seems false: because the analogous term per se and primarily signifies many things with attribution; therefore it does not primarily signify only the principal analogate, but all of them, although the principal significate is first in dignity.

> 44 Tertia opinio est Ferra. & Caiet. vbi suprà quòd analogum significet immediatè, & per se omnia analogata, in quantum inter sese habent attributionem, & ens significet immediatè decem prædicamenta, in quantum nouem accidentium, dicuntur per attributionem ad substantiam. & hæc est probabilior, & tenenda.

44 The third opinion is that of Ferrara and Cajetan, in the places cited above: that the analogous term signifies immediately and per se all the analogates, inasmuch as they have attribution among themselves; and that being signifies immediately the ten categories, inasmuch as the nine of accidents are so called by attribution to substance. And this is the more probable and is to be held.

> Sed pro eius explicatione tanquam certum debet præsupponi; Quòd analogum aliquo modo sit superius cuiuslibet analogato, vt bene Caiet. in opusc. de analogia, cap. 5. non solùm secũdùm vocem, quæ communis est analogatis: nam hoc etiam habet æquiuocum, sed aliquo modo secundùm rationem, aut conceptum significatum, qui cùm aliquo modo debeat etiam communis esse, consequenter debet esse superior: & si communis est aliquo modo, debet esse abstractus ab eis.

But for its explanation it must be presupposed as certain that the analogous term is in some way superior to each analogate, as Cajetan rightly says in the opuscule On Analogy, ch. 5: not only according to the word, which is common to the analogates (for the equivocal term also has this), but in some way according to the ratio or concept signified; which, since it must also be in some way common, must consequently be superior; and if it is in some way common, it must be abstracted from them.

> Sed vt hæc intelligantur melius, adnotat bene Caiet. vbi suprà, duplicem esse abstractionem, qua vnum abstrahitur ab aliis. Vna est, per quam vnum cognoscitur sine alio, aut eo non cognito. Alia, per quam eadem res cognoscitur alio modo, quàm sit in se: vt cùm in se habeat modum expressum, atque distinctum, cognoscitur quasi implicitè & confusè. Et primus modus abstractionis cõstituit abstractionem simpliciter, & pertinet ad vniuoca, quæ sic abstrahuntur à suis vniuocatis. Secundus non facit, nisi abstractionem secundùm quid, & pertinet ad analoga: quæ non possunt primo modo abstrahi, nec alio, nisi secundo. Itaque substantia duobus modis considerabilis est: aut secundùm conceptum expressum per proprium nomen substantiæ, significatũ: aut secundùm cõceptum confusum, & quasi implicitum, qui non videtur esse alius, quàm entitas principalis, cui attribuuntur acicdentia. Et hoc modo significatur nomine entis, cuius proprius conceptus est entitatis primæ, ac principalis: & minùs principalium: quæ sunt accidentia secundùm particulares modos inhærendi ei, attributa, quæ est substantia. Et conceptus iste aliquo modo est abstractus respectu conceptum expressorum, inter quos, vt sic expressos, nulla attributio, nullus ordo, nulla dependentia, aut [p. 223] similitudo significatur, & ratio abstractionis in eo consistit, quòd licèt per conceptum entis, omnia concipiamus actu, & similiter dum omnia simul cõcipimus per propria nomina, per conceptum tamen entis concipimus ea, cum attributione, & similitudine: quæ per conceptus proprios repræsentata, nullam habẽt attributionem, nullum ordinem, nullam similitudinem, vnde sequitur, conceptum entis, ita prędicari de quocunque, vt suo etiam modo prædicetur, de aliis, & hoc est esse aliquo modo superiorem respectu singulorum, & ex consequenti, abstractum eodem modo ab eis, & vt talem prædicari de singulis.

But in order that these things may be better understood, Cajetan rightly notes, in the place cited above, that there is a twofold abstraction by which one thing is abstracted from others. One is that by which one thing is known without another, or with the other not known. The other, by which the same thing is known in another way than it is in itself: as when, though in itself it has an express and distinct mode, it is known as it were implicitly and confusedly. And the first mode of abstraction constitutes abstraction simply, and pertains to univocals, which are thus abstracted from their univocates. The second makes only abstraction in a certain respect, and pertains to analogous terms, which cannot be abstracted in the first mode, nor in any other except the second. Thus substance can be considered in two ways: either according to the express concept signified by the proper name substance; or according to a confused and as it were implicit concept, which seems to be nothing other than the principal entity to which accidents are attributed. And in this way it is signified by the name being, whose proper concept is of the first and principal entity, and of the less principal ones, which are accidents, attributed according to their particular modes of inhering to it, which is substance. And this concept is in some way abstracted with respect to the express concepts, among which, as thus expressed, there is no attribution, no order, no dependence, or [p. 223] similarity is signified; and the ratio of the abstraction consists in this, that although through the concept of being we conceive all things in act, and likewise while we conceive all of them together through their proper names, yet through the concept of being we conceive them with attribution and similarity, whereas, represented through their proper concepts, they have no attribution, no order, no similarity. Whence it follows that the concept of being is so predicated of any one whatever that it is also, in its own way, predicated of the others; and this is to be in some way superior with respect to each, and consequently abstracted from them in the same way, and as such to be predicated of each.

> 45 Sed vt modus prædicandi entis de singulis prędicamentis intelligatur, adnotamus secundò, Quòd licèt conceptus entis includat substantiam, & accidens actu confuso, vt explicatum est, in prædicatione tamen applicatur singulis, iuxta propriam naturam, vt dum prædicatur de substantia, applicatur ei, vt primo enti, cui attribuuntur accidentia, & dum prædicatur de aliquo accidenti, applicatur eidem, vt attributo substantiæ. Sensus igitur huius propositionis, *Substantia est ens*, iste est: Substantia est entitas prima, cui attribuuntur accidentia, & quantitas est ens, id est, habet entitatem per modum extensionis, attributam substantiæ. Et ratio huius est, quia omnia significantur secundùm attributionem ad vnum: ergo de illo vno prædicatur, tanquam de eo, cui attribuuntur cætera, & de cæteris, vt illi attribuuntur, & eadem attributio, est ratio propter quam, licèt conceptus entis multa ac diuersa contineat, verè possit prædicari de singulis: quia dum de quolibet prædicatur, ex proprio modo ipsius applicationis, & attributionis, illud tantùm dicit in recto, cætera verò in obliquo, vt attributio ipsa significata inter eos petit.

45 But in order that the mode of predicating being of the individual categories may be understood, we note second that, although the concept of being includes substance and accident in confused act, as has been explained, yet in predication it is applied to each according to its proper nature: so that when it is predicated of substance, it is applied to it as to the first being, to which accidents are attributed; and when it is predicated of some accident, it is applied to it as attributed to substance. The sense, then, of this proposition, Substance is a being, is this: Substance is the first entity, to which accidents are attributed; and of Quantity is a being: that is, it has entity by way of extension, attributed to substance. And the reason for this is that all things are signified according to attribution to one: therefore it is predicated of that one as of that to which the others are attributed, and of the others as they are attributed to it; and this same attribution is the reason why, although the concept of being contains many and diverse things, it can truly be predicated of each: because, while it is predicated of any one whatever, by the proper mode of its application and attribution it says that one only in recto, but the others in obliquo, as the very attribution signified among them requires.

> 46 Si autem dicas secundùm sensum harũ prædicationum, non prędicari ens de singulis prędicamentis, tanquam superius, sed tanquam æquale, imò prædicatione identica, aduersus id, quod dictum est, superius esse, saltem secundùm quid. Probatur vtrumque. Primum quidem, nam prædicatum huius propositionis, *Substantia est ens*, non est aliud, quàm substantia est entitas prima, cui proportionantur accidentia, & hoc patet cõuerti cum subiecto, imò esse idem prorsus cum eo, & ideo non solùm esse propositionem æqualis, sed identicam Respondeo prædicari prædicatione æquali simpliciter, superioris verò secundùm quid, identica verò nullo modò. Primum manifestum erit, si consideremus conceptum entis secundùm diuersos modos: quibus prædicatur de omnibus: nam de substantia, vt de primo, cui cætera attribuuntur: de singulis verò accidentibus [p. 224] secundùm particulares modos, quibus attribuuntur substantię. Consideratus igitur conceptus entis cum his omnibus modis, qui ei conueniunt, vt analogo adæquatè sumpto, cùm ei conueniant ratione analogiæ attributionis, superior erit formaliter respectu singulorum analogatorum, licèt tantùm secundùm quid, quamuis æqualis simpliciter seclusa hac consideratione. Et quòd sit superior formaliter secundùm quid, probo: quia dum prædicatur de vno secundùm modum applicationis ad illud, prædicari potest de cæteris, secundùm proprios modos eorum, quod manifestum est, non habere subiectum: ergo secundùm modum prædicandi non conuertuntur, licèt quantum ad rem significatam conuertantur.

46 But if you say that, according to the sense of these predications, being is not predicated of the individual categories as superior, but as equal, indeed by an identical predication, contrary to what was said, that it is superior at least in a certain respect: both points are proved. The first, indeed, because the predicate of this proposition, Substance is a being, is nothing other than Substance is the first entity, to which accidents are proportioned; and this is plainly convertible with the subject, indeed altogether the same as it; and therefore the proposition is not only one of equality, but identical. I reply that it is predicated by a predication of equality simply, of a superior in a certain respect, but identical in no way. The first will be manifest if we consider the concept of being according to the different modes in which it is predicated of all: for of substance, as of the first, to which the others are attributed; but of the individual accidents [p. 224] according to the particular modes by which they are attributed to substance. The concept of being, therefore, considered with all these modes that belong to it as to the analogous term taken adequately, since they belong to it by reason of the analogy of attribution, will be formally superior with respect to the individual analogates, although only in a certain respect, while it is equal simply if this consideration is set aside. And that it is formally superior in a certain respect I prove: because while it is predicated of one according to the mode of application to it, it can be predicated of the others according to their proper modes, which the subject manifestly does not have: therefore according to the mode of predicating they are not convertible, although they are convertible as regards the thing signified.

> 47 Et ex hoc sequitur, easdem propositiones non esse identicas, sed formales analogi, quia licèt eadem res sit prędicatum, & subiectum, diuersum habet modum in prædicato, quàm in subiecto in duobus consistentem. In primo quidem: nam in prædicato maiorem habet extensionem, cùm sic prædicetur de vno secundùm proprium modum illius, vt possit etiam prædicari de cæteris, secundùm proprios modos eorum: In secundo verò quia licèt tam prædicatum, quàm subiectum huius prædicationis, *Substantia est ens*, significet eandem rem, expressiùs tamen atque distinctiùs significatur per subiectum, tanquàm per proprium nomen, quàm per prædicatum, tanquam per nomen commune. Et modus iste significandi diuersus efficit, vt propositio sit formalis, & ideò non identica, sicut non est identica prædicatio, in qua definitio prædicatur de definito, licèt eadem res sint, ex eo solùm, quòd expressius significatur per prædicatum, quàm per subiectum.

47 And from this it follows that the same propositions are not identical, but formal propositions of the analogous term: because, although the same thing is predicate and subject, it has a different mode in the predicate than in the subject, consisting in two things. In the first, indeed: for in the predicate it has greater extension, since it is so predicated of one according to the proper mode of that one that it can also be predicated of the others according to their proper modes. In the second, however: because, although both the predicate and the subject of this predication, Substance is a being, signify the same thing, yet it is signified more expressly and distinctly through the subject, as through a proper name, than through the predicate, as through a common name. And this different mode of signifying makes the proposition formal, and therefore not identical; just as the predication in which a definition is predicated of the defined is not identical, although they are the same thing, from this alone, that it is signified more expressly through the predicate than through the subject.

> 48 Et ex his non erit difficile arg. contrariæ opinionis soluere: Nam testimonium Arist. verum continet, quòd *Metaphysica considerat ens, in quantum eius*, hoc est nõ secundùm aliquam rationem particularem alicuius prædicamenti, nec secundùm rationes omnium expressas, atque distinctas: sed secundùm rationem attributionis ad vnum, nempe ad substantiam: hanc enim non habent sub propriis nominibus significata, sed sub nomine entis omnibus communi, sub quo similitudinem quandam in entitate habent, & vnitatem secundùm quid, sub qua abstrahi possunt, etiam secundùm quid à propriis rationibus expressè significatis. Et sic abstractum ens consideratur in quantum ens, & potest esse obiectum Metaphysicæ, quia licèt sit analogum, consideratum tamen sub tali modo abstrahendi à materia vt consideratur in metaphysica, vnam rationem, sub qua, obiectiuã habet, à qua scientia ipsa sumit vnitatẽ specificã.

48 And from these things it will not be difficult to solve the arguments of the contrary opinion. For the testimony of Aristotle contains the truth, that Metaphysics considers being inasmuch as it is being: that is, not according to some particular ratio of some category, nor according to the express and distinct rationes of all, but according to the ratio of attribution to one, namely to substance. For they do not have this as signified under their proper names, but under the name of being, common to all, under which they have a certain similarity in entity, and unity in a certain respect, under which they can be abstracted, again in a certain respect, from the proper rationes expressly signified. And thus being, abstracted, is considered inasmuch as it is being, and can be the object of Metaphysics: because, although it is analogous, yet, considered under such a mode of abstracting from matter as it is considered in metaphysics, it has one objective ratio, under which and from which the science itself takes its specific unity. The

[p. 225]

> 49 Testimonium verò D. Th. petit modum, quo ens contrahatur per modos particulares substantiæ, & accidentis. Et difficultas consistit in hoc: Quia si non datur communis conceptus eius ab iisdem modis abstractus, sed includens, eos, non videtur posse contrahi per illos, quia contrahens debet esse extra rationem contrahibilis: nam si in eo includatur, iam erit contractum per illud. Respondeo, Eodem modo contrahi ens per modos per se, & in alio, quo ab eisdem abstractum est, sed abstrahitur ab eis solùm secundùm quid, hoc est, sicut idem à seipso diuersó modo significato, ideo solùm potest contrahi per seipsum, vt diuerso modo significatum. Gratia exempli, ens in suo conceptu includit modos intrinsecos per se, & in alio, actu quidem, non tamen sub expresso conceptu, sed sub implicito, & confuso, hoc est, non vt propriis nominibus significantur, sed nomine communi entis, & diuersus iste modus includendi eos sufficit, vt dicatur abstractus ab eis secundùm quid, conceptus verò non contrahitur, nisi vt abstractus est: nam contractio, & abstractio, mutuò sibi correspondent: ergo eodem modo contrahitur conceptus entis per modos intrinsecos sub expresso conceptu significatos, quos tamen hoc modo non includit, sed sub confusa ratione, vt semper sit verum (adhuc in contractione analogi, quæ solùm est secũdùm quid, sicut abstractio) quòd contrahens sit extra rationem contrahibilis. Hunc sensum explicuit D. Th. in alio loco, & ita vnum testimonium explicamus per alterum. Locus autem est: quæst. 1. de veritate, art. 1. vbi sic ait: *Quod primò intellectu concipit quasi notissimum, & in quo omnes conceptiones resoluit, ens: vnde oportet, quòd omnes aliæ conceptiones intellectus, accipiantur ex additione ad ens, sed enti nihil potest addi, quasi extranea natura per modum, quo differentia additur generi, quia qualibet natura essentialiter est ens, sed secundùm hoc aliqua dicuntur addere supra ens, in quantum exprimunt ipsius modum, qui nomine ipsius entis non exprimitur*. Et infrà: *Substantia non addit supra ens aliquam differentiam, sed nomine substantiæ exprimitur specialis modus essendi.*

49 The testimony of St. Thomas, however, asks for the mode by which being is contracted through the particular modes of substance and accident. And the difficulty consists in this: because, if there is not given a common concept of it abstracted from those modes, but one including them, it does not seem that it can be contracted through them, because the contracting must be outside the ratio of the contractible; for if it is included in it, it will already be contracted by it. I reply that being is contracted through the modes per se and in another in the same way in which it is abstracted from them; but it is abstracted from them only in a certain respect, that is, as the same thing from itself signified in a different mode; therefore it can be contracted only through itself, as signified in a different mode. For example, being in its concept includes the intrinsic modes per se and in another, in act indeed, yet not under an express concept but under an implicit and confused one, that is, not as they are signified by their proper names, but by the common name of being; and this different mode of including them suffices for it to be said to be abstracted from them in a certain respect. But a concept is not contracted except as it is abstracted: for contraction and abstraction correspond mutually to each other; therefore the concept of being is contracted in the same way through the intrinsic modes signified under an express concept, which, however, it does not include in this mode, but under a confused ratio; so that it is always true (even in the contraction of the analogous term, which is only in a certain respect, like the abstraction) that the contracting is outside the ratio of the contractible. St. Thomas explained this sense in another place, and so we explain one testimony by the other. The place is On Truth, q. 1, a. 1, where he speaks thus: That which the intellect first conceives as most known, and into which it resolves all conceptions, is being: whence all the other conceptions of the intellect must be taken by addition to being. But nothing can be added to being as a nature extraneous to it, in the way in which a difference is added to a genus, because every nature is essentially being; but according to this some things are said to add above being, inasmuch as they express a mode of it which is not expressed by the name of being itself. And below: Substance does not add above being some difference, but by the name of substance a special mode of being is expressed.

> 50 Ad primum arg. Concesso primo enthymemate, distinguenda est minor syllogismi, quia qualis fuerit conuenientia multorum, talis erit abstrahibilis conceptus ab eis. Si conueniant simpliciter abstrahibilis erit conceptus simpliciter communis, & vnus, vt in vniuocis: si verò solùm conueniant secundùm quid, solùm erit abstrahibilis conceptus communis, & vnus secundùm quid. Et ita est in analogis, atque etiam in ente, tùm sit analogum. Quid autem sit abstrahi secundùm [p. 226] quid, iam explicatum est.

50 To the first argument: granting the first enthymeme, the minor of the syllogism is to be distinguished: because such as the agreement of many things is, such will be the concept abstractable from them. If they agree simply, the abstractable concept will be simply common and one, as in univocals; but if they agree only in a certain respect, the abstractable concept will be common and one only in a certain respect. And so it is in analogous terms, and also in being, since it is analogous. But what it is to be abstracted in a certain respect P [p. 226] has already been explained.

> Ad secundum: Concesso antecedenti, distinguendum est consequens: Nam actualis inclusio duplex est, confusa seu implicita, & distincta, vel expressa, & de hac concedendum est, negandum verò de illa, dicendumque, ex eo posse dubitationem procedere, An substantia sit, vel accidens illud, de quo certò scimus esse ens, quia conceptus entis confusè tantùm includit rationes particulares substantiæ, & accidentis, non distinctè, ratione verò confusionis occurrit dubitatio, in eo consistens, quòd intellectus non cognoscit distinctè, ad quod significatum determinetur ens.

To the second: granting the antecedent, the consequent is to be distinguished.
