But it is not so taken by Aristotle, but in the second acceptation, and insofar as the property of standing under belongs to it; and in this way it is true that the first substance is more perfect than the second, because it stands under by its own power, but the second only by the power of the first.

> 43 Tertium argumentũ, alia distinctione soluendũ est: nam substare, duobus modis sumitur, Intensiuè, & Extensiuè: Intensiuè, accipitur in ordine ad virtutem substandi, & hoc modo, illud dicitur magis substare, quod propria virtute substat, & illud minus, quod virtute alterius: Extensiuè autem, in ordine ad plura, vel pauciora, quibus aliquid substat. Et ex hoc respondetur ad argumentum, quòd dum Aristoteles ait, *Primam substantiam esse magis substantiam quàm secundam*, vtroque modo [p. 302] intelligit hanc comparationem: tam intensiuè, quàm extensiuè. Et vtroque modo verum est: quia prima substantia pluribus substat, quàm secunda: & etiam propria virtute substat, secunda verò non nisi virtute primæ: aliæ verò comparationes intensiuè intelliguntur, non extensiuè: & ideo verum est inter species, nullam esse, quæ substet virtute alterius. Argumentum verò solùm probat, magis substare extensiuè, quod est, pluribus substare: & eodem modo, verum est, inter primas substantias, vnam, non magis substare, quàm alteram intensiuè: quia vna non substat virtute alterius, sed quælibet virtute propria. Species verò magis substantia dicitur, quàm genus, vtroque modo: extensiuè quidem: nam & pluribus substat, cùm substet ipsi generi, & cæteris. Et etiam intensiuè, quia licèt non substet propria virtute, sicut nec genus, tamen propinquiùs accedit ad id, quod substat propria virtute, nempe ad primam substantiam: & hoc sufficit, vt dicatur, magis substare intensiuè.

43 The third argument is to be solved by another distinction: for to stand under is taken in two ways, Intensively and Extensively. Intensively it is taken in order to the power of standing under, and in this way that is said to stand under more which stands under by its own power, and that less which does so by the power of another. But Extensively, in order to the more or fewer things under which something stands. And from this it is replied to the argument that when Aristotle says that the first substance is more a substance than the second, in both [p. 302] he understands this comparison both intensively and extensively. And in both ways it is true: because the first substance stands under more things than the second, and also stands under by its own power, while the second does so only by the power of the first. But the other comparisons are understood intensively, not extensively: and therefore it is true that among species there is none that stands under by the power of another. The argument, however, proves only that one stands under more extensively, that is, that it stands under more things. And in the same way it is true that among first substances one does not stand under more than another intensively: because one does not stand under by the power of another, but each by its own power. But the species is said to be more a substance than the genus in both ways: extensively indeed, for it stands under more things, since it stands under the genus itself and the rest. And also intensively, because, although it does not stand under by its own power, any more than the genus does, yet it comes nearer to that which stands under by its own power, namely to the first substance; and this suffices for it to be said to stand under more intensively.

## SECOND DOUBT CONCERNING THE THIRD

> DVBIVM SECVNDVM CIRCA tertiam proprietatem substantiæ.

P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

> *An verum sit, & in quo sensu, Secundas substantias significare Quale quid.*

Whether it is true, and in what sense, that Second substances signify Quale quid.

> QVòd secundæ substantiæ, non significent Quale quid, vt Aristoteles docet, duobus argumentis probo. Primo, quia duo tantùm possunt considerari in nomine aliquo, ex quibus intelligatur significare, Quid, vel Quale quid: nempe, res significata, an sit Substantia, vel qualitas, & modus eam significandi. Nomina secundarum substantiarum ex parte vtriusque significant Quid, hoc est, Substantiam, & non Quale quid: ergo falsum est, Quale quid significare. Probatur minor: quia ex parte rei significatæ, substantiam, significant, & etiam ex parte modi, cùm sint nomina substantiua, significantia rem per modum subsistentis.

That second substances do not signify Quale quid, as Aristotle teaches, I prove by two arguments. First, because only two things can be considered in any name from which it may be understood to signify Quid or Quale quid: namely, the thing signified, whether it is Substance or quality; and the mode of signifying it. The names of second substances, on the part of both, signify Quid, that is, Substance, and not Quale quid; therefore it is false that they signify Quale quid. The minor is proved: because on the part of the thing signified they signify substance, and also on the part of the mode, since they are substantive names, signifying the thing by way of something subsisting.

> Secundò: Ex modo significandi, sumitur modus prædicandi, ergo si secundæ substantiæ, quæ sunt genera, & species, significant Quale quid, sequitur, quòd prędicẽtur de primis in Quale quid. Consequens est falsum, ergo & antecedens, probo minorem auctoritate, & ratione: nam Porphyrius cap. de genere, & specie docuit expressè, *Genus & speciem prædicari in Quid*. Et ratio ipsa coniunxit: quia ad interrogationem factam de specie, per Quid, respondemus, per genus: & ad interrogationem factam de indiuiduo, per speciem, vt si inquiras, quid est [p. 303] homo? respondemus esse animal: & si inquiras, quid sit Petrus? Esse hominem: ergo vtraque secunda substantia prædicatur in Quid, & non in Quale quid.

Second: the mode of predicating is taken from the mode of signifying; therefore if second substances, which are genera and species, signify Quale quid, it follows that they are predicated of the first in Quale quid. The consequent is false; therefore so is the antecedent. I prove the minor by authority and by reason: for Porphyry, in the chapter on genus and species, expressly taught that Genus and species are predicated in Quid. And reason itself joins with this: because to a question asked about the species by Quid, we reply by the genus; and to a question asked about the individual, by the species: as if you ask what is Peter [p. 303] man, we reply that it is an animal; and if you ask what Peter is, that he is a man: therefore each second substance is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid.

> Circa sensum huius proprietatis, diuerso modo loquuntur auctores: & primus modus dicendi, est Alberti Magni, tract. 7. prædicamentorum, cap. 8. vbi inquit: *Genera, & species, quę sunt secundę substantię, ratione naturę genericę, significare Quid: sed propter differentiam, quam species continet actu, & genus potentia: significant Quale, & ideo ratione vtriusque, Quale quid: & hunc fuisse sensum Arist.*

Concerning the sense of this property, authors speak in different ways. And the first way of speaking is that of Albert the Great, Categories, tract. 7, ch. 8, where he says: Genera and species, which are second substances, by reason of the generic nature signify Quid; but on account of the difference, which the species contains in act and the genus in potency, they signify Quale, and therefore by reason of both, Quale quid; and that this was the sense of Aristotle.

> Hic tamen modus dicendi, hoc arg. probatur falsus: Si genus, & Species, ratione vtriusque partis essentialis, significant Quale quid, ergo prędicantur in Quale quid, contra sententiã Porph. qui sciens speciem continere genus & differentiam, & genus differentiã, docuit expressè, *vtrumque prædicari in Quid*, & non in Quale quid, & est contra rationem: quia si prędicarẽtur in Quale quid, non distinguerentur à prędicabili differentiæ. Ideo hanc sententiã meritò refutauit Caiet. cap. præsenti.

This way of speaking, however, is proved false by this argument: If genus and Species, by reason of each essential part, signify Quale quid, then they are predicated in Quale quid, against the opinion of Porphyry, who, knowing that the species contains genus and difference, and the genus difference, expressly taught that each is predicated in Quid, and not in Quale quid; and it is against reason: because if they were predicated in Quale quid, they would not be distinguished from the predicable difference. Therefore Cajetan rightly refuted this opinion, in the present chapter.

> Ipse verò Caiet. secundum modum dicendi proponit, duo distinguens in genere, & specie nempe naturam genericam, aut specificam, quæ denominatur genus: & secundam intentionem, à qua denominantur: & propter naturam genericam, atque specificam, quę sunt substantiæ, significant aliquid: sed propter secundam intentionem: quæ est accidens, & modum habet qualitatis, sicut albedo, & color, significant Quale, & ideo propter vtramque significant Quale quid.

Cajetan himself proposes a second way of speaking, distinguishing two things in genus and species: namely, the generic or specific nature, which is denominated genus; and the second intention, by which they are denominated. And on account of the generic and specific nature, which are substance, they signify something; but on account of the second intention, which is an accident and has the mode of a quality, as whiteness and color, they signify Quale; and therefore on account of both they signify Quale quid.

> Sed hic modus dicendi, non est minùs falsus, quàm primus: quod sic probo: Secundæ substantiæ significant Quale, ratione secundæ intentionis, quæ est accidens: ergo significant Quale accidentale: sicut album, significat Quale, ratione albedinis: & ideo Quale accidentale. Ex quo sequitur: quòd prędicentur de primis substantiis, in Quale accidentale, & ideo prædicatione quinti prędicabilis, quod est absurdum. Et si aliquis pro Caiet. respondeat, significare Quale accidentale, sed circa substantiam quæ naturæ generis, & speciei denominatæ, substantiales sunt. Non satis facit solutio: quia etiam album, significat qualitatem circa substantiam: cùm subiectum, cui inhæret albedo substantia sit: ergo eodem modo significant Quale, ac album, aut coloratum: sed hæc prædicantur in Quale accidentale: ergo etiam secundæ substantiæ de primis.

But this way of speaking is no less false than the first, which I prove thus: Second substances signify Quale by reason of the second intention, which is an accident; therefore they signify an accidental Quale, just as white signifies Quale by reason of whiteness, and therefore an accidental Quale. From which it follows that they are predicated of first substances in an accidental Quale, and therefore by the predication of the fifth predicable, which is absurd. And if someone should reply for Cajetan that they signify an accidental Quale, but concerning substance, since the natures of genus and species which are denominated are substantial: the solution does not satisfy, because white also signifies a quality concerning substance, since the subject in which whiteness inheres is a substance; therefore they signify Quale in the same way as white or colored; but these are predicated in an accidental Quale; therefore so too are second substances predicated of the first.

> Pro solutione igitur huius dubij, & argumentorum, notandum est, Quale quid, duobus modis accipi posse, Proprio, & Communi. Et cùm vtroque modo sumatur: per similitudinem [p. 304] ad veram qualitatem, quæ est forma accidentalis, quarti prædicamenti: ex propria, & communi similitudine ad illam, accipiendus est vterque modus: nam Qualitas duo habet. Primum habet inhærere subiecto, à quo abesse potest, ipsumq; circumstare, ac tali modo determinare, vt ad interrogationem de ipso factam, per Quale, propriè respondeamus per illam. Et hæc est ratio propria eius: cui assimilatur differentia quæ ad genus comparatur tanquam ad potentiam, extra cuius rationem est: & cui adesse, & abesse potest: & ideo tanquam determinans genus, ad constitutionem speciei, per modum adiacentis, adiectiuo nomine significata, prædicatur de specie: & hoc est assimilari qualitati, secundùm propriam rationem eius. Aliud habet Qualitas, commune cum cæteris accidentibus, quòd à subiecto determinetur, quantum ad actualem eius inhærentiam, & aliquo saltem modo, quantum ad indiuiduationem: & secundæ substantiæ assimilantur qualitati: secundùm hanc rationem communem, & impropriam consideratæ: quia sunt quasi communes conceptus, & communes formæ: quæ determinantur, quantum ad subsistentiam, & indiuiduationem, à primis substantiis, in quibus subsistunt: & propter hanc similitudinem docuit Aristoteles non significare Hoc aliquid: hoc est, substantiam singularem, & subsistentem, aduersus Platonem, qui *substantias ponebat separatas à singularibus, & extra illa subsistentes*: sed significare Quale, ita sint quasi formæ abstractæ à singularibus, solùm per intellectum: & ab eisdem determinabiles: quantum ad subsistentiam, & indiuiduationem, ad modum accidentalium: & quia verè sunt substantiæ, significare Quale quid. Deinde, cùm ratio substantialis conueniat eis propriè, ratio verò qualitatis: solùm per similitudinem, in ratione communi, & impropria, qualitatis nominibus substantiuis significantur: prædicata quidditatiua appellantur: & in Quid, non in Quale quid, sicut differentia, dicuntur prædicari: quia differentia, similitudinem propriam habet cum qualitate: secundæ verò substantiæ, eidem secundùm communem, & impropriam rationem assimilantur: & ideo non prædicantur in Quale quid: quia modus specialis prædicandi, ex propria ratione, non ex communi sumi debet. Et hæc est ratio propter quam Arist. docuit, *Secundas substantias significare Quale quid: & non prædicari, in Quale quid*.

For the solution, then, of this doubt and of the arguments, it should be noted that Quale quid can be taken in two ways, in a Proper and in a Common sense. And since in both ways it is taken by similitude [p. 304] to true quality, which is an accidental form of the fourth category, each mode is to be understood from a proper and a common similitude to it. For Quality has two things. The first is to inhere in a subject, from which it can be absent, and to surround it, and to determine it in such a way that to a question asked about it by Quale we properly reply by means of the quality. And this is its proper ratio, to which the difference is likened, which is compared to the genus as to a potency, outside whose ratio it is, and to which it can be present and from which it can be absent; and therefore, as determining the genus for the constitution of the species, by way of something adjacent, signified by an adjectival name, it is predicated of the species: and this is to be likened to quality according to its proper ratio. Quality has another thing, common with the other accidents: that it is determined by the subject as to its actual inherence, and in some way at least as to individuation. And second substances are likened to quality, considered according to this common and improper ratio: because they are as it were common concepts and common forms, which are determined, as to subsistence and individuation, by the first substances in which they subsist. And on account of this similitude Aristotle taught that they do not signify This something, that is, singular and subsisting substance, against Plato, who posited substances separated from singulars and subsisting outside them; but that they signify Quale, since they are as it were forms abstracted from singulars by the intellect alone, and determinable by those same singulars as to subsistence and individuation, after the manner of accidental forms; and, because they are truly substances, that they signify Quale quid. Next, since the substantial ratio belongs to them properly, but the ratio of quality only by similitude, in the common and improper ratio of quality, they are signified by substantive names, they are called quidditative predicates, and they are said to be predicated in Quid, not in Quale quid, as difference is: because difference has a proper similitude with quality, whereas second substances are likened to it according to the common and improper ratio; and therefore they are not predicated in Quale quid, because the special mode of predicating must be taken from the proper ratio, not from the common. And this is the reason for which Aristotle taught that Second substances signify Quale quid, and are not predicated in Quale quid.

> 51 Ad primum arg. in principio positum: Concedendum est totum, quod assumit: sed distinguendum consequens, dum infertur, non significare Quale quid: nam si de proprio Quale quid intelligatur, verum est: si de improprio falsum. Itaque [p. 305] bene stat simul, significare Quid simpliciter, propter rem significatam, quæ est substantia, & propter modum significandi nominum substantiuorum, & significare etiam Quale improprium, propter quandam similitudinem cum qualitate: & ideo quodam modo Quale quid.

51 To the first argument posited at the beginning: all that it assumes is to be granted; but the consequent is to be distinguished, when it is inferred that they do not signify Quale quid: for if the proper Quale quid is understood, it is true; if the improper, false. Therefore rightly [p. 305] it is rightly consistent that they signify Quid simply, on account of the thing signified, which is substance, and on account of the mode of signifying of substantive names, and that they also signify an improper Quale, on account of a certain similitude with quality; and therefore in a certain way Quale quid.

> Ad secundum, distinguenda est maior: nam ex modo significandi proprio, sumitur modus prędicandi, non ex improprio: & quia secundæ substantiæ, propriè significant Quid, & quadam ratione communi, & impropria Quale quid, potiùs prædicantur in Quid, quàm in Quale quid.

To the second, the major is to be distinguished: for the mode of predicating is taken from the proper mode of signifying, not from the improper; and because second substances properly signify Quid, and by a certain common and improper ratio Quale quid, they are predicated rather in Quid than in Quale quid.

## THIRD DOUBT CONCERNING THE

> DVBIVM TERTIVM CIRCA quartam proprietatem substantiæ.

F O U RT H P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

> *An verum sit, substantiam non habere contrarium.*

Whether it is true that substance has no contrary.

> 52 IN hac proprietate substantię, videtur Arist. sibi cõtrarius: quod ita probo: Nam 1. Physicorum tex. 50. asserit, *Principia, ex quibus substantia generatur, & componitur, esse contraria: imò esse prima contraria: & in vno quoque genere, seu prædicamento, esse vnam contrarietatem: & ideo in substantia, quę vnum genus est, vnam contrarietatem reperiri*: falsum est ergo, quod capite præsenti docet, *Proprium esse substantiæ, non habere contrarium*.

52 In this property of substance Aristotle seems to contradict himself, which I prove thus: for in Phys. 1, text 50, he asserts that the principles from which substance is generated and composed are contraries; indeed, that they are the first contraries; and that in each genus or category there is one contrariety; and therefore that in substance, which is one genus, one contrariety is found. It is false, then, what he teaches in the present chapter, that it is proper to substance to have no contrary.

> Et ratione probatur, quòd substantia habeat contrarium: nam elementa contraria sunt, vt ignis, & aqua, aer, & terra, & tamen sunt substantię quędam. Et si respondeas: Elementa esse contraria, non vt sunt substantiæ: sed ratione primarum qualitatum, quæ sunt accidentia eorum: vt ratione caloris, & frigoris, humiditatis, & siccitatis: Contra hoc est, quòd qualitates istæ, procedunt ab ipsa substantia elementorum, ergo ab ea accipiunt contrarietatem: quare primò erit in substantia, & per participationem ab ea, in accidentibus.

And it is proved by argument that substance has a contrary: for the elements are contraries, as fire and water, air and earth, and yet they are certain substances. And if you reply that the elements are contraries not as they are substances, but by reason of the first qualities, which are their accidents, as by reason of heat and cold, moistness and dryness: against this is the fact that these qualities proceed from the very substance of the elements; therefore they receive their contrariety from it. Wherefore it will be first in substance, and by participation from it in the accidents.

> Pro huius dubij solutione, notandum est: *Quatuor esse genera oppositionis*, vt docet Aristoteles in hoc libro, capite de oppositis, & 5. Metaphysicæ, cap. Vna est oppositio priuatiua, inter formam, & priuationem, vt inter lucem, & tenebras: Alia contradictoria, inter affirmationem, & negationem: vt inter hominem, & non hominem, seu inter propositionem affirmatiuam, & negatiuam: Tertia, relatiua, vt inter patrem, & filium: Quarta denique contraria, vt inter calidum, & frigidum: quæ explicanda est, cùm de ea sit dubium, an reperiatur in substantia.

For the solution of this doubt it should be noted that there are four genera of opposition, as Aristotle teaches in this book, in the chapter on opposites, and in Metaph. 5, ch. One is privative opposition, between form and privation, as between light and darkness. Another is contradictory, between affirmation and negation, as between man and not-man, or between an affirmative and a negative proposition. The third is relative, as between father and son. The fourth, finally, is contrary, as between hot and cold; and this is to be explained, since the doubt concerns it, whether it is found in substance.

> Contrarietas duobus modis accipitur. Primò, sub ratione Communi, & impropria, pro quacunque oppositione. In qua [p. 306] acceptione, contraria appellamus, quocunque modo opposita. Secundò, Propriè, pro vltimo tantùm genere oppositionis, ex quatuor enumeratis. Cuius talis definitio colligitur ex Arist. locis citatis: *Contraria sunt, quæ sub eodem genere, maximè distant, & ab eodem subiecto, mutuò se expellunt*. Vt calidum & frigidum, sub genere qualitatis, maximè distant: hoc est, quasi extrema sunt, & à corpore, in vnum inhæret, expellitur aliud: vt ab aqua, in qua est frigiditas, expellitur calor. Duas igitur conditiones, ad propositum necessarias, debent habere contraria. Primam, quòd sint formæ positiuæ: quia sunt species eiusdem generis. Secundam, quòd respiciant idem subiectum, in quo vtraque inhærere potest, & aliam ab eo expellere.

Contrariety is taken in two ways. First, under a Common and improper ratio, for any opposition whatever. In which V [p. 306] acceptation we call contraries things opposed in any way whatever. Second, Properly, for the last genus of opposition only, of the four enumerated, whose definition is gathered from Aristotle in the places cited: Contraries are those which under the same genus are most distant, and mutually expel each other from the same subject. As hot and cold under the genus of quality are most distant, that is, they are as it were extremes; and when one inheres in a body, the other is expelled, as heat is expelled from water, in which there is coldness. Contraries, then, must have two conditions necessary to the purpose. The first, that they be positive forms, because they are species of the same genus. The second, that they regard the same subject, in which each can inhere and expel the other from it.

> 53 Ex quibus intelligitur. Primò, quòd ex quatuor generibus oppositionis, tria reperiuntur in substantia: nempe, Priuatiua, quia substantia, dum generatur, fit ex priuatione sui: vt homo, ex nõ homine: id est, ex materia, in qua est priuatio animæ rationalis. Contradictoria, vt inter hominem, & non hominem: Relatiua, vt inter Petrum & Ioannem, quatenus sunt eiusdem speciei. Sola oppositio contraria, ei repugnat, propter perfectionem suæ naturæ: quia cùm substantia tam perfectæ naturæ sit, vt ei debeatur subsistentia per se, repugnat ei, quòd sit forma inhærens subiecto: & ideo, quòd cùm alia forma se expellat ab illo, vt in definitione contrariorum dicitur: nec in tota latitudine sui prædicamenti, potest talis imperfectio reperiri. Et hoc est potissimum fundamentum huius proprietatis, quam ei tribuit Aristoteles.

53 From which it is understood, First, that of the four genera of opposition three are found in substance: namely, Privative, because substance, when it is generated, comes to be from its own privation, as man from not-man, that is, from matter, in which there is the privation of the rational soul; Contradictory, as between man and not-man; Relative, as between Peter and John, insofar as they are of the same species. Contrary opposition alone is repugnant to it, on account of the perfection of its nature: because, since substance is of so perfect a nature that subsistence per se is owed to it, it is repugnant to it to be a form inhering in a subject; and therefore that it should expel another form from it, as is said in the definition of contraries. Nor can such an imperfection be found in the whole latitude of its category. And this is the chief foundation of this property which Aristotle attributes to it.

> 54 Secundò intelligitur, quonam modo concedendum sit, substantiam habere contrarium, & quo etiam modo negandum: nam de impropria contrarietate, pro quacunque oppositione, concedendum est: de propria verò, pro vltimo tantùm genere oppositionis suprà posito, negandum. Et quia quarta proprietas, intelligitur ab Arist. solùm de propria, verissima est eius sententia. *Quòd substantiæ nihil sit contrarium*.

54 Second, it is understood in what way it is to be granted that substance has a contrary, and also in what way it is to be denied: for of improper contrariety, taken for any opposition whatever, it is to be granted; but of proper contrariety, taken for the last genus of opposition only, posited above, it is to be denied. And because the fourth property is understood by Aristotle only of proper contrariety, his opinion is most true: That nothing is contrary to substance.

> 55 Pro solutione argumentorum notandum est, quòd inter oppositiones, prima, & quasi fundamentum cæterarum, est priuatiua, quæ in quocunque genere, & prædicamento reperitur: nam ex duabus differentiis oppositis, per quas diuiditur genus, vna se habet respectu alterius, tanquam priuatio: quia imperfectior est illa: & ideo quasi priuatur perfectione alterius, vt in differentiis, per quas diuiditur viuens, in sensibile, & in insensibile: & animal in rationale, & irrationale, patet: nam insensibile, quasi priuatio sensus intelligitur: & irrationale, quasi rationale carens. Quòd verò sit fundamentum aliarum, [p. 307] probatur: quia substantia est fundamentum aliarum rerum, inter quas reperiuntur aliæ oppositiones: sed priuatiua oppositio, reperitur in prima generatione eiusdem substantiæ: quia quælibet substantia generatur, ex priuatione sui in materia: vt homo ex non homine, & ex consequenti, quæcunque alia generantur, vel fiunt, ex sui priuatione fieri intelliguntur: vt calidum ex non calido, hoc est, ex priuatione caloris in subiecto, in quo, & ex quo fit. Vnde sequitur, quòd sicut priuatiua oppositio est prima, fundamentum aliarum, ita substantia, in qua primò reperitur, est quasi radix, à qua procedunt omnes oppositiones: quæ ideo primò reperiuntur in ea formaliter quidem priuatiua, contradictoria, & relatiua: contraria verò non formaliter, sed solùm virtualiter: quia formalis repugnat perfectioni eius.

55 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that among the oppositions the first, and as it were the foundation of the rest, is the privative, which is found in any genus and category whatever: for of the two opposed differences by which a genus is divided, one is related to the other as a privation, because it is more imperfect than the other, and therefore is as it were deprived of the perfection of the other; as is plain in the differences by which living is divided into sensible and insensible, and animal into rational and irrational: for insensible is understood as it were as a privation of sense, and irrational as lacking rationality. But that it is the foundation of the others [p. 307] is proved: because substance is the foundation of the other things among which the other oppositions are found; but privative opposition is found in the first generation of substance itself, because every substance is generated from its own privation in matter, as man from not-man; and consequently whatever other things are generated or come to be are understood to come to be from their own privation, as hot from not-hot, that is, from the privation of heat in the subject in which and from which it comes to be. From which it follows that, just as privative opposition is the first, the foundation of the others, so substance, in which it is first found, is as it were the root from which all oppositions proceed; which are therefore first found in it: privative, contradictory and relative formally; but contrary not formally, but only virtually, because formal contrariety is repugnant to its perfection.

> Ex hac doctrina, facilè soluuntur argumenta: nam testimonia Aristot. loquuntur de contrarietate, sub ratione communi, & impropria, pro quocunque genere oppositionis, sed præcipuè pro oppositione priuatiua: de qua intelligitur: quòd principia generationis substantiæ, sint contraria: & quòd prima contrarietas, reperiatur in substantia: hoc est, prima oppositio quæ est priuatiua. Dum verò substantiam asserit, in hoc prædicamento, non habere contrarium: loquitur de contrarietate propria, vt expositum est.

From this doctrine the arguments are easily solved: for the testimonies of Aristotle speak of contrariety under its common and improper ratio, taken for any genus of opposition whatever, but chiefly for privative opposition; of which it is understood that the principles of the generation of substance are contraries, and that the first contrariety is found in substance, that is, the first opposition, which is the privative. But when he asserts that substance in this category has no contrary, he speaks of proper contrariety, as has been explained.

> 56 Ad arg. Respondetur, distinguendo antecedens: nam elementa ratione substantiæ, non sunt formaliter, nec propriè contraria, sed ratione qualitatum. Et dum dicitur, Qualitates procedere à substantia: concedendum est, sed distinguendum consequens: quòd in substantia, primò reperiatur vera contrarietas: nam virtualiter reperitur, tanquam in prima radice, à qua procedit, non formaliter. Aristoteles verò dum negat in hac proprietate quarta, *substantiam habere contrarium*, de formali intelligit, non de virtuali: quia hæc non dicit imperfectionem, repugnantem naturæ substantiali, illa verò cum eius perfectione pugnat.

56 To the argument it is replied by distinguishing the antecedent: for the elements, by reason of substance, are not formally nor properly contraries, but by reason of their qualities. And when it is said that the Qualities proceed from substance, it is to be granted; but the consequent is to be distinguished, that true contrariety is first found in substance: for it is found there virtually, as in the first root from which it proceeds, not formally. But when Aristotle denies in this fourth property that substance has a contrary, he understands it of formal contrariety, not of virtual: because the latter does not imply an imperfection repugnant to the substantial nature, whereas the former conflicts with its perfection.

> DVBIVM QVARTVM CIRCA vltimam proprietatem substantiæ.

F O U RT H D O U B T C O N C E R N I N G T H E L A S T P RO P E RT Y O F S U B S TA N C E .

> *An solùm primis substantiis conueniat esse susceptiuas contrariorum: vel etiam secundis, & accidentibus.*

Whether it belongs to first substances alone to be receptive of contraries, or also to second substances and to accidents.

> VLtimam proprietatem substantiæ, dixit Aristoteles esse, *Quòd vna numerò cùm sit, contraria possit in se suscipere*. [p. 308] Et cùm sola prima substantia, sit vna numero, secundæ verò, vnitatẽ tantùm specificam, & genericam habeant, ei soli videtur attributa ab Aristotele, ita vt secundis non conueniat, & multò minùs accidentibus, sed primæ substantiæ, quarto modo: hoc est, omni, soli, & semper.

The last property of substance, Aristotle said, is That, being one in number, it can receive contraries in itself. V ij [p. 308] And since the first substance alone is one in number, while second substances have only specific and generic unity, it seems to be attributed by Aristotle to it alone, so that it does not belong to second substances, and much less to accidents, but to first substance in the fourth mode, that is, to every one, to it alone, and always.

> 57 Sed videtur, nec omnibus primis substantiis conuenire, nec solis, sed etiam accidentibus: nam propositio accidens est, & tamen eadem permanens, nunc est vera, si res ita se habeat, vt per eam enunciatur, postea verò falsa, si res mutetur: ergo suscipit contraria. Probatur consequentia: quia veritas, & falsitas contraria sunt. Nec videtur satisfacere solutio, quam tribuit Aristoteles huic argumento, dicens: *Suscipere contraria, idem esse, ac mutari de vno ad alterum*: quod verò mutatur, mutationem ipsam in se recipit, atque etiam terminum eiusdem mutationis: vt quod mutatur, dum fit calidum ex frigido, vtrumque in se recipit: sed propositio non mutatur, dum fit vera ex falsa, sed solùm mutatur res, & ex eius mutatione, fit propositio vera, aut falsa: & ideo non dicitur suscipere contraria: hęc inquam solutio non satisfacit argumento, quod ita probo: Veritas, & falsitas, aut complexa, non est formaliter in rebus, sed virtualiter tantùm, vt in causa: quia causant in intellectu: in hoc verò, reperitur formaliter, vt enunciante, aut iudicante: nec reperitur, nisi media propositione mẽtali, per quam enunciat, ergo in propositione mentali, aut in intellectu, per eam enunciante, reperitur veritas, & falsitas, tanquam in subiecto, quod formaliter mutatur, dum propositio fit falsa ex vera: quare necesse est concedere, quòd suscipiat contraria, cùm per veram sui mutationem ea suscipiat. Sed intellectus, & propositio mentalis, sunt accidentia: ergo accidentibus conuenit suscipere contraria, & non solis, primis substantiis. Quod etiam de quantitate verum est: nam accidentia corporea, verè conporea verè contraria, priùs in quantitate recipiuntur, quàm in substantia: vt calor, & frigus: ergo quantitas etiam vna numero cùm sit, erit susceptiua contrariorum.

57 But it seems that it belongs neither to all first substances, nor to them alone, but also to accidents: for a proposition is an accident, and yet, remaining the same, it is now true, if the thing is as it is enunciated through it, and afterwards false, if the thing changes: therefore it receives contraries. The consequence is proved: because truth and falsity are contraries. Nor does the solution which Aristotle gives to this argument seem to satisfy, saying: To receive contraries is the same as to be changed from one to the other; but what is changed receives the change itself in itself, and also the term of that change, as what is changed when it becomes hot from cold receives both in itself; but the proposition is not changed when it becomes true from false, but only the thing is changed, and from its change the proposition becomes true or false; and therefore it is not said to receive contraries. This solution, I say, does not satisfy the argument, which I prove thus: Truth and falsity, as complex, are not formally in things, but only virtually, as in a cause, because they cause them in the intellect; but in the intellect they are found formally, as enunciating or judging; nor are they found there except by means of the mental proposition through which it enunciates; therefore in the mental proposition, or in the intellect enunciating through it, truth and falsity are found as in a subject, which is formally changed when the proposition becomes false from true. Wherefore it is necessary to grant that it receives contraries, since it receives them through a true change of itself. But the intellect and the mental proposition are accidents; therefore it belongs to accidents to receive contraries, and not to first substances alone. Which is also true of quantity: for bodily accidents that are truly contraries are received in quantity before they are received in substance, as heat and cold; therefore quantity also, since it is one in number, will be receptive of contraries.

> 58 Iam quòd non conueniat omnibus primis substantiis, probatur: quia substantia spiritualis, vt Angelus, non suscipit in se vlla contraria: imò nec substantia corporea incorruptibilis: qualis est cœlum, ergo non omnis substantia prima est susceptiua contrariorum. Antecedens probatur: quia contraria disponunt subiectum, in quo sunt ad corruptionem, vt calor, & frigus: sed Angeli, & corporea cœlestia, sunt incorruptibiles substantiæ, ergo non sunt capaces contrariorum. Probatur antecedens: quia contrariæ qualitates, disponunt subiectum [p. 309] ad diuersas formas substantiales, vt calor ad formam ignis, & frigus, ad formam aquæ: sed diuersæ formæ substantiales, non possunt simul esse in eadem materia, vel subiecto, nec vna expelli ab eo, nisi per corruptionem compositi: ergo contraria ordinantur ad corruptionem eius, quare non possunt esse in subiecto incorruptibili.

58 Now, that it does not belong to all first substances is proved: because a spiritual substance, as an Angel, does not receive any contraries in itself; indeed, neither does an incorruptible bodily substance, such as the heavens; therefore not every first substance is receptive of contraries. The antecedent is proved: because contraries dispose the subject in which they are toward corruption, as heat and cold; but Angels and celestial bodies are incorruptible substances; therefore they are not capable of contraries. The antecedent is proved: because contrary qualities dispose the subject [p. 309] to different substantial forms, as heat to the form of fire, and cold to the form of water; but different substantial forms cannot be at the same time in the same matter or subject, nor can one be expelled from it except through the corruption of the composite; therefore contraries are ordered to its corruption, wherefore they cannot be in an incorruptible subject.

> 59 Vt hoc dubium plenè soluatur, tria sunt determinanda. Primum: An hæc proprietas conueniat solis substantiis, vel etiam accidentibus. Secundum: An dato, quod conueniat solis substantiis, conueniat, non solùm primis, sed etiam secundis. Tertium: An si solis primis conueniat, quibusdam tantùm conueniat, vel etiam omnibus: & ex determinatione horum trium colligi poterit, An sit proprietas hæc substantiæ, quarto modo ei conueniens.

59 In order that this doubt may be fully resolved, three things are to be determined. First: Whether this property belongs to substances alone, or also to accidents. Second: Whether, granted that it belongs to substances alone, it belongs not only to first substances but also to second. Third: Whether, if it belongs to first substances alone, it belongs only to some, or to all. And from the determination of these three it can be gathered Whether this is a property of substance, belonging to it in the fourth mode.

> Pro solutione primi notandum est, Primam substantiam duo habere, quorum ratione conuenit illi hæc proprietas. Primum est, *quòd sit hoc aliquid* (vt verbis Arist. vtamur) hoc est, substantia singularis, & per se subsistens, & ideo independens ab aliis. Secundum: quòd sit primum subiectum omnium accidentium: & ratione primi, conuenit illi esse vnam numero, manentem sub diuersis accidentibus: ratione secundi, quòd sit contrariorum susceptiua: Nam contrariè opposita, accidentia sunt: & ideo ratione vtriusque conuenit illi integra proprietas, nempe, vt vna numero cùm sit, contraria in se suscipiat: sed cùm neutrum conueniat accidentibus (vt notum est) nec potest eis conuenire eadem proprietas.

For the solution of the first, it should be noted that the First substance has two things by reason of which this property belongs to it. The first is that it is this something (to use Aristotle’s words), that is, a singular substance, subsisting per se, and therefore independent of others. The second, that it is the first subject of all accidents. And by reason of the first it belongs to it to be one in number, remaining under different accidents; by reason of the second, that it is receptive of contraries: for things contrarily opposed are accidents. And therefore by reason of both the entire property belongs to it, namely that, being one in number, it receives contraries in itself. But since neither belongs to accidents (as is known), neither can the same property belong to them.

> 60 Ad arg. verò de propositione, Respondetur hac distinctione: Propositio duplex est: Vna vocalis, aut scripta, & mentalis alia: & de vocali, & scripta, euidens est, non recipere in se veritatem, aut falsitatem formalem: sed solùm est in eis veritas, tanquam in signo: quod est, esse per solam denominationem extrinsecam: vnde licèt transeat de veritate in falsitate, non per sui mutationem id fit, quia non recipiunt hæc accidentia in se formaliter, sed solùm per mutationem rei: vnde nec suscipiunt in se contraria. De mentali verò, negari non potest, quin contineat in se veritatem, aut falsitatem formalem, cùm formaliter repræsentet rem, sicuti est, aut sicut non est; nec etiam negari potest, quin in intellectu iudicante sit veritas formaliter: sed adhuc sic, non dicitur propositio mentalis, aut intellectus iudicans, suscipere contraria: quia non est principale subiectum veritatis, aut falsitatis, sed medium, per quod ista recipiuntur in anima, & adhuc, nec sic sunt tanquam medium contraria suscipiens ratione sui, aut virtute propria: & ex consequenti [p. 310], nec ea habent simpliciter: sed virtute substantiæ, cuius accidentia sunt: & ideo substantia sola est, quæ tanquam præcipuum subiectum, propriaque virtute suscipit contraria, non accidentia.

60 But to the argument about the proposition, it is replied by this distinction: A proposition is twofold: One vocal or written, and the other mental. And of the vocal and written it is evident that they do not receive formal truth or falsity in themselves, but truth is in them only as in a sign, that is, by extrinsic denomination alone. Whence, although it passes from truth to falsity, this does not happen through a change of itself, because they do not receive these accidents in themselves formally, but only through the change of the thing; whence neither do they receive contraries in themselves. But of the mental proposition it cannot be denied that it contains formal truth or falsity in itself, since it formally represents the thing as it is or as it is not; nor can it be denied either that truth is formally in the judging intellect. But even so, the mental proposition, or the judging intellect, is not said to receive contraries, because it is not the principal subject of truth or falsity, but the means through which these are received in the soul; and moreover, not even so are they, as a means, receiving contraries by reason of themselves or by their own power: and from the con V iij [p. 310] sequence, nor do they have them simply, but by the power of the substance whose accidents they are; and therefore it is substance alone that, as the chief subject and by its own power, receives contraries, not accidents.

> 61 Circa secundum, An proprietas hæc conueniat secundis substantiis, Caiet. cap. præsenti, ait, hanc particularem, (vnam numero) distinguẽdam esse: nam vel à parte subiecti ponitur, vel à parte prędicati: & à parte subiecti positam, hunc sensum efficere. Proprium est substantiæ, quæ est vna numero, esse contrariorum susceptiuam, in qua euidens est, soli primæ substantiæ conuenire: quia sola est vna numero. Si verò ponatur à parte prædicati, talis erit sensus: Proprium est substantiæ, vt seruata vnitate numerica, possit contraria suscipere: & sic intellectam proprietatem, etiam est euidens, conuenire secundis substantijs: quia seruata vnitate numerica, quam habent in primis, contraria suscipere possunt: vt homo seruata vnitate numerica, quam habet in Petro, potest suscipere colorem & frigus. Hoc etiam modo, intelligitur proprietas hæc ab aliis expositoribus, vt Alberto Magno, Simplicio, & Villalpando: dicuntque sic esse locutum Aristotelem: vt hanc proprietatem communem esse omnibus substantiis efficeret.

61 Concerning the second, Whether this property belongs to second substances, Cajetan, in the present chapter, says that this particle (one in number) must be distinguished: for it is placed either on the part of the subject or on the part of the predicate. And placed on the part of the subject it makes this sense: It is proper to substance which is one in number to be receptive of contraries; in which sense it is evident that it belongs to first substance alone, because it alone is one in number. But if it is placed on the part of the predicate, the sense will be this: It is proper to substance that, numerical unity being preserved, it can receive contraries; and the property understood in this way, it is also evident, belongs to second substances: because, the numerical unity which they have in first substances being preserved, they can receive contraries; as man, the numerical unity which he has in Peter being preserved, can receive color and cold. In this way too this property is understood by other expositors, as Albert the Great, Simplicius and Villalpando; and they say that Aristotle spoke thus, so as to make this property common to all substances.

> Alij verò, negant posse secundis substantiis accommodari, vt Ammonius, & Cant. in expositionibus huius capitis.

But others deny that it can be accommodated to second substances, as Ammonius and Cant., in their expositions of this chapter.

> 62 Sed nostra sententia est, hac distinctione respondendum esse. De hac proprietate substãtiæ, duobus modis loqui possumus. Primo, in eo sensu, in quo locutus est Arist. Secundo, sine vlla limitatione verborum. Et si primo modo loquendum est, solis primis substantiis conuenit hæc proprietas, secundis verò nullo modo, probatur hęc contra Caiet. Primò Arist. asserit, *Maximè proprium esse substantiæ, vna numero cùm sit, contraria suspicere posse*, ergo proprietas hæc non potest conuenire substantiæ, nisi sit vna numero: sed secunda substantia, neque in se, neque in prima substantia, habet vnitatem numericam, ergo nullo modo ei conuenit. Probatur minor. Secunda substantia in se consideratur, vt est abstracta à prima: sed, vt abstracta à prima, non est vna numero, cùm sit communis omnibus primis substantiis, sed solùm vna genere, aut specie: ergo non conuenit ei hæc proprietas. Cæterùm, vt est contracta ad primam, est quidem vna numero, non tamen est secunda substantia. sed prima: quia homo, vt est contractus ad Petrum realiter & formaliter, est hic homo: sed hic homo formaliter, est singularis homo: ergo formaliter prima substantia, & nullo modo secunda. Quare idem est dicere, quòd secundis [p. 311] substantiis conueniat hæc proprietas, vt habent vnitatem numericam in primis, ac dicere, quòd solis primis conueniat.

62 But our view is that one must reply with this distinction. We can speak of this property of substance in two ways. First, in the sense in which Aristotle spoke. Second, without any limitation of the words. And if we are to speak in the first way, this property belongs to first substances alone, and to second substances in no way. This is proved against Cajetan. First, Aristotle asserts that It is most proper to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries; therefore this property cannot belong to a substance unless it is one in number; but second substance has numerical unity neither in itself nor in first substance; therefore it belongs to it in no way. The minor is proved. Second substance is considered in itself as it is abstracted from the first; but as abstracted from the first it is not one in number, since it is common to all first substances, but one only in genus or in species; therefore this property does not belong to it. But as it is contracted to the first, it is indeed one in number, yet it is not second substance but first: because man, as contracted to Peter really and formally, is this man; but this man formally is a singular man; therefore formally first substance, and in no way second. Wherefore it is the same to say that sec [p. 311] ond substances have this property as they have numerical unity in first substances, and to say that it belongs to first substances alone.

> Secundò probatur, ex definitione secundarum substantiarum, quæ ita habet: *Secundæ substantiæ sunt genera, & species, quibus primæ substantiæ insunt*. Sed non sunt genera, & species, vt sunt contractæ ad primam, vel vt in ea habent subsistentiam, sed in quantum considerantur, ab eadem abstractæ: sub hac autem consideratione, repugnat eis conuenire, cùm non habeant vnitatem numericam, ergo secundis substantiis, vt sunt secundæ substantiæ, non potest accommodari hæc proprietas, vt ab Arist. assignata: sed idem fuit dicere: *Proprium esse substantiæ, vt vna numero cùm sit, contraria possit suscipere*, ac excludere ab hac proprietate, secundas substantias.

Second, it is proved from the definition of second substances, which runs thus: Second substances are the genera and species in which first substances are. But they are not genera and species as they are contracted to the first, or as they have subsistence in it, but insofar as they are considered as abstracted from it; and under this consideration it is repugnant that it belong to them, since they do not have numerical unity; therefore this property, as assigned by Aristotle, cannot be accommodated to second substances as they are second substances. But to say It is proper to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries, was the same as to exclude second substances from this property.

> 63 Si verò accipiatur eadem proprietas, secundo modo, sine vlla limitatione verborum, scilicet ita, vt dicamus maximè proprium esse substantiæ, suscipere contraria, conuenit omni substantiæ, eodem modo, atque proprietas substandi, sed analogicè: hoc est, per se primo, & ratione sui, primæ, secundis verò, non nisi cum dependentia, & attributione ad illam.

63 But if the same property is taken in the second way, without any limitation of the words, namely so that we say that it is most proper to substance to receive contraries, it belongs to every substance in the same way as the property of standing under, but analogically: that is, to first substances per se primarily and by reason of themselves, but to second substances only with dependence on and attribution to the first.

> Circa tertium, An proprietas hæc conueniat omnibus primis substantiis, non conueniunt omnes: Sed primus modus dicendi est, Solis primis substantiis corporeis, & corruptibilibus conuenire, propter argumẽtum à nobis factum in principio: ita Porphyrius, & Ammonius, in explicatione huius proprietatis.

Concerning the third, Whether this property belongs to all first substances, not all agree. But the first way of speaking is that it belongs to bodily and corruptible first substances alone, on account of the argument we made at the beginning: so Porphyry and Ammonius, in their explanation of this property.

> 64 Secundus modus dicendi est, cõmunis omnium aliorum Interpretum, Quòd omnibus primis substantiis conueniat. Et ita tenendum est. Sed duo sunt breuiter notanda, vt intelligatur. Primum, Quòd Arist. non loquitur de solis contrariis strictè acceptis, qualia sunt primæ, & secundæ qualitates: nam veritas, & falsitas, non sunt propriè contraria, de quibus loquitur in textu, negans, *quòd propositio dicatur eas suscipere*: sed loquitur de contrariis, vniuersaliùs. Secundò notandum est, Quòd vt proprietas hæc conueniat alicui substantiæ, non est necessarium eam suscipere omnia contraria: sed sufficit aliqua posse suscipere, secundùm conuenientiam, suę naturę. Vnde satis est, vt corpora Cælestia sint susceptiua contrariorum, quòd possint suscipere motus contrarios, vnum ab Oriente in Occidentem, alterum ab Occidente in Orientem. Aut motum augmẽti, & decrementi circa lucem: quos constat suscipere Lunam à Sole. Sufficit etiam, quòd Angeli possint suscipere veritatem & falsitatem, medio intellectu, & bonitatem, & malitiam moralem, media voluntate, & actibus eius, vt dicantur esse primæ substantiæ susceptiuæ contrariorum.

64 The second way of speaking, common to all the other Interpreters, is That it belongs to all first substances. And so it is to be held. But two things are briefly to be noted in order that it may be understood. The first, That Aristotle does not speak only of contraries taken strictly, such as the first and second qualities are: for truth and falsity, of which he speaks in the text, denying that the proposition is said to receive them, are not properly contraries; but he speaks of contraries more universally. Second, it should be noted That for this property to belong to some substance, it is not necessary that it receive all contraries, but it suffices that it can receive some, according to what befits its nature. Whence it is enough, for the Celestial bodies to be receptive of contraries, that they can receive contrary motions, one from East to West, the other from West to East; or the motion of increase and decrease in light, which it is certain the Moon receives from the Sun. It also suffices that Angels can receive truth and falsity by means of the intellect, and moral goodness and malice by means of the will and its acts, for them to be called first substances receptive of contraries. V iiij

[p. 312]

> 65 Ad arg. verò, Distinguendum est antecedens: quia contraria duplicia sunt. Propria quidem, vt primæ, & secundæ qualitates, quæ ad corruptionem subiecti solent disponere: alia minùs propria, non respicientia corruptionem subiecti; & licèt Angeli, & corpora cælestia, non possint suscipere contraria illa priora & propria: quia neque corrumpi possunt, susceptiua tamen sunt aliorum contrariorum: & hoc sufficit, vt proprietas hæc illis conueniat: quia non de solis primis contrariis intelligitur ab Arist. sed de his, vel aliis.

65 But to the argument, the antecedent is to be distinguished: because contraries are of two kinds. Some proper, as the first and second qualities, which are wont to dispose toward the corruption of the subject; others less proper, not regarding the corruption of the subject. And although Angels and celestial bodies cannot receive those former and proper contraries, because they cannot be corrupted either, yet they are receptive of other contraries; and this suffices for this property to belong to them, because it is not understood by Aristotle of the first contraries alone, but of these or others.

> Ex his, quæ dicta sunt, sequitur hanc proprietatem vltimam substantiæ, conuenire primis substantiis, quarto modo: quia omni primæ substantiæ, soli, & semper conuenit. Et ideo Arist. dixit, *Maximè proprium esse substantiæ, vt vna numero cùm sit, contraria suscipere possit*: vt significaret, alias proprietates non conuenire ei quarto modo, sed accidentibus esse communes: hanc solis primis substantiis, *cum quibus conuertitur*.

From what has been said it follows that this last property of substance belongs to first substances in the fourth mode, because it belongs to every first substance, to it alone, and always. And therefore Aristotle said, It is most proper to substance that, being one in number, it can receive contraries: to signify that the other properties do not belong to it in the fourth mode, but are common to accidents; this one to first substances alone, with which it is convertible.

## CHAPTER VI

### CAP. VI. Continens prædicamentum quantitatis, cum exposit. tex. — Containing the category of quantity.

> Continens prædicamentum quantitatis.

[…]

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Quantum autem, aliud quidem est discretum, aliud autem continuum.*

Of quantity, however, one kind is discrete, another continuous.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 1 Post substantiam, statim disputat Aristoteles de quãtitate: quia inter accidentia corporea, primum est, proximè consequens naturam eiusdem substantiæ, & medium, quo illi cætera inhærent. Et intentum eius est, explicare naturam quantitatis. Diuiditur autem caput hoc in tres partes. In prima, diuidit quantitatem, tribus diuisionibus, ex quibus colligit numerum specierum quantitatis. In secunda, explicat singulas species. In tertia, enumerat tres proprietates eiusdem quantitatis.

1 After substance, Aristotle immediately disputes about quantity, because among the bodily accidents it is the first, most immediately following the nature of substance itself, and the medium by which the rest inhere in it. And his intention is to explain the nature of quantity. This chapter is divided into three parts. In the first, he divides quantity by three divisions, from which he gathers the number of the species of quantity. In the second, he explains the single species. In the third, he enumerates three properties of the same quantity.

> Prima diuisio quantitatis, non assignatur expressè ab Arist. sed præsupponitur, & insinuatur: nam eo ipso, quòd agit de Quantitate per se, præsupponit diuisionem eius, in Quantitatem per se, & Per accidens: Quantum per se, est illud, quod à se habet partes extensionis, vt linea, aut superficies: Quantum per accidens, est, quod non habet à se extensionem, sed ab alio extenditur: vt album dicitur quantum per accidens: quia albedo, non habet à se partes extensas, sed eas accipit, à superficie illius corporis, in quo extenditur.

The first division of quantity is not assigned expressly by Aristotle, but is presupposed and insinuated: for by the very fact that he treats of quantity per se, he presupposes its division into Quantity per se and Per accidens. A Quantity per se is that which has parts of extension of itself, as a line or a surface. A Quantity per accidens is that which does not have extension of itself, but is extended by another: as white is called a quantity per accidens, because whiteness does not have extended parts of itself, but receives them from the surface of the body in which it is extended.

[p. 313]

> Secunda diuisio est, (licèt tertio loco ponatur ab Aristot.) Quantum, aliud est Continuum, aliud Discretum. Continuum est, cuius partes copulantur termino communi, vt partes lineæ, copulantur punctis. Discretum verò, cuius partes non copulantur termino communi, vt numerus, discreta quantitas est: quia vnitates, non coniunguntur aliquo termino, sed separatæ permanent.

The second division is (although it is placed in the third place by Aristotle): Of Quantity, one kind is Continuous, another Discrete. The Continuous is that whose parts are joined by a common term, as the parts of a line are joined by points. But the Discrete is that whose parts are not joined by a common term: as number is a discrete quantity, because its units are not joined by any term, but remain separate.

> 2 Tertia diuisio, Quantum, aliud habet Positionem partium in continuo, aliud non habet talem positionem. Positio autem in continuo, duplex est: Vna, quam habent partes quantitatis, in ordine ad locum: ratione cuius dicitur aliquid, sedere, iacere aut stare. Et hæc Positio partium, non pertinet ad hoc prædicamentum, sed ad prædicamentum Situs: alia est Positio, quam habent partes, non in ordine ad locum, sed inter se, secundùm quam vna dicitur anterior, alia posterior, vna dextera, alia sinistra, vna sursum, alia deorsum: & hæc est propria huius prædicamenti: secundùm quam intelligitur diuisio, quæ ait, Quibusdam quantis id conuenire, aliis non. Duæ sunt enim conditiones necessariæ, vt quantum aliquod dicatur habere positionem in continuo. Prima, quòd continuum sit. Secunda, quòd sit permanens. Et defectu primæ conditionis: nulla species quantitatis discretæ, habet talem positionem. Defectu secundæ, ex quantitatibus continuis, tempus habet positionem, sed reliquæ quatuor illam habent: vt linea, superficies, corpus, & locus: quia habent vtramque conditionem.

2 The third division: Of Quantity, one kind has Position of parts in the continuum, another does not have such position. Now position in the continuum is twofold. One, which the parts of quantity have in order to place, by reason of which something is said to sit, to lie, or to stand. And this Position of parts does not pertain to this category, but to the category of Situation. The other is the Position which the parts have, not in order to place, but among themselves, according to which one is called prior, another posterior, one right, another left, one up, another down. And this is proper to this category; according to it is understood the division which says that this belongs to some quantities and not to others. For two conditions are necessary for some quantity to be said to have position in the continuum. The first, that it be continuous. The second, that it be permanent. Through defect of the first condition, no species of discrete quantity has such position. Through defect of the second, among the continuous quantities time does not have position; but the remaining four have it, as line, surface, body and place, because they have both conditions.

> 3 Species quantitatis continuæ sunt quinque: *Linea, Superficies, Corpus, Tempus, & Locus*: Species verò quantitatis Discretæ, duæ tantùm, nempe *Numerus, Oratio*. Sed probatur de singulis, quòd sint species quantitatis: vel si hoc notum sit, de aliquibus. Probat Arist. saltem, quòd sint quantitates continuæ, vel discretæ: & incipit à Numero, de quo, non probat esse quãtitatem: quia per se est notum, sed quòd sit quantitas discreta, hac ratione probat: Quantitas discreta est, cuius partes non copulantur termino communi: sed partes numeri quæ sunt vnitas, non copulantur aliquo termino communi, sed separatæ manent: ergo numerus est quantitas discreta.

3 The species of continuous quantity are five: Line, Surface, Body, Time and Place. But the species of Discrete quantity are two only, namely Number and Speech. But it is proved of each that they are species of quantity; or, if this is known of some, Aristotle at least proves that they are continuous or discrete quantities. And he begins from Number, of which he does not prove that it is a quantity, because that is known per se, but that it is a discrete quantity he proves by this argument: A discrete quantity is that whose parts are not joined by a common term; but the parts of number, which are units, are not joined by any common term, but remain separate; therefore number is a discrete quantity.

> De Oratione verò vtrumque probat, & esse quantitatem, & esse discretam: quia neutrum est per se manifestum. Probat quòd sit quantitas, hoc arg. Longum & breue, sunt passiones quantitatis, sed oratio mensuratur syllaba longa, & breui (loquitur enim de sola vocali, quia hæc sola potest esse species quantitatis) ergo est quantitas. Quòd verò sit quantitas [p. 314] discreta, probat, sicut probauerat de numero: quia partes orationis quæ sunt syllabæ, non copulantur termino communi, sed separatæ manent.

But of Speech he proves both, that it is a quantity and that it is discrete, because neither is manifest per se. He proves that it is a quantity by this argument: Long and short are attributes of quantity; but speech is measured by the long and short syllable (for he speaks of vocal speech alone, because this alone can be a species of quantity); therefore it is a quantity. But that it is a dis [p. 314] crete quantity he proves as he had proved of number: because the parts of speech, which are syllables, are not joined by a common term, but remain separate.

> 4 De continuis etiam, probat eodem modo: & primò de Linea, Superficie, & Corpore, quòd sint quantitates continuæ præposito tanquam manifesto, quòd sint quantitates (hac ratione: Quantitas continua est, cuius partes copulantur termino communi, sed partes harum trium specierum, copulantur termino communi: ergo sunt quantitates continuæ. Minorem ita probat: Linea, est longitudo sine latitudine, cuius partes copulantur punctis: Superficies, est longitudo, & latitudo, sine profunditate, cuius partes copulantur lineis: & Corpus, est longitudo, latitudo, & profunditas, cuius partes copulantur superficiebus; ergo partes harum trium specierum copulantur termino communi.

4 Of the continuous species also he proves it in the same way. And first of Line, Surface and Body, that they are continuous quantities, presupposing as manifest that they are quantities, by this argument: A continuous quantity is that whose parts are joined by a common term; but the parts of these three species are joined by a common term; therefore they are continuous quantities. He proves the minor thus: A Line is length without breadth, whose parts are joined by points; a Surface is length and breadth without depth, whose parts are joined by lines; and a Body is length, breadth and depth, whose parts are joined by surfaces; therefore the parts of these three species are joined by a common term.

> De Tempore verò, & Loco, supponit tanquam manifestum quòd sint quanta, & probat, quòd sint continua: de Tempore quidem hac ratione: Partes temporis, quæ sunt præsens, præteritum, & futurum, copulantur instanti: ratione cuius fiunt vnum tempus: ergo tempus est quantum continuum. De Loco verò hoc modo: Locus, ita continet corpus locatum, vt aqua arborem, vt partibus eiusdem locati, correspondeant partes loci: sed partes locati, cùm sit corpus, copulantur termino communi: ergo etiam partes loci: & ita erit locus quantitas continua, sicut corpus locatum.

But of Time and Place he supposes as manifest that they are quantities, and proves that they are continuous: of Time, indeed, by this argument: The parts of time, which are present, past and future, are joined in the instant, by reason of which they become one time; therefore time is a continuous quantity. But of Place in this way: Place so contains the located body, as water contains a tree, that the parts of the place correspond to the parts of the located thing; but the parts of the located thing, since it is a body, are joined by a common term; therefore so are the parts of the place; and thus place will be a continuous quantity, just as the located body is.

> Prima proprietas quantitatis est, *Non habere contrarium*, vt bicubitum, aut tricubitum, quæ sunt quantitates, nullum habent contrarium: & hæc proprietas, communis est quantitati cum substantia, vt cap. præcedenti docuit Aristoteles.

The first property of quantity is To have no contrary: as two cubits long or three cubits long, which are quantities, have no contrary. And this property is common to quantity with substance, as Aristotle taught in the preceding chapter.

> Secunda proprietas est, *Non suscipere gradus intensionis, aut remissionis*: aut quod aliis verbis dicitur, *non suscipere magis, & minus*: sicut suscipit calor, quem dicimus esse intensum, secundùm duos, aut tres gradus: non est enim vnum tempus magis tempus, quàm aliud: quia nec habet plures gradus perfectionis: & sic de cæteris speciebus quantitatis. Hæc etiam est communis proprietas quantitatis, cum substantia, & aliis: & ideo non conuenit quarto modo quantitati, sicut nec prima.

The second property is Not to receive degrees of intension or remission, or, as is said in other words, not to receive more and less, as heat receives them, which we call intense according to two or three degrees: for one time is not more time than another, because it does not have more degrees of perfection either; and so of the other species of quantity. This too is a property common to quantity with substance and the others; and therefore it does not belong to quantity in the fourth mode, just as the first does not.

> Tertia proprietas quantitatis est, *Quòd secundùm eam res dicantur æquales, & inæquales*, vt duo corpora, quæ verè sunt substantiæ: si habeant eandem longitudinem, dicuntur æqualia, sed ratione quantitatis: quia longitudo quantitas est: & hæc proprietas conuenit quarto modo quantitati, qui conuenit omnibus speciebus eius, solis, & semper.

The third property of quantity is That according to it things are called equal and unequal: as two bodies, which are truly substances, if they have the same length, are called equal, but by reason of quantity, because length is a quantity. And this property belongs to quantity in the fourth mode, since it belongs to all its species, to them alone, and always.

[p. 315]

## QUESTION I

> *In quonam sit ponenda essentialis ratio quantitatis.*

In what the essential ratio of quantity is to be placed.

> 6 Prima opinio, ponit *Rationem essentialem quantitatis in mensura*. hoc est in eo, quòd quælibet quantitas sit mensurabilis per alteram: vel saltem suis partibus mensuretur, atque etiam sit aliarum rerum mensura. Et potest probari testimonio Arist. qui 4. lib. Physicorum, agens de tempore, quod est vna species quantitatis: illud definit, dicens: *Esse numerum, seu mensuram motus secundùm prius, & posterius*.

6 The first opinion places the essential Ratio of quantity in measure, that is, in the fact that every quantity is measurable by another, or at least is measured by its own parts, and is also the measure of other things. And it can be proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in Phys. 4, treating of time, which is one species of quantity, defines it, saying that it is the number or measure of motion according to before and after.

> Probatur etiam ratione: quia species quantitatis, debent distingui per rationes essentiales, sed quædam sunt, quæ non possunt distingui: nisi per rationem mensuræ: ergo hæc erit ratio essentialis quantitatis. Probatur minor: In loco, & superficie, quæ non distinguuntur, nisi ex eo quòd superficies est mensura extrinseca corporis continentis, in quo est, vt aeris, aut aquæ: & locus est superficies extrinseca corporis contenti: hoc enim modo considerata, habet rationem loci. Hæc sententia attribuitur D. Th. opusc. 53. de natura loci, in fine.

It is proved also by argument: because the species of quantity must be distinguished by essential rationes; but there are some which cannot be distinguished except by the ratio of measure; therefore this will be the essential ratio of quantity. The minor is proved: In place and surface, which are not distinguished except by the fact that the surface is the extrinsic measure of the containing body in which it is, as of air or water; and place is the extrinsic surface of the contained body, for considered in this way it has the ratio of place. This opinion is attributed to St. Thomas, opusc. 55, On the Nature of Place, at the end.

> Secunda opinio, est Scoti in prædicamentis, quæst. 17. & 5. Meta. q. 9. vbi *Essentiam quantitatis* asserit, *esse diuisibilitatem in proprias partes integrantes*: ita etiam Anto. Andr. 5. Meta. qu. 10. Capr. in 2, d. 3. q. 1. Soci. 5. Met. q. 12. Iauel. q. 10. & eadem tenere videtur D. Th. lect. 15. eiusdem lib. & in 1. d. 39. q. 1. ar. 1. ad 1. Probatur eam Scot. testimonio Arist. & ratione. Arist. enim 5. lib. Meta. cap. 23. definit Quantum: *Quòd sit diuisibile in ea, quæ insunt*: hoc est, in proprias partes integrantes, ex quibus componitur: sed definitio illa explicat essentiam quantitatis, ergo hæc erit ratio diuisibilitatis.

The second opinion is that of Scotus, on the Categories, q. 17, and Metaph. 5, q. 9, where he asserts that the Essence of quantity is divisibility into its own integral parts: so too Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 5, q. 10; Capreolus, in 2, d. 3, q. 1; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 12; Javelli, q. 10; and St. Thomas seems to hold the same, lect. 15 of the same book, and in 1, d. 39, q. 1, a. 1, ad 1. Scotus proves it by the testimony of Aristotle and by argument. For Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 23, defines Quantity: That which is divisible into those things which are in it, that is, into its own integral parts, of which it is composed; but that definition explains the essence of quantity; therefore this will be the ratio, namely of divisibility.

> 7 Ratione verò: quia omnes distinguunt species quantitatis, per diuisibilitatem, dicentes, diuisibile secũdùm vnam dimensionem longitudinis, esse lineam, secundùm duas dimensiones, longitudinis, & latitudinis, superficiem, & secundùm tres diuisiones, longitudinis, latitudinis, & profunditatis, corpus: sicque de cæteris, secundùm proprias rationes diuisibilitatis: sed distinctio specifica, debet esse essentialis; ergo distinguuntur essentialiter, per diuisibilitatem: quare hæc erit ratio essentialis quantitatis.

7 And by argument: because all distinguish the species of quantity by divisibility, saying that what is divisible according to one dimension, of length, is a line; according to two dimensions, of length and breadth, a surface; and according to three dimensions, of length, breadth and depth, a body; and so of the rest, according to their own rationes of divisibility. But the specific distinction must be essential; therefore they are distinguished essentially by divisibility; wherefore this will be the essential ratio of quantity.

> Tertia opinio, negat *Essentiam quantitatis esse mensuram*, aut diuisibilitatem, sed eam ponit, in extensione partium, quæ est, vnam partem esse extra aliam. Ita Duran. in 1. d. 34. quæst. 1. num. 26. Niphus 5. Meta. quæst. 9. Sotus, & Toletus, quæst. 1. [p. 316] huius prædicamenti, Canterus in expositione textus, Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 13 q. 1. sect. 3. Et hæc est probabilior sententia.

The third opinion denies that the Essence of quantity is measure or divisibility, but places it in the extension of parts, which is for one part to be outside another. So Durandus, in 1, d. 34, q. 1, no. 26; Nifo, Metaph. 5, q. 9; Soto and Toledo, q. 1 [p. 316] of this category; Canterus, in his exposition of the text; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 13, q. 1, sect. 5. And this is the more probable opinion.

> Sed non eodem modo explicatur ab omnibus. Pro eius tamen intelligentia, notanda est prima distinctio quantitatis: quam tradit D. Th. 1. p. q 42 art. 1 ad 2. acceptam ex D. Aug. 6. li. de Trinitate, cap. 8. circa medium: *Quantitas, alia est Molis, alia Virtutis*, *Quantitas Molis* est, quę in substantia corporea inhærens, partes eius sic facit extensas vt molem, aut magnitudinem eis tribuat. *Quantitas Virtutis*, est perfectio essẽtialis cuiuscunque rei, secundùm quam magna dicitur, vel parua: id est, in maiori, vel minori gradu perfectionis constituta: vt Angelus dicur maior homine, & homo maior leone: quia essentialiter perfectior. Hæc autem quantitas virtutis, seu perfectionis, ad omnia prædicamenta pertinet: ideo non agimus modò de illa: sed solùm de quantitate molis, quæ constituit hoc prædicamentum. Et eam definit Arist. 5. lib. Meta. cap. 13 his verbis: *Quantum est diuisibile in ea, quæ insunt, quorum vtrumque, aut singulum, vnum quid, aut quodquid, aptum est esse*.

But it is not explained in the same way by all. For its understanding, however, there should be noted the first distinction of quantity, which St. Thomas gives, 1 p., q. 42, a. 1, ad 1, taken from St. Augustine, On the Trinity 6, ch. 8, about the middle: One Quantity is of Bulk, another of Power. The Quantity of Bulk is that which, inhering in a bodily substance, so makes its parts extended as to give them bulk or magnitude. The Quantity of Power is the essential perfection of any thing whatever, according to which it is called great or small, that is, constituted in a greater or lesser degree of perfection: as an Angel is called greater than man, and man greater than a lion, because essentially more perfect. Now this quantity of power, or of perfection, pertains to all the categories; therefore we are not treating of it now, but only of the quantity of bulk, which constitutes this category. And Aristotle defines it, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, in these words: A quantity is that which is divisible into those things which are in it, each of which, whether both or each one, is apt to be some one thing and a this something.

> 8 Sic autem explicanda est definitio, vt *Diuisibile*, appelletur. *Quantum*, ad differentiam punctorum, & aliorum indiuisibilium: & in ea, quæ insunt, diuisibile dicitur, id est, in partes integrantes, ex quibus componitur: quæ ideo formaliter ei insunt, & non solùm virtualiter, sicut elementa dicuntur esse in mixto, ex eo solùm, quòd virtutes eorũ, vt calor, frigus, humor & siccitas, in mixtis sunt, non tamen elementa ipsa secundùm formas substantiales: & ideo non dicuntur esse in eis formaliter. Quorum vtrumque, si duas partes habeat, vel certè duas medietates, in quas diuidi solet quodlibet continuum: vel vnumquodque, si plures. Sic autem in eas diuiditur, vt post diuisionem, quælibet possit separata ab eo existere, per se. Gratia exempli: Lignum vnius palmi, diuisibile est in duas medietates, ita, vt quælibet earum, facta diuisione, existat iam per se, & independenter à toto: in quo distinguitur continuum à toto Physico, quod componitur ex materia & forma, tanquam ex partibus, & à toto Meta. quod componitur ex genere, & differentia: ita tamen, vt non posset diuidi in has partes, potentes per se separatas existere naturaliter: quia nec forma materialis, sine materia, nec materia sine forma, materialiter esse potest. De partibus igitur integrantibus intelligitur definitio, dum dicitur: *Concretum esse diuisibile in ea, quæ insunt*.

8 Now the definition is to be explained thus: it is called Divisible to distinguish Quantity from points and other indivisibles. And it is said to be divisible into those things which are in it, that is, into the integral parts of which it is composed, which are therefore formally in it, and not only virtually, as the elements are said to be in a mixed body only from the fact that their powers, as heat, cold, moistness and dryness, are in mixed bodies, but not the elements themselves according to their substantial forms; and therefore they are not said to be in them formally. Each of which, both, if it has two parts, or certainly two halves, into which any continuum is wont to be divided; or each one, if more. But it is divided into them in such a way that after the division each can exist separated from it, per se. For example: A piece of wood a palm long is divisible into two halves in such a way that each of them, once the division is made, now exists per se and independently of the whole: in which the continuum is distinguished from the Physical whole, which is composed of matter and form as of parts, and from the Metaphysical whole, which is composed of genus and difference; yet in such a way that it could not be divided into these parts, able to exist separated per se naturally, because neither can the material form exist materially without matter, nor matter without form. The definition, then, is understood of integral parts, when it is said: Quantity is that which is divisible into those things which are in it.

> 9 Secundò notãdum est, *partes integrantes* esse in duplici differentia.
