Vt in homine, forma partialis est illa, quæ cum materia componit naturam hominis: & natura ipsa composita ex materia, & forma, dicitur forma totalis: vt humanitas, dicitur forma totalis hominis: quia simul cum suo modo substantiali, qui est subsistentia, componit hominem: significantem naturam completam in supposito. Formam igitur partialem numeri, ait esse vltimam vnitatem, quæ determinat præcedentes: & ita se habet, per modum actus, & formæ: & præcedentes per modum materiæ: vt forma binarij, est secunda vnitas, determinans primam, ad constitutionem talis speciei: forma ternarij, est tertia, præsupponens duas tanquam materiam, & eas determinans per modum formæ. Formam verò totalem (inquit) non esse [p. 347] vltimam vnitatem, neque omnes, sed naturam ipsam numeri, resultantem ex compositione: ex qua natura simul, cum modo actualis inhærentiæ, fit completus numerus in concreto. Probat hoc vltimum hac ratione, quia in quibuscunque rebus, forma totalis, quæ est natura, resultat ex vnione partium: sed nec vltima vnitas, nec omnes simul, resultant ex vnione partium: sed potiùs sunt partes, ex quibus resultat natura ipsa numeri: ergo non possunt esse forma totalis eius. Primum verò non probat, quia per se est manifestum. Hanc sententiam sequutus est priùs Albert. Mag. in prædicamentis, tit. 8. quantitate, & in Comment. sup. 5. c. D. Dionys. de diuinis nominibus, Imò & D. Th. 8. Met. lect. 3. & postea Iauel. 8. Meta. q. 10.

The first opinion, then, is that of Capreolus, on 1, d. 24, q. 1, concl. 5, who distinguishes a twofold form of number, Partial and Total, as must be distinguished in any species of substance whatever. As in man, the partial form is that which with matter composes the nature of man; and the nature itself, composed of matter and form, is called the total form: as humanity is called the total form of man, because together with its substantial mode, which is subsistence, it composes man, signifying the complete nature in the supposit. The partial form of number, then, he says is the last unity, which determines the preceding ones; and thus it stands by way of act and form, and the preceding ones by way of matter: as the form of the number two is the second unity, determining the first to the constitution of such a species; the form of the number three is the third, presupposing two as matter and determining them by way of form. But the total form (he says) is not [p. 347] the last unity, nor all of them, but the very nature of number resulting from the composition; from which nature, together with the mode of actual inherence, the complete number in the concrete comes to be. He proves this last point by this argument: because in any things whatever the total form, which is the nature, results from the union of the parts; but neither the last unity nor all of them together result from the union of the parts, but rather they are the parts from which the very nature of number results; therefore they cannot be its total form. The first point, however, he does not prove, because it is manifest of itself. This opinion was followed earlier by Albert the Great, in the Categories, the treatise on quantity, and in his Commentary on ch. 5 of St. Dionysius, On the Divine Names; indeed also by St. Thomas, Metaph. 8, lect. 3; and afterward by Javelli, Metaph. 8, q. 10.

> 64 Secundam opinionem tenet Sonci. 10. Meta. q. 9. vbi alio modo distinguit numerum, *In eum qui abstrahitur à particularibus vnitatibus*: & solùm dicit duo, tria, vel quatuor: & *in eum, qui contrahitur ad particulares vnitates*, & in eis consideratur: vt dum dicimus tria corpora, tres lapides, vel tres homines. Formam igitur numeri abstracti, dicit esse vltimam vnitatem, non tamen numeri contracti: sed numerum contractum seipso cõstitui, in specie, hoc est, per suas vnitates simul acceptas, absque ordine primę, vel vltimæ: vt ternarium hominum, aut quaternarium lapidum. Et hæc sententia, videtur opposita præcedenti: quia quæstio hæc de numero reali pro quantitatibus ipsis accepto, procedit: cuius formam, dicit, prima opinio, sumendam esse ab vltima vnitate, quod negat hæc secunda.

64 The second opinion is held by Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 9, where he distinguishes number in another way: into that which is abstracted from particular unities, and signifies only two, three, or four; and into that which is contracted to particular unities and is considered in them, as when we say three bodies, three stones, or three men. The form of abstract number, then, he says is the last unity, but not that of contracted number; rather contracted number is constituted in its species by itself, that is, by its unities taken together, without an order of first or last: as the number three of men, or the number four of stones. And this opinion seems opposed to the preceding one, because this question proceeds concerning real number, taken for the quantities themselves, whose form the first opinion says is to be taken from the last unity, which this second one denies.

> 65 Probat porrò Sonc. 1. par. suæ opinionis, *Quòd forma numeri abstracti, sit vltima vnitas*, hac ratione: Quia numerus abstractus, solùm reperitur obiectiuè in intellectu, constituente ordinem prioris, & posterioris, inter vnum, duo, & tria: ita vt sicut ad binarium, non perueniat, nisi per vnitatem, & ad ternarium, per binarium; sicque ad cæteros semper: ergo vltima vnitas, in apprehensione intellectus, præsupponit cæteras: & ideo habet se ad illas, per modum formæ determinantis.

65 Soncinas, further, proves the first part of his opinion, that the form of abstract number is the last unity, by this argument: because abstract number is found only objectively in the intellect, which constitutes the order of prior and posterior among one, two, and three, so that just as it does not arrive at two except through one, so it does not arrive at three except through two, and so always to the others; therefore the last unity, in the apprehension of the intellect, presupposes the others, and therefore stands to them by way of a determining form.

> Secundam verò partem, quòd *forma numeri contracti, non sit vltima vnitas*, probat duplici argument. Primò, quia vbi est primum, & vltimum realiter, aliquis est ordo realis inter ea: sed inter vnitates numeri, nullus est ordo realis: ergo nec datur prima vnitas realiter, neque vltima, quæ possit esse forma numeri. Probatur minor, quia si ordo realis daretur inter vnitates: aut ille ordo esset naturæ aut dignitatis, loci, vbi, vel situs, sed nullus talis datur: ergo nec habebunt realem ordinem. Probo iterum minorem, quia simul tempore, possunt fieri duo, vel tria corpora, ex quibus efficitur ternarius: & ita vt [p. 348] vnum non sit causa alterius, nec sit eo dignius: sed nec necesse est habere ordinem loci, vel situs, cùm possint in vacuo constitui: quare nullum habebunt ordinem realem.

But the second part, that the form of contracted number is not the last unity, he proves by a twofold argument. First, because where there is a first and a last really, there is some real order between them; but among the unities of number there is no real order; therefore neither is there really a first unity, nor a last, which could be the form of number. The minor is proved: because, if a real order were given among the unities, that order would be either of nature, or of dignity, of place, of where, or of position; but none such is given; therefore they will not have a real order. I prove the minor again: because two or three bodies, from which the number three is made, can come to be at the same time; and thus [p. 348] one is not the cause of another, nor is it more worthy than it; nor is it necessary that they have an order of place or of position, since they can be constituted in a vacuum: wherefore they will have no real order.

> Secundò: Vel vltima vnitas, est forma numeri realis, in quantum est vnitas, vel in quantum est vltima; non vt vnitas, quia hæc ratio communis est omnibus: sed nec, vt vltima, propter duo. Primum quia esse vltimam, habet ab intellectu numerante: ergo non potest esse forma realis. Secundò, quia forma rei, debet esse fixa, & inuariabilis: sed esse vltimam, sæpe variatur, pro voluntate numerantis: ita vt vnitas, quæ modò numeratur post alias, possit rursus numerari prima; vnde esse vltimam, per omnes variatur: quare non potest esse forma numeri.

Second: Either the last unity is the form of real number inasmuch as it is a unity, or inasmuch as it is last. Not as a unity, because this ratio is common to all; but neither as last, for two reasons. First, because it has its being last from the intellect that numbers; therefore it cannot be a real form. Second, because the form of a thing must be fixed and invariable; but being last often varies according to the will of the one numbering, so that a unity which is now numbered after the others can in turn be numbered first; hence being last varies through all of them; wherefore it cannot be the form of number.

> 66 Pro solutione huius quæst. notandum est, ex D. Th. 12. q. 54. art. 4. in corpore: In accidentibus, non esse compositionem essentialem Physicam, ex materia, & forma, sed esse naturas quasdam adeò imperfectas, vt potiùs sint formæ subiectorum, per actualẽ inhęrentiam in eo: & huius ratio est manifesta, quia materia, & forma, sunt partes essentiales entis naturalis, quod est substantia: accidentia verò, non sunt entia naturalia: sed aliquid entis naturalis: ergo non possunt habere compositionem ex materia, & forma. Vnde ex tribus compositionibus, quæ reperiuntur in substantia, nempe Physica essentialis ex materia, & forma: & quasi Entitatiua, aut substantialis, ex partibus integrantibus: & Metaphysica, essentialis ex genere, & differentia: solùm in accidentibus reperiuntur duæ postremæ: in quibus explicandum est: an vltima vnitas habeat rationem differentiæ: vel ab ea sumatur differentia essentialis.

66 For the solution of this question it should be noted, from St. Thomas, 1- 2, q. 54, a. 4, in the body, that in accidents there is no essential physical composition of matter and form, but that they are certain natures so imperfect that they are rather forms of the subject, through actual inherence in it. And the reason for this is manifest: because matter and form are essential parts of a natural being, which is substance; but accidents are not natural beings, but something of a natural being; therefore they cannot have composition of matter and form. Hence, of the three compositions which are found in substance, namely the physical essential one, of matter and form; the quasi-entitative or substantial one, of integral parts; and the metaphysical essential one, of genus and difference, only the last two are found in accidents; in which it must be explained whether the last unity has the ratio of difference, or whether the essential difference is taken from it.

> Et à compositione ex genere & differentia tanquam ab essentiali incipiamus: idem est in ea forma, & differentia: quia cùm fiat ex genere, & differentia, genus se habet, vt materia, & differentia tanquam forma. Videudum igitur est, à quo sumatur differentia in speciebus numerorum, an ab vltima vnitate, vel ab omnibus. Et de genere certum est, ab omnibus simul sumptam definiendum esse: quia genus proximum numeri, est quantitas discreta: discretio verò, non reperitur in vna sola vnitate, sed in omnibus: quare ab omnibus sumitur genus: differentia verò, ab omnibus etiam sumi debet: quia differentia continet gradum perfectionis, determinantem genus: vnde cùm genus contineat communem rationem extensionis, aut diuisibilitatis discretæ, differentia debet continere gradum perfectionis, talis extensionis, aut diuisibilitatis: quæ etiam non repetitur in vna sola vnitate, sed in multis, [p. 349] Ideo non vt est à sola vltima: sed etiam ab omnibus, sub ratione speciali debet sumi: & ita genus numeri ternarij, erit quantitas discreta: differentia verò extensio, vel diuisibilitas, in tres vnitates: sicque definitur numerus ternarius, *Est quantitas discreta, extensa secundum tres vnitates, ita ordinatas secundum prius & posterius.*

And let us begin with the composition of genus and difference, as with the essential one. In it form and difference are the same: because, since it is made of genus and difference, the genus stands as matter and the difference as form. It must be seen, then, from what the difference in the species of numbers is taken: whether from the last unity, or from all. And concerning the genus it is certain that it must be defined from all taken together: because the proximate genus of number is discrete quantity, and discreteness is not found in one single unity, but in all; wherefore the genus is taken from all. But the difference too must be taken from all: because the difference contains a grade of perfection determining the genus; hence, since the genus contains the common ratio of extension, or of discrete divisibility, the difference must contain a grade of perfection of such extension or divisibility, which likewise is not found in one single unity, but in many, [p. 349] and therefore it must be taken not from the last alone, but from all, under a special ratio. And thus the genus of the number three will be discrete quantity, and the difference the extension or divisibility into three unities; and so the number three is defined: It is a discrete quantity extended according to three unities, so ordered according to prior and posterior.

> 67 In compositione verò totius, ex partibus integrantibus, non reperitur materia, neque forma: quia omnes partes integrantes, sic sunt in actu, vt nulla recipiat aliam, nec recipiatur ab alia: vt inter brachiũ, caput, & pedes non est materia, neque forma propriè loquendo: nihilominus inter partes integrantes numeri, vna pars se habet ad alias, tanquam forma, in quãtum eas determinat: & ita se habet vltima vnitas in numero, determinans aliam, vel alias, ad certum numerum efficiẽdum: vt secunda vnitas determinat primam, ad efficiendum binarium, & tertia determinat duas, ad efficiẽdũ ternariũ, sicque de cęteris.

67 But in the composition of the whole from integral parts neither matter nor form is found: because all the integral parts are in act in such a way that none receives another nor is received by another: as among arm, head, and feet there is no matter or form, properly speaking. Nevertheless, among the integral parts of number one part stands to the others as form, inasmuch as it determines them; and thus the last unity stands in number, determining another or others to make a certain number: as the second unity determines the first to make two, and the third determines two to make three, and so of the rest.

> Nostra igitur sententia duo asserit. Primum est: Forma essentialis, quam potest habere numerus, non sumitur à sola vltima vnitate, sed ab omnibus, in quantum habent specialem rationem extensionis discretæ.

Our view, therefore, asserts two things. The first is: The essential form which number can have is not taken from the last unity alone, but from all, inasmuch as they have a special ratio of discrete extension.

> Probatur hac ratione, deducta ex doctrina tradita. Forma essentialis duplex tantùm est, Physica & Metaphysica: sed numerus non habet formam essentialem Physicam: & Metaphysica, quam habet, sumitur ab omnibus vnitatibus sic ordinatis, secundùm prius & posterius: ergo non à sola vltima. Probatur minor: quia differentia in quibuscunque rebus, sumitur à tota natura, sub gradu speciali concepta, vt in homine, à tota eius natura, sub gradu rationalitatis: ergo differentia numeri sumitur à tota eius natura, sub tali gradu extensionis discretæ considerata: talis autem gradus extensionis discretæ, non reperitur in sola vltima vnitate: sed in omnibus sic ordinatis, sicut nec discretio ipsa, in vno solo reperitur, sed inter multa: ergo nec differentia numeri, à sola vltima vnitate desumi potest, sed ab omnibus sic ordinatis: vt forma ternarij, à quibus vnitatibus sic ordinatis, vt duæ sint præsuppositæ, & ab vltima determinentur.

This is proved by this argument, drawn from the doctrine delivered: Essential form is only twofold, physical and metaphysical; but number does not have a physical essential form; and the metaphysical one which it has is taken from all the unities so ordered according to prior and posterior; therefore not from the last alone. The minor is proved: because the difference in any things whatever is taken from the whole nature, conceived under a special grade, as in man from his whole nature under the grade of rationality; therefore the difference of number is taken from its whole nature, considered under such a grade of discrete extension. But such a grade of discrete extension is not found in the last unity alone, but in all so ordered, just as discreteness itself is not found in one alone, but among many; therefore neither can the difference of number be taken from the last unity alone, but from all so ordered: as the form of the number three from the unities so ordered that two are presupposed and are determined by the last.

> 68 Secundum, quod asserit, nostra sententia est: In numero considerato, vt toto integrali, licèt non inueniatur propria forma Physica nec Metaphysica, inuenitur tamen quædam similitudo formæ: & sumitur à sola vltima vnitate: imò ista sola se habet vt forma. Probatur hac ratione: Id quod est determinabile per aliud, habet modum materiæ: & id quod determinat aliud, habet modum formæ: sed inter partes integrantes [p. 350] numeri, vltima vnitas se habet, vt determinans præcedentes, & istę vt determinabiles per eam: ergo istæ se habent tanquam materia, & illa tanquam forma. Et hoc voluit prima sententia, dum asseruit, Vltimam vnitatem esse quasi partialem formam numeri. & præsertim D. Th. qui hoc idem intellexit, non de vera forma, sed de aliqua similitudine eius. Et ideo argumentis eiusdem sententiæ, non est necessarium respondere.

68 The second thing our view asserts is: In number considered as an integral whole, although no proper physical or metaphysical form is found, yet a certain likeness of form is found, and it is taken from the last unity alone; indeed that alone stands as form. This is proved by this argument: That which is determinable by another has the mode of matter, and that which determines another has the mode of form; but among the integral parts [p. 350] of number, the last unity stands as determining the preceding ones, and these as determinable by it; therefore these stand as matter and that one as form. And this is what the first opinion meant when it asserted that the last unity is as it were the partial form of number, and especially St. Thomas, who understood this same point not of a true form but of some likeness of it. And therefore it is not necessary to reply to the arguments of that opinion.

> Solùm hoc est notandum: Hoc habere speciale partes integrantes numeri, quòd cùm vna se habeat per modum formæ, & aliæ per modum materiæ, variata illa, quæ se habeat vt forma, ex consequenti variatur differentia essentialis numeri: quia variatur modus extensionis, ex quo accipitur: vt variata tertia vnitate, idem numerus habet extensionem, in ordine ad duo, vel ad quatuor, quæ diuersa est.

This only should be noted: the integral parts of number have this special feature, that, since one stands by way of form and the others by way of matter, when the one that stands as form is varied, the essential difference of number is consequently varied: because the mode of extension from which it is taken is varied; as, when the third unity is varied, the same number has an extension in order to two or to four, which is different.

> Secunda autem sententia, distinctionem illam de numero abstracto, & contracto, minùs bene adduxit: quia nunc loquimur de numero prædicamentali, qui est species, quantitatis discretæ, & reperitur in rebus: numerus verò abstractus, transcendentalis est, cùm in substantiis, ac cæteris accidentibus reperiatur: & ideo non magis ad hoc prædicamentum, quàm ad cætera pertinet: imò ad nullũ: & ideo non est de illo curandũ.

The second opinion, however, did not do well in adducing that distinction of abstract and contracted number: because we are now speaking of categorial number, which is a species of discrete quantity and is found in things; but abstract number is transcendental, since it is found in substances and in the other accidents; and therefore it pertains no more to this category than to the others; indeed, to none; and therefore we need not concern ourselves with it.

> Ad primum igitur arg. eiusdem sententiæ, Neganda est minor: quòd non sit ordo realis inter vnitates numeri: nam licèt non sit ordo tẽporis, nec naturæ loci, vel situs, est tamen ordo numerabilitatis, quem dicit vnitas quælibet ad alias: in quantum prius, ac posterius, numerabilis est ab intellectu, hoc est, præsupponendo eas, vel eisdem præsupposita.

To the first argument, then, of that opinion: the minor must be denied, namely that there is no real order among the unities of number. For although there is no order of time, nor of nature, of place, or of position, yet there is an order of numerability, which each unity signifies to the others, inasmuch as it is numerable by the intellect as prior or posterior, that is, as presupposing them or as presupposed to them.

> Ad secundum, Distinguenda est maior: quia vnitates numeri dupliciter considerari possunt, vel vt actu numerantur, vel vt sunt numerabiles: & ideo quęlibet habet duplicem considerationem vltimæ: nempe in actuali numeratione, aut in aptitudine. Dum ergo dicitur, vel vltima est forma, vt vnitas est, vel vt est vltima: distinguendum est: nam vt vltima in ratione numerabilitatis, habet modum formæ realis, non vt vltima in actuali numeratione: quia hæc est ratio extrinseca, & variabilis, illa extrinseca, & inuariabilis, eodem modo cõueniens omnibus, cùm possit quælibet numerari post alias: & ideo cuilibet inuariabiliter conuenit, esse vltimam secundùm aptitudinem: & hoc non habet ab intellectu: sed ex propria natura: quamuis non sine respectu ad intellectum: bene tamen habent id ante operationem eius: realis igitur est ratio vltimę in qualibet vnitate, sicut ratio primæ, aut mediæ, vt explicatum est.

To the second. The major must be distinguished: because the unities of number can be considered in two ways, either as they are actually numbered or as they are numerable; and therefore each has a twofold consideration of being last, namely in the actual numbering or in the aptitude. When, then, it is said that the last is the form either as it is a unity or as it is last, a distinction must be made: for as last in the ratio of numerability it has the mode of a real form; not as last in the actual numbering, because this is an extrinsic and variable ratio, that one intrinsic and invariable, belonging in the same way to all, since any one can be numbered after the others; and therefore being last according to aptitude belongs invariably to each one. And they do not have this from the intellect, but from their own nature; although not without respect to the intellect, yet they have it before its operation. The ratio of last, therefore, is real in each unity, as is the ratio of first or of middle, as has been explained.

[p. 351]

## QUESTION VIII

> QVÆSTIO VIII.

[…]

> *An numerus prædicamentalis, non solùm reperiatur in corporibus, sed etiam in rebus spiritualibus.*

Whether categorial number is found not only in bodies, but also in spiritual things.

> 70 SEnsus quæstionis est, An sicut tres homines, tres lapides, aut tria quælibet alia corpora, efficiunt numerum qui est species quantitatis discretæ: ita tres Angeli, aut tres animæ: & procedit quæstio, supposito, quòd numerus sit per se in prædicamento.

70 The sense of the question is: whether, just as three men, three stones, or any three other bodies make a number which is a species of discrete quantity, so three angels or three souls do; and the question proceeds on the supposition that number is per se in the category.

> Prima opinio affirmat, *Numerum rerum spiritualium, non minùs esse speciem quantitatis discretæ, quàm numerum corporum.* Ita Richard. in 1. dist. 10. q. 1. ad 4. & dist. 24. art. 1. q. 1. & art. 2. q. 1. Marsil. in 3. q. 27. ar. 1. & 2. Greg. d. 24. q. 2. ar. 3. Aureol. apud Capreol. eadem dist. & q. vbi etiam Maior. Ocham, & Gabriel, quos sequitur magna modernorum pars.

The first opinion affirms that the number of spiritual things is no less a species of discrete quantity than the number of bodies. So Richard, on 1, d. 10, q. 1, ad 4, and d. 24, a. 1, q. 1, and a. 2, q. 1; Marsilius, on 3, q. 27, a. 1 and 2; Gregory, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3; Auriol, as reported by Capreolus in the same distinction and question, where also Major, Ockham, and Gabriel, whom a great part of the moderns follow.

> Probatur testimoniis D. Aug. lib. 2. de libero arbitrio, cap. 16. vbi asserit, *Numerum esse aliquid intelligibile, & in omnibus rebus inueniri*, & Damas. 3. lib. Fidei, cap. 8. docentis, *Numerũ in quibuslibet rebus inter se diuersis, sic reperiri, vt duæ naturæ, Diuina, & humana in Christo, ad quantitatem discretam pertineant.*

It is proved by the testimonies of St. Augustine, On Free Choice, bk. 2, ch. 16, where he asserts that number is something intelligible, and is found in all things; and of Damascene, On the Faith, bk. 3, ch. 8, who teaches that numbers in any things whatever, different among themselves, are so found that the two natures, divine and human, in Christ pertain to discrete quantity.

> Probatur etiam ratione, quia integra ratio numeri, constat ex multis vnitatibus realibus, & inter se separatis, atque numerabilibus ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius: sed hoc totum conuenit tribus Angelis: ergo veram habent rationem numeri prædicamentalis. Probatur minor, quia tres Angeli, sunt distincti realiter, atque etiam realiter separati, & quilibet est numerabilis ab intellectu ante alios, & post alios.

It is also proved by reason: because the entire ratio of number consists of many real unities, separated from one another and numerable by the intellect according to prior and posterior; but all this belongs to three angels; therefore they have the true ratio of categorial number. The minor is proved: because three angels are really distinct, and also really separated, and each is numerable by the intellect before the others and after the others.

> 71 Secunda opinio, negat, *Numerum prædicamentalem reperiri in rebus spiritualibus*, sed solùm putat ponendum esse in corporibus. Ita D. Th. q. 9. de Potentia, at. 7. in 1. dist. 24. qu. 1. art. 3. & 1. part. qu. 3. art. 3. Capreol. in 1. di. 24. quæst. 1. Soncin 10. Metaph. q. 13. Iauel. lib. 8. quæst. 11. & colligitur ex doctrina Aristot. 4. lib. Phys. 6. & 7. vbi docet, *Numerum fieri ex diuisione continui.* & 2. de anima, 6. *Numerum*, asserit, *esse sensibile per se.* Sed numerus rerum spiritualium, nec fit ex diuisione continui, nec est sensibilis: quia sensus non possunt percipere nisi corporea: ergo non est numerus prædicamentalis ex mente Aristo.

71 The second opinion denies that categorial number is found in spiritual things, and thinks that it is to be posited only in bodies. So St. Thomas, q. 9 On Power, a. 7; on 1, d. 24, q. 1, a. 3; and 1 p., q. 3, a. 3; Capreolus, on 1, d. 24, q. 1; Soncinas, Metaph. 10, q. 13; Javelli, bk. 8, q. 11. And it is gathered from the doctrine of Aristotle, Phys. 4, 6 and 7, where he teaches that number comes to be from the division of the continuous; and On the Soul 2, 6, he asserts that number is sensible per se. But the number of spiritual things neither comes to be from the division of the continuous nor is sensible, because the senses can perceive only bodily things; therefore it is not categorial number in the mind of Aristotle.

> 72 Ratione item probatur: Primò quia omnis species, debet participare naturam sui generis proximi, atque remoti, in eadem linea prædicamentali positi: sed genus proximũ numeri, [p. 352] est quantitas discreta: & remotum quantitas communis, continuæ, atque discretæ: ergo repugnat aliquem esse numerum prædicamentalem, nisi ex his duobus generibus participet. Tunc vltrà, numerus rerum spiritualium ex neutro genere participat, ergo non est species huius prædicamenti. Probatur antecedens: talis numerus non est quantitas, ergo non est quantitas discreta. Euidens est consequentia à superiori ad inferius negatiuè: & antecedens per se notum est.

72 It is likewise proved by reason. First, because every species must participate the nature of its proximate and remote genus, placed in the same categorial line; but the proximate genus of number [p. 352] is discrete quantity, and the remote one common quantity, continuous and discrete; therefore it is repugnant that any number be categorial unless it participates in these two genera. Further: the number of spiritual things participates in neither genus; therefore it is not a species of this category. The antecedent is proved: such a number is not quantity; therefore it is not discrete quantity. The consequence is evident, from the superior to the inferior negatively; and the antecedent is known per se.

> Secundò: quia transcendentia non pertinent ad aliquod speciale prædicamentum, vt de ente, & accidente manifestum est: sed numerus eo modo, quo reperitur in rebus spiritualibus, reperitur in quibuscunque rebus cuiuslibet prædicamenti: ergo transcendentalis est, & non prædicamentalis. Minorem probo: nam sicut dicimus, tres Angelos, aut tres animas; sic dicimus tres albedines, tres relationes, tres actiones, & passiones, sicque de cæteris prædicamentis.

Second: because transcendentals do not pertain to any special category, as is manifest of being and accident; but number, in the way in which it is found in spiritual things, is found in any things whatever of any category; therefore it is transcendental and not categorial. I prove the minor: for just as we say three angels or three souls, so we say three whitenesses, three relations, three actions and passions, and so of the other categories.

> 73 Pro solutione argumentorum oppositę opinionis, notandum est, quòd sicut vnitas sumitur duobus modis, primò, prout vnum est passio entis, & vnitas conuertitur cum entitate: & sic accepta est transcendentalis: quia in omnibus rebus reperitur. Secundò, vt est vnitas specialis, quę fundatur in quantitate rei: & hæc est propria huius prædicamenti. Ita numerus, est duplex, transcendentalis, qui constat ex vnitatibus transcendentalibus: & specialis, qui fit ex quantitatibus: & iste est species quantitatis discretæ, ille vagatur per omnia prædicamenta: & ideo neque ad hoc, neque ad aliquod aliud pertinet.

73 For the solution of the arguments of the opposite opinion it should be noted that, just as unity is taken in two ways: first, as one is an attribute of being, and unity is convertible with entity, and so taken it is transcendental, because it is found in all things; second, as it is a special unity, which is founded on the quantity of a thing, and this is proper to this category: so number is twofold, transcendental, which consists of transcendental unities, and special, which is made of quantities; and the latter is a species of discrete quantity, while the former ranges through all the categories, and therefore pertains neither to this one nor to any other.

> Hæc distinctio explicat sensum sanctorum Patrum, qui, vt constat ex antecedentibus & cõsequentibus, de numero transcendentali loquuntur, non prędicamentali. Et etiam si aliquod verbum eorum videatur significare numerum prædicamentalem, solùm per similitudinem intelligi debet.

This distinction explains the sense of the holy Fathers, who, as is evident from what precedes and what follows, are speaking of transcendental number, not categorial. And even if some word of theirs seems to signify categorial number, it must be understood only by way of likeness.

> Ad argu. Distinguendum est antecedens: quia si de numero prædicamentali intelligatur, non est verum, quòd solùm dicat vnitates quascunque discretas, & numerabiles, secũdùm prius, & posterius: sed debet dicere vnitates speciales, & quantitatiuas, quas cùm non habeat numerus rerum spiritualium, sed transcendentales: non est numerus prædicamentalis, sed transcendentalis.

To the argument. The antecedent must be distinguished: because if it is understood of categorial number, it is not true that it signifies only any discrete unities whatever, numerable according to prior and posterior; rather it must signify special and quantitative unities; and since the number of spiritual things does not have these, but transcendental ones, it is not categorial number, but transcendental.

## QUESTION IX

### Quæst. 9. An oratio sit vera species quantitatis — Whether speech is a true species of quantity.

> QVÆSTIO IX.

[…]

> *An oratio sit vera species quantitatis.*

[…]

> DIfficilior est quæstio de oratione, An sit vera species quantitatis discretæ. Intelligimus autem quæstionem, de [p. 353] sola oratione vocali: nam mentalis, & scripta, non pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum: cùm vtraque sit qualitas, illa naturalis, hæc verò quasi per artem facta: vocalis verò, quæ aut voce humana profertur, vel aliis instrumentis fit, quandam extensionem syllabarum habere videtur: & ideo quærimus de illa: An sit species quantitatis discretæ.

More difficult is the question concerning speech: whether it is a true species of discrete quantity. And we understand the question as concerning [p. 353] spoken speech alone: for mental and written speech do not pertain to this category, since each is a quality, the former natural, the latter as it were made by art; but spoken speech, which is either uttered by the human voice or made by other instruments, seems to have a certain extension of syllables; and therefore we ask concerning it whether it is a species of discrete quantity.

> Et est prima opinio Louaniensium, in expositione huius capitis, qui negant, *orationem esse speciem quantitatis discretæ*, putantes esse quantum quoddam per accidens, sicut album, aut motus: & hanc videtur sequi Caiet. cap. præsenti, & sequuntur moderni omnes, qui numerum excludunt ab hoc prædicamento.

And the first opinion is that of the Louvain commentators, in their exposition of this chapter, who deny that speech is a species of discrete quantity, thinking that it is a certain quantified thing per accidens, like white or motion; and Cajetan seems to follow it, in the present chapter, and all the moderns who exclude number from this category follow it.

> 74 Et probatur, illis omnibus argumentis, quibus probatum est de numero, esse ens per accidens: & ideo non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum q. 6. quæ non sunt hoc loco repetenda,

74 And it is proved by all those arguments by which it was proved of number that it is a being per accidens, and therefore does not pertain to this category, q. 6; which are not to be repeated in this place.

> Sed duobus aliis specialibus probanda est. Primò, Quia hæc tantùm sunt in oratione, nempe soni syllabarum, motus instrumentorum, aut prolationis: per quem fiunt tempora consumpta eiusdem prolationibus, ordo syllabarum, & significatio totius orationis: sed ex nullo horum potest oratio esse quanta per se: ergo non est admittenda ad hoc prædicamentum. Probatur minor: quia soni sunt qualitates: motus quantus per accidens: tempora quanta quidem per se continua, sed quæ non possunt efficere aliam speciem quantitatis discretæ: ordo syllabarum, secundùm longitudinem, & breuitatem, pro libito mutari potest: & ideo non potest efficere quantam per se orationẽ: & longè minùs significatio syllabarum, quam certum est non habere ex propria natura, sed ex libera impositione hominum.

But it must be proved by two other special ones. First, because only these things are in speech: namely the sounds of the syllables; the motion of the instruments or of the utterance, through which come to be the times consumed in that utterance; the order of the syllables; and the signification of the whole speech; but from none of these can speech be quantified per se; therefore it is not to be admitted to this category. The minor is proved: because sounds are qualities; motion is quantified per accidens; times are indeed quantified per se, but continuous ones, which cannot make another species of discrete quantity; the order of the syllables, according to length and shortness, can be changed at will, and therefore cannot make speech quantified per se; and far less the signification of the syllables, which it is certain they do not have from their own nature, but from the free imposition of men.

> Secundò: Quia successiua non possunt habere vnitatem, nisi per continuationem: vt patet in motu, cuius partes, si semel interrumpantur per moram temporis, sic fiunt diuersæ, vt nullo modo efficiant vnum: sed syllabæ sunt quidam motus prolationis instrumentorum interrupti: ergo sunt omnino diuersi, nullam habentes vnionem, aut vnitatem: quare non possunt efficere vnam quantitatem. Et si respondeas, Ordinabiles esse ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius, sicut vnitates numeri: & per talem ordinabilitatem habere vnitatem. Contra hoc est: quia si semel interrupti motus prolationis, sunt ordinabiles secundùm prius, & posterius: ergo etiam si per longum tempus interrumpantur, erunt ordinabiles, vnde si vna syllaba proferatur hodie, & altera post annum, efficient orationem, non minùs, quàm si pòst dimidiam horam proferretur [p. 354]: imò etiam si a diuersis hominibus: quæ non solùm falsa sed absurda videntur.

Second: because successive things cannot have unity except through continuation, as is plain in motion, whose parts, if they are once interrupted by a delay of time, become so diverse that they in no way make one thing; but syllables are certain interrupted motions of the utterance of the instruments; therefore they are altogether diverse, having no union or unity; wherefore they cannot make one quantity. And if you reply that they are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, like the unities of number, and through such orderability have unity, against this is the following: because if motions of utterance once interrupted are orderable according to prior and posterior, then even if they are interrupted for a long time they will be orderable; hence if one syllable is uttered today and another after a year, they will make a speech no less than if it were uttered after half an hour, Z [p. 354] indeed even if by different men: which seem not only false but absurd.

> 75 Secunda opinio est Iauelli in Epitome, in 5. lib. Met. c. 8. distinguentis duplicem considerationem orationis. Nam si consideretur, ait, in ratione extensionis quantitatiuæ, non est oratio distincta à motu, neque quantum per se, sed per accidens, sicut motus: cùm syllabæ non sint aliud, quàm motus quidam prolationis. Si verò consideretur in ratione mensuræ, est quantum per se, & vera species quantitatis discretæ, distincta à numero: cùm sit mensura discreta, & successiua. Et propterea, inquit, considerans Arist. in Dialectica, rationem mensuræ in quantitatibus, docuit *orationem esse speciem quantitatis.* Et probauit etiam ex eadem ratione mensuræ: quia mensuratur, inquit, syllaba longa, & breui. At in Metaph. vbi præcipuè considerabat rationem extensionis eiusdem quantitatis, cùm connumerasset alias species, nullam mentionem orationis fecit, quod probatur ex mente eius, non esse speciem quantitatis in ratione extensionis, sed solùm in ratione mensuræ.

75 The second opinion is that of Javelli, in his Epitome of the Metaph., bk. 5, ch. 8, who distinguishes a twofold consideration of speech. For if it is considered, he says, in the ratio of quantitative extension, speech is not distinct from motion, nor is it quantified per se, but per accidens, like motion, since syllables are nothing other than certain motions of utterance. But if it is considered in the ratio of measure, it is quantified per se, and a true species of discrete quantity, distinct from number, since it is a discrete and successive measure. And therefore, he says, Aristotle, considering in the Dialectic the ratio of measure in quantities, taught that speech is a species of quantity; and he also proved it from the same ratio of measure, because, he says, it is measured by the long and the short syllable. But in the Metaph., where he principally considered the ratio of extension of that same quantity, when he had enumerated the other species he made no mention of speech; by which it is proved, from his mind, that it is not a species of quantity in the ratio of extension, but only in the ratio of measure.

> Tertia opinio tenet, *Orationem esse secundam speciem quantitatis discretæ*: quod Arist. non solùm asseruit, cap. præsenti, sed probauit. Ita D. Th. opusc. 42. & in 4. d. 3. q. vnica, art. 2. ad 5. Albertus Mag. tract. de quantitate, c. 2. Scotus cap. præsenti, q. 8. Soncinas 5. Meta. q. 4. Sotus q. 2. huius capitis, & in eodem Cant. & Tolet. atque moderni plures. Et hæc sententia quamuis difficilis, videtur nobis probabilior, & tenenda.

The third opinion holds that speech is the second species of discrete quantity: which Aristotle not only asserted, in the present chapter, but proved. So St. Thomas, opusc. 42, and on 4, d. 3, the single question, a. 2, ad 5; Albert the Great, the treatise on quantity, ch. 2; Scotus, the present chapter, q. 8; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 4; Soto, q. 2 of this chapter, and in the same place Cant. and Toledo, and many moderns. And this opinion, although difficult, seems to us more probable and to be held.

> 76 Et probatur hac ratione: Oratio constat syllabis verè extensis secundùm prius, & posterius, sicut numerus constat vnitatibus: ergo sicut numerus est species quantitatis discretæ, sic oratio. Probatur antecedẽs: quia syllaba vna longior est, maioremq; habet extensionem soni, quàm alia: non solùm ratione tẽporis consumpti, quod patet esse maius, sed ratione sui, nempe vt est sonus extensus: quemadmodum tres lapides, habent substantiam extensam per quantitatem: & ideo eius ratione efficiunt speciẽ numeri. Quòd verò syllabę sint ordinabiles ab intellectu, secũdùm prius, & posterius, ratione lõgitudinis, aut breuitatis: probatur, quia distincta oratio est, aut distinctus pes carminis ille, qui cõstat vtraque syllaba longa, ab eo, qui constat vtraq; breui, vel vna breui, & altera longa, ex eo quòd distincto modo ordinantur syllabæ: ergo ex se sunt ordinabiles

76 And it is proved by this argument: Speech consists of syllables truly extended according to prior and posterior, as number consists of unities; therefore, just as number is a species of discrete quantity, so is speech. The antecedent is proved: because one syllable is longer, and has a greater extension of sound, than another, not only by reason of the time consumed, which is plainly greater, but by reason of itself, namely as it is an extended sound; just as three stones have a substance extended through quantity, and by reason of it they make a species of number. That syllables are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, by reason of length or shortness, is proved: because the speech, or the foot of verse, which consists of two long syllables is distinct from that which consists of two short ones, or of one short and the other long, from the fact that the syllables are ordered in a distinct way; therefore of themselves they are orderable

#### In quonam sit ponenda quantitas orationis — In what the quantity of speech is to be placed.

> *In quonam sit ponenda quantitas orationis.*

[…]

> 77 TOta difficultas nostræ sententiæ consistit, in explicanda quantitate orationis, assignandáque ratione illa, in [p. 355] catur consistere: circa quam, non eodem modo sentiunt ii, qui nostram sententiam sequuntur.

77 The whole difficulty of our view consists in explaining the quantity of speech and in assigning that ratio in [p. 355] which it is said to consist; concerning which those who follow our view do not think in the same way.

> Sed prima opinio, est multorum modernorum, qui *quantitatem orationis, nec in syllabis, nec in alio vllo ex his, quæ possunt considerari in oratione, consistere docent, sed in motibus prolationis discontinuis, & ordinabilibus ab intellectu*: vt in tribus motibus prolationis, quibus profertur hæc oratio: Dominus, dicunt consistere quantitatem discretam, & successiuam eius,

But the first opinion is that of many moderns, who teach that the quantity of speech consists neither in the syllables nor in anything else of those which can be considered in speech, but in the motions of utterance, discontinuous and orderable by the intellect: as in the three motions of utterance by which this speech, Dominus [Lord], is uttered, they say its discrete and successive quantity consists.

> Hæc tamen sententia falsa est, quod probo hoc arg. Motus est quantum per accidens, ergo numerus plurium motuum, nõ est prædicamentalis Probatur consequentia, à superiori ad inferius negatiuè: numerus trium motuum, non est quantitas per se, ergo nec est quantitas discreta. Secundò, quia numerus motuum, est sicut numerus alborum, aut Angelorum, est transcendentalis, & non prædicamentalis.

This opinion, however, is false, which I prove by this argument: Motion is quantified per accidens; therefore a number of several motions is not categorial. The consequence is proved, from the superior to the inferior negatively: the number of three motions is not quantity per se; therefore neither is it discrete quantity. Second, because the number of motions is like the number of white things or of angels: it is transcendental, and not categorial.

> Ideo secunda opinio, multorum est, *non in syllabis, nec in motibus prolationis earum: sed solùm in temporibus, quibus motus ipsi prolationis, atque etiam syllabæ mensurantur, quantitatem orationis ponens*, in quantum duo, vel tria tempora consumpta in eis, ordinabilia sunt ab intellectu, secundùm prius & posterius.

Therefore the second opinion, that of many, places the quantity of speech not in the syllables, nor in the motions of their utterance, but only in the times by which the motions of the utterance themselves, and also the syllables, are measured, inasmuch as two or three times consumed in them are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior.

> Quod colligunt ex Arist. c. præsenti, qui *orationem esse quantitatem* probauit: quia mensuratur syllaba longa, & breui: sed longitudo, aut breuitas syllabarum, sumitur ex maiori, aut minori tempore, quo mensurantur: ergo in his temporibus consistit quantitas orationis, ex mente Aristotelis.

This they gather from Aristotle, in the present chapter, who proved that speech is a quantity because it is measured by the long and the short syllable; but the length or shortness of syllables is taken from the greater or lesser time by which they are measured; therefore the quantity of speech consists in these times, in the mind of Aristotle.

> Sed nec sententia hæc videtur mihi vera, quod ita probo Sicut numerus, est multitudo vnitatum ordinabilium ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius, ita oratio, est multitudo syllabarum ordinabilium, secundùm longitudinem, & breuitatem, ex quarum diuersitate distinguunt omnes diuersas orationes: sed tempora non sunt syllabæ, imò valde ab eis diuersa: ergo multitudo temporum non potest esse oratio.

But neither does this opinion seem true to me, which I prove thus: Just as number is a multitude of unities orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, so speech is a multitude of syllables orderable according to length and shortness, from whose diversity all distinguish the diverse speeches; but times are not syllables; indeed, they are very different from them; therefore a multitude of times cannot be speech.

> Secundò, Vel tempora distincta constituunt orationem, secundùm se, vel in quantum sunt mensura syllabarum, vterque modus est impossibilis: ergo non possunt orationem constituere. Probatur minor: quia species quantitatis constituuntur per diuersas rationes extensionis: sed tempora ex eo, quòd sint mensura syllabarum, non habent specialem rationem extensionis, distinctam ab ea, quam habent, secundùm quod sunt multa tempora: nam temporibus non aduenit noua ratio extensionis, ex eo, quòd sint mensura syllabarum, sicut nec ex eo quòd sint mensura syllabarum motuum, prolatio namq; syllabarũ, motus quidam localis est instrumentorum, ergo si hoc [p. 356] modo sumpta non efficiunt speciem quantitatis discretæ, nec efficient, vt sunt mensura syllabarum. Quòd verò vt sunt discreta tempora, non efficiant orationem, probatur, quia si sic efficerent orationem: ergo vbicunque reperirentur, etiam sine syllabis eam efficerent. Euidens est consequentia, quia quod alicui conuenit vt talis vbicumque reperiatur, ei conueniet. Et præterea, quia tria tempora, nihil accipiunt à syllabis, ratione cuius efficiant quantitatem discretam: consequens autem falsum est: quia nullus vnquam dixit; nec intelligi potest, quòd tres durationes trium calefactionum, sine oratio.

Second: Either distinct times constitute speech according to themselves, or inasmuch as they are the measure of syllables; each way is impossible; therefore they cannot constitute speech. The minor is proved: because the species of quantity are constituted through diverse rationes of extension; but times, from the fact that they are the measure of syllables, do not have a special ratio of extension distinct from the one they have according as they are many times; for no new ratio of extension accrues to times from their being the measure of syllables, just as none does from their being the measure of motions; for the utterance of syllables is a certain local motion of the instruments: therefore, if this Z ij [p. 356] taken in this way they do not make a species of discrete quantity, neither will they make one as they are the measure of syllables. That distinct times as such do not make speech is proved: because if they did so make speech, then wherever they were found, even without syllables, they would make it. The consequence is evident, because what belongs to something as such will belong to it wherever it is found. And moreover, because three times receive nothing from the syllables by reason of which they could make a discrete quantity. But the consequent is false: because no one has ever said, nor can it be understood, that three durations of three heatings are speech.

> Vt igitur intelligamus, in quo consistat quantitas orationis: Notandum est, in voce duo esse consideranda. Primum, quòd sit sonus, per motum localem linguæ, dentium, ac palati, aliorumque instrumentorum factus. Secundum, est extensio, seu corpulentia eiusdem soni, vel vocis: quæ non est aliud, quàm dilatatio, vel prolongatio eiusdem. Notum est enim, syllabam morosè prolatam, maiorem habere dilatationem, aut prolongationem, quàm eam, quę citò profertur: quin natura ipsa talis est, syllabarum è pluribus literis conflatarum, & quarundam aliarum, vt tardiùs proferantur. v.g. (stirps,) (traps) quàm istæ duæ, (e) a) Eiusmodi igitur dilatatio, aut prolongatio vocis, est quasi corpulentia, vel magnitudo eius, & ita dicitur eius extensio: quemadmodum longitudo, aut latitudo substantiæ, est extensio eius: vnde sicut substantia est extensa per accidens, & longitudo eius aut latitudo, est quantitas, aut extensio per se: ita sonus, aut vox, est extẽsa per accidens, eius tamen dilatatio, prolongatio, & corpulentia, est quantitas per se: & ita ex multis extensionibus syllabarum sibi succedentium, fit oratio: sicut ex multis extensionibus substantiæ, fit numerus. Nec mirum est, suam habere extensionem sonum ita factum, cùm sit qualitas corporea: sicut albedo, & aliæ qualitates, suam habent extensionem, accidentaliter eis conuenientẽ: Hæc autem extensio orationis, quam prolongationem, aut dilatationem soni vocamus: non est alia realiter distincta ab extensione, seu quantitate aeris verberati: sicut nec vox est aliud, quam sonus, ex verberatione aeris, per talia instrumenta causatus & in eodem aere extensus, sed eadem extensio aeris, à qua sonus ipse, (qui qualitas quædam corporea est extenditur. Hęc autem extensio syllabarum, distincta est à motu prolationis, vt constat, & etiam à tempore consumpto in prolatione: sed sub syllaba comprehenditur, & nomine syllabæ significatur: & ideo oratio vocatur, multitudo syllabarum sibi succedentium, vt ordinabiles [p. 357] sunt ab intellectu secundùm prius, & posterius ratione longitudinis, ac breuitatis.

In order, then, that we may understand in what the quantity of speech consists, it should be noted that two things are to be considered in a vocal sound. The first, that it is a sound made through the local motion of the tongue, teeth, and palate, and of the other instruments. The second is the extension or corpulence of that same sound or vocal sound, which is nothing other than its dilation or prolongation. For it is known that a syllable uttered slowly has a greater dilation or prolongation than one which is uttered quickly; indeed, the very nature of syllables composed of several letters, and of certain others, is such that they are uttered more slowly, e.g. (stirps), (traps), than these two, (e), (a). Such a dilation or prolongation of the vocal sound, then, is as it were its corpulence or magnitude, and so it is called its extension: just as the length or breadth of a substance is its extension. Hence, just as substance is extended per accidens, and its length or breadth is quantity or extension per se, so sound or vocal sound is extended per accidens, but its dilation, prolongation, and corpulence is quantity per se. And thus from many extensions of syllables succeeding one another speech comes to be, as from many extensions of substance number comes to be. Nor is it surprising that sound so made has its own extension, since it is a bodily quality: as whiteness and the other qualities have their own extension, belonging to them accidentally. But this extension of speech, which we call the prolongation or dilation of the sound, is not another one really distinct from the extension or quantity of the struck air; just as the vocal sound is not anything other than a sound caused by the striking of the air through such instruments and extended in the same air; but it is the same extension of the air by which the sound itself (which is a certain bodily quality) is extended. And this extension of the syllables is distinct from the motion of utterance, as is evident, and also from the time consumed in the utterance; but it is comprehended under the syllable and signified by the name of syllable. And therefore a multitude of syllables succeeding one another, as orderable [p. 357] by the intellect according to prior and posterior by reason of length and shortness, is called speech.

> 79 Et ex hac doctrina facilè explicatur testimonium Arist. pro secundo modo dicendi, de temporibus adductum: nam argum. eius quo probauit, *orationem esse quantitatem*, quia mensuratur syllaba longa, & breui, quasi ab exteriori signo est: nam tempora mensura sunt extrinseca syllabarũ, sed per talem, mensurationem extrinsecam, cognoscimus propriam extensionem orationis, in magnitudine syllabarum, seu dilatione, aut corpulentia earum consistentem, per quam formaliter dicuntur longæ, aut breues formaliter, & quasi intrinsecè.

79 And from this doctrine the testimony of Aristotle adduced for the second way of speaking, concerning times, is easily explained: for his argument by which he proved that speech is a quantity, because it is measured by the long and the short syllable, is as it were from an exterior sign: for times are an extrinsic measure of the syllables, but through such extrinsic measuring we know the proper extension of speech, consisting in the magnitude of the syllables, or in their dilation or corpulence, through which they are formally called long or short, formally and as it were intrinsically.

> Facilè etiam soluuntur argumenta primæ opinionis: Nam ad primum respondetur, quòd in antecedenti non numerantur sufficienter ea, quæ sunt in oratione, sed præcipuum relinquitur: nempe extensio, seu dilatio, & corpulentia soni, in qua consistit propria quantitas syllabarum: sicut in latitudine, aut profunditate, consistit extensio substantiæ, aut aliarum qualitatum.

The arguments of the first opinion are also easily solved. For to the first the reply is that in the antecedent the things that are in speech are not sufficiently enumerated, but the principal one is left out, namely the extension or dilation and corpulence of the sound, in which the proper quantity of syllables consists; just as the extension of substance, or of other qualities, consists in breadth or depth.

> Ad secundum, Neganda est minor: quòd syllabæ sint motus prolationis, sed sunt soni quidam dearticulati, per motus prolationum facti: de quibus neganda est: quòd non habeant vnitatem sufficientem, ad constituendam orationem: habent enim eandem, quam numeru: nempe ordinabiles esse ab intellectu, secundùm prius, & posterius, pro ratione longitudinis, & breuitatis. Negandum est etiam: quòd syllaba hodie prolata, possit ordinari in modum orationis: cum ea, quæ profertur post annum: quia cùm syllabæ sint ordinabiles ab intellectu proferentis, & in ordine ad concentum, & harmoniam, humanam, interruptionem habere debent, in ordine ad talem finem: hoc est, tantam, & non maiorem, quæ repugnet eidem fini: repugnaret autem, si secunda proferretur post annum: imò si post mensem, aut diem: & fortè si post horam: quare non erunt ordinabiles cum tanta interruptione, nec efficiens orationem.

To the second. The minor must be denied, namely that syllables are motions of utterance; rather they are certain articulated sounds, made through the motions of utterance; of which it must be denied that they do not have a unity sufficient to constitute speech: for they have the same unity as number, namely that they are orderable by the intellect according to prior and posterior, by reason of length and shortness. It must also be denied that a syllable uttered today can be ordered in the manner of speech with one that is uttered after a year: because, since syllables are orderable by the intellect of the one uttering them, and in order to human concord and harmony, they must have an interruption in order to such an end, that is, so much and no greater as would be repugnant to that same end; and it would be repugnant if the second were uttered after a year, indeed if after a month or a day, and perhaps if after an hour. Wherefore they will not be orderable with so great an interruption, nor make speech.

## QUESTION X

> QVÆSTIO X.

[…]

> *An si daretur linea, superficies, aut corpus, vel alia quantitas actu infinita, collocaretur in hoc prædicamento.*

Whether, if a line, surface, or body, or another quantity infinite in act were given, it would be placed in this category.

> 80 QVæstio hæc nõ est absoluta, sed cõditionalis: quia non disputamus modò, An possibile sit, quòd detur aliqua quantitas actu infinita, vel impossibile: sed titulus quæstionis sub conditione quærit; An si daretur per possibile, vel impossibile [p. 358], quantitas aliqua actu infinita, collocaretur in hoc prædicamento.

80 This question is not absolute but conditional: because we are not now disputing whether it is possible or impossible that some quantity infinite in act be given; but the title of the question asks under a condition: whether, if it were given, whether possibly or impossibly, Z iij [p. 358] some quantity infinite in act, it would be placed in this category.

> Et pars negatiua, quòd non collocaretur in prædicamento, Probatur testimonio Arist. & D. Tho. Arist. enim 5. lib. Meta. tex. 10. ita ait: *Multitudo igitur quantum quid, si numerabilis est, magnitudo verò, si mensurabilis.* Sed si multitudo daretur actu infinita, non esset numerabilis: nec corpus actu infinitum, mensurabile: ergo non essent quanta ex mente Arist. nec proinde collocarentur in hoc prædicamento.

And the negative part, that it would not be placed in the category, is proved by the testimony of Aristotle and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, Metaph. 5, text 10, speaks thus: A multitude, then, is a quantity if it is numerable; and a magnitude, if it is measurable. But if a multitude infinite in act were given, it would not be numerable, nor would a body infinite in act be measurable; therefore they would not be quantified things in the mind of Aristotle, nor consequently would they be placed in this category.

> Et D Tho in Comment. eiusdem loci, lect. 15. docet: quòd si longitudo esset actu infinita, non esset linea: quia linea est longitudo mensurabilis, & ideo in definitione lineæ ponitur, quòd sit longitudo, clausa duobus extremis punctis.

And St. Thomas, in his Commentary on the same place, lect. 15, teaches that if a length were infinite in act, it would not be a line: because a line is a measurable length, and therefore it is placed in the definition of line that it is a length closed by two extreme points.

> 81 Et ratione probatur, Primò, quia ita se habet quantitas, in suo ordine prædicamentali, sicut substantia in suo, sed substantia actu infinita, qualis est Deus, non ponitur in prędicamento: sicut diximus in 2. qu. præcedentis capitis: ergo nec poneretur infinita quantitas in prædicamento.

81 And it is proved by reason. First, because quantity stands in its categorial order as substance does in its own; but a substance infinite in act, such as God is, is not placed in the category, as we said in q. 2 of the preceding chapter; therefore neither would an infinite quantity be placed in the category.

> Secundò: Eadem est ratio de quantitate continua, & discreta, quantum pertinet ad præsentem quæst. sed si daretur multitudo infinita corporum, non poneretur in prædicamento, sub genere quantitatis discretæ: ergo si daretur quantitas continua actu infinita, non poneretur in prædicamento, sub genere quantitatis continuæ. Minor probatur: quia species numeri variantur, per additionem vnitatis: vt si binario addideris vnam, transit iam in aliam speciem ternarij: si ergo daretur multitudo actu infinita, non haberet determinatam speciem, & quod non habet determinatam speciem, non potest esse sub determinato genere: ergo nec sub determinato prędicamento. Quare infinita multitudo, non posset in hoc prædicamento collocari.

Second: The ratio of continuous and discrete quantity is the same, as far as pertains to the present question; but if an infinite multitude of bodies were given, it would not be placed in the category under the genus of discrete quantity; therefore, if a continuous quantity infinite in act were given, it would not be placed in the category under the genus of continuous quantity. The minor is proved: because the species of number are varied by the addition of a unity: as, if you add one to two, it passes at once into another species, of three; if, therefore, a multitude infinite in act were given, it would not have a determinate species; and what does not have a determinate species cannot be under a determinate genus; therefore neither under a determinate category. Wherefore an infinite multitude could not be placed in this category.

> Communis tamen sententia scholæ tenet, Quòd si daretur linea vel corpus, actu infinitum, poneretur in hoc prędicamento, non minùs, quàm corpus finitum. Ita Soncinas 5. Meta. qu. 15. Iauellus ibidem, quæst. 17. Durand. in 4. d. 3. quæst. 3. Niphus 8. lib. Topicorum, loco 73. Sotus quæst. prima huius prædicamenti,

The common opinion of the school, however, holds that if a line or body infinite in act were given, it would be placed in this category no less than a finite body. So Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 15; Javelli, in the same place, q. 17; Durandus, on 4, d. 5, q. 3; Nifo, Topics 8, topic 73; Soto, q. 1 of this category.

> Probatur testimonio Aristotelis, 8. lib. Topicorum, loco 73. vbi docet, *Lineam finitam, & infinitam, esse eiusdem speciei*: ex quo sequitur, idem habere genus, & differentiam: & ideo in eodem prædicamento collocari: & hoc idem sentit D. Tho. 1. par. qu. 58. ar. 8. ad 2.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Topics 8, topic 73, where he teaches that a finite and an infinite line are of the same species: from which it follows that they have the same genus and difference, and therefore are placed in the same category. And St. Thomas holds this same, 1 p., q. 58, a. 8, ad 2.

> Idem probatur ratione: Quia quidquid componitur ex genere [p. 359], & differentia, collocatur in prædicamento: sed linea actu infinita, componeretur ex genere, & differentia: ergo collocaretur in hoc prædicamẽto. Probatur minor, quia genus lineæ, est quantitas continua: differentia verò, extensio secundùm dimensionem formalem lõgitudinis: sed linea infinita, vtrumque haberet: nam esset quantitas continua: quia copularetur punctis: & esset extensa secundùm formalem dimensionem longitudinis: ergo esset in hoc prędicamento. Et si respondeas, esse quantitatem finitam, ex qua efficitur prædicamentum, non infinitam, & ideo excludi à prædicamento. Contra hoc est: quòd *esse actu infinitam*, solùm est habere partes integrantes, actu infinitas: sed partes integrantes, non pertinent ad essentiam rei, vt per se est manifestum: ergo etiam si sint actu infinitæ, non variabunt essentiã lineæ, sed erit linea infinita eiusdem speciei, cum linea finita, vt ex Arist. adduximus. Et ideo collocabitur sub eodẽ genere, & erit in eodem prædicamento.

The same is proved by reason: Because whatever is composed of genus [p. 359] and difference is placed in a category; but a line infinite in act would be composed of genus and difference; therefore it would be placed in this category. The minor is proved: because the genus of line is continuous quantity, and its difference extension according to the formal dimension of length; but an infinite line would have both: for it would be a continuous quantity, because it would be joined by points; and it would be extended according to the formal dimension of length; therefore it would be in this category. And if you reply that it is finite quantity, not infinite, from which the category is made, and that therefore it is excluded from the category, against this is the following: that being infinite in act is only having integral parts infinite in act; but integral parts do not pertain to the essence of a thing, as is manifest of itself; therefore, even if they are infinite in act, they will not vary the essence of line, but the infinite line will be of the same species as the finite line, as we adduced from Aristotle. And therefore it will be placed under the same genus, and will be in the same category.

> 83 Pro solutione argumentorum, notandum est: aliud esse, quòd aliquid sit infinitum secũdùm substantiam, aliud, secundùm aliquam rationem accidentalem: quia substantia dicit essentiam rei: ergo idem est aliquid esse infinitum, secundùm substantiam, & esse infinitum secundùm essentiam: & quod est infinitum secundùm essentiam, est infinitum simpliciter: sed quod est infinitum secundùm rationem accidentalem, potest esse finitum secundùm essentiam: quia accidentia sunt extra essentiam rei. Vnde sequitur, quòd cùm res omnes collocentur in prædicamento, secundùm essentias, si sint infinitæ secundùm essentiam, non possint collocari in prædicamento. Cuius hæc est ratio: quia prædicamenta sunt gradus essendi, finitæ, ac limitatæ perfectionis: & quæ in eis collocantur, sub genere supremo, debent esse composita ex determinato genere, & determinata differentia, continente gradum limitatum perfectionis, sub tali genere: ergo quod est infinitum secundùm essentiam, nec potest collocari sub determinato genere, nec constitui per determinatam differentiam: & cõsequenter nec collocari in determinato prædicamento. Sed quæ solùm sunt infinita, secundùm rationem accidentalem, bene possunt comprehendi sub determinato genere, & componi etiam ex determinata differentia: & ideo collocari in prædicamento: quia cùm ratio accidentalis extra essentiam sit, eam non variat, sed sub propria limitatione relinquit. Esse autem lineam, vel corpus actu infinitum, ratio accidentalis est: quia non est aliud, quàm habere plures partes integrantes, ex quibus non variatur essentia, nec in perfectione crescit.

83 For the solution of the arguments it should be noted that it is one thing for something to be infinite according to substance, another according to some accidental ratio: because substance signifies the essence of a thing; therefore it is the same for something to be infinite according to substance and to be infinite according to essence; and what is infinite according to essence is infinite simply; but what is infinite according to an accidental ratio can be finite according to essence, because accidents are outside the essence of a thing. Hence it follows that, since all things are placed in a category according to their essences, if they are infinite according to essence they cannot be placed in a category. The reason for this is: because the categories are grades of being, of finite and limited perfection; and the things placed in them under the supreme genus must be composed of a determinate genus and a determinate difference containing a limited grade of perfection under such a genus; therefore what is infinite according to essence can neither be placed under a determinate genus, nor be constituted by a determinate difference, and consequently cannot be placed in a determinate category. But things which are infinite only according to an accidental ratio can well be comprehended under a determinate genus, and also be composed of a determinate difference, and therefore be placed in a category: because, since the accidental ratio is outside the essence, it does not vary it, but leaves it under its proper limitation. And for a line or body to be infinite in act is an accidental ratio: because it is nothing other than having more integral parts, from which the essence is not varied, nor does it grow in perfection. Z iiij

[p. 360]

> 84 Vt si corpus plures aut maiores partes integrantes habeat, non est propter eas perfectius alio, quod pauciores, vel minores habet, sed solùm accidentaliter: ergo habere partes infinitas, etiam est perfectio accidentalis: à qua non variatur essentia, & ideo non minùs erit finita & limitata ad certum genus, atque ad prædicamentum.

84 As, if a body has more or greater integral parts, it is not on their account more perfect than another which has fewer or smaller ones, except only accidentally; therefore having infinite parts is also an accidental perfection, by which the essence is not varied; and therefore it will be no less finite and limited to a certain genus and to a category.

> Ad testimonia Aristotelis, & D. Tho. Respondetur, vtrunque loqui de quantitatibus existentibus, quæ sunt actu finitæ. Quid vero sentiant de infinitis, si darentur, quantum ad collocationem in prædicamento, in aliis locis à nobis citatis, pro communi sententia, explicant: asseruntque non minùs in prædicamento collocari, quàm alias quantitates actu finitas. Illa verò definitio lineæ, mathematicorum est, qui de solis lineis finitis agunt, & ideo eas solùm describunt.

To the testimonies of Aristotle and St. Thomas the reply is that each is speaking of existing quantities, which are finite in act. But what they think of infinite ones, if they were given, as regards their placement in the category, they explain in other places cited by us for the common opinion; and they assert that they are placed in the category no less than other quantities finite in act. That definition of line, however, is the mathematicians’, who deal only with finite lines and therefore describe only these.

> Ad primum arg. Distinguendum est antecedens: quia substantia, & quantitas, duobus modis cõsiderari possunt: aut secundùm rationem finiti, & infiniti: & hoc modo, non ita se habet quantitatis ad prædicamentum, sicut substantia: quia hæc si actu sit infinita, non potest esse sub terminato genere, nec componi ex genere, & differentia, & ideo nec in prædicamento collocari: bene tamen potest omnia hæc habere quantitas infinita: & rationem huius discriminis tradidimus iam. Si verò considerentur secundùm ordinem prædicamentalem, eodem modo ordinantur, per diuisionem generum, in suas species.

To the first argument. The antecedent must be distinguished: because substance and quantity can be considered in two ways. Either according to the ratio of finite and infinite; and in this way quantity does not stand to the category as substance does: because the latter, if it is infinite in act, cannot be under a determinate genus, nor be composed of genus and difference, and therefore cannot be placed in a category either; but infinite quantity can well have all these, and we have already given the reason for this difference. But if they are considered according to the categorial order, they are ordered in the same way, through the division of genera into their species.

### An numerus infinitus esset in prædicamento — Whether infinite number would be in the category.

> *An numerus infinitus esset in prædicamento.*

[…]

> 85 SEd an eadem sit ratio, de quantitate continua, & discreta, ita vt sicut continua, actu infinita, collocaretur in prædicamento, ita etiam discreta, vt numerus infinitus, non est certum. Nam Soncinas, vbi suprà, eandem asserit rationem esse de vtraque. Et probat; quia sicut lineam esse actu infinitam, solùm est habere plures partes integrantes; quod non pertinet ad eius essentiam: ita numerum esse actu infinitum, solum est habere plures vnitates, quæ sunt partes integrantes eius: ergo sicut linea actu infinita esset in prædicamento: ita numerus actu infinitus.

85 But whether the ratio is the same for continuous and discrete quantity, so that, just as continuous quantity infinite in act would be placed in the category, so also would discrete quantity, such as an infinite number, is not certain. For Soncinas, in the place cited above, asserts that the ratio is the same for both. And he proves it: because, just as for a line to be infinite in act is only to have more integral parts, which does not pertain to its essence, so for a number to be infinite in act is only to have more unities, which are its integral parts; therefore, just as a line infinite in act would be in the category, so would a number infinite in act.

> Ego verò contrarium sentio: *Quòd si daretur multitudo corporum actu infinita, non esset per se collocanda in hoc prædicamento.* Quod colligo ex doctrina Aristot. 8. lib. Meta. tex. 15. vbi de numero ita loquitur: *Quemadmodum de numero, ablato aut addito aliquo, ex quibus numerus est, non est ampliùs idem numerus, sed diuersus, etiam si minimum auferatur, aut addatur: ita nec definitio [p. 361], nec ipsum quid erat esse, erit ampliùs, ablato aliquo, aut addito*, &c. Ex quibus verbis sequitur manifesta differentia inter quãtitatem continuam, & discretam, in eo, quòd continua per additionem alicuius partis, vel plurium, non variatur, sed eadem linea, vel corpus permanet: numerus verò per additionem vnitatis variatur: vnde intelligitur, vnitates non omnino se habere in numero, tanquam partes integrantes: sed ita esse fundamentum generis, & differentiæ, vt per additionem, vel detractionem vnitatis, varietur differentia, & species numeri. Cuius ratio satis probabilis est: quia addita vnitate, variatur dispositio totius numeri, atque adeo discretio eius, seu discreta extensio, quæ consistebat in tali dispositione vnitatum: vt extensio specialis ternarij, in eo, quòd duæ sint dispositæ sub tertia, in qua consistit differentia essentialis eius: & ideò addita vnitate, soluitur species numeri, & fit alia. Et quòd hæc sit mens Aritelis, non est dubium: quia si non defineret esse species numeri, vel non transiret in aliam, non teneret similitudo numerorum cum speciebus, vt per se est manifestum.

But I hold the contrary: that if a multitude of bodies infinite in act were given, it would not be per se to be placed in this category. This I gather from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph. 8, text 15, where he speaks thus of number: Just as with number, when something of those of which the number consists is taken away or added, it is no longer the same number, but a different one, even if the least is taken away or added, so neither the definition [p. 361] nor the what-it-was-to-be itself will any longer remain, once something has been taken away or added, etc. From these words there follows a manifest difference between continuous and discrete quantity, in that continuous quantity is not varied by the addition of some part, or of several, but the same line or body remains; whereas number is varied by the addition of a unit. From which it is understood that the units are not related in number altogether as integral parts, but are the foundation of the genus and difference in such a way that through the addition or subtraction of a unit the difference and the species of number is varied. The reason for this is quite probable: because when a unit is added, the disposition of the whole number is varied, and so too its discreteness, or discrete extension, which consisted in such a disposition of the units: as the specific extension of the ternary consists in this, that two are disposed under a third, in which its essential difference consists; and therefore, when a unit is added, the species of number is dissolved, and another comes to be. And that this is the mind of Aristotle is not doubtful: because if it did not cease to be a species of number, or did not pass into another, the likeness of numbers with species would not hold, as is manifest of itself.

> 86 Vnde ex hoc colligitur, numerum apud Aristotelem, esse speciem subalternam, quæ diuiditur tanquam genus, in binarium, ternarium, & reliquos: qui omnes sunt species infimæ, solùm habentes sub se indiuidua: vt ternarius, hunc & illum ternarium.

86 Hence from this it is gathered that number, in Aristotle’s view, is a subalternate species, which is divided as a genus into the binary, the ternary, and the rest: all of which are lowest species, having under them only individuals: as the ternary has this and that ternary.

> Colligitur tandem, numerum actu infinitum non collocari in prædicamento. Quod sic probo: Addita vnitate mutatur species numeri, & fit alia: ergo additis vnitatibus in infinitum, crescet etiam in infinitum perfectio essentialis numeri: & ideo numerus actu infinitus, habebit essentialem perfectionem actu infinitam, in ratione quantitatis discretæ: quare non poterit habere speciem: quia species, constituitur per differentiam determinatæ perfectionis: nec erit sub genere, aut prædicamento.

It is gathered, finally, that number infinite in act is not placed in the category. I prove it thus: When a unit is added, the species of number is changed, and another comes to be; therefore, when units are added to infinity, the essential perfection of number will also grow to infinity; and therefore number infinite in act will have an essential perfection infinite in act in the ratio of discrete quantity: wherefore it will not be able to have a species, because a species is constituted through a difference of determinate perfection; nor will it be under a genus or a category.

> Secundò: Differentia numeri sumitur ex vnitatibus, ordinabilibus secundùm prius, & posterius, ita vt sub aliqua ordinentur cæteræ, tanquam ei præsuppositæ: sed vnitates actu infinitæ, non sunt ordinabiles ab intellectu, ergo non possunt constituere determinatam speciem numeri: & quod non est determinatum secundùm speciem, non potest esse sub genere: ergo nec erit in prædicamento.
