Probatur minor, quia inter infinita actu, non est dabilis determinata vnitas, sub qua ordinentur cęteræ: ergo nec erunt ordinabiles ab intellectu.

Second: The difference of number is taken from units orderable according to prior and posterior, so that the rest are ordered under some one, as presupposed to it; but units infinite in act are not orderable by the intellect; therefore they cannot constitute a determinate species of number; and what is not determinate according to species cannot be under a genus; therefore neither will it be in the category. The minor is proved: because among things infinite in act no determinate unit can be given under which the rest may be ordered; therefore neither will they be orderable by the intellect.

> Argumentum verò, pro opposita sententia de quantitate continua, ex doctrina à nobis tradita, solutum est.

But the argument for the opposite view concerning continuous quantity has been solved from the doctrine we have handed down.

[p. 362]

## LAST QUESTION

### Quæst. 11. An quantitas sit res distincta à substantia corporea, & cæteris accidentibus absolutis — Whether quantity is a thing distinct from corporeal substance and from the other absolute accidents.

> QVÆSTIO VLTIMA.

[…]

> *An quantitas sit res distincta à substantia corporea, & cæteris accidentibus absolutis.*

[…]

> 87 NOn solùm de distinctione reali quantitatis à substantia corporea quærimus, sed etiam ab aliis accidentibus absolutis, quibus tribuit extensionem partium, vt à qualitatibus: quia eadem est ratio de illis, ac de substantia.

87 We inquire not only about the real distinction of quantity from corporeal substance, but also from the other absolute accidents to which it gives extension of parts, as from qualities: because the ratio is the same for them as for substance.

> Et prima opinio: Negat esse distinctam, quam tenuerunt Ocham, in sua Dialectica, cap. de quantitate, in 4. q. 4. quodlib. etiam 4. q. 30. & in tract. de venerabili Sacramento Eucharistiæ, per plura capita: quibus locis affirmat, quantitatem esse ipsammet substantiam: prout habet partes situ disiunctas, & locabiles, diuersisque partibus loci correspondentes. Gabriel. in 4. d. 10. q. vnica, & d. 12. q. 1. art. 1. & lect. 43. super canonem Missæ. Adamus in 4. q. 5. Aureolus apud Capreol. in 2. d. 10. quæst. vnica, art. 1. & videtur fuisse sententia antiquorum Philosophorum, vt Platonis, qui, vt affirmat Arist. 1. lib. Metaph. tex. 5. loquens de materiali principio rerum posuit *vnam materiam pro rebus naturalibus*: cuius differentias esse dicebat *magnum, & paruum*, sentiens, *Eandem rem esse materiam, & quantitatem.*

And the first opinion denies that it is distinct. It was held by Ockham, in his Dialectic, the chapter on quantity; on 4, q. 4; Quodlibet 4, q. 30 also; and in the treatise on the venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, through several chapters: in which places he affirms that quantity is substance itself, inasmuch as it has parts disjoined in position and locatable, and corresponding to the different parts of place. Gabriel on 4, d. 10, single q., and d. 12, q. 1, a. 1, and lect. 45 on the Canon of the Mass; Adam on 4, q. 5; Aureolus in Capreolus on 2, d. 10, single quest., a. 1. And it seems to have been the opinion of the ancient Philosophers, such as Plato, who, as Aristotle affirms in Metaph. 1, text 5, speaking of the material principle of things, posited one matter for natural things, whose differences he said were the great and the small, meaning that matter and quantity are the same thing.

> 88 Et ratione probatur. Primò: Quia Deus potest separare substantiam corpoream, ab omni accidente absoluto, cùm ab eo non dependeat essentialiter: ergo si quantitas est accidens absolutum, realiter à substantia distinctum, poterit separari ab ea substantia: & tunc, si manet sine quantitate, quæritur, an haberet partes loco distinctas, sicut prius, vel non si dicas habere, sequitur, non habere extensionem à quantitate, sed à se esse extensam, & occupatiuam loci: quod est esse ipsammet quantitatem, & ab ea non distingui. Si verò dixeris, non habere, sequitur, partes eius, loco esse coniunctas: quòd est impossibile: quia non potuerunt coniungi, cùm priùs essent separatæ, nisi pet motum localem, cuius non sunt capaces sine quantitate: ergo ab ea non distinguuntur realiter.

88 And it is proved by reason. First: Because God can separate corporeal substance from every absolute accident, since it does not depend on it essentially; therefore, if quantity is an absolute accident really distinct from substance, it will be able to be separated from that substance. And then, if it remains without quantity, it is asked whether it would have parts distinct in place, as before, or not. If you say that it would have them, it follows that it does not have extension from quantity, but is extended and occupies place of itself: which is to be quantity itself, and not to be distinct from it. But if you say that it would not have them, it follows that its parts are conjoined in place: which is impossible, because, since they were separated before, they could not have been conjoined except through local motion, of which they are not capable without quantity; therefore they are not really distinguished from it.

> Secundò: Si quantitas est res distincta à substantia, ei inhærebit: & tunc, vel recipitur tota quantitas, in tota substantia, & pars in parte, vel tota in tota substantia, & tota etiam in qualibet eius parte, eo modo, quo anima rationalis, recipitur tota in toto corpore per informationem, & tota etiam in qualibet parte: sed hoc vltimum repugnat accidenti corporeo, ac diuisibili, habenti partes integrantes: ergo necessarium est primum. [p. 363] Ex quo sequitur, substantiam habere à se partes integrantes, & non à quantitate, cùm partes eius præsupponantur partibus quantitatis, tanquam subiecta, in quibus recipiuntur: sed nihil habet à se partes integrantes, nisi sola quantitas, à qua cætera eas recipiunt: ergo substantia eas habens à se, erit ipsamet quantitas, & non distinguetur ab eo realiter.

Second: If quantity is a thing distinct from substance, it will inhere in it; and then either the whole quantity is received in the whole substance and part in part, or the whole in the whole substance and the whole also in each of its parts, in the way in which the rational soul is received whole in the whole body through information and whole also in each part. But this last is repugnant to a corporeal and divisible accident having integral parts; therefore the first is necessary, [p. 363] From which it follows that substance has integral parts of itself, and not from quantity, since its parts are presupposed to the parts of quantity as subjects in which they are received; but nothing has integral parts of itself except quantity alone, from which the other things receive them; therefore substance, having them of itself, will be quantity itself, and will not be distinguished from it really.

> 89 Secunda opinio tenet: *Quantitatem distingui realiter à substantia, & cæteris accidentibus absolutis.* Ita D. Aug. 5. lib. de Trinitate, c. 10 D. Th. 5. Meta. lect. 15. in fine, Scotus in 2. d. 2. quæst. 9. & in 4. d. 14. q. 2. Rich. in 4. d. 12. art. 1. q. 1. Duran. & Argengentinas ibidem, q. 5. Ægydius Roma, in 1. d. 2. q. 2. Albertus Magnus 5. Physic. tract. 2. art. 4. Socin. 5. Meta. q. 19. & cæteri interpretes, Arist. c. præsenti. Et hæc est vera, & tenenda.

89 The second opinion holds: Quantity is distinguished really from substance and from the other absolute accidents. So St. Augustine, On the Trinity 5, ch. 10; St. Thomas, Metaph. 5, lect. 15, at the end; Scotus on 2, d. 2, quest. 9, and on 4, d. 14, q. 2; Richard on 4, d. 12, a. 1, q. 1; Durandus and Thomas of Strasbourg in the same place, q. 5; Giles of Rome on 1, d. 2, q. 4; Albert the Great, Phys. 5, tract. 2, a. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 19; and the other interpreters of Aristotle in the present chapter. And this is true and to be held.

> Colligitur euidenter ex doctrina Arist. 1. lib. Physic. tex 15. vbi ita arguit, contra Melissum antiquum Philosophum, ponentem, *Vnum tantùm principium rerum naturalium, & illud infinitum. Si vnum tantùm est principium infinitum, cùm finitum, vel infinitum sit propria passio quantitatis, sequitur præter substantiam, continere etiam quantitatem: & ideo non esse vnam rem, aut vnum principium, sed multiplex*, &c. Quod argum. patet nihil probare: nisi quantitas distinguatur realiter à substantia: ergo ex mente Aristo. realiter distinguitur Et lib. 2. de Anima, tex. 65. docet, *Substantiam esse sensibilem per accidens, quantitatem verò per se*: quod non potest esse verum, sine distinctione reali.

It is gathered evidently from the doctrine of Aristotle, Phys. 1, text 15, where he argues thus against Melissus, an ancient Philosopher, who posited only one principle of natural things, and that infinite: If there is only one principle, and infinite, since the finite or the infinite is a proper attribute of quantity, it follows that besides substance there is also quantity, and that therefore there is not one thing or one principle, but a manifold one, etc. Which argument plainly would prove nothing unless quantity were distinguished really from substance; therefore, in the mind of Aristotle, it is really distinguished. And in On the Soul 2, text 65, he teaches that substance is sensible per accidens, but quantity per se: which cannot be true without a real distinction.

> Idem probatur duplici ratione. Primò: Quia naturaliter repugnat plures magnitudines aut quantitates esse, in eodem loco: quia hoc nõ posset esse sine penetratione earum, naturaliter impossibili: ex eo, quòd quælibet est occupatiua distincti loci, & nata appellere aliam ab eodem: sed vtrumque sequitur, si quantitas non distinguatur realiter à substantia, & accidentibus absolutis: ergo necesse est realiter distingui. Probatur minor: Quia si quantitas est idem realiter cum substantia, & albedine in ea existente, ergo quælibet habebit propriam, & distinctam magnitudinem, atque extensionem ab alia: sed constat esse in eodem loco, ergo se penetrabunt.

The same is proved by a twofold reason. First: Because it is naturally repugnant that several magnitudes or quantities be in the same place, since this could not be without their penetration, which is naturally impossible, from the fact that each occupies a distinct place and is naturally apt to expel another from the same; but both follow if quantity is not distinguished really from substance and the absolute accidents; therefore it is necessary that it be really distinguished. The minor is proved: Because if quantity is the same really with substance, and with the whiteness existing in it, then each will have its own magnitude and extension, distinct from the other; but it is established that they are in the same place; therefore they will penetrate one another.

> Secundò: Quia certum est in fide Catholica, in Eucharistia non manere substantiam panis, sed totam conuerti in corpus Christi, at experientia visus, & tactus, docet, remanere eandem quantitatem panis: ergo separatur realiter quantitas à substantia. Et quæ ita se habent, vt vnum possit esse sine alio, distinguuntur realiter: ergo distinguitur realiter quantitas à substantia. Vbi illud obiter aduerto, periculosum esse negare, quòd in Eucharistia non remaneat eadem quantitas [p. 364] panis, & asserere, corpus illud quantum, specierum Sacramentalium, non esse dimensiones, vel quantitatem veram huius prædicamenti, sed propriam extensionem aliorum accidentium, vt albedinis, & aliorum.

Second: Because it is certain in the Catholic faith that in the Eucharist the substance of the bread does not remain, but is wholly converted into the body of Christ; yet the experience of sight and touch teaches that the same quantity of the bread remains; therefore quantity is separated really from substance. And things that are so related that one can be without the other are distinguished really; therefore quantity is distinguished really from substance. Here I note in passing that it is dangerous to deny that in the Eucharist there remains the same quantity [p. 364] of the bread, and to assert that that quantified body of the sacramental species is not the dimensions or true quantity of this category, but the proper extension of the other accidents, such as of whiteness and the others.

> Ad primum arg. Concedimus primum enthymema: ad id verò quod postea quæritur, An substantia permanens sine quantitate, haberet partes occupantes locum, vel separatas secundùm locum: respondeo non occupare locum substantiam sic permanentem, nec eius partes: nec habere extensionem localem: sed modum indiuisibilem, quantum ad occupandum locum pertinet: nec tamen coniungi partes per motum localem: quia nec positiuè essent coniunctæ coniunctione locali sed negatiuè tantùm, ex eo, quòd ablata quantitate, nullam habent distantiam, aut ordinem localem. Sed de his in libris Physicorum, ex professo disputamus.

To the first argument: We grant the first enthymeme. But to what is asked afterwards, whether substance remaining without quantity would have parts occupying place, or separated according to place, I reply that substance so remaining does not occupy place, nor do its parts; nor does it have local extension, but an indivisible mode, as far as occupying place is concerned. Nor, however, are the parts conjoined through local motion: because they would not be positively conjoined by a local conjunction, but only negatively, from the fact that, quantity being taken away, they have no distance or local order. But we dispute these things expressly in the books of the Physics.

> Ad secundum, Concedimus, substantiam habere proprias partes integrantes entitatiuas: sed non extensas, nec loci occupatiuas, quæ tamen extenduntur à quantitate in eis recepta. In his ergo partibus recipiuntur partes quantitatis: & ita tota quantitas recipitur in tota substantia, & partes in partibus. Negamus tamen consequentiam: quòd substantia sit ipsamet quantitas: quia aliud est habere per se partes integrantes entitatiuas, aliud partes extensionis: & primum conceditur substantiæ, & accidentibus absolutis, secundum verò soli quantitati, à qua omnia recipiunt extensionem: quod sufficit ad distinctionem realem.

To the second: We grant that substance has its own integral entitative parts, but not extended nor occupying place, which nevertheless are extended by the quantity received in them. In these parts, then, the parts of quantity are received; and so the whole quantity is received in the whole substance, and the parts in the parts. We deny, however, the consequence, that substance is quantity itself: because it is one thing to have integral entitative parts per se, another to have parts of extension; and the first is granted to substance and to the absolute accidents, but the second to quantity alone, from which all things receive extension: which suffices for a real distinction.

## CHAPTER VII

### CAP. VII. Continens prædicamentum ad aliquid, cum exposit. text. — Containing the category of relation.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Ad aliquid verò talia dicuntur, quæcunque hæc ipsa, quæ sunt, aliorum esse dicuntur, &c.*

Those things are called relatives which, the very things that they are, are said to be of others, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 1 INtentum Arist. capite præsenti est, explicare naturam relatiuorum. Diuiditur autem caput hoc, in tres partes. In quarum prima, definitionem relatiuorum, quæ suo tempore in scholis circumferebatur, proponit, cum quatuor proprietatibus, quæ ex ea sequuntur. In secunda, dubium quoddam circa eãdem definitionem; [p. 365] ex cuius solutione minùs bonam esse probat. Et tandem in tertia, propriam definitionem, ex qua veram proprietatem relatiuorum colligit.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na1 T          ture of relatives. And this chapter is divided into three parts. In the first of these he proposes the definition of relatives which was going around in the schools in his time, with four properties which follow from it. In the second, a certain doubt about the same definition; [p. 365] from the solution of which he proves that it is not good. And finally, in the third, he gives a proper definition, from which he gathers the true property of relatives.

> Definitio antiqua relatiuorum talis erat: *Ad aliquid talia dicuntur, quæcunque hæc ipsa, quæ sunt aliorum esse dicuntur, vel quomodolibet alter ad alterum.* Vt duplum dicitur ad dimidium, & magnum, respectu parui, scientia habitus, atque potentia, ad sua obiecta.

The ancient definition of relatives was this: Those things are called relatives which, the very things that they are, are said to be of others, or are in any way whatever referred one to another: as the double is said with respect to the half, and the great with respect to the small, a habit, a science, and a power with respect to their objects.

> Prima proprietas, antiqua relatiuorum erat, *Quòd relatiua habeant contrarium*: cuius exemplum facilè designari potest: quia si habitus, & virtutes sunt relatiua, inter eas reperiuntur virtus, & vitium, & alij habitus particulares contrarij: ex quibus probatur relatiua habere contrarium.

The first property of relatives was, in the ancient view, that relatives have a contrary: an example of which can easily be pointed out: because if habits and virtues are relatives, among them are found virtue and vice, and other particular contrary habits; from which it is proved that relatives have a contrary.

> Secunda proprietas est: *Quòd relatiua suscipiunt magis & minus*: nam vnum dicitur magis simile alteri, quàm aliud, & idemmet, vno tempore magis, quàm alio simile eidem.

The second property is that relatives admit of more and less: for one thing is said to be more like another than something else is, and the same thing is more like the same thing at one time than at another.

> 2 Tertia proprietas est: *Quòd relatiua dicãtur ad conuertentiam.* Dici autem ad conuertentiam, non est conuersim prædicari vnum de altero, in recto, quia vnum relatiuũ, non potest prædicari hoc modo de alio: nam falsum est, quòd pater sit filius. Sed prędicari vnũ de altero in obliquo, vt petit natura relatiuorum, ita vt si aliquis est pater, filij pater sit, & si est simile, alicui simile esse debet. Vt autem hęc proprietas conueniat omnibus relatiuis, debet fieri debita assignatio termini: debita autẽ assignatio termini fiet, si terminus per se, & non per accidens assignetur.

2 The third property is that relatives are said by reciprocation. Now to be said by reciprocation is not to be predicated conversely one of the other in recto, because one relative cannot be predicated of the other in this way: for it is false that the father is the son. But it is for one to be predicated of the other in obliquo, as the nature of relatives requires: so that if someone is a father, he is the father of a son, and if he is like, he must be like to something. But in order that this property may belong to all relatives, the due assignment of the term must be made; and the due assignment of the term will be made if the term per se, and not per accidens, is assigned.

> 3 Terminus autem per se ille est, qui formalem rationem terminandi significat. Et ratio formalis terminandi est illa, quæ sufficienter terminat relationem, exclusis quibuscunque aliis, quæ in termino relationis esse possunt. Gratia exempli: pater est relatiuum, cui pro termino, non bene assignatur homo, aut album, vel musicum, sed filius: quia licèt, filius necessariò debeat esse homo, & aliquando sit albus, vel musicus, etiam si hęc per impossibile ab eo remoueantur, & sola filiatio remaneat, terminabit sufficienter relationem patris, & dicetur cum eo, ad conuertentiam, non cum aliis: non enim dicimus patrem esse hominis patrem, aut albi, vel musici: quia isti sunt materiales, aut accidentales termini, sed esse filii patrem: quia filius est terminus per se, & formalis.

3 Now the term per se is that which signifies the formal ratio of terminating. And the formal ratio of terminating is that which sufficiently terminates the relation, all other things whatever that can be in the term of the relation being excluded. For example: father is a relative, for which man, or white, or musical is not well assigned as the term, but son: because, although the son must necessarily be a man, and is sometimes white or musical, even if these were per impossibile removed from him and filiation alone remained, it would sufficiently terminate the relation of the father, and it is said by reciprocation with it, not with the others: for we do not say that a father is the father of a man, or of a white thing, or of a musical thing, because these are material or accidental terms, but that he is the father of a son, because the son is the term per se and formal.

> 4 Vltima proprietas est, Quòd relatiua sint simul natura: ad quam duæ requiruntur conditiones: quarum primam tangit Arist. cap. præsenti, secundam verò in post prædicamentis, ca. 3. Prima igitur conditio est, quòd vno existente in rerum natura, necesse sit existere aliud: & vno sublato, necesse etiam sit [p. 366] auferri aliud: vt posito patre, necesse est poni filium, quocunque autem deficiente, necesse est deficere aliud, saltem sub ratione relatiui: vt mortuo filio, etiam si permaneat homo, qui erat pater, iam non permanet in ratione patris. Sed hæc conditio non est sufficiens: quia homo, & risibile, ita se habent, & non sunt simul natura, sed homo est natura prior. Alia igitur conditio est, quòd vnum relatiuum, non sit causa alterius, secundùm formalem rationem relatiui: licèt secundum rationem materialem, causa esse possit: vt pater, in quantum homo, est causa filii, non in quantum pater. His igitur duabus conditionibus concurrentibus explicata manet proprietas hæc, quòd relatiua sint simul natura.

4 The last property is that relatives are simultaneous by nature: for which two conditions are required, of which Aristotle touches the first in the present chapter, but the second in the Postpredicaments, ch. 3. The first condition, then, is that when one exists in the nature of things, it is necessary that the other exist; and when one is taken away, it is necessary also that [p. 366] the other be taken away: as, when a father is posited, it is necessary that a son be posited; and when either one fails, it is necessary that the other fail, at least under the ratio of relative: as, when the son is dead, even if the man remains who was a father, he no longer remains in the ratio of father. But this condition is not sufficient, because man and risible are so related, and are not simultaneous by nature, but man is prior by nature. The other condition, then, is that one relative not be the cause of the other according to the formal ratio of relative, although it can be a cause according to the material ratio: as the father, inasmuch as he is a man, is the cause of the son, not inasmuch as he is a father. When these two conditions concur, then, this property remains explained: that relatives are simultaneous by nature.

> 5 Sed aduersus hanc definitionem antiquam, proponit dubium Arist. *An conueniat substantiæ, aut secundùm se, vel secundùm suas partes?* Et respondet, quòd substantiæ secundùm se, non potest conuenire: nam aqua, non dicitur esse alicuius tanquam termini ( licèt possit esse alicuius possessoris ) ergo substantia secundùm se, non est relatiua: sed partibus eius, vt brachio, vel capiti, conuenire ait: quia caput, alicuius hominis, vel animalis est caput, & etiam brachium. Ex hoc autem, quòd substantiæ conueniat talis definitio, saltem secundùm partes, colligit Arist. non esse bonam: quia substantia omnino absoluta est, & prædicamentum constituit, primò diuersum à prædicamento ad aliquid: quare vt substantia non potest esse relatiua.

5 But against this ancient definition Aristotle proposes a doubt: whether it belongs to substance, either according to itself or according to its parts. And he replies that it cannot belong to substance according to itself: for water is not said to be of something as of a term (although it can be of some possessor); therefore substance according to itself is not relative. But he says that it belongs to its parts, such as the arm or the head: because a head is the head of some man or animal, and so also is an arm. But from the fact that such a definition belongs to substance, at least according to its parts, Aristotle gathers that it is not good: because substance is altogether absolute, and constitutes a category primarily diverse from the category of relation; wherefore, as substance, it cannot be relative.

> Ideo in vltima parte capitis, necessarium esse docet Arist. assignare aliam definitionem, quæ solùm conueniat veris relatiuis. Assignat autem hanc: *Ad aliquid ea sunt, quorum totum suum est, referri ad aliud*: Vt totum esse patris, est referri ad filium, & totum esse filij, est referri ad patrem Nihil ergo absolutum debent habere relatiua, vt relatiua, sed totum esse quod habent, est referri ad aliud.

Therefore in the last part of the chapter Aristotle teaches that it is necessary to assign another definition, which belongs only to true relatives. And he assigns this one: Relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to another: as the whole being of the father is to be referred to the son, and the whole being of the son is to be referred to the father. Relatives, then, as relatives, must have nothing absolute, but the whole being they have is to be referred to another.

> 6 Ex hac definitione, colligit Arist. *Proprietatem relatiuorum esse: non solùm, quòd sint simul natura, sed etiam simul cognitione: in definitione*: ita vt qui definitè cognoscit vnum relatiuum: definitè etiam cognoscat alterum: quasi dicat, qui cognoscit vnum relatiuum, necesse est simul cognoscat alterum: & qui propriam definitionem vnius scit designare, necesse, est, vt sciat designare definitionem alterius: vt si quis cognoscat patrem, necesse est eo ipso filium cognoscere: qui scit definire patrem, necesse est, sciat etiam definire filium. Hæc Aristoteles in litera.

6 From this definition Aristotle gathers that the property of relatives is not only that they are simultaneous by nature, but also simultaneous in cognition and in definition: so that whoever knows one relative definitely also knows the other definitely: as if to say, whoever knows one relative must at the same time know the other; and whoever knows how to designate the proper definition of one must know how to designate the definition of the other: as, if someone knows a father, he must by that very fact know a son; whoever knows how to define father must also know how to define son. This is what Aristotle says in the letter.

[p. 367]

## QUESTION I

> QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

> *An ad aliquid, vel relatiuum constituat speciale prædicamentum.*

Whether relation, or the relative, constitutes a special category.

> 7 DVobus modis considerare possumus prædicamenta accidentium, nempe secundùm ordinem dignitatis, & secundùm ordinem, quo inhærent substantiæ prius aut posterius, magis aut minus immediatè. Et primam considerationem habuit Arist. in Metaph. vbi de eis agebat secundùm proprias entitates: sed secundam in Dialectica, vbi modum potiùs, quo prædicantur de substantia, & ei inhærent, attendere debuit: & ideo in 5. Meta. priùs posuit prædicamentum qualitatis, quàm ad aliquid: quia nobilior est qualitas, cùm sit accidens absolutum: sed in Logica, priùs posuit relationem: quia priùs inhæret substantiæ, quàm qualitas: quod sic probatur: Quantitas est, quæ proximæ inhæret substantiæ corporeæ, extendendo partes eius: sed post quantitatem statim sequitur relatio: quia antequam intelligatur habere qualitates, intelligitur magna, aut parua, dupla, ac dimidia, & qualis alteri: ergo priùs intelligitur relatiua, quàm effecta qualitatibus: vnde priùs relatio, quàm qualitas afficit substantiam: non quidem prioritate temporis, sed rationis: quia cùm in primò instanti temporis, in quo genita est, habeat relationes, & qualitates, priùs intelligimus habere illas, quàm has.

7 We can consider the categories of accidents in two ways: namely, according to the order of dignity, and according to the order in which they inhere in substance, prior or posterior, more or less immediately. And Aristotle had the first consideration in the Metaphysics, where he treated of them according to their proper entities; but the second in Dialectic, where he had rather to attend to the mode in which they are predicated of substance and inhere in it. And therefore in Metaph. 5 he placed the category of quality before relation, because quality is nobler, since it is an absolute accident; but in Logic he placed relation first, because it inheres in substance before quality does. Which is proved thus: Quantity is what most proximately inheres in corporeal substance, extending its parts; but immediately after quantity relation follows, because before substance is understood to have qualities it is understood to be great or small, double and half, and equal to another; therefore it is understood to be relative before it is understood to be affected by qualities. Hence relation affects substance before quality does: not indeed by a priority of time, but of reason; because, although in the first instant of time in which it is generated it has relations and qualities, we understand it to have the former before the latter.

> De relatione verò, quam per nomen, *Ad aliquid*, intelligimus, primò inquirendum est, An sit speciale genus entis, quod non est aliud ac inquirere, An sit ratio vniuersalissima, transcendens prædicamenta omnia, vel specialis, quæ specialem modum, aut genus entis contineat, sicut quantitas, & qualitas:

But concerning relation, which we understand by the name relative, it must first be inquired whether it is a special genus of being: which is nothing other than to inquire whether it is a most universal ratio, transcending all the categories, or a special one, which contains a special mode or genus of being, as quantity and quality do.

> Et fuit prima opinio, antiquorum Philosophorum, qui Zenonem secuti, dixerunt: *Ad aliquid esse permixtum, vel inclusum in omnibus prædicamentis*: & ideo non esse vnum speciale genus entis. Probatur hac ratione: quia relatio præsupponit necessariò alia accidentia in subiecto: vt si sit relatio æqualitatis, præsupponit quantitatem: & si relatio similitudinis, qualitatem, & sic de cæteris accidentibus: quia inter omnia reperitur relatio: ergo in omnibus includitur, & omnibus permixta est: quare non potest esse speciale genus entis.

And the first opinion was that of the ancient Philosophers who, following Zeno, said that the relative is intermixed with, or included in, all the categories, and therefore is not one special genus of being. It is proved by this reason: because relation necessarily presupposes other accidents in the subject: as, if it is a relation of equality, it presupposes quantity; and if a relation of likeness, quality; and so of the other accidents: because relation is found among all; therefore it is included in all and intermixed with all; wherefore it cannot be a special genus of being.

> 8 Secunda opinio fuit Platonis, à quo eam accepit Aristot. *Quòd ad aliquid sit speciale genus entis.* Et hæc est iam communis in schola, & omnino vera. Probatur hac ratione: Ens diuiditur in decem prædicamenta: tanquam in diuersos modos essendi: & accidens diuiditur in nouem, tanquam in diuersos [p. 368] modos afficiendi substantiam: sed relatio continet diuersum modum essendi, & afficiendi substantiam: ergo erit speciale genus entis. Probatur minor: quia esse relationis, est ad aliud se habere, & substantiam afficit distincto modo ac cætera accidentia: nam quantitas, eam extendendo afficit, qualitas eam qualificando: relatio verò ordinando eam ad aliud: quem modum, nullum aliud accidentium habet: ergo tam modus essendi, quàm afficiendi substantiam, specialis est, & distinctus à cæteris: quare speciale genus entis erit.

8 The second opinion was that of Plato, from whom Aristotle took it: that the relative is a special genus of being. And this is also the common one in the school, and altogether true. It is proved by this reason: Being is divided into ten categories as into diverse modes of being; and accident is divided into nine, as into diverse [p. 368] modes of affecting substance; but relation contains a diverse mode of being and of affecting substance; therefore it will be a special genus of being. The minor is proved: because the being of relation is to be toward another, and it affects substance in a mode distinct from the other accidents: for quantity affects it by extending it, quality by qualifying it, but relation by ordering it to another: which mode no other accident has; therefore, as its mode both of being and of affecting substance is special and distinct from the others, it will therefore be a special genus of being.

> 9 Vt autem veritas huius sententiæ intelligatur, & argumentum alterius meliùs solui possit, Vnum est notandum, nempe, Relationem vniuersaliter sumptam, in tria membra diuidi. Prima relatio est: Vniuersalis respectus, & intrinsecus omnibus accidentibus, quod respiciunt subiectum, vt ei inhærere possunt. Alia est respectus quidam minùs vniuersalis, qui includitur essentialiter, non in omnibus, sed in quibusdam tantùm specialibus accidentibus absolutis: vt respectus, quem habitus, & scientiæ, atque etiam potentię, dicunt ad obiectum, per quem respectum, simul cum ratione absoluta, per eum explicata, distinguuntur specie, Postrema relatio est, Respectus, non pertinens ad essentiam alicuius accidentis absoluti, nec ordinans rem, in qua est ad aliud, tanquam ad subiectum, aut obiectum, vel quid simile, sed solùm tanquam ad terminum. Et primum genus relationis, dicitur transcendentale: quia in omnibus accidentibus, essentialiter includitur, & ideo non est speciale genus entis. Secundum verò, vocatur relatio secundùm dici: & pertinet reductiuè ad illa prædicamenta absoluta, in quorum ratione intrinseca clauditur: vt respectus scientiæ, ad obiectum, pertinet ad speciem habitus: & relatio potentiæ ab obiectum, ad speciem naturalis potentiæ, reductiuè quidem, quia aliquid sunt, quasi complens essentiam harum specierum. Tertium genus relationis, duplicem conditionem habet. Prima non conuenit omnibus accidentibus, sed quibusdam tantùm, vt quantitati, actioni, & passioni, in quibus fundatur: & non essentialiter, sed accidentaliter. Et in hoc distinguitur à primò, & secundo genere relationum: quia nec transcendit omnia prædicamenta accidentium, sicut primum, quamuis de multis eorum accidentaliter prædicetur: hoc enim non sufficit, vt ad prædicamenta eorũ reducatur: sed requiritur essentialis inclusio, alioqui omnia accidentia pertinerent ad prædicamentum substantiæ, cùm de illa prædicentur accidentaliter. Nec pertinet ad aliquod prædicamentum absolutum, vt ad secundum: quia non est de essentia alicuius absoluti: [p. 369] vnde sequitur specialem esse rationem eius, ab omnibus distinctam, & hæc est secunda conditio eius. Tertia verò: quòd eius essentia habeat modum entis completi, & totius potentialis, contrahibilis per differentias, vt quæstione sequenti explicabitur.

9 But in order that the truth of this view may be understood, and the argument of the other may be better solved, one thing should be noted: namely, that relation taken universally is divided into three members. The first relation is a universal respect, intrinsic to all accidents, by which they regard the subject, as being able to inhere in it. Another is a certain less universal respect, which is included essentially not in all but only in certain special absolute accidents: such as the respect which habits and sciences, and also powers, bear to their object, by which respect, together with the absolute ratio explained through it, they are distinguished in species. The last relation is a respect that does not pertain to the essence of any absolute accident, nor orders the thing in which it is to another as to a subject or object or something similar, but only as to a term. And the first genus of relation is called transcendental, because it is included essentially in all accidents, and therefore is not a special genus of being. But the second is called relation according to being said, and pertains reductively to those absolute categories in whose intrinsic ratio it is enclosed: as the respect of science to its object pertains to the species of habit, and the relation of power to its object, to the species of natural power: reductively indeed, because they are something as it were completing the essence of these species. The third genus of relation has a twofold condition. The first: it does not belong to all accidents, but only to some, such as quantity, action, and passion, in which it is founded; and not essentially but accidentally. And in this it is distinguished from the first and second genera of relations: because it does not transcend all the categories of accidents, as the first does, although it is predicated accidentally of many of them; for this does not suffice for it to be reduced to their categories, but essential inclusion is required; otherwise all accidents would pertain to the category of substance, since they are predicated of it accidentally. Nor does it pertain to some absolute category, as the second does, because it is not of the essence of anything absolute: [p. 369] hence it follows that its ratio is special, distinct from all others; and this is its second condition. And the third: that its essence has the mode of a complete being and of a potential whole, contractible by differences, as will be explained in the following question.

> 11 Ad argumentum igitur oppositæ sententiæ, Concesso antecedente, distinguendum est consequens, quòd in omnibus includantur: nam si de essentiali inclusione intelligitur, falsum est: si verò de accidentali, concedi potest, quòd includatur in omni prædicamento, aliquo modo, non tamen essentiali, sed accidentali: vnde non sequitur, quòd sit transcendens, aut quòd pertineat ad plura prædicamenta: nam ad vtrumque requiritur inclusio essentialis, vt per se est manifestum.

11 To the argument of the opposite view, then: granting the antecedent, the consequent must be distinguished, namely that it is included in all: for if it is understood of essential inclusion, it is false; but if of accidental, it can be granted that it is included in every category in some mode, not however an essential one but an accidental one. Hence it does not follow that it is transcendent, or that it pertains to several categories: for to both essential inclusion is required, as is manifest of itself.

## QUESTION II

> QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

> *An ad aliquid sit speciale genus entis realis.*

Whether relation is a special genus of real being.

> COnstituto iam in præcedenti quæstione, quòd *Ad aliquid* sit speciale genus entis: sequitur disputandum in præsenti, An sit speciale genus entis realis: quod idem est, ac si quæratur, An detur relatio realis, quæ constituat speciale prædicamentum.

Having established in the preceding question that relation is a special genus of being, it follows that we should dispute in the present one whether it is a special genus of real being: which is the same as if it were asked whether there is given a real relation which constitutes a special category.

> Et est prima opinio, negans omnino, *Relationem realem, & reale prædicamentum ad aliquid*, tenensque per solam relationem rationis, dici tale, quidquid ad aliud refertur, vt pater, & simile. Ita plures ex antiquioribus Philosophis, quos citat commentator 12. lib. Meta. commento 19. quos secuti sunt ex Theologis, Henricus quodlib. 9. quæst. 3. Ocham in 1 d. q. 1. Aureolus apud Capreolum in 1. d. 3. qu. 1. in argument. contra primam conclusionem: & ita tenent moderni quidam: quia putant, nullam esse rationem conuincentem, quòd aliqua sit relatio realis ponenda in rebus.

And the first opinion altogether denies a real relation and a real category of relation, and holds that whatever is referred to another, such as a father and a like thing, is called such through a relation of reason alone. So hold many of the more ancient Philosophers, whom the Commentator cites in Metaph. 12, comment 19; whom have followed, among the Theologians, Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 9, quest. 3; Ockham on 1, d., q. 1; Aureolus in Capreolus on 1, d. 3, q. 1, in the arguments against the first conclusion. And certain moderns hold the same: because they think that there is no convincing reason why some real relation should be posited in things.

> 12 Probatur testimonio Arist. 5. lib. Phys. textu 10. vbi affirmat, *Ad relationem, non terminari per se motum*: & probat, quia acquiritur sine mutatione subiecti: vt si vno albo Compluti existente, fiat aliud Romæ, incipit primum album esse simile, sine noua sui mutatione, per solam mutationem alterius, in quo de nouo producitur Romæ albedo. Ex quo tale arg. colligitur: Aliquid fit relatiuum, sine reali mutatione sui, ergo sine aliqua entitate reali noua in se recepta, ergo relatio non est entitas realis. Probatur euidenter vltima consequentia: quia si esset entitas realis cùm de nouo acquiratur, non fieret aliquid de nouo relatiuũ, sine noua entitate in se recepta, nec sine reali [p. 370] mutatione sui: quia repugnat aliquid recipere de nouo in se entitatem realem sine sui mutatione.

12 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, Phys. 5, text 10, where he affirms that motion does not terminate per se at relation; and he proves it because it is acquired without change of the subject: as, if while one white thing exists at Alcalá another comes to be at Rome, the first white thing begins to be like without a new change of itself, through the change alone of the other, in which whiteness is newly produced at Rome. From which such an argument is gathered: Something becomes relative without real change of itself; therefore without some new real entity received in itself; therefore relation is not a real entity. The last consequence is proved evidently: because if it were a real entity, since it is newly acquired, nothing would newly become relative without a new entity received in itself, nor without a real Aa [p. 370] change of itself: because it is repugnant that something newly receive a real entity in itself without change of itself.

> Probatur deinde ratione. Primò: Quia ens reale, adæquatè diuiditur in substantiam, & accidens: sed relatio nõ est substantia, neque accidens, ergo non ens reale. Probatur minor, quòd non sit accidens: (nam quòd relatio non sit substantia, euidens est) de intrinseca ratione accidentis realis est, inhærere subiecto: si non actu, saltem aptitudine: sed relatio non inhæret subiecto vllo modo, ergo non est accidens, Minorem probo: quia proprius conceptus relationis, est esse rationem referendi aliud ad terminum: ergo relatio vt relatio, non respicit subiectum, sed terminum, nec potest inhærere: quare non erit accidens.

It is proved next by reason. First: Because real being is adequately divided into substance and accident; but relation is neither substance nor accident; therefore it is not real being. The minor is proved, that it is not an accident (for that relation is not substance is evident): it is of the intrinsic ratio of a real accident to inhere in a subject, if not in act, at least in aptitude; but relation does not inhere in a subject in any way; therefore it is not an accident. I prove the minor: because the proper concept of relation is to be the ratio of referring something to a term; therefore relation as relation does not regard the subject but the term, nor can it inhere; wherefore it will not be an accident.

> 13 Secundò: Si relatio esset speciale prędicamentum, ex propria natura esset accidens reale, cùm constet non esse substantiam: quare nec posset esse substantia, neque ens rationis: sed aliquando est substantia, & aliquando ens rationis, ergo non erit speciale prædicamentum.

13 Second: If relation were a special category, it would be of its own nature a real accident, since it is established that it is not a substance; wherefore it could not be either a substance or a being of reason; but it is sometimes a substance and sometimes a being of reason; therefore it will not be a special category.

> Probatur minor: quia in personis diuinis, sunt rationes reales paternitatis, filiationis, & spirationis, seu processionis: & nõ sunt accidentia, quia accidens repugnat Deo, sed sunt relationes substantiales, ergo relatio potest esse substantia. Deinde relatio generis ad speciem, & speciei ad indiuidua, est vera relatio, cùm totum esse generis sit ad speciem, & totum esse speciei ad indiuidua: & non est accidens reale, sed rationis, vt vidimus in prædicabilibus, ergo vera relatio potest esse ens rationis: & ideo non erit ex se speciale genus entis realis.

The minor is proved: because in the divine persons there are real rationes of paternity, filiation, and spiration, or procession; and they are not accidents, because accident is repugnant to God, but they are substantial relations; therefore relation can be substance. Next, the relation of the genus to the species, and of the species to the individuals, is a true relation, since the whole being of the genus is toward the species, and the whole being of the species toward the individuals; and it is not a real accident but one of reason, as we saw in the Predicables; therefore a true relation can be a being of reason; and therefore it will not of itself be a special genus of real being.

> Tertiò: Quia relatio non est aliud, quam comparatio duorum extremorum, vt similitudo, comparatio duorum alborum eiusdem gradus: sed comparatio est opus rationis, quam facit intellectus, postquam naturam vtriusque cognouit, ergo non erit ens reale, sed rationis.

Third: Because relation is nothing other than a comparison of two extremes, as likeness is a comparison of two white things of the same degree; but comparison is a work of reason, which the intellect makes after it has known the nature of both; therefore it will not be a real being, but one of reason.

> Secunda opinio est totius scholæ, quæ cum Arist. *ponit speciale prædicamentũ relationis realis, sub nomine prædicamenti ad aliquid*. Et hæc est vera, & tenenda: quæ (nisi ego fallor) efficaciter probari potest, his rationibus: non quidem ex doctrina Aristotelis deductis, quam in hac parte non recipiunt aduersarij, sed ex ipsa natura rerum, & ex fide Catholica.

The second opinion is that of the whole school, which with Aristotle posits a special category of real relation, under the name of the category of the relative. And this is true and to be held; which (unless I am mistaken) can be proved efficaciously by these reasons: not indeed reasons drawn from the doctrine of Aristotle, which in this matter our adversaries do not accept, but from the very nature of things and from the Catholic faith.

> 14 Prima ratio, in natura rerum fundatur, hoc modo: Ex natura rei, & ante operationẽ intellectus, magis assimilatur vnus homo alteri homini, quàm equo vel leoni: & etiam vnum album, alteri eiusdem gradus, magis, quàm ei, quod non habet tam intensam albedinem: sed simile non dicitur tale respectu sui, sed alterius, ergo si naturaliter est alteri simile, [p. 371] naturaliter ordinatur ad alterum, & naturalis ordinatio est realis: ergo vnum ad alterum ordinatur ex natura rei, & ordinatione reali: & ordinatio realis est relatio realis, ergo dantur in rebus relationes reales. Et confirmari potest ex creatione: nam anima rationalis, ex eo quòd creatur à Deo, vocatur, & est creatura: sed creatura non dicitur ad se, sed ad aliud, ergo refertur realiter ad creatorem, dabiturque in ea relatio realis,

14 The first reason is founded on the nature of things, in this way: From the nature of the thing, and before the operation of the intellect, one man is more assimilated to another man than to a horse or a lion; and also one white thing to another of the same degree more than to one that does not have so intense a whiteness; but a like thing is not called such with respect to itself, but to another; therefore, if it is naturally like another, by nature [p. 371] it is ordered to the other, and a natural ordering is real; therefore the one is ordered to the other from the nature of the thing and by a real ordering; and a real ordering is a real relation; therefore real relations are given in things. And it can be confirmed from creation: for the rational soul, from the fact that it is created by God, is called and is a creature; but a creature is not said with respect to itself, but to another; therefore it is referred really to the creator, and there will be given in it a real relation.

> 15 Secunda ratio, deducitur ex fide Catholica, secũdùm quã in personis Diuinis ponuntur relationes reales Paternitatis, Filiationis, & Spirationis: sed vna persona Diuina refertur realiter ad aliam, quia procedit ab ea, aut quia est principium, à quo alia procedit: vt Filius ad Patrem, quia procedit ab eo, per naturalem generationem: & in creaturis vnus homo, procedit ab alio, per naturalem generationem, vt genitus à generante, ergo iste erit filius, & ille pater per veras relationes reales.

15 The second reason is deduced from the Catholic faith, according to which real relations of Paternity, Filiation, and Spiration are posited in the Divine persons; but one Divine person is referred really to another because it proceeds from it, or because it is the principle from which another proceeds: as the Son to the Father, because he proceeds from him by natural generation. And in creatures one man proceeds from another by natural generation, as the begotten from the begetter; therefore the latter will be son and the former father through true real relations.

> 16 Sed, vt natura relationis meliùs intelligatur, & argumenta faciliùs solui possint: Notandum est illud, quod D. Th, asserit, 1. p. q. 28. art. 1. nempe: *Quodlibet prædicamentum, duplicem conceptum habere*: Communem, in quo omnia conueniunt, saltem analogicè: & particularem, per quem distinguntur. Communis conceptus est, esse in subiecto, actu, vel aptitudine: in quo conuenit relatio cum accidentibus absolutis: conceptus verò Particularis, & proprius, non sumitur eodem modo in absolutis, & relatione: sed in illis, per modos speciales inhærendi in subiecto: & ideo absoluta vocantur, quia subiectum afficiunt, vt in se est. Vt conceptus particularis quantitatis, est inhærere substantiæ extendendo partes eius: qualitatis verò, qualificando eam, sicque de cæteris: sed particularis conceptus, & proprius relationis, non sumitur per ordinem ad subiectum: sed ad terminum, ad quem refert subiectum: vt conceptus proprius paternitatis, per ordinem ad filium, tanquam ad terminum: vnde accidentia absoluta his duobus conceptibus complentur, nempe inhærendi subiecto, & tali modo inhærendi: relatio verò duobus aliis. Primò quidem inhærendi subiecto, ideo communi cum absolutis: & secundò, ordinando illud ad terminum: ideo dici solet, habere duplicem conceptum: vnum qui dicitur esse, *In*, alium, qui dicitur esse, *Ad*.

16 But in order that the nature of relation may be better understood and the arguments more easily solved, note what St. Thomas asserts, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1: namely, that every category has a twofold concept: a Common one, in which all agree, at least analogically; and a particular one, through which they are distinguished. The common concept is to be in a subject, in act or in aptitude; in which relation agrees with the absolute accidents. But the Particular and proper concept is not taken in the same way in the absolute accidents and in relation, but in the former through special modes of inhering in the subject; and therefore they are called absolute, because they affect the subject as it is in itself. As the particular concept of quantity is to inhere in substance by extending its parts, and that of quality by qualifying it, and so of the others. But the particular and proper concept of relation is not taken through order to the subject, but to the term to which it refers the subject: as the proper concept of paternity is taken through order to the son, as to its term. Hence the absolute accidents are completed by these two concepts, namely of inhering in the subject and of inhering in such a mode; but relation by two others: first, of inhering in the subject, therefore common with the absolute accidents; and second, of ordering it to the term. Therefore it is customarily said to have a twofold concept: one which is called esse in [being in], the other which is called esse ad [being toward].

> 17 Testimonium Arist. hac distinctione explicandum est: Mutatio duplex est: Vna propria, & per se talis, à naturáque intenta, quæ procedit à principio intrinseco rei, per quam mouetur corpus, ad recipiendum in se aliquam perfectionem absolutam: vt materia, ad recipiendam formam substantialem: vel corpus, ad recipiendam accidentalem. *Alia Communis*, [p. 372] impropria, & per accidens, quæ non procedit à principio intrinseco, rei, nec per se primò intenditur à natura, sed quasi per accidens sequitur. Et per primum genus mutationis, non potest acquiri, aut fieri relatio: quia natura non intendit per se relationem, cùm non sit perfectio absoluta rei: sed sequitur quasi per accidens, in vtroque extremo, ad acquisitionem alicuius formæ absolutæ atque per se intentæ in eis: vel saltem in aliquo eorum. Vt in exemplo adducto in arg. de albo Romæ facto de nouo, ex cuius mutatione intrinseca, mutatur ab extrinseco aliud album, quod Compluti erat. Bene ergo Arist. asserit, *ad relationem non terminari per se mutationem, aut motum proprium, & per se, sed acquiri sine illa*: non tamen vult, quòd sine impropria saltem & communi acquiratur, cùm verum sit, ac necessarium, vt subiectum quomodocũque acquirat de nouo relationem realem aliter se habeat nunc, quàm priùs: quæ est definitio communis, & impropriæ mutationis: satis est autem per impropriam mutationem acquiri, vt sit ens reale.

17 The testimony of Aristotle is to be explained by this distinction. Change is twofold. One is proper and per se such, and intended by nature, which proceeds from an intrinsic principle of the thing, through which a body is moved to receive in itself some absolute perfection: as matter, to receive a substantial form; or a body, to receive an accidental one. The other, Common, Aa ij [p. 372] improper and per accidens, which does not proceed from an intrinsic principle of the thing, nor is intended per se primarily by nature, but follows as it were per accidens. And relation cannot be acquired or come to be through the first genus of change: because nature does not intend relation per se, since it is not an absolute perfection of the thing; but it follows as it were per accidens, in both extremes, upon the acquisition of some absolute form, intended per se in them, or at least in one of them. As in the example adduced in the argument, of the white thing newly made at Rome: from whose intrinsic change another white thing, which was at Alcalá, is changed extrinsically. Aristotle rightly asserts, then, that a proper and per se change or motion does not terminate at relation, but that it is acquired without it: he does not, however, mean that it is acquired without an improper and common one at least, since it is true and necessary that the subject, in whatever way it newly acquires a real relation, should be otherwise now than before: which is the common definition of improper change. And it is enough that it be acquired through improper change for it to be a real being.

> 18 Ad primum arg. Negandum est, relationem non esse accidens: & dum dicitur, secundùm proprium conceptum non inhærere, distinguendum est, nam si sensus sit, quòd proprius conceptus relationis, non sit inhęrendi, sed referendi ad terminum, verum est. Et si rursus dicatur, secundùm hunc conceptum proprium, qui est, *Ad*, non esse accidens: concedendum est: quia non est accidens, nisi secundùm conceptum communem inhærendi: sed est tale accidens: sicut quodlibet aliud prædicamentum, secundùm proprium conceptum, non est accidens, sed secundùm communem inhærendi: in quo conueniunt omnia. Et si tandem dicatur: Communem conceptum inhærendi, esse transcendentalem: & ideo inclusum: necessariò, in conceptibus particularibus prædicamentorum: quia si illum non includunt, non erunt cõceptus accidentium, nec proinde reales. Respondeo, Necessariò illum includere, propter transcendentiam, sicut necessariò includunt conceptum entis: eum tamen non exprimere, aut non expressè significare, sed quasi implicitè, aut confusè: quemadmodum rationale, includit conceptum entis, sed non exprimit: quia expressè non significat, nisi gradum naturæ rationalis: in quo tamen cùm includatur ens, dicitur conceptum entis implicitè, aut confusè significare, non distinctè, aut expressè: itaque conceptus proprius relationis, per quem distinguitur relatio ab accidentibus absolutis, non exprimit, nisi modum referendi ad terminum: sed quia est conceptus formæ realis, inhærentis, & referentis subiectum, quod constituit ad terminum, etiam [p. 373] includit implicitè esse, sicut includit conceptum entis,

18 To the first argument: It must be denied that relation is not an accident. And when it is said that according to its proper concept it does not inhere, a distinction must be made: for if the sense is that the proper concept of relation is not of inhering but of referring to a term, it is true. And if again it is said that according to this proper concept, which is toward, it is not an accident, it must be granted: because it is not an accident except according to the common concept of inhering; but it is such an accident, just as any other category whatever is not an accident according to its proper concept, but according to the common concept of inhering, in which all agree. And if finally it is said that the common concept of inhering is transcendental, and therefore necessarily included in the particular concepts of the categories, because if they do not include it they will not be concepts of accidents, nor consequently real: I reply that they necessarily include it, on account of its transcendence, just as they necessarily include the concept of being; yet they do not express it, or do not signify it expressly, but as it were implicitly or confusedly: just as rational includes the concept of being, but does not express it, because expressly it signifies only the grade of rational nature; in which, however, since being is included, it is said to signify the concept of being implicitly or confusedly, not distinctly or expressly. And so the proper concept of relation, through which relation is distinguished from the absolute accidents, expresses only the mode of referring to the term; but because it is the concept of a real form, inhering in and referring the subject, which it constitutes toward the term, it also includes [p. 373] implicitly the being in, just as it includes the concept of being.

> 19 Ratio autem, ob quam non exprimit, est: quia nomen relationis, non est impositum ad significandum conceptum inhærendi, sed conceptum referendi: in quo tamen implicitè, includitur idem conceptus inhærendi.

19 And the reason why it does not express it is that the name of relation was not imposed to signify the concept of inhering, but the concept of referring; in which, however, the same concept of inhering is implicitly included.

> Ad secundum, Distinguendum est antecedens: nam relatio duobus modus accipitur. Primò, communissimè prout solùm dicit rationem referendi ad terminum, abstrahendo à ratione reali, vel rationis: imò à ratione substantiali, vel accidentali: & hoc modo non efficit prædicamentum reale: quia non determinationem accidentis realis. Secundò, sumitur specialiori modo, pro ratione referendi reali, & accidentali: in qua acceptione constituit tertium prædicamentum: à quo excluduntur in primis relationes: quia non sunt reales: & ad quod non pertinent relationes substantiales, aut diuinæ: quia diuina, propter sui excellentiam, & immensitatem, non limitantur ad ordinem prædicamentalem.

To the second: The antecedent must be distinguished. For relation is taken in two ways. First, most commonly, inasmuch as it only implies the ratio of referring to a term, abstracting from a real ratio or one of reason, indeed from a substantial or accidental ratio; and in this way it does not make a real category, because it does not imply the determination of a real accident. Second, it is taken in a more special way, for a real and accidental ratio of referring; in which acceptation it constitutes the third category: from which are excluded, first of all, relations of reason, because they are not real; and to which substantial or divine relations do not pertain, because the divine ones, on account of their excellence and immensity, are not limited to the categorial order.

> 20 Ad tertium, Concessa maiori, distinguẽda est minor: quia duobus modis comparantur aliqua: Primò, ex natura rei, quia rationes naturales eorum non sunt tales absolutè, sed ad alterum, vt sunt similia, aut æqualia: & talis comparatio non est opus intellectus: sed sine dependentia ab eo reperitur in natura aliquarum rerum. Alia est comparatio, quam non habent res ex propria natura: quia non sunt distinctæ: aut cùm sint absolutæ, concipiuntur in ordine ad aliud: & talis comparatio est opus rationis. Primam igitur comparationem, includunt relationes reales, aliam verò, relationes rationis: & ideo prima comparatio, tanquam realis, pertinet ad hoc prædicamentum, secunda verò, tanquam non realis, excluditur ab eo.

20 To the third: Granting the major, the minor must be distinguished: because things are compared in two ways. First, from the nature of the thing, because their natural rationes are not such absolutely, but toward another, as they are like or equal; and such a comparison is not a work of the intellect, but is found without dependence on it in the nature of certain things. The other is a comparison which things do not have from their own nature, because they are not distinct, or, though they are absolute, they are conceived in order to another; and such a comparison is a work of reason. Real relations, then, include the first comparison, but relations of reason the other; and therefore the first comparison, as real, pertains to this category, but the second, as not real, is excluded from it.

## QUESTION III

### Quæst. 3. Quodnam sit supremum genus prædicamenti ad aliquid — What is the supreme genus of the category of relation.

> QVÆSTIO III.

[…]

> *Quidnam sit supremum genus prædicamenti ad aliquid.*

[…]

> 21 SPecialis est ratio inquirendi de supremo genere huius prædicamenti. Quia hoc arg. videtur probari, nullum posse habere, & ideo nec ordinationem prædicamentalem ex relatiuis fieri posse. Quia intrinseca ratio relatiuorum est, ordinari ad terminum: ergo siue ponatur pro supremo genere relatiuum in communi, vel ad aliquid, ordinabitur ad terminum; & tunc vel ad terminum inferiorem, vel superiorem, vel æqualem; non ad superiorem, neque inferiorem, propter duo. Primum, quia relatio realis debet esse, inter extrema realia, & realiter distincta, vt inferiùs probabitur: superius autem, & [p. 374] inferius sunt prædicata solùm ratione distincta, vt est manifestum, ergo non potest inter illa dari relatio realis. Secundum, quia relatiua sunt simul natura, *superius* verò *prius natura est inferiori*, vt docet Arist. in postprædicamentis: ergo inter illa non potest esse relatio realis. Quare relatiuum in communi, ad terminum sibi æqualem ordinabitur, & realiter à se distinctum. Vnde sequitur, aut duo esse suprema genera huius prædicamenti, aut nullum. Probatur consequentia: quia neutrum ponitur sub alterno: sed duo esse repugnat, sicut in eodem corpore duo capita: alioqui duo essent prædicamenta ad aliquid: ergo nullum habebit supremum genus.

21 There is a special reason for inquiring about the supreme genus of this category: because by this argument it seems to be proved that it can have none, and that therefore no categorial ordering can be made of relatives either. Because the intrinsic ratio of relatives is to be ordered to a term; therefore, whether the relative in common, or relation, is posited as the supreme genus, it will be ordered to a term; and then either to an inferior term, or a superior one, or an equal one; not to a superior or an inferior, for two reasons. First, because a real relation must be between real extremes, really distinct, as will be proved below; but the superior and the inferior Aa iij [p. 374] are predicates distinct only by reason, as is manifest; therefore a real relation cannot be given between them. Second, because relatives are simultaneous by nature, but the superior is prior by nature to the inferior, as Aristotle teaches in the Postpredicaments; therefore there cannot be a real relation between them. Wherefore the relative in common will be ordered to a term equal to itself and really distinct from itself. Hence it follows that there are either two supreme genera of this category, or none. The consequence is proved: because neither is placed under the other; but that there be two is repugnant, as are two heads in the same body: otherwise there would be two categories of relation; therefore it will have no supreme genus.

> 22 Propter hoc arg. diuisi sunt autores. Et prima opinio tenet *supremum genus huius prædicamenti*, propriè loquendo, *nin esse relatiuum in concreto, vel ad aliquid, sed relationem in abstracto*: quæ est ratio referendi ad aliud: & hoc modo videntur difficultatem argumenti effugere: quia relatio non refertur ad aliud, sed est ratio referendi: ideo non colligitur esse duo genera suprema. Ita Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 25 q. 6. sect. 2. & 3 quod ratione vniuersali probat; quia abstracta accidentium potiùs quàm concreta in prædicamento collocantur, cùm significentur tanquam entia per se: concreta verò tanquam entia per accidens. Hæc tamen sententia non potest satisfacere argu. quia licèt verum esset, abstracta magis propriè in prædicamento collocari, nihilominus quod etiam concreta aliquo modo collocentur, necessariò concedendum est, & concedit hæc sententia: quo supposito non soluit arg.

22 On account of this argument the authors are divided. And the first opinion holds that the supreme genus of this category, properly speaking, is not the relative in the concrete, or ad aliquid, but relation in the abstract, which is the ratio of referring to another; and in this way they seem to escape the difficulty of the argument: because relation is not referred to another, but is the ratio of referring; therefore it is not gathered that there are two supreme genera. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 6, sect. 2 and 3; which he proves by a universal reason: because the abstracts of accidents, rather than the concretes, are placed in the category, since they are signified as beings per se, but the concretes as beings per accidens. This opinion, however, cannot satisfy the argument: because, although it were true that abstracts are more properly placed in the category, nevertheless that concretes too are placed there in some way must necessarily be granted, and this opinion grants it; and on that supposition it does not solve the argument.

> Secunda opinio, *Ad aliquid*, aut *relatiuum, dicit esse supremum genus, potius quàm relationem*: ita Albertus Mag. tract. de prædicamento ad aliquid, c 2 & 10. Scotus in 1. d. 21 q. vnica. Et tunc ad arg. respondent: Supremum genus prædicamenti esse ad aliquid, vel relatiuum in communi, prout dicit conceptum abstractum: in quo conueniunt omnia relatiua. Et hoc modo sumptum, non refertur per se ad alterum, sed per inferiora relatiua, in quibus exercetur actus referendi: vt per paternitatem, & filiationem, per simile, & dissimile: ipsum verò solùm dicit rationem communem eorum, quæ referuntur: & ita vnicum est supremum genus in concreto, habens sub se inferiora genera, & species: in quibus habet exercitium referendi.

The second opinion says that ad aliquid, or the relative, is the supreme genus, rather than relation. So Albert the Great, treatise on the category of relation, ch. 2 and 10; Scotus on 1, d. 21, single q. And then to the argument they reply: The supreme genus of the category is ad aliquid, or the relative in common, inasmuch as it implies an abstracted concept in which all relatives agree. And taken in this way it is not referred per se to another, but through the inferior relatives in which the act of referring is exercised: as through paternity and filiation, through like and unlike; but it itself implies only the common ratio of those things that are referred. And so there is a single supreme genus in the concrete, having under it the inferior genera and species, in which it has the exercise of referring.

> 23 Sed hac sententia falsa probatur, duplici arg. Primò, Conceptus communis abstractus ab inferioribus, debet continere rationem essentialem inferiorum, vt conceptus hominis, abstractus à Petro, & Ioanne: rationem essentialem hominis: sed ratio essentialis quorumcunq; relatiuorum particularium, [p. 375] est referri ad terminum: ergo hanc debet continere conceptus communis relatiui, abstractus à particularibus: vnde sequitur relatiuum in communi, referri ad terminum in communi, sicut relatiuum in particulari, refertur ad terminum in particulari: vel non esse conceptum relatiui abstractum à particularibus.

23 But this opinion is proved false by a twofold argument. First: A common concept abstracted from the inferiors must contain the essential ratio of the inferiors, as the concept of man abstracted from Peter and John contains the essential ratio of man; but the essential ratio of any particular relatives whatever, [p. 375] is to be referred to a term; therefore the common concept of the relative, abstracted from the particulars, must contain this. Hence it follows that the relative in common is referred to a term in common, just as the relative in particular is referred to a term in particular; or else that it is not the concept of the relative abstracted from the particulars.

> Secundò: Qui vult definire patrem in communi, non potest, nisi per communem etiam terminum eum definire, videlicet per genitum in communi, aut per filium in communi: ergo pater in communi, refertur ad filium in communi: sicut hic pater ad hunc filium: & consequenter relatiuum in communi, ad terminum in communi.

Second: Whoever wishes to define father in common cannot define him except also through a common term, namely through the begotten in common, or through son in common; therefore father in common is referred to son in common, just as this father to this son; and consequently the relative in common to a term in common.

> 24 Quod verò dicitur, *Exercitium referendi solùm habere relationem in singularibus*, falsum est, & ex ignorantia procedere videtur; quia exercitium relationis, non consistit in aliqua efficientia, neque in actu aliquo ipsius relationis, quem in singularibus habeat, & non in conceptu communi considerata; sed solùm est ordinatio naturalis vnius ad alterum eodem modo se habens semper: ergo non solùm in singularibus exercetur, sed etiam in vniuersalibus. Hæc solùm differentia esse potest: quòd in singularibus exercetur secundùm actualem existentiam in eis: in vniuersali verò considerata, abstrahit ab existentia: & solùm in hoc sensu, vera esse potest distinctio relationis, à quibusdam assignata: in relationem, vt *Conceptam*, & vt *Exercitam*: quasi dicatur, relationem, vt actu existentem, inter singularia exerceri, quod non habet in vniuersali, sed conceptum tantùm eiusdem exercitij. Et si aliquid aliud velit eadem sententia, vel eadem distinctio, non est admittenda.

24 But what is said, that relation has the exercise of referring only in singulars, is false, and seems to proceed from ignorance: because the exercise of relation does not consist in some efficiency, nor in some act of the relation itself which it would have in singulars and not when considered in the common concept; but it is only the natural ordering of one to another, always holding itself in the same way; therefore it is exercised not only in singulars but also in universals. This alone can be the difference: that in singulars it is exercised according to the actual existence in them, but considered in the universal it abstracts from existence. And only in this sense can the distinction of relation assigned by some be true, into relation as Conceived and as Exercised: as if to say that relation, as actually existing, is exercised among singulars, which it does not have in the universal, but only the concept of the same exercise. And if the same opinion, or the same distinction, means anything else, it is not to be admitted.

> 25 Ideo tertia opinio tenet, *Supremum genus huius prædicamenti, in abstracto, esse Relationem in communi, & in concreto Relatiuum vel Ad aliquid, etiam in communi*. Hanc tenet Toletus q. 2. huius prædicamenti. Et est probabilior, & sequenda. Probaturque, ex communi modo concipiendi, & loquẽdi, de aliis prædicamentis accidentium quæ, vt in anteprędicamẽtis probauimus, vtroque modo sumi possunt: in Cõcreto, & in Abstracto: & vtroque modo accipiuntur, in diuersis locis ab Arist. nec excludi potest omnino concretum à prædicamento, nec etiam Abstractum.

25 Therefore the third opinion holds that the supreme genus of this category in the abstract is Relation in common, and in the concrete the Relative or Ad aliquid, also in common. Toledo holds this, q. 2 on this Category. And it is more probable and to be followed. And it is proved from the common mode of conceiving and speaking about the other categories of accidents, which, as we proved in the Antepredicaments, can be taken in both ways, in the Concrete and in the Abstract; and they are taken in both ways in different places by Aristotle; nor can the concrete be altogether excluded from the category, nor the Abstract either.

> Pro solutione autẽ argumẽti, notãdum primò, Diuersam esse rationẽ formalẽ relatiui, & termini: nã ratio formalis relatiui, est referri ad terminũ, ratio verò formalis termini, nõ est referri ad aliud, sed terminare relationẽ alterius: terminare verò nõ est aliud, quàm esse id ad quod relatiuum ordinatur: & hoc nõ videtur ponere aliquid in re, quæ terminat, sed est quasi denominatio extrinseca: sicut visum esse in pariete, aut quid simile.

But for the solution of the argument it should be noted, first, that the formal ratio of the relative and of the term is diverse: for the formal ratio of the relative is to be referred to the term, but the formal ratio of the term is not to be referred to another, but to terminate the relation of another; and to terminate is nothing other than to be that to which the relative is ordered; and this does not seem to posit anything in the thing which terminates, but is as it were an extrinsic denomination: as being seen in a wall, or something similar. Aa iiij

[p. 376]

> 26 Secundò notandum, Quòd licèt diuersæ sint opiniones circa terminum relationis, an sit absolutus, vel relatiuus: certum tamen est, quòd in relationibus tertii generis, quæ sunt mensurabilis, & mensuræ, terminus non est relatiuus, sed absolutus: nam mensura absolutum quid est, non dependens à mensurabili, Gratia exempli: Scientia sub ratione mensurabilis, per suum obiectum, refertur ad illud relatione tertij generis: quam relationem terminat obiectum, sub ratione mensuræ: obiectum verò non dependet à scientia, licèt hæc dependeat ab obiecto: & ideo scientia dicitur mensurabilis, per veram relationem: sed obiectum non dicitur mensura, per relationem propriam, aut intrinsecam, sed per solam denominationem extrinsecam, mensurabilis existentis in scientia: & ideo dixit Aristot, *Obiectum non dici mensuram*, quia referatur ad mensurabile: sed quia mensurabile refertur ad ipsum, tanquam ad absolutum quid. Vnde sequitur, quòd vel omnis terminus relationis absolutus est, vel aliquis saltem: quod sufficit, vt dicamus: terminum relationis in communi consideratum, vel esse absolutum, vel abstrahere ab absoluto, & relatiuo: quia in quibusdam relationibus absolutus est, & in aliis, relatiuus.

26 It should be noted, second, that although there are diverse opinions about the term of relation, whether it is absolute or relative, it is nevertheless certain that in relations of the third genus, which are those of the measurable and the measure, the term is not relative but absolute: for the measure is something absolute, not depending on the measurable. For example: science, under the ratio of the measurable through its object, is referred to it by a relation of the third genus; which relation the object terminates under the ratio of measure; but the object does not depend on the science, although the latter depends on the object. And therefore science is called measurable through a true relation; but the object is not called measure through a proper or intrinsic relation, but through the extrinsic denomination alone of the measurable existing in the science. And therefore Aristotle said that the object is not called a measure because it is referred to the measurable, but because the measurable is referred to it as to something absolute. Hence it follows that either every term of relation is absolute, or at least some one is: which suffices for us to say that the term of relation, considered in common, either is absolute or abstracts from the absolute and the relative: because in some relations it is absolute, and in others relative.

> 27 Et ex hoc non est difficile respondere ad formam arg. Concedẽdo primam consequentiam quòd relatiuum in communi, aut aliquid in communi, sit supremum genus huius prædicamenti: & etiam, quòd referatur ad terminum in communi, non inferiorem, nec superiorem, sed æqualem sibi. Negando tamen secundam consequentiam, quòd duo sint suprema genera: quia terminus in communi, sub ratione formali termini, non est relatiuum: sed abstrahit ab absoluto, & relatiuo: & solùm dicit quandam denominationem extrinsecam terminandi: non prædicamentalem, sed quæ reduci potest ad idem prædicamentum, quod cõstituit relatiuum in communi, tanquam supremum genus, cuius terminus ipse est. Itaque terminus in communi, non potest esse supremum genus prædicamẽti: quia non est formaliter relatiuus: imò nec ad prædicamentum per se pertinere, sed solùm reduci ad idem prædicamentum ad aliquid: in quantum aliquo modo pertinet ad relatiuum in communi, constituens per se hoc prædicamentum.

27 And from this it is not difficult to reply to the form of the argument: by granting the first consequence, that the relative in common, or ad aliquid in common, is the supreme genus of this category, and also that it is referred to a term in common, not inferior nor superior, but equal to itself; but by denying the second consequence, that there are two supreme genera: because the term in common, under the formal ratio of term, is not a relative, but abstracts from the absolute and the relative, and implies only a certain extrinsic denomination of terminating, not a categorial one, but one which can be reduced to the same category which the relative in common constitutes as the supreme genus, of which it is itself the term.
