And so the term in common cannot be the supreme genus of the category, because it is not formally relative; indeed it cannot even pertain per se to the category, but only be reduced to the same category of relation, inasmuch as it pertains in some way to the relative in common, which per se constitutes this category.

> QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

### Quæ. 4. An definitio relatiuorum, tradita ab Arist. ex propria sententia sit bona — Whether the definition of relatives handed down by Aristotle in his own view is good.

> *An definitio relatiuorum, tradita ab Aristotele, ex propria sententia, sit bona.*

[…]

> 18 DEfinitio his verbis continetur in textu: *Ad aliquid sunt: quibus hoc ipsum est esse, ad aliquid quodam modo se habere*. [p. 377] Cuius sensus est, relatiua sunt, quorum totum suum esse, est ad terminum referri. His autem argumentis probari potest, non esse bonam. Primò, quia relatio duo respicit, nempe subiectum, cui inhæret, tale denominat formaliter, & etiam terminum, ad quem refert: ergo duplicem habebit rationem formalem, vnam, secundùm quam respicit subiectum, & ei inhæret, aliam secundùm quam respicit terminum, & ad eum refert. Ex quo infero, totum esse relationis, non esse ad terminum referre, aut ordinare, sed aliquid habere absolutum, quatenus respicit subiectum, & ei inhæret Et ideo falsum esse quod in definitione dicitur: Relatiuum esse, cuius totum suum esse, est referri ad aliud. Probatur consequentia: quia relatiuum dicitur tale à relatione, sed totum esse relationis, non est referre ad terminum: ergo nec totum esse relatiui erit referri ad terminum,

18 The definition is contained in the text in these words: Relatives are those for which to be is the same as to be related in some way to something. [p. 377] Its sense is: relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to a term. But that it is not good can be proved by these arguments. First, because relation regards two things: namely the subject in which it inheres, which it formally denominates such, and also the term to which it refers; therefore it will have a twofold formal ratio: one according to which it regards the subject and inheres in it, the other according to which it regards the term and refers to it. From which I infer that the whole being of relation is not to refer or order to the term, but to have something absolute, insofar as it regards the subject and inheres in it. And therefore what is said in the definition is false: that the relative is that whose whole being is to be referred to another. The consequence is proved: because the relative is called such from relation; but the whole being of relation is not to refer to the term; therefore neither will the whole being of the relative be to be referred to the term.

> Et confirmari potest: quia hæc definitio æquè conuenit relatiuis rationis, atque realibus: imò relatiuis diuinis, & creatis: de quibus iam diximus, non collocari in prædicamento; ergo non est bona. Probatur antecedens, quia commune est omnibus quòd totum suum esse, sit referri ad terminum, non enim minùs verum est totum esse speciei, esse, ordinari ad genus, & totum esse Patris æterni, ordinari ad filium, quàm totum esse similis ad aliud simile.

And it can be confirmed: because this definition belongs equally to relatives of reason and to real ones; indeed to divine and created relatives, of which we have already said that they are not placed in the category; therefore it is not good. The antecedent is proved: because it is common to all that their whole being is to be referred to a term; for it is no less true that the whole being of the species is to be ordered to the genus, and that the whole being of the eternal Father is to be ordered to the son, than that the whole being of a like thing is toward another like thing.

> Secunda: Verba in definitione non dicunt actum, sed aptitudinem: sed definitio hæc, non potest dicere solam aptitudinem referendi, sed etiam actum: ergo non est bona. Probatur minor: quia relatiuum non est, quod potest referri, sed quod actu refertur: alioqui illud, quod non habet relationem, ex eo solùm, quod potest eam habere, esset relatiuum: quia sicut potest eam habere, potest etiam referri, quod patet esse falsum.

Second: The words in a definition do not imply act but aptitude; but this definition cannot imply the aptitude of referring alone, but also the act; therefore it is not good. The minor is proved: because the relative is not that which can be referred, but that which is referred in act; otherwise that which does not have a relation would be a relative from this alone, that it can have one: because just as it can have it, it can also be referred; which is plainly false.

> Vt definitio intelligatur, notandum est, Aristotelem, priùs quàm singula prædicamenta proponere, tradidisse vniuersalem diuisionem entis realis in decem prædicamenta, & consequenter diuisionem accidentis in nouem. Vnde sequitur ex mente illius, subintelligendum esse ens reale, in explicatione substantiæ: ita vt dicamus, Substantia est ens reale, per se; & in explicationibus prædicamentorum accidentium, accidens reale: & ita definitio relatiuorum sic debet assignari: *Ad aliquid sunt accidentia realia, quorum totum suum esse, est ad aliud referri*: Et per primam particulam excluduntur relationes diuinæ, quæ non sunt accidentia: per secundam, relationes rationis, quæ non sunt accidentia realia: per cæteras verò excluduntur relationes secundùm dici, & transcendentales: quia non sunt rationes referẽdi ad terminum: sed ad subiectum, aut obiectum: [p. 378] vel quid simile, relatiua verò huius prædicamenti, ad aliud ordinantur, tanquam ad purum terminum, de quo illam particulam ad aliud intellexit Arist. secundùm communem expositionem omnium interpretum.

In order that the definition may be understood, it should be noted that Aristotle, before proposing the several categories, handed down the universal division of real being into ten categories, and consequently the division of accident into nine. Hence it follows, in his mind, that real being is to be understood in the explanation of substance, so that we say: Substance is a real being per se; and in the explanations of the categories of accidents, real accident. And so the definition of relatives must be assigned thus: Relatives are real accidents whose whole being is to be referred to another. And by the first particle divine relations are excluded, which are not accidents; by the second, relations of reason, which are not real accidents; but by the rest, relations according to being said and transcendental relations are excluded, because they are not rationes of referring to a term, but to a subject or an object; [p. 378] or something similar; whereas the relatives of this category are ordered to another as to a pure term, of which Aristotle understood that particle to another, according to the common exposition of all the interpreters.

> Conclusio igitur nostra est, Definitionem Arist. ita explicatam esse bonam, quod probatur ex communi consensu totius scholæ, eam recipientis, & etiam ratione. Nam bona definitio est, quæ explicat naturam definiti, & illud distinguit à cæteris: sed hoc efficit præsens definitio relatiuorum: vt constat ex tradita expositione eius: ergo est bona.

Our conclusion, then, is that Aristotle’s definition, so explained, is good: which is proved from the common consent of the whole school, which accepts it, and also by reason. For a good definition is one which explains the nature of the defined and distinguishes it from the others; but the present definition of relatives does this, as is established from the exposition of it handed down; therefore it is good.

> Ad primum arg. respondent quidam, Relationem duplicem conceptum habere: Communem cum cæteris accidentibus, qui est inhærentiæ in subiecto, actu, vel aptitudine: & vocatur esse, *In*: & Particularem, per quem distinguitur ab eis, qui est referre ad terminum, & vocatur esse, *Ad*: & ratione primi conceptus, concedunt relationem respicere subiectum, sicut cætera accidentia, sed ratione particularis, non respicere subiectum, sed terminum: & ideo totum esse relationis, vt relationis, esse ad terminum, non relationis, vt accidentis. Et posset probari hic modus dicendi, ex D. Thom. 1. p. q. 28. art. 1. vbi aduersus Gilbertum quendam (qui asserebat, *Relationem nihil ponere in subiecto, aut relatiuo, & ideo non esse inhærentem in eo, sed quasi extrinsecus assistentem*) docet relationem secundùm communem conceptum inhærendi in subiecto, aliquid ponere in relatiuo: & rationem huius, inhęrentem esse. Sed secundùm conceptum proprium relationis, nihil ponere in eo, sed solùm esse rationem referendi ad aliud.

To the first argument some reply that relation has a twofold concept: a Common one, with the other accidents, which is that of inherence in a subject, in act or in aptitude, and is called esse in [being in]; and a Particular one, through which it is distinguished from them, which is to refer to a term, and is called esse ad [being toward]. And by reason of the first concept they grant that relation regards the subject, as the other accidents do, but by reason of the particular one, that it does not regard the subject but the term; and therefore that the whole being of relation as relation is to be toward the term, not of relation as accident. And this way of speaking could be proved from St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, where, against a certain Gilbert (who asserted that relation posits nothing in the subject or relative, and therefore is not inherent in it, but as it were assisting from outside), he teaches that relation, according to the common concept of inhering in a subject, posits something in the relative, and that by reason of this it is inherent; but that according to the proper concept of relation it posits nothing in it, but is only the ratio of referring to another.

> 31 Hæc tamen solutio falsa est, & eidem doctori sancto contraria. Probo primum: quia relatio secundùm proprium conceptum, *Ad*, est forma relatiua, & constituit subiectum formaliter relatiuum: vt paternitas, sub proprio conceptu paternitatis, est forma relatiua, & constituit hominem in ratione formali, & intrinseca patris: ergo secundùm proprium conceptum, ponit aliquid reale, & intrinsecum in subiecto, aut relatiuo. Euidens est consequentia: & probatur antecedens: quia denominatio patris, aut similis, & quæcunque alia relatiua, non est extrinseca, sed formalis: sicut denominatio albi, aut calidi: ergo ponit effectum formalem in subiecto: effectus autem formalis cuiuslibet realis formæ, realis esse debet: ergo necesse est, aliquid reale in subiecto ponere.

31 This solution, however, is false, and contrary to the same holy doctor. I prove the first: because relation according to its proper concept, toward, is a relative form and constitutes the subject formally relative: as paternity, under the proper concept of paternity, is a relative form and constitutes the man in the formal and intrinsic ratio of father; therefore according to its proper concept it posits something real and intrinsic in the subject or relative. The consequence is evident; and the antecedent is proved: because the denomination of father, or of like, and any other relative denomination whatever, is not extrinsic but formal, just as the denomination of white or hot; therefore it posits a formal effect in the subject; but the formal effect of any real form whatever must be real; therefore it is necessary that it posit something real in the subject.

> Secundò, quia si relatio secundùm esse, *Ad*, nihil ponit in subiecto, aut relatiuo, ergo secundùm hunc cõceptum non est aliquid reale. Probatur cõsequẽtia: quia omne ens reale aut est [p. 379] substantia aut accidens: ergo aut est ens per se, aut in alio. Sed relatio secundùm esse, *Ad*, non est ens per se: cùm non sit substantia, nec in alio, cùm non ponat aliquid in subiecto: ergo non erit aliquid reale, nec efficiet prædicamentum reale.

32 Second, because if relation according to being toward posits nothing in the subject or relative, then according to this concept it is not something real. The consequence is proved: because every real being either is [p. 379] substance or accident; therefore it is either a being per se or in another. But relation according to being toward is not a being per se, since it is not substance; nor in another, since it posits nothing in the subject; therefore it will not be something real, nor will it make a real category.

> 32 Pro vera igitur solutione arg. notandum est, Relationem realem, secundùm vtrumque conceptum, *In*, & *Ad*, aliquid ponere in subiecto, diuersa tamen ratione: nam secundùm esse, *In*, ponit aliquam rationem communem, & abstrahentem à particularibus prædicamentorum: (eo modo, quo superiùs diximus analogum abstrahi ab analogatis) sed secundùm esse, *Ad*, ponit rationem propriam relatiuam, distinctam à particularibus, quas ponunt cætera prædicamenta. Vt relatio paternitatis, ponit rationem realem patris in homine: sed hæc ratio licèt ponatur in subiecto, purè relatiua est: quia sic ponitur in subiecto, vt per illam non sit tale ad se, sed solùm ad aliud, nẽpe ad terminum: cætera verò prędicamenta, ita ponunt aliquid in subiecto, secundùm proprios conceptus, vt per illam rationem propriam, ad se sit subiectum, & non referatur ad aliud. Gratia exẽpli: quãtitatis secundùm propriũ conceptũ, ponit extensiodem partiũ in subiecto, per quã in se, & ad se dicitur extensum: sed paternitas ita ponit rationẽ realem patris in homine, vt per illã non sit tale ad se, sed ad filiũ, sicque de cæteris relationibus.

32 For the true solution of the argument, then, it should be noted that real relation, according to both concepts, in and toward, posits something in the subject, yet in a different ratio. For according to being in it posits a certain common ratio, abstracting from the particular ratios of the categories (in the way in which we said above that the analogous is abstracted from the analogates); but according to being toward it posits a proper relative ratio, distinct from the particular ratios which the other categories posit. As the relation of paternity posits the real ratio of father in the man; but this ratio, although it is posited in the subject, is purely relative: because it is posited in the subject in such a way that through it the subject is not such toward itself, but only toward another, namely toward the term. The other categories, however, posit something in the subject according to their proper concepts in such a way that through that proper ratio the subject is such toward itself, and is not referred to another. For example: quantity, according to its proper concept, posits the extension of parts in the subject, through which it is called extended in itself and toward itself; but paternity posits the real ratio of father in the man in such a way that through it he is not such toward himself, but toward the son; and so of the other relations.

> Et hoc modo intelligi debet D. Th. dum in citato loco asserit, *Relationem secundùm esse, In, ponere aliquid in subiecto: sed secundùm esse, Ad, nihil ponere speciale, per quod sit tale ad se*, sicut ponũt cætera prędicamẽta, sed purè, & omninò ad aliud. Quẽ sensum clarissimè posuit alio loco, per quem hunc explicauimus, nempe in 1. lib. sent. d. 8. q. 4. ar. 3. ad 4. vbi ita ait: *Debilitas esse relationis, consideratur secũdùm inhærentiã sui ad subiectũ, quia nõ ponit aliquid absolutũ in subiecto, sed tantũ per respectũ ad aliud*.

And in this way St. Thomas must be understood when in the place cited he asserts that relation according to being in posits something in the subject, but according to being toward posits nothing special through which it is such toward itself, as the other categories posit, but purely and altogether toward another. Which sense he set down most clearly in another place, through which we have explained this one, namely on bk. 1 of the Sentences, d. 8, q. 4, a. 3, ad 4, where he says thus: The weakness of the being of relation is considered according to its inherence in its subject, because it posits nothing absolute in the subject, but only by respect to another.

> 33 Si autem aliquis dicat: Iam ergo relatio non solùm secundùm conceptum communem accidentis, inhærebit subiecto, sed etiam secundùm proprium, & vltimum relationis, qui vocatur esse, *Ad*, aduersus illud, quod ex D. Th. adduximus, quęstione præcedenti, videlicet conceptum proprium relationis, non sumi in ordine ad subiectum, sicut sumuntur conceptus proprij accidentium absolutorum, sed in ordine ad terminum: Præterea habebit relatio duos conceptus qui vocentur, *In*, vnum communem cum accidentibus absolutis, & alium sibi proprium. Probatur consequentia: quia tam secundùm cõmunem rationem, quàm secundùm particularem, ponit aliquid in subiecto: ergo secundùm vtramque ei inhæret, & in eo est.

33 But if someone should say: Then relation will inhere in the subject not only according to the common concept of accident, but also according to the proper and ultimate concept of relation, which is called being toward; against what we adduced from St. Thomas in the preceding question, namely that the proper concept of relation is not taken in order to the subject, as the proper concepts of the absolute accidents are taken, but in order to the term. Moreover, relation will have two concepts which are called in: one common with the absolute accidents, and another proper to itself. The consequence is proved: because it posits something in the subject both according to the common ratio and according to the particular one; therefore according to both it inheres in it and is in it.

> Respondeo ad primum: Secundùm vtrumque conceptum, [p. 380] inhærere subiecto: diuersa tamen ratione: nam secũdùm communem inhæret inhærentia communi, cum cæteris, & abstrahente ab inhærentia absoluta, & respectiua: sed secundùm conceptum proprium inhæret inhærentia purè relatiua: quod est inhærere referendo ad aliud. Quod verò D. Th. dixit, proprium conceptum relationis, non sumi in ordine ad subiectum, vt in accidentibus absolutis, verissimum est: sic autem intelligendum, vt non sumatur in ordine ad subiectum, vt *In se*, & *Ad se* est, sed vt refertur ad aliud, per eandem rationem relatiuam, in eo positam. In quo valde differt ratio, propria relationis, à rationibus particularibus accidentium absolutorum, quæ sumuntur in ordine ab subiectum, vt est in se, & ad se, non vt est ad aliud, per tales rationes.

I reply to the first: According to both concepts, [p. 380] it inheres in the subject, yet in a different ratio: for according to the common concept it inheres by a common inherence, together with the others, abstracting from absolute and respective inherence; but according to its proper concept it inheres by a purely relative inherence, which is to inhere by referring to another. And what St. Thomas said, that the proper concept of relation is not taken in order to the subject, as in the absolute accidents, is most true; but it must be understood thus: that it is not taken in order to the subject as it is in itself and toward itself, but as it is referred to another through the same relative ratio placed in it. In which the proper ratio of relation differs greatly from the particular rationes of the absolute accidents, which are taken in order to the subject as it is in itself and toward itself, not as it is toward another, through such rationes.

> 34 Ad aliud verò respondeo, Relationem habere esse, *In*, commune, cum cæteris accidentibus, & esse, *In*, particulare, per quod subiectum refert ad terminum, & per hoc esse, *In*, particulare, determinatur aliud, *In*, commune, & fit vna ratio prædicamentalis ex vtroque: quia ex determinante per se, & determinabili, per se, semper fit vnum per se: sicut quodlibet accidens absolutum, habet esse, *In* commune, & particulare, & ex vtroque efficitur vnum.

34 To the other I reply that relation has a common being in, with the other accidents, and a particular being in, through which the subject is referred to the term; and by this particular being in the other, common being in is determined, and one categorial ratio is made from both: because from what determines per se and what is determinable per se there always comes to be something one per se: just as any absolute accident whatever has a common and a particular being in, and from both one thing is made.

> Ad formam igitur primi argu. Concedendum est primum enthymema, quo probatur relationem habere duplicem conceptum: Vnum, quo respicit subiectum, Alium, quo respicit terminum. Negandum tamen est, quod infertur, totum esse relationis, & relatiui, non esse ad terminum: quia illud esse, quod habet in subiecto, si consideretur in communi, abstrahit ab absoluto, & relatiuo, & contrahitur per esse ad terminum: & per talem contractionem, ordinatur ad illũ, & fit relatiuum: si verò consideretur in particulari, est esse proprium relationis, & ideo est esse relatiuum: vnde sequitur, relatiuum esse, quidquid habet relatio, & quidquid habet relatiuum: & hoc est *totum esse relationis, & relatiui, esse ad aliud*, vt dicitur in definitione Arist. Ad confirmationem, responsum est, per explicationem definitionis.

To the form of the first argument, then: The first enthymeme must be granted, by which it is proved that relation has a twofold concept: One by which it regards the subject, Another by which it regards the term. But what is inferred must be denied, that the whole being of relation and of the relative is not to be toward the term: because that being which it has in the subject, if it is considered in common, abstracts from the absolute and the relative, and is contracted through being toward the term; and through such contraction it is ordered to it, and becomes relative; but if it is considered in particular, it is the proper being of relation, and therefore it is a relative being. Hence it follows that whatever relation has, and whatever the relative has, is relative; and this is the whole being of relation and of the relative to be toward another, as is said in Aristotle’s definition. To the confirmation the reply has been given through the explanation of the definition.

> 35 Circa solutionem secundi arg. aliqui distinguunt relatum, & relatiuum, dicentes: Relatiuum dicere potentiam ad referendum, relatum verò, actuale exercitium referendi: & in definitione potiùs explicari ad aliquid, vt relatum, quàm vt relatiuum. Hæc tamen distinctio, non habet fundamentum: quia vt superiùs probauimus, exercitium referendi, vel actus referendi, non est aliud quàm naturalis ipsa ordinatio, vnius relatiui ad aliud: quæ semper eodem modo se habet, & semper est [p. 381] actualis, & semper exercetur inter relatiua: quòd necessariò dicendum est: nam eo ipso, quòd vnum relatiuum non referatur actu, vel in exercitio ad aliud, nõ habebit actu in se relationem, nec erit relatiuum formaliter: & eo ipso, quòd habet in se relationem, non potest non referri actu, & secundùm exercitium. Idem ergo prorsus sunt, secundùm rem, & secundùm rationem, relatum, & relatiuum: sed illud magis distinctè explicat actum referendi, quia etiam minus distinctè dicit aliud: ideo in definitione Arist. pro vtroque sumitur nomen, ad aliquid: & actum referendi dicit, non potentiam.

35 Concerning the solution of the second argument, some distinguish the related and the relative, saying that the relative implies a potency for referring, but the related the actual exercise of referring; and that in the definition the relative (ad aliquid) is explained as related rather than as relative. This distinction, however, has no foundation: because, as we proved above, the exercise of referring, or the act of referring, is nothing other than the natural ordering itself of one relative to another, which always holds itself in the same way, and is always [p. 381] actual, and is always exercised between relatives: which must necessarily be said; for by the very fact that one relative is not referred in act, or in exercise, to another, it will not have relation in act in itself, nor will it be a relative formally; and by the very fact that it has relation in itself, it cannot fail to be referred in act and according to exercise. Therefore related and relative were altogether the same, according to the thing and according to the ratio; but the former explains the act of referring more distinctly, because the latter also says the same thing less distinctly; and therefore in Aristotle’s definition the name toward something is taken for both, and it says the act of referring, not the potency.

> Ad argum. ergo respondetur, Distinguendo illud axioma, quòd verba in definitione non dicũt actum, sed aptitudinem: nam res quæ definiuntur, sunt in duplici differentia. Quædam enim sunt, quarum ratio, vel essentia in aptitudine, vel potentia consistit: & istæ, licèt definiantur per verba significantia actum, non pro actu, sed pro potentia accipiuntur in definitione: & ratio huius est: quia actus in his, non potest esse essentialis: & ideo non bene definiuntur per actum. Aliæ sunt, quarum ratio, vel essentia, non consistit in aptitudine, sed in actu: & in definitione harum, non possunt verba accipi pro aptitudine, quia si ita accipiantur, non explicabunt naturam definiti: Sed pro actu debent accipi, vt rationem eius explicent. Vt si definiatur quantum, pro eo, quòd habet partem extra partem, secundùm extensionem molis: non possunt verba huius definitionis, dicere aptitudinem, sed actum: quia ratio extensionis, in actu consistit, non in aptitudine: sicque de cæteris. Et ita se habet relatiuum, cuius ratio, in actuali ordinatione, & relatione consistit: ideo verba definitionis eius pro actu, & non pro aptitudine accipiuntur.

To the argument, then, the reply is made by distinguishing that axiom, that the words in a definition do not say act but aptitude: for the things that are defined are of two different kinds. For some are those whose ratio or essence consists in aptitude or potency; and these, although they are defined through words signifying act, are taken in the definition not for act but for potency; and the reason for this is that act in these cannot be essential, and therefore they are not well defined through act. Others are those whose ratio or essence consists not in aptitude but in act; and in the definition of these the words cannot be taken for aptitude, because if they were so taken they would not explain the nature of the thing defined; but they must be taken for act, in order to explain its ratio. As, if the quantum is defined as that which has part outside part according to the extension of bulk, the words of this definition cannot say aptitude but act: because the ratio of extension consists in act, not in aptitude; and so of the others. And so it is with the relative, whose ratio consists in actual ordering and relation: therefore the words of its definition are taken for act and not for aptitude.

> QVÆSTIO V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

### Quæ. 5. Vtrùm omnes relationes pertineant ad prædicamentum ad aliquid — Whether all relations belong to this category.

> *Vtrùm omnes relationes petineant ad hoc prædicamentum.*

[…]

> 36 TAnquam certum præsupponendum est, nec Diuinas relationes, nec etiam relationes rationis, collocari in hoc prædicamento: quia vt in præcedenti quæst. probauimus, præditamentum ad aliquid, est membrum quoddam generalis diuisionis accidentis realis, in nouem prædicamenta: & ideo relatiuum, quod est supremum genus, est accidens reale, atque finitum: quare nec relationes Diuinæ, cùm sint substantiales, & infinitæ, possunt pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum, nec relationes rationis: quia non sunt accidentia realia,

36 As something certain it must be presupposed that neither the Divine relations nor even relations of reason are placed in this category: because, as we proved in the preceding question, the category of relation is a certain member of the general division of real accident into nine categories; and therefore the relative, which is the supreme genus, is a real and finite accident. Wherefore neither can the Divine relations, since they are substantial and infinite, belong to this category, nor relations of reason: because they are not real accidents.

[p. 382]

> Solùm ergo procedit quæst. de relationibus realibus creaturarum: *An omnes ponantur in hoc prædicamento?* verùm non distinguntur ab omnibus eodem modo: nam quidam asserunt, *Esse eas res in triplici differentia*: Quædam sunt transcendentales, quæ in rebus diuersorum prædicamentorum reperiuntur, eisque essentialiter conueniunt, quasi complementum essentiæ: tales sunt respectus inclusi, in essentia cuiuslibet accidentis, per quos ordinatur ad subiectũ, cui inhęrere aptũ est.

The question, therefore, proceeds only concerning the real relations of creatures: whether all are placed in this category? But they are not distinguished by all in the same way. For some assert that they are things of three different kinds. Some are transcendental, which are found in things of diverse categories and belong to them essentially, as it were a complement of the essence: such are the respects included in the essence of any accident whatever, through which it is ordered to the subject in which it is apt to inhere.

> 38 Aliæ sunt relationes, quæ non omnibus accidentibus vniuersaliter conueniunt, sed quibusdam tantùm: in quorum essentiis, etiam includuntur: vt respectus, quem dicunt habitus, potentiæ, & scientiæ ad propria obiecta, & istæ vocantur relationes secundùm dici.

38 Others are relations which belong not to all accidents universally, but only to certain ones, in whose essences they are also included: as the respect which habit, power, and science bear to their proper objects; and these are called relations according to being said.

> Aliæ denique sunt relationes, quæ nulli conueniunt essentialiter, sed accidentaliter conueniunt multis: & dicuntur relationes secundùm esse: vt paternitas, similitudo, & æqualitas. Alij verò solùm has vltimas relationes admittunt: & nullam prorsus ex iis, quæ ad essentiam alicuius absoluti pertineant. Sic videtur sentire Scot. in 4. d. 12. q. vnica. Probántque non esse admittendas. Primò, quia quidquid pertinet ad essentiam substantiæ, est substantiæ: & quidquid pertinet ad essentiam quantitatis, est quantitas: ergo si relationes tales dantur, quæ pertineant ad essentiam omnium rerum absolutarum, erunt res absolutæ: vt in substantia, erunt substantiæ, in quantitate, quantitas, & in qualitate, qualitas. Et si ad essentiam aliquarum rerum tantùm pertineant, vt ad essentiam habitus aut potentiæ, erunt etiam potentiæ, & habitus. Hæc autem falsa sunt: ideo falsum erit tales relationes ponere.

Others, finally, are relations which belong to none essentially, but belong accidentally to many; and they are called relations according to being: as paternity, similarity, and equality. But others admit only these last relations, and none at all of those that would pertain to the essence of something absolute. So Scotus seems to hold, in 4, d. 12, single q. And they prove that they are not to be admitted. First, because whatever pertains to the essence of substance is substance, and whatever pertains to the essence of quantity is quantity; therefore, if such relations are given as pertain to the essence of all absolute things, they will be absolute things: in substance they will be substances, in quantity quantity, and in quality quality. And if they pertain to the essence of certain things only, as to the essence of habit or power, they will also be powers and habits. But these things are false; therefore it will be false to posit such relations.

> Probatur secundò: quia si intra essentiam absolutorum admittantur relationes istæ, aliud absurdum erit concedendum: nempe, quòd tales essentiæ componantur, ex entitate absoluta, & relatiua, diuersis non solùm specie, sed genere.

It is proved second: because if these relations are admitted within the essence of absolute things, another absurdity will have to be conceded: namely, that such essences are composed of an absolute and a relative entity, diverse not only in species but in genus.

> 39 Alij denique præter relationes accidentales, vel secũdùm esse, admittunt intra essentiam absolutorum trãscendentales: non tamen relationes secundùm dici, nisi solo nomine: nam habitus inquiunt, potentia, & scientia, purè absoluta sunt, nec dicunt respectum realem ad obiecta, sed absolutam proportionem cum eis: quam proportionem non possumus intelligere, nec explicare, nisi per quendam respectum, quem intellectus concipit in eis: & ideo de eis loquitur, quasi de respectiuis: cùm tamen non sint verè respectiua, sed absoluta: licèt in communi modo loquendi, respectiua dicantur: & propterea appellentur relatiua secundùm dici.

39 Others, finally, besides the accidental relations, or relations according to being, admit transcendental ones within the essence of absolute things, yet not relations according to being said, except in name only. For habit, they say, power, and science are purely absolute, and do not say a real respect to their objects, but an absolute proportion with them; which proportion we cannot understand or explain except through a certain respect which the intellect conceives in them; and therefore it speaks of them as of respective things, although they are not truly respective but absolute, though in the common manner of speaking they are called respective; and for this reason they are called relatives according to being said.

[p. 383]

> Vltimus modus dicendi, concedit, præter relationes secundùm esse, transcendentales, & secundùm dici, & vtraque pertinere ad essentiam absolutorũ: sed eas ita confundit, vt omnes esse appellandas transcẽdentales asserat: & ita relationem realẽ creatam, in duo tantùm membra diuidendam esse, nempe in transcendentalem, & prędicamentalem: ita vt sub primo membro, tam respectus, qui omnibus prędicamentis absolutis essentialiter conueniunt, quàm qui aliquibus tantùm comprehendantur. Sub secundo verò, solùm relationes accidentales, quæ vocantur secundùm esse, & pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum. Nostra sententia tribus conclusionibus explicatur.

The last way of speaking grants that, besides relations according to being, there are transcendental relations and relations according to being said, and that both pertain to the essence of absolute things; but it so confounds them as to assert that all are to be called transcendental; and so that created real relation is to be divided into only two members, namely into transcendental and categorial: so that under the first member are comprehended both the respects which belong essentially to all the absolute categories and those which belong to certain ones only; but under the second only the accidental relations, which are called according to being and pertain to this category. Our view is explained in three conclusions.

> 40 Prima est: Necesse est ponere respectus quosdam reales, pertinentes ad essentiam *accidentium absolutorum: vt respectus, quem includit inhærentia aptitudinalis eorum ad subiectum, & habitus, & potentiæ ad obiectum, & respectus isti, diminutæ quædam relationes sunt, complentes essentiam absolutorum*. Hanc conclusionem tenet. D. Thom. 1. par. q. 13. art. 7. ad 1. & q. 28 ar. 1. Caiet. in opusc. de ente & essentia, ca. 7. q. 15. Et probatur testimonio Arist. 2. lib. de anima, tex. 33. vbi docet, *Essentiam specificam potentiarum, ab actibus, & obiectis sumendam esse*: quod non potest esse verum, nisi respectum essentialem ad obiectum includant. Nam euidens est, non sic accipiendam esse essentiam specificam potentiæ ab obiecto vt obiectum sit de essentia eius cùm sit semper res diuersa ab ea, ergo necesse est sumi per respectum eiusdem potentiæ ad obiectum: ideo talem respectum esse ei essentiale. Probatur consequentia: quia si nec obiectum, nec respectus ad ipsum est de essentia potentiarum, nullo modo accipietur species earum ab obiectis.

40 The first is: It is necessary to posit certain real respects pertaining to the essence of absolute accidents, such as the respect which the aptitudinal inherence of these includes to the subject, and of habit and power to the object; and these respects are certain diminished relations completing the essence of absolute things. This conclusion is held by St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, ad 1, and q. 28, a. 1; Cajetan, in the opuscule On Being and Essence, ch. 7, q. 15. And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, On the Soul 2, text 33, where he teaches that the specific essence of powers is to be taken from their acts and objects: which cannot be true unless they include an essential respect to the object. For it is evident that the specific essence of a power is not to be taken from the object in such a way that the object is of its essence, since it is always a thing diverse from it; therefore it must necessarily be taken from the respect of that same power to the object; and therefore such a respect is essential to it. The consequence is proved: because if neither the object nor the respect to it is of the essence of the powers, their species will in no way be taken from the objects.

> 41 Probatur deinde ratione, quia accidentia non sunt entia simpliciter, sed entis entia, hoc est, aliquid substantiæ, ad quam intrinsecam attributionem dicunt: sed talis attributio, non potest esse, neque intelligi, nisi per aliquem respectum ad eandem substantiam, inclusum in essentia accidentium: ergo necessariò ponendi sunt respectus isti essentiales, in omnibus accidentibus absolutis.

41 It is proved next by reason: because accidents are not beings simply, but beings of a being, that is, something of substance, to which they say an intrinsic attribution; but such an attribution can neither exist nor be understood except through some respect to that same substance included in the essence of accidents; therefore these essential respects must necessarily be posited in all absolute accidents.

> Secunda conclusio: *Ex his respectibus ad essentiam absolutorum pertinentibus, plures sunt transcendentales, & plures etiam prædicamentales*. Probatur primum: quia transcendentale dicitur illud, cuius propria ratio, transcendit omnia prædicamenta, vel saltem plura: sed respectus aptitudinalis: inhærentiæ ad subiectum, quem in sua essentia includit accidens, transcendit omnia prædicamenta accidentium sicut accidens ipsum: ergo erit relatio transcendentalis.

The second conclusion: Of these respects pertaining to the essence of absolute things, many are transcendental, and many also categorial. The first is proved: because that is called transcendental whose proper ratio transcends all the categories, or at least several; but the aptitudinal respect of inherence to the subject, which an accident includes in its essence, transcends all the categories of accidents, just as accident itself does; therefore it will be a transcendental relation.

[p. 384]

> Probatur secundum, ratione opposita, nam transcendens est, quod multis prædicamentis est commune: sed dantur plures respectus essentiales rebus absolutis, qui non possunt ad plura prædicamenta pertinere: ergo non erunt transcendentales. Probatur minor: quia respectus habituum, & potentiarum ad sua obiecta, non possunt ad plura se extendere, quàm habitus ipsi, atque potentiæ, quibus sunt essentiales: sed habitus, & potentia solùm pertinent ad prædicamentum qualitatis, imò solùm ad determinata genera huius prædicamenti: ergo nec sunt, nec dici debent transcendentales.

The second is proved by the opposite reason: for that is transcendent which is common to many categories; but there are many essential respects in absolute things which cannot pertain to several categories; therefore they will not be transcendental. The minor is proved: because the respects of habits and powers to their objects cannot extend themselves to more than the habits and powers themselves to which they are essential; but habit and power pertain only to the category of quality, indeed only to determinate genera of this category; therefore they neither are nor ought to be called transcendental.

> Tertia conclusio, *Ex tribus generibus relationum, nempe transcendentalium, secundùm dici, & secundùm esse, transcendentales ad nullum prædicamentum pertinent, relationes secundùm dici pertinent ad prædicamentum absoluti, cuius essentiam complent, relationes verò secundùm esse, aut accidentales, constituunt prædicamentum relationis*.

The third conclusion: Of the three genera of relations, namely transcendental, according to being said, and according to being, the transcendental pertain to no category; relations according to being said pertain to the category of the absolute thing whose essence they complete; but relations according to being, or accidental relations, constitute the category of relation.

> Probanda sunt tria hæc: & primum, de respectibus transcendentalibus facilè probatur, ex ipsamet transcendentia: nam quod transcendens est, ad nullum speciale prædicamentum pertinere potest: ergo relationes istæ transcendentales, ab omni prædicamento excluduntur, Probatur antecedens, quia prædicamenta continent determinatum modum essendi, vt substantia modum per se, quantitas modum entensionis: sed transcendens non est determinatum ad aliquem modum essendi, sed comprehendit multos: ergo non potest ad speciale prædicamentum pertinere.

These three things must be proved. And the first, concerning transcendental respects, is easily proved from transcendence itself: for what is transcendent can pertain to no special category; therefore these transcendental relations are excluded from every category. The antecedent is proved: because the categories contain a determinate mode of being, as substance the mode of being per se, quantity the mode of extension; but the transcendent is not determined to any mode of being, but comprehends many; therefore it cannot pertain to a special category.

> 43 Secũdum verò, de relationibus secundùm dici, sic probo: Respectus quem dicunt potẽtia, & habitus ad obiecta, cõplent essentiam eorum: ergo pertinent ad essentias, quas complent, tanquam aliquid earum: quare necesse est in eodem prædicamento collocari, & sub eodem genere: sub quo sunt tales essentiæ. Quod intelligendum est reductiuè tantùm, sicut partes reducuntur ad prædicamentum, & speciem totius, & non per se, & directè: quia incompletum aliquid sunt, atque diminutum, & qui non possunt per se efficere speciem, nisi simul cum absoluto, cuius essentiam complent: vt si solum respectum potentiæ, aut habitus ad obiectum intelligas, non intelligendo absolutam rationem qualitatis, nihil completum, aut prædicamentale intelligis: quia respectus isti, essentialiter coniunguntur cum absoluta ratione qualitatis, quam complent: & ideo nihil completum sine illa intelliguntur constituere: vnde nec nomina potentiarum, & habituum imponuntur ad significandos hos respectus, sed principalem rationem [p. 385] qualitatis, quam consequuntur, vt bene ait D. Th. 1. p. q. 13. ar. 7. ad 1. & qu. 7. de potentia. art. 10. ideo nec per se constituuntur in prædicamento, sed per absolutum. Et hinc sequitur non pertinere ad prædicamentum ad aliquid, nec vocari relationes prędicamentales, sed secundùm dici ab Arist. Et ratio huius denominationis est: quia tales ab antiquis dicebantur, & cum veris, & prædicamẽtalibus confundebantur: cùm tamen non sint relationes secundùm esse, sed solo nomine harum gaudeant.

43 The second, concerning relations according to being said, I prove thus: the respect which power and habit bear to their objects completes their essence; therefore they pertain to the essences which they complete, as something of them; wherefore they must necessarily be placed in the same category and under the same genus under which such essences are. Which is to be understood only reductively, as parts are reduced to the category and species of the whole, and not per se and directly: because they are something incomplete and diminished, and they cannot of themselves make up a species except together with the absolute thing whose essence they complete: as, if you understand only the respect of a power or habit to its object, without understanding the absolute ratio of quality, you understand nothing complete or categorial; because these respects are essentially conjoined with the absolute ratio of quality, which they complete; and therefore they are not understood to constitute anything complete without it. Hence neither are the names of powers and habits imposed to signify these respects, but the principal ratio of quality, [p. 385] which they follow, as St. Thomas well says, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, ad 1, and q. 7 On Power, a. 10; and therefore they are not constituted in a category per se, but through the absolute thing. And hence it follows that they do not pertain to the category of relation, nor are they called categorial relations, but relations according to being said, by Aristotle. And the reason for this denomination is that such were so called by the ancients, and were confused with true and categorial relations, although they are not relations according to being, but enjoy only their name.

> 44 Tertium denique, quòd relationes, quæ nulli sunt essentiales, sed accidentaliter semper conueniunt, efficiant per se hoc prædicamentum, communis est consensus totius scholæ, Et ratio eius colligitur, ex differentia earum à relationibus transcendentibus, & secundùm dici: quæ cùm pertineant ad essentiam absolutorum, quam complent, incompleti quidam respectus sunt, & aliquid eorum: & ideo non possunt per se constituere rationem prędicamentalem, sed simul cum eisdem absolutis. Relationes verò, quæ extra essentiam omnium absolutorum sunt, primò habent modum naturæ completæ: quia nihil essentiale alicuius sunt, sed per se habent proprium modum essendi, ad aliquid, qui sit integra, atque completa ratio prædicamentalis, sicut cætera accidentia prædicamentalia, & consequenter sua genera, species, ac differentias, ex quibus per se potest fieri ordinatio prædicamentalis. Habent etiam secundò, quòd sint totum esse essentiale relatiuorum, ita vt nihil præter relationes ipsas essentialiter includant: & ideo sic definita sunt ab Arist. *Relatiua sunt quorum totum suum esse sit, ad aliud se habere*.

44 The third, finally, that the relations which are essential to nothing but always belong accidentally make up this category per se, is the common consensus of the whole school. And its reason is gathered from their difference from the transcendental relations and those according to being said: which, since they pertain to the essence of the absolute things which they complete, are certain incomplete respects and something of them; and therefore they cannot constitute a categorial ratio per se, but only together with those same absolute things. But the relations which are outside the essence of all absolute things have, first, the mode of a complete nature: because they are nothing essential of anything, but have per se their own mode of being, toward something, which is an entire and complete categorial ratio, like the other categorial accidents, and consequently their own genera, species, and differences, from which a categorial ordering can be made per se. They have also, second, that they are the whole essential being of relatives, so that these include nothing essentially besides the relations themselves; and therefore they are so defined by Aristotle: Relatives are those whose whole being is to be disposed toward another.

> 45 Conueniunt igitur relationes istæ cum transcendentalibus, in eo, quòd nihil absolutum dicunt, sed totum esse earum est, esse rationes referendi ad aliud: differunt tamen in duobus. In primo quidem: quia respectus secundùm dici, non sunt tota ratio, totum esse, aut tota essentia relatiuorum: sed quoddam complemẽtum eorum: & ideo ea, quorum complementum sunt, non sunt relatiua simpliciter, sed simpliciter absoluta: & ex consequenti dicuntur quodam modo relatiua, & ex hoc sequitur secunda differentia, quòd respectus isti non sunt ad aliud, tanquam ad terminũ, sed tanquam ad subiectũ, vel obiectum, vt petit natura absoluti, quod complẽt: relationes verò prædicamentales, non solùm non dicunt aliquid absolutum, sed sunt tota ratio, tota essentia, totum esse relatiuorum, quæ constituunt: & ideo relatiua ab eis constituta, nihil absolutum dicunt, sed totum suum esse, est referri ad aliud, non quidem tanquam ad obiectum, vel subiectum, sed [p. 386] tanquam ad purum terminum: quia relatio à qua sola constituuntur, non petit aliud sub aliqua ratione particulari, ad quam ordinet relatiuum, quod constituit, sed sub ratione præcisa termini.

45 These relations, therefore, agree with the transcendental ones in this, that they say nothing absolute, but their whole being is to be rationes of referring to another; yet they differ in two respects. In the first, indeed: because respects according to being said are not the whole ratio, the whole being, or the whole essence of relatives, but a certain complement of them; and therefore the things whose complement they are are not relatives simply but absolute simply, and consequently they are called relatives in a certain way. And from this follows the second difference: that these respects are not toward another as toward a term, but as toward a subject or object, as the nature of the absolute thing which they complete requires; whereas categorial relations not only do not say anything absolute, but are the whole ratio, the whole essence, the whole being of the relatives which they constitute; and therefore the relatives constituted by them say nothing absolute, but their whole being is to be referred to another, not indeed as to an object or subject, but as Bb [p. 386] toward a pure term: because the relation by which alone they are constituted does not require another thing under some particular ratio, to which it orders the relative which it constitutes, but under the precise ratio of term.

> 46 Ad primum arg. secundæ opinionis, contrariæ relationis secundùm dici, distinguendum est antecedens. nam esse Substantiam, quidquid pertinet ad essentiam substantiæ: & quantitatem, quidquid pertinet ad essentiam quantitatis duobus modis intelligi potest: In recto, & in obliquo. Et primo modo negandum est, quia non est necessarium, rem aliquam prædicari in recto: de quocunque eius modo, aut complemento: ita vt dicatur simpliciter substantia, aut quantitas: bene tamen in obliquo: ita vt dicatur aliquid substantiæ, vel quantitatis: & hoc modo verum est, hos respectus esse absolutos, vel substantias, id est, aliquid rerum absolutarum, vel substantiæ.

46 To the first argument of the second opinion, contrary to relation according to being said, the antecedent must be distinguished. For that whatever pertains to the essence of substance is substance, and whatever pertains to the essence of quantity is quantity, can be understood in two ways: in recto and in obliquo. In the first way it must be denied, because it is not necessary that a thing be predicated in recto of any mode or complement of it whatever, so that it be called simply substance or quantity; but it may well be in obliquo, so that it be called something of substance or of quantity; and in this way it is true that these respects are absolute things or substances, that is, something of absolute things, or of substance.

> Ad secundum: Negandum est, quòd sequatur absoluta illa, in quibus clauduntur isti respectus, composita esse ex absoluto, & respectiuo: quia non includuntur in rebus absolutis, per modum generis, aut differentiæ, aut per modum compositionis. sed tam in genere, quàm in differentia, atque in specie ipsa ex eis composita, per modum cuiusdam complementi: tam compositorum, quàm componentium, vnde non sequitur compositionem aliquam cum eis facere.

To the second: it must be denied that it follows that those absolute things in which these respects are enclosed are composed of an absolute and a respective entity: because they are not included in absolute things by way of genus or of difference, or by way of composition, but both in the genus and in the difference, and in the species itself composed of them, by way of a certain complement, both of the composites and of the components; whence it does not follow that they make any composition with them.

## QUESTION VI

> QVÆSTIO VI.

[…]

> *An species relationis prædicamentalis, à termino sit accipienda.*

Whether the species of categorial relation is to be taken from the term.

> 47 DE sola relatione prædicamentali procedit quæstio, non de relationibus transcendentalibus, nec secũdùm dici: quas probauimus quæstione præcedenti, non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum. Vt autem meliùs intelligantur, quæ de relatione dicenda sunt, quasdam diuisiones relatiuorum adducere oportet. Relatiuum igitur, quod est supremum genus huius prædicamenti, primò diuiditur in tria genera intermedia, secundùm tria fundamenta, in quibus fundatur, enumerata ab Aristot, 5. lib. Metaph. cap. 15. Primum genus relatiuorum est eorum, quæ fundantur in vnitate, vel diuersitate generica, aut specifica, & habet sub se tria alia genera, vel species, secundùm diuersa fundamenta, in quibus reperitur vnitas, aut diuersitas. Nam si reperiatur in Substantia, erit relatio identitatis, vel diuersitatis, si in Qualitate, relatio similitudinis, aut dissimilitudinis, & si in Quantitate, relatio æqualitatis, vel inæqualitatis. Secundum genus relatiuorum est eorum, quæ [p. 387] fundantur in actione, & passione: vt relationes paternitatis, & filiationis: & habet alia genera, vel species subalternas: secundùm diuersas actiones, de præsenti, præterito, & futuro. Tertium, eorum, quæ fundantur in mensura, vt relationes potentiarum, & scientiarum, sub nomine mensurabilis, ad sua obiecta sub nomine mensuræ: nam obiectum dicitur mensura scientiæ, & potentiæ: scientia, atque potentia, mensurabilis per obiectum: ex eo, quod ad nihil potest vtraque extendi, aut circa nihil versari, quod non contineatur sub proprio obiecto.

47 The question proceeds only concerning categorial relation, not concerning transcendental relations, nor those according to being said, which we proved in the preceding question do not pertain to this category. But in order that what is to be said about relation may be better understood, it is necessary to adduce certain divisions of relatives. The relative, then, which is the supreme genus of this category, is first divided into three intermediate genera, according to the three foundations on which it is founded, enumerated by Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15. The first genus of relatives is of those which are founded on generic or specific unity or diversity, and it has under it three other genera, or species, according to the diverse foundations in which unity or diversity is found. For if it is found in Substance, it will be a relation of identity or diversity; if in Quality, a relation of similarity or dissimilarity; and if in Quantity, a relation of equality or inequality. The second genus of relatives is of those which are founded [p. 387] on action and passion: as the relations of paternity and filiation; and it has other genera, or subalternate species, according to the diverse actions, present, past, and future. The third, of those which are founded on measure: as the relations of powers and sciences, under the name of the measurable, to their objects under the name of measure; for the object is called the measure of science and of power, and science and power measurable by the object, from the fact that neither can extend to anything, or be concerned with anything, which is not contained under its proper object.

> 48 Secunda diuisio, minùs vniuersalis est: qua diuiditur relatiuum, in Mutuum, & non mutuum. Relatiua mutua sunt, quorum vtrumque dicitur tale, per relationem realem: vt pater, & filius: Non mutua, quorum vnum tantùm dicitur tale, per relationem realem: in altero verò, talis relatio non est, vt mensurabile, & mensura: nam illud dicitur tale, per relationem realem: hæc verò non habet talem relationem.

48 The second division is less universal: by it the relative is divided into Mutual and non-mutual. Mutual relatives are those each of which is called such through a real relation: as father and son. Non-mutual, those of which only one is called such through a real relation, while in the other such a relation does not exist: as the measurable and the measure; for the former is called such through a real relation, but the latter does not have such a relation.

> Tertia diuisio est: Relatiua alia sunt Æquiparantiæ, alia disquiparantiæ. Æquiparantiæ, quæ eiusdem rationis, & denominationis sunt, vt similia æqualia. Disquiparantiæ dicuntur, quæ diuersæ rationis sunt, & denominationis, vt pater, & filius. Quodlibet autem horum generum, suas habet species, & de omnibus, & singulis, quærit titulus quæstionis, *A quo sumant distinctionem specificam, an à termino, vel ab aliquo alio*.

The third division is: some relatives are of Equiparance, others of Disquiparance. Of equiparance are those which are of the same ratio and denomination, as like things and equal things. Those are called of disquiparance which are of diverse ratio and denomination, as father and son. Now each of these genera has its own species, and of all and each the title of the question asks from what they take their specific distinction, whether from the term or from something else.

> Et prima opinio, videtur esse D. Tho. 3 p. q. 35. ar. 5. & quodlib 9. ar. 4. *Quòd relatio, aut relatiuum, non sumat speciem à termino, sed potiùs à causa, per quam producitur*: Quod probat hoc argum. Quia si relatio sumeret speciem à termino, sequeretur in vtroque parente, eandem esse relationem ad filium. Probatur consequentia: quia filius vnicus terminus est, ergo relatio patris, & matris, ad eum terminata, erit eadem. Sed consequens est falsum, ergo etiam antecedens, quòd relatio sumat speciem à termino. Probatur minor: quia pater est causa efficiens filij, mater verò passiua tantùm, ergo habent rationes causarum, specie diuersas: quas necessariò consequitur diuersa relatio in vtroque: paternitatis in patre, & maternitatis in matre.

And the first opinion seems to be that of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 35, a. 5, and Quodlibet 9, a. 4: that relation, or the related, does not take its species from the term, but rather from the cause through which it is produced. Which this argument proves: because if relation took its species from the term, it would follow that in both parents there is the same relation to the son. The consequence is proved: because the son is the single term; therefore the relation of the father and of the mother, terminated at him, will be the same. But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent also, that relation takes its species from the term. The minor is proved: because the father is the efficient cause of the son, but the mother only a passive one; therefore they have rationes of causes diverse in species, which a diverse relation in each necessarily follows: of paternity in the father, and of maternity in the mother.

> 49 Secundò probatur: quia species debet sumi ab aliquo intrinseco, quòd sit differentia essentialis eius: sed terminus relationis, est res diuersa à relatione, & ei extrinseca, vt pater respectu filiationis, ergo non potest sumi ab eo species. Et si respondeas, non ita sumi speciem à termino, vt terminus ipse sit differentia specifica relationis: sed ordinatio ad terminum. Contra hoc est: quòd relatio ipsa, est ordinatio ad terminum: ergo si ex ordine, aut ordinatione ad terminum, sumitur [p. 388] species eius, sumet speciem à seipsa: quod patet esse falsum.

49 It is proved second: because the species must be taken from something intrinsic, which is its essential difference; but the term of a relation is a thing diverse from the relation and extrinsic to it, as the father with respect to filiation; therefore the species cannot be taken from it. If you reply that the species is not taken from the term in such a way that the term itself is the specific difference of the relation, but the ordering to the term: against this is that the relation itself is the ordering to the term; therefore, if it is taken from the order or ordering to the term, B b ij [p. 388] which is its species, it will take its species from itself: which is plainly false.

> Pro hac etiam sententia, adduci potest testimonium Arist. quia tria genera relationum distinguit (vt vidimus) non per diuersos terminos, sed per diuersa fundamenta: ergo sentit non esse sumendam speciem relationis à termino.

For this opinion, too, the testimony of Aristotle can be adduced: because he distinguishes the three genera of relations (as we have seen) not by diverse terms but by diverse foundations; therefore he holds that the species of relation is not to be taken from the term.

> 50 Secunda opinio est communis, & vera, Quòd relatio, aut relatiuum, sumit suam speciem à termino: ita vt illæ relationes sint eiusdem speciei: quæ habent terminum eiusdem speciei: vt omnes paternitates omnes similitudines: illæ verò sint specie distinctæ, quæ habent terminos specie distinctos: vt similitudo, & dissimilitudo. Probatur ex definitione Arist. quæ ait: *Relatiua esse, quorum totum suum esse, est referri ad aliud*, hoc est, ad terminum, ergo talis erit relatio, qualis fuerit terminus, ad quem refert: & hoc est ab eo accipere speciem. Et D. Th. absque dubio tenet eandem sententiam, 3. p. q. 32. art. 2. vbi sic ait: *Cùm ratio specifica relationis, consistat in hoc, quod aliud se habet, necesse est dicere, quòd duæ relationes, non sunt diuersæ secundùm speciem, si opposito vna relatio eis correspondeat.*

50 The second opinion is the common and true one: that relation, or the relative, takes its species from the term; so that those relations are of the same species which have a term of the same species, as all paternities, all similarities; but those are distinct in species which have terms distinct in species, as similarity and dissimilarity. It is proved from Aristotle’s definition, which says that relatives are those whose whole being is to be referred to another, that is, to the term; therefore the relation will be such as the term is to which it refers; and this is to receive its species from it. And St. Thomas without doubt holds the same opinion, 3 p., q. 32, a. 2, where he says thus: Since the specific ratio of relation consists in this, that it is disposed toward another, it must be said that two relations are not diverse according to species if an opposite relation corresponds to them.

> Probatur etiam ratione: Quia ex quatuor generibus causarum, relatio non habet materiam, & formam, quæ sunt causæ intrinsecæ, à quibus (saltem à forma) posset sumere speciem: quia, vt superiùs probauimus, accidentia non componuntur ex materia, & forma, solùm ergo habet causam efficientem, à qua producitur: & finem, seu terminum, in quem ordinatur relatiuum: sed à causa efficiente, non sumunt res suam speciem: quia extrinseca prorsus est: ergo solùm restat causa finalis, quæ est terminus, in quem essentialiter ordinatur relatiuum: quare ab eo sumet suam speciem.

It is proved also by reason: because of the four genera of causes, relation does not have matter and form, which are intrinsic causes from which (at least from the form) it could take its species, because, as we proved above, accidents are not composed of matter and form; therefore it has only the efficient cause, by which it is produced, and the end, or term, to which the relative is ordered; but things do not take their species from the efficient cause, because it is altogether extrinsic; therefore there remains only the final cause, which is the term to which the relative is essentially ordered; wherefore it will take its species from it.

> 51 Sed, vt meliùs intelligatur hæc specificatio relationis, Notandum est, Relationem, sicut cætera accidentia, non habere compositionem Physicam, ex materia, & forma, sed Metaphysicam, ex genere, & differentia. Vt ergo intelligatur, à quo sumat speciem, explicandum est, à quo sumatur genus, & differentia eius: & quonam modo assignari possit definitio quidditatiua cuiuslibet relationis. Genus igitur relationis, sumitur à tota eius natura, sub communi conceptu referendi ad terminum considerata. Differentia verò, ab eadem concepta, sub conceptu speciali, & vltimo determinante genus: nempe ex eo, quòd sit ordinatio ad talem terminum: vt Genus paternitatis, erit communis conceptus relationis realis, qui dicit esse ordinem, vel ordinationem ad terminum. Differentia verò, esse ordinationem ad filium: & ideo definitio paternitatis talis erit: Paternitas est ordo, aut ordinatio patris, ad filium: & sic de cæteris [p. 389] relationibus. Itaque terminus relationis, non est differentia specifica relationis, seu esse ordinationem ad talem terminum, qui extrinsecus est relationi: sed esse ordinationem ad illum intrinsecum: & quia talis est ordinatio, quod est ad talem terminum, ideo dicitur relationem sumere speciem à termino, per quem cognoscenda, & definienda est relatio, & relatiuum.

51 But in order that this specification of relation may be better understood, it should be noted that Relation, like the other accidents, does not have a Physical composition from matter and form, but a Metaphysical one from genus and difference. In order, then, that it may be understood from what it takes its species, it must be explained from what its genus and difference are taken, and in what way the quidditative definition of any relation whatever can be assigned. The genus of relation, then, is taken from its whole nature considered under the common concept of referring to a term; but the difference from the same nature conceived under a special concept, ultimately determining the genus: namely, from the fact that it is an ordering to such a term. As the Genus of paternity will be the common concept of real relation, which says being an order or ordering to a term; but the Difference, being an ordering to a son; and therefore the definition of paternity will be such: Paternity is the order, or ordering, of a father to a son; and so of the other [p. 389] relations. Thus the term of the relation is not the specific difference of the relation, nor is being an ordering to such a term, which is extrinsic to the relation; but being an ordering to it is intrinsic; and because such an ordering is that which is to such a term, therefore relation is said to take its species from the term, through which the relation and the relative are to be known and defined.

> 52 Ex hac doctrina constat solutum esse secundum arg. quia nec relatio sic specificatur à termino vt terminus: vt sit differentia essentialis eius, nec specificatur à seipsa, sed à propria differentia: quæ ab eius natura sumitur, vt consideratur sub conceptu determinato, & vltimo ordinationis ad talem terminum: per quem conceptum contrahitur communis, & genericus.

52 From this doctrine it is plain that the second argument has been solved: because relation is not specified by the term as term, so that it would be its essential difference, nor is it specified by itself, but by its proper difference, which is taken from its nature as considered under the determinate and ultimate concept of ordering to such a term, through which concept the common and generic one is contracted.

> Vt testimonium Arist. explicetur, notandum est: Fundamenta esse causas relationum: vel quia ab eis aliquo modo producuntur: vel si aliquando non producuntur ab eis, naturali saltem sequela, positis fundamentis sequuntur: vnde ex fundamentis diuersæ rationis, semper sequuntur relationes diuersæ speciei. Et ita concedi potest, quòd à fundamentis sumatur species relationum, aut relatiuorum, quasi causaliter: sed à terminis, quasi formaliter. Inter hos autem duos modos sumendi speciem relationem, patet secundum esse magis proprium, quem posuit Arist. in definitione relatiuorum: & hæc est causa: propter quam communis modus loquendi scholæ, eo potiùs quàm primo vtitur: sed Arist. & D. Thom. per fundamenta distinguunt illis locis: quia aliquando notiora nobis sunt & quia modus ille distinguendi, non contradicit proprio, & formali, sed eum infert: vnde per illum distinguentes, non negant proprium, quo ferè semper vtuntur.

That the testimony of Aristotle may be explained, it should be noted that foundations are causes of relations: either because relations are in some way produced by them, or, if sometimes they are not produced by them, at least they follow by natural sequel once the foundations are posited; whence from foundations of diverse ratio there always follow relations of diverse species. And so it can be granted that the species of relations, or of relatives, is taken from the foundations as it were causally, but from the terms as it were formally. But between these two ways of taking the species of relations, it is plain that the second is more proper, which Aristotle posited in the definition of relatives; and this is the reason why the common manner of speaking of the school uses it rather than the first. But Aristotle and St. Thomas distinguish them in those places through the foundations, because these are sometimes better known to us, and because that way of distinguishing does not contradict the proper and formal one, but implies it; whence those who distinguish through it do not deny the proper one, which they almost always use.

### An filio correspondeat duplex relatio, vna in patre, & alia in matre, vel eadem in vtroque parente — Whether to the son there corresponds a twofold relation, one in the father and another in the mother, or the same in both parents.

> *An filio correspondeat duplex relatio, vna in patre, & alia in matre, vel eadem in vtroque parente.*

[…]

> 53 SOlutionem primi arg. in vltimũ locum remisimus: quia circa illam dubium hoc (licèt breuissimè) disputandũ est, An in patre, & matre vnica sit relatio ad filium, vel duplex, atq; diuersa: nempe paternitatis in patre, & maternitatis in matre.

53 We have put off the solution of the first argument to the last place, because concerning it this doubt (though very briefly) must be disputed: whether in the father and the mother there is a single relation to the son, or a twofold and diverse one, namely of paternity in the father and of maternity in the mother.

> Et est prima opinio D. Tho. 3 p. qu. 35. art. 5. quam sequitur ibidem Caiet. & Ferrar. 4. lib. contra gentes, ca. 14. *Quòd duplex sit, ac diuersa relatio in patre, & matre*: quæ in eo fundatur, quòd Aristot. quem sequitur D. Thom. asserit, *Patrem, & matrem diuerso modo, aut in diuerso genere causæ concurrere ad generationem filij*: patrem quidem tanquam causam efficientem, matrem verò [p. 390] tanquam materialem: sed effectus, diuerso modo, diuersaque dependentia dependet à diuersis generibus causarum, & diuerso modo ab eis respicitur, ergo per diuersas relationes: & ita pater refertur ad filium, relatione causæ efficientis: quæ dicitur paternitas: mater verò per relationem principij passiui, significatam nomine maternitatis. Et hæc sententia consequenter ponit, duplicem relationem, ratione saltem diuersam in filio: vnam, per quam refertur ad patrem, & aliam, per quam refertur ad matrem: nam cùm relatio sumat speciem à termino, impossibile est, quòd duæ relationes specie diuersæ, habeant eundem terminum formalem: vnde cùm filius terminet relationes diuersas, vtriusque parentis, necesse est per duas alias relationes, formaliter diuersas eas terminare, sed ambæ significantur eodem nomine filiationis.

And the first opinion is that of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 35, a. 5, which Cajetan follows in the same place, and Ferrara on Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 14: that there is a twofold and diverse relation in the father and the mother; which is founded on this, that Aristotle, whom St. Thomas follows, asserts that the father and the mother concur in the generation of the son in a diverse way, or in a diverse genus of cause: the father as an efficient cause, but the mother B B iij [p. 390] as a material one; but the effect depends with a diverse mode and a diverse dependence on diverse genera of causes, and regards them in a diverse way; therefore through diverse relations; and so the father is referred to the son by the relation of efficient cause, which is called paternity, but the mother by the relation of passive principle, signified by the name of maternity. And this opinion consequently posits a twofold relation, diverse at least in ratio, in the son: one through which he is referred to the father, and another through which he is referred to the mother; for since relation takes its species from the term, it is impossible that two relations diverse in species should have the same formal term; whence, since the son terminates diverse relations of each parent, he must terminate them through two other relations, formally diverse, but both are signified by the same name of filiation.

> 54 Secũda opinio opposita tenet: *In patre, & matre, esse vnam relationem totalem, & completam*, sed quasi compositam ex duabus relationibus partialibus, & eiusdem rationis patris, & matris: & in filio non nisi vnicam ei correspondere: per quam refertur ad vtrumque parentem, tanquam ad terminum adæquatum, & ad vtrumlibet, tanquam ad terminum inadæquatum. Ita Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 15. q. 5. sect. 3. & habet oppositum fundamentum, videlicet patrem, & matrem, in eodem genere causæ efficientis, concurrere ad generationem filij: tanquam vnam causam totalem, & adæquatam, quasi ex duplici causa partiali compositam. Ita enim sentit Galenus: quem omnes Medici sequuntur, & (quibus magna fides in hac re tribuenda est) cum eis Scotus in 3. d. q. 1. Ex hoc autem fundamento euidenter sequitur, quòd in patre, & matre, non sint relationes eiusdem speciei, Probatur consequentia: quasi si eodem modo, atque in eodem genere causæ efficientis, & proximè concurrunt ad generationem filij eodem modo ab eis dependebit: eodem etiam modo ab eis respicietur: quare per relationem eiusdem speciei, sed partialiter distinctam in vtroque: quia diuersæ sunt causæ partiales, & diuersa subiecta, in quibus non potest idem numero accidens reperiri, & possumus exemplum adducere, de multis hominibus trahentibus nauim, in quibus diuersæ sunt relationes partiales, & inadæquatæ, ad eundem effectum: sed ex omnibus integratur vna totalis, & adæquata.

54 The second, opposite opinion holds: that in the father and the mother there is one total and complete relation, but as it were composed of two partial relations, of the same ratio, of the father and of the mother; and that in the son only a single one corresponds to it, through which he is referred to both parents as to an adequate term, and to either one as to an inadequate term. So Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 5, sect. 3; and it has the opposite foundation, namely that the father and the mother concur in the same genus of efficient cause in the generation of the son, as one total and adequate cause, as it were composed of a twofold partial cause. For so Galen holds, whom all the Physicians follow (to whom great credit is to be given in this matter), and with them Scotus, in 3, d., q. 1. And from this foundation it evidently follows that in the father and the mother there are relations of the same species. The consequence is proved: because if they concur in the same way, and in the same genus of efficient cause, and proximately, in the generation of the son, he will depend on them in the same way; he will also regard them in the same way; wherefore through a relation of the same species, but partially distinct in each: because the partial causes are diverse, and the subjects diverse, in which the same accident in number cannot be found. And we can adduce the example of many men hauling a ship, in whom there are diverse partial and inadequate relations to the same effect, but from all of them one total and adequate relation is integrated.

> Nostra autem sententia est: probabilem esse vtramque opinionem, non solùm propter patrones doctissimos, sed propter probabilia fundamenta: *ideo liberum erit cuique hanc vel illam pro libitu sequi.*

Our view, however, is that both opinions are probable, not only on account of their most learned patrons but on account of their probable foundations; and therefore each will be free to follow this one or that at his pleasure.

[p. 391]

## QUESTION VII

> *An terminus relationis, sit formaliter absolutus, vel formaliter relatiuus.*

Whether the term of a relation is formally absolute or formally relative.

> 55 TRia sunt in relatiuo, Subiectum, Fundamentũ, & Relatio. Subiectum, est res ipsa, quæ denominatur à relatione. Fundamentum verò ratio, aut medium, per quod consurgit in ea relatio; & hęc est, per quam formaliter dicuntur relatiua: vt in patre est homo, qui denominatur pater, à relatione; est generatio, vel potentia generandi, in qua fundatur relatio: & est Relatio ipsa paternitatis. Ex his tribus certum est, Subiectũ non esse terminum relationis, nisi materialem, & quasi remotum: de quo non procedit quæstio, sed de duobus aliis: quorũ ratione subiectum potest proximè terminare relationem. Et cùm fundamentũ absolutum sit vel modum absoluti habeat, ideo titulus quæsti. quærit: *An terminus relationis, per quam vnum refertur ad aliud sit subiectũ ipsum, ratione fundamenti, quod absoluta res est, vel ratione relationis*: nam si ratione primi sit terminus, terminabitur relatio ad absolutum formaliter: si verò ratione relationis, terminabitur formaliter ad relatiuum.

55 There are three things in a relative: the Subject, the Foundation, and the Relation. The subject is the thing itself which is denominated by the relation. The Foundation is the ratio or means through which the relation arises in it. And the relation is that through which they are formally called relatives: as in the father, the man is what is denominated father by the relation; generation, or the power of generating, is that on which the relation is founded; and the Relation is paternity itself. Of these three it is certain that the Subject is not the term of the relation except a material and as it were remote one, about which the question does not proceed, but about the two others, by reason of which the subject can proximately terminate the relation. And since the foundation is absolute, or has the mode of something absolute, therefore the title of the question asks: whether the term of the relation through which one thing is referred to another is the subject itself by reason of the foundation, which is an absolute thing, or by reason of the relation: for if it is the term by reason of the first, the relation will be terminated formally at something absolute; but if by reason of the relation, it will be terminated formally at a relative.

> 56 Sed duo possumus cõsiderare in relatione. Primum, quòd sit ratio referendi vnum ad alterum. Secundum, quòd sit ratio terminandi relationem alterius: vt in paternitate, quòd sit ratio referendi patrem ad filium: & quòd sit ratio, per quam idem pater, terminet relationem filiationis: & cùm rationes istæ sint diuersæ, in eadem relatione, certũ est, per relationem, secundùm primam considerationem, vnum relatiuum non terminare relationem alterius: solùm potest esse dubium, an terminet per eam secundo modo consideratam.

56 But we can consider two things in a relation. The first, that it is the ratio of referring one thing to another. The second, that it is the ratio of terminating the relation of the other: as in paternity, that it is the ratio of referring the father to the son, and that it is the ratio through which the same father terminates the relation of filiation.
