And since these rationes are diverse in the same relation, it is certain that through the relation according to the first consideration one relative does not terminate the relation of the other; it can only be doubtful whether it terminates it through the relation considered in the second way.

> Et in hoc sensu quæritur, *An terminus relationis sit formaliter relatiuus?* id est an terminet per suam relationem, saltem secundo modo consideratam, relationem alterius.

And in this sense it is asked whether the term of a relation is formally relative, that is, whether it terminates the relation of the other through its own relation, at least considered in the second way.

> Et circa quæstionem sic explicatam, sunt tres opiniones: duæ extremæ, & tertia media. Prima opinio extrema, asserit, *Vnum relatiuum semper, & in quocunque genere relationum, terminare relationem alterius, per propriam relationem, & nunquam per fundamentum, aut rationem absolutam.* Ita Caiet. 1. part. q. 13. art. 7. quem sequuntur nonnulli ex modernis.

And concerning the question so explained there are three opinions: two extreme, and a third middle one. The first, extreme opinion asserts that one relative always, and in whatever genus of relations, terminates the relation of the other through its own relation, and never through the foundation or absolute ratio. So Cajetan, 1 p., q. 13, a. 7, whom not a few of the moderns follow.

> 57 Probant, ex duplici proprietate relatiuorum, approbata ab Arist. & omnibus, nempe, *Quòd relatiua sint simul natura, & simul cognitione, & definitione*: ita vt nec vnum possit esse prius natura quàm alterum: nec cognosci sine cognitione alterius: [p. 392] nec definiri, nisi alio definito: quæ omnia manifesta sunt in patre, & filio: sed nihil horum potest eis conuenire, nisi vt relatiuus: ergo vt talia, referuntur vnum ad alterum, & vnum terminat relationem alterius. Probatur minor: quia pater, ratione fundamenti est prior natura filio: & filius posterior: cùm per potentiam generandi, & generationem actiuam, quæ sunt fundamentum relationis, sit causa illius: & causa sit prior natura effectu: & eadem ratione potest cognosci, & definiri sine filio, ergo hoc modo, non poterit vnum terminare relationem alterius: & ideo solùm per relationem possunt se terminare.

57 They prove it from a twofold property of relatives approved by Aristotle and by all, namely, that relatives are simultaneous in nature, and simultaneous in cognition and in definition: so that neither can be prior in nature to the other, nor be known without the cognition of the other B b iiij [p. 392] nor be defined unless the other is defined: all of which are manifest in the father and the son; but none of these can belong to them except as relatives; therefore as such they are referred to one another, and one terminates the relation of the other. The minor is proved: because the father, by reason of the foundation, is prior in nature to the son, and the son posterior, since through the power of generating and active generation, which are the foundation of the relation, he is his cause, and a cause is prior in nature to its effect; and for the same reason he can be known and defined without the son; therefore in this way one will not be able to terminate the relation of the other; and therefore they can terminate each other only through the relation.

> Sed quia relationis aliæ sunt mutuæ, & aliæ non mutuæ: quę solùm reperiuntur in vno extremo, aliud verò absolutum est: & ideo tale non videtur posse terminare aliud per relationem, sed per rationem absolutam: non apparet igitur, quomodo vera esse possit hæc opinio in omnibus relationibus.

But since some relations are mutual and others not mutual, which are found only in one extreme, while the other is absolute; and therefore such an extreme does not seem able to terminate the other through a relation, but through an absolute ratio: it is not apparent, therefore, how this opinion can be true in all relations.

> Propterea duobus modis defenditur, quantum ad relationes non mutuas à diuersis qui eam sequuntur. Primò, à Caiet. qui ait, *In his relationibus, vnum extremum esse relatiuum formaliter, per relationem sibi inhærentem: aliud verò, non per relationem sibi inhærentem, sed per relationem existentem in altero.* Gratia exempli: Scientia, quæ mensurabilis dicitur, refertur per relationem sibi inhærentem ad obiectum, tanquam ad mensuram: obiectum verò, quod mensura dicitur, refertur ad scientiam, non per relationem sibi inhærentem, sed per eandem relationem existentem in scientia: & ita vnum relatiuum est intrinsecum. Probatur ex Arist. 5. Meta. c. 15. expressè asserente, *In relatiuis tertij generis quæ sunt mensura, & mensurabile, vnum referri per relationem, quam in se habet, alterum verò per relationem, qua aliud refertur ad ipsum.*

Therefore it is defended in two ways, as regards non-mutual relations, by the diverse authors who follow it. First, by Cajetan, who says: In these relations one extreme is formally relative through a relation inhering in it; the other, however, not through a relation inhering in it, but through the relation existing in the other. For example: science, which is called measurable, is referred to the object as to a measure through a relation inhering in it; but the object, which is called the measure, is referred to the science not through a relation inhering in it, but through the same relation existing in the science; and so one relative is intrinsic. It is proved from Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, who expressly asserts: In relatives of the third genus, which are the measure and the measurable, one is referred through the relation which it has in itself, the other through the relation by which the other is referred to it.

> Secunda via defenditur ab aliis modernis, asserentibus, *Extremum illud, in quo non est relatio realis, terminare relationem realem alterius*, non per eandem illius relationem, sed per relationem propriam: non realem, quam supponimus non habere, sed rationis: quia eo ipso quòd scientia refertur, per relationem realem mensurabilis ad obiectum, acquirit obiectum nouam commensurationem, & correspondentiam cum illa, ratione cuius commensurationis, debita est ei denominatio relatiua mensuræ: & cùm non possit eam habere realem, quia res absoluta est, habebit à relatione rationis: quæ licèt non sit ante operationem intellectus, satis est debitam ei esse, & quasi in potentia proxima, vt tribuat ei denominationem relatiui, licèt non relati: nam relatiuum dicit potentiam, vt aliquid referatur ad aliud: relatum verò actuale exercitium referendi.

In the second way it is defended by other moderns, who assert that the extreme in which there is no real relation terminates the real relation of the other not through that same relation of the other, but through its own relation: not a real one, which we suppose it does not have, but one of reason: because by the very fact that science is referred to the object through the real relation of the measurable, the object acquires a new commensuration and correspondence with it, by reason of which commensuration the relative denomination of measure is due to it; and since it cannot have it as real, because it is an absolute thing, it will have it from a relation of reason; which, although it does not exist before the operation of the intellect, it is enough that it be due to it, and as it were in proximate potency, to give it the denomination of relative, though not of related: for relative says the potency for something to be referred to another, but related the actual exercise of referring.

[p. 393]

> Hæc tamen sententia, siue hoc, siue illo modo defendatur, improbabilis mihi videtur: quia vterque modus eam defendendi, euidenter ostenditur falsus. Et primò, modum Caiet. sic impugno: Effectus formalis relationis est, facere relatiuum, sicut effectus formalis albedinis est facere album: sed repugnat aliquid esse album: nisi ab albedine sibi inhærente: ergo repugnabit esse relatiuum, nisi à relatione sibi inhærente, falsum ergo est, quod asserit Caiet. mensuram referri ad mensurabile, per relationem existentem in eodem mensurabili.

This opinion, however, whether it be defended in this way or in that, seems to me improbable: because each way of defending it is evidently shown to be false. And first I attack Cajetan’s way thus: the formal effect of relation is to make a relative, just as the formal effect of whiteness is to make a white thing; but it is repugnant for something to be white except by whiteness inhering in it; therefore it will be repugnant for it to be relative except by a relation inhering in it. It is false, therefore, as Cajetan asserts, that the measure is referred to the measurable through a relation existing in that same measurable.

> 60 Secundò: Quia relatio, cùm sit forma relatiua, non potest referre ad alterum, nisi illud, quod constituit relatiuum: sed constituere aliquid relatiuum, est tribuere illi proprium effectum formalem: sicut constituere albedinem, vel subiectum album, est tribuere illi proprium effectum formalem: & effectum formalem, non tribuit forma, nisi per informationem: ergo repugnat aliquid constitui relatiuum, aut referri ad aliud per relationem existentem in altero, & non in se.

60 Second: because relation, since it is a relative form, cannot refer to another anything except that which it constitutes a relative; but to constitute something a relative is to confer on it its proper formal effect, just as to constitute whiteness, or a white subject, is to confer on it its proper formal effect; and a form does not confer its formal effect except through information; therefore it is repugnant for something to be constituted a relative, or to be referred to another, through a relation existing in the other and not in itself.

> Secunda via hac ratione probatur falsa: Relatiuum, & relatum, vt superiùs probauimus, non se habent sicut potentia & actus; quia cùm relatio sit actualis ordinatio vnius ad alterum, eo ipso, quod est in subiecto, refert illud actu ad terminum: & ideo impossibile est, aliquid habere relationem in se, per quam dicatur relatiuum, quin per eandem etiam dicatur relatum. Impossibile est etiam dici relatiuum, ex eo solùm, quòd potest habere relationem, nisi eam actu habeat: nam homo, priusquam relationem habeat paternitatis, non dicitur relatiuum ad filium. Et sicut hæc vera sunt, & necessaria, in relationibus realibus: ita non minus sunt necessaria, in relationibus rationis; quia relatio rationis, concipitur ab intellectu, ad similitudinem relationis realis: eodem igitur modo erit impossibile, quòd mensura referatur ad mensurabile, per relationem rationis, priusquam illam actu habeat ab intellectu, eam cognoscente, etiam si sit ei debita: sicut est impossibile, quòd aliquid dicatur relatiuum à relatione reali, priusquam eam actu habeat.

The second way is proved false by this reason: the relative and the related, as we proved above, are not related as potency and act; because, since relation is the actual ordering of one thing to another, by the very fact that it is in a subject it refers that subject in act to the term; and therefore it is impossible for something to have in itself a relation through which it is called relative without also being called related through the same. It is impossible, too, for it to be called relative solely from the fact that it can have a relation, unless it has it in act: for a man, before he has the relation of paternity, is not called relative to a son. And just as these things are true and necessary in real relations, so they are no less necessary in relations of reason: because a relation of reason is conceived by the intellect after the likeness of a real relation. In the same way, then, it will be impossible for the measure to be referred to the measurable through a relation of reason before it has it in act from the intellect knowing it, even if it is due to it: just as it is impossible for something to be called relative by a real relation before it has it in act.

> 16 Secunda opinio extrema tenet: *Terminum, non solùm in relationibus non mutuis, sed etiam in mutuis, esse formaliter absolutum.* Ita Scot. in 1. d. 30. q. 1. quem sequuntur omnes eius discipuli, & ex modernis multi; & in eandem sententiam, videtur inclinare Capreol. in 1. d. 30. q. 1. art. 2. ad 3. Sonc. 5. Meta. q. 3. ad 2. Et de relationibus non mutuis, tanquam certum præsupponit hæc sententia, quòd ad absolutum terminentur.

16 The second, extreme opinion holds: that the term, not only in non-mutual relations but also in mutual ones, is formally absolute. So Scotus, in 1, d. 30, q. 1, whom all his disciples follow, and many of the moderns; and Capreolus seems to incline to the same opinion, in 1, d. 30, q. 1, a. 2, ad 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 3, ad 2. And concerning non-mutual relations this opinion presupposes as certain that they are terminated at something absolute.

> Sed ita esse etiam in relationibus mutuis, probatur primò. [p. 394] Quia aut relatio, in quantum relatio, postulat terminum relatiuum, aut in quantum relatio mutua: sed neutro modo postulare potest talem terminum: ergo non terminatur per se ad relatiuum, sed per accidens, & ideo ad absolutum per se. Probatur minor: Primò, quòd non vt relatio: nam si vt relatio peteret terminum relatiuum, omnis relatio deberet illum habere, & nulla poterit terminari ad absolutum: sed relationes tertij generis, terminantur omnes ad absolutum, vt manifestum est: ergo relatio, vt relatio, non petit terminum relatiuum. Quòd autem eum non petat, vt relatio mutua, probatur primò: Quia relatio non dicitur mutua, per rationem terminandi, sed per rationem referendi: quia vtrumque extremũ refertur ad aliud: ergo non est necessarium, vt relatio sit mutua: quòd sit ratio terminandi, sed satis est esse rationem referendi, in vtroque extremo: quod verum esse potest etiam si absolutum terminetur.

That it is so in mutual relations too is proved first: [p. 394] because relation demands a relative term either insofar as it is relation or insofar as it is mutual relation; but in neither way can it demand such a term; therefore it is terminated at a relative not per se but per accidens, and therefore at something absolute per se. The minor is proved. First, that it does not do so as relation: for if as relation it required a relative term, every relation would have to have one, and none could be terminated at something absolute; but the relations of the third genus are all terminated at something absolute, as is manifest; therefore relation, as relation, does not require a relative term. And that it does not require one as mutual relation is proved, first: because a relation is not called mutual by the ratio of terminating but by the ratio of referring, because each extreme is referred to the other; therefore it is not necessary, for a relation to be mutual, that it be the ratio of terminating, but it is enough that it be the ratio of referring in each extreme: which can be true even if it is terminated at something absolute.

> 62 Secundò: Quia neque omnis relatio mutua, terminatur semper ad relatiuum, sed aliquando ad absolutum: nam paternitas, aut maternitas, & filiatio, sunt relationes mutuæ: & tamen aliquando datur vna sine altera, vt in beatissima Virgine, secundùm sententiam D. Th. 3. p. q. 35. art. 5. datur relatio realis maternitatis, ad Christum hominem, in quo non est relatio, realis filiationis: ergo relatio maternitatis, non terminabitur ad Christum tanquam ad relatiuum, sed tanquam ad absolutum, per passiuam generationem, quæ accidens absolutum est) terminantem relationem maternitatis.

62 Second: because not every mutual relation is always terminated at a relative either, but sometimes at something absolute: for paternity, or maternity, and filiation are mutual relations; and yet sometimes one is given without the other, as in the most blessed Virgin, according to the opinion of St. Thomas, 3 p., q. 35, a. 5, there is a real relation of maternity to Christ the man, in whom there is no real relation of filiation; therefore the relation of maternity will be terminated at Christ not as at a relative, but as at something absolute, through the passive generation (which is an absolute accident) terminating the relation of maternity.

> 63 Secundò: Si vnum relatiuum terminaretur ad alterum, etiam vt relatiuum, sequeretur, non posse vnum cognosci, aut definiri, nisi per alterum. Probatur consequentia: quia non potest cognosci, neque definiri relatiuum, nisi per terminum, sed consequens est falsum: ergo falsum erit etiam antecedens. Probatur minor: quia loco nominis in definitione positi, licet ponere suam definitionem: vt loco animalis, positi in definitione hominis, licet ponere viuens sensibile, quæ est eius definitio, dicereque, Homo est viuens sensibile rationale: ergo si pater definitur per filium, dicemus, Pater est, qui habet filium & tunc, loco filij, licebit ponere definitionem eius, quæ talis erit: filius est, qui habet patrem: & ita definitio patris erit, Pater est qui genuit eum, qui habet patrem: in qua tria vitia committuntur. Primũ est nugationis, seu inutilis repetitionis: quia pater ipse, qui definitur, in definitione reperitur. Secundùm est, quòd ignotum per ignotius definiatur: nam dum patrem definimus per filium, non solùm æquè ignotus est filius, sed minus notus: cùm nihil de eo possimus cognoscere, nisi per [p. 395] patrem. Tertium, viciosus quidam circulus: nam vnum relatiuum definitur per alterum, & hoc idem per illud: quod non est aliud, quàm definire idem per semetipsum: nam si pater definitur per filium, & rursus filius per patrem, à primo ad vltimum, definietur pater per seipsum. Quod reprobauit Arist. 5. li. Meta. ca. 13 his verbis: *Non est autem intellectus ad illud, cuius intellectus est: idem enim profectò bis esset dictum.* Et 1. lib. de poster. resolutione, ca. 3. eundem circulum reprobauit, in demonstrationibus.

63 Second: if one relative were terminated at the other also as relative, it would follow that one could not be known or defined except through the other. The consequence is proved: because a relative cannot be known or defined except through its term. But the consequent is false; therefore the antecedent will also be false. The minor is proved: because in place of a name posited in a definition it is permissible to put its definition: as in place of animal, posited in the definition of man, it is permissible to put sensible living thing, which is its definition, and to say: Man is a sensible rational living thing. Therefore, if father is defined through son, we shall say: A father is one who has a son; and then, in place of son, it will be permissible to put its definition, which will be such: A son is one who has a father; and so the definition of father will be: A father is one who begot him who has a father: in which three faults are committed. The first is that of nugation, or useless repetition: because the father himself, who is defined, is found in the definition. The second is that the unknown is defined through the more unknown: for when we define father through son, the son is not only equally unknown, but less known, since we can know nothing about him except through [p. 395] the father. The third, a certain vicious circle: for one relative is defined through the other, and this same one through that; which is nothing other than to define the same thing through itself: for if father is defined through son, and in turn son through father, from first to last father will be defined through himself. Which Aristotle reproved, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, in these words: But the understanding is not toward that of which it is the understanding: for indeed the same thing would have been said twice. And in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 3, he reproved the same circle in demonstrations.

> 64 Tertia opinio media, inter hæc extrema, affirmat, *Relationes non mutuas terminari ad absolutum formaliter, mutuas verò formaliter ad relatiuum, & ideo relationem in communi, vel relationem, vt relatio est ad terminum, abstrahentem ab absoluto, & relatiuo.* Ita Ferrar. 2. contra gentes, cap. 11. Nip. 5. Meta. d. 14. Deca His. in 1. d. 3. q. 1. nota. 3. & ex modernis plures. Et hanc existimo esse certam in doctrina Aristo. & Tho. & probabiliorem cæteris. Quam efficaciter probauimus, quantum ad relationes non mutuas, vt mensurabilis, & mensuræ, creaturæ, & creatoris aduersus primam opinionem Caie.

64 The third opinion, midway between these extremes, affirms that non-mutual relations are terminated formally at something absolute, but mutual ones formally at a relative; and therefore relation in common, or relation as it is relation to a term, abstracts from the absolute and the relative. So Ferrara on Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 11; Nifo, Metaph. 5, d. 14; Deza of Seville, in 1, d. 3, q. 1, note 3; and several of the moderns. And I consider this to be certain in the doctrine of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and more probable than the others. Which we have effectively proved, as regards non-mutual relations, such as of the measurable and the measure, of the creature and the creator, against the first opinion, of Cajetan.

> Probatur etiam aduersus secundam opinionem, *Quòd relationes mutuæ terminentur formaliter ad relatiuum*: expressis testimoniis Arist. Porph. & D. Th. Arist. enim ca. præs. agens de termino relationis, & docens qualis esse debeat, ita ait: *Amplius, si quidem conuenienter assignetur, ad quod dicitur, omnibus aliis sublatis, quæcunque accidentia sunt: relicto autem solo illo, ad quod assignatum est, conuenienter semper ad ipsum dicetur, circumscriptis omnibus, quæ accidentia sunt domino: vt esse bipedem, vel scientia susceptibilem, vel hominem; relicto verò solo, quòd dominus est, semper: seruus enim, domini seruus dicitur. Si autem non conuenienter ad id, ad quod dicitur, assignetur, circumscriptis omnibus aliis, relicto autem eo solo, ad quod assignatum est, non dicetur ad ipsum. Assignetur seruus hominis, aut alicuius, & circumscribatur ab homine, esse dominum, non amplius seruus ad hominem dicetur, cùm enim dominus non sit, nec seruus est.* Quibus verbis expressè docet, seruum terminari formaliter ad dominum, vt dominus est: & dominum ad seruum, vt seruus est: quia ablatis relationibus dominii, & seruitutis, neuter potest terminare relationem alterius, & relationibus positis: etiam si omnia alia auferantur, sufficienter per eas vtrumque terminat relationem alterius.

It is proved also against the second opinion, that mutual relations are terminated formally at a relative, by express testimonies of Aristotle, Porphyry, and St. Thomas. For Aristotle, in the present chapter, treating of the term of relation and teaching what it ought to be, says thus: Further, if that to which it is said is suitably assigned, when all the other things that are accidents have been taken away and that alone left to which it was suitably assigned, it will always be said toward it; as, if the master is assigned, all the things that are accidents to the master being set aside, such as being two-footed, or capable of science, or a man, and that alone left, that he is master, the slave will always be said toward him: for the slave is called the master’s slave. But if that to which it is said is not suitably assigned, all the other things being set aside and that alone left to which it was assigned, it will not be said toward it. Let the slave be assigned to man, or to something, and let being master be set aside from the man: the slave will no longer be said toward the man; for when there is no master, neither is there a slave. In which words he expressly teaches that the slave is terminated formally at the master as he is master, and the master at the slave as he is slave: because, if the relations of mastership and servitude are taken away, neither can terminate the relation of the other; and if the relations are posited, even if all other things are taken away, through them each sufficiently terminates the relation of the other.

> 65 Porph. etiam c. de specie, idem tenet, non minùs expressè: nam asserit se definisse genus per speciem, & rursus: speciem per genus: quia sunt relatiua, & vnum relatiuum debet definiri per alterum, tanquam per terminum suæ relationis.

65 Porphyry also, in the chapter on species, holds the same no less expressly: for he asserts that he defined genus through species, and in turn species through genus, because they are relatives, and one relative must be defined through the other, as through the term of its relation.

[p. 396]

> Quod D. Thom. non minùs expressè docet, 1. p. q. 40. art. 2. ad 4. vbi explicans definitionem relatiuorum, traditam ab Aristot. & docens quomodo conueniat relatiuis mutuis, inquit: *Cùm dicitur, quòd relatiui esse, est ad aliud se habere, per ad aliud, intelligitur correlatiuum: quod non est prius sed simul natura.*

Which St. Thomas teaches no less expressly, 1 p., q. 40, a. 2, ad 4, where, explaining the definition of relatives handed down by Aristotle and teaching how it belongs to mutual relatives, he says: When it is said that the being of a relative is to be disposed toward another, by “toward another” is understood the correlative, which is not prior but simultaneous in nature.

> Probatur deinde duplici ratione. Prima, ex intrinseca ratione relatiuorum deducta. Oppositio relatiua reperitur inter relatiua, vt relatiua sunt formaliter, ergo mutua relatio includit essentialiter mutuam oppositionem relatiuam: sed mutua oppositio relatiua essentialiter includit vtramque rationem, referendi, & terminandi: ergo vtrumque officium exercent relatiua per relationes, & non per fundamenta absoluta. Omnia constant euidenter, præter minorem, quam non minùs euidenter probo. Mutua oppositio, consistit in hoc, quòd relatiua mutuò se respiciant, & relationes, sint rationes mutuò se respicienti, sed mutuò se respicere est, quodlibet respicere aliud, & ab eo respici: & ab eo respici, est terminare relationem eius: ergo euidens est, quòd in mutua oppositione, includatur essentialiter vtrumque officium, referendi, & terminandi: & ex consequenti, quòd vtrumque exerceant relatiua per relationes, & non per fundamenta: quia per relationes, & non per fundamenta, habent formalem oppositionem.

It is proved next by a twofold reason. The first, deduced from the intrinsic ratio of relatives. Relative opposition is found between relatives as they are formally relatives; therefore mutual relation essentially includes mutual relative opposition; but mutual relative opposition essentially includes both rationes, of referring and of terminating; therefore relatives exercise both offices through their relations, and not through their absolute foundations. All of this is evidently plain except the minor, which I prove no less evidently. Mutual opposition consists in this, that the relatives regard each other mutually, and the relations are the rationes of their regarding each other mutually; but to regard each other mutually is for each to regard the other and to be regarded by it; and to be regarded by it is to terminate its relation; therefore it is evident that in mutual opposition both offices, of referring and of terminating, are essentially included; and consequently that relatives exercise both through their relations, and not through their foundations: because it is through the relations, and not through the foundations, that they have formal opposition.

> 66 Secunda ratio ex Diuinis relationibus sumitur, in quibus euidenter probari videtur, vnum relatiuum, non posse per absolutum, sed per relationem terminare alterum. Duo autem præsupponit hæc ratio, tanquam certa. Primum est; Relationem realem, esse non posse, nisi inter extrema realiter distincta: quia nihil potest ad seipsum referri relatione reali. Secundum, in Diuinis non posse vnum distingui realiter ab altero, per aliquid absolutum: sed solùm per relationes oppositas. Quibus suppositis, ita procedit ratio: Pater refertur ad Filium, & Filius ad Patrem, vt realiter distinguuntur, ergo vterque terminat relationem alterius, vt realiter ab eo distinctus: quia sicut relatio realis, non potest esse eiusdem ad seipsum realiter, ita nec terminari ad se ipsum: sed pater, & filius non distinguuntur realiter, nisi per solas relationes oppositas: ergo nec refertur vnus ad alterum, nec terminat relationem alterius, nisi per relationem: vt relatiuum igitur, & non vt absolutum: sed eadem est ratio, de relationibus Diuinis, & creatis, quantum pertinet ad rationem referendi, & terminandi: ergo etiam relationes creatæ terminantur ad relatiuum, & non ad absolutum.

66 The second reason is taken from the Divine relations, in which it seems to be evidently proved that one relative cannot terminate the other through something absolute, but through the relation. Now this reason presupposes two things as certain. The first is that a real relation cannot exist except between extremes really distinct: because nothing can be referred to itself by a real relation. The second, that in Divine things one cannot be really distinguished from another through something absolute, but only through opposed relations. These being supposed, the reason proceeds thus: the Father is referred to the Son, and the Son to the Father, as they are really distinguished; therefore each terminates the relation of the other as really distinct from it: because, just as a real relation cannot be of the same thing to itself really, so neither can it be terminated at itself; but the father and the son are not really distinguished except through the opposed relations alone; therefore neither is one referred to the other, nor does he terminate the relation of the other, except through the relation: therefore as a relative, and not as something absolute. But the reason is the same concerning Divine and created relations as regards the ratio of referring and terminating; therefore created relations too are terminated at a relative, and not at something absolute.

> 67 Huic arg. duobus modis conantur respondere moderni, [p. 397] Primò, quòd licet in diuinis personis nihil distinguat realiter nisi relatio: & ideo relatiuum sit, quod terminat secundùm se, tamen, vt à nobis concipiuntur Diuinæ Personę, potest distingui fundamentum relationis, à relatione ipsa, & concipi per modum absoluti, & per ipsum ita conceptum, terminabit vna persona relationem alterius: vt in filio, possumus considerare generationem passiuam, à qua dicitur genitus per modum absoluti, tanquam fundamentum filiationis: & per illam terminabit filius relationem paternitatis, non per filiationem: & sic etiam pater, per generationem actiuam, per modum absoluti consideratam.

67 To this argument the moderns try to reply in two ways, [p. 397] First, that although in the divine persons nothing distinguishes really except relation, and therefore it is the relative that terminates according to itself, yet, as the Divine Persons are conceived by us, the foundation of the relation can be distinguished from the relation itself and conceived by way of something absolute; and through it, so conceived, one person will terminate the relation of the other: as in the son we can consider passive generation, from which he is called begotten, by way of something absolute, as the foundation of filiation; and through it the son will terminate the relation of paternity, not through filiation; and so too the father, through active generation considered by way of something absolute.

> Hæc tamen solutio, nec vera est, nec soluit arg. Probo primò: Quia in personis Diuinis, non solùm paternitas, & filiatio sunt relationes, sed etiam generatio actiua, & passiua, quæ vocantur origo actiua & passiua, dicunt formaliter relationem, alioqui non possent distingui realiter, sicut certum est distingui. Deinde à nobis, qui scimus nihil distingui in Diuinis, nisi per relationes, concipiuntur tanquam relatiuæ: ergo si per illas terminat vna persona relationem alterius, terminabit, vt relatiua formaliter. Probo secundum, Quòd solutio non soluat argumentum. Quia licèt à nobis imperfectè intelligentibus, conciperentur generatio actiua, & passiua, per modum absoluti, cùm tamen sint relatiuæ: nihilominus secundùm se, nihil habent absolutum: ergo cùm relationes terminentur secundùm se, & non solùm, vt imperfectè concipiuntur à nobis, sequitur euidenter, secundùm se terminari ad relatiuum formaliter, & non ad absolutum: & etiam vt intelliguntur à Deo, & beatis qui eas cognoscunt, vt sunt in se.

This solution, however, is neither true nor does it solve the argument. I prove the first: because in the Divine persons not only paternity and filiation are relations, but also active and passive generation, which are called active and passive origin, say relation formally; otherwise they could not be distinguished really, as it is certain that they are distinguished. Next, by us, who know that nothing is distinguished in Divine things except through relations, they are conceived as relative; therefore, if through them one person terminates the relation of the other, it will terminate it as formally relative. I prove the second, that the solution does not solve the argument: because, although by us, who understand imperfectly, active and passive generation should be conceived by way of something absolute, since nevertheless they are relative, they have nothing absolute according to themselves; therefore, since relations are terminated according to themselves, and not only as they are imperfectly conceived by us, it evidently follows that according to themselves they are terminated formally at a relative and not at something absolute; and also as they are understood by God and by the blessed, who know them as they are in themselves.

> Propterea iidem moderni, videntes prædictam solutionem insufficientem esse, aliam tradiderunt. Concedentes, relationes Diuinas terminari ad relatiuum formaliter, non tamen creatas. Et differentiam in eo consistere, quòd relationes Diuinæ, sunt subsistentes, aut substantiales, ideo non habent aliud fundamentum, præter seipsas, per quod possit vnum relatiuum terminare relationem alterius: sed relationes creatæ, sunt accidentales: & ideo præsupponunt aliud accidens absolutum, tanquam fundamentum, quo medio consurgunt: & per tale fundamentum, potest vnum relatiuum terminare alterum.

Therefore the same moderns, seeing that the aforesaid solution was insufficient, handed down another, granting that the Divine relations are terminated formally at a relative, but not created ones; and that the difference consists in this, that the Divine relations are subsistent, or substantial, and therefore do not have another foundation besides themselves through which one relative could terminate the relation of the other; but created relations are accidental, and therefore presuppose another absolute accident as a foundation, by means of which they arise; and through such a foundation one relative can terminate the other.

> Sed nec differentia hæc aliquid valet, quod ita probo: Relationem esse subsistentem aut inhærentem, seu substantialem, aut accidentalem, non pertinent ad rationem formalem relationis, aut relatiui, sed materiale quid est: relationes verò [p. 398], aut relatiua mutua, ex ratione formali talium relationum & relatiuorum, habent mutuam oppositionem, formaliter includentem vtramque rationem, referendi, & terminandi: quæ eadem est in Diuinis, & creatis: ergo eadem erit ratio terminandi in vtrisque: sicut eadem est ratio referendi: quare si ad relatiuum formaliter terminantur Diuinę relationes, & non ad absolutum, etiam terminabuntur creatæ.

But neither is this difference worth anything, which I prove thus: for a relation to be subsistent or inhering, or substantial or accidental, does not pertain to the formal ratio of relation or of relative, but is something material; but relations [p. 398] or mutual relatives, from the formal ratio of such relations and relatives, have mutual opposition, formally including both rationes, of referring and of terminating; which is the same in Divine and in created things; therefore the ratio of terminating will be the same in both, just as the ratio of referring is the same; wherefore, if the Divine relations are terminated formally at a relative and not at something absolute, created ones too will be so terminated.

> 69 Argumenta primæ opinionis, non sunt contra nostram: & ideo non est necessarium ad ea respondere. Sed ad primum argu. secundæ opinionis, Concessa maiori, concedenda est etiam minor, secundùm illam partem, qua asserit, *Relationem, vt relatio est, non terminari ad relatiuum formaliter*: sed neganda, quantùm ad aliam, Quòd, *vt est relatio mutua, non petat terminum relatiuum*: quia relatio, vt relatio, consideratur tanquam genus, abstractum à mutua, & non mutua: sed vt relatio mutua, consideratur in specie: certum est autem, plura conuenire alicui rei, ratione suæ differentiæ, vel speciei, quæ non conueniunt ei, ratione generis: & ideo conuenire potest relationi vt mutuæ, terminari ad relatiuum, licèt non conueniat ei sub communi ratione relationis: sed sicut hoc modo abstrahit à mutua, & non mutua, ita petit terminum abstrahentem, ab absoluto, & relatio. Vt autem aliud, quod in eodem arg. adducitur, de relationibus mutuis, carentibus aliquando relatione in vno extremo, vt est relatio creaturæ ad creatorem, & relatio maternitatis B. Virginis, ad Christum Dominum, apud D. Tho. soluatur, notandum est, Primò, *Relatiua duobus modis considerari posse*, Maternaliter, dum pro subiectis, aut fundamentis accipiuntur, vt dum dicitur, hunc hominem album, referri ad alium hominem album, aut generans ad genitum: quo etiam modo, solùm dicuntur relatiua accidentaliter, quia accidentalis est hæc generans est pater, vel album est simile. Alio modo accipiuntur Formaliter, prout significantur nominibus relatiuis, patris, aut similis: & sicut relatiua, sic etiam termini accipiuntur eisdem modis: vt dum dicimus, simile referri ad album, aut patrem ad genitum: formaliter verò, si dicamus patrem referri ad filium.

69 The arguments of the first opinion are not against ours, and therefore it is not necessary to reply to them. But to the first argument of the second opinion: the major being granted, the minor too must be granted according to that part which asserts that relation, as it is relation, is not terminated formally at a relative; but it must be denied as regards the other part, that as it is mutual relation it does not require a relative term: because relation as relation is considered as a genus, abstracted from mutual and non-mutual; but as mutual relation it is considered in species; and it is certain that many things belong to a thing by reason of its difference, or species, which do not belong to it by reason of its genus; and therefore to be terminated at a relative can belong to relation as mutual, although it does not belong to it under the common ratio of relation; but just as in this way it abstracts from mutual and non-mutual, so it requires a term abstracting from the absolute and the relative. And in order that the other point adduced in the same argument may be solved, concerning mutual relations that sometimes lack the relation in one extreme, as is the relation of the creature to the creator, and the relation of maternity of the Blessed Virgin to Christ the Lord, according to St. Thomas, it should be noted, first, that relatives can be considered in two ways: Materially, when they are taken for the subjects or foundations: as when it is said that this white man is referred to another white man, or the one generating to the one generated; in which way also they are called relatives only accidentally, because This one generating is a father or The white thing is like is accidental. In another way they are taken Formally, as they are signified by relative names, of father or of like; and as relatives, so too terms are taken in the same ways: as when we say that the like is referred to the white, or the father to the one generated; but formally, if we say that the father is referred to the son.

> 70 Secundò notandum est: *Relationes mutuas, perfectas esse*: quia oppositionem relatiuam includunt: non verò mutuas, quasi mancas, & imperfectas, in quibus vnum tantũ extremum relatiuæ oppositionis reperitur: vnde solùm intelliguntur habere materiales terminos, non formales. Vt relatio mensurabilis, ad mensuram, solùm materialiter dicitur terminata: & idem de relationibus mutuis, si in altero extremo suspendereretur [p. 399] relatio, per possibile, vel impossibile: vt si, consurgente relatione similitudinis in vno albo, suspenderetur relatio in alio (si hoc sit possibile, de quo non agimus) tunc enim solùm materialiter maneret terminata relatio alterius.

70 It should be noted, second, that mutual relations are perfect, because they include relative opposition; but not so non-mutual ones, which are as it were maimed and imperfect, in which only one extreme of relative opposition is found; whence they are understood to have only material terms, not formal ones. As the relation of the measurable to the measure is said to be terminated only materially; and the same of mutual relations, if in the other extreme they were suspended [p. 399] through a possible or impossible case: as if, when a relation of similarity arose in one white thing, the relation in the other were suspended (if this be possible, which we are not discussing); for then the relation of the other would remain terminated only materially.

> Ex his respondetur, Relationes illas quæ in arg. adducũtur, esse non mutuas: quia relationes mutuæ, non versantur, nisi inter extrema eiusdem ordinis: Deus autem & creatura diuersi ordinis sunt: & ideo non habent mutuas relationes: propterea quoque solùm materialiter terminatas: & hoc est, terminari ad absolutum: mutuæ verò, oppositionem relatiuam essentialiter dicunt, ratione cuius, quælibet est ratio referendi ad aliam, & simul ratio terminandi: quia non potest oppositio intelligi, sine vtraque ratione: & ideo relatiua mutua, vt talia, ad relatiuum formaliter terminantur.

From these things the reply is that the relations adduced in the argument are not mutual: because mutual relations are found only between extremes of the same order; but God and the creature are of diverse orders, and therefore do not have mutual relations; and for this reason they are also terminated only materially, and this is to be terminated at something absolute. But mutual relations essentially say relative opposition, by reason of which each is the ratio of referring to the other and at the same time the ratio of terminating: because opposition cannot be understood without both rationes; and therefore mutual relatives, as such, are terminated formally at a relative.

### An vnum relatiuum possit, & debeat definiri per alterum — Whether one relative can and must be defined through the other.

> *An vnum relatiuum possit, & debeat definiri per alterum.*

[…]

> 71 SEcundum arg. petit, *An vnum relatiuum possit, & debeat definiri per alterum.* Et circa hoc dubium, est duplex opinio. Prima negat, quòd sic debeat definiri: quam tenent oẽs illi, qui defendunt, relationem non terminari ad relatiuum, sed ad absolutum: & probant ex inconuenientibus, quæ sequuntur ex tali modo definiendi, in eodem arg. adductis.

71 The second argument asks whether one relative can and must be defined through the other. And concerning this doubt there is a twofold opinion. The first denies that it must be so defined: which all those hold who maintain that relation is terminated not at a relative but at something absolute; and they prove it from the inconveniences which follow from such a way of defining, adduced in the same argument.

> Secunda opinio, est eorum, qui sequuntur nostram sententiam, *Quòd vnum relatiuum, debeat definiri per aliud*: & hæc apud Arist. & D. Th. est certissima, vt probant testimonia eorum adducta in confirmationem nostræ sententiæ: est etiam expressa apud Porph. cap. de specie, vbi asserit, se egisse statim post genus de specie: *quia sunt relatiua*: & ideo necesse est vnũ cognoscere, & definire per alterum. Huic autem testimonio, respondent moderni, non posuisse Porph. speciem, in definitione generis, vt refertur ad genus: sed vt ad indiuidua, & ideo non definisse vnum relatiuum per alterum formaliter. Sed miror sanè solutionem tam apertè falsam excogitasse: quia luce clarius est, genus definisse per speciem, tanquam per subiectum: de quo prædicatur: sed non est subiectum, de quo prædicatur genus, vt respicit indiuidua, sed vt respicit genus ipsum, vt ex se patet: ergo per illam tanquam relatiuum generis, definiuit genus ipsum. Sed in rationibus est probabilior, & (nisi ego fallor) euidenter concluditur ex Diuinis relationibus, in quibus fatentur, quòd licèt nostro modo intelligendi imperfecto, possumus intelligere, quòd terminentur ad fundamentum, per modum absoluti à nobis conceptum; tamen si sumantur vt sunt in se, vel vt à Deo ipso, aut beatis [p. 400] cognoscuntur, non possunt vllo modo terminari ad absolutum: quia cùm sint subsistentes, & substantiales, non habent fundamentum aliud, præter seipsas: ideo necesse est per seipsas terminare.

The second opinion is that of those who follow our view, that one relative must be defined through the other; and this is most certain in Aristotle and St. Thomas, as their testimonies adduced in confirmation of our view prove. It is also express in Porphyry, chapter on species, where he asserts that he treated of species immediately after genus because they are relatives, and therefore it is necessary to know and define one through the other. To this testimony, however, the moderns reply that Porphyry did not posit species in the definition of genus as it is referred to genus, but as it is referred to individuals, and therefore he did not define one relative through the other formally. But I truly wonder that they devised a solution so openly false: because it is clearer than daylight that he defined genus through species as through the subject of which it is predicated; but the subject of which genus is predicated is not species as it regards individuals, but as it regards the genus itself, as is plain of itself; therefore he defined genus itself through it as the relative of the genus. But in reasons it is more probable, and (unless I am mistaken) it is evidently concluded from the Divine relations, in which they admit that, although by our imperfect mode of understanding we can understand that they are terminated at the foundation, conceived by us by way of something absolute, yet if they are taken as they are in themselves, or as by God himself or by the blessed [p. 400] know them, they cannot in any way be terminated at something absolute: because, since they are subsistent and substantial, they have no other foundation besides themselves; and therefore they must terminate through themselves.

> 72 Ex hoc deduco euidens arg. hoc modo: Relationes Diuinæ, vt sunt in se, & vt cognoscuntur à Deo, & beatis, terminantur ad relatiuum formaliter: ergo terminus formalis vnius relatiui, vt patris, erit aliud relatiuum, nempe filius, vt filius: sed relatiuum, non potest definiri, nisi per terminum: ergo non potest definiri, nisi per aliud relatiuum. Si igitur beatus, quadam explicatione explicaret, quid sit pater Æternus, non posset alio modo, nisi dicendo, Pater Æternus est, qui habet filium eiusdem naturæ. Tunc ergo, vel ex tali definitione sequuntur illa inconuenientia, nempe circulus vitiosus, definiendo idem per seipsum, ignotum per ignotim, atque etiam nugatio, vel inutilis repetitio, vel non: si non sequuntur: ergo nec sequuntur ex modo definiendi vnum relatiuum creatum per aliud: & si sequuntur, non erit verum, quòd Diuinæ relationes terminentur ad relatiuum. Probatur euidenter paritas rationis: quia tam in diuinis quàm in humanis erit verum, quòd loco nominis in definitione positi licet ponere suam definitionem: ex quo sequuntur illa inconuenientia: vel in vtrisque erit falsum. & non admittendum in relatiuis.

72 From this I deduce an evident argument in this way: the Divine relations, as they are in themselves and as they are known by God and the blessed, are terminated formally at a relative; therefore the formal term of one relative, as of the father, will be the other relative, namely the son as son; but a relative cannot be defined except through its term; therefore it cannot be defined except through the other relative. If, then, one of the blessed were to explain by some explanation what the Eternal Father is, he could not do so in any other way than by saying: The Eternal Father is he who has a son of the same nature. Then, therefore, either those inconveniences follow from such a definition, namely a vicious circle, by defining the same thing through itself, the unknown through the unknown, and also nugation, or useless repetition, or they do not. If they do not follow, therefore neither do they follow from the way of defining one created relative through the other; and if they do follow, it will not be true that the Divine relations are terminated at a relative. The parity of reasoning is evidently proved: because both in divine and in human things it will be true that in place of a name posited in a definition it is permissible to put its definition, from which those inconveniences follow; or in both it will be false, and not to be admitted in relatives.

> 73 Ad arg. igitur, Concedenda est consequentia primi enthymematis. Dum autem dicitur, loco nominis in definitione positi, licere definitionem eius ponere, Distinguendum est: quia vel id, quod ponitur in definitione, ponitur, tanquam pars definitionis intrinseca: & tunc licebit quidem: si verò non ponatur, nisi tanquam additamentum extrinsecum, non licebit: & quia vnum relatiuum, non ponitur in definitione alterius, tanquam pars definitionis, sed tanquam additamentum extrinsecum, in ordine, ad quod sumitur differentia relationis, propterea non licet loco eius ponere suam definitionem. Et ratio huius differentię est: quia pars definitionis, est pars essentialis definiti, secundùm propriam naturam illud componens: vnde idem est, quòd ipsa ponatur, vel eius definitio continens naturam propriam. Quod autem ponitur tanquam additamentum, non est pars definitionis, aut definiti, nec illud componit, sed solùm extrinsecè terminat, aut respicit: quod non potest præstare per suam definitionem, sed per se: quia per se respicitur ab alio, & per se ei opponitur relatiuè: quemadmodum vnum contrarium per se opponitur alteri, & per se expellit illud à subiecto, & non per propriam definitionem. Quod [p. 401] considerans Arist. 6. lib. Topic. c. 2. docet, *Relatiuum, vt in definitione alterius positum, diuersum esse à seipso, extra definitionem, aut secundùm se sumpto*: nam in definitione non ponitur secundùm se: sed solùm vt extrinsecum additamentum. Præterea in definitione, non ponitur tanquam relatiuum: sed tanquam terminus: ideo non licet ponere definitionem eius, vt relatiua: vt terminus verò, solùm habet extrinsecam denominationem, quasi eius, in quo finitur relatio alterius.

73 To the argument, then: the consequence of the first enthymeme must be granted. But when it is said that in place of a name posited in a definition it is permissible to put its definition, a distinction must be made: because either that which is posited in the definition is posited as an intrinsic part of the definition, and then indeed it will be permissible; or it is posited only as an extrinsic addition, and then it will not be permissible. And because one relative is posited in the definition of the other not as a part of the definition but as an extrinsic addition, in order to which the difference of the relation is taken, therefore it is not permissible to put its definition in its place. And the reason for this difference is that a part of the definition is an essential part of the thing defined, composing it according to its proper nature; whence it is the same whether the part itself is posited or its definition, containing its proper nature. But what is posited as an addition is not a part of the definition or of the thing defined, nor does it compose it, but only extrinsically terminates or regards it; which it cannot accomplish through its definition, but through itself: because it is regarded by the other through itself, and is relatively opposed to it through itself, just as one contrary is opposed to the other through itself, and expels it from the subject, and not through its proper definition. Which [p. 401] considering which, Aristotle, Topics 6, ch. 2, teaches that a relative, as placed in the definition of another, is different from itself outside the definition, or taken according to itself: for in the definition it is not placed according to itself, but only as an extrinsic addition. Moreover, in the definition it is not placed as a relative but as a term; therefore it is not permitted to put its definition as of a relative; but as a term it has only an extrinsic denomination, as that in which the relation of the other is terminated.

> 74 Ad testimonium verò Aristotelis, Respondetur, non loqui de definitione vnius relatiui per alterum, sed solùm asserere, quòd potentia, non refertur ad suum subiectum, in quo est, relatione speciali potentiæ, sed solùm ad proprium obiectum: vt intellectus, non ad hominem, sed ad intelligibile: & visus ad visibile: Nam si diceretur, inquit, relatiuè ad hominem, idem in quantum idem, bis diceretur: hoc est, ad duos terminos, & per duas relationes: quod patet esse impossibile. Itaque vt potentia, solùm dicitur relatiuè, ad obiectum, hoc est ad intelligibile: ad subiectum verò non dicitur vt potentia: sed sub alia ratione communi accidentis. Ita exponunt verba Aristo. Commentator, D. Thom. & Alexander, in Commentariis eorum verborum: & ideo hunc esse germanum sensum eorundem credendum est.

74 To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that he is not speaking of the definition of one relative through another, but only asserts that a potency is not referred to its subject, in which it is, by the special relation of a potency, but only to its proper object: as the intellect not to man but to the intelligible, and sight to the visible. For if it were said, he says, relatively to man, the same thing as the same would be said twice: that is, to two terms and through two relations, which is plainly impossible. Thus, as a potency, it is said relatively only to its object, that is, to the intelligible; but to its subject it is not said as a potency, but under another, common ratio of accident. So the Commentator, St. Thomas, and Alexander expound Aristotle’s words in their Commentaries on those words; and therefore this must be believed to be their genuine sense.

> 75 Ad aliud verò, quod in argumento dicitur: Definiri ignotum per ignotius, si vnum relatiuum definiatur per alterum: negandum est: sed definitur per extrinsecum, æquè ignotum, & sine quo non potest per notiora explicari: & hoc nihil refert: quia non requiritur, quòd magis notum sit definito, quidquid ponitur in definitione eius, per se sumptum: sed satis est, si sit æquè notum, vel ignotum, dummodo ex eo, & aliis notioribus, resultet integra definitio, notior simpliciter definito: & hoc habet definitio relatiui: licèt terminus in ea positus. tanquam extrinsecum additamentum, æquè ignotus sit, si per se sumatur, ac definitum.

75 To the other point made in the argument, that the unknown is defined through the more unknown if one relative is defined through the other: this must be denied; rather it is defined through something extrinsic, equally unknown, and without which it cannot be explained through better-known things; and this makes no difference, because it is not required that whatever is placed in the definition, taken by itself, be better known than the definitum; but it is enough if it be equally known or unknown, provided that from it and from other better-known things there results an entire definition, better known absolutely than the definitum. And the definition of a relative has this, although the term placed in it as an extrinsic addition is equally unknown if it is taken as the definitum.

## QUESTION VIII

### Quæ. 8. An vnum relatiuum ordinetur ad duos terminos eiusdem speciei, per eandem, vel diuersas rationes — Whether one relative is ordered to two terms of the same species through the same relation or through different relations.

> *An vnum relatiuum, ordinetur ad duos terminos eiusdem speciei, per eandem, vel diuersas relationes.*

[…]

> 76 EXplicatum est iam in præcedentibus, id quod pertinet ad vnitatem, & distinctionem specificam relationis: ideo in hac octaua quæstione quærimus, de vnitate numerica, An quando vnum relatiuum respicit plures terminos eiusdem [p. 402] speciei, vt pater plures filios, aut simile plura similia, respiciat singulos per singulas atque distinctas numero paternitates, aut similitudines, vel per vnam, & eandem numero extensam ad omnes. Sed respicere vnum & relatiuũ plures terminos, dupliciter contingit. Primò, ita vt quilibet sit quasi partialis, & inadæquatus, & ex multis constituatur vnus totalis, & adæquatus, atque etiam necessarius ad terminandam relationem: & hoc modo species respicit indiuidua, & totum, plures partes. Et hoc modo certum est, relatiuum per eãdem numero relationem, & non per plures, respicere plures terminos. Secundo modo, contingit vnum relatiuum respicere plures terminos, adęquatos, & totales, ita, vt quilibet solus, & per se, posset terminare sufficienter relationem: & hoc modo procedit quæstio, An multiplicatis his terminis, multiplicentur relationes: ita vt pater referatur ad plures filios, per plures relationes, vel non multiplicentur, sed per eandem numero paternitatem referatur ad omnes.

76 What pertains to the specific unity and distinction of relation has already been explained in what precedes; therefore in this eighth question we inquire about numerical unity: whether, when one relative regards several terms of the same Cc [p. 402] species, as a father several sons, or a similar thing several similar things, it regards each of them through single paternities or similitudes, numerically distinct, or through one and the same in number, extended to all. But it happens in two ways that one relative regards several terms. First, so that each is as it were partial and inadequate, and out of many one total and adequate term is constituted, which is also necessary for terminating the relation: and in this way the species regards the individuals, and the whole its several parts. And in this way it is certain that the relative regards several terms through the same relation in number, and not through several. In the second way it happens that one relative regards several adequate and total terms, so that each one alone and by itself could sufficiently terminate the relation: and in this way the question proceeds, whether, when these terms are multiplied, the relations are multiplied, so that a father is referred to several sons through several relations; or they are not multiplied, but he is referred to all through the same paternity in number.

> 77 Et prima opinio tenet, *Relatiuum ad plures terminos, non eadem relatione referri, sed multis numero diuersis: ita vt tot habeat relationes: quot filios*: ita Scotus in 3. d. 8. q. vnica, quem sequuntur sui discipuli, & plures moderni: & probatur ex doctrina Aristo. qui docet in hoc capite, *Relatiua esse simul natura, & cognitione*, ita vt quoque eorum existente in rerum natura, ponatur necessariò aliud, & ablato etiam vno, necessariò auferatur aliud, cognito etiam vno: necessariò cognoscatur aliud: sed hæc proprietas, non potest conuenire relatiuis, si per vnam relationem referantur ad plures terminos, ergo hoc non est possibile. Probatur minor, quia posito primo termino, ponitur relatio: sed semper ponitur priùs tempore vnus primus: quàm sint alij: ergo non erit relatiuum simul tempore, nec natura cum eis, sed solùm cum primo: nec etiam simul cognitione: quia priùs cognoscitur primus, quàm illi alij cognoscantur. Deinde sublatis omnibus præter vltimum, qui non periit, non aufertur relatiuum.

77 And the first opinion holds that a relative is not referred to several terms by the same relation, but by many numerically different ones, so that it has as many relations as sons. So Scotus, in 3, d. 8, the single q., whom his disciples follow, and many moderns; and it is proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, who teaches in this chapter that relatives are simultaneous in nature and in cognition, so that when either of them exists in the nature of things the other is necessarily posited, and when one is taken away the other is also necessarily taken away, and when one is known the other is also necessarily known. But this property cannot belong to relatives if they are referred to several terms through one relation; therefore this is not possible. The minor is proved: because when the first term is posited the relation is posited; but one first term is always posited earlier in time than the others come to be; therefore the relative will not be simultaneous in time, nor in nature, with them, but only with the first; nor yet simultaneous in cognition, because the first is known before those others are known. Further, when all except the last, who has not perished, are taken away, the relative is not taken away.

> 78 Probatur deinde ratione. Primò: Quia si pater vnum habeat filium, per vnam relationem realem ordinabitur ad illum, ergo habitu secundo, consurget in eo noua relatio. Probatur consequentia: Relatio est ordinatio ad terminum, erga noua ordinatio erit noua relatio: sed ordinatur de nouo ad nouum filium, cùm priùs non ordinaretur, ergo noua est in eo ordinatio, & ideo noua relatio: & sic multiplicabuntur relationes, multiplicatis terminis.

78 It is proved, next, by reason. First: because if a father has one son, he will be ordered to him through one real relation; therefore, when he has a second, a new relation will arise in him. The consequence is proved: relation is an ordering to a term; therefore a new ordering will be a new relation; but he is ordered anew to a new son, since he was not ordered before; therefore there is in him a new ordering, and therefore a new relation; and thus relations will be multiplied when terms are multiplied.

> Secundò: Posito fundamento proximo relationis, & termino, ponitur necessariò relatio, vt posita albedine in hoc pariete [p. 403]: quæ est fundamentum similitudinis, & posito alio albo, quod est terminus, consurgit necessariò similitudo, ergo posito nouo fundamento, & nouo termino, consurgit noua relatio: sed genito nouo filio, ponitur noua generatio actiua in patre, quæ est nouum fundamentum relationis: ponitur nouus terminus, qui est nouus filius: ergo ponitur noua relatio. Et confirmari potest hoc modo: Si primus filius moriatur, ante generationem secundi, desinit esse in patre relatio paternitatis & per generationem secundi, consurgit noua: quia nouum est fundamentum, & nouus terminus, ergo etiã si non moreretur primus, consurgeret noua relatio. Probatur consequentia quia eodem modo est nouum fundamentum, & nouus terminus.

Second: when the proximate foundation of the relation and the term are posited, the relation is necessarily posited, as when whiteness is posited in this [p. 403] wall, which is the foundation of similitude, and another white thing is posited, which is the term, similitude necessarily arises; therefore, when a new foundation and a new term are posited, a new relation arises. But when a new son is begotten, a new active generation is posited in the father, which is a new foundation of the relation; a new term is posited, which is the new son; therefore a new relation is posited. And it can be confirmed in this way: if the first son dies before the generation of the second, the relation of paternity ceases to be in the father, and through the generation of the second a new one arises, because there is a new foundation and a new term; therefore, even if the first did not die, a new relation would arise. The consequence is proved, because in the same way there is a new foundation and a new term.

> 79 Et si respondeas, viuente primo non consurgere nouam relationem: quia relatio est accidens: & vna paternitas, est accidens solo numero diuersum ab alia: sed duo accidentia solo numero distincta, non possunt esse in eodem subiecto: quia accidentia indiuiduantur ab eo, ergo nec potest consurgere noua relatio permanente prima. Itaque subiectum habens vnam relationem, incapax est alterius solo numero distinctæ: & ideo vno relatio impedit, ne consurgat alia. Contra hoc est: quòd licèt accidentia purè absoluta, indiuiduentur à subiecto: & ideo non possint plura esse in eodem, solo numero distincta: accidentia tamen respectiua, non indiuiduantur à solo subiecto: sed cum ordine ad terminũ, vel ad aliquid aliud, quod respiciunt. Vnde plures species visibiles (quas vocant intentionales) simul sunt in eodem oculo, vidente simul duo alba, aut duo alia obiecta: ergo cùm relatio sit accidens respectiuum, non indiuiduatur à subiecto solo, sed cum ordine ad talem terminum: qui si fuerit nouus, capax erit subiectum recipiendi nouam relationem, solo numero distinctam: quia nullum erit impedimentum, ratione cuius non multiplicentur relationes, multiplicatis terminis.

79 And if you reply that while the first is living a new relation does not arise, because relation is an accident, and one paternity is an accident differing from another in number alone; but two accidents distinct in number alone cannot be in the same subject, because accidents are individuated by it; therefore neither can a new relation arise while the first remains. Thus a subject having one relation is incapable of another distinct in number alone, and therefore one relation prevents another from arising. Against this is the fact that, although purely absolute accidents are individuated by the subject, and therefore several distinct in number alone cannot be in the same subject, nevertheless respective accidents are not individuated by the subject alone, but together with the order to the term, or to something else which they regard. Hence several visible species (which they call intentional) are at once in the same eye when it sees two white things, or two other objects, at once. Therefore, since relation is a respective accident, it is not individuated by the subject alone, but together with the order to such a term; and if this is new, the subject will be capable of receiving a new relation, distinct in number alone, because there will be no impediment by reason of which relations should not be multiplied when terms are multiplied.

> Secunda opinio, *negat multiplicari sed primam relationem extendi affirmat ad nouos terminos superuenientes: & ita per vnam numero relationem, referri patrem ad omnes filios* Ita D. Th. in 3. d. 8. q. 1. & 3. p. q. 35 art. 5. Caiet ibid. Ferra. 1. lib. contra gentes, c. 4. Soncin. 5. Met. q. 32. concl 3. Tolet. q. 2. huius prædicamenti.

The second opinion denies that it is multiplied, but affirms that the first relation is extended to the new terms that supervene, and thus that the father is referred to all his sons through one relation in number. So St. Thomas in 3, d. 8, q. 1, and 3 p., q. 35, a. 5; Cajetan, ibid.; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles, bk. 1, ch. 4; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 32, concl. 3; Toledo, q. 2 of this category.

> 80 Potissimum fundamentum D. Tho est, Natura accidentium: quæ sicut essentialiter sunt aliquid substantiæ, sic nata sunt ab ea indiuiduari. Duplicia autem esse possunt accidentia: nam vel sunt distincta specie, vel eiusdem speciei: & si specie distincta sint, iam supponuntur distincta numero: quia [p. 404] distinctio specifica, cùm sit maior, continet minorem, quæ est numerica: & ideo nullus vnquam dubitauit, quin duo accidentia specie distincta, simul sint in eodem subiecto: quia experientia notum est, in colore, & calore simul existentibus in homine: si verò sint eiusdem speciei, non supponuntur distincta, sed nata sunt à subiecto suscipere indiuiduationem, ac distinctionem: & propterea non possunt multa simul esse in eodem subiecto, siue purè absoluta sint, siue respectiua: nam cùm sint aliquid substantiæ, cui inhærent, & quam denominant, quodlibet natum est esse hoc, in quantum natum est efficere substantiam hanc, in specie talis accidentis, nempe hoc album, aut hoc calidum: sed repugnat, quòd idem numero subiectum, sit simul diuersum numero, in eadem specie accidentali: vt quòd sint duo numero alba, aut calida, ergo repugnabit habere duplicem albedinem, aut calorem: & ex hoc infertur, subiectum indiuiduitate accidentia, eiusdem speciei: quia licèt admitteretur, habere plura simul, nihilominus vnum tantùm numero esset in specie eorum, vt vnum numero albũ, & non plura, ergo ea traheret ad propriam indiuiduationem, ita vt vnum numero fierent: & hoc est à subiecto accipere indiuiduationem. Et cùm relationes ordinentur ex propria natura, ad constituendum subiectum relatiuum, & non possit constitui duplex numero pater, aut duplex numero simile, repugnabit habere simul duas relationes eiusdem speciei: sed si termini multiplicentur, per eandem relationem numero ordinabitur ad omnes. Illi verò, quia plura sunt subiecta, per plures relationes terminabunt eandem relationem existentem in patre, ad omnes se extendentem: & sic est intelligenda, & explicanda opinio D. Th. quam sequimur.

80 The chief foundation of St. Thomas is the nature of accidents, which, just as they are essentially something of substance, so are apt to be individuated by it. Now accidents can be of two kinds: for either they are distinct in species or of the same species; and if they are distinct in species, they are thereby presupposed to be distinct in number, because C c ij [p. 404] specific distinction, since it is greater, contains the lesser, which is numerical; and therefore no one has ever doubted that two accidents distinct in species are at once in the same subject, as is known by experience in the case of choler and heat existing at once in a man. But if they are of the same species, they are not presupposed to be distinct, but are apt to receive individuation and distinction from the subject; and on that account many cannot be at once in the same subject, whether they are purely absolute or respective. For since they are something of the substance in which they inhere and which they denominate, each is apt to be this one inasmuch as it is apt to make the substance this one in the species of such an accident, namely this white thing or this hot thing. But it is repugnant that the same subject in number should at the same time be diverse in number in the same accidental species, as that there should be two white or hot things in number; therefore it will be repugnant for it to have a double whiteness or heat. And from this it is inferred that the subject individuates accidents of the same species: because, even if it were admitted to have several at once, nevertheless it would be only one in number in their species, as one white thing in number, and not several; therefore it would draw them to its own individuation, so that they would become one in number; and this is to receive individuation from the subject. And since relations are ordered by their own nature to constituting a relative subject, and a double father in number, or a double similar thing in number, cannot be constituted, it will be repugnant for it to have at once two relations of the same species; but if the terms are multiplied, it will be ordered to all through the same relation in number. Those terms, however, since they are several subjects, will terminate through several relations the same relation existing in the father and extending itself to all. And so the opinion of St. Thomas, which we follow, is to be understood and explained.

> 81 Probatur primò: Quia hæc paternitas ponitur, vt homo per illam sit, & denominetur formaliter hic numero pater, sed per vnam paternitatem, fit hic numero pater, & per plures, etiam si multiplicentur, non fit alius pater numero, ergo nec est capax plurium relationum: vel si ponantur plures: eo ipso efficientur vna numero omnes: quia per omnes non fit alius numero pater, sed idem. Si verò respondeas, fieri hunc numero patrem per hanc paternitatem, in ordine ad hunc filium; & per aliam quoque eundem, in ordine ad alterum, & hoc sufficere, vt plures possint, & debeant multiplicari. Contra hoc sic arguo: In ordine ad vnum, & plures filios, est idem numero pater: ergo per vnam numero formam relatiuam, & non per plures. Probatur consequentia: quia si quælibet est distincta numero ab alia, propter distinctum numero terminum, ergo [p. 405] quælibet nata est efficere distinctum numero patrem: vnde si non facit distinctum, nec potest esse distincta numero ab alia, etiam si ad distinctum numero filium ordinetur. Quare non poterunt multiplicari in eodem patre: sed sicut idem numero pater est, respiciens plures filios, ita eos respicit per eandem numero paternitatem.

81 It is proved, first: because this paternity is posited so that through it a man may be, and be formally denominated, this father in number; but through one paternity he becomes this father in number, and through several, even if they are multiplied, he does not become another father in number; therefore he is not capable of several relations; or, if several are posited, by that very fact they will all be made one in number, because through all of them he does not become another father in number, but the same. But if you reply that he becomes this father in number through this paternity in order to this son, and through another also the same father in order to another, and that this suffices for several to be able and obliged to be multiplied: against this I argue thus. In order to one son and to several sons he is the same father in number; therefore through one relative form in number, and not through several. The consequence is proved: because if each is distinct in number from another on account of a term distinct in number, therefore [p. 405] each is apt to make a father distinct in number; hence, if it does not make a distinct one, neither can it be distinct in number from another, even if it is ordered to a son distinct in number. Wherefore they cannot be multiplied in the same father; but just as he is the same father in number while regarding several sons, so he regards them through the same paternity in number.

> 82 Secundò probatur: Quia non sunt multiplicandæ entitates reales, sine vrgenti necessitate, sed si multiplicentur relationes eiusdem speciei per multiplicationem terminorum, multiplicantur ferè infinitæ entitates reales, sine vrgenti necessitate: ergo non debent multiplicari. Probatur minor: quia infinita ferè sunt alba eiusdem gradus, ad quæ refertur vnum, & idem per relationem similitudinis, infiniti ferè homines, ad quos refertur quilibet relatione identitatis specificæ, ergo ferè infinitas habebit entitates reales quilibet, numero distinctas, si pro singulis multiplicentur singulæ relationes. Quòd verò necessitas non vrgeat, probatur, quia secundùm cõmunem sententiam scholę pro singulis conclusionibus eiusdem rationis, non multiplicantur in eodem homine singuli habitus scientiæ, sed idem habitus numero se extendit ad omnes: & posset se extendere: etiam si essent infinitæ: sed æquè facile est, quòd eadẽ numero relatio se extendat ad omnes terminos eiusdem rationis, ergo nulla est necessitas multiplicandi singulas pro singulis.

82 It is proved, second: because real entities are not to be multiplied without urgent necessity; but if relations of the same species are multiplied through the multiplication of terms, almost infinite real entities are multiplied without urgent necessity; therefore they ought not to be multiplied. The minor is proved: because there are almost infinite white things of the same degree, to which one and the same thing is referred through the relation of similitude, and almost infinite men, to whom each is referred by the relation of specific identity; therefore each will have almost infinite real entities, distinct in number, if single relations are multiplied for single terms. That necessity does not urge is proved: because, according to the common opinion of the school, single habits of science are not multiplied in the same man for single conclusions of the same ratio, but the same habit in number extends itself to all, and could extend itself even if they were infinite; but it is equally easy for the same relation in number to extend itself to all the terms of the same ratio; therefore there is no necessity to multiply single relations for single terms.

> Ad testimonium Arist. Respondetur, Patrem esse simul natura, & cognitione cum filio, duobus modis intelligi posse: Aut secundùm substantiam relationis. Aut secundùm extensionem eius accidentalem ad plures: & primo modo, solùm est simul natura cum primo filio, secundo modo cum omnibus, & singulis superuenientibus: & eodem modo loquendum est de conseruatione eiusdem relationis: nam cùm singulos respiciat, tanquam adæquatos terminos, ab vna tontum dependet, vt conseruetur, quantum ad substantiam: ab omnibus verò, & singulis, vt conseruetur, quantum ad extensionem: quare quolibet desinente, non conseruabitur in eadem extensione, sed in minori.

To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that the father’s being simultaneous in nature and in cognition with the son can be understood in two ways: either according to the substance of the relation, or according to its accidental extension to several; and in the first way he is simultaneous in nature only with the first son, in the second way with all and each of those that supervene. And in the same way we must speak of the conservation of the same relation: for since it regards each as an adequate term, it depends on one only in order to be conserved as to its substance, but on all and each in order to be conserved as to its extension. Wherefore, when any one of them ceases, it will not be conserved in the same extension, but in a lesser one.

> Ad primum arg. neganda est consequentia primi enthymematis: & cùm dicitur nouam ordinationem, esse nouam relationem: concedi potest. Sed negandum est, quòd adueniente nouo filio, consurgat noua ordinatio in patre: sed solùm consurgit noua extensio eiusdem ordinationis, siue eiusdem relationis: sicut adueniente noua conclusione, non multiplicatur nouus habitus, sed solùm habetur de nouo extensio noua eiusdem.

To the first argument, the consequence of the first enthymeme must be denied; and when it is said that a new ordering is a new relation, this can be granted. But it must be denied that, when a new son comes, a new ordering arises in the father; rather there arises only a new extension of the same ordering, or of the same relation: just as when a new conclusion comes, a new habit is not multiplied, but only a new extension of the same is had anew. C c iij

[p. 406]

> Ad secundum: Concesso antecedente, neganda est consequentia: quia nouum fundamentum inducit nouam relationem, si subiectum sit capax: habita autem prima relatione, non est capax subiectum nouæ alterius relationis numero distinctæ (vt probatum est) ideo nouum fundamentum, quod ex se posset nouam inducere relationem, per accidens non inducit eam: quia per accidens fuit subiectum impeditum, per relationem iam acquisitam. Et datur euidens instantia in conclusionibus, quarum quælibet est productiua habitus, sed per accidens non producitur ab aliis, præter primam: quia inueniunt iam productum, & impeditum subiectum.
