To the second: granting the antecedent, the consequence must be denied; because a new foundation induces a new relation if the subject is capable; but once the first relation is had, the subject is not capable of another new relation distinct in number (as has been proved); therefore the new foundation, which of itself could induce a new relation, per accidens does not induce it, because the subject was per accidens impeded by the relation already acquired. And an evident instance is given in conclusions, each of which is productive of a habit, but per accidens the habit is not produced by the others besides the first, because they find it already produced and the subject impeded.

> 84 Secundò respondetur: Concedendo eandem consequentiam, sed negando minorem subsumentem, quòd per generationem secundi filij nouum ponatur fundamentum. Nam licèt ponatur noua generatio, hæc tamen non est fundamentum relationis, sed solùm ratio fundandi: fundamentum verò est potentia generandi, vt reducta ad actum, per generationem: potentio verò nõ multiplicatur: ideo nec ponitur nouum fundamentum, nec proinde noua relatio. Ad aliud tandem, quod dicitur de indiuiduatione accidentium: negari posset, quòd plures species intentionales sint in eodem subiecto, hoc est, in sensu, aut intellectu: qui non potest simul plura intelligere, nisi per modum vnius: hoc est, nisi vt aliquo modo ordinentur, vel per vnam speciem repræsentetur, si sint obiecta eiusdem speciei. Sed meliùs fortè dicetur diuersam esse rationem de accidentibus intentionalibus: quæ nec denominant subiectum, nec producuntur propter illud, nec ab eo præcipuè dependent, sed ab obiecto, propter quod producuntur, vt potentiæ vniatur, atque de accidentibus realibus, habentibus esse physicum, & secundùm illud denominantibus, & propter subiectum productis. Quæ proinde ab eodem subiecto indiuiduantur: intentionalia verò, potiùs ex propria entitate, cum ordine ad talem actionem per quam producuntur ab obiectis: sed de hoc suo loco.

84 Second, I reply by granting the same consequence but denying the subsuming minor, that through the generation of the second son a new foundation is posited. For although a new generation is posited, this nevertheless is not the foundation of the relation but only the ratio of founding; the foundation is the potency of generating, as reduced to act through generation; and the potency is not multiplied; therefore neither is a new foundation posited, nor, consequently, a new relation. To the other point, finally, which is said about the individuation of accidents: it could be denied that several intentional species are in the same subject, that is, in the sense or the intellect, which cannot understand several things at once except by way of one, that is, unless they are in some way ordered, or are represented through one species if they are objects of the same species. But it will perhaps be better said that the ratio is different for intentional accidents, which neither denominate the subject, nor are produced for its sake, nor depend principally on it, but on the object, for the sake of which they are produced, in order that it may be united to the power, and for real accidents, which have physical being, and denominate according to it, and are produced for the sake of the subject. These, accordingly, are individuated by the same subject; but intentional ones rather by their own entity, together with the order to such an action through which they are produced by the objects. But of this in its own place.

## QUESTION IX

> QVÆSTIO IX.

[…]

> *An entis realis ad non ens, aut ad ens rationis, detur relatio realis.*

Whether there is a real relation of a real being to non-being, or to a being of reason.

> 85 Sensus quæstionis est: An necesse sit terminum relationis realis, esse realem, hoc est, actu existentem: vel etiam si sit ens rationis, aut ens in potentia, referatur ad illud ens actu existens, relatione reali.

85 The sense of the question is: whether it is necessary that the term of a real relation be real, that is, actually existing; or whether, even if it is a being of reason or a being in potency, a being actually existing is referred to it by a real relation.

[p. 407]

> 86 Triplex est relatio. Prima, *pertinens ad essentiam absoluti*, vt transcendentes, & secundùm dici, quales sunt respectus, quos dicunt accidentia ab subiecta, & scientiæ, atque potentiæ, ad obiecta: & de his certum est apud omnes, quod reales esse possunt & terminari ad ens in potentia, vel ens rationis, quia realis est respectus aptitudinalis inhærentiæ, quem dicit quantitas Eucharistiæ ad substantiam panis, in qua erat, iam non existentem. Realis est etiam respectus, quem dicit Dialectica ad ens rationis, tanquam ad proprium obiectum. Alia est relatio, *non pertinens ad essentiam absoluti*, sed quæ omnibus accidit: & hæc est prædicamentalis, sed est duplex: quædam mutua, quæ ex parte vtriusque extremi realis est, vt similitudo, & æqualitas. Et de hac etiam est certum, quòd nõ possit versari, inter ens actu, & ens in potentia, aut inter ens reale, & rationis. Quod probat euidenter hoc argumentum, Relatio realis mutua debet esse ex parte vtriusque extremi realis, sed ens in potentia, aut ens rationis, non est capax relationis realis: ergo non potest referri ad ens actu relatione reali, & ex consequenti, repugnat relationem realem mutuam dari entis in actu, ad ens in potentia, vel ad ens rationis.

86 Relation is threefold. The first, pertaining to the essence of something absolute, as transcendental relations and relations secundum dici, such as are the respects which accidents bear to their subjects, and sciences and powers to their objects; and concerning these it is certain among all that they can be real and be terminated to a being in potency, or a being of reason: for real is the aptitudinal respect of inherence which the quantity of the Eucharist bears to the substance of the bread in which it was, which no longer exists; real also is the respect which Dialectic bears to a being of reason as to its proper object. The other relation is one not pertaining to the essence of something absolute, but which befalls all things; and this is categorial. But it is twofold: one mutual, which is real on the part of both extremes, as similitude and equality. And concerning this also it is certain that it cannot obtain between a being in act and a being in potency, or between a real being and a being of reason. This argument proves it evidently: a mutual real relation must be real on the part of both extremes; but a being in potency, or a being of reason, is not capable of a real relation; therefore it cannot be referred to a being in act by a real relation; and consequently it is repugnant that a mutual real relation be given of a being in act to a being in potency or to a being of reason.

> 87 Difficultas igitur quæstionis, ad solas relationes prædicamentales non mutuas, ex quibus constat tertium genus, reducitur: *An possint terminari ad ens in potentia, vel ad ens rationis, vel necesse sit habere terminum realem, & actu existentem, quamuis absolutum.*

87 The difficulty of the question, therefore, is reduced to the non-mutual categorial relations alone, of which the third genus consists: whether they can be terminated to a being in potency, or to a being of reason; or whether it is necessary that they have a real and actually existing term, albeit an absolute one.

> Et prima opinio affirmat, *Entis in actu ad ens in potentia, vel ad non ens, dari posse relationem realem, non mutuam*; Ita Greg. in 1. d. 28. q. 3. Soncinas 5. Meta. q. 7. & ex modernis nonnulli.

And the first opinion affirms that a real, non-mutual relation can be given of a being in act to a being in potency, or to non-being. So Gregory in 1, d. 28, q. 3; Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 7; and some of the moderns.

> Et probatur, testimonio Arist. ca. præsenti, vbi ait: *Calefactiuum referri ad calefactibile, & agens in actu, ad passum in potentia, in secundo genere relationum*: ergo sentit entis in actu, ad ens in potentia, dari relationem realem.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he says that the calefactive is referred to the calefactible, and the agent in act to the patient in potency, in the second genus of relations; therefore he holds that a real relation is given of a being in act to a being in potency.

> Probatur deinde ratione. Primò: Quia relatio non sumit entitatem realem à termino, sed à fundamento: ergo vt realis sit, non habet à termino, sed à fundamento: quare realis esse poterit, etiam si terminus sit ens rationis, vel ens in potentia. Quod probat Dialectica, quæ cùm scientia realis sit, & realis habitus, habet pro obiecto ens rationis.

It is proved, next, by reason. First: because relation does not take its real entity from the term but from the foundation; therefore, in order to be real, it has this not from the term but from the foundation. Wherefore it could be real even if the term is a being of reason or a being in potency. Dialectic proves this, which, though it is a real science and a real habit, has a being of reason for its object.

> 88 Secundò: Potentiæ habitus, & scientiæ, sunt mensurabiles per sua obiecta: ergo referuntur ad ea relatione reali, mensurabilis ad mensuram, in tertio genere posita: non tamen referuntur ad illa, vt actu existentia, sed sufficit, quòd sint in potentia: ergo hæc est relatio non mutua, potest dari inter ens actu, & [p. 408] ens in potentia. Probatur minor, quia visibile non dicit actualem existentiam, sed potentiam tantùm: & rosa non existente in hyeme, datur vera, & realis scientia de illa. Et confirmari potest hoc modo: Hæc est differentia inter officium referendi, & terminandi, quòd illud dicit intrinsecam ordinationem relatiui ad terminum: & ideo requirit veram relationem inhærentem relatiuo, & est consequenti actualem existentiam eiusdem relatiui: sed terminare, solùm dicit extrinsecam denominationem: & extrinseca denominatio potest conuenire rei non existenti: quia cùm nihil intrinsecum ponat in ea, non necessariò præsupponit actualem existentiam eius: ergo ens in potentia sufficienter potest terminare relationem non mutuam.

88 Second: powers, habits, and sciences are measurable by their objects; therefore they are referred to them by a real relation, of the measurable to the measure, placed in the third genus; yet they are not referred to them as actually existing, but it suffices that these be in potency; therefore this is a non-mutual relation, which can be given between a being in act and C c iiij [p. 408] a being in potency. The minor is proved: because the visible does not say actual existence, but only potency; and when the rose does not exist, in winter, there is a true and real science of it. And it can be confirmed in this way: this is the difference between the office of referring and that of terminating, that the former says an intrinsic ordering of the relative to the term, and therefore requires a true relation inhering in the relative, and consequently the actual existence of the same relative; but terminating says only an extrinsic denomination, and an extrinsic denomination can belong to a thing that does not exist, because, since it posits nothing intrinsic in it, it does not necessarily presuppose its actual existence; therefore a being in potency can sufficiently terminate a non-mutual relation.

> Secunda opinio negat, *Relationem prædicamentalem non mutuam, posse dari ad ens rationis, vel ad ens in potentia, sed asserit relationem necessariò requirere terminum realem actu existentem*. Hæc est D. Tho 2. contra gentes, c. 12. & 1. par. qu. 13. quem sequuntur in eisdem locis Caiet. & Ferrar. Scotus in 1. d. 3. quæstione vnica. Capreol. d. 31. q. 1. Sotus quęst. 1. huius capitis. Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 15. q. 1. sectio. 2. Pater Franciscus Suarius 2. tomo suæ Meta. & moderni ferè omnes. Et videtur nobis probabilior, & sequenda.

The second opinion denies that a non-mutual categorial relation can be given to a being of reason or to a being in potency, but asserts that relation necessarily requires a real, actually existing term. This is St. Thomas’s, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 12, and 1 p., q. 13, whom Cajetan and Ferrara follow in the same places; Scotus in 1, d. 3, the single question; Capreolus, d. 31, q. 1; Soto, q. 1 of this chapter; Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 15, q. 1, sect. 2; Father Francisco Suárez, vol. 2 of his Metaphysics; and almost all the moderns. And it seems to us more probable and to be followed.

> 89 Sed explicanda est priùs, deinde probanda. Pro explicatione verò, notanda est distinctio, inter relationes trãscendentales, & secundùm dici ex vna parte, & relatione prædicamentales, quòd illæ sunt de essentia absolutorum, quorũ essentiam complent: ideo non dicuntur habere fundamentum, nec ex fundamento aliqua consurgere, sed naturam absoluti, cuius essentiam complent, sequuntur: quòd si ens prædicamentale fuerit, ad prædicamentum, & speciem eius reductiuè pertinebunt. Relationes verò prædicamentales, extra essentiam omnium absolutorum sunt: nec per se intenduntur, aut producuntur à natura, vel agente aliquo: sed consequũtur rem absolutam per se intentam, atque productam: nec sequuntur illam: vt in se est, sed vt commensuratur, aut proportionatur alteri. Gratia exempli: relatio similitudinis, extra essentiam albi, aut nigri est, nec per se intenditur, aut producitur à natura: sed consequitur albedinem, aut nigredinem per intentam, & productam: nec sequitur illam vt est in se, sed vt commensuratur alteri albedini: quia si sola vna albedo produceretur in rerum natura, non consequeretur eam relatio similitudinis: & quod de similitudine dicimus, de cæteris relationibus intelligendum est.

89 But it must first be explained, then proved. For the explanation, the distinction should be noted between transcendental relations and relations secundum dici on the one hand, and categorial relations on the other: that the former belong to the essence of the absolute things whose essence they complete; therefore they are not said to have a foundation, nor to arise from any foundation, but they follow the nature of the absolute thing whose essence they complete; and if this is a categorial being, they will pertain reductively to its category and species. But categorial relations are outside the essence of all absolute things; nor are they intended per se or produced by nature or by any agent, but they follow upon the absolute thing intended and produced per se; nor do they follow it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate or proportioned to another. For example: the relation of similitude is outside the essence of white or black, nor is it intended per se or produced by nature, but it follows upon whiteness or blackness intended and produced per se; nor does it follow it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate to another whiteness: because if only one whiteness were produced in the nature of things, the relation of similitude would not follow upon it. And what we say of similitude is to be understood of the other relations.

> 90 Secundò notandum est, *In potentiis, habitibus, & scientiis, duplicem esse relationem*; Primam, per quam completur essentia [p. 409] eius: & hæc non significatur nomine scientiæ, sed imbibitur in ratione absoluta eius, ad quam significandam per se est impositum. Alia est relatio, Quæ non pertinet ad essentiam scientiæ, nec sequitur eam, vt est in se, sed vt commensuratur, & adęquatur obiecto: ita vt non possit circa aliquid versari, quod non contineatur sub eo: nec possit non versari, circa quodcunque sub eo contentum. Et hæc est relatio mensurabilis, per quam refertur scientia ad obiectum: non sub ratione scibilis, sed sub ratione mensuræ. Itaque naturam scientiæ iam completæ, per respectum ad obiectum, in ratione scibilis, consequitur relatio adæquationis aut mensurabilitatis: vnde respectus scientiæ, vt significatur nomine scientiæ ad scibile, est relatio secundùm dici: respectus verò eiusdem scientiæ, vt mensurabilis, est relatio secundùm esse, & prædicamentalis, pertinens ad tertium genus huius prædicamenti.

90 It should be noted, second, that in powers, habits, and sciences there is a twofold relation: the first, through which the essence is completed [p. 409] of it; and this is not signified by the name of science, but is imbibed in its absolute ratio, which the name is imposed per se to signify. The other relation is one which does not pertain to the essence of science, nor follows it as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate and adequated to its object, so that it cannot be concerned with anything that is not contained under it, nor can it fail to be concerned with whatever is contained under it. And this is the relation of the measurable, through which science is referred to its object, not under the ratio of the knowable, but under the ratio of measure. Thus upon the nature of science, already completed through its respect to the object under the ratio of the knowable, there follows the relation of adequation or measurability. Hence the respect of science, as signified by the name of science, to the knowable is a relation secundum dici; but the respect of the same science as measurable is a relation secundum esse, and categorial, pertaining to the third genus of this category.

> 91 Ex hac doctrina colligitur, efficax argum. ad probandum nostram sententiam. Quia relatio prædicamentalis, cùm sit extra essentiam absoluti, fundatur in commensuratione eius cum alio: & cùm sit realis, fundatur in commensuratione reali: sed nihil potest habere commensurationem, vel adæquationem realem, cum altero, nisi etiam sit reale: ergo nec potest consurgere relatio realis, in ente reali, ad ens rationis, vel ad ens in potentia. Probatur minor: Quia commensuratio realis, est realis, & naturalis proportio vnius rei cum altera: in qua proportione fundatur relatio realis: ergo non potest esse talis commensuratio, aut proportio, cum ente rationis, non habente esse, nisi per operationem intellectus: sed nec cum ente in potentia, quia ens in potentia, non habet esse reale in rerum natura: ergo nec ad illud comparari potest realiter & naturaliter, ens reale actu existens, sed solùm per operationem intellectus, considerantis ipsum, ac si actu esset: quare nec potest esse fundamentum reale in ente reali, ex quo consurgat relatio prædicamentalis, respectu entis rationis, vel entis in potentia.

91 From this doctrine an efficacious argument is gathered for proving our opinion: because a categorial relation, since it is outside the essence of the absolute thing, is founded on its commensuration with another; and since it is real, it is founded on a real commensuration; but nothing can have a real commensuration or adequation with another unless that other too is real; therefore neither can a real relation arise in a real being toward a being of reason or toward a being in potency. The minor is proved: because real commensuration is a real and natural proportion of one thing with another, on which proportion the real relation is founded; therefore there cannot be such a commensuration or proportion with a being of reason, which has no being except through an operation of the intellect; nor yet with a being in potency, because a being in potency does not have real being in the nature of things; therefore a real being actually existing cannot be compared to it really and naturally either, but only through an operation of the intellect considering it as if it were in act. Wherefore neither can there be a real foundation in a real being from which a categorial relation may arise in respect of a being of reason or of a being in potency.

> Ad testimonium Aristotelis, pro prima sententia, Respondeo, Relationem motiui ad mobile, & productiui ad productibile, realem esse, si extrema sint actu existentia in rerum natura: ita vt de illis verum sit, vnum habere realem potentiam actiuam, producendi, vel mouendi aliud, verbi gratia, motiuum, mobile verò habere potentiam passiuam, per quam procedit, aut mouetur ab alio: si verò vtrumque, vel alterum solùm sit in potentia, non erit relatio realis, sed rationis tantùm.

To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, I reply that the relation of the motive to the mobile, and of the productive to the producible, is real if the extremes actually exist in the nature of things, so that it is true of them that one has a real active potency of producing or moving the other, for example the motive, while the mobile has a passive potency through which it is produced or moved by the other; but if both, or one of them, is only in potency, the relation will not be real, but of reason only.

> 92 Ad primum, Distinguendũ est antecedens, quia duplicem sensum habere potest. Primum materialem, nempe, relationem [p. 410] sumere entitatem realem à re materiali, quæ est fundamentum, vt in se consideratur: & in hoc sensu, negandum est: quia relatio non sequitur rem, in qua fundatur, vt est in se, sed vt commensuratur, vel comparatur naturaliter ad alteram. Secundus sensus est: Relationem sumere entitatem realem, à fundamento, vt alteri commensurato: & est verus. Sed neganda est consequentia, quòd realis possit esse relatio, etiam si terminus, sit ens rationis, vel ens in potentia: quia res quæ est fundamentum, non potest cum his habere realem, & naturalem commensurationem: & ideo non potest tribuere entitatem relationi reali: nec proinde esse fundamentum eius.

92 To the first, the antecedent must be distinguished, because it can have a twofold sense. The first, material, namely: the relation [p. 410] takes its real entity from the material thing which is the foundation, as it is considered in itself; and in this sense it must be denied, because relation does not follow the thing on which it is founded as it is in itself, but as it is commensurate or naturally compared to another. The second sense is: relation takes its real entity from the foundation as commensurate to another; and this is true. But the consequence must be denied, that the relation can be real even if the term is a being of reason or a being in potency: because the thing that is the foundation cannot have a real and natural commensuration with these, and therefore cannot give entity to a real relation, nor, consequently, be its foundation.

> Ad secundum, Concedendum est primum enthymema, sed minor distinguenda, nam Scientia duobus modis accipitur, atque etiam potentia, & habitus: Aut secundùm essentialia: & hoc modo respiciunt obiecta, vt scibilis & ideo non, vt actu existentia: Aut secundùm realem commensurationem, vel adæquationem, quam habent cum obiectis: quia ratione consequitur eas relatio mensurabilitatis realis ad obiecta: non sub ratione vniuersali scibilium accepta, sed sub speciali mensuræ: & hoc modo respiciunt obiecta, actu existentia: non ita, vt actualis existentia sit ratio obiectiua: sed potiùs natura eorum, secundùm quam attinguntur ab eodem scientia: existentia verò, necessaria conditio est, ad conditionem realem mensurabilitatis: quia nisi actu existant, non potest scientia realiter commensurari, aut comparari ad illa: sed solùm dicentur scientiæ mensurabiles, per relationem rationis mensurabilitatis, consurgentem ex comparatione, qua eas comparat intellectus cum obiecto, tanquam cum mensura earum.

To the second, the first enthymeme must be granted, but the minor must be distinguished; for science is taken in two ways, and likewise power and habit. Either according to their essentials, and in this way they regard their objects as knowable, and therefore not as actually existing. Or according to the real commensuration or adequation which they have with their objects, by reason of which the relation of real measurability to the objects follows upon them, taken not under the universal ratio of knowables but under the special ratio of measure; and in this way they regard their objects as actually existing: not so that actual existence is the objective ratio, but rather their nature, according to which they are attained by the same science; existence, however, is a necessary condition for the real relation of measurability, because unless they actually exist, the science cannot be really commensurated or compared to them; but the sciences will be called measurable only through a relation of reason of measurability, arising from the comparison by which the intellect compares them with the object as with their measure.

> 93 Ratio autem huius differentiæ, inter vtramue relationem, scientiæ, vt scientiæ, ad obiectum, vt scibile: & relationem eiusdem scientiæ, ad obiectum, vt mensuram: est, quòd cùm relatio illa sit complementum scientiæ, (quæ absoluta qualitas est: ideo non dependens in sua entitate absoluta, ab entitate obiecti, sed ab actibus circa illud, per quos producitur) realis esse potest: etiam si obiectum sit ens rationis, vel solùm ens in potentia. Cuius ea est ratio: quia non minùs versatur intellectus, per actus reales, circa obiectum reale, aut actu existens, quàm circa ens rationis, vel ens in potentia: nec minùs per tales actus reales, producit verum, & realem habitum. Relatio verò realis mensurabilis, accidit scientiæ, ex commensuratione, & comparatione reali, & naturali cum obiecto: non vt scibili, sed vt mensuræ eius: commensurationem verò, & comparationem realem, habere non potest cum eo, nisi actu [p. 411] existente: & ideo nec relationem realem mensurabilis: sed rationis tantùm, per comparationem intellectus cum eo, existente in potentia, Non ergo sequitur, quòd si relatio secundùm dici, scientiæ ad scibile, realis sit respectu obiecti in potentia, aut respectu entis rationis, realis quoque esse possit, relatio prædicamentalis non mutua, eiusdem scientiæ, vt mensurabilis, ad idem obiectum, vt mensuram,

93 The reason for this difference between the two relations, that of science as science to the object as knowable, and the relation of the same science to the object as measure, is that, since the former relation is the complement of the science (which is an absolute quality, and therefore does not depend in its absolute entity on the entity of the object, but on the acts concerning it, through which it is produced), it can be real even if the object is a being of reason, or only a being in potency. The reason for this is that the intellect is no less concerned, through real acts, with a being of reason or a being in potency than with a real or actually existing object; nor does it produce a true and real habit any less through such real acts. But the real relation of the measurable befalls science from a real and natural commensuration and comparison with the object, not as knowable but as its measure; and it cannot have a real commensuration and comparison with it unless it actually exists [p. 411] and therefore neither can it have a real relation of the measurable, but only one of reason, through the comparison of the intellect with it as existing in potency. It does not follow, therefore, that if the relation secundum dici of science to the knowable is real in respect of an object in potency, or in respect of a being of reason, the non-mutual categorial relation of the same science as measurable to the same object as measure can also be real.

> 94 Ad confirmationem, Concedenda est maior, sed minor distinguenda: nam licèt aliqua denominatio extrinseca, conuenire fortè possit enti in potentia, non tamen denominatio extrinseca terminandi relationem realem: quia relatio realis fundatur in commensuratione reali relatiui, cum termino: commensuratio autem realis, non potest esse, nisi inter entia realia actu existentia.

94 To the confirmation, the major must be granted, but the minor must be distinguished: for although some extrinsic denomination can perhaps belong to a being in potency, not, however, the extrinsic denomination of terminating a real relation; because a real relation is founded on a real commensuration of the relative with the term, and a real commensuration cannot exist except between real beings actually existing.

## QUESTION X

### Qu. 10. An aliqua relatio prædicamentalis fundetur proximè in substantia — Whether any categorial relation is founded proximately in substance.

> QVÆSTIO X.

[…]

> *An aliqua relatio prædicamentalis, fundetur proximè in substantia.*

[…]

> 95 Explicato termino relationis, iam agimus de fundamento eius, *Tria fundamenta relationum prædicamentalium* assignauit Arist. 5. lib. Met. c. 15. Primum est. Vnitas, quam etiam vocauit numerum: quia principium numeri est. Vnitas verò triplex est, *Numerica, Specifica, & Generica*. Et de numerica, non intelligit esse fundamentum relationis, quia repugnat naturæ eius: nam relatio realis, prædicamentalis, dicit oppositionem realem, inter extrema, & ex consequenti distinctionem realem: quia nihil opponitur realiter sibiipsi: sed indiuiduum, vt est vnum numero, non est vnum cum altero indiuiduo vnitate numerica: sed sibiipsi tantùm: & sibiipsi non opponitur realiter: quia non distinguitur à seipso realiter, ergo non potest fundare relationem vnitatis. Specifica verò, & generica, possunt: quia in diuersis indiuiduis, aut speciebus fundantur: & ideo habent extrema realiter distincta; vt natura humana, distincta indiuidua, nempe Petrum, & Ioannem, & natura sensitiua, distinctas species, vt hominem, & leonem.

95 Having explained the term of relation, we now treat of its foundation. Three foundations of categorial relations Aristotle assigned in Metaph. 5, ch. 15. The first is unity, which he also called number, because it is the principle of number. But unity is threefold: numerical, specific, and generic. And of numerical unity he does not understand that it is a foundation of relation, because this is repugnant to its nature: for a real categorial relation says a real opposition between the extremes, and consequently a real distinction, because nothing is really opposed to itself; but the individual, as it is one in number, is not one with another individual by numerical unity, but only with itself; and it is not really opposed to itself, because it is not really distinguished from itself; therefore it cannot found the relation of unity. But specific and generic unity can, because they are founded in different individuals or species, and therefore have really distinct extremes: as human nature in distinct individuals, namely Peter and John, and sensitive nature in distinct species, as man and lion.

> 96 Secundum fundamentum relationis, dicit, *Esse actionem, & passionem*. Vt generatio, per quam vnus homo generat alterum, est actio, & generatio passiua, per quam vnus homo dicitur genitus ab alio, dicitur passio: & illa fundat relationem paternitatis, hæc relationem filiationis.

96 The second foundation of relation, he says, is action and passion. As generation, through which one man begets another, is an action; and passive generation, through which one man is said to be begotten by another, is called passion; and the former founds the relation of paternity, the latter the relation of filiation.

[p. 412]

> Tertium fundamentum est *Mensura*, hoc est, adæquatio vnius rei ad aliam, quæ reperitur in potentiis, habitibus, scientiis, & virtutibus cum suis obiectis: in quantum ad omnia se extendunt, quæ sub obiectis propriis continentur, & ad nihil aliud, quod sub eis non contineatur: ex qua adæquatione, dicuntur obiecta, mensura earum: & illæ dicuntur mensurabiles ab eisdem obiectis, & secundùm hæc tria fundamenta, distinguit Arist. tria genera relationum, Primum vocans, *Quod fundatur in vnitate*, sub vnitate etiam intelligens diuersitatem: quia eadem est ratio oppositorum. Secundum genus vocat illud, *Quod fundatur in actione, passione*. Et tertiũ, *Quod fundatur in mensura*. Et quantum pertinet ad hanc quæstionem, supponimus relationes secundi generis, non fundari proximè in substantia, sed mediis his accidentibus, nempe actione, passione, & mensura. Quare solùm procedit quæstio de relationibus primi generis, quæ fundantur in vnitate: *An fundentur proximè in substantia*. Et de vnitate numerica, probauimus, non fundare relationem realem: ideo difficultas quæstionis, reducitur ad vnitatem genericam, & specificam. In qua tres alias species relationum fundari, vt docet Arist. nam si vnitas specifica sit in substantia, dicit fundare relationem identitatis specificæ: vt vnitas specifica Petri, & Ioannis, est fundamentum relationis identitatis specificæ, inter eos repertæ. Si sit in qualitate, dicit fundare relationem similitudinis: vt inter duo alba. Si sit in quantitate, fundat relationem æqualitatis: qualis est ea, quæ reperitur inter duo corpora, eiusdem longitudinis.

The third foundation is measure, that is, the adequation of one thing to another, which is found in powers, habits, sciences, and virtues with their objects, inasmuch as they extend to all the things contained under their proper objects, and to nothing else not contained under them; from which adequation the objects are called their measure, and they are called measurable by the same objects. And according to these three foundations Aristotle distinguished three genera of relations, calling the first that which is founded in unity, understanding under unity diversity also, because the ratio of opposites is the same. The second genus he calls that which is founded in action and passion. And the third, that which is founded in measure. And as far as pertains to this question, we suppose that relations of the second genus are not founded proximately in substance, but by means of these accidents, namely action, passion, and measure. Wherefore the question proceeds only about relations of the first genus, which are founded in unity: whether they are founded proximately in substance. And of numerical unity we have proved that it does not found a real relation; therefore the difficulty of the question is reduced to generic and specific unity, in which three species of relations are founded, as Aristotle teaches: for if specific unity is in substance, he says it founds the relation of specific identity, as the specific unity of Peter and John is the foundation of the relation of specific identity found between them. If it is in quality, he says it founds the relation of similitude, as between two white things. If it is in quantity, it founds the relation of equality, such as is that found between two bodies of the same length.

> 97 Sed in fundamentis harum trium specierum relationis, duo considerantur, nempe, Fundamentum, & ratio fundandi: Fundamentum est, res ipsa fundans relationem: vt substantia, qualitas, & quantitas. Ratio verò fundandi, est vnitas, aut diuersitas specifica, aut generica: quia ratione illius, substantia qualitas, & quantitas fundant relationem: ita vt vnitas sit ratio fundandi relationem identitatis, similitudinis, aut æqualitatis: diuersitas verò, sit ratio fundandi relationem, diuersitatis, dissimilitudinis, & inæqualitatis. Et hanc rationem fundandi, vocant alij fundamentum proximum, ipsam verò rem, quæ fundat, remotum. Vt albedinem, vocant fundamentum remotum, vnitatem verò, proximum.

97 But in the foundations of these three species of relation two things are considered, namely the foundation and the ratio of founding. The foundation is the thing itself founding the relation, as substance, quality, and quantity. The ratio of founding is specific or generic unity or diversity, because by reason of it substance, quality, and quantity found the relation; so that unity is the ratio of founding the relation of identity, similitude, or equality, and diversity is the ratio of founding the relation of diversity, dissimilitude, and inequality. And this ratio of founding others call the proximate foundation, and the thing itself which founds, the remote one; as they call whiteness the remote foundation, and unity the proximate one.

> Ex his tribus speciebus relationem, nempe, Identitatis, Similitudinis, & Æqualitatis, certum est duas postremas, non fundari proximè in substantia, sed in qualitate, & quantitate, per duas dicuntur res similes, vel æquales. Solùm ergo potest esse quæstio, de relationibus identitatis, & diuersitatis genericæ [p. 413], aut specificæ, an proximum fundamentum earum sit substantia.

Of these three species of relations, namely identity, similitude, and equality, it is certain that the two last are not founded proximately in substance, but in quality and quantity, through which two things are called similar or equal. The question, therefore, can only be about the relations of identity and diversity, generic [p. 413] or specific: whether their proximate foundation is substance.

> Et prima opinio asserit, *Non esse relationes reales, sed rationis* vt relationem identitatis specificæ, inter Petrum, & Ioannem: & consequenter tenet, nullam relationem realem fundari proximè in substantia. Ita Fons. 4. lib. Meta. c. 2. q. 7. sect. 8. & li. 5. cap. 1. q. 1. sect. 7.

And the first opinion asserts that they are not real relations, but of reason, as the relation of specific identity between Peter and John; and consequently it holds that no real relation is founded proximately in substance. So Fonseca, Metaph. bk. 4, ch. 2, q. 7, sect. 8, and bk. 5, ch. 1, q. 1, sect. 7.

> Probat primò: Quia vnitas specifica aut generica, est ratio fundandi has relationes: sed istæ vnitates, non dantur à parte rei, sed per operationem intellectus, abstrahentis naturam ab inferioribus, aut comparantis ad illa: vt quæst. 3. vniuersalium dictum est: ergo relationes, quæ consequuntur has vnitates, non dabuntur à parte rei, sed per intellectum: & ideo non erunt reales, sed rationis.

He proves it, first: because specific or generic unity is the ratio of founding these relations; but these unities are not given on the part of the thing, but through an operation of the intellect abstracting the nature from its inferiors, or comparing it to them, as was said in q. 3 on Universals; therefore the relations which follow upon these unities will not be given on the part of the thing, but through the intellect; and therefore they will not be real, but of reason.

> Secundo: Relationes, quæ eodem modo conueniunt rebus, dum actu existunt, & dum solùm sunt in potentia, non possunt esse reales: vt ex quæst. præcedenti patet: sed relationes identitatis, & diuersitatis specificæ, atque genericæ, ita se habent: ergo non sunt reales, sed rationis. Probatur minor: quia non minùs sunt eiusdem speciei Petrus & Ioannes mortui quàm viui: hæc minùs distinguuntur specie, equus, & leo, siue actu existant, siue solùm in potentia: quod etiam de rosa certum est, non minùs specie distincta ab aliis floribus in hyeme quàm verno tempore: ergo vtroque modo se habentes, fundant relationes identitatis, & diuersitatis: quæ ideo non poterunt esse reales, sed rationis.

Second: relations which belong to things in the same way while they actually exist and while they are only in potency cannot be real, as is plain from the preceding question; but the relations of specific and generic identity and diversity are of this kind; therefore they are not real, but of reason. The minor is proved: because Peter and John are no less of the same species dead than alive; the horse and the lion are no less distinguished in species, whether they actually exist or only in potency; which is also certain of the rose, which is no less distinct in species from other flowers in winter than in springtime; therefore, being in either condition, they found relations of identity and diversity, which therefore cannot be real, but of reason.

> Secunda opinio *concedit tales relationes esse reales, & proximè conuenire substantiis, sed negat esse prædicamentales: & transcendentales esse vult: & ideo nullam relationem prædicamentalem, proximè fundari in substantia*. Hanc sententiam citat Soncin. 5. Met. q. 31. & sequitur Mercatus cap. præsenti, qu. 1. probatque testimonio D. Tho. 4. contra gentes, c. 14. vbi inquit: *Relatio non solum præexigit esse substantiæ, sed esse aliorum accidentium, ex quibus causatur: sicut vnum in quantitate, causat æqualitatem, & vnum in qualitate similitudinem*. Deinde hoc arg. Vnum, & distinctum, seu diuersum, sunt passiones entis: ergo conuertuntur cum eo: sed ens est transcendens: ergo & illa: quare relationes consequentes vnitatem, & diuersitatem, & transcendentales erant, non prædicamentales. Quod probatur etiam hac ratione, quia vnitas specifica, atque generica, in omnibus prædicamentis reperitur: ergo transcendentalis est: & consequenter relatio in ea fundata, est talis.

The second opinion grants that such relations are real and belong proximately to substances, but denies that they are categorial, and holds that they are transcendental; and therefore that no categorial relation is founded proximately in substance. Soncinas cites this opinion, Metaph. 5, q. 31, and Mercado follows it in the present chapter, q. 1; and he proves it by the testimony of St. Thomas, Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 14, where he says: Relation presupposes not only the being of substance, but the being of other accidents, by which it is caused: as one in quantity causes equality, and one in quality similitude. Next, by this argument: one and distinct, or diverse, are attributes of being; therefore they are convertible with it; but being is transcendental; therefore they are too. Wherefore the relations following upon unity and diversity will also be transcendental, not categorial. This is also proved by this reason: because specific and generic unity is found in all the categories; therefore it is transcendental; and consequently the relation founded on it is such.

> 99 Tertia opinio duo asserit. Primum, *Relationes identitatis* [p. 414] *& diuersitatis esse reales, & prædicamentales*. Secundum, *Proximè fundari in substantia*. Ita Auicenna 3. Metaph. cap. 10. Albertus Magnus tract. de prædicamento ad aliquid, cap. 3. Caiet. 1. part. qu. 28. art. 1. ad 2. Ferra. 4. contra gentes, cap. 1. Soncin. 5. Meta. q. 31. Sotus cap. præsenti, qu. 1. & est expressa sententia Arist. & D. Thom. & non solùm probabilis, sed vera. Aristotelis quidem 5. Meta. c. 15 vbi assignat fundamentum relationum primi generis, his verbis: *Secundùm vnum etenim, omnia dicuntur: Eadem enim sunt, quorum substantia vna. Similia verò, quorum qualitas vna, Æqualia autem, quorum quantitas vna*. Et D. Th. opusc. 48. tract. 5. de prædicamento ad aliquid, cap. 4. ait: *Nihil tamen obstat, quin relatio possit fundari immediatè in substantia: nam in vno in substantia fundatur identitas, in vno in quantitate, fundatur æqualitas, in vno in qualitate, similitudo*. Et 1. p. q. 28. art 1 ad 2. docet identitatem numericam, esse relationem rationis, genericam verò, & specificam, realem, & prædicamentalem.

99 The third opinion asserts two things. First, that the relations of identity [p. 414] and diversity are real and categorial. Second, that they are founded proximately in substance. So Avicenna, Metaph. 3, ch. 10; Albert the Great, treatise on the category of relation, ch. 3; Cajetan, 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, ad 2; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 4, ch. 1; Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 31; Soto, present chapter, q. 1; and it is the express opinion of Aristotle and St. Thomas, and not only probable but true. Of Aristotle, indeed, in Metaph. 5, ch. 15, where he assigns the foundation of relations of the first genus in these words: For all these are said according to one: for those things are the same whose substance is one; similar, those whose quality is one; and equal, those whose quantity is one. And of St. Thomas, opusc. 48, tract. 5, on the category of relation, ch. 4, who says: Nothing, however, prevents a relation from being able to be founded immediately in substance: for in one in substance identity is founded, in one in quantity equality, in one in quality similitude. And in 1 p., q. 28, a. 1, ad 2, he teaches that numerical identity is a relation of reason, but generic and specific identity real and categorial.

> Idem probatur ratione: Quia vnitas specifica albedinis fundat relationem realem, & prædicamentalem similitudinis, & vnitas specifica quantitatis, relationem æqualitatis: ergo vnitas specifica substantiæ, fundat relationem realem, & prædicamentalem identitatis. Antecedens euidens est, & conceditur ab aduersariis, sed non est minùs euidens consequentia: quia omnes conditiones necessariæ ad fundandam relationem realem, & prædicamentalem, quæ reperiuntur inter æqualia, & similia, reperiuntur etiam inter ea quæ sunt eiusdem, aut diuersæ speciei in substantia: ergo non minùs fundant relationem realem, & prædicamentalem identitatis.

The same is proved by reason: because the specific unity of whiteness founds the real and categorial relation of similitude, and the specific unity of quantity the relation of equality; therefore the specific unity of substance founds the real and categorial relation of identity. The antecedent is evident, and is granted by the adversaries; but the consequence is no less evident, because all the conditions necessary for founding a real and categorial relation which are found between equal and similar things are found also between things that are of the same or of different species in substance; therefore they no less found the real and categorial relation of identity.

> 100 Quòd verò substantia, sit proximum fundamentum harum relationum, probatur: Quia priùs quàm intelligatur substantia cum aliquo accidente, intelligitur, & est eadem, vel diuersa specie, per proprium genus, & differentiam: ergo proximum fundamentum est relationis identitatis, aut diuersitatis.

100 That substance is the proximate foundation of these relations is proved: because before substance is understood together with any accident, it is understood to be, and is, the same or diverse in species through its own genus and difference; therefore it is the proximate foundation of the relation of identity or diversity.

> Ad primum arg. primæ opinionis, Respondetur ex doctrina tradita, q 3. vniuersalium, distinguendo minorem: nam vnitas specifica, & generica formalis, non datur ante operationem intellectus, datur tamen virtualis, quæ est fundamentum remotum vniuersalitatis, & sufficiens ratio fundandi has relationes reales identitatis.

To the first argument of the first opinion, I reply from the doctrine delivered in q. 3 on Universals, by distinguishing the minor: for formal specific and generic unity is not given before the operation of the intellect; but virtual unity is given, which is the remote foundation of universality and a sufficient ratio for founding these real relations of identity.

> Ad secundum, Neganda est minor: quòd istæ relationes identitatis, eodem modo reperiantur in extremis actu existentibus, & non existentibus: quia dum non existunt Petrus, & [p. 415] Paulus, non sunt eiusdem speciei, secundùm entitatem realem specificam, sed solùm, in quantum possunt apprehendi ab intellectu, sub eisdem prædicatis essentialibus: & ideo non possunt fundare relationem realem, sed rationis: quia fundamentum relationis realis, debet esse entitas realis, quæ non est nisi actu existens.

To the second, the minor must be denied, that these relations of identity are found in the same way in extremes actually existing and not existing: because while Peter and [p. 415] Paul do not exist, they are not of the same species according to real specific entity, but only inasmuch as they can be apprehended by the intellect under the same essential predicates; and therefore they cannot found a real relation, but one of reason: because the foundation of a real relation must be a real entity, which is only one actually existing.

> Ad testimonium D. Tho. pro secunda opinione adductum, Respondet Ferra. ibidem quòd substantia fundat relationem identitatis, media vnitate tanquam ratione fundandi: quæ vnitas, licèt verè sit substantialis, tamen habet modum accidentalem, in quantum intelligitur, vt quid superadditum extremis: vt Petro, & Ioanni, quasi superaddita intelligitur vnitas specifica, eo ferè modo, quo intelligitur superaddita vnitas albedini: itaque vniuersaliter verum est, substantiam fundarè relationem, medio accidente superaddito, vero quidem, aut per similitudinem accidentis apprehenso. Vel secundò, possumus respondere: non de relationibus loqui D. Tho. maiori ex parte: quia maior pars earum, conuenit substantiæ medio accidente: non tamen de omnibus: cùm in primo loco expressè doceat, quasdam fundari proximè in substantia.

To the testimony of St. Thomas adduced for the second opinion, Ferrara replies in the same place that substance founds the relation of identity by means of unity as the ratio of founding; which unity, although it is truly substantial, nevertheless has an accidental mode, inasmuch as it is understood as something superadded to the extremes, as to Peter and John, to whom specific unity is understood as if superadded, in almost the same way as unity is understood to be superadded to whiteness. Thus it is universally true that substance founds a relation by means of a superadded accident, either a true one or one apprehended after the likeness of an accident. Or, second, we can reply that St. Thomas is speaking of relations for the greater part, because the greater part of them belong to substance by means of an accident, but not of all, since in the first place he expressly teaches that some are founded proximately in substance.

> 101 Ad argument. eiusdem sententiæ: Distinguendum est primum antecedens, quia vnitas duplex est: *Generalis*, quæ consequitur entitatem: & *Specialis*, quæ vocatur specifica, aut generica: & illa est transcendens: & ideo non potest fundare relationem prædicamentalem: hæc verò quia est specialis, potest. Quòd verò reperiatur in omnibus prædicamentis, nihil obstat: quia cùm ratio eius specialis sit, specialis semper censetur: & secundùm specialem, & propriam rationem, fundat relationem identitatis.

101 To the argument of the same opinion: the first antecedent must be distinguished, because unity is twofold: general, which follows upon entity; and special, which is called specific or generic; and the former is transcendental, and therefore cannot found a categorial relation; but the latter, because it is special, can. That it is found in all the categories is no obstacle, because, since its ratio is special, it is always deemed special; and according to its special and proper ratio it founds the relation of identity.

## QUESTION XI

### Quæst. 11. An vna relatio realis possit esse fundamentum alterius — Whether one real relation can be the foundation of another.

> QVÆSTIO XI.

[…]

> *An vna relatio realis, possit esse fundamentum alterius.*

[…]

> Quælibet relatio per se primò, habet esse rationẽ referendi relatiuum, quod constituit, ad terminum sibi oppositum: vt paternitas, esse rationem referendi patrem ad filium, habet etiam esse eiusdem generis, aut speciei, vel diuersæ, ab altera relatione: vt paternitas, est eiusdem speciei, cum alia paternitate, & etiam ei similis vocari potest. Quærimus ergo, An per se referatur ad quamlibet aliam, cui est similis, vel cum qua est eadem, aut non per se, sed per aliam, relationem identitatis: nam si per se refertur, non indigens alia [p. 416] relatione, nec erit fundamentum eius: si verò per alium referatur, sicut quodlibet indiuiduum eiusdem speciei, refertur ad alterum, per relationem identitatis, sibi superadditam, fundamentum talis relationis, absque dubio erit.

Every relation has per se primarily to be the ratio of referring the relative which it constitutes to the term opposed to it, as paternity has to be the ratio of referring the father to the son; it has also to be of the same genus or species as another relation, or of a different one, as paternity is of the same species as another paternity, and can also be called similar to it. We ask, therefore, whether it is referred per se to any other to which it is similar, or with which it is the same; or not per se, but through another relation of identity. For if it is referred per se, not needing another, [p. 416] relation, it will not be its foundation either; but if it is referred through another, as each individual of the same species is referred to another through a relation of identity superadded to it, it will without doubt be the foundation of such a relation.

> Primam sententiam, omnibus modis negantem, *quòd vna relatio sit fundamentum alterius*, tenent Ferr. 4. lib. contra gentes, c. 4. Soncinas 5. Meta. q. 29. ad 1. Et probatur ex doctrina Arist. lib. Meta. ca. 15. vbi tria tantùm fundamenta relationum posuit, nempe, *Vnitatem substantiæ, qualitatis & quantitatis, pro primo genere, actionem, & passionem, pro secundo, & pro tertio mensuram*: sed relatio nihil horum est, vt constat: ergo ex mente Arist. non potest esse fundamentum relationis.

The first opinion, denying in every way that one relation is the foundation of another, is held by Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 4, ch. 4, and Soncinas, Metaph. 5, q. 29, ad 1. And it is proved from the doctrine of Aristotle, Metaph., ch. 15, where he posited only three foundations of relations, namely the unity of substance, quality, and quantity, for the first genus; action and passion, for the second; and for the third, measure; but relation is none of these, as is plain; therefore, according to Aristotle’s mind, it cannot be the foundation of a relation.

> 102 Probatur etiam testimonio D. Tho. 1. par. qu. 42 art. 1. ad 4 vbi vniuersaliter videtur negare, quòd vna relatio sit fundamentum alterius, his verbis: *Vna relatio non refertur ad aliam per aliquam aliam relationem: cùm enim dicimus, quòd paternitas opponitur filiationi, oppositio non est relatio media, inter paternitatem & filiationem*.

102 It is proved also by the testimony of St. Thomas, 1 p., q. 42, a. 1, ad 4, where he seems universally to deny that one relation is the foundation of another, in these words: One relation is not referred to another through some other relation: for when we say that paternity is opposed to filiation, the opposition is not a relation midway between paternity and filiation.

> Deinde ratione probatur. Primò: Quia relatio, essentialiter est ratio referendi vnum alterum: ergo per seipsam, & non per aliud, refertur ad quodcunque ordinari potest. Sicut albedo, quia ex se est ratio albi, non potest per aliam, albedinem fieri alba: sed si vna relatio fundaret aliam, ordinaretur per illam ad alterum, quemadmodum ordinantur cætera, quæ fundant relationem: ergo impossibile est, quòd relatio sit fundamentum alterius.

Next, it is proved by reason. First: because relation is essentially the ratio of referring one thing to another; therefore through itself, and not through another, it is referred to whatever it can be ordered to. Just as whiteness, because it is of itself the ratio of white, cannot become white through another whiteness. But if one relation founded another, it would be ordered to another through it, in the way in which the other things that found a relation are ordered; therefore it is impossible that a relation be the foundation of another.

> Secundò: Sit vna relatio fundaret alteram, daretur processus in infinitum in relationibus: at iste non est admittendus, quia ex eo sequitur dari infinitas relationes actu: ergo nec admittendum est, quòd vna relatio sit fundamentum alterius. Probatur antecedens, quia si paternitas fundat aliam relationem, cùm illa secunda sit vera relatio, erit etiam fundamentum alterius relationis: & sic de tertia, vsque ad infinitas.

Second: if one relation founded another, there would be a process to infinity in relations; but this is not to be admitted, because from it it follows that infinite relations in act are given; therefore neither is it to be admitted that one relation is the foundation of another. The antecedent is proved: because if paternity founds another relation, since that second one is a true relation, it will also be the foundation of another relation; and so of the third, up to infinitely many.

> 103 Secunda opinio, Concedit, *Vnam relationem esse fundamentum alterius*: quam tenet Scotus in 2. d. 1. quæst. 4. & 5. & in 4. d. 6 q. 10. & cum eo Lyquetus, & Mayronius eisdem locis. & Antonius Andreas, 5. Meta. quæst. 13. & lib. de sex principiis quæst 10,

103 The second opinion grants that one relation is the foundation of another. Scotus holds it in 2, d. 1, q. 4 and 5, and in 4, d. 6, q. 10; and with him Lychetus and Mayronis in the same places, and Antonius Andreas, Metaph. 5, q. 13, and on the Book of Six Principles, q. 10.

> Probat primò, ex Euclide 5. Geometriæ, in principio, Vbi definit proportionalitatem, dicens, *Esse similitudinem duarum proportionum*: quod non potest esse verum, nisi in proportione fundetur similitudo: sed proportio est etiam relatio, apud omnes: ergo vna relatio, ex mente Euclidis, est fundamentum alterius.

He proves it, first, from Euclid, Geometry 5, at the beginning, where he defines proportionality, saying that it is the similitude of two proportions; which cannot be true unless similitude is founded on proportion; but proportion too is a relation, according to all; therefore one relation, according to Euclid’s mind, is the foundation of another.

[p. 417]

> Deinde ratione: Quia sicut duæ albedines sunt similes, quia sunt eiusdem speciei: & ideo sunt fundamenta relationis similitudinis, per quam vna ordinatur ad aliã: ita duæ paternitates aut aliæ relationes similitudinis, sunt similes: ergo fundãt alias relationes similitudinis, per quas ordinatur quælibet ad aliam.

Next, by reason: because just as two whitenesses are similar because they are of the same species, and are therefore foundations of the relation of similitude through which one is ordered to the other, so two paternities, or other relations of similitude, are similar; therefore they found other relations of similitude through which each is ordered to the other.

> Pro solutione huius quæstionis, Notandum est, Relationem duobus modis posse considerari: *Primò per se formaliter & essentialiter*: & hoc modo est ratio referendi vnum extremum ad alterum sibi oppositum, vt relatio paternitatis, est ratio referendi patrem ad filium.

For the solution of this question, it should be noted that relation can be considered in two ways. First, per se, formally and essentially; and in this way it is the ratio of referring one extreme to the other opposed to it, as the relation of paternity is the ratio of referring the father to the son.

> 104 Secundò consideratur *materialiter, & accidentaliter*, in quantum conuenit cum alia relatione in essentia: aut est diuersa ab ea: vt vna paternitas, aut vna similitudo, in quantum conuenit cum alia paternitate, vel alia similitudine, aut differt à filiatione, & dissimilitudine: & hoc modo non consideratur, vt ratio referẽdi, sed vt id, quod refertur ad aliud: & propterea dicitur, consideratio materialis relationis: quia communis est ei cum rebus absolutis, quæ ad alias referuntur, à quibus separatur per primam considerationem formalem, & essentialem. Dicitur etiam consideratio accidentalis: quia sicut accidentale est Petro: quòd sit idem in specie cum Ioanne: & huic albedini, quòd sit similis alteri: Eadem ratione, accidentale est paternitati, quòd sit eiusdem speciei cum altera, aut ei similis. *Probatur paritas rationis euidenter*, quia, sicut hæc prædicatio: Petrus est idem cum Ioanne, aut ei similis, est in 5. prædicabili: sic etiam ista, hæc paternitas est eadem cum illa, aut ei similis.

104 Second, it is considered materially and accidentally, inasmuch as it agrees with another relation in essence, or is different from it: as one paternity, or one similitude, inasmuch as it agrees with another paternity or another similitude, or differs from filiation and dissimilitude; and in this way it is not considered as the ratio of referring, but as that which is referred to another. And on that account it is called the material consideration of relation, because it is common to it with absolute things, which are referred to others, from which it is separated by the first, formal and essential, consideration. It is also called the accidental consideration, because just as it is accidental to Peter that he is the same in species with John, and to this whiteness that it is similar to another, by the same reasoning it is accidental to paternity that it is of the same species as another, or similar to it. The parity of reasoning is proved evidently: because, just as this predication, Peter is the same as John, or similar to him, is in the fifth predicable, so also is this one: this paternity is the same as that one, or similar to it.

> Hoc supposito, nostra sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur, secundùm sensum huius distinctionis. Prima est, *Relatio formaliter, & essentialiter considerata, hoc est, vt ratio referendi relatiuum ad terminum sibi oppositum, non potest esse fundamentum alterius relationis*. Vt paternitas, in quantum est ratio referendi patrem ad filium, non fundat aliam relationem: sed per se ipsam, & non per aliam, est ratio referendi. Hæc conclusio videtur mihi euidens, ideo non indigeret probatione.

This supposed, our opinion is explained in two conclusions, according to the sense of this distinction. The first is: relation considered formally and essentially, that is, as the ratio of referring the relative to the term opposed to it, cannot be the foundation of another relation. As paternity, inasmuch as it is the ratio of referring the father to the son, does not found another relation, but is the ratio of referring through itself, and not through another. This conclusion seems to me evident, and therefore would not need proof.

> Nihilominus probatur primò: Id quod fundat relationem, refertur per illam ad aliud: vt albedo fundat relationem similitudinis: & per eam refertur ad aliam albedinem. Sed relatio formaliter, & essentialiter sumpta, non refertur ad aliam, sed est ratio referendi vnum ad aliud: ergo non est fundamentum alterius relationis.

Nevertheless it is proved, first: that which founds a relation is referred through it to another, as whiteness founds the relation of similitude and through it is referred to another whiteness. But relation taken formally and essentially is not referred to another, but is the ratio of referring one thing to another; therefore it is not the foundation of another relation.

> 105 Secundò: Vna relatio formaliter sumpta, dicit formalem oppositionem cum alia relatione termini, ad quem per se ordinat relatiuum, ergo per se, atque essentialiter est ei opposita, [p. 418] & non per aliam: quare per se, & non per aliam, erit ratio referendi: sicut per se, & non per aliam opponitur eidem relationi: & ideo hoc modo sumpta, non indiget alia relatione, cuius fundamentum sit.

105 Second: one relation taken formally says a formal opposition with the other relation, of the term to which it orders the relative per se; therefore it is per se and essentially opposed to it, Dd [p. 418] and not through another; wherefore it will be the ratio of referring through itself, and not through another, just as through itself, and not through another, it is opposed to the same relation; and therefore, taken in this way, it does not need another relation of which it would be the foundation.

> Probatur prima consequentia: Quia si per aliam relationem esset illi opposita, non essentialiter, sed accidentaliter ei opponeretur. Et hoc modo sumpsit D. Th. in illo testimonio relationem, dum negauit, posse esse fundamentum alterius: vt verba citata ostendunt.

The first consequence is proved: because if it were opposed to it through another relation, it would be opposed to it not essentially but accidentally. And in this way St. Thomas took relation in that testimony, when he denied that it could be the foundation of another, as the words cited show.

> Secunda conclusio: *Relatio materialiter & accidentaliter considerata, tanquam id, quod refertur ad aliud: quo pacto comparatur ad relationem non sibi oppositam, sed ad aliam, cui est similis, vel cum qua est eiusdem speciei, fundamentum est alterius relationis, per quam ad eandem relationem refertur*. Vt relatio paternitatis, non comparata ad filiationem, sed ad aliam paternitatem, tanquam ad id, quod ad eam refertur, vt est eiusdem speciei cum ea, fundat non aliam relationem paternitatis: sed aliam rationem identitatis, in primo genere: sicut Petrus, vt est eiusdem speciei cum Ioanne. Vtramque conclusionem nostram, tenet pater Franciscus Suarius tomo 1. suæ Metaph. disp. 47. sect. 1. num. 5.

Second conclusion: relation considered materially and accidentally, as that which is referred to another, in which manner it is compared not to the relation opposed to it, but to another to which it is similar, or with which it is of the same species, is the foundation of another relation, through which it is referred to the same relation. As the relation of paternity, compared not to filiation but to another paternity, as that which is referred to it, inasmuch as it is of the same species with it, founds not another relation of paternity, but another relation of identity, in the first genus: just as Peter, inasmuch as he is of the same species with John. Father Francisco Suárez holds both our conclusions, vol. 1 of his Metaphysics, disp. 47, sect. 1, no. 5.

> 106 Probatur quoque hæc primò: Vna relatio, solùm ordinatur per se ad oppositam, & ad quamcunque aliam accidentaliter, vt probatum est: ergo licèt non ordinetur ad oppositam per aliam relationem, sed per seipsam, ad aliam tamen non potest ordinari, nisi per relationem superadditam accidentaliter. Probatur consequentia: quia ordinatur accidentaliter ad aliam, sequitur talem ordinationem esse ei accidentalem: sed ordinatio est relatio: ergo per relationem sibi accidentalem ordinatur, quæ non potest fundari in alio, præter eandem relationem.

106 This one too is proved, first: one relation is ordered per se only to the opposite one, and to any other accidentally, as has been proved; therefore, although it is not ordered to the opposite one through another relation, but through itself, yet to another it cannot be ordered except through a relation superadded accidentally. The consequence is proved: because if it is ordered accidentally to another, it follows that such an ordering is accidental to it; but an ordering is a relation; therefore it is ordered through a relation accidental to it, which cannot be founded in anything other than the same relation.

> Secundò: Duæ paternitates, sunt eiusdem speciei, & vtraque est id, quod refertur ad alteram, in ratione identitatis specificæ, sicut Petrus refertur ad Ioannem: ergo sic sumptæ, pertinent ad primum genus relationis: & non vt paternitates, quia vt sic, pertinent ad secundum, ergo sub ratione eiusdem, hoc est, vt extrema sunt identitatis specificæ, sed identitas specifica, per se fundat relationem primi generis: ergo duæ paternitates sub tali ratione, erunt fundamentum relationis identitatis: & ideo necessariò erit concedendum, quòd vna relatio, sit fundamentum alterius, non eiusdem generis, sed diuersi.

Second: two paternities are of the same species, and each is that which is referred to the other under the ratio of specific identity, just as Peter is referred to John; therefore, taken thus, they pertain to the first genus of relation, and not as paternities, because as such they pertain to the second; therefore under the ratio of the same, that is, as they are extremes of specific identity; but specific identity per se founds a relation of the first genus; therefore two paternities under such a ratio will be the foundation of a relation of identity; and therefore it will necessarily have to be granted that one relation is the foundation of another, not of the same genus, but of a different one.

> 107 Quod hoc modo potest confirmari: Hæc prædicatio est [p. 419] vera de vtraque paternitate, hæc paternitas est eadem in specie cum illa: & identitas, est relatio primi generis: ergo est eadem, per relationem primi generis: sed ipsa secundùm se aut essentialiter, non pertinet ad primum genus, sed ad secundum: ergo pertinet ad primum accidentaliter: & ideo accidentaliter de ea prædicabitur relatio primi generis: sed impossibile est, relationem prædicari accidentaliter, nisi de eo, quod est fundamentum eius: vt patet in qualibet relatione: ergo prædicabitur relatio identitatis, de duabus paternitatibus, tanquam de his, à quibus fundatur. Probatur tandem in relationibus rationis, in quibus euidens est, quòd vna relatio materialiter sumpta, sit fundamentum alterius. Nam relatio generis constituens primum prædicabile, per se, & essentialiter est ratio prædicandi, de speciebus, sed materialiter sumpta, vt est, quod prædicatur de hac & illa secunda intentione generis, tanquam de indiuiduis, pertinet ad prædicabile speciei, & fundat relationem eius, à qua denominatur accidentaliter: ergo etiam in relationibus realibus, vna fundabit aliam sumpta materialiter.

107 Which can be confirmed in this way: this predication is [p. 419] true of each paternity: this paternity is the same in species as that one; and identity is a relation of the first genus; therefore it is the same through a relation of the first genus; but the paternity itself, according to itself or essentially, does not pertain to the first genus, but to the second; therefore it pertains to the first accidentally; and therefore a relation of the first genus will be predicated of it accidentally. But it is impossible for a relation to be predicated accidentally except of that which is its foundation, as is plain in any relation; therefore the relation of identity will be predicated of the two paternities as of the things by which it is founded. It is proved, finally, in relations of reason, in which it is evident that one relation taken materially is the foundation of another. For the relation of genus constituting the first predicable is per se and essentially the ratio of predicating of the species; but taken materially, as it is that which is predicated of this and that second intention of genus, as of individuals, it pertains to the predicable of species, and founds its relation, by which it is denominated accidentally; therefore in real relations also one will found another when taken materially.

> Ad testimonium Aristotelis: Respondeo, ex hoc non multiplicari fundamenta, cùm relatio vna fundet aliam in primo genere. Testimonium D. Thom. iam est expositum, per nostram primam conclusionem, cuius sensum continet: loquitur enim de relatione sumpta formaliter, & essentialiter: & hoc modo verum est, non posse fundare aliam relationem, sed materialiter tantùm, & accidentaliter consideratam.

To the testimony of Aristotle, I reply that the foundations are not multiplied by this, since the one relation founds the other in the first genus. The testimony of St. Thomas has already been expounded through our first conclusion, whose sense it contains: for he speaks of relation taken formally and essentially; and in this way it is true that it cannot found another relation, but only when considered materially and accidentally.

> Ad primum argumentum: Distinguendum est consequens primi enthymematis. Nam duobus modis potest ordinari vna relatio, ad aliam. Primò *formaliter*, & vt ratio referendi relatiuum ad terminum sibi oppositum: & hoc modo seipsa: & non alia relatione ordinatur, & hoc solum probat similitudo albedinis. Secundò, *per accidens, & materialiter*, hoc est tanquam id quod accidentaliter refertur, non ad relationem sibi oppositam, sed aliam, cum qua est idem in specie: ad quam non refertur vt paternitas, vel filiatio, sed vt eadem: imò nec per modum relationis, sed absoluti, quod est idem in specie cum alio: quare non potest seipsa referri sed per aliam sibi superadditam, cuius fundamentum esse necessarium est.

To the first argument: the consequence of the first enthymeme must be distinguished. For one relation can be ordered to another in two ways. First, formally, and as the ratio of referring the relative to the term opposed to it; and in this way it is ordered by itself, and not by another relation; and the example of whiteness proves only this. Second, per accidens and materially, that is, as that which is accidentally referred, not to the relation opposed to it, but to another, with which it is the same in species; to which it is not referred as paternity or filiation, but as the same; indeed, not even by way of a relation, but of an absolute thing which is the same in species as another. Wherefore it cannot be referred by itself, but through another superadded to it, of which it must necessarily be the foundation.

> 108 Ad secundũ, respondent quidã, concedendo processum infinitum in relationibus, & nullum esse inconueniens asserunt: quia tenent relationem sola ratione distingui, à fundamento: quo supposito, solùm sequitur, quòd dentur relationes per intellectum distinctæ, actu infinitæ, non verò à parte rei: sicut concedendæ sunt in partibus continui, relationes [p. 420] actu infinitæ. Hæc tamen solutio non placet: quia probabilius est, relationes distingui ex natura rei à fundamentis, vt inferiùs probabitur: & ideo concedenda erunt infinita entia distincta à parte rei. Et completa quidem, hoc est, prædicamentalia & composita, ex genere, & differentia: quod est inconueniens. Relationes verò partium continui, incompletæ sunt & partiales, ex quibus quasi vna totalis efficitur: & ideo non est inconueniens admittere, quòd sint actu infinitæ.

108 To the second, some reply by granting a process to infinity in relations, and they assert that there is nothing unfitting in it, because they hold that relation is distinguished from its foundation by reason alone; on which supposition it follows only that relations distinguished by the intellect are given infinite in act, but not on the part of the thing, just as in the parts of the continuum there are to be granted relations D d ij [p. 420] infinite in act. This solution, however, does not please me, because it is more probable that relations are distinguished from their foundations from the nature of the thing, as will be proved below; and therefore infinite beings distinct on the part of the thing will have to be granted, and complete ones at that, that is, categorial and composed of genus and difference, which is unfitting. But the relations of the parts of the continuum are incomplete and partial, from which as it were one total relation is made; and therefore it is not unfitting to admit that they are infinite in act.

> Respondeo igitur: Negando, quòd detur processus in infinitum in relationibus: nam aliud est dari processum in infinitũ in aliquibus, aliud verò quòd in infinitum multiplicari possint: nam illud est dari actu infinitum, hoc verò solùm in potentia: dari autem infinitum in potentia, nullum est inconueniens, sed necessarium est in diuisionibus continui, & in indiuiduis cuiuslibet speciei: & hoc tantùm datur in relationibus, ex eo, quòd vna fundet alteram, non actu infinitæ relationes. Quod sic ostendo: nam etiam si duæ paternitates, fundent alias relationes identitatis, non sequitur, quòd tales relationes identitatis fundatę, fundẽt alias, sed per illas referuntur inter se, & ad quascunque alias eiusdem speciei: sicut per easdem paternitates referuntur patres, in quibus sunt, ad hos filios, & ad omnes alios, quos habebunt. Quòd verò possint multiplicari per alias relationes diuersitatis, ad quas istæ referantur per alias rationes etiam diuersitatis, nihil refert: quia eodem modo, per singulas relationes diuersitatis, ordinabuntur ad omnes alias diuersas specieis & non erit vltrà procedendum in relationibus actualibus, nec multiplicantur plures, ex eo, quòd vna relatio sit fundamentum alterius Quòd verò semper possint multiplicari aliæ, si de nouo fiant relationes in aliis rebus solùm est, posse multiplicari in infinitum, & dari infinitum in potentia: vt in diuisionibus continui, & quibuscunque indiuiduis aliarum specierum: & ideo nullum est inconueniens.

I reply, therefore, by denying that there is a process to infinity in relations: for it is one thing for there to be a process to infinity in some things, and another for them to be able to be multiplied to infinity: for the former is for there to be an infinite in act, the latter only in potency. But for there to be an infinite in potency is nothing unfitting, but is necessary in the divisions of the continuum and in the individuals of any species whatever; and only this is given in relations from the fact that one founds another, not relations infinite in act. Which I show thus: for even if two paternities found other relations of identity, it does not follow that such founded relations of identity found others; but through them they are referred to each other and to any others of the same species, just as through the same paternities the fathers in whom they are are referred to these sons and to all the others whom they will have. That they can be multiplied through other relations of diversity, to which these are referred through other relations, also of diversity, makes no difference; because in the same way, through single relations of diversity, they will be ordered to all the others of diverse species, and there will be no proceeding further in actual relations, nor are more multiplied from the fact that one relation is the foundation of another. That others can always be multiplied, if relations come to be anew in other things, is only for them to be able to be multiplied to infinity, and for there to be an infinite in potency, as in the divisions of the continuum and in any individuals of other species; and therefore there is nothing unfitting.

## CHAPTER XII

> CAPVT XII.

[…]

> *Vtrùm relationes secundi generis, fundentur in potentia, vel in actione.*

Whether relations of the second genus are founded in potency or in action.

> 109 TRes modos relationum diuersos enumerauit Aristo. in hoc secundo genere, 5. lib. Metaph. cap. 15 & Primum dixit fundari *in actione præsenti*, vt calefacientis ad calefactum, & vniuersaliter agentis in actu, ad passum in actu. Secundum, *in actione futura*, vt calefactiui ad calefactibile. Tertium [p. 421] *in actione præterita*, vt pater, & filius: ille enim fundat relationem paternitatis, quia genuit: iste verò relationem filiationis, quia genitus est. Ex his autem, quædam sunt relationes secundùm dici tantùm: aut etiam relationes rationis: sed omnes quasi permixtas enumerat Aristoteles, quia ex omnibus simul cognitis, meliùs cognoscitur natura relationum prædicamentalium. Ex his autem omnibus relationibus illius saltem recipiunt omnes, pro prædicamentalibus, quæ fundantur in actione præterita: & de his, atque etiam de cæteris prædicamentalibus huius secundi generis inquirimus: *An fundentur in actione præterita, præsenti, aut futura, vel in potentia, à qua procedit actio*: vt an paternitas, & filiatio fundentur in actione, & passione præterita, quas significare solent his nominibus, genuisse, & genitum esse, vel solùm in potentia generandi actiua patris, & in potentia passiua filij, per quam dicitur genitus?

109 Three different modes of relations Aristotle enumerated in this second genus, Metaph. 5, ch. 15. And the first he said is founded in present action, as of the calefacient to the heated thing, and universally of the agent in act to the patient in act. The second, in future action, as of the calefactive to the calefactible. The third [p. 421] in past action, as father and son: for the former founds the relation of paternity because he begot, the latter the relation of filiation because he was begotten.
