This is proved evidently: because he says it is a quality; but quality is a positive entity, while negation and privation are not positive entities, as is self-evident: therefore they are not qualities, nor are they understood by Aristotle by natural impotency; but by impotency he understands a positive quality, bestowed on substance by nature, for doing something or for resisting contraries, but each with difficulty. And so substance through this natural quality can do something, or can resist contraries, yet hardly and with difficulty: whence it is a principle of some operation or resistance, but a weak and as it were infirm one; and therefore it is called not so much a potency as an impotency, so that its defect and imperfection may be made manifest.

> 24 Secundò: Certum est, *Impotentiam naturalem, non solùm sumi ab Aristot. in ordine ad resistendum cum difficultate: sed etiam ad agendum cum difficultate*: vtrumque enim expressis verbis explicuit in textu. Tertiò, Certum est, *Naturalem potentiam, & impotentiam, dum ordinantur ad operationes specie diuersas, vel vna ad agendum, & alia ad resistendum, specie distingui*. Vt hebetudo ingenij, quæ ordinatur ad intelligendum cum difficultate, specie distinguitur, à potentia visiua, ordinata ad videndum. Probatur efficaciter: quia potentiæ distinguuntur specie per actus, ad quos ordinantur: sed videre, & intelligere sunt actus specie [p. 452] distincti: ergo potentiæ ad eos ordinatæ, distinguuntur specie. Nec minùs euidenter probatur, de potentia ad agendum, & impotentia ad resistendum: quia agere, & resistere contrariis, diuersa sunt: vt potentia nutritiua, distincta est, à mollitudine ceræ, quæ est impotentia, ad ægrè resistendum diuisioni.

24 Second: it is certain that natural impotency is taken by Aristotle not only in relation to resisting with difficulty, but also to acting with difficulty: for he explained both in express words in the text. Third, it is certain that natural potency and impotency, when they are ordered to different operations, or one to acting and the other to resisting, are distinguished in species. As dullness of wit, which is ordered to understanding with difficulty, is distinguished in species from the visual power, ordered to seeing. This is proved efficaciously: because potencies are distinguished in species through the acts to which they are ordered; but seeing and understanding are acts Ff ij [p. 452] distinct in species: therefore the potencies ordered to them are distinguished in species. Nor is it less evidently proved of a potency for acting and an impotency for resisting: because to act and to resist contraries are different things: as the nutritive power is distinct from the softness of wax, which is an impotency for resisting division with difficulty.

> 25 Difficultas igitur quæstionis, in hoc posita est: *An naturalis potentia ad aliquid agendum, & naturalis impotentia, ad illud idem ægre, aut difficulter agendum, distinguentur specie: & eodem modo, naturalis potentia ad resistendum fortiter diuisioni, & naturalis impotentia ad ægre resistendum, an distinguantur specie*: vt durities ferri per quam fortiter resistit diuisioni, distinguatúrne à mollitudine ceræ, per quam modo quodam debili resistit eidem diuisioni hæc enim quasi durities quædam imperfecta videtur, & prima opinio *distingui specie* docet: Nostra verò, talem distinctionem negat.

25 The difficulty of the question, then, lies in this: Whether a natural potency for doing something, and a natural impotency for doing the same thing hardly or with difficulty, are distinguished in species; and in the same way, whether a natural potency for resisting division strongly and a natural impotency for resisting it hardly are distinguished in species: as, whether the hardness of iron, by which it strongly resists division, is distinguished from the softness of wax, by which it resists the same division in a certain weak manner; for this seems to be as it were a certain imperfect hardness. And the first opinion teaches that they are distinguished in species; ours denies such a distinction.

> Probatur autem testimonio Arist. capite præsenti, vbi *potentiam naturalem* vocat qualitatem, per quam substantia simpliciter potest aliquid agere, vel contrario resistere: impotentiam verò, qualitatem quandam debilem, & quasi infirmam, ad eadem præstanda: sed debili quodam modo, & cum difficultate, quod est imperfectè illa præstare: sed perfectè, & imperfectè idem agere, aut eidem contrario resistere, non distinguuntur essentialiter: ergo nec naturalis potentia, & impotentia, ad idem agendum, vel eidem resistendum, distinguuntur essentialiter, ex mente Arist. Probatur consequentia, quia perfectè aut imperfectè efficere eandem operationem, solùm potest esse differentia accidentalis.

And it is proved by the testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he calls natural potency a quality through which substance can simply do something or resist a contrary; and impotency a certain weak and as it were infirm quality for accomplishing the same things, but in a certain weak manner and with difficulty, which is to accomplish them imperfectly. But to do the same thing, or to resist the same contrary, perfectly and imperfectly, are not distinguished essentially: therefore neither are natural potency and impotency, for doing the same thing or resisting the same thing, distinguished essentially, in the mind of Aristotle. The consequence is proved: because to effect the same operation perfectly or imperfectly can be only an accidental difference.

> 26 Probatur deinde ratione: Quia potentiæ distinguuntur specie, per actus, & obiecta: sed potentia, & impotentia, sunt facultates quædam naturales, aut potentiæ: ergo si ordinentur ad eundem actum, erunt eiusdem speciei. Probatur consequentia: quia solùm differunt, tanquam principium eiusdem actus, aut eiusdem resistentiæ, perfectum & imperfectum, quod patet solùm esse differentiam accidentalem.

26 It is proved next by reason: Because potencies are distinguished in species through their acts and objects; but potency and impotency are certain natural faculties or potencies: therefore, if they are ordered to the same act, they will be of the same species. The consequence is proved: because they differ only as perfect and imperfect principle of the same act or of the same resistance, which plainly is only an accidental difference.

> Ad argu. primæ opinionis negandum est antecedens: Quòd naturalis potentia, & impotentia, dicant rationes formales verè oppositas: nam licèt nomina ipsa potentiæ, & impotentiæ, videantur opposita, ratione negationis, quam videtur significare impotentia, tamen verè, nec rationes significatæ opponuntur: nec nomina: quia impotentia non dicit puram negationem, sed qualitatem positiuam, debilem tamen atque imperfectam: & imperfectio hæc, quasi negatio est perfectionis, quam dicit potentia: & propter ea negationem videtur significare nomen [p. 453] impotentia: sed quia perfecta, & imperfecta facultas, aut potentia: respectu eiusdem actus, non possunt distingui Specie, nec esse verè oppositæ: ideo nec rationes formales earum oppositæ sunt, nec nomina significant rationes verè oppositas: sed se habent, sicut hæc duo nomina, perfectum, & imperfectum: quæ etiam videntur significare oppositas rationes, & specie diuersas, cùm tamen semper sint eiusdem speciei, si solùm secundùm rationem perfectæ, & imperfectæ distinguantur. Et eodem modo intelligendum est, de mollitudine, & duritie, vt ordinatis, ad fortiter, & debiliter resistendum: quæ licèt videantur specie differre, non tamen differunt: quia mollitudo hoc modo considerata, quasi durities quædam imperfecta est.

To the argument of the first opinion, the antecedent must be denied, that natural potency and impotency imply truly opposite formal rationes: for although the names themselves, of potency and impotency, seem opposed by reason of the negation which impotency seems to signify, yet in truth neither are the rationes signified opposed, nor the names: because impotency does not imply a pure negation, but a positive quality, yet a weak and imperfect one; and this imperfection is as it were a negation of the perfection which potency implies; and on account of this negation the name seems to signify [p. 453] impotency. But because a perfect and an imperfect faculty or potency, with respect to the same act, cannot be distinguished in species nor be truly opposed, therefore neither are their formal rationes opposed, nor do the names signify truly opposed rationes; but they stand as these two names, perfect and imperfect: which also seem to signify opposed rationes, different in species, although they are always of the same species, if they are distinguished only according to the ratio of perfect and imperfect. And the same is to be understood of softness and hardness, as ordered to resisting strongly and weakly: which, although they seem to differ in species, nevertheless do not differ; because softness, considered in this way, is as it were a certain imperfect hardness.

> QVÆSTIO IV.

Q U E S T I O N I V.

> *De his quæ pertinent ad passionem, & passibilem qualitatem.*

On the things that pertain to passion and passible quality.

> 27 QVatuor sunt disputanda, circa passionem, & passibilem qualitatem. Primum, *An sint veræ species qualitatis*. Secundum, *An sint species distinctæ*: vel vna tantùm, & ita solùm distinguantur accidentaliter. Tertium, *An passiones animæ*, vt ira, gaudium, & similes, pertineant ad hanc speciem. Quartum, *An etiam in eadem ponantur obiecta omnium sensuum externorum*. Ideo, quatuor dubiis propositis, & solutis, maioris distinctionis, & claritatis gratia, soluta erit quæstio.

our things are to be disputed concerning passion and passible 27 F quality. First, whether they are true species of quality. Second, whether they are distinct species, or only one, and so are distinguished only accidentally. Third, whether the passions of the soul, such as anger, joy, and the like, pertain to this species. Fourth, whether the objects of all the external senses are also placed in it. Therefore, four doubts having been proposed and solved, for the sake of greater distinction and clarity, the question will be solved.

> Primum dubium.

F I R S T D O U B T.

> *An passio, & passibilis qualitas, sint veræ species qualitatis.*

Whether passion and passible quality are true species of quality.

> PAssio, vt à significatione nominis incipiamus: *quatuor modis accipitur*. Primò, pro *quacunque, siue sit rei disconuenientis, aut nociuæ affectio, siue conuenientis, ac perficientis*: in qua acceptione, non minùs vocatur passio, receptio speciei visibilis, aut visionis in oculo, quàm receptio caloris in aqua: vnde hæc acceptio passionis communissima est, & impropria.

Passion, to begin from the signification of the name, is taken in four ways. First, for any affection whatever, whether of a thing disagreeing or harmful, or of one agreeing and perfecting: in which acceptation the reception of a visible species, or of vision, in the eye is no less called passion than the reception of heat in water; whence this acceptation of passion is the most common and improper.

> Ideo accipitur secundò modo, pro *sola receptione contrariæ qualitatis, aut disconuenientis*, per quam subiectum recipiens, disponitur ad corruptionem: & hæc receptio propriè vocatur passio.

It is taken, therefore, in a second way, for the sole reception of a contrary or disagreeing quality, through which the receiving subject is disposed toward corruption; and this reception is properly called passion.

> Sed accipitur tertiò, pro *operatione animæ sensitiuæ, facta cum [p. 454] aliqua passione corporali secundæ acceptionis*. in qua acceptione, ira, gaudium, dolor, & tristitia dicuntur passiones: quia ex propria natura, fiunt cum aliqua alteratione corporali: hoc est, cum calefactione, aut frigefactione, aut alia simili: vnde passiones istæ, duo includunt, nempe operationem sensibilem appetitus sensitiui: & alterationem naturalem corporis: nempe calefactionem, aut infrigidationem: illam formaliter, hanc verò quasi materialiter, & antecedenter, vel concomitanter. Ex quo factum est, vt duobus modis definiantur, definitione *materiali*, & *formali*, seu finali. *Materialiter* definiuntur pro alteratione reali. *Formaliter* verò, pro operatione sensitiua.

But it is taken, third, for an operation of the sensitive soul, accompanied Ff iij [p. 454] by some bodily passion in the second acceptation: in which acceptation anger, joy, pain, and sadness are called passions, because by their own nature they come about with some bodily alteration, that is, with heating or cooling or something similar. Whence these passions include two things, namely the sensible operation of the sensitive appetite, and the natural alteration of the body, namely heating or chilling: the former formally, the latter as it were materially, and antecedently or concomitantly. From which it has come about that they are defined in two ways, by a material definition and by a formal or final one. Materially they are defined by the real alteration; formally, by the sensitive operation.

> 28 Vt ira definitur, materialiter, quòd sit accensio sanguinis circa cor: formaliter verò, quòd sit appetitus vindictæ. Et hæc acceptio tertia, includit primam, & secũdam. Nam actus appetitus sensitiui, non est disconueniens, nec disponit appetitum sensitiuum, in quo recipitur ad corruptionem, sed potiùs eum perficit: & ideo receptio eius propriè dicitur passio, secundùm primam acceptionem: sicut receptio speciei visibilis, aut visionis in oculo: sed ex parte alterationis realis, cum qua fit, propriè dicitur passio, iuxta secundam acceptionem: & ideo acceptio tertia: quasi mixta ex prima, & secunda vocari potest.

28 As anger is defined materially as the kindling of the blood around the heart; formally, as the appetite for revenge. And this third acceptation includes the first and the second. For the act of the sensitive appetite is not disagreeing, nor does it dispose the sensitive appetite in which it is received toward corruption, but rather perfects it; and therefore its reception is properly called passion according to the first acceptation, as the reception of a visible species, or of vision, in the eye; but on the side of the real alteration with which it comes about, it is properly called passion according to the second acceptation; and therefore the third acceptation can be called as it were mixed of the first and the second.

> Quarto modo, accipitur passio, pro *qualitate*, quæ est effectus passionis tertio modo sumptæ: vt rubor, qui apparet in facie ex verecundia, & pallor ex timore, dicuntur passiones: & passio in hac acceptione, est tertia species qualitatis.

In the fourth way passion is taken for a quality which is the effect of passion taken in the third way: as the redness which appears in the face from shame, and the pallor from fear, are called passions; and passion in this acceptation is the third species of quality.

> Distinguitur autem à passibili qualitate: quia non solùm est effectus passionis, sed etiam modum illius habet *citò transiens*: passibilis autem qualitas, licèt sit effectus passionis, *permanet tamen in subiecto*, vt color rubeus ostendit, quem permanenter habent quidam homines. Ex hac autem differentia, *citò transeuntis, & permanentis*: prouenit alia, quam Aristot. assignauit in litera, inter passionem, & passibilem qualitatem: quòd *passio non denominat subiectum simpliciter quale, sed bene passibilis qualitas id denominat*. Non enim dicitur homo rubeus, vel pallidus, ab illo colore rubeo apparente in facie, ex verecundia, aut ex timore, sed ruborem vel pallorem passus: sed ab eodem colore à natiuitate habito, rubeus vocatur, aut pallidus simpliciter.

And it is distinguished from passible quality: because it not only is an effect of passion, but also has its mode, passing quickly; whereas passible quality, although it is an effect of passion, nevertheless remains in the subject, as the red color shows which certain men have permanently. And from this difference, of passing quickly and of remaining, there arises another, which Aristotle assigned in the text, between passion and passible quality: that passion does not denominate the subject simply qualified, but passible quality does denominate it. For a man is not called red or pale from that red color appearing in the face from shame or from fear, but is said to have suffered redness or pallor; but from the same color possessed from birth he is called red, or pale, simply.

> 29 Ex hac doctrina, sumitur hoc arg. pro ratione dubitandi, ad probandum passionem, & passibile qualitatem, non esse veras species qualitatis, sed quædam analogata eius: quia passio non est qualitas simpliciter, sed secundùm quid: at verò [p. 455] passibilis qualitas, simpliciter est qualitas: ergo qualitas in cõmuni, quæ est supremum genus huius prædicamenti, non vniuocè, sed analogicè de vtraque prædicatur: & ideo non tanquam genus de speciebus, sed tanquam analogum de analogatis. Probatur antecedens: quia *Qualitas*, vt definit Arist. *est à qua denominamur quales*: sed à passione nõ denominamur quales simpliciter: bene tamen à passibili qualitate, vt ex eodem Aristot. & communi modo loquendi probatum est: ergo sola passibilis qualitas, erit simpliciter qualitas, passio verò non nisi secundùm quid.

29 From this doctrine this argument is taken, as a reason for doubting, to prove that passion and passible quality are not true species of quality, but certain analogates of it: because passion is not quality simply, but in a certain respect; but [p. 455] passible quality is quality simply: therefore quality in common, which is the supreme genus of this category, is predicated of both not univocally but analogically; and therefore not as a genus of its species, but as an analogous term of its analogates. The antecedent is proved: because quality, as Aristotle defines it, is that by which we are denominated qualified; but from passion we are not denominated qualified simply, though we are from passible quality, as was proved from the same Aristotle and from the common manner of speaking: therefore passible quality alone will be quality simply, but passion only in a certain respect.

> Respondetur nihilominus ad dubium propositum: quòd passio, & passibilis qualitas, vniuocè conueniunt, in ratione qualitatis in communi: & hæc prædicatur de illis, tanquam genus de sua specie, vel de suis speciebus.

It is replied nonetheless to the proposed doubt that passion and passible quality agree univocally in the ratio of quality in common; and this is predicated of them as a genus of its species, or of its species.

> 30 Vt autem hoc explicetur, & simul probetur, notandum est, duobus modis, posse considerari passionem: nempe, *secundùm entitatem*, vel *essentiam*, aut *secundùm modum inhærendi in subiecto*. Entitas, aut essentia eius est, esse qualitatem productam per passionem: quod est esse effectum passionis (vt vidimus) Modus verò inhærendi, est per modum citò transeuntis: quem habet ex eadem passione: à qua causatur citò etiam transeunte: sed modus iste accidentalis est: quia accidit rubori, quod per causam permanentem, vel citò transeuntem producatur. Vnde sequitur, passionem secundùm essentiam consideratam esse qualitatem simpliciter: sed secundùm modum inhærendi accidentalem, esse qualitatem secundùm quid. Et quia ex modo inhærendi sumitur denominatio, non dicitur denominare subiectum simpliciter, passibilis verò qualitas, simpliciter denominat subiectum tale: quia modum permanentis habet: si verò sumeretur ex sola essentia: simpliciter denominaret: sicut qualitas passibilis.

30 But that this may be explained and at the same time proved, it is to be noted that passion can be considered in two ways: namely, according to its entity or essence, or according to its mode of inhering in the subject. Its entity or essence is to be a quality produced through passion: which is to be an effect of passion (as we have seen). But its mode of inhering is by way of something passing quickly, which it has from the same passion, by which it is caused, itself also passing quickly; but this mode is accidental, because it is accidental to redness that it be produced by a permanent or by a quickly passing cause. Whence it follows that passion considered according to its essence is quality simply, but according to its accidental mode of inhering is quality in a certain respect. And since denomination is taken from the mode of inhering, it is not said to denominate the subject simply; whereas passible quality denominates the subject simply such, because it has the mode of something permanent; but if denomination were taken from the essence alone, it would denominate simply, just as passible quality does.

> Ex hac igitur doctrina colligitur arg. ad probandum, quòd vniuocè dicatur qualitas de passione, & passibili qualitate: & ideo tanquam genus: quia illud est vniuocum, cuius essentia simpliciter, & æqualiter participatur ab inferioribus: sed essentia qualitatis, participatur æqualiter, & simpliciter à passione, & passibili qualitate: ergo vniuocè, & tanquam genus prædicatur de illis. Probatur minor: quia ad essentiam qualitatis pertinet determinare, & qualificare subiectum: quòd verò sit per modũ impermanentis, vel citò transeuntis, accidentale est, ex breui, aut longo tempore desumptum: sed passio determinat, & qualificat subiectum simpliciter, quamuis parũ in eo duret: ergo est qualitas simpliciter: & ideo vniuocè, & tanquã genus, [p. 456] de ea, & passibili qualitate prædicatur, qualitas in communi.

From this doctrine, then, an argument is gathered to prove that quality is said univocally of passion and of passible quality, and therefore as a genus: because that is univocal whose essence is participated simply and equally by its inferiors; but the essence of quality is participated equally and simply by passion and by passible quality: therefore it is predicated of them univocally and as a genus. The minor is proved: because to determine and qualify the subject pertains to the essence of quality; but that it be by way of something permanent, or of something passing quickly, is accidental, taken from a short or a long time; but passion determines and qualifies the subject simply, although it lasts little in it: therefore it is quality simply, and therefore univocally and as a genus Ff iiij [p. 456] quality in common is predicated of it and of passible quality.

> 31 Ad arg. verò allatum in contrarium: Negandum est antecedens, & dum dicitur, qualitatem esse, à qua denominamur quales: Respondetur per denominationem, non tam impositionem nominis significare Aristotelem, quàm effectum formalem qualitatis. Vnde sensus definitionis est, Qualitas est, à qua sumus formaliter quales: denominatio verò aliquando sumitur, ab essentia, aliquando ex modo inhærendi accidentali. vnde quòd à passione non denominemur quales simpliciter, non tollit, quin sit simpliciter qualitas: quia formaliter efficit nos quales, vt probatum est. Exemplum adducere possumus in albedine, de qua constat esse qualitatem simpliciter, & eiusdem speciei cum albedine parietis: quia habet essentiam albedinis, & effectum formalem in subiecto, sicut illa: sed non denominat Æthiopem album simpliciter: quia modus inhærendi in toto corpore, aut solùm in vna parte, à quo sumitur denominatio, & de quo constat esse accidentalem, propter maiorem, aut minorem extensionem, diuersus est: nemo tamen dixit albedinem non prædicari vniuocè, tanquam speciem de suis indiuiduis de albedine Æthiopis, & parietis: ita ergo iudicandum est de passione, & passibili qualitate.

31 But to the argument brought to the contrary: the antecedent must be denied. And when it is said that quality is that by which we are denominated qualified, it is replied that by denomination Aristotle signifies not so much the imposition of the name as the formal effect of quality. Whence the sense of the definition is: Quality is that by which we are formally qualified; but denomination is sometimes taken from the essence, sometimes from the accidental mode of inhering. Whence the fact that we are not denominated qualified simply from passion does not prevent it from being quality simply, because it formally makes us qualified, as has been proved. We can adduce an example in whiteness, of which it is plain that it is quality simply, and of the same species as the whiteness of a wall, because it has the essence of whiteness and the formal effect in the subject, just as that one does; but it does not denominate an Ethiopian white simply, because the mode of inhering in the whole body or only in one part, from which the denomination is taken, and which it is plain is accidental, is different on account of the greater or lesser extension; yet no one has said that whiteness is not predicated univocally, as a species of its individuals, of the whiteness of the Ethiopian and of the wall: so, then, must one judge of passion and passible quality.

> Dubium Secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

> *An passio, & passibilis qualitas sint diuersæ species, vel vna tantùm.*

Whether passion and passible quality are different species, or only one. 32

> 32 PRima opinio tenet, *Passionem, & passibilem qualitatem, esse distinctas species, non minùs, quàm habitum, & dispositionem*: quam probabilem iudicat Sotus, quæstione vnica huius prædicamenti, in solutione ad confirmationem quarti argumenti: & sequuntur nonnulli ex modernis.

The first opinion holds that passion and passible quality are distinct species, no less than habit and disposition: which Soto judges probable, in the single question on this category, in the solution to the confirmation of the fourth argument; and some of the moderns follow it.

> Probaturque hoc arg. Habitus, & dispositio distinguuntur specie: quia ille est difficilè mobilis à subiecto, ex natura suæ causæ, dispositio verò facilè remouetur: sed ita se habent passio, & passibilis qualitas: ergo distinguentur etiam in specie. Probatur minor: quia *passio* ex sententia Arist. *citò transit, passibilis qualitas permanet in subiecto*: & id habet vtraque ex natura suæ causæ: nam qualitas quæ est passio, ideo citò transit, quia est effectus passionis citò transeuntis: vt rubor causatus ex verecundia, sed rubor, qui habetur à natiuitate, habet causas permanentes & ideo permanens est ex propria natura, & vocatur passibilis qualitas: & hanc differentiam manifestat denominatio [p. 457]. Nam passio, quia ex sua natura non permanet, nec subiectum denominat simpliciter: quod tamen præstat passibilis qualitas, propter permanentiam: ergo non minùs distinguuntur specie, quàm habitus & dispositio.

And it is proved by this argument: Habit and disposition are distinguished in species because the former is not easily removable from the subject, from the nature of its cause, while disposition is easily removed; but passion and passible quality are so related: therefore they too will be distinguished in species. The minor is proved: because passion, in the opinion of Aristotle, passes quickly; passible quality remains in the subject; and each has this from the nature of its cause: for the quality which is passion passes quickly for this reason, that it is the effect of a quickly passing passion, as redness caused by shame; but redness which is had from birth has permanent causes, and therefore is permanent by its own nature, and is called passible quality. And this difference is made manifest by the denomination, [p. 457] for passion, because by its nature it does not remain, does not denominate the subject simply; which passible quality nevertheless does, on account of its permanence: therefore they are distinguished in species no less than habit and disposition.

> 33 Secunda opinio, opposita est, quòd *passio, & passibilis qualitas, non sint species distinctæ, sed vna, & eadem & solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter*. Hanc sequuntur Sotus vbi supra, Fonseca 5. Meta. c. 14. qu. 2. sect. 3. & plures moderni. Et nobis videtur probabilior.

33 The second opinion, the opposite one, is that passion and passible quality are not distinct species, but one and the same, and are distinguished only accidentally. It is followed by Soto in the place cited above, by Fonseca, Metaph. 5, ch. 14, q. 2, sect. 3, and by many moderns. And it seems to us more probable.

> Et probatur ratione: Quia intrinseca conditio vtriusque qualitatis est, quòd sit causa, vel effectus passionis: quòd verò citò transeuntis, aut diu permanentis accidentalis est ratio: tamen in prima illa ratione essentiali conueniunt: ergo solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter. Probatur minor: quia rubor causatus ex verecundia, est passio: si verò habeatur à natiuitate, est passibilis qualitas, sed rubores isti, sunt eiusdem speciei: & solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter ergo passio, & passibilis qualitas, sic se habebunt. Minorem probo. Quia essentia qualitatis, euidenter colligitur ex effectu formali, quem habet in subiecto: sed rubores isti, habet eundem effectum formalem, qui est constituere hominem rubeum: & solùm diuersum ex eo, quod parum, vel multum duret, ratione causæ permanentis, aut transeuntis: quod patet esse accidentalem differentiam, respectu rubei formaliter: cùm non sit minùs rubeus formaliter homo, pro illo breui tempore, quàm alter, qui habet eandem qualitatem à natiuitate: ergo non possunt distingui essentialiter, nec esse diuersæ species. Et confirmari potest, ac declarari simul: quia ad rationem ruboris essentialem, per accidens se habet, quod ab hac vel illa causa efficiente producatur: hoc est, permanente, vel transeunte, sicut ad rationem caloris: ergo ex hac parte, non distinguuntur specie rubores diuersi: sed non habent aliam differentiam essentialem, sed genere qualitatis: ergo non distinguuntur essentialiter.

And it is proved by reason: Because the intrinsic condition of each quality is that it be a cause or an effect of passion; but the ratio of passing quickly or of remaining long is accidental; yet they agree in that first essential ratio: therefore they are distinguished only accidentally. The minor is proved: because redness caused by shame is a passion; but if it is had from birth, it is a passible quality; but these rednesses are of the same species and are distinguished only accidentally: therefore passion and passible quality will be so related. I prove the minor: Because the essence of a quality is evidently gathered from the formal effect which it has in the subject; but these rednesses have the same formal effect, which is to constitute a man red, and differ only in that one lasts a short time and the other a long time, by reason of a permanent or a passing cause; which is plainly an accidental difference with respect to being formally red, since a man is no less formally red for that brief time than another who has the same quality from birth: therefore they cannot be distinguished essentially, nor be different species. And this can be confirmed and at the same time declared: because it is per accidens to the essential ratio of redness that it be produced by this or that efficient cause, that is, a permanent or a passing one, just as to the ratio of heat: therefore on this side different rednesses are not distinguished in species; but they have no other essential difference, but agree in the genus of quality: therefore they are not distinguished essentially.

> 34 Ad arg. verò contrariæ opinionis, neganda est minor, quòd sic se habeat passio, & passibilis qualitas, sicut habitus, & dispositio. Et ratio differentiæ colligitur ex eodem Aristot. 5. Met. c. 20. tex. 25. vbi docet, *Ad rationem habitus pertinere permanentiam*: quia habitus ex se dicit habere, aut possidere, quasi ex cõsuetudine, & cum diuturnitate: ergo vt qualitas sit habitus, diuturna esse debet: & si hoc habeat ex propria natura, habebit essentialiter: si verò ex aliqua causa extrinseca, vel accidentali, solùm habebit accidẽtaliter: & si ab intrinseco habeat oppositam conditionem, vt si facilè mobilis à subiecto, necesse [p. 458] erit distingui essentialiter ab habitu. Et ita se habent dispositio, & habitus: vt in scientia, & opinione ostendimus superiùs. Itaque duæ istæ qualitates, non propter solam denominationem, aut significationem nominis distinguuntur, sed quia dicunt ex propria natura, rationes diuersas, facilè ac difficilè mobilem esse à subiecto. Passio verò, & passibilis qualitas: solùm ex parte denominationis differunt quæ tamen non desumitur ex ratione essentiali earum, sed ex modo inhærendi in subiecto, quem constat esse accidentalem: ex eo enim passio dicitur rubor, & ex eo non denominat subiectum simpliciter rubeum, quia per modum transeuntis inhæret.

34 But to the argument of the contrary opinion, the minor must be denied, that passion and passible quality are so related as habit and disposition. And the reason of the difference is gathered from the same Aristotle, Metaph. 5, ch. 20, text 25, where he teaches that permanence pertains to the ratio of habit: because habit of itself means to have or possess, as it were from custom and with long duration: therefore, for a quality to be a habit, it must be lasting; and if it has this from its own nature, it will have it essentially; but if from some extrinsic or accidental cause, it will have it only accidentally; and if from within it has the opposite condition, so that it is easily removable from the subject, necessarily [p. 458] it will be distinguished essentially from habit. And so disposition and habit are related, as we showed above in science and opinion. And so these two qualities are distinguished not on account of the denomination alone, or the signification of the name, but because by their own nature they imply different rationes, of being easily and not easily removable from the subject. But passion and passible quality differ only on the side of denomination, which, however, is not taken from their essential ratio but from the mode of inhering in the subject, which it is plain is accidental: for from it redness is called passion, and from it it does not denominate the subject simply red, because it inheres by way of something passing.

> 35 Quòd verò hoc sit ei accidentale, probatum est: cùm non variet effectum formalem eius: ergo passio, & passibilis qualitas solùm accidentaliter differunt: quia ad essentiam earum solùm pertinet, esse causam, vel effectum passionis, in quo distinguuntur à cæteris speciebus qualitatis: citò verò transire, vel diu permanere, à quo sumitur denominatio, accidentalis ratio est: cùm tamen ad rationem formalem habitus pertineat, naturalis permanentia in subiecto: Et ex hoc cognoscitur satis probabiliter, differentia vtriusque speciei, & solutio argumenti intelligitur.

35 And that this is accidental to it has been proved, since it does not vary its formal effect: therefore passion and passible quality differ only accidentally: because to their essence there pertains only to be a cause or an effect of passion, in which they are distinguished from the other species of quality; but to pass quickly or to remain long, from which the denomination is taken, is an accidental ratio; whereas natural permanence in the subject pertains to the formal ratio of habit. And from this the difference of the two species is known with sufficient probability, and the solution of the argument is understood.

> Dubium tertium.

T H I R D D O U B T.

> *An passiones animæ pertineant ad hanc speciem qualitatis.*

Whether the passions of the soul pertain to this species of quality.

> PAssiones animæ sunt, ira, gaudium, tristitia, delectatio, & similes: de quibus superiùs diximus, eas duo habere. Vnum pro formali, quod est esse operationes appetitus sensitiui: aliud pro *materiali*, nempe alterationem corpoream, cum qua fiunt: vt calefactionem, aut infrigidationem corporis, aut alicuius partis eius: quærit ergo dubium, *An collocentur in hac specie*.

The passions of the soul are anger, joy, sadness, delight, and the like: of which we said above that they have two things. One as formal, which is to be operations of the sensitive appetite; the other as material, namely the bodily alteration with which they come about, as the heating or chilling of the body or of some part of it. The doubt therefore asks, whether they are placed in this species.

> Et prima opinio asserit, *has passiones non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum*, vt sunt operationes appetitus sensitiui: sed solùm, vt de materiali dicunt qualitates reales receptas in corpore, per veram alterationem: ita plures moderni.

And the first opinion asserts that these passions do not pertain to this category as they are operations of the sensitive appetite, but only as, on the material side, they imply real qualities received in the body through a true alteration: so many moderns.

> 36 Probatur testimonio Arist. qui tristitiam & delectationem collocauit in prædicamẽto actionis, non alia ratione, nisi quia sunt actiones appetitus sensitiui: ergo hoc modo sumptæ, non possunt pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum. Probatur consequentia: quia impossibile est eandem rem, secundùm eandem rationem formalem, pertinere ad duo prædicamenta.

36 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who placed sadness and delight in the category of action, for no other reason than that they are actions of the sensitive appetite: therefore, taken in this way, they cannot pertain to this category. The consequence is proved: because it is impossible for the same thing, according to the same formal ratio, to pertain to two categories.

> Probatur etiam ratione. Quia tristitia, & delectatio, procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo, per quem tristari, aut delectari [p. 459] dicitur homo: sicut per visum videre, & per auditum audire: ergo sunt actiones immanentes: quæ ab eodem: vt agente, procedunt, & in eodem, vt in subiecto, recipiuntur: & vt in eo receptæ, dicuntur passiones: quia actio, vt recepta in passo, dicitur passio: sed actio, & passio, vt tales sunt, nihil de qualitate habent, sed in propriis prædicamentis, actionis, & passionis, collocantur: ergo passiones istæ, vt procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo, & in eo recipiuntur, non pertinent ad hoc prędicamentum: bene tamen ratione qualitatis materialis, nempe caloris, aut frigiditatis, quæ simul dum fiunt imprimitur subiecto, vel alicui parti eius, per alterationem realem, pertinere possunt.

It is proved also by reason: Because sadness and delight proceed from the sensitive appetite, by which to be saddened or delighted [p. 459] is said of man, just as through sight he is said to see and through hearing to hear: therefore they are immanent actions, which proceed from the same power as agent and are received in the same as in a subject; and as received in it they are called passions, because action, as received in the patient, is called passion. But action and passion, as such, have nothing of quality, but are placed in their own categories, of action and of passion: therefore these passions, as they proceed from the sensitive appetite and are received in it, do not pertain to this category; but by reason of the material quality, namely of the heat or cold which, at the same time as they come about, is impressed on the subject or on some part of it through a real alteration, they can pertain to it.

> 37 Secunda opinio est opposita: quòd *passiones istæ, non solùm ratione materialis, sed ratione formalis, pertineant ad hanc speciem*: quam plures moderni tenent: & mihi videtur necessario tenenda in doctrina Arist. Quod sic probo: Aristoteles cap. præsenti asserit, Iram, & amentiam, & alias passiones, si permanentes sint, vt dum habentur à natiuitate, denominare hominem simpliciter amentem, vel iracundum, & esse passibiles qualitates: si verò citò transeant, non denominare hominem iracundum, aut amẽtem, sed solùm dici earum ratione iram, aut amentiam passum, & tunc esse passiones: ergo sentit in hoc prædicamento aliquo modo collocari, vt procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo. Quod enim autores primæ opinionis asserunt, Aristotelem solùm de eis loqui sub ratione materiali alterationis, cum qua fiunt, & non sub ratione formali, qua procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo: friuolum est, & euidẽter falsum: quod sic probo: Passiones istæ non denominant iracundos, vel amentes homines: ratione caloris, vel calefactionis, cum qua fiunt, sed, vt procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo, turbante, aut tollente vsum rationis: sed Arist. docet pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum, vt denominant hominem iracundum, vel amentem, ergo non solùm secundùm materialem calorem, aut frigiditatem, quę imprimitur in corpore, dum fiunt, sed, vt procedunt ab appetitu sensitiuo, intelligit esse qualitates huius speciei.

37 The second opinion is the opposite: that these passions pertain to this species not only by reason of the material, but by reason of the formal: which many moderns hold, and which seems to me necessarily to be held in the doctrine of Aristotle. I prove it thus: Aristotle in the present chapter asserts that anger, madness, and the other passions, if they are permanent, as when they are had from birth, denominate a man simply mad or irascible, and are passible qualities; but if they pass quickly, they do not denominate a man irascible or mad, but he is only said by reason of them to have suffered anger or madness, and then they are passions: therefore he thinks that they are placed in some way in this category as they proceed from the sensitive appetite. For what the authors of the first opinion assert, that Aristotle speaks of them only under the ratio of the material alteration with which they come about, and not under the formal ratio by which they proceed from the sensitive appetite, is frivolous and evidently false. I prove it thus: These passions do not denominate men irascible or mad by reason of the heat or heating with which they come about, but as they proceed from the sensitive appetite, disturbing or taking away the use of reason; but Aristotle teaches that they pertain to this category as they denominate a man irascible or mad: therefore he understands them to be qualities of this species not only according to the material heat or cold which is impressed in the body while they come about, but as they proceed from the sensitive appetite.

> 38 Sed tota difficultas huius rei consistit, in inuenienda ratione qualitatis, quam passiones istæ habeant, vt sunt actiones appetitus sensitiui: atque etiam in distinguenda, in eis eadem ratione qualitatis inuenta à rationibus actionis, & passionis. Vtrumque autem colligi debet ex doctrina D. Tho. 1. 2 quęst. 21. art. 1. & 3. vbi distinguit appetitum sensitiuum à rationali, qui est voluntas: quòd rationalis, non est potentia corporea, nec existens in organo corporeo. sed cùm sit spiritualis, immediatè inhæret animæ, & per animã communicatur corpori: [p. 460] appetitus verò sensitiuus, potentia corporea est, sicut visus, & auditus: & ideo est in organo corporeo, tãquam in proximo, & adęquato subiecto. Vnde sequitur alia differentia, quòd operatio voluntatis, procedit immediatè à voluntate, & non medio organo corporeo, operatio verò appetitus sensitiui, procedit immediatè à composito, hoc est, ab illa parte corporis, in qua est hæc potentia, tanquam in subiecto, sicut visus ab oculo: & ideo fit medio organo corporeo, sicut visus medio oculo.

38 But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in finding the ratio of quality which these passions have as they are actions of the sensitive appetite, and also in distinguishing the same ratio of quality found in them from the rationes of action and passion. And both must be gathered from the doctrine of St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 21, a. 1 and 3, where he distinguishes the sensitive appetite from the rational, which is the will: that the rational is not a corporeal power, nor existing in a corporeal organ, but, since it is spiritual, inheres immediately in the soul, and through the soul is communicated to the body; [p. 460] but the sensitive appetite is a corporeal power, like sight and hearing, and therefore is in a corporeal organ as in its proximate and adequate subject. Whence there follows another difference: that the operation of the will proceeds immediately from the will, and not by means of a corporeal organ; but the operation of the sensitive appetite proceeds immediately from the composite, that is, from that part of the body in which this power is as in a subject, as sight from the eye; and therefore it comes about by means of a corporeal organ, as sight by means of the eye.

> 39 Et hæc est causa, ob quam fit cum alteratione corporali eiusdem organi, aut partis in qua residet: & quo vehementiores sunt actus appetitus, eo maiorem commotionem, & alterationem corporis excitant. Hæc autem alteratio: aut contraria est complexioni corporis, aut non: si cõtraria non sit, excessum tamen habet semper ratione cuius disconueniens est ei, multò magis, si est contraria. Vnde fit, vt semper disponat aliquo modo corpus, in quo recipitur ad corruptionem: & propterea vocatur propriè passio: à qua actus appetitus, qui cum ea fiunt, vocantur passiones animæ: quia semper habent coniunctam hanc passionem.

39 And this is the cause why it comes about with a bodily alteration of the same organ, or of the part in which it resides; and the more vehement the acts of the appetite are, the greater the commotion and alteration of the body they excite. And this alteration either is contrary to the complexion of the body or not: if it is not contrary, it nevertheless always has an excess, by reason of which it is disagreeable to it; much more if it is contrary. Whence it comes about that it always disposes in some way the body in which it is received toward corruption; and on that account it is properly called passion: from which the acts of the appetite that come about with it are called passions of the soul, because they always have this passion conjoined.

> Duæ igitur sunt actiones realiter distinctæ, in quacunque passione animæ, vt in ira, & gaudio: vna appetitus in eodem recepta: alia verò alteratio corporalis, recepta in corpore: & vtraque habet terminum per ipsam productum: & terminus quidem alterationis per sensum cognoscitur, vt rubor in verecundia, cognoscitur per visum. Terminus verò productus per actionem appetitus, non cognoscitur sensu, quia interiùs producitur, & manet: nam iram non cognoscimus, nisi per ruborem, vel alio signo, aut verbo manifestetur. Est autem qualitas quædam corporea, sicut actus ipse appetitus, corporea actio est: verum non habet nomen proprium, quo significetur, sed nomine eiusdem actionis solet significari: quemadmodum actus amoris à voluntate procedens, suum habet terminum productum, cùm sit vera actio: sed non habet proprium nomen: & ideo vocamus eum amorem actualem: & est qualitas quædam producta, per modum actualis impressionis.

There are, then, two really distinct actions in any passion of the soul, as in anger and joy: one of the appetite, received in the same appetite; the other the bodily alteration, received in the body; and each has a term produced by it. And the term of the alteration is known by sense, as redness in shame is known by sight. But the term produced by the action of the appetite is not known by sense, because it is produced and remains within: for we do not know anger except through redness, or unless it is manifested by some other sign or by a word. And it is a certain corporeal quality, just as the act of the appetite itself is a corporeal action; but it has no proper name by which it is signified, but is wont to be signified by the name of the same action: just as the act of love proceeding from the will has its own produced term, since it is a true action, but has no proper name; and therefore we call it actual love; and it is a certain quality produced by way of an actual impression.

> 40 Ita ergo terminum actionis appetitus, vocamus nomine actionis, & dicimus esse iram actualem, vel actualem tristitiam: estque qualitas, quam idemmet appetitus sibi imprimit, per suã actionem: sicut intellectus, imprimit sibi per actionem vitalem propriam, speciem impressam, quæ est qualitas quædam per modum actus, per quam rem ab ea repræsentatam intelligit. Hos igitur terminos actionum appetitus, vocamus etiam passiones, tribuentes eis nomina earundem actionum: & si per [p. 461] actiones citò transeuntes producantur, dicuntur passiones: vt qualitas interior: producta per actionem appetitus, quæ dicitur verecundia: si verò per actionem quasi permanentem producatur, vt est iracundia, aut dementia ab ipsa natiuitate habita, vocatur passibilis qualitas.

40 So, then, we call the term of the action of the appetite by the name of the action, and say that it is actual anger, or actual sadness; and it is a quality which the appetite itself impresses on itself through its action: just as the intellect impresses on itself, through its own proper vital action, an impressed species, which is a certain quality by way of an act, through which it understands the thing represented by it. These terms of the actions of the appetite, then, we also call passions, attributing to them the names of the same actions; and if by [p. 461] are produced by quickly passing actions, are called passions: as the interior quality produced by an action of the appetite which is called shame; but if it is produced by an action that is as it were permanent, as is irascibility, or madness had from birth itself, it is called a passible quality.

> 41 Ex quibus iam patet: Primò veritas Aristotelicę sententię, quam sequimur: nam quatuor sunt in his passionibus. Primum, est materiale, nempe alteratio corporea. Secundum, *Terminus eius*, qui est corporea qualitas, cum qua fiunt, vt color, seu calefactio, aut infrigidatio. Tertium *formale*, & est actio appetitus, habens proprium terminum: qui est qualitas quædam quam sibi imprimit appetitus, per eandem actionem: & hæc qualitas est. Quartum, & vocatur *passio*: sicut actio appetitus, passio vocatur: quia fit cum passione corporali. Ex his autem quatuor, duæ sunt actiones: nempe alteratio corporea, & actus appetitus: & duo sunt termini earum, qui verè sunt qualitates: nempe calor, aut frigiditas producta per alterationem: & ira, aut amẽtia actualis, producta per actionem appetitus, quæ vocatur ira. De actionibus autem certum est, non pertinere ad hoc prædicamentum ratione sui: quia non sunt qualitates, sed ad prædicamentum actionis: & vt recipiuntur in subiecto, ad prædicamentum passionis: termini verò, propriè pertinent ad hoc prædicamentum: & ratione eorum actiones ipsæ: quamuis nomen passionis, & possibilis qualitatis, ab eisdem actionibus sumant termini: nam si per actiones citò transeuntes producantur, passiones dicuntur: si verò per diuturnas passibiles qualitates.

41 From this there is now plain, first, the truth of Aristotle’s opinion, which we follow: for there are four things in these passions. The first is material, namely the bodily alteration. The second, its term, which is the bodily quality with which they come about, as color, or heating, or cooling. The third is formal, and it is the action of the appetite, having its own term, which is a certain quality that the appetite impresses on itself through the same action: and this is a quality. The fourth is also called a passion, just as the action of the appetite is called a passion, because it comes about with a bodily passion. Of these four, two are actions, namely the bodily alteration and the act of the appetite; and two are their terms, which are truly qualities, namely the heat or cold produced by the alteration, and the actual anger or madness produced by the action of the appetite, which is called anger. Now concerning the actions it is certain that they do not belong to this category by reason of themselves, because they are not qualities, but to the category of action; and, as they are received in the subject, to the category of passion. The terms, however, properly belong to this category, and by reason of them the actions themselves: although the terms take the name of passion and of passible quality from the same actions; for if they are produced by quickly passing actions they are called passions, but if by lasting ones, passible qualities.

> 42 Secundò patet falsitas primæ opinionis, asserentis, passiones appetitus, solùm pertinere ad prædicamentum hoc, & ad hanc eius speciem, ratione materialis alterationis, cũ qua fiunt, & non ratione actus ipsius appetitus. Patet autem ex doctrina tradita, etiam actiones appetitus, ratione sui termini, propriè, & formaliter pertinere ad hanc Categoriam. Quod probatur hac ratione: Passio, & passibilis qualitas, dicuntur tales, quia sunt effectus passionis citò trãseuntis, aut diu permanentis: sed qualitates interiores, productæ in appetitu, per actiones eius, quæ dicuntur ira, vel amentia, vel aliis nominibus nominantur, sunt effectus earundem actionum, quæ vocantur passiones: ergo verè, & propriè dicentur etiam passiones huius speciei, si citò transeant, vel passibiles qualitates, si diu permaneant.

42 Second, there is plain the falsity of the first opinion, which asserts that the passions of the appetite belong to this category, and to this species of it, solely by reason of the material alteration with which they come about, and not by reason of the act of the appetite itself. And it is plain from the doctrine given that the actions of the appetite too, by reason of their term, belong properly and formally to this Category. This is proved by the following argument: passion and passible quality are so called because they are effects of a passion that passes quickly or remains for a long time; but the interior qualities produced in the appetite by its actions, which are called anger or madness, or are named by other names, are effects of those same actions which are called passions: therefore they will truly and properly be called passions of this species too, if they pass quickly, or passible qualities, if they remain for a long time.

> 43 Ad testimonium Arist. pro prima opinione, respondetur, Passiones appetitus, collocasse Aristotelem in prædicamento actionis, sumendo eas pro actionibus eiusdem appetitus: in hoc autem prædicamento, & in hac specie, pro terminis earundem [p. 462] actionem: qui verè & propriè sunt qualitates, vt explicatum est. Et hæc eadem distinctio soluit argumentum eiusdem sententiæ.

43 To the testimony of Aristotle for the first opinion, the reply is that Aristotle placed the passions of the appetite in the category of action taking them for the actions of the same appetite; but in this category, and in this species, for their terms [p. 462] of the same action, which are truly and properly qualities, as has been explained. And this same distinction solves the argument of the same opinion.

> Dubium quartum.

F O U R T H D O U B T.

> *An obiecta omnium sensuum externorum, vt obiecta eorum sunt, pertineant ad hanc speciem qualitatis.*

Whether the objects of all the external senses, as they are their objects, belong to this species of quality.

> 43 OBiectum visus est color, atque etiam lux, obiectum auditus, sonus, olfactus, odores, obiectum gustus, sunt sapores, & obiectum tactus, sunt quatuor primæ qualitates: quæ ideo vocantur communiter qualitates tangibiles, vt calor, frigus, humor, & siccitas. Et de his omnibus obiectis sensuum, certum est, primò, esse veras qualitates, & pertinere ad hoc prędicamentum. Certum est secundò: pertinere ad hanc speciem, in quantum sunt effectus passionis: quia vel per aliquam alterationem realem producuntur, & ideo impressio earum, propriè appellatur passio, aut passibilis qualitas huius speciei: vel ex communi permixtione, aut actione primarum qualitatum inter sese generantur: & hoc etiam modo, appellantur qualitates passibiles si sint permanentes, vel passiones, si citò transeant: dubium verò solùm esse potest: *An sub ratione formali obiectiua, per quam causant sensationem, vt visionem, & auditionem in sensibus, sint qualitates passibiles huius speciei*.

43 The object of sight is color, and also light; the object of hearing, sound; of smell, odors; the object of taste is flavors; and the object of touch is the four primary qualities, which are therefore commonly called tangible qualities, such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. And concerning all these objects of the senses it is certain, first, that they are true qualities and belong to this category. It is certain, second, that they belong to this species inasmuch as they are effects of a passion: because either they are produced through some real alteration, and therefore their impression is properly called a passion or a passible quality of this species; or they are generated from the common mixture, or action, of the primary qualities among themselves: and in this way too they are called passible qualities if they are permanent, or passions if they pass quickly. The doubt, then, can only be: Whether under the formal objective ratio through which they cause sensation in the senses, such as vision and hearing, they are passible qualities of this species.

> Et ratio dubitandi, ex vna parte est: quia sensatio, quam causant in sensu, procedit ab eis, simul concurrentibus cum potentia sensitiua, & recipitur in eadem: & quatenus recipitur, appellatur passio: ergo sunt causa passionis in sensu: sed passibilem qualitatem vocat Arist. *Eam quæ causat passionem in sensu*: ergo obiecta omnium sensuum, vt talia sunt, erunt passibiles qualitates huius speciei.

And the reason for doubting, on the one side, is: because the sensation which they cause in the sense proceeds from them, concurring together with the sensitive power, and is received in that same power; and inasmuch as it is received, it is called a passion: therefore they are the cause of a passion in the sense; but Aristotle calls a passible quality that which causes a passion in the sense: therefore the objects of all the senses, as such, will be passible qualities of this species.

> 44 Ex alia verò parte, habemus expressum testimonium Arist. c. præsenti, vbi de solis obiectis gustus, & tactus, concedit esse passibiles qualitates: quia causant passionem in sensu: de coloribus verò, quæ sunt obiecta visus, negat hac ratione esse passibiles qualitates: sed solùm id habere eas concedit, in quantum sunt effectus alicuius passionis, per quam producuntur.

44 On the other side, however, we have an express testimony of Aristotle in the present chapter, where he concedes that the objects of taste and touch alone are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but of colors, which are the objects of sight, he denies that they are passible qualities for this reason, and concedes only that they have this inasmuch as they are effects of some passion through which they are produced.

> Prima opinio est, quorundam modernorum, asserentium, *omnia obiecta sensuum, vt talia esse passibiles qualitates*, quia causant passionem in sensu: sed Aristo. quia manifestum hoc erat, in sensu gustus, & tactus: ideo solùm id concessit expresse obiectis [p. 463] eorum: non tamen negauit obiectis aliorum sensuum: sed quia in eis non erat res ita clara, de illis docuit alia ratione, esse passibiles qualitates, nempe, quia sunt effectus passionis.

The first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that all the objects of the senses, as such, are passible qualities, because they cause a passion in the sense; but that Aristotle, because this was manifest in the senses of taste and touch, therefore conceded it expressly only [p. 463] of their objects; yet he did not deny it of the objects of the other senses, but, because the matter was not so clear in them, he taught of them, by another reason, that they are passible qualities, namely because they are effects of a passion.

> 45 Hæc sententia non potest defendi in doctrina Arist. quia expressis verbis negat obiecta visus esse passibiles qualitates, quia causant passionem in sensu. Sed nec tenenda est, considerata natura huius speciei, quod ita probo: Solùm dicitur qualitas passibilis huius speciei, in quantum effectus est passionis: vt illa, quæ est effectus veræ passionis, aut eius actionis, quæ cum vera passione fit: vnde species expressa, quæ producitur per intellectionem, vel quæ producitur in sensibus internis, ex sensationibus sensuum externorum, non dicuntur passibiles qualitates: quia operatio intellectus, nec est vera passio, sed impropriissima, nec fit cum vera passione: ergo nec dicetur aliqua qualitas passibilis, in quantum causa passionis: nisi sit causa veræ ac propriæ passionis: sed colores non causant veram passionem in visu: quia visio, nec est vera passio, vt recepta in visu, sed communissima: nec fit cum vera passione: ergo non sunt passibiles qualitates, quia causant passionem in sensu. Vera igitur mens Arist. est, & vera sententia, ac tenenda, *Quòd solum obiectum gustus, olfactus, & tactus sunt passibiles qualitates*. quia causant passionem in sensu: obiecta verò visus & auditus, non hac ratione, sed solùm, quia sunt effectus alicuius passionis.

45 This opinion cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle, because in express words he denies that the objects of sight are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense. But neither is it to be held, considering the nature of this species, which I prove thus: a quality is called a passible quality of this species only inasmuch as it is the effect of a passion, as is that which is the effect of a true passion, or of an action of its own which comes about with a true passion; whence the expressed species, which is produced through intellection, or which is produced in the internal senses from the sensations of the external senses, are not called passible qualities, because the operation of the intellect neither is a true passion (but a most improper one), nor comes about with a true passion: therefore neither will any quality be called passible inasmuch as it is the cause of a passion, unless it is the cause of a true and proper passion; but colors do not cause a true passion in sight, because vision neither is a true passion, as received in sight, but a most common one, nor does it come about with a true passion: therefore they are not passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense. The true mind of Aristotle, therefore, and the true opinion, and the one to be held, is That only the objects of taste, smell, and touch are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but the objects of sight and hearing not for this reason, but only because they are effects of some passion.

> 46 Quod vt explicemus simul, & probemus, notanda est differentia, inter obiecta gustus, olfactus, & tactus ex vna parte, & obiecta visus, & auditus ex altera: quòd illa natura mouent sensus, vt percipiantur ab eis, cum reali alteratione organi: nempe cum humectatione, aut calefactione, vel alia simili qualitate: quæ vt recipiuntur in organis, propriè appellantur passiones: cùm aliquo modo disponant subiectum, in quo recipiuntur, ad corruptionem: vnde sensationes horum sensuum, propriè dicuntur passiones: quia licèt ipsæ secundùm se passiones propriæ, non essent tales, nihilominus sic appellantur: quia fiunt cum vera passione, sicut de passionibus appetitus dictum est. Obiecta verò visus, & auditus, nec secundùm se propriè appellantur passiones, nec per se fiunt cum vera passione: licèt aliquando fortè contingat per accidens, cum vera passione fieri.

46 To explain and at the same time prove this, the difference must be noted between the objects of taste, smell, and touch on the one side, and the objects of sight and hearing on the other: that the former by their nature move the senses, so as to be perceived by them, with a real alteration of the organ, namely with moistening, or heating, or some other similar quality; and these, as they are received in the organs, are properly called passions, since in some way they dispose the subject in which they are received toward corruption. Whence the sensations of these senses are properly called passions: because, although in themselves they would not be such proper passions, nevertheless they are so called because they come about with a true passion, as was said of the passions of the appetite. But the objects of sight and hearing neither are properly called passions in themselves, nor do they of themselves come about with a true passion, although sometimes it may perhaps happen per accidens that they come about with a true passion.

> 47 Ex hac differentia sequitur, verum esse, quod asserit Arist. *Solùm obiecta trium sensuum esse passibiles qualitates*. quia causant passionem in sensu: obiecta verò visus, & auditus, non hac ratione, sed solũ quia sunt effectus passionis. Et probatur [p. 464] hac ratione. Passibilis qualitas dicitur illa, quæ causat passionem in sensu, ergo qualis fuerit passio causata, talis erit denominatio qualitatis passibilis: sed sola obiecta trium sensuum causant passionem propriè dictam in sensibus, cùm moueant sensus cum vera, ac reali alteratione, quæ passio propriè appellatur: cætera verò solùm causant passionem impropriissimam: ergo illæ solùm erunt passibiles qualitates propriè loquendo, quia causant passionem in sensu: hæc verò non, sed alia ratione.

47 From this difference it follows that what Aristotle asserts is true: that only the objects of three senses are passible qualities because they cause a passion in the sense; but the objects of sight and hearing not for this reason, but only because they are effects of a passion. And this is proved [p. 464] by this argument. A passible quality is called that which causes a passion in the sense; therefore, of whatever kind the passion caused is, of such kind will be the denomination of the passible quality; but only the objects of three senses cause a passion properly so called in the senses, since they move the senses with a true and real alteration, which is properly called a passion; the others cause only a most improper passion: therefore those alone will be passible qualities, properly speaking, because they cause a passion in the sense; but these not, but for another reason.

> Ad arg. pro ratione dubitandi propositum, distinguenda est minor, nam Arist. non definit passibilem qualitatem, per id quod causet passionem quamlibet in sensu, sed propriè dictam: obiectum verò visus, & auditus, solùm sunt causa passionis communis, & impropriæ: & ideo sunt passibiles qualitates, in quantum passibilis qualitas causat passionem sensu: sed alia titulo, vel ratione, quia sunt effectus passionis: testimonium autem Arist. nostram sententiam confirmat, vt vidimus.

To the argument proposed for the reason for doubting, the minor is to be distinguished: for Aristotle does not define a passible quality by its causing any passion whatever in the sense, but a passion properly so called; but the object of sight and hearing is only the cause of a common and improper passion; and therefore they are passible qualities, not inasmuch as a passible quality causes a passion in the sense, but by another title or reason, because they are effects of a passion. And the testimony of Aristotle confirms our opinion, as we have seen.

> QVÆSTI V.

Q U E S T I O N V.

> *Quid per Formam, & Figuram intelligat Arist. & an sint diuersæ species qualitatis, vel eadem.*

What Aristotle understands by Form and Figure, and whether they are diverse species of quality, or the same.

> 48 CIrca primum, variæ sunt acceptiones *Formæ*. Nam primò, accipitur pro pulchritudine rei, quæ resultat ex debita ordinatione partium. Secundò, pro *forma substantiali*, à qua res accipit esse: vt ab anima homo. Tertiò, pro *exteriori figura rerum*, non solùm naturalium, sed etiam artificialium: vt quod artificiosum est in cathedra, vocamus formam eius.

48 Concerning the first, there are various acceptations of Form. For first, it is taken for the beauty of a thing, which results from the due ordering of its parts. Second, for the substantial form, from which a thing receives its being, as man from the soul. Third, for the exterior figure of things, not only natural but also artificial: as what is artful in a chair we call its form.

> Et secundùm has diuersas acceptiones, diuerso modo sumuntur ab expositoribus, *forma*, & *figura*. nam quidam per figuram intelligunt, eam quæ in rebus non viuentibus reperitur: per formam verò, eam quæ in viuentibus. Ita Ammonius cap. præsenti. Hæc tamen expositio non est tenenda, quia nulla videtur differentia in figuris harum rerum, propter quam vna sit, aut dicatur forma, & altera figura.

And according to these diverse acceptations, form and figure are taken by the expositors in diverse ways: for some understand by figure that which is found in non-living things, and by form that which is found in living things. So Ammonius, on the present chapter. This exposition, however, is not to be held, because there seems to be no difference in the figures of these things on account of which one should be, or be called, form, and the other figure.

> Ideo Boëtius, & Simplicius ibidem, formam asserunt appellari ab Arist. *Pulchritudinem resultantem ex debita membrorum coaptatione, ac distinctione: Figuram verò eam, quæ resultat ex sola quantitate*: vt triangularem, & quadrangularem: Sed nec expositio hæc potest esse ad mentem Arist. qui in hoc cap. pulchritudinem collocauit in specie habitus.

Therefore Boethius and Simplicius, in the same place, assert that Aristotle calls form the beauty resulting from the due adjustment and distinction of the members; but figure, that which results from quantity alone, as triangular and quadrangular. But neither can this exposition be according to the mind of Aristotle, who in this chapter placed beauty in the species of habit.

[p. 465]

> Albertus Mag. tract. de prædicamento qualitatis, c. 8 *figuram*, ait, *respectu solius quantitatis dici*: quia non videtur esse aliud, quàm terminatio quantitatis: nam anguli, quibus constat figura triangularis, & quadrangularis, non videntur esse aliud, præter lineas, qui sunt termini quantitatis: formam verò, per ordinem ad substantiam: nam sicut forma substantialis continet totam perfectionem speciei: ita qualitas huius speciei, totam perfectionem eius manifestat: vnde res diuersarum specierum, propter diuersas formas substantiales, diuersas habent figuras.

Albert the Great, treatise on the category of quality, ch. 8, says that figure is so called with respect to quantity alone, because it does not seem to be anything other than the termination of quantity: for the angles of which the triangular and quadrangular figure consists do not seem to be anything besides lines, which are the terms of quantity; but form, by order to substance: for just as the substantial form contains the whole perfection of the species, so the quality of this species manifests its whole perfection; whence things of diverse species, on account of their diverse substantial forms, have diverse figures.

> 49 Sententia D. Tho. probabilior est, quam iam ferè omnes moderni Interpretes sequuntur: eam verò his verbis explicat 7. lib. Phys. lect. 7. *Considerandum est, quòd forma & figura, in hoc ab inuicem differunt, quòd figura importat terminationem quantitatis: est enim figura, quæ termino, vel terminis comprehenditur: forma verò dicitur, quæ dat esse specificum artificiato: nam formæ artificiatorum, sunt accidentia.* Quibus clarè docet, figuram esse nudam terminationem quantitatis: formam verò, dicere ordinem ad compositum artificiale. Et huius veritatis signum est: quòd *figura reperitur in quantitatibus Mathematicis, abstrahentibus à materia sensibili*, vt docet Aristot. 5. Meta. c. 14. vbi res Mathematicas immobiles, hoc est, abstrahentes à motu, *figuras* vocat. Et hæc non solùm reperitur in quantitatibus continuis, sed etiam in numeris: non quidem simplicibus, sed compositis: nam binarius non dicit aliquam figuram, senarius verò, qui ex duobus ternariis componitur, præter vnitates ipsas quæ sunt quantitates, certam habet figuram, ex ipsamet compositione resultantem: vt docet expressè Arist. 5 Meta. ca 14.

49 The opinion of St. Thomas is more probable, which almost all modern Interpreters now follow; and he explains it in these words, Phys. 7, lect. 7: It should be considered that form and figure differ from each other in this, that figure implies the termination of quantity: for figure is that which is comprehended by a term or terms; but that is called form which gives specific being to the thing made by art: for the forms of artificial things are accidents. By these words he clearly teaches that figure is the bare termination of quantity, but that form expresses an order to the artificial composite. And a sign of this truth is that figure is found in Mathematical quantities, which abstract from sensible matter, as Aristotle teaches in Metaph. 5, ch. 14, where he calls mathematical things immobile, that is, abstracting from motion, figures. And this is found not only in continuous quantities but also in numbers: not indeed in simple ones, but in composite ones; for the number two does not express any figure, but the number six, which is composed of two threes, has, besides the units themselves which are quantities, a certain figure resulting from the composition itself, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Metaph. 5, ch. 14.

> 50 Sed hoc debet notari, circa hanc expositionem: quòd dum figura appellatur terminus, vel terminatio quantitatis: duobus modis intelligi potest. Primò, de termino proprio, & intrinseco quantitatis: vt de punctis lineæ, & lineis superficierum & superficiebus corporis: in quo sensu non est verum, quia isti termini, essentiales sunt quantitati: figura verò accidens eius est, ad prædicamentum qualitatis pertinens. Secundò, de termino accidentali, & quasi extrinseco: qui intrinsecos terminos, & intrinsecam terminationem consequitur: & eiusmodi termini, vel terminatio, propriè loquendo, habent rationem figuræ. Et huius ratio est: quia tres anguli, ex quibus constituitur figura triangularis, præsupponunt tres lineas, suis punctis iam terminatas: & ex eis iam terminatis, atque completis in sua specie, figura triangula fit. Ex quibus intelligitur: potiùs dicendum esse, claritatis, ac proprietatis gratia figuram resultare [p. 466] ex terminis, vel ex terminatione quantitatis, quàm esse terminum, aut terminationem quantitatis: nam terminus quantitatis, aut terminatio eius, incompletum quid est, cùm sit indiuisibile, vel ab indiuisibilibus facta: ideo non habet aliam speciem vel prædicamentum, ab ipsis quantitatibus: figura verò, completum quid est, ex genere, & differentia compositum, & per se habet speciem, atque prædicamentum.

50 But this ought to be noted concerning this exposition: that when figure is called the term or termination of quantity, it can be understood in two ways. First, of the proper and intrinsic term of quantity, as of the points of a line, and of the lines of a surface, and of the surfaces of a body; in which sense it is not true, because these terms are essential to quantity, whereas figure is an accident of it, belonging to the category of quality. Second, of an accidental and as it were extrinsic term, which follows upon the intrinsic terms and the intrinsic termination; and such a term or termination, properly speaking, has the ratio of figure. And the reason for this is: because the three angles of which the triangular figure is constituted presuppose three lines already terminated by their points; and from these, already terminated and complete in their species, the triangular figure comes about. From which it is understood that, for the sake of clarity and propriety, it should rather be said that figure results Gg [p. 466] from the terms or from the termination of quantity, than that it is the term or termination of quantity: for the term of quantity, or its termination, is something incomplete, since it is indivisible or made of indivisibles; therefore it has no other species or category than the quantities themselves; but figure is something complete, composed of genus and difference, and has of itself a species and a category.

> Circa secundum verò, An forma, & figura distinguantur specie: quidam interpretes, diuersas species eas faciunt, ex eo distinctas, quòd figura abstrahit à materia sensibili: forma verò dicit ordinem ad materiam sensibilem, tribuens speciem artificialibus, & manifestam faciens speciem rerum naturalium: vt constat in forma statuæ, & exteriori hominis.

Concerning the second, whether form and figure are distinguished in species: some interpreters make them diverse species, distinguished by the fact that figure abstracts from sensible matter, whereas form expresses an order to sensible matter, giving species to artificial things and making manifest the species of natural things, as is plain in the form of a statue and in the exterior of a man.

> Tenendum tamen est: Formam & figuram non esse diuersas species qualitatis, sed vnam, & eandem: & solùm distingui accidentaliter. Probatur hac ratione: Eadem res, prout magis, vel minùs abstracta à materia consideratur, non distinguitur specie: sed solùm accidentaliter: in quantum diuersum ordinem dicit ad materiam: vt homo Physicè consideratus, prout componitur ex materia, & forma, & habet in se principium motus, non distinguitur specie à se ipso, prout composito ex genere, & differentia: quo pacto non dicit ordinem ad materiam sensibilem: sed forma, & figura, solùm ex eo distinguuntur, quod figura abstrahit à materia sensibili, forma verò eandem respicit: ergo non distinguuntur specie, sed solùm accidentaliter. Probatur consequentia: quia accidentalis est ei ordo ad materiam sensibilem, vel abstractio ab ea: licèt enim ad diuersas scientias pertineat res, vt diuerso modo abstrahitur à materia, tamen pertinere ad eandem, vel diuersam scientiam, sic vel aliter esse abstrahibilem à materia, accidit ei: quamuis scientiæ, essentialis sit talis modus abstrahendi à materia.

It must be held, however, that form and figure are not diverse species of quality, but one and the same, and are distinguished only accidentally. This is proved by the following argument: the same thing, according as it is considered as more or less abstracted from matter, is not distinguished in species, but only accidentally, inasmuch as it expresses a diverse order to matter: as man considered physically, according as he is composed of matter and form and has in himself a principle of motion, is not distinguished in species from himself according as he is composed of genus and difference, in which way he does not express an order to sensible matter; but form and figure are distinguished only by the fact that figure abstracts from sensible matter, whereas form regards it: therefore they are not distinguished in species, but only accidentally. The consequence is proved: because the order to sensible matter, or the abstraction from it, is accidental to it; for although a thing belongs to diverse sciences according as it is abstracted from matter in a diverse way, yet to belong to the same or to a diverse science, and thus to be abstractable from matter in one way or another, is accidental to it; although such a mode of abstracting from matter is essential to the science.

## CHAPTER IX

### CAP. IX. De prædicamento Actionis & passionis — On the Category of Action and Passion.

> QVatuor explicanda sunt, circa hæc duo prædicamenta actionis, & passionis. Primum est, *Quid nomine actionis, & passionis significetur*. Secundum: *Quid vtraque sit*. Tertium, *Quæ sint genera suprema vtriusque prædicamenti, & in quas species diuidantur*, (ex his enim ordinatio prædicamentalis fit.) Quartum, *Quot, & quæ sint proprietates actionis, & passionis*.
