First, from the intrinsic condition of the infinite noun, which is such that it posits no form in the subject, indeed not even any positive ratio, but the pure negation of the thing to which it is joined: as non-man posits only the negation of man; but negation alone does not require the existence of the subject, indeed not even its possibility, because the negation of man is verified even of an impossible thing, such as the chimera: therefore the infinite noun can be verified of all these. The consequence is proved: because there is an evident argument from a negative proposition to an affirmative one with an infinite predicate in the same terms, as A lion is not a man: therefore a lion is non-man; but the infinite noun is denied of impossible things, because this is true: A chimera is not a man: therefore it will be affirmed of the same in a proposition with an infinite predicate; and so this too will be true: A chimera is non-man. The consequence is proved again: for the reason a negative proposition about an impossible subject is true is that the negation posits nothing positive in the subject; but the infinite noun posits nothing positive in the subject, but only a negation: therefore according to this it can be verified of the same possible thing in an affirmative proposition.

> Secundò, Prædicata contradictoria, habent immediatam oppositionem: ergo de quolibet ente, aut non ente, necesse est alterum eorum verificari: sed homo, & non homo sunt prædicata contradictoria: ergo necesse est alterum eorum verificari de quacunque re possibili, vel impossibili: sed de re impossibili vt de chimæra, non verificatur homo: ergo verificabitur non homo: sicque de cæteris nominibus infinitis, quæ de rebus etiam impossibilibus verificari debent.

Second, contradictory predicates have an immediate opposition: therefore of any being or non-being whatever one of them must be verified; but man and non-man are contradictory predicates: therefore one of them must be verified of any thing whatever, possible or impossible; but of an impossible thing, such as the chimera, man is not verified: therefore non-man will be verified; and so of the other infinite nouns, which must be verified even of impossible things.

> 16 Pro solutione arg. alterius opinionis: Notandum est, *Prædicatum propositionis affirmatiuæ duobus modis se habere ad subiectum*, nam vel accidens eius est, modùmve accidentis habet, [p. 516] vel ad essentiam eius pertinet, aut tanquam propria passio se habet. Et si primo modo se habeat, certum est subiecto actu existenti attribui: quia accidentia non conueniunt subiectis, nisi secundùm actualem inhærentiam in eis: quam constat necessariò supponere actualem existentiam: Si verò secundo modo se habeat, certum est non conuenire ei secundùm actualem existentiam, sed secundùm naturalem connexionem cum eo: quæ cùm nullum tempus determinet, sed perpetua sit, eodem modo semper se habens, propositio etiam perpetuæ veritatis est: & copula (vt aiunt) absoluitur à tempore: quod est, extrema non coniungere, pro vlla differentia temporis: cùm tamen in propositione accidentali, pro determinata differentia temporis, in qua existunt extrema, ea coniungat.

16 For the solution of the argument of the other opinion it should be noted that the predicate of an affirmative proposition stands toward the subject in two ways: for either it is its accident, or it has the mode of an accident, Kk ij [p. 516] or it pertains to its essence, or stands toward it as a proper attribute. And if it stands in the first way, it is certain that it is attributed to an actually existing subject: because accidents do not belong to subjects except according to actual inherence in them, which, it is agreed, necessarily presupposes actual existence. But if it stands in the second way, it is certain that it does not belong to it according to actual existence, but according to a natural connection with it; and since this determines no time, but is perpetual, always standing in the same way, the proposition too is of perpetual truth, and the copula (as they say) is absolved from time: that is, it does not join the extremes for any difference of time; whereas in an accidental proposition it joins them for a determinate difference of time, in which the extremes exist.

> Ex quibus sequitur, solùm in propositionibus accidentalibus, extrema supponi: & ideo solùm in his requiri actualem existentiam extremorum, ad veritatem propositionis affirmatiuæ. Et etiam in his solùm intelligi illam regulam summulistarum, quòd propositio affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente est falsa: ac tandem solùm in his esse bonam consequentiam, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo. In propositionibus autem necessariis, nec supponuntur subiecta, nec vniuntur secundùm actualem existentiam, nec secundùm aliquam differentiam temporis, sed solùm secundùm naturalem connexionem, abstrahentem ab existentia, & tempore: vnde in eis hæc sola regula vera semper est, & obseruanda: quòd omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ, sunt semper veræ: & omnes negatiuæ semper falsæ. Quare nec in his valet consequentia, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo: quia in propositione de tertio, prædicatum coniungitur subiecto, secundùm naturalem connexionem cum eo: in propositione verò de secundo, dicit actualem existentiam, vt si dicas: Homo est rationalis, ergo homo est: antecedens erit verum, nullo homine existente, & consequens falsum. Quam doctrinam, si ad nomen infinitum applicemus, inueniemus significare omnia possibilia, & impossibilia, quasi modo essentiali, cùm per se omnia significet. Et ex hoc sequitur, de illis verificari in propositione, quasi per modum naturalis connexionis, & non secundùm actualem existentiam: quare omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ sunt veræ: & omnes negatiuæ falsæ: quia extrema non supponuntur nec valet in eis consequentia, à propositione de tertio adiacente, ad propositionem de secundo.

From which it follows that only in accidental propositions do the extremes supposit, and therefore only in these is the actual existence of the extremes required for the truth of an affirmative proposition. And also that only in these is that rule of the summulists to be understood, that an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject is false; and finally that only in these is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second good. But in necessary propositions the subjects neither supposit, nor are united according to actual existence, nor according to any difference of time, but only according to a natural connection, abstracting from existence and from time: whence in them this rule alone is always true and to be observed, that all affirmative propositions are always true, and all negative ones always false. Wherefore neither is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in these: because in the proposition of the third adjacent the predicate is joined to the subject according to a natural connection with it, but in the proposition of the second it denotes actual existence: as if you say, Man is rational: therefore man is, the antecedent will be true when no man exists, and the consequent false. If we apply this doctrine to the infinite noun, we shall find that it signifies all possible and impossible things in an as it were essential mode, since it signifies them all per se. And from this it follows that it is verified of them in a proposition as it were by way of a natural connection, and not according to actual existence: wherefore all affirmative propositions are true, and all negative ones false, because the extremes do not supposit; nor is the consequence from a proposition of the third adjacent to a proposition of the second valid in them.

> Ad formam igitur arg. Concedenda est maior, quòd nomen [p. 517] infinitum non possit verificari de impossibilibus, aut non existentibus, nisi in propositione affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente: sed minor distinguẽda, quòd affirmatiua de subiecto non supponente sit falsa: nam si accidentalis sit, concedendum est, quia vniuntur extrema secundùm actualem existentiam, quam habere debet tempore significato per copulam: & si eam non habuerint, falsa erit propositio. In propositionibus verò necessariis, nõ requiritur actualis existentia extremorum: quia solùm vniuntur secundùm naturalem connexionem: & ideo affirmatiua, licèt sit de subiecto non supponente, vera est. Et cùm propositiones affirmatiuæ de prædicato infinito, modum habeant necessarium, negandum est etiam in eis quòd affirmatiua de subiecto, non supponente sit falsa.

To the form of the argument, then: The major is to be granted, that the infinite [p. 517] noun cannot be verified of impossible or non-existing things except in an affirmative proposition about a non-suppositing subject; but the minor is to be distinguished, that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false. For if it is accidental, it is to be granted, because the extremes are united according to actual existence, which they must have at the time signified by the copula; and if they do not have it, the proposition will be false. But in necessary propositions the actual existence of the extremes is not required, because they are united only according to a natural connection; and therefore the affirmative, although it is about a non-suppositing subject, is true. And since affirmative propositions with an infinite predicate have the mode of necessary ones, it is to be denied in them too that an affirmative about a non-suppositing subject is false.

### An transcendentia nomina possint infinitari — Whether transcendental nouns can be made infinite.

> *An transcendentia nomina possint infinitari.*

[…]

> 17 PRima opinio, tenet, *infinitari non posse transcendentia*, si in tota sua vniuersalitate accipiantur: vt ens absolutè sumptum: Si verò cum limitatione, vt pro ente reali tantùm, aut pro ente rationis, infinitari posse. Ita Alber. Magnus in Comment. huius lib. tract. 2. c. 5. cum Auicenna, quos sequuntur Toletus, & alij c. præsenti. Probatur ex natura nominis infiniti, quod tam de entibus, quàm de non entibus dicitur: sed si infinitetur ens absolutè sumptum, solùm de entibus dici poterit: ergo non potest infinitari.

17 The first opinion holds that transcendentals cannot be made infinite if they are taken in their whole universality, as being taken absolutely; but if they are taken with a limitation, as for real being only, or for being of reason, that they can be made infinite. So Albert the Great in the commentary on this book, tract. 2, ch. 5, with Avicenna, whom Toledo and others follow on the present chapter. It is proved from the nature of the infinite noun, which is said as much of beings as of non-beings; but if being taken absolutely were made infinite, it could be said only of beings: therefore it cannot be made infinite.

> Secunda opinio, adhuc hoc modo sumpta, *transcendentia infinitari posse*, concedit: ita Sotus 2. li. Summularum, c. 1. notab. 6. Suesanus, & Louanienses c. præsenti. Probãt: Quia prædicationes istæ, Chimæra est non ens; Nihil est, non ens, sunt de prædicato infinito: & prędicatum est ens in sua vniuersalitate: ergo transcendentia in sua vniuersalitate sumpta, infinitari possunt.

The second opinion grants that transcendentals can be made infinite even when taken in this way. So Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 1, notable 6, Suesanus, and the Louvain commentators on the present chapter. They prove it: Because these predications, A chimera is non-being, Nothing is non-being, have an infinite predicate; and the predicate is being in its universality: therefore transcendentals taken in their universality can be made infinite.

> Pro solutione dubij: Distinguenda sunt transcendentia, hoc modo: Quædam sunt Vniuersalissima, *vt Ens*, alia minùs vniuersalia: *vt passiones eius, Verum, Bonum, & Vnum*, quæ minùs vniuersalia dicuntur: quia secundùm rationes formales non se includunt, nec enim bonum, est verum formaliter; nec verum, est formaliter vnum. Et rursus, vniuersalissimum transcendens, vt ens, potest sumi *absolutè, vel cum alia limitatione.* Videlicet pro solo ente reali, vel pro sola substantia. Et de transcendentibus minùs vniuersalibus, euidens est infinitari posse: quia non verum, aut non bonum, adhuc verificari possunt de entibus, & non entibus: nam verum est non bonum: & vnum est non verum formaliter. Certum est etiam, ens cum limitatione acceptum, infinitari posse, propter eandem rationem: sed an possit [p. 518] possit sine limitatione acceptum; de hoc solùm potest esse dubium.

For the solution of the doubt, transcendentals are to be distinguished in this way: some are Most universal, as Being; others less universal, as its attributes, True, Good, and One, which are called less universal because according to their formal ratios they do not include one another: for neither is good formally true, nor is true formally one. And again, the most universal transcendental, such as being, can be taken absolutely, or with some limitation: namely for real being alone, or for substance alone. And of the less universal transcendentals it is evident that they can be made infinite, because non-true or non-good can still be verified of beings and non-beings: for the true is non-good, and the one is formally non-true. It is certain also that being taken with a limitation can be made infinite, for the same reason; but whether it can Kk iij [p. 518] be made infinite when taken without limitation: about this alone can there be doubt.

> Et nostra sententia est infinitari posse. Probatur, ex propria definitione nominis infiniti, à nobis assignata in principio, secundùm quam solum dicit esse compositum ex nomine simplici, & negatione ei adiuncta: sed non ens, componitur ex vtroque: ergo simpliciter est nomen infinitum: & hoc etiam probat arg. secundæ opinionis.

And our view is that it can be made infinite. This is proved from the proper definition of the infinite noun assigned by us at the beginning, according to which it means only that it is composed of a simple noun and a negation joined to it; but non-being is composed of both: therefore it is simply an infinite noun. And the argument of the second opinion also proves this.

> Ad argu. verò primæ opinionis, negandum est antecedens; quòd de ratione nominis infiniti sit, de entibus, & non entibus verificari: sed hoc solùm pertinet ad rationem nominis infiniti particularis: de quo Aristot. & omnes communiter loquuntur. Ad rationem verò nominis infiniti, vt sic, solùm pertinet, quòd ex nomine simplici particulari, vel transcendente, & ex negatione ei adiuncta componatur.

But to the argument of the first opinion, the antecedent is to be denied, namely that it belongs to the ratio of the infinite noun to be verified of beings and non-beings; this pertains only to the ratio of the particular infinite noun, of which Aristotle and all speak commonly. But to the ratio of the infinite noun as such it pertains only that it be composed of a simple noun, particular or transcendental, and a negation joined to it.

### An nomina infinita sint enumeranda inter absoluta, vel inter connotatiua — Whether infinite nouns are to be counted among absolute or among connotative terms.

> *An nomina infinita sint numeranda inter absoluta, vel inter connotatiua.*

[…]

> CErtum est; nec esse absoluta simpliciter, nec connotatiua: cùm nec simpliciter sint nomina, sed solùm secundũ quid. Solùm ergo potest esse dubium, An ad hæc potiùs, quàm ad illa reducantur. Toletus in Comment. huius capitis asserit, *inter absoluta numerari*: quia non habent materiale, & formale significatum, vt connotatiua: sed solùm significant negationem in concreto.

It is certain that they are neither absolute simply nor connotative, since they are not nouns simply, but only in a certain respect. There can therefore be doubt only whether they are to be reduced to the latter rather than to the former. Toledo, in the commentary on this chapter, asserts that they are counted among absolute terms: because they do not have a material and a formal significate, as connotatives do, but signify only a negation in the concrete.

> Nostra verò sententia est, ad connotatiua potiùs reducenda esse: quia de formali dicunt negationem rei, cui adiunguntur, de materiali verò, rem aliam quamcunque: ideo connotatiuorum similitudinem habent.

Our view, however, is that they are rather to be reduced to connotative terms: because formally they denote the negation of the thing to which they are joined, but materially any other thing whatever; therefore they have a likeness to connotatives.

### An nomen infinitum dicatur vniuocè de entibus & non entibus, vel analogicè — Whether the infinite noun is said univocally of beings and non-beings, or analogically.

> *An nomen infinitum dicatur vniuocè de entibus & non entibus, vel analogicè.*

[…]

> REspondetur vniuocè dici de omnibus. Cuius ratio est; quia significatum formale eius, est sola negatio eius rei, cui adiungitur: negatio verò æquè conuenit entibus, & non entibus: ergo æquè dicitur de omnibus; atque adeò vniuocè: non quidem propria vniuocatione; quia denominatiua non sunt propriè vniuoca: sed impropria, qualis in denominatiuis reperitur.

The answer is that it is said univocally of all. The reason for this is: because its formal significate is only the negation of the thing to which it is joined; but negation belongs equally to beings and non-beings: therefore it is said equally of all, and so univocally; not indeed by proper univocation, because denominatives are not properly univocal, but by improper univocation, such as is found in denominatives.

> Adnotandum tandem est, Circa definitionem nominis, non esse ei addendas duas illas particulas; *finita & recta*, vt exeludantur [p. 519] nomina infinita, & obliqui casus: quia per alias particulas definitionis, iam exclusa censentur: nec Arist. eas posuit in definitione, sed post integram explicationem eius.

It should be noted, finally, concerning the definition of the noun, that those two particles, finite and direct, are not to be added to it in order to exclude [p. 519] infinite nouns and oblique cases: because they are judged to be already excluded by the other particles of the definition; nor did Aristotle put them in the definition, but after the complete explanation of it.

## CHAPTER III

> De Verbo.

On the Verb.

> *TEX. ARISTOTELIS.*

TEXT OF ARISTOTLE.

> *Verbum autem est, quid consignificat tempus, cuius pars nihil significat seorsum: & est semper eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur, nota, &c.*

The verb, moreover, is that which consignifies time, no part of which signifies anything separately; and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> INtentum Arist. est explicare naturam *Verbi.* Diuiditur autem caput in tres partes. In prima, *Definitionem verbi proponit, & explicat.* In secunda, *Excludit à ratione verbi, infinitum verbum, & casus verbi*: hoc est verba aliorum temporum à præsenti. In tertia, *Colligit, verbum cum nomine, in duobus conuenire.*

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the nature of the Verb. The chapter T          is divided into three parts. In the first, he proposes and explains the definition of the verb. In the second, he excludes from the ratio of verb the infinite verb and the cases of the verb: that is, verbs of tenses other than the present. In the third, he gathers that the verb agrees with the noun in two things.

> Definitio verbi talis est: *Verbum est, quod consignificat tempus, cuius pars nihil significat seorsum: & est semper eorum: quæ de altero, prædicantur, nota.* In qua definitione subintelligi debent, duæ istæ particulæ, vox significatiua ad placitum, ex definitione nominis: secundùm communem expositionem interpretum: quia communes sunt nomini, & verbo: sed quia hoc satis erat notum, noluit Aristotel. eas in definitione verbi repetere, sed à consignificatione temporis initium eius sumere: quia iam incipit verbum, per hanc particulam à nomine differre. Consignificare verò tempus: idem est, ac connotare tempus: vel ex consequenti illud significare. Itaque, quia verbum actionem aut passionem per se significat, aut aliquid per modum actionis, aut passionis: & actio aut passio fiunt in tempore, dicitur tempus simul, & ex consequenti significare cum actione ipsa, aut passione, per se primò significata. Itaque diuersum quid est, *significare tempus, & consignificara.* Significare enim tempus est, rem, quæ est tempus, sicut quamlibet aliam, per se significare: sed consignificare tempus, vel significare cum tempore, est significare rem aliam, vt in tempore factam: ex hoc enim, licèt non significetur tempus, sed res alia, simul tamen denotatur, & simul quasi ex consequentia significatur: quod est consignificari: & hoc soli verbo conuenit, nomini verò solùm conuenit, significare tempus, vt dies, & [p. 520] nox determinata quædam tempora significant, nõ tamen consignificant tempus.

The definition of the verb is this: The verb is that which consignifies time, no part of which signifies anything separately; and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another. In this definition, according to the common exposition of the interpreters, these two particles from the definition of the noun must be understood, significative word by convention: because they are common to the noun and the verb; but because this was well enough known, Aristotle did not wish to repeat them in the definition of the verb, but to take its beginning from the consignification of time, because by this particle the verb already begins to differ from the noun. Now to consignify time is the same as to connote time, or to signify it consequently. And so, because the verb per se signifies action or passion, or something by way of action or passion, and action or passion take place in time, it is said to signify time together with, and consequently upon, the action or passion itself, which is per se and primarily signified. And so to signify time and to consignify it are different things. For to signify time is to signify per se the thing which is time, as any other thing; but to consignify time, or to signify with time, is to signify another thing as done in time: for from this, although time is not signified but another thing, yet it is at the same time denoted and at the same time signified as it were consequently, which is to be consignified; and this belongs to the verb alone, whereas to the noun belongs only to signify time, as day, and Kk iiij [p. 520] and night signify certain determinate times, yet they do not consignify time.

> Alia verò particula, cuius pars nihil significat seorsum, distinguit verbum ab oratione: & satis fuit explicata in definitione nominis. Solùm restat vltima, & est semper eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur, nota. quasi dicat, verbum esse signum, aut significare coniunctionem prædicati cum subiecto, quam facit. Nomen enim prædicatur, aut subiicitur in propositione: sed verbum vnit prædicatum cum subiecto, & talem vnionem significat: in quo etiam distinguitur à nomine, & oratione.

The other particle, no part of which signifies anything separately, distinguishes the verb from speech, and was sufficiently explained in the definition of the noun. There remains only the last, and it is always a sign of those things which are predicated of another: as if to say that the verb is a sign of, or signifies, the conjunction of the predicate with the subject, which it brings about. For the noun is predicated or made subject in a proposition, but the verb unites the predicate with the subject and signifies such a union; in which it is also distinguished from the noun and from speech.

> In secunda parte, excludit verba infinita, & casus verbi, à definitione, propter easdem rationes, quibus exclusit nomen infinitum, & casus obliquos à definitione nominis. Quia verbum debet significare determinatam actionem & passionem, determinatamque, coniunctionem prædicati cum subiecto: sed verbum infinitum, nihil determinatum significat: ergo non est simpliciter verbum, sed secundùm quid: & propterea excludendum est à definitione verbi, atque etiam casus verbi, hoc est, verba aliorum temporum, quàm præsentis. Quia non ratione sui: sed ratione verbi præsentis, conuenit eis officium verbi: nec actionem, aut passionem simpliciter talem significant, sed præteritam, aut futuram; quæ cùm non sit actu in rerum natura solùm est talis secundùm quid.

In the second part he excludes infinite verbs and the cases of the verb from the definition, for the same reasons for which he excluded the infinite noun and the oblique cases from the definition of the noun. Because the verb must signify a determinate action or passion, and a determinate conjunction of the predicate with the subject; but the infinite verb signifies nothing determinate: therefore it is not a verb simply, but in a certain respect; and for this reason it is to be excluded from the definition of the verb; and so too the cases of the verb, that is, verbs of tenses other than the present. Because the office of the verb belongs to them not by reason of themselves but by reason of the present verb; nor do they signify an action or passion that is such simply, but a past or future one, which, since it is not actually in the nature of things, is such only in a certain respect.

> In tertia tandem parte capitis: Duo colligit, in quibus *verbum conuenit cum nomine*. Primum est, quòd verbum per se sumptum, hoc est, extra propositionẽ, significat aliquam rem, sicut nomen: vt curro, significat cursum. Secundò: quòd sicut nomen per se sumptum, non significat verum, vel falsum, nisi adiungatur ei verbum: ita verbum per se sumptum hoc est extra propositionem, non significat verum aut falsum, nisi ei aliquo modo adiungatur nomen Cuius rationem assignat: quia veritas, & falsitas, solùm reperiuntur in compositione, & diuisione: sed verbum per se sumptum, non significat talem compositionem: quia non potest intelligi sine extremis, hoc est, sine prædicato, & subiecto: ergo verbum sine nomine sibi adiuncto, non potest veritatem, aut falsitatem significare.

In the third part of the chapter, finally, he gathers two things in which the verb agrees with the noun. The first is that the verb taken by itself, that is, outside a proposition, signifies some thing, as the noun does: as I run signifies running. Second, that just as the noun taken by itself does not signify the true or the false unless a verb is joined to it, so the verb taken by itself, that is, outside a proposition, does not signify the true or the false unless a noun is in some way joined to it. And he assigns the reason for this: because truth and falsity are found only in composition and division; but the verb taken by itself does not signify such a composition, because it cannot be understood without the extremes, that is, without the predicate and the subject: therefore the verb without a noun joined to it cannot signify truth or falsity.

## QUESTION I

> QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

> *An verum sit verbum consignificare tempus,*

Whether it is true that the verb consignifies time.

> NOn videtur hæc particula definitionis conuenire omni verbo: ergo non bene fuit posita ab Arist. in definitione, [p. 521] Probatur antecedens: quia si verbum consignificat tempus, maximè quia significat actionem, cui conuenit mensurari tempore: sed non omne verbum significat actionem, vt probat verbum substantiuum, *est*: ergo neque omne verbum consignificabit tempus. Quod magis etiam fit manifestum: dum idem verbum, *est*, vnit extrema secundùm naturalem connexionem eorum, quod facit quotiescunque prædicatum est de essentia subiecti: aut propria passio eius: tunc enim non vnit ea pro aliqua differentia temporis: cùm tales propositiones, ante omne tempus, & post omne tempus sint veræ: & ideo dicantur esse perpetuæ veritatis: in quibus copula absoluitur à tempore: ergo in eis non potest consignificare tempus.

This particle of the definition does not seem to belong to every verb: therefore it was not rightly put by Aristotle in the definition, [p. 521] The antecedent is proved: because if the verb consignifies time, this is chiefly because it signifies action, to which it belongs to be measured by time; but not every verb signifies action, as the substantive verb is proves: therefore neither will every verb consignify time. Which becomes even more manifest: since the same verb is unites the extremes according to their natural connection, which it does whenever the predicate is of the essence of the subject, or its proper attribute; for then it does not unite them with any difference of time, since such propositions are true before all time and after all time, and are therefore said to be of perpetual truth; in them the copula is absolved from time: therefore in them it cannot consignify time.

> 20 Nec soli verbo conuenit: sed etiam nomini: ergo etiam ex hac parte, non bene fuit in definitione collocata eadem particula; sed probatur antecedens, quia prandium, cœna, & similia nomina, significant actionem comedendi, connotando quòd tali tempore fiat: ergo consignificant tempus. Præterea participium, vt amans, currens, est verum nomen, cùm ponatur pro subiecto, aut prædicato propositionis: & tamen consignificat tempus cùm significet actionem tempore præsenti, aut futuro exercendam: ergo nominibus etiam conuenit consignificare tempus.

20 Nor does it belong to the verb alone, but also to the noun: therefore on this score too the same particle was not well placed in the definition. The antecedent is proved: because lunch, dinner, and similar nouns signify the action of eating, connoting that it takes place at such a time: therefore they consignify time. Moreover, the participle, as loving, running, is a true noun, since it is placed as the subject or predicate of a proposition; and yet it consignifies time, since it signifies an action to be exercised in present or future time: therefore it also belongs to nouns to consignify time.

> Circa hanc particulam definitionis, duo explicanda sunt. Primum, *An soli verbo conueniat consignificare, tempus, vel etiam participio, & aliis nominibus*. Secundum, *An omnibus verbis, & semper conueniat*. Circa primum præsupponendum est, quid sit consignificare tempus. Non est enim aliud, quàm significare cum tempore: & vtrumque est significare aliquid, nempe actionem, cui conuenit mensurari tempore: ex hoc enim simul cum re illa, significatur tempus, quod est consignificari: vel res illa notatur, vt mensurata tempore, quod est significari cum tempore.

Concerning this particle of the definition, two things must be explained. First, Whether it belongs to the verb alone to consignify time, or also to the participle and to other nouns. Second, Whether it belongs to all verbs, and always. Concerning the first, it must be presupposed what it is to consignify time. For it is nothing other than to signify with time; and each of these is to signify something, namely an action to which it belongs to be measured by time: for from this, together with that thing, time is signified, which is to be consignified; or that thing is noted as measured by time, which is to be signified with time.

> Quo supposito, circa participium non loquuntur omnes eodem modo, sed plures negant consignificare tempus: quia licèt significet actionem tempore mensuratam, non tamen per modum actionis, sed per modum formæ inhærentis subiecto: vt currens, significat actionem currendi, per modum formæ inhærentis: sicut inhæret albedo: & ideo non significat eam, vt mensuratam tempore: nec proinde consignificat tempus.

This supposed, not all speak in the same way about the participle, but most deny that it consignifies time: because, although it signifies an action measured by time, yet it does so not by way of action but by way of a form inhering in a subject: as running signifies the action of running by way of an inhering form, as whiteness inheres; and therefore it does not signify it as measured by time, nor consequently does it consignify time.

> Communis tamen sententia tenet, *participium consignificare tempus*. Et hoc est verum. Ita D. Thom. cap. præsenti, vbi asserit: *Participium separari à verbo, per vltimam particulam definitionis [p. 522]*, nempe, *& est semper eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur, nota. Et conuenire cum eo in cæteris omnibus*: ita etiam Sotus 2 lib Summularum, cap. 2. & ibidem Mercatus, Venetus, tract. 2. de partibus propositionis, cap. 2. Toletus cum cæteris modernis, in hoc cap.

The common opinion, however, holds that the participle consignifies time. And this is true. So St. Thomas on the present chapter, where he asserts: The participle is separated from the verb by the last particle of the definition [p. 522] namely, and it is always a sign of those things that are predicated of another. And it agrees with it in all the others. So too Soto, Summulae bk. 2, ch. 2, and Mercado in the same place; Paul of Venice, tract. 2, on the parts of the proposition, ch. 2; Toledo with the other moderns, on this chapter.

> Probatur testimonio Arist. qui vltimam particulam, explicantem proprium officium verbi, posuit, ad excludendum participium, vt docuit D. Tho. non enim excludi potest per eam aliud: ergo sensit in reliquis particulis conuenire, quarum prima est, consignificare tempus.

It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who placed the last particle, which explains the proper office of the verb, in order to exclude the participle, as St. Thomas taught; for nothing else can be excluded by it: therefore he thought that it agrees with the verb in the remaining particles, the first of which is to consignify time.

> Probatur etiam ratione: Quia participium significat actionem; vt egreditur ab agente: vt calefaciens significat calefactionem: vt à se egressam: ergo significat actionem per modum actionis. Probatur consequentia: quia modus actionis, est egredi ab agente: sed actio fit in tempore: ergo participiũ significat cum tempore: cuius euidens signum est, quòd ei adiunguntur aduerbia hæc, tarde & velociter: quæ non conueniunt, nisi his, quæ significant motum, vel actionem, vt actio est. Distinguitur verò participium à verbo, per vltimam particulam, vt asserit D. Thom. quia licèt significet cum tempore, non vnit tamen extrema: in quo consistit propria, & vltima ratio verbi. Et ex his habemus, quòd consignificare tempus, non conuenit soli verbo, sed etiam participio: quòd videtur esse medium inter nomen, & verbum:

It is proved also by reason: Because the participle signifies action as it goes out from the agent: as heating signifies heating as going out from itself: therefore it signifies action by way of action. The consequence is proved: because the mode of action is to go out from the agent; but action takes place in time: therefore the participle signifies with time; a clear sign of which is that these adverbs, slowly and quickly, are joined to it, which do not belong except to those words that signify motion, or action as it is action. But the participle is distinguished from the verb by the last particle, as St. Thomas asserts: because, although it signifies with time, yet it does not unite the extremes, in which the proper and ultimate ratio of the verb consists. And from these things we have that to consignify time belongs not to the verb alone but also to the participle, which seems to be a medium between noun and verb.

> 21 Sed an puris nominibus conueniat, vt cœnæ, & prandio, ac similibus, Dicendum est, non conuenire: quia solùm significat actionem materialiter, vel vt res quædam est, non formaliter, & per modum actionis: vnde nec per modum, quo mensuratur tempore, gratia exẽpli, cœna significat actionem comedendi vt rem quandam: sicut albedo significat abedinem, non tamen significat eam ex parte sua, vt factam tali tempore: sed solùm habet tali tempore fieri, ex consuetudine hominum, non ex eo, quòd per tale nomen significatur: quod necessarium est ad consignificandum tempus. Nam verbum, ex eo dicitur consignificare tempus: quia significat actionem per modum actionis: & ideo, vt mensuratam tempore. Quare, ex vi suæ significationis, & non ex consuetudine, vel alia ratione extrinseca, dicitur simul cum actione significare tempus: & proinde illud consignificare. Et ex hoc intelligitur, consignificare tempus soli verbo, & participio conuenire, non puris nominibus.

21 But whether it belongs to pure nouns, as to dinner and lunch and the like: It must be said that it does not belong to them: because they signify action only materially, or as it is a certain thing, not formally and by way of action; hence not by the mode in which it is measured by time either. For example, dinner signifies the action of eating as a certain thing, just as whiteness signifies whiteness; yet it does not signify it on its own part as done at such a time, but it only has being done at such a time from the custom of men, not from the fact that it is signified by such a noun: which is what is necessary for consignifying time. For the verb is said to consignify time from the fact that it signifies action by way of action, and therefore as measured by time. Wherefore it is by force of its signification, and not from custom or some other extrinsic reason, that it is said to signify time together with the action, and consequently to consignify it. And from this it is understood that to consignify time belongs only to the verb and to the participle, not to pure nouns.

> Circa secundum verò, *An omnibus verbis & semper conueniat*: solùm est difficultas de verbo substantiuo, est: nam de cæteris satis est manifestum, quòd significent cum tempore. Et ratio, [p. 523] dubitandi est: quia solùm significat existentiam simpliciter, vel existentiam rei, sub aliqua forma accidentali: primum habet, in hac propositione, Homo est: secundum in hac, Homo est albus. Dicendum tamen est, communi sententia interpretum: *Non significare actionem veram, sed existentiam rei per modum actionis*, hoc satis esse, vt significet cum tempore: quia existentia significata per modum actionis, significatur vt mensurata tempore: nam sicut actio, ex se mensuratur tempore, ita etiam, quod per modum actionis significatur: & ideo verbum, est, significans existentiam rei per modum actionis, consequenter significat tempus: quod propriè est consignificare tempus, vel significare cum tempore.

But concerning the second, Whether it belongs to all verbs, and always, the only difficulty is about the substantive verb is: for about the others it is manifest enough that they signify with time. And the reason [p. 523] for doubting is: because it signifies only existence simply, or the existence of a thing under some accidental form: it has the first in this proposition, Man is; the second in this one, Man is white. It must nevertheless be said, with the common opinion of the interpreters: It does not signify true action, but the existence of a thing by way of action; and this is enough for it to signify with time: because existence signified by way of action is signified as measured by time; for just as action is of itself measured by time, so too is what is signified by way of action; and therefore the verb is, signifying the existence of a thing by way of action, consequently signifies time: which is properly to consignify time, or to signify with time.

> Sed, *an semper hoc habeat*: hoc est, in propositionibus etiam, in quibus solùm vnit extrema, secundùm naturalem connexionem prædicati cum subiecto: in quibus dicitur absolui à tempore, maxima difficultas est: quia non ab omnibus eodem modo explicatur, quid sit verbum in his propositionibus absolui à tempore, vel quo modo possit absolui à tempore, & simul significare cum tempore.

But whether it always has this, that is, even in propositions in which it unites the extremes only according to the natural connection of the predicate with the subject, in which it is said to be absolved from time, is the greatest difficulty: because it is not explained by all in the same way what it is for the verb in these propositions to be absolved from time, or in what way it can be absolved from time and at the same time signify with time.

> 21 Omissis autem aliorum explicationibus: quia non videntur satisfacere difficultati; Notandum est, *Verbum duo habere*: duabus particulis definitionis, ab Arist. explicatæ, contenta. Primum, Consignificare tempus. Secundum, Vnire extrema, quod explicuit Arist. vltima particula definitionis. *Et est semper eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur, nota*. Hoc est coniunctionis prædicati cum subiecto, quam facit. Extrema autem vnit, secundùm naturam eorum: ita, vt si prædicatum dicat actualem existentiam, vel actualem inhærentiam in subiecto, illud cum eo vniat secundùm actualem existẽtiam, vel inhærentiam in eo: & in hoc sensu vera, vel falsa, iudicanda sit propositio. Si verò prædicatum non dicat actualem existentiam, vel inhærentiam in subiecto, sed essentialem, aut necessariam connexionem cum eo, secundùm hanc, & non secundùm illam, ipsum vniat subiecto: exemplum vtriusque habemus in his propositionibus, homo est albus: homo est rationalis: nam in prima, prædicatum dicit actualem inhęrentiam in subiecto, & secundùm eam ei vnitur: in secunda verò, essentialem connexionem gradus rationalis, cum homine: abstrahentem ab actuali existentia: nam licèt nullus sit homo in rerum natura, tamen verum est, hominem esse rationalem.

21 Leaving aside, however, the explanations of others, because they do not seem to satisfy the difficulty: It should be noted that the verb has two things, contained in two particles of the definition explained by Aristotle. First, To consignify time. Second, To unite the extremes, which Aristotle explained by the last particle of the definition, And it is always a sign of those things that are predicated of another: that is, of the conjunction of the predicate with the subject, which it effects. Now it unites the extremes according to their nature: so that if the predicate expresses actual existence, or actual inherence in the subject, it unites it with the subject according to actual existence or inherence in it, and in this sense the proposition is to be judged true or false. But if the predicate does not express actual existence or inherence in the subject, but an essential or necessary connection with it, it unites it to the subject according to this and not according to that. We have an example of each in these propositions, Man is white, Man is rational: for in the first the predicate expresses actual inherence in the subject, and according to it is united to it; but in the second it expresses the essential connection of the grade rational with man, abstracting from actual existence: for although no man exists in the nature of things, yet it is true that man is rational.

> Circa consignificationem etiam temporis, & extremorum vnionem, duo consideramus in verbo. Primum, *Quòd essentiale est ei*, nempe consignificare tempus, vniendo extrema. [p. 524] Secundum, *Quasi accidentale*, nempe consignificare tempus, & vnire extrema pro tempore significato. Itaque essentiale est verbo vnire extrema, consignificando tempus: sed ea vnire, pro determinata differentia temporis significata, solùm est accidentale: & ideo ex natura extremorum, iudicandum est, an hoc efficiat verbum in propositione, vel non. Nam si apta sint pro ea differentia coniungi, ita coniungentur: si verò non sint apta pro ea coniungi, suspendetur talis modus coniunctionis, & vnientur simpliciter, absque tali determinatione, vel restrictione, & quidem extrema propositionum accidentalium vel modum accidentalem habentium, non necessariò, sed contingenter vniuntur; cùm accidens, aut habens modum accidentis, possit vniri subiecto: quare non sunt apta vniri, nisi pro determinata differentia temporis; & ideo in talibus propositionibus, verbum vnit extrema, pro determinata differentia temporis, quam consignificat: nempe pro tempore præsenti, præterito, & futuro.

Concerning the consignification of time also, and the union of the extremes, we consider two things in the verb. First, What is essential to it, namely to consignify time in uniting the extremes. [p. 524] Second, What is as it were accidental, namely to consignify time and to unite the extremes for the time signified. Thus it is essential to the verb to unite the extremes while consignifying time; but to unite them for a determinate difference of time signified is only accidental; and therefore it must be judged from the nature of the extremes whether the verb effects this in the proposition or not. For if they are apt to be conjoined for that difference, they will be so conjoined; but if they are not apt to be conjoined for it, such a mode of conjunction will be suspended, and they will be united simply, without such determination or restriction. And indeed the extremes of accidental propositions, or of those having an accidental mode, are united not necessarily but contingently, since an accident, or what has the mode of an accident, is able to be united to the subject; wherefore they are not apt to be united except for a determinate difference of time; and therefore in such propositions the verb unites the extremes for a determinate difference of time, which it consignifies, namely for present, past, and future time.

> 22 Extrema verò propositionum necessariarum, dicunt naturalem connexionem cum verbo eodem modo se habentem semper: quare non petunt vniri pro determinata differentia temporis, sed absolutè, & simpliciter, abstrahendo à qualibet differentia temporis: & ideo non vniuntur cum limitatione, vel restrictione ad aliquam differentiam temporis, sed secundùm naturalem, & necessariam connexionem, abstrahentem ab illa. Vnit igitur verbum, in his propositionibus extrema, sed non coarctat vnionem, ad differentiam temporis, quam consignificat, sed relinquit in propria natura, & conditione. Et hoc est *absolui à tempore*, hoc est etiam tales propositiones esse perpetuæ veritati: quemadmodum eorum connexio necessaria est, atque perpetua, & semper eodem modo se habens, nec à tempore vllo modo dependens. Igitur sat est explicatum, quomodo conueniat omni verbo, consignificare tempus, & semper ei conueniat: & quid sit absolui à tempore: & quomodo non repugnet semper consignificare tempus, & aliquando absolui à tempore.

22 But the extremes of necessary propositions express a natural connection, holding always in the same way, with the verb; wherefore they do not demand to be united for a determinate difference of time, but absolutely and simply, abstracting from any difference of time whatever; and therefore they are not united with a limitation or restriction to some difference of time, but according to their natural and necessary connection, which abstracts from it. The verb, therefore, unites the extremes in these propositions, but does not narrow the union to the difference of time which it consignifies; rather it leaves it in its own nature and condition. And this is to be absolved from time, that is, also, that such propositions are of perpetual truth, just as their connection is necessary and perpetual, always holding in the same way, and in no way depending on time. It has therefore been sufficiently explained how to consignify time belongs to every verb, and always belongs to it; and what it is to be absolved from time; and how it is not inconsistent always to consignify time and sometimes to be absolved from time.

> Et ex hac doctrina soluta sunt argumenta, in principio posita. Nam ad primum, Distinguenda est minor, quia quædam sunt verba, quæ significant veram actionem: alia, quæ significant aliquid per modum actionis: vt substantiua, nempe existentiam rei: & cùm existentia, significata per modum actionis: significetur ex consequenti per modum eius, quod mensuratur tempore, etiam verba substantiua consignificant tempus quod etiam habent in propositionibus necessariis, in quibus dicuntur absolui à tempore: quia non repugnat significare [p. 525] tempus, & absolui à tempore, vt explicatum est.

And by this doctrine the arguments placed at the beginning are solved. For to the first: The minor must be distinguished, because some verbs signify true action, others something by way of action, as the substantive verbs, namely the existence of a thing; and since existence signified by way of action is consequently signified by way of that which is measured by time, the substantive verbs too consignify time; which they have also in necessary propositions, in which they are said to be absolved from time: because there is nothing inconsistent in signifying [p. 525] time and being absolved from time, as has been explained.

> Ad secundum, Distinguendum est antecedens, quòd cœna, & prandium, significent actionem, per modum actionis: solùm enim eam significant materialiter, vt rem quandam, sicut cætera nomina: & ideo non connotando, quòd tali tempore fiat: sed hoc quod est tali tempore fieri, ab extrinseco prouenit, ex hominum consuetudine, & non ex vi significationis eorum: quare non sufficit, vt dicantur significare cum tempore, vel consignificare tempus.

To the second: The antecedent, that dinner and lunch signify action by way of action, must be distinguished: for they signify it only materially, as a certain thing, like the other nouns; and therefore not by connoting that it takes place at such a time; but this, its taking place at such a time, comes from without, from the custom of men, and not from the force of their signification: wherefore it does not suffice for them to be said to signify with time, or to consignify time.

## QUESTION II

> QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

> *An verbum sit vera pars propositionis.*

Whether the verb is a true part of the proposition.

> PRima opinio, tenet *verbum non esse partem propositionis*: sed quasi partium ligamentum. Ita Scotus in 1. editione Summularum, & alij cum eo, & probatur primò, ex compositione domus: in qua ligna, & lapides, concurrunt tanquam partes: claui verò quibus vniuntur ligna, & ligamentum, quo vniuntur lapides, non sunt partes, sed partium nexus: sed ita se habet verbum in propositione, cùm sit copula per quam vniuntur partes: ergo non est pars propositionis.

he first opinion holds that the verb is not a part of the proposition, but T          as it were the binding of the parts. So Soto in the 1st edition of the Summulae, and others with him; and it is proved first from the composition of a house, in which the timbers and the stones concur as parts, but the nails by which the timbers are united, and the mortar by which the stones are united, are not parts but the bond of the parts: but the verb stands so in the proposition, since it is the copula through which the parts are united: therefore it is not a part of the proposition.

> Secundò, ex eisdem partibus componitur res quælibet, in quas absoluitur: sed propositio solùm resoluitur in extrema quæ sunt subiectum, & prædicatum: ergo solùm componitur ex subiecto, & prædicato, tanquam ex partibus: quare non verbum erit pars, cùm nec subiectum, nec prædicatum. Probatur minor, ex Arist. 1. lib. de Priori resolutione, c. 1. sic definiente terminum: *Terminus est extremum propositionis, in quod propositio resoluitur, tanquam in subiectum & prædicatum*.

Second: every thing is composed of the same parts into which it is resolved; but the proposition is resolved only into the extremes, which are the subject and the predicate: therefore it is composed only of the subject and the predicate as of parts: wherefore the verb will not be a part, since it is neither subject nor predicate. The minor is proved from Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, who defines the term thus: A term is the extreme of a proposition, into which the proposition is resolved, as into subject and predicate.

> 23 Secunda opinio, de verbo saltem substantiuo, *est*, asserit, *non esse partem propositionis*: quia nullam actionem significat, quæ possit prædicari de subiecto: ita Villalpandeus, & Suesanus c. præsenti.

23 The second opinion asserts, at least of the substantive verb is, that it is not a part of the proposition: because it signifies no action that can be predicated of the subject: so Villalpando and Suessanus on the present chapter.

> Tertia opinio, tenet, *verbum duo habere*. Primum, quod significet aliquam rem, in quo conuenit cum nomine. Secundum quòd vnit extrema: & ratione primi, est pars propositionis, ratione verò secundi, non est pars, sed nexus partium: ita tenent quidam moderni.

The third opinion holds that the verb has two things. First, that it signifies some thing, in which it agrees with the noun. Second, that it unites the extremes: by reason of the first it is a part of the proposition, but by reason of the second it is not a part but the bond of the parts. So certain moderns hold.

> Communis sententia & vera, duo asserit. Primum, *Verbum esse partem propositionis, quasi materialem ratione rei significatæ*. Secundum, *Esse partem formalem, per proprium officium verbi, quod est vnire extrema*. Ita Porphy. Ammonius, Boëtius, Albertus [p. 526] Magnus, D. Thom. & Toletus cap. præsenti.

The common and true opinion asserts two things. First, That the verb is a part of the proposition, as it were material, by reason of the thing signified. Second, That it is a formal part, through the proper office of the verb, which is to unite the extremes. So Porphyry, Ammonius, Boethius, Albert [p. 526] the Great, St. Thomas, and Toledo on the present chapter.

> Vt autem vtrumque explicamus, atque probemus simul: Norandum est duo habere. Verbum Primum, *Rem aliquam significare cum tempore*, nempe, actionem, vel aliquid per modum actionis quod habet non solùm in propositione, sed etiam extra illam: vt expressè docuit Arist. in fine præcedentis ca. *Curro* enim, significat actionem currendi cum tempore: & verbum substantiuum, *est*, existentiam rei per modum actionis. Habet secundùm, Quod est, *esse notam eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur*, (vt verbis Aristot. vtamur) quod non est aliud, quàm esse signum compositionis prædicati cum subiecto: nam ita consignificat cum tempore: vt ea applicet subiecto: vnde hoc secundum, est quasi propria, & vltima differentia verbi, per quam constituitur in ratione formali, & essentiali verbi, quod non exercet, nisi in propositione, licèt aptum semper sit, exercere talem actum. Gratia exempli, in hac propositione, homo currit, sic actionem currendi significat cum tempore, vt eam applicet homini. Et cùm hæc applicatio sit formalis compositio prædicati cum subiecto, verum est, quòd verbum continet, atque significat formalem compositionem prædicati cum subiecto. Itaque cursus, in eadem propositione est, qui componitur cum homine, & prædicatur de illo: sed verbum *curro* est, quod illum cum homine componit, quod illum de homine prædicat: cursus etiam est prædicatum, *quod*, sed verbum curro, est quasi prædicatum, *quo*: cùm sit ratio, & quasi forma enunciandi: & tandem cursus, est quasi materiale prædicatum, verbum verò quasi formale. Et ideo D. Thom. asseruit, *Verbum non solùm ratione rei significatæ, se tenere ex parte prædicati, cùm de subiecto illa enuncietur, sed etiam vt est nota compositionis*: cùm hoc modo sit quasi prædicatum formale: & ita ex vtroque est prædicatum propositionis: ex primo quidem, quasi materiale, & vt quod: cùm res ab eo significata sit: quæ prædicatur: ex secundo, verò, quasi forma, & vt quo: cùm sit signum compositionis, & prædicationis eiusdem prædicati cum subiecto.

But in order that we may explain and prove both at once, it should be noted that the verb has two things. First, To signify some thing with time, namely an action, or something by way of action, which it has not only in the proposition but also outside it, as Aristotle expressly taught at the end of the preceding chapter. For I run signifies the action of running with time; and the substantive verb is, the existence of a thing by way of action. It has, second, What is to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another (to use Aristotle’s words), which is nothing other than to be a sign of the composition of the predicate with the subject: for it consignifies with time in such a way as to apply the thing to the subject; whence this second is as it were the proper and ultimate difference of the verb, through which it is constituted in the formal and essential ratio of a verb, which it does not exercise except in the proposition, although it is always apt to exercise such an act. For example, in this proposition, Man runs, it signifies the action of running with time in such a way as to apply it to man. And since this application is the formal composition of the predicate with the subject, it is true that the verb contains and signifies the formal composition of the predicate with the subject. Thus in the same proposition it is running that is composed with man and is predicated of him; but it is the verb runs that composes it with man, that predicates it of man: running is also the predicate which, but the verb I run is as it were the predicate by which, since it is the ratio and as it were the form of enunciating; and finally running is as it were the material predicate, but the verb as it were the formal one. And therefore St. Thomas asserted that the verb, not only by reason of the thing signified, holds itself on the side of the predicate, since that is enunciated of the subject, but also as it is a sign of composition: since in this way it is as it were the formal predicate; and so on both counts it is the predicate of the proposition: on the first, as it were material, and as that which, since the thing signified by it is what is predicated; on the second, as it were the form, and as that by which, since it is the sign of the composition and predication of the same predicate with the subject.

> Secundò, Norandum, duobus modis contingere, *Verbum applicare subiecto rem à se significatam*. Vno modo, nudam quidem aut solam, dum propositio non habet aliud prædicatum, præter verbum. Quod patet in propositionibus de secundo adiacente, vt homo currit: in quibus solam actionem significatam componit verbum cum subiecto, vel eam de illo prædicat. Altero modo, nudam aut solam: sed coniunctam alteri prędicato, & modificatam per illud, vt in propositionibus de tertio adiacente [p. 527], vt Homo est albus, in quibus non solũ esse, quod significatur per verbum, enunciatur, se coniunctum cum albedine: & ita sensus eiusdem propositionis est, homo est ens, affectum albedine: & primo modo, totale prædicatum est significatum verbis, secundo verò modo quasi partiale, sed vtroque modo est prædicatum materiale, & verbũ semper formale: quia semper significat, & facit compositionem prædicati cum subiecto.

Second, it should be noted that it can happen in two ways that the verb applies to the subject the thing signified by it. In one way, bare or alone, when the proposition has no other predicate besides the verb. Which is plain in propositions of the second adjacent, as Man runs, in which the verb composes only the signified action with the subject, or predicates it of him. In the other way, not bare or alone, but conjoined to another predicate and modified by it, as in propositions of the third adjacent [p. 527] as Man is white, in which there is enunciated not only being, which is signified by the verb, but being conjoined with whiteness; and so the sense of the same proposition is: man is a being affected with whiteness. And in the first way the total predicate is what is signified by the verb, but in the second way it is as it were a partial one; but in both ways it is the material predicate, and the verb is always the formal one: because it always signifies and makes the composition of the predicate with the subject.

> Ex hac doctrina, colliguntur duo argumenta: quibus efficaciter probantur duo illa, quæ nostra sententia, & communis asserit. Primum arg. probat, *Verbum, ratione rei à se significatæ, esse prædicatum propositionis materiale, & vt quod, & ex consequenti veram partem eius*: & est tale: Verbum significat actionem vel aliquid per modum actionis, sed hoc est, quod prædicatur de subiecto: nudum quidem, in propositionibus de secundo adiacente: vel coniunctum cum alio prædicato, vt in propositionibus de tertio adiacente: ergo verbum per rem à se significatam, semper est prædicatum totale, vel partiale propositionis: & proinde semper est pars propositionis.

From this doctrine two arguments are gathered, by which those two things which our opinion, and the common one, asserts are efficaciously proved. The first argument proves that the verb, by reason of the thing signified by it, is the material predicate of the proposition, and as that which, and consequently a true part of it; and it is this: The verb signifies an action, or something by way of action; but this is what is predicated of the subject: bare, indeed, in propositions of the second adjacent, or conjoined with another predicate, as in propositions of the third adjacent: therefore the verb, through the thing signified by it, is always the total or the partial predicate of the proposition; and consequently it is always a part of the proposition.

> Secundum arg probat, *Verbum semper esse prædicatum propositionis formale, & vt quo: atque adeò, partem formalem eius*: & procedi, hoc modo: Propositio formaliter, est cõpositio prædicati cum subiecto: sed verbũ est signũ formale huius cõpositionis, eam faciens: ergo est ratio formalis eius: & ideo formalis pars: sicut anima est pars formalis viuentis, quod componit, tribuẽs ei esse tanquam vera eius forma. Verbum namque vnit de subiecto per rem à se significatam, & simul est signum formale, efficiens eandem vnionem: & ideo est quasi forma, tribuens propositioni vitam, ea similitudine, qua anima tribuit corpori esse, & viuere, per informationem. Et veritas hæc ostendit deceptionem aliarum opinionum, quę putant verbum solùm esse materialem nexum propositionis, ita, vt solùm materialiter vniat prædicatum cum subiecto: sicut lapides domus vniuntur calce, vel ligna clauo: cùm tamẽ hoc plenè sit falsum, nam verbum sic vnit prædicatum subiecto, vt semper vniat rem à se significatam: ratione cuius, verũ prædicatum propositionis est, veraque pars eius: sic etiam vnit, vt formale signum sit, eiusdẽ compositionis prædicati cum subiecto: & signum quidem non solùm significatiuum, sed simul factiuum formaliter: quod est esse formam totius propositionis: & ideo partẽ formalem eius.

The second argument proves that the verb is always the formal predicate of the proposition, and as that by which, and so its formal part; and it proceeds in this way: The proposition, formally, is the composition of the predicate with the subject; but the verb is the formal sign of this composition, making it: therefore it is its formal ratio, and therefore a formal part: just as the soul is the formal part of the living thing which it composes, giving it being as its true form. For the verb unites with the subject through the thing signified by it, and at the same time it is the formal sign effecting the same union; and therefore it is as it were the form, giving life to the proposition, by that likeness by which the soul gives being and living to the body through informing it. And this truth shows the error of the other opinions, which think that the verb is only the material bond of the proposition, such that it unites the predicate with the subject only materially, as the stones of a house are united by mortar, or timbers by a nail: whereas this is entirely false; for the verb so unites the predicate to the subject that it always unites the thing signified by it, by reason of which it is a true predicate of the proposition and a true part of it; it also unites in such a way that it is the formal sign of the same composition of the predicate with the subject; and a sign not only significative but at the same time formally effective: which is to be the form of the whole proposition, and therefore its formal part.

> 25 Et si dicatur, Prædicatum esse partem formalem propositionis. Respõdeo: Comparatione subiecti, se habere tanquam formam: quia illud determinat, sed in ordine ad totam propositionem, tam subiectum, quàm prædicatum, sunt partes [p. 528] materiales, & forma totius propositionis, & earundem partium materialium, est verbum.

25 And if it is said, The predicate is the formal part of the proposition: I reply: in comparison with the subject it stands as form, because it determines it; but in relation to the whole proposition, both the subject and the predicate are [p. 528] material parts, and the form of the whole proposition, and of the same material parts, is the verb.

> Ex his facilè soluuntur argumenta primæ opinionis. Nam ad primum, neganda est minor: quòd verbum ita se habeat in propositione, sicut se habet ligamentum partium domus: non enim vnit prædicatum & subiectum materialiter, sed per modum formæ totius compositionis, vt explicatum est.

From these things the arguments of the first opinion are easily solved. For to the first, the minor must be denied: that the verb stands in the proposition as the binding of the parts of a house stands: for it does not unite the predicate and the subject materially, but by way of the form of the whole composition, as has been explained.

> Ad secundum: neganda est etiam minor: quòd propositio solùm soluatur in subiectum, & prædicatum, tanquam in partes: solùm enim in hæc resoluitur, tanquam in extremas partes, quas ideo vocat Aristoteles terminos eius: quia terminus non quamlibet partem rei significat, sed extremam: & aliquando non partem, sed indiuisibile extremum: quod nõ est vera pars, vt patet in termino lineæ. Verbum igitur, vera pars formalis propositionis est, licèt non sint extrema: quod intelligo in ratione formali verbi: nam per rem à se significatam, quam applicat subiecto, & de eo prædicat, etiam est extrema pars propositionis, cùm sit prædicatum eius.

To the second: the minor too must be denied: that the proposition is resolved only into the subject and the predicate as into parts: for it is resolved into these alone as into its extreme parts, which Aristotle therefore calls its terms: because a term signifies not any part whatever of a thing, but the extreme one; and sometimes not a part but an indivisible extreme, which is not a true part, as is plain in the term of a line. The verb, therefore, is a true formal part of the proposition, although it is not an extreme: which I understand of the formal ratio of the verb: for through the thing signified by it, which it applies to the subject and predicates of it, it is also an extreme part of the proposition, since it is its predicate.

## QUESTION III

> QVÆSTIO III.

[…]

> *An verbum infinitum possit collocari in propositione.*

Whether the infinite verb can be placed in a proposition.

> QVæstio hæc, vnum præsupponit, tanquam certum apud Arist. & omnes, videlicet *dari verbum infinitum extra propositionem*: quod docuit expressè Aristot. cap. præsenti illud excludens à definitione verbi: & cum eo omnes interpretes. Sed quærit aliud, An verbum infinitum, non solùm detur extra propositionem, sed etiam possit in propositione collocari.

his question presupposes one thing as certain with Aristotle and with Tall, namely that there is an infinite verb outside the proposition: which Aristotle expressly taught in the present chapter, excluding it from the definition of the verb; and with him all the interpreters. But it asks something else: Whether the infinite verb is not only found outside the proposition but can also be placed in the proposition.

> Et est prima opinio, antiquorum Interpretum, Alberti Magni, & Boëtij, in hoc capite: *non posse collocari in propositione*. Quod probatur duplici arg. Primo: Quia verbum fit infinitũ, sicut nomen, per negationem, non neganter, sed infinitanter sumptam: ita vt vis eius vlteriùs non transeat, sed nomen, aut verbum cui adiungitur, solùm neget: at repugnat negationem adiungi verbo in propositione, nisi neganter sumptam: ergo repugnat infinitari: verbum in propositione. Probatur minor, quia repugnat negationem adiungi verbo in propositione, quin propositio negetur: sed nõ potest esse propositio negatiua, nisi negatio adiuncta verbo sumatur neganter, vt per se est manifestum: ergo repugnat sumi infinitanter additam verbo in propositione: & ex consequenti, repugnat verbum infinitari.

And the first opinion, that of the ancient Interpreters, Albert the Great and Boethius, on this chapter, is that it cannot be placed in a proposition. This is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because the verb becomes infinite, like the noun, through a negation taken not as negating but as infinitizing, so that its force does not pass further, but it negates only the noun or verb to which it is joined; but it is inconsistent for a negation to be joined to the verb in a proposition unless it is taken as negating: therefore it is inconsistent for the verb to be infinitized in a proposition. The minor is proved: because it is inconsistent for a negation to be joined to the verb in a proposition without the proposition being negated; but it cannot be a negative proposition unless the negation joined to the verb is taken as negating, as is manifest of itself: therefore it is inconsistent for it to be taken as infinitizing when added to the verb in a proposition; and consequently it is inconsistent for the verb to be infinitized.

[p. 529]

> Secundo negatio infinitanter sumpta, negat omninò illud, cui adiungitur, licèt vis eius vlteriùs non transeat: ergo adiuncta verbo, nõ solùm negat significatum eius, sed propriũ etiam officium verbi, quòd est esse notam eorum, quæ de altero prædicantur: atqui negato officio verbi, redditur propositio negatiua: ergo non infinitatur verbum. Probatur cõsequentia: quia non potest esse negatiua propositio, nisi negatio eius neganter accipiatur: Sumpta autem neganter non potest verbum infinitũ reddere, sed negatiuũ, vt patet in propositionibus negatiuis.

Second: a negation taken as infinitizing altogether negates that to which it is joined, although its force does not pass further: therefore, joined to the verb, it negates not only its significate but also the proper office of the verb, which is to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another; but when the office of the verb is negated, the proposition is rendered negative: therefore the verb is not infinitized. The consequence is proved: because a proposition cannot be negative unless its negation is taken as negating; but taken as negating it cannot render the verb infinite, but negative, as is plain in negative propositions.

> Secunda opinio tenet, *non solùm extra propositionem dari verbum infinitum, sed etiam in propositione*: ita Ammonius, Suesanus. Toletus c. præsenti, Sotus, & Mercatus, 1. lib. Summularum, ca. 2. de verbo, & omnes moderni interpretes. Videtúrque nobis probabilior. Probatur primò duobus testimoniis Arist. nam c. præsenti, sic loquitur de verbo infinito: *Non valet autem, & non laborat, non verbum dico: consignificat enim tempus, & semper de aliquo est*. Quasi dicat, semper de aliquo prædicatur: sed non potest prædicari, nisi in propositione: ergo sentit Arist. in propositione posse infinitari. Secundum testimonium habetur lib. 1. posteriorum, c. 10. vbi hanc demonstrationem constituit Arist. in prima figura: *Stellæ non micantes, sunt prope nos: planetæ non micant: ergo planetæ sunt prope nos*. Quæ tamen vitiosus erit syllogismus, si negatio in minori sumatur neganter: nam tunc constituet propositionem negatiuam: minore autem negatiua, viua, vitiosus est syllogismus in prima figura: ergo necesse est infinitanter accipi ab Arist. ita vt sensus sit, planetæ sunt non micantes: & ita efficiet verbum infinitum in propositione. Probatur etiam ratione: quia verbum extra propositionem est infinitum: ergo negatio ei adiuncta, non accipitur neganter, sed infinitanter: vel ergo negat totum, quod habet verbum, nempe significatum eius, & officium copulæ, vel solùm significatum: si primum dicatur, sequitur posse esse infinitum in propositione, licèt totum, quod habet, negetur: & etiam sequitur, si dicatur secundum: quia si solùm negetur significatum eius, non efficiet propositionem negatiuam: sed affirmatiuam de prædicato infinito: vt contingit in demonstratione Aristotelis adducta.

The second opinion holds that the infinite verb is found not only outside the proposition but also in the proposition: so Ammonius, Suessanus, Toledo on the present chapter, Soto and Mercado, Summulae bk. 1, ch. 1, on the verb, and all the modern interpreters. And it seems to us more probable. It is proved first by two testimonies of Aristotle: for in the present chapter he speaks thus of the infinite verb: But not-is-well and not-is-ill I do not call a verb: for it consignifies time, and is always of something. As if to say, it is always predicated of something; but it cannot be predicated except in a proposition: therefore Aristotle thinks that it can be infinitized in a proposition. The second testimony is found in Posterior Analytics 1, ch. 10, where Aristotle sets up this demonstration in the first figure: Things that do not twinkle are near us; the planets do not twinkle: therefore the planets are near us. This syllogism, however, will be faulty if the negation in the minor is taken as negating: for then it will make a negative proposition; but with a negative minor the syllogism in the first figure is faulty: therefore it must be taken by Aristotle as infinitizing, so that the sense is, the planets are non-twinkling; and so it will make an infinite verb in the proposition. It is proved also by reason: because the verb outside the proposition is infinite: therefore the negation joined to it is taken not as negating but as infinitizing: either, then, it negates the whole that the verb has, namely its significate and the office of the copula, or only the significate: if the first is said, it follows that it can be infinite in the proposition, even though the whole that it has is negated; and the same also follows if the second is said: because if only its significate is negated, it will not make a negative proposition, but an affirmative one with an infinite predicate, as happens in the demonstration of Aristotle adduced.

> Vt autem veritas huius sententiæ fiat manifesta, & faciliùs soluantur argumenta alterius, notandum est, Differentiam sententiæ vtriusque in eo solùm consistere: quòd prima asserit, *E duobus, quæ habet verbum*, nempe significare rem cum tempore, & esse notam eorum, quæ de altero prędicantur, *primum tantùm ei conuenire extra propositionem: secundum verò non nisi in propositione [p. 530] exerceri*: & ideò extra propositionem posse infinitari: quia potest negari totum, quod in eo statu habet: in propositione verò, non posse: quia non potest ei adiungi negatio, nisi negetur vtrumque: negato autem vtroque, propositio constituitur negatiua: & ideo negatio sumitur neganter, & non potest ipsum efficere infinitum.

But in order that the truth of this opinion may become manifest, and the arguments of the other be more easily solved, it should be noted that the difference between the two opinions consists only in this: that the first asserts that, of the two things which the verb has, namely to signify a thing with time and to be a sign of those things that are predicated of another, the first alone belongs to it outside the proposition, but the second only in the proposition Ll [p. 530] is exercised; and therefore that outside the proposition it can be infinitized, because the whole which it has in that state can be negated; but in the proposition it cannot, because a negation cannot be joined to it without both being negated; and when both are negated, the proposition is constituted negative; and therefore the negation is taken as negating and cannot make it infinite.

> Secunda verò opinio, quam sequimur: non putat necessarium, *quòd negatio adiuncto verbo in propositione neget vtrumque*: sed sicut extra propositionem ei adiunctã, potest negare solùm significatum, non negata compositionis nota: ita in propositione potest illud solùm negare: non negata eadem compositionis nota: & ita potest verbum infinitari, & constituere propositionem affirmatiuam, de prædicato infinito, & huius ratio est, quia duo illa distincta sunt in verbo: ergo potest negari primum, non negato secundo. Præterea, In eo, quod est rem aliquam significare, conuenit verbum cum nomine: & ideò quantum ad hoc, infinitari potest, per negationem, non tamen quantum ad notam compositionis: quia cùm hæc limitetur ad hoc prædicatum, & hoc subiectum, siquidem verbum coniungit necesse est coniunctione hac, seu compositione negata, totam propositionem negari: & ideo negationem neganter sumi: non enim datur medium in compositione ipsa inter negatiuam: & affirmatiuam nec infinita esse potest propositio, vt propositio est formaliter: licèt possit esse infinita, ex parte prædicati, aut ex parte subiecti.

But the second opinion, which we follow, does not think it necessary that the negation joined to the verb in the proposition negate both; but just as, joined to it outside the proposition, it can negate only the significate, without the mark of composition being negated, so in the proposition it can negate that alone, without the same mark of composition being negated; and so the verb can be infinitized and constitute an affirmative proposition with an infinite predicate. And the reason of this is that those two things are distinct in the verb: therefore the first can be negated without the second being negated. Moreover, in that which is to signify some thing, the verb agrees with the noun; and therefore as to this it can be infinitized through negation, but not as to the mark of composition: because, since this is limited to this predicate and this subject, inasmuch as the verb conjoins them, it is necessary that, when this conjunction or composition is negated, the whole proposition be negated, and therefore that the negation be taken as negating: for there is no medium in the composition itself between negative and affirmative; nor can a proposition be infinite as it is formally a proposition, although it can be infinite on the side of the predicate or on the side of the subject.

> 28 Ad primum arg. neganda est minor: quòd non possit negatio adiungi verbo in propositione, nisi neganter sumpta, aut nisi fiat eo ipso propositio negatiua: potest enim solùm negare significatum verbi, non negata vnione eiusdem cum subiecto: vt fit extra propositionem: quia distincta est vtraque ratio in verbo: & ideo potest negatio cadere sub vna, & non sub alia, vt probatum est, in verbum.

28 To the first argument, the minor must be denied: that a negation cannot be joined to the verb in a proposition unless it is taken as negating, or unless by that very fact the proposition becomes negative: for it can negate only the significate of the verb, without its union with the subject being negated, as happens outside the proposition: because each ratio is distinct in the verb; and therefore the negation can fall under the one and not under the other, as has been proved, upon the verb.
