He says, therefore, that the question proceeds only about singular propositions about the contingent future: whether one of them is determinately true and the other determinately false. And the reason for doubting is manifest: because a contingent or free cause is not determined to a future effect, but can determine itself and can not determine itself; and therefore, as long as its future determination is enunciated by a singular proposition about the future, so long does it remain as it were suspended; and therefore the truth of that same proposition always seems indeterminate.

> Respondet autem Arist. In his propositionibus, determinatè verum esse totum disiunctum, ex vtraque contradictoria constans. Vt Petrus peccabit, aut non peccabit: nam peccare, aut non peccare, ita necessarium est, sicut esse, vel non esse: ergo ita determinatè verum Sed vtramlibet contradictoriam per se sumptam, non esse determinatè veram, aut falsam, vt Petrus peccabit, atque etiam Petrus non peccabit. Quod probat duplici arg. ducente ad impossibile. Primò: Quia si determinatè essent veræ, nihil esset in rebus contingens, sed omnia euenirent necessariò: vt si determinatè verum esset, Petrus hoc efficiet, aut illud: studiosus, aut vitiosus erit: bellum erit futurum cras, vel non erit futurum, necessariò euenirent effectus isti: & ideo non possent non euenire: quare nihil esset in rebus contingens, quod est absurdum.

Aristotle replies, however, that in these propositions the whole disjunction made up of both contradictories is determinately true, as Peter will sin or will not sin: for to sin or not to sin is as necessary as to be or not to be; therefore it is likewise determinately true. But either contradictory taken by itself is not determinately true or false, as Peter will sin, and also Peter will not sin. This he proves by a twofold argument leading to the impossible. First: because if they were determinately true, nothing in things would be contingent, but all things would come about necessarily; as, if it were determinately true that Peter will do this or that, will be virtuous or vicious, that a battle will take place tomorrow or will not take place, those effects would come about necessarily, and therefore could not fail to come about; wherefore nothing in things would be contingent, which is absurd.

> Secunda ratio: Quia si propositiones istæ singulares de futuro contingenti essent determinatè veræ, & omnes futuri effectus, necessariò euenirent, neque aliquis esset effectus contingens, non esset consultandum de rebus futuris, nec deliberandum: quare nec esset consilium, nec libertas: nam deliberatio [p. 547], & consultatio, solùm est de rebus contingentibus: quæ possunt esse, & non esse: de his enim quæ necessariò futura sunt, vt de ortu solis crastino, nullus vnquam suæ mentis consultandum esse dixit. Tollere autem contingentiam, consilium, deliberationem, imò, & libertatem nostram, absurdum est: ergo non est dicendum propositiones singulares de futuro contingenti esse determinatè veras, aut determinatè falsas.

The second reason: because if these singular propositions about the contingent future were determinately true, and all future effects came about necessarily, and no effect were contingent, there would be no need to take counsel about future things, nor to deliberate; wherefore there would be neither counsel nor freedom: for delibe [p. 547] ration and consultation concern only contingent things, which can be and not be; for about things that will necessarily come to be, such as tomorrow’s sunrise, no one in his right mind ever said that one must take counsel. But to take away contingency, counsel, deliberation, nay, even our freedom, is absurd; therefore it must not be said that singular propositions about the contingent future are determinately true or determinately false.

> Explicat tandem duplicem distinctionem necessitatis rerum, & enunciationum. Prima talis est: *Quædam res sunt necessariæ ex propria natura*, vt cœlum: *aliæ verò, non nisi ex conditione temporis, quo mensurantur*: cùm tamen ex propria natura contingentes sint: vt Petrum ambulare, dum ambulat, necessarium est, non ex propria natura, sed ex conditione temporis, quo mensuratut ambulatio eius: & hoc modo verum esse vniuersaliter ait, quòd omnis res quando est, necessariò sit: & omnis propositio pro tempore, quo vera est, necessariò est vera, sed necessitatem primam simpliciter esse talem affirmat: secundam verò, non nisi secundùm quid: hoc est ab extrinseco, & ex suppositione temporis, in quo res est, vel in quo propositio vera est.

Finally he explains a twofold distinction of the necessity of things and of enunciations. The first is this: Some things are necessary from their own nature, as the heavens; others only from the condition of the time by which they are measured, although from their own nature they are contingent: as it is necessary that Peter walk while he walks, not from his own nature but from the condition of the time by which his walking is measured. And in this way he says it is universally true that every thing, when it is, necessarily is, and every proposition, for the time at which it is true, is necessarily true; but he affirms that the first necessity is such simply, while the second is such only in a qualified sense, that is, extrinsically and from the supposition of the time at which the thing is, or at which the proposition is true.

> Secunda est distinctio necessarij: *Quædam sunt necessaria absolutè*, id est, sine comparatione ad aliud: vt hominem esse animal. *Alia non nisi ex comparatione ad suum oppositum*: ita, vt quod per se sumptum contingens est, sumptum cum suo opposito fit necessarium: vt contingens est hæc, Petrus ambulabit, at si sumatur cum sua opposita, necessarium facit totum, disiunctum, vt, Petrus ambulabit, aut non ambulabit. Et hunc etiam modum necessitatis extrinsecum esse ait, & secundùm quid talem: cùm tamen primus simpliciter sit talis, & ab intrinseco. Et hunc modum necessitatis, atque etiam secundum, primæ distinctionis, reperiri docet in enunciationibus singularibus contingentibus de præsenti, præterito, & futuro: nam dum Petrus ambulat, necessarium est ex suppositione, ambulare: & etiam quòd ambulauerit, supposito, quòd ambulauit: & etiam est necessaria hæc de futuro, Petrus ambulabit, ex suppositione, quòd ambulabit. Necessarium quoque est disiunctum hoc, Petrus ambulabit, vel non ambulabit: sed cum vtraque hac necessitate totius disiuncti, & etiam cuiuslibet partis per se sumptæ, ex suppositione temporis verum est, quamlibet per se sumptam esse contingentem, & indeterminatè veram.

The second is the distinction of the necessary: Some things are necessary absolutely, that is, without comparison to another, as that man is an animal. Others only from comparison to their opposite, so that what, taken by itself, is contingent, taken together with its opposite is necessary: as this is contingent, Peter will walk; but if it is taken with its opposite, it makes the whole disjunction necessary, as Peter will walk or will not walk. And he says that this mode of necessity too is extrinsic and such in a qualified sense, whereas the first is such simply and intrinsically. And he teaches that this mode of necessity, and also the second of the first distinction, is found in singular contingent enunciations about the present, the past, and the future: for while Peter walks it is necessary, on the supposition, that he walk; and also that he has walked, on the supposition that he did walk; and this one about the future is also necessary, Peter will walk, on the supposition that he will walk. This disjunction too is necessary, Peter will walk or will not walk; but with both of these necessities, of the whole disjunction and also of each part taken by itself from the supposition of time, it is true that each, taken by itself, is contingent and indeterminately true. MM ij

[p. 548]

## Quæst. vnic. An singulares enunciationes de futuro contingenti habeant veritatem, aut falsitatem determinatam — SINGLE QUESTION. Whether singular enunciations about the contingent future have determinate truth or falsity.

> QVÆSTIO VNICA.

[…]

> *An singulares enunciationes de futuro contingenti, habeant veritatem, aut falsitatem determinatam.*

[…]

> De solis singularibus, & contingentibus procedit quæstio: nam propositiones necessariæ, atque etiam ex materia remota constantes, necessariò veræ sunt, vel necessariò falsæ: siue sint vniuersales, siue singulares: & ideo determinata est earum veritas, aut falsitas: determinatè etiam veræ sunt contingentes de subiecto vniuersali, aut determinatè falsæ: vt omnis homo ambulabit: nullus homo ambulabit: &, homo ambulabit: homo non ambulabit. Quia licèt effectus futurus, atque contingens, in singulari possit esse, & non esse, vniuersaliter tamen verum est, quòd causa contingens determinabitur ad operandum: imò necessaria est determinatio eius in singulari vago, licèt sit omnino contingens in quolibet singulari determinato. Necessitate quidem morali: quia moraliter loquendo, hoc est, more humano, vel vt res humanæ solent euenire, necesse est, homines ambulare: & ideo determinatè vera hæc, homo ambulabit: & aliquis homo ambulabit: & determinatè falsa, omnis homo ambulabit: nullus homo ambulabit. In hoc enim sensu accipitur illud Christi apud Matthæum: *Necesse est, vt veniant scandala.* Certum quoque est, singulares propositiones contingentes de præsenti, & præterito, esse determinatè veras, vel falsas: imò necessarias, non quidem ab intrinseco, vel simpliciter, sed ab extrinseco, & ex suppositione temporis: vt iã fuit à nobis expositum. Solùm ergo de singularibus de futuro contingenti quæstio esse potest: *An determinatam habeant veritatẽ, vel indeterminatam*: quia determinatio causæ futuræ, à qua pendet veritas earum, quamdiu futura enunciatur, indeterminata est: & ideo non videtur posse tribuere veritatem determinatam eisdem propositionibus.

The question proceeds only about singular and contingent ones: for necessary propositions, and also those consisting of remote matter, are necessarily true or necessarily false, whether they are universal or singular; and therefore their truth or falsity is determinate. Contingent ones with a universal subject are also determinately true or determinately false: as every man will walk, no man will walk; and, man will walk, man will not walk. Because, although a future and contingent effect can, in the singular, be and not be, it is nevertheless universally true that the contingent cause will be determined to operate; nay, its determination is necessary in the vague singular, although it is wholly contingent in any determinate singular. By a moral necessity, that is: because, speaking morally, that is, in the human manner, or as human affairs are wont to turn out, it is necessary that men walk; and therefore this is determinately true, man will walk, and some man will walk; and determinately false, every man will walk, no man will walk. For in this sense is taken that saying of Christ in Matthew: It must needs be that scandals come. It is also certain that singular contingent propositions about the present and the past are determinately true or false; nay, necessary, not indeed intrinsically or simply, but extrinsically and from the supposition of time, as was expounded by us. The question, then, can be only about singular ones about the contingent future: whether they have determinate truth, or indeterminate; because the determination of the future cause, on which their truth depends, is indeterminate as long as it is enunciated as future; and therefore it does not seem able to confer determinate truth on those same propositions.

> Ideò prima opinio asserit: *Nullam prorsus habere veritatem, aut falsitatem tales propositiones, sed neutras esse*: hoc est, nec veras, nec falsas. Ita Antonius Cordubensis, lib. 1. sui Quæstionarij, q. 55. dub. 2. Probatur: quia veritas, vel falsitas enunciationis sumitur, per conformitatem, aut difformitatem, ad rem significatam: sed res significata per hanc enunciationem: Petrus peccabit, non est in rerum natura, quamdiu enunciatur futura: ergo enunciatio ipsa non est ei conformis, nec deformis: quare non erit vera, neque falsa, sed neutra, & certè si vera, aut falsa [p. 549] concedatur, sequitur simul esse veram, & falsam, quod repugnat. Probatur consequentia: quia cùm res significata indifferens sit ad essendum, & non essendum, & non magis ad vnum, quàm ad alterum determinata, non est maior ratio, ob quam enunciatio sit vera, potiùs quàm falsa: quare vel neutrum habebit, vel vtrumque: & hoc impossibile: ergo aliud necessarium, quod est esse neutram.

Therefore the first opinion asserts: that such propositions have no truth or falsity at all, but are neutral, that is, neither true nor false. So Antonio de Córdoba, bk. 1 of his Quaestionarium, q. 55, doubt 2. It is proved: because the truth or falsity of an enunciation is taken from its conformity or disconformity to the thing signified; but the thing signified by this enunciation, Peter will sin, is not in the nature of things as long as it is enunciated as future; therefore the enunciation itself is neither conformed nor disconformed to it; wherefore it will be neither true nor false, but neutral. And certainly, if true or false [p. 549] is granted, it follows that it is at once true and false, which is repugnant. The consequence is proved: because, since the thing signified is indifferent to being and not being, and not determined to the one more than to the other, there is no greater reason why the enunciation should be true rather than false; wherefore it will have either neither or both; and the latter is impossible; therefore the other is necessary, namely that it is neutral.

> Secunda opinio: *Aliquam veritatem tribuit his enunciationibus*, non quidem determinatam, sed confusam, aut indeterminatam: ita vt totum disiunctum ex vtraque contradictoria cõpositum, sit determinatè verum, ac necessarium, vt Petrus disputabit, vel non disputabit: sed vtraque, earum per se sumpta indeterminatè, vera sit aut falsa, quod est dicere indifferentem esse ad veritatem, aut falsitatem: & ideo non esse actu veram, nec actu falsam, sed quasi in potentia, nondum determinata. Ita Alber. Mag. 1. lib. de interpretatione, tract. de oppositione, cap. 4. Catherinus in opus. de veritate enunciationum, Louanien. & Tolet. cap. præsenti. Et hæc videtur expressa sententia Aristotelis, qui eam probauit hac ratione: *Quod determinatè verum est, necessarium existimatur*: ergo si enunciatio singularis de futuro contingenti, determinatè vera est, erit necessaria. Ex quo sequitur, futura omnia necessariò euenire. Probatur consequentia: quia si hæc est necessariò vera, Petrus disputabit, disputatio Petri, à qua sumit suam veritatem, erit necessariò futura, & non contingens: quare nulla relinquetur libertas, nec locum habebit consilium, aut deliberatio: quia de rebus necessariò futuris non deliberamus: nec dicuntur esse in nostra potestate necessaria, sed contingentia solùm, quæ possunt euenire, & non euenire: sic, vel alio modo fieri.

The second opinion attributes some truth to these enunciations, not indeed determinate, but confused or indeterminate: so that the whole disjunction composed of both contradictories is determinately true and necessary, as Peter will dispute or will not dispute; but either of them, taken by itself, is indeterminately true or false, which is to say that it is indifferent to truth or falsity, and therefore is neither actually true nor actually false, but as it were in potency, not yet determined. So Albert the Great, On Interpretation bk. 1, tract. on opposition, ch. 4; Catharinus in his opuscule on the truth of enunciations; the Louvain commentators and Toledo on the present chapter. And this seems to be the express view of Aristotle, who proved it by this argument: What is determinately true is judged necessary; therefore, if a singular enunciation about the contingent future is determinately true, it will be necessary. From which it follows that all future things come about necessarily. The consequence is proved: because, if this is necessarily true, Peter will dispute, the disputation of Peter, from which it takes its truth, will be necessarily future and not contingent; wherefore no freedom will be left, nor will counsel or deliberation have any place, because we do not deliberate about things necessarily future; nor are necessary things said to be in our power, but only contingent ones, which can come about and not come about, be done in this way or in another.

> Probatur secundò: Nam ab eo quod res est, vel non est, enunciatio dicitur vera, vel falsa: sed res significata per enunciationem singularem de futuro contingenti, ita est determinata, vt quamdiu futura est, & vt talis enunciatur, nullam determinationem habeat: ergo nec propositio de futuro eam enuncians determinatam habebit veritatem: sed indeterminata, atque indifferens semper erit ad veritatem, & falsitatem.

It is proved, second: for from the fact that the thing is or is not, an enunciation is called true or false; but the thing signified by a singular enunciation about the contingent future is so determined that, as long as it is future and is enunciated as such, it has no determination; therefore neither will a proposition about the future enunciating it have determinate truth, but it will always be indeterminate and indifferent to truth and falsity.

> Tertia opinio, tenet, *Tales enunciationes habere determinatam veritatem, aut falsitatem: sed contingentem*: Et hæc est vera, & valde conformis fidei Catholicæ, quam tenet Scotus in 1. d. 3. qu. 1. §. ad argumeta principalia, D. Bona. d. 38. art. 3. qu. 1. ad 1. Richar. ar. 1. quæst. 5. ad 1. Greg. qu. 1. art. 2. Ocham, quæst. 1. ad principale, Gabriel quæst. 1. art. 1. notab. 7. Mars. quæ. 40. ad 3. Holcoth. in 2. quæ. art. 7. Sotus in cap. 9. Epistolæ ad Rom. p. 5. [p. 550] Pater Franciscus Suarius opus. de absoluta scientia futurorum contingentium, cap. 2. num. 6. P. Gabriel Vazques, tom. 1. primæ partis, disp. 67. cap. 3. & iam ferè omnes moderni nostri temporis.

The third opinion holds that such enunciations have determinate truth or falsity, but contingent. And this is true, and very much in conformity with the Catholic faith; it is held by Scotus on 1, d. 3, q. 1, § to the principal arguments; St. Bonaventure, d. 38, a. 3, q. 1, ad 1; Richard, a. 1, q. 5, ad 1; Gregory, q. 1, a. 2; Ockham, q. 1, to the principal argument; Gabriel, q. 1, a. 1, notable 7; Marsilius, q. 40, ad 3; Holcot on 2, q., a. 7; Soto on ch. 9 of the Epistle to the Romans, p. 5, Mm iij [p. 550] Father Francisco Suárez, opuscule on the absolute knowledge of future contingents, ch. 2, no. 6; Father Gabriel Vázquez, vol. 1 on the First Part, disp. 67, ch. 3; and by now almost all the moderns of our time.

> Sed vt eam simul explicemus, & probemus, notandum est, *Quid sit determinata veritas*: nam ex hoc constabit, an tribuenda sit singularibus enunciationibus de futuro contingenti. Determinata autem veritas, duo habere debet. Primum, *Quòd sit distincta, & non confusa*: sicut confusa est ea, quæ reperitur in propositionibus æquiuocis, vt in hac, Canis mouetur: in qua non verificatur prædicatum de aliquo subiecto distinctè, sed confusa, & quasi suspensa manet veritas eius. Secundò requiritur, *Quòd sit actualis*: quæ in ordine ad actuale significatum accipiatur, nam si solùm sit in potentia indifferenti, suspensa dicetur enunciatio à veritate. Actuale autem significatum enunciationis, illud dicitur, quod actu est in rerum natura, tempore significato per copulam eius: ita vt si enunciatio sit de præsenti, actualem habeat veritatem, ac determinatam, si res significata existat tempore præsenti: & si sit de præterito, determinatè vera erit, si eius significatum aliquando fuit in rerum natura eius. Si verò sit enunciatio de futuro, erit determinatè vera, si eius significatum aliquando futurum sit in rerum natura: vt hæc enunciatio, Sol orietur cras, determinatè vera est hodie: quia significatum eius crastina die erit in rerum natura.

But in order that we may at once explain and prove it, it should be noted what determinate truth is: for from this it will be clear whether it is to be attributed to singular enunciations about the contingent future. Now determinate truth must have two things. First, that it be distinct and not confused: as that truth is confused which is found in equivocal propositions, as in this one, Canis movetur [The dog moves], in which the predicate is not verified of any subject distinctly, but its truth remains confused and as it were suspended. Second, it is required that it be actual, which is taken in relation to an actual significate: for if it is only in indifferent potency, the enunciation will be said to be suspended from truth. Now the actual significate of an enunciation is said to be that which actually is in the nature of things at the time signified by its copula: so that, if the enunciation is about the present, it has actual and determinate truth if the thing signified exists at the present time; and if it is about the past, it will be determinately true if its significate at some time was in the nature of things. But if the enunciation is about the future, it will be determinately true if its significate is at some time to be in the nature of things: as this enunciation, The sun will rise tomorrow, is determinately true today, because its significate will be in the nature of things on the morrow.

> Secundò notandum est, *Propositionem de futuro, sicut de præterito, duplicem esse*: Vnam, quæ determinat aliquod tempus: vt hæc, Petrus disputabit cras. Aliam, quæ nullum determinat sed totum tempus futurum quasi indefinitè significat: vt Petrus disputabit. Et vt determinatè vera sit prior, necesse est disputationem Petri futuram esse die crastino: vt autem posterior, sufficit, quòd aliquo tempore habitura sit esse actuale in rerum natura: ita vt verum sit tunc de præsenti enunciare Petrus disputat.

Second, it should be noted that a proposition about the future, like one about the past, is twofold: one, which determines some time, as this, Peter will dispute tomorrow; another, which determines none, but signifies the whole future time as it were indefinitely, as Peter will dispute. And for the former to be determinately true, it is necessary that the disputation of Peter be future on the morrow; but for the latter it suffices that at some time it is to have actual being in the nature of things, so that it is then true to enunciate about the present, Peter is disputing.

> His suppositis: Probatur iam nostra sententia, Quòd propositiones singulares de futuro contingenti, sint determinatè veræ, aut falsæ: Ex fide Catholica, quæ docet Deum ab æterno euidenter cognouisse veritatem earum: ex quo sequitur, eam habuisse ab æterno. Probatur consequentia: quia Deus non cognoscit futura esse, nisi quæ verè futura sunt. Gratia exẽpli: Deus ab æterno cognouit hanc singularẽ, de futuro cõtingẽti, veram esse, Antichristus est peccaturus: ergo cognouit, quòd [p. 551] aliquando erit vera de præsenti: sed propositio, quæ aliquando est vera de præsenti, semper fuit vera de futuro, & determinatè vera, cùm aliquando sit de præsenti determinatè vera: ergo cognouit Deus ab æterno, determinatam vnitatem eius de futuro: quod non potest esse, nisi eam habuerit. Alioqui cognouisset Deus tanquam futurum, id, quod futurum non est.

These things supposed, our view is now proved: that singular propositions about the contingent future are determinately true or false. From the Catholic faith, which teaches that God from eternity evidently knew their truth; from which it follows that they had it from eternity. The consequence is proved: because God does not know things to be future unless they truly are future. For example: God knew from eternity that this singular about the contingent future is true, Antichrist will sin; therefore he knew that [p. 551] it will at some time be true about the present; but a proposition which is at some time true about the present was always true about the future, and determinately true, since at some time it is determinately true about the present; therefore God knew from eternity its determinate truth about the future, which cannot be unless it had it. Otherwise God would have known as future that which is not future.

> Probatur etiam ratione. Primò: Quia, si Petrus hodie disputat, determinatè verum erit, de præsenti enunciare, Petrus disputat: ergo etiam fuit determinatè verum, heri enunciare de futuro, Petrus disputabit. Probatur euidenter consequentia: quia veritas enunciationis de futuro, mensuratur per significatum eius: & determinata veritas, per determinationem eiusdem significati: sed disputatio præsens, habet nunc esse determinatum de præsenti: ergo habuit heri esse determinatum de futuro: & ideo enunciatio de futuro: quæ illud enunciabat, determinatam veritatem habuit, quam sicut heri habuit certum est ante mille annos habuisse.

It is proved also by reason. First: because, if Peter is disputing today, it will be determinately true to enunciate about the present, Peter is disputing; therefore it was also determinately true yesterday to enunciate about the future, Peter will dispute. The consequence is evidently proved: because the truth of an enunciation about the future is measured by its significate, and determinate truth by the determination of that same significate; but the present disputation now has determinate being about the present; therefore yesterday it had determinate being about the future; and therefore the enunciation about the future which enunciated it had determinate truth, which, just as it had it yesterday, it is certain it had a thousand years before.

> Secundò, Determinata veritas enunciationis, sumitur ex significato eius determinato: sed significatum huius enunciationis, Petrus disputabit, habebit aliquando esse determinatum de præsenti: ergo habet modò esse determinatum de futuro: & ideo propositio, quæ illud de futuro enunciat, erit determinatè vera, cùm eius significatum sit determinatè futurum. Probatur minor: quia disputatio Petri aliquando habebit esse actuale, atque distinctum extra causas.

Second: the determinate truth of an enunciation is taken from its determinate significate; but the significate of this enunciation, Peter will dispute, will at some time have determinate being about the present; therefore it now has determinate being about the future; and therefore the proposition which enunciates it about the future will be determinately true, since its significate is determinately future. The minor is proved: because the disputation of Peter will at some time have actual being, and distinct, outside its causes.

> Probatur tandem: Quia si propositiones istæ non habent determinatam veritatem: ergo nullo modo sint veræ, aut falsæ, nec erunt aliquando: hoc est, nec actu, nec potentia, quod est absurdum. Probatur consequentia: quia frustra est potentia, quæ nec reducitur, nec reduci potest ad actum: sed istæ enunciationes, nunquam erunt de futuro veræ: imò nec esse poterunt, si modò non sunt sunt determinatè veræ: quia cùm effectus præsens fuerit, iam non sunt verè de futuro, sed de præsenti: ergo nec habent veritatem de futuro, determinatam actu, nec potentia: quod est nullo prorsus modo esse veras de futuro.

It is proved, finally: because, if these propositions do not have determinate truth, then they are in no way true or false, nor will they be at any time, that is, neither in act nor in potency, which is absurd. The consequence is proved: because a potency is in vain which neither is reduced nor can be reduced to act; but these enunciations will never be true about the future, nay, will not be able to be so, if they are not now determinately true: because, when the effect has become present, they are no longer true about the future, but about the present; therefore they have determinate truth about the future neither in act nor in potency, which is to be in no way at all true about the future.

> Ad arg. primæ opinionis, Distinguenda est minor, quòd significatum propositionis, singularis de futuro contingenti, non sit in rerum natura: quia licèt non sit in differentia temporis præsentis, est tamen in differentia temporis futuri, significata per copulam, in qua habebit esse determinatum, & actuale, & in hoc sufficit, vt determinatè sit vera enunciatio, [p. 552] de futuro: sicut, nec modò est in rerum natura significatum propositionis de præterito: sed quia in propria differentia temporis, habuit esse actuale, ac determinatum, sufficit, vt enunciatio de præterito, sit determinatè vera. Aliud verò, quod infertur, simul esse veram, & falsam, si determinatè vera concedatur: negandum est: quia ideo est determinatè vera, quia significatum eius habebit esse determinatum, tempore significato per copulam: quod licèt possit non esse, cùm sit contingens: erit tamen, & ideo propositio erit vera, non autem falsa: quia licèt possit non esse, non est tamen verum, quòd non sit habiturum esse in propria differentia temporis. Itaque cùm enunciatur futurum, & non solùm possibile, non satis est, quòd possit non esse, vt falsa sit propositio: sed requiritur, vt omnino non sit futurum: quod patet esse falsum: & ideo malè infertur, propositionem simul esse, veram & falsam.

To the argument of the first opinion: the minor must be distinguished, that the significate of a singular proposition about the contingent future is not in the nature of things; for although it is not in the difference of present time, it is nevertheless in the difference of future time signified by the copula, in which it will have determinate and actual being; and this suffices for the enunciation to be determinately true, Mm iiij [p. 552] about the future; just as the significate of a proposition about the past is not now in the nature of things either, but because it had actual and determinate being in its own difference of time, this suffices for the enunciation about the past to be determinately true. But the other thing that is inferred, that it is at once true and false if it is granted to be determinately true, must be denied: because it is determinately true for this reason, that its significate will have determinate being at the time signified by the copula; and although this can fail to be, since it is contingent, it nevertheless will be; and therefore the proposition will be true, but not false: because, although it can fail to be, it is nevertheless not true that it will not have being in its own difference of time. And so, since it is enunciated as future, and not only as possible, it is not enough for the proposition to be false that it can fail to be; rather it is required that it be not future at all, which is plainly false; and therefore it is badly inferred that the proposition is at once true and false.

> Pro solutione arg. secundæ opinionis, notandum est, *Effectum futurum duplicem esse, Necessarium, & contingentem*. Necessariò futurus est ille, qui non potest non esse futurus: quia per causam necessariam futurus est, vt ortus solis crastinus, necessariò futurus est: quia per causam necessariam, ac determinatam ad vnum. Contingenter verò futurus esse dicatur ille, qui tempore quidem futuro habiturus est esse, non minùs quàm effectus necessarius, contingenter tamen: ita vt possit non esse futurus: quia per causam sit liberam, aut contingentẽ: quæ sic eum producit in differentia temporis futuri, vt possit illum non producere: sic se ad operandum determinabit, vt possit se non determinare. Et cùm veritas, aut falsitas enunciationis mensuretur per rem significatam, duplex est etiam enunciatio de futuro, vna *Necessaria*, vt Sol orietur cras, & alia *Contingens*, vt Petrus disputabit: & quidem vtraque determinatè vera, aut falsa: sed illa prior necessariò: quia ita est vera, vt non possit esse falsa: hæc verò posterior contingenter: quia ita est vera, vt possit esse falsa. Vnde sequitur: hanc non esse bonam consequentiam: Hæc enunciatio, Petrus disputabit, est determinatè vera: ergo necessaria, vel necessariò vera: nam ita est determinatè vera, vt contingens, & contingenter sit vera: quia sic est vera vt possit esse falsa: sicut effectus per eam significatus, sic est determinatè futurus, vt possit non esse futurus.

For the solution of the arguments of the second opinion, it should be noted that a future effect is twofold, necessary and contingent. That one is necessarily future which cannot fail to be future, because it is future through a necessary cause: as tomorrow’s sunrise is necessarily future, because it is so through a necessary cause, determined to one. But that one is said to be contingently future which, at a future time, is indeed to have being no less than a necessary effect, yet contingently: so that it can fail to be future, because it is so through a free or contingent cause, which so produces it in the difference of future time that it can not produce it; it will so determine itself to operate that it can not determine itself. And since the truth or falsity of an enunciation is measured by the thing signified, the enunciation about the future is also twofold: one necessary, as The sun will rise tomorrow, and the other contingent, as Peter will dispute; and indeed both determinately true or false, but the former necessarily, because it is so true that it cannot be false, the latter contingently, because it is so true that it can be false. Whence it follows that this is not a good consequence: This enunciation, “Peter will dispute,” is determinately true; therefore it is necessary, or necessarily true; for it is so determinately true as to be contingent and contingently true, because it is so true that it can be false; just as the effect signified by it is so determinately future that it can fail to be future.

> Ex hac doctrina soluitur argum. Arist. Cuius negandum est antecedens: quia nõ omne, quod futurum est, habebit esse per causam necessariam, siquidem habebunt plura per contingentem: & ideo nec sunt necessaria, nec necessariò futura, sed contingentia, & contingenter futura: & ex consequenti nunciationes, [p. 553] per quas significantur, licèt sint determinatè verè, non tamen necessariæ, sed contingentes: quia sic sunt veræ, vt possint esse falsæ.

By this doctrine the argument of Aristotle is solved. Its antecedent must be denied: because not everything that is future will have being through a necessary cause, since many things will have it through a contingent one; and therefore they are neither necessary nor necessarily future, but contingent and contingently future; and consequently the enunciations [p. 553] by which they are signified, although they are determinately true, are nevertheless not necessary but contingent, because they are so true that they can be false.

> Pro solutione alterius, Aliud est notandum: in quo consistit deceptio huius opinionis: Nempe, *causam liberam, vel contingentem indeterminatam esse, atque indifferentem*: quia potest se determinare, & potest se non determinare. Certum tamen est, quòd determinabit se: vel non se determinabit: & ideo, certum est etiam, effectum eius futurum esse, vel non esse futurum: & si futurus est, potuisse non esse futurum, & si futurus non est, potuisse etiam esse futurum.

For the solution of the other, another thing should be noted, in which the deception of this opinion consists: namely, that a free or contingent cause is indeterminate and indifferent, because it can determine itself and can not determine itself. Yet it is certain that it will determine itself or will not determine itself; and therefore it is also certain that its effect will be future or will not be future; and if it is future, that it could have failed to be future; and if it is not future, that it could also have been future.

> Gratia exempli: Voluntas Petri semper est indeterminata, & indifferens, ad disputandum, vel non disputandum, quousque se determinet crastino die, tali hora ad disputandum: & tunc cessabit indifferentia eius. Quare disputatio, determinata erit tali hora diei crastini: ita tamen vt potuerit non esse: sed sicut verum erit tunc de præsenti, esse determinatam contingenter. & potuisse non habere esse determinatum illa eadem hora: quia posset causa libera se non determinare: ita verum est hodie, quòd habitura sit cras esse determinatum, contingenter tamen; quia verum est, potuisse non esse: & ideo est verum, quod disputatio sit esse determinatum. Enunciatio igitur futura, Petrus disputabit die crastino, tali hora, non comparatur ad voluntatem eius, vt indeterminatam: sed vt se determinantem tali hora ad disputandum: nec significat disputationem, vt in potentia, vel vt in potestate voluntatis nondum determinatæ: sed, vt determinatum, & habentem esse actuale: non præsens, sed futurum crastino die, tali hora: & ex hoc determinatam habet veritatem, non minùs quàm propositio de præsenti, eodem tempore, quo fit disputatio prolata: Petrus disputat. Quia sicut tunc habet disputatio esse determinatum de præsenti: Ita nunc habet esse determinatum de futuro. Et in hoc consistit deceptio secundæ opinionis: quia putat propositionem de futuro, comparari ad causam, vt indeterminatam tantùm: cùm tamen non comparetur ad eam: vt nunc interminatam: (licèt verè nunc indeterminata sit:) sed ad eandem, vt se determinantem tempore futuro, per copulã significato: ex quo determinatam habet veritatem enunciatio, licèt contingentem: quia comparatur ad causam, vt se determinantem in futuro, contingenter tamen, iuxta propriam naturam: & ideo potentem se non determinare.

For example: the will of Peter is always indeterminate and indifferent to disputing or not disputing, until it determines itself on the morrow, at such an hour, to dispute; and then its indifference will cease. Wherefore the disputation will be determined at such an hour of tomorrow, yet in such a way that it could have failed to be; but just as it will then be true about the present that it is determined contingently, and that it could have failed to have determinate being at that same hour, because the free cause could have not determined itself, so it is true today that it will have determinate being tomorrow, yet contingently, because it is true that it could have failed to be; and therefore it is true that the disputation will have determinate being. The future enunciation, therefore, Peter will dispute tomorrow at such an hour, is not compared to his will as indeterminate, but as determining itself at such an hour to dispute; nor does it signify the disputation as in potency, or as in the power of the will not yet determined, but as determined and having actual being, not present, but future on the morrow at such an hour; and from this it has determinate truth, no less than the proposition about the present uttered at the same time at which the disputation takes place: Peter is disputing. Because, just as then the disputation has determinate being about the present, so now it has determinate being about the future. And in this consists the deception of the second opinion: because it thinks that the proposition about the future is compared to the cause only as indeterminate; whereas it is not compared to it as now indeterminate (although it truly is now indeterminate), but to that same cause as determining itself at the future time signified by the copula; from which the enunciation has determinate truth, although contingent, because it is compared to the cause as determining itself in the future, yet contingently, according to its own nature, and therefore as able not to determine itself.

> Ad formam igitur arg. Distinguenda est minor, quòd res significata per enunciationem de futuro: quamdiu enunciatur [p. 554] futura, nullam habeat determinationem: nam licèt nullam habeat determinationem præsentem, habet tamen determinationem futuram, quam significat: & contingentem quidem cùm sic futura sit disputatio determinata, vt possit non esse: hoc enim non tollit futuram eius determinationem, sed ostendit esse contingentem: & ideo non tollit determitam veritatem enunciationis de futuro, sed ostendit determinatam eius veritatem, non esse necessariam, sed contingentem.

To the form of the argument, then: the minor must be distinguished, that the thing signified by an enunciation about the future, as long as it is enunciated [p. 554] as future, has no determination; for although it has no present determination, it nevertheless has a future determination, which it signifies; and a contingent one indeed, since the disputation is so future and determined that it can fail to be: for this does not take away its future determination, but shows that it is contingent; and therefore it does not take away the determinate truth of the enunciation about the future, but shows that its determinate truth is not necessary but contingent.

> Sed quid dicendum ad Arist. qui videtur sentire, *tales enunciationes non esse determinatè veras*. Respondeo, plures adhiberi solutiones à pluribus, quæ quidem non videntur ad mentem eius esse. Et ideo eas non refero. Alij verò quibus prædictæ solutiones non satis faciunt, asserunt ita sensisse Arist. quòd *tales enunciationes non habeant determinatam veritatem*: sed errasse in hoc, aduersus fidem nostram, quæ cùm ponat à Deo euidenter cognosci ab æterno, quasdam esse veras, & alias falsas, necesse est concedere, determinatè veras esse, aut falsas: quia quòd Deus cognoscit futurum esse, determinatè futurum est. licèt contingens. Quare non est audiendus in hac parte Arist. Ego verò credere non possum Aristotelem errasse: quia certum est cognouisse eum libertatem nostræ voluntatis, & contingentiam aliarum causarum: quæ sunt duæ radices totius contingentiæ futurorum effectuum, quos enunciationes singulares de futuro contingenti enunciant. Et cùm cognouerit eosdem effectus, habituros esse determinationem actualem, licèt contingentem, tempore futuro per copulam earum significato, impossibile est eundem non intellexisse, quòd tales enunciationes habeant determinatam veritatem licèt contingentem.

But what is to be said to Aristotle, who seems to hold that such enunciations are not determinately true? I reply that several solutions are applied by several authors, which indeed do not seem to be according to his mind; and therefore I do not report them. Others, however, whom the aforesaid solutions do not satisfy, have asserted that Aristotle did hold that such enunciations do not have determinate truth, but that he erred in this, against our faith: which, since it holds that God knows evidently from eternity that some are true and others false, it is necessary to grant that they are determinately true or false; because what God knows to be future is determinately future, although contingent. Wherefore Aristotle is not to be listened to in this part. I, however, cannot believe that Aristotle erred: because it is certain that he knew the freedom of our will and the contingency of the other causes, which are the two roots of the whole contingency of the future effects that singular enunciations about the contingent future enunciate. And since he knew that those same effects will have actual determination, although contingent, at the future time signified by their copula, it is impossible that he did not understand that such enunciations have determinate truth, although contingent.

> In eo igitur sensu, determinatam veritatem eis denegauit: in quo eam concessit enũciationibus materię necessarię, & remotę: atque etiam contingentibus de subiecto vniuersali: imò & singularibus de præsenti, & præterito, atque etiam toti disiuncto, ex vtraque contradictoria singulari de futuro constanti, quale est hoc, Petrus disputabit, vel non disputabit. His autem omnibus concessit veritatem determinatam, sumptam pro necessaria, quam negauit singularibus de futuro contingenti: non tamen eis denegauit determinatam veritatem contingentem. Itaque sensus eius fuit, Regulam contradictionis, quòd ex duabus contradictoriis, vna determinatè est vera, & alia determinatè falsa, id est, vna necessariò est vera, alia necessariò est falsa, in omnibus enunciationibus cuiuscunq; materiæ esse [p. 555] veram, exceptis singularibus de futuro contingenti, in quibus solis deficit: quia neutra per se sumpta est determinatè vera, id est, non est necessariò vera, sed contingenter veræ sunt vel falsæ: & ob id, non est de illis humana scientia: hanc nihilominus veritatem contingentem, determinatam habent propter determinationem contingentem effectus tempore futuro, per copulam earũ significato. Quòd autem iste fuerit sensus eius: ex duobus ostendo.

He denied determinate truth to them, therefore, in that sense in which he granted it to enunciations of necessary and remote matter, and also to contingent ones with a universal subject; nay, even to singular ones about the present and the past, and also to the whole disjunction made up of the two singular contradictories about the future, such as this, Peter will dispute or will not dispute. Now to all these he granted determinate truth taken for necessary, which he denied to singulars about the contingent future; yet he did not deny them determinate contingent truth. So his sense was that the rule of contradiction, that of two contradictories one is determinately true and the other determinately false, that is, one is necessarily true, the other necessarily false, is in all enunciations of whatever matter [p. 555] true, except singulars about the contingent future, in which alone it fails: because neither, taken by itself, is determinately true, that is, it is not necessarily true, but they are contingently true or false; and for that reason there is no human science of them. Nevertheless they have this truth, contingently determinate, on account of the contingent determination of the effect at the future time signified by their copula. That this was his sense I show from two things.

> Primò ex argumentis, quibus id probauit: in quibus arguit à determinata veritate, ad necessariam. Et ex determinata veritate harum enunciationum infert, tolli consilium, & deliberationem: esset autem friuolum argumentum, nisi determinationem veritatis pro necessitate acciperet.

First, from the arguments by which he proved it, in which he argues from determinate truth to necessary truth. And from the determinate truth of these enunciations he infers that counsel and deliberation are taken away; but the argument would be frivolous unless he took determination of truth for necessity.

> Secundò, ex his verbis, quibus apertè eundem sensum significauit: *Sed & in contradictione eadem ratio est, esse quidem, vel non esse omne, necesse est, & futurum esse, vel non.* Non tamen diuidentem dicere alterum necessarium. Dico autem, vt necesse est: Futurum esse bellum nauale cras, vel non futurum esse, nõ tamen cras fieri bellum nauale necesse est, neque non fieri: fieri tamen, vel non fieri necesse est. Et in hoc sensu explicant Aristote. Rich. in 1. distinctione 38. arti. 1. quæst. 5. ad 1. & Maior ibidem, quæst. 1.

Second, from these words, in which he openly signified the same sense: But in contradiction too the reason is the same: it is altogether necessary to be or not to be, and to be future or not. Yet it is not necessary, dividing, to say that one of the two is necessary. I mean, as it is necessary that there will be a naval battle tomorrow or will not be, yet it is not necessary that a naval battle take place tomorrow, nor that it not take place; but that it take place or not take place is necessary. And in this sense Aristotle is explained by Richard on 1, distinction 38, a. 1, q. 5, ad 1, and Major in the same place, q. 1.

> *Breue dubium, an effectus contingens quando est, sit necessarius, vel adhuc contingens.*

Brief Doubt: whether a contingent effect, when it is, is necessary, or still contingent.

> Non parum iuuabit, ad meliùs intelligendum præcedentem quæstionem, determinatio huius dubij, ex qua etiam explicabitur vniuersalis illa propositio Aristotelis, frequenter in hac materia repetita, nempe, *Omne quod est, quando est, necesse est, esse.* Quæ si vera sit, sequitur ex ea, futurum contingens, dum iam est in rerum natura, non esse contingens, sed necessarium. Quod etiam sic probo, nam causa libera priusquam se determinet ad operandum, indeterminata, & contingens est, sed dum de præsenti operatur, cessat iam indeterminatio: ergo cessat contingentia eius: & ex consequenti cessabit contingentia effectus: & erit necessarius.

It will help not a little toward better understanding the preceding question to determine this doubt, from which will also be explained that universal proposition of Aristotle frequently repeated in this matter, namely: Everything that is, when it is, necessarily is. If this is true, it follows from it that a future contingent, once it is in the nature of things, is not contingent but necessary. Which I also prove thus: for a free cause, before it determines itself to operate, is indeterminate and contingent; but while it operates in the present, its indetermination now ceases; therefore its contingency ceases; and consequently the contingency of the effect will cease, and it will be necessary.

> Dubium hoc hac distinctione soluendum est: *Necessarium* dupliciter sumitur. Primò, *Ex propria natura*, & hoc dicitur [p. 556] necessarium simpliciter, vt ortus solis: quia ita est, vt non possit non esse, propter necessitatem suæ causæ Secundò, dicitur aliquid necessarium, non ex propria natura, sed *Ab extrinseco*: vt ex determinatione temporis in quo producitur extra causas, licèt à causa contingente fiat. Quo supposito dicimus, *Effectum contingentem, dum iam est, adhuc esse contingentem simpliciter: sed necessarium solùm ab extrinseco, ex determinatione temporis.*

This doubt is to be solved by this distinction: the necessary is taken in two ways. First, from its own nature; and this is said [p. 556] necessary simply, as the sunrise: because it is such that it cannot fail to be, on account of the necessity of its cause. Second, something is said to be necessary not from its own nature but extrinsically: as from the determination of the time in which it is produced outside its causes, although it comes about from a contingent cause. This supposed, we say that a contingent effect, once it is, is still contingent simply, but necessary only extrinsically, from the determination of time.

> Probatur primum: Quia causa libera, liberè se determinat ad operandum: ergo ita se determinat, vt possit se non determinare: & consequenter ita operatur, vt possit non operari: quare dum operatur, non necessariò, sed liberè, & contingenter operatur: & ideo operatio ipsa, aut effectus etiam dum fit, vel præsens est, contingenter procedit à sua causa, & contingens esse habet simpliciter. Probatur secundum, quòd sit necessarium ex suppositione: quia supposito quod iam habet esse, non potest non esse: alioqui simul posset esse, & non esse: quod repugnat. Et in hoc sensu intelligitur propositio Arist. *Omne quod est, quando est, necesse est esse*: quasi dicat ex suppositione temporis, in quo præsens est, non potest non esse: & hoc tantum probat argumentum factum: quia licèt per determinationem causæ liberæ ad operandum, cesset indeterminatio, atque indifferentia eius: liberè tamen cessat, & ideo liber semper est effectus, atque contingens ex propria natura, etiam tum, quando præsens est: licèt ex suppositione præsentialitatis sit necessarius, ab extrinseco, & ex suppositione.

The first part is proved: because a free cause freely determines itself to operate; therefore it so determines itself that it can not determine itself; and consequently it so operates that it can not operate; wherefore, while it operates, it operates not necessarily but freely and contingently; and therefore the operation itself, or the effect, even while it comes to be or is present, proceeds contingently from its cause and has contingent being simply. The second is proved, that it is necessary on a supposition: because, supposing that it already has being, it cannot fail to be; otherwise it could at once be and not be, which is repugnant. And in this sense is understood the proposition of Aristotle, Everything that is, when it is, necessarily is: as if to say, from the supposition of the time in which it is present, it cannot fail to be. And this is all that the argument made proves: because, although through the determination of the free cause to operate its indetermination and indifference cease, yet they cease freely; and therefore the effect is always free and contingent from its own nature, even then when it is present, although from the supposition of presentiality it is necessary extrinsically and from a supposition.

> In secundo libro huius operis, solùm agit Aristoteles, de enunciationibus modalibus, & oppositione earum: de quibus copiosè in Summulis disseritur: & cùm ex hoc libro desumpta sint, quæ à Summulistis repetuntur, & inculcantur, non iudicamus necessarium, ea nunc repetere, nec capita huius libri exponere, cùm iam sit tota eorum doctrina ab adolescentibus satis intellecta: sed ad libros de Priori resolutione procedendum esse.

In the second book of this work Aristotle treats only of modal enunciations and their opposition, of which there is copious discussion in the Summulae; and since the things that are repeated and inculcated by the Summulists are taken from this book, we have not judged it necessary to repeat them now, nor to expound the chapters of this book, since their whole doctrine is by now sufficiently understood by the young; but rather that we must proceed to the books of the Prior Analytics.

> *Finis huius operis.*

End of this work.

[p. 557]

## COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK

> COMMENTARII IN LIBRVM ARISTOT. DE PRIORI ANALYSI, seu Resolutione.

O F A R I S T O T L E O N P R I O R A N A LY S I S , or Resolution.

### Proœmium huius operis — P RO E M O F T H I S WO R K .

> Opus hoc initium est tertiæ partis Dialecticæ, in quo Arist. incipit agere de tertia operatione intellectus, ad quam pertinet syllogismus. Inscribitur autem de priori resolutione: & Resolutio Logica, siue intellectualis, de qua intelligitur inscriptio, non est dissolutio syllogismi, sicut materialis, & physica resolutio rei, est eius dissolutio: sed est quasi examinatio partium, ex quibus syllogismus: qui est instrumentum Dialecticæ, constare debet. Finis quoque resolutionis est, perfectio eiusdem syllogismi: quę nota debet esse, ex modo ipso resolutionis, aut examinationis eum componente, vt vim habere possit ad inueniendam, ac probandam veritatem: vt copiosiùs explicabimus in proœmio librorum de posteriori resolutione.

his work is the beginning of the third part of Dialectic, in which T Aristotle begins to treat of the third operation of the intellect, to which the syllogism pertains. And it is entitled On Prior Resolution; and logical or intellectual resolution, of which the title is understood, is not the dissolution of the syllogism, as the material and physical resolution of a thing is its dissolution; but it is as it were an examination of the parts of which the syllogism, which is the instrument of Dialectic, ought to consist. The end of the resolution, too, is the perfection of that same syllogism, which ought to be known from the very mode of the resolution, or examination, composing it, so that it may have power for finding and proving the truth, as we shall explain more copiously in the proem of the books of the Posterior Analytics.

#### De inscriptione huius operis — On the title of this work.

> Sed cur de priori resolutione inscribantur, non satis constat, complures quippe dicunt, ideo de priori dici hos libros, sequentes verò de posteriori resolutione: quia in his agitur de forma syllogismi, in sequentibus de materia. Hæc tamen ratio insufficiens est: quia licèt verum sit, in his libris agi de syllogismo, secundùm formam: falsum tamen, quòd in sequentibus solùm agatur de eodem, secundùm materiam: quia si verum hoc esset, demonstratio non distingueretur à syllogismo in communi: nec è syllogismo topico, & sophystico, nisi per materiam: quod est apertè falsum: nam ex eo sequeretur, nec demonstrationem esse speciem syllogismi, nec distingui specie à syllogismis Dialecticis, & sophisticis. Probatur euidenter consequentia: quia à materia non sumitur differentia essentialis constituens speciem, & distinguens eam ab aliis, sed à forma. Propterea dicendum est: hos libros appellari de resolutione priori, sequentes verò de resolutione posteriori: quia in his agitur de forma syllogismi communi atque generica, quæ [p. 558] sumitur ex dispositione eius in figura, & modo: & quam constat communem esse omnibus syllogismis. In lib. verò sequentibus, agitur de forma speciali, nempe, de modo concludendi necessariò vnam veritatem de altera; per quem constituitur demonstratio in specie syllogismi, & distinguitur ab aliis: vt etiam explicatur copiosiùs in proœmio operis sequentis. Forma autem communis, atque generica, prior est, & notior nobis: ideo de priori resolutione meritò inscribuntur libri isti.

But why they are entitled On Prior Resolution is not sufficiently clear. Indeed, many say that these books are called “prior,” and the following ones “on posterior resolution,” because in these the form of the syllogism is treated, in the following ones its matter. This reason, however, is insufficient: because, although it is true that in these books the syllogism is treated according to its form, it is nevertheless false that in the following ones the same is treated only according to its matter; because, if this were true, demonstration would not be distinguished from the syllogism in common, nor from the topical and sophistical syllogism, except by matter, which is openly false; for from it would follow that demonstration is neither a species of syllogism nor distinguished in species from dialectical and sophistical syllogisms. The consequence is evidently proved: because the essential difference constituting a species and distinguishing it from others is not taken from the matter, but from the form. Therefore it must be said that these books are called “on prior resolution,” and the following “on posterior resolution,” because in these the common and generic form of the syllogism is treated, which [p. 558] is taken from its disposition in figure and mood, and which is clearly common to all syllogisms. But in the following books the special form is treated, namely the mode of concluding one truth necessarily from another, by which demonstration is constituted in the species of syllogism and distinguished from the others, as is also explained more copiously in the proem of the following work. Now the common and generic form is prior and better known to us; therefore these books are rightly entitled On Prior Resolution.

#### Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis — What the object of this work is.

> Prima opinio asserit; *Demonstrationem esse subiectum*: quia ex his, & sequentibus lib. vnum opus efficitur; cuius scopus est demonstratio; tanquam finis, in quem proximè ordinatur. Vnde Arist. cap. 1. huius lib. proponens intentum huius operis asserit esse, de *Demonstratione, & disciplina demonstratiua disputare.*

The first opinion asserts that demonstration is the subject: because from these and the following books one work is made, whose aim is demonstration, as the end to which it is proximately ordered. Whence Aristotle, in ch. 1 of this book, proposing the intent of this work, asserts that it is to dispute about demonstration and demonstrative discipline.

> Secunda opinio: *Opus hoc à sequenti distinguit*: & ideo negat demonstrationem esse obiectum: sed neque asserit syllogismum esse adæquatum obiectum: verum argumentationem in communi: quia Arist. non de solo syllogismo agit, sed etiam de aliis argumentationibus: vt de inductione, enthymemate, & exemplo: quare aliquid his commune, debet esse obiectum huius operis.

The second opinion distinguishes this work from the following one, and therefore denies that demonstration is the object; but neither does it assert that the syllogism is the adequate object, but rather argumentation in common: because Aristotle treats not of the syllogism alone, but also of other argumentations, such as induction, the enthymeme, and the example; wherefore something common to these must be the object of this work.

> Nostra tamen sententia, & magis communis inter expositores huius loci est; supposita distinctione huius operis, à sequenti, necessariò admittenda; cùm diuersa sint ea, de quibus in vtroque agitur: *Solum syllogismum in communi esse adæquatum obiectum eius.* Quia vel nihil de cæteris argumentationibus agit in ea Arist. vel si agit aliquid, solùm, vt deseruire possunt syllogismo. Idipsum ratione probatur: Quia adæquatum obiectum scientiæ alicuius est, cuius partes ex professo explicat scientia, cuius definitionem tradit, cuius passiones probat: sed in hoc opere traduntur partes syllogismi, assignatur definitio eius, & passiones probantur, vt in 1. & 2. libr. est manifestum: ergo syllogismus est obiectum huius partis adæquatum. Quod verò Aristo. dicit; propositum sibi esse, agere de demonstratione: solum probat; quòd libri sequentes, quasi finis sint, in quem ordinatur opus hoc: de quo fine patet, non agi in hoc opere: & ideo neque ad eius obiectum pertinet.

Our view, however, and the more common one among the expositors of this place, which, supposing the distinction of this work from the following, must necessarily be admitted, since the things treated in each are different, is that the syllogism in common alone is its adequate object. Because either Aristotle treats nothing of the other argumentations in it, or, if he treats something, it is only inasmuch as they can serve the syllogism. This very thing is proved by reason: because the adequate object of any science is that whose parts the science expressly explains, whose definition it delivers, whose attributes it proves; but in this work the parts of the syllogism are delivered, its definition is assigned, and its attributes are proved, as is manifest in bks. 1 and 2; therefore the syllogism is the adequate object of this part. But what Aristotle says, that his purpose is to treat of demonstration, proves only that the following books are as it were the end to which this work is ordered; of which end it is plain that it is not treated in this work, and therefore it does not pertain to its object either.

[p. 559]

#### Diuisio totius operis — Division of the whole work.

> 3 In duos libros, aut partes diuiditur opus hoc. In quorum primo *de syllogismo, & partibus eius* agit Arist. In secundo de eius proprietatibus, seu passionibus: quas potestates seu potentias, & impotentias vocat Aristoteles.

3 This work is divided into two books or parts. In the first of them Aristotle treats of the syllogism and its parts; in the second, of its properties or attributes, which Aristotle calls powers or potencies and impotencies.

> Primus autem hic liber, diuiditur in tres partes. In prima quæ proœmij rationem habet, proponit Arist. materiam totius operis syllogismúmque, & partes eius (quæ sunt *propositio*, & *terminus*) definit. In secunda agit de conuersionibus propositionum. In tertia de figuris, & modis syllogismorum: & de his, quæ ad easdem figuras pertinent.

This first book, moreover, is divided into three parts. In the first, which has the character of a proem, Aristotle proposes the matter of the whole work, and defines the syllogism and its parts (which are the proposition and the term). In the second he treats of the conversions of propositions. In the third, of the figures and moods of syllogisms, and of the things that pertain to those figures.

## CHAPTER I

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Primum dicere circa quid, & cuius sit consideratio, quoniam circa demonstrationem.*

First, to say about what, and of what, the consideration is: that it is about demonstration.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 4 Caput hoc quasi proœmium est totius operis, in quo Arist. intendit proponere finem eius in quem ordinetur, atque etiam ea, de quibus in eo acturus est. Diuiditur in duas partes. In quarum prima, proposito fine, proponit ea de quibus agendum est: nempe, propositionem, terminum, syllogismum perfectum, & imperfectum: & singula hæc definit: ac item diuidit, quæ multiplicia sunt: nempe, propositionem & syllogismum.

his chapter is as it were the proem of the whole work, in 4 T which Aristotle intends to propose its end, to which it is ordered, and also the things he is going to treat in it. It is divided into two parts. In the first of them, having proposed the end, he proposes the things to be treated, namely the proposition, the term, the perfect and the imperfect syllogism; and he defines each of these, and likewise divides those that are manifold, namely the proposition and the syllogism.

> Finem huius operis, asserit esse demonstrationem: quæ cùm sit potissimum instrumentum Dialecticæ, ad illam ordinantur omnia, remotè quidem simplicia: proximè verò propositiones, & forma syllogistica: de qua in hoc opere agendum est. Forma est, eo ferè modo, quo genus, ordinatur ad constituendam potissimam eius speciem.

He asserts that the end of this work is demonstration: which, since it is the most excellent instrument of Dialectic, all things are ordered to it, remotely indeed the simple ones, but proximately propositions and the syllogistic form, of which this work is to treat. The form is ordered, in roughly the way a genus is, to constituting its most excellent species.

> Definit ergo primò propositionem: quia notior nobis erat, cùm de ea iam egerit in libr. de Interpretatione, & definitio eius talis est: *Propositio est oratio affirmatiua, vel negatiua, alicuius de aliquo.* In qua pro genere ponitur oratio, quæ secundùm se nihil affirmat, aut negat. Contrahitur autem, per affirmationem, & negationem, tanquam per differentias essentiales [p. 560]: vt 1. lib. de Interpretatione diximus: & per has definitur potiùs, quàm per verum, vel falsum: quia in ordine ad syllogismum, ad quem proximè ordinatur, nihil refert, quòd vera sit, vel falsa: cùm forma syllogistica, tam in falsis quàm in veris propositionibus consistere possit: sed necesse est, affirmatiuam esse, aut negatiuam, vt syllogismo deseruiat.

He defines, then, first the proposition, because it was better known to us, since he had already treated of it in the book On Interpretation; and its definition is this: A proposition is an expression affirmative or negative of something about something. In which expression is put in place of the genus, which of itself affirms or denies nothing. And it is contracted by affirmation and negation, as by essential differences [p. 560] as we said in bk. 1 of On Interpretation; and it is defined by these rather than by true or false, because in relation to the syllogism, to which it is proximately ordered, it makes no difference whether it is true or false, since the syllogistic form can consist as much in false as in true propositions; but it is necessary that it be affirmative or negative in order to serve the syllogism.

> Diuidit eandem propositionem, duplici diuisione, Prima est, in *Vniuersalem, Particularem, & Indefinitam. Vniuersalis*, illa est, cuius subiectum pro omnibus inferioribus sub se contentis, distribuitur: vt omnis homo est animal. *Particularis*, cuius subiectum afficitur signo particulari: vt aliquis homo est animal. *Indefinita*, cuius subiectum est terminus communis, nullo signo effectus, vt homo est animal. De propositione singulari non facit mentionem, quia non pertinet per se ad artem, vel scientiam, nec ad formam syllogisticam.

He divides the same proposition by a twofold division. The first is into universal, particular, and indefinite. The universal is that whose subject is distributed for all the inferiors contained under it, as every man is an animal. The particular, that whose subject is affected by a particular sign, as some man is an animal. The indefinite, that whose subject is a common term affected by no sign, as man is an animal. He makes no mention of the singular proposition, because it does not pertain per se to an art or science, nor to the syllogistic form.

> Secunda diuisio propositionis est, *in Dialecticam, & Demonstratiuam. Dialectica*, est probabilis, ex qua efficitur probabilis syllogismus: sed quæ formam habet interrogationis, in eo qui interrogat: in eo verò, qui syllogismum constituit, solùm est simplex propositio probabilis: vt si dicas, Putásne, animal rationale, est definitio hominis? modum habet interrogationis. Si verò interrogationem auferas, habet modum simplicis propositionis, ex qua fit syllogismus. Alia est propositio *Demonstratiua*, quæ vera debet esse, ac necessaria: & ex vtraque potest fieri syllogismus: & ideo propositio syllogistica, vtrique communis est.

The second division of the proposition is into dialectical and demonstrative. The dialectical is the probable one, from which a probable syllogism is made; but it has the form of an interrogation in the one who asks, while in the one who constructs the syllogism it is only a simple probable proposition: as if you say, Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? it has the mode of an interrogation. But if you take away the interrogation, it has the mode of a simple proposition, from which a syllogism is made. The other is the demonstrative proposition, which must be true and necessary; and from either a syllogism can be made; and therefore the syllogistic proposition is common to both.

> Definit deinde terminum, tali definitione: *Terminum voco in quem resoluitur propositio, vt in prædicatum, & de quo prædicatur*: vt homo, & animal.

Next he defines the term by this definition: I call a term that into which a proposition is resolved, as into the predicate and that of which it is predicated: as man and animal.

> Definit tandem syllogismum, hac definitione: *Syllogismus est oratio, in qua positis quibusdam, alterum quid, à positis, necesse est contingere, eo quòd hæc sint.* In qua definitione, *Oratio*, ponitur pro genere: quia communis est ad omnes argumentationes, cum quibus in ea conuenit syllogismus: *In qua quibusdam positis*, hoc est, duabus promissis, dispositis in modo, & figura: vt distinguatur ab exemplo, quòd ex vna tantùm singulari, colligit aliam: ab enthymemate, quòd ex vna tantùm procedit, quasi supprimens aliam: atque etiam ab inductione, quæ licèt ex multis singularibus colligat vniuersale, non tamen dispositis in modo, & figura, sed solùm numeratis. Addit autem, *eo quòd hæc sunt*: vt explicet conclusionem syllogismi, sequi ex virtute præmissarum, sic dispositarum: absque aliquo extrinseco additamento.

Finally he defines the syllogism by this definition: A syllogism is an expression in which, certain things being posited, something other than the things posited necessarily follows, by the fact that these are. In which definition expression is put in place of the genus, because it is common to all argumentations, with which the syllogism agrees in it. In which, certain things being posited, that is, two premises disposed in mood and figure, so that it may be distinguished from the example, which from one singular only gathers another; from the enthymeme, which proceeds from one only, as it were suppressing the other; and also from induction, which, although it gathers a universal from many singulars, does so not from singulars disposed in mood and figure, but only enumerated. And he adds, by the fact that these are, to explain that the conclusion of the syllogism follows by virtue of the premises so disposed, without any extrinsic addition.

[p. 561]

> Diuidit syllogismum, *in perfectum, & imperfectum. Perfectum* esse ait, qui nullo indiget, vt appareat necessarius: & tales sunt syllogismi primæ figuræ, *Imperfectum verò*, qui reductione quadam indiget, ad perfectum, vt appareat necessarius.

He divides the syllogism into perfect and imperfect. Perfect, he says, is the one that needs nothing in order to appear necessary; and such are the syllogisms of the first figure. Imperfect, however, is the one that needs some reduction to a perfect one in order to appear necessary.

> Principia tandem per se nota, quibus innititur tota ars syllogistica, duo esse docet, nempe: *Dici de omni*, cui innituntur syllogismi affirmatiui: & *Dici de nullo*, cui innituntur negatiui. *Et dici de omni*, sic explicat, quando nihil est sumere sub subiecto, de quo non dicatur prædicatum: sed minor propositio sumitur sub maiori, quia subiectum eius continetur sub subiecto eiusdem maioris: ergo euidens est, quòd si prædicatum maioris dicitur de subiecto, dicentur etiam de omni contento sub illo: quod colligitur in conclusione: vt ostendit hic syllogismus, Omne animal est substantia: omnis homo est animal: ergo omnis homo est substantia: in cuius conclusione, prædicatum maioris, quod dicitur maior extremitas, prædicatur de subiecto minoris, quod dicitur extremitas minor, & continetur sub subiecto eiusdem minoris. *Dici autem de nullo*, tale est, Si prædicatum maioris negatur de subiecto minoris, negabitur etiam de quolibet contento sub eo, & hoc fit in conclusione, vt si dicamus, Nullum animal est lapis: omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis. Euidens est enim, quòd si lapis negatur de omni animali in maiori, negatur etiam de omni homine, in conclusione, quod sub eo assumptum fuit in minori. His autem duobus principiis, Dici de omni, & Dici de nullo, non indiget syllogismus perfectus, vt appareat necessarius: sed vt appareat, quibus efficacitas eius innitatur: & ideo necesse est, vt sciamus eam probare per illa, vt certi simus de ea. Nam si quis eam probare nesciat, quod est reducere formam syllogisticam ad sua principia indemonstrabilia, non habet scientiam de efficacitate eius. Et ideo hæc principia dicuntur, *Dici de omni, & de nullo prioristicè*: quia in posterioribus sumuntur secundùm veritatem, ac necessitatem propositionum: & dicuntur *posterioristica*, quibus innititur tota ars demonstratoria.

Finally, he teaches that the principles known per se on which the whole syllogistic art rests are two, namely: Said of all, on which affirmative syllogisms rest, and Said of none, on which negative ones rest. And said of all he explains thus: when nothing can be taken under the subject of which the predicate is not said. But the minor proposition is taken under the major, because its subject is contained under the subject of that same major: therefore it is evident that if the predicate of the major is said of the subject, it will also be said of everything contained under it; which is gathered in the conclusion, as this syllogism shows: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. In its conclusion the predicate of the major, which is called the major extreme, is predicated of the subject of the minor, which is called the minor extreme and is contained under the subject of that same minor. Said of none, moreover, is this: If the predicate of the major is denied of the subject of the minor, it will also be denied of anything whatever contained under it; and this takes place in the conclusion, as if we say: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. For it is evident that if stone is denied of every animal in the major, it is also denied, in the conclusion, of every man, who was assumed under it in the minor. Now a perfect syllogism does not need these two principles, Said of all and Said of none, in order to appear necessary, but in order that it may appear on what its efficacy rests; and therefore it is necessary that we know how to prove it through them, in order to be certain of it. For if someone does not know how to prove it, that is, to reduce the syllogistic form to its indemonstrable principles, he does not have science of its efficacy. And therefore these principles are called Said of all and Said of none prioristically: because in the Posterior Analytics they are taken according to the truth and necessity of the propositions; and they are called posterioristically the principles on which the whole demonstrative art rests. Nn

[p. 562]

## CHAPTER II

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Quoniam verò omnis propositio est, aut inesse, aut necessariò inesse, aut contingenter inesse.*

But since every proposition is either of inherence, or of inhering necessarily, or of inhering contingently.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 7 Intentum *Arist.* est explicare modum, quo propositiones *de inesse* conuertantur. Diuiditur autem in duas partes, In prima, diuidit propositionem, in eam, quam vocat *de inesse*, & aliã, quæ vocatur *Modalis*. In secunda, docet, quonam modo conuertantur, *propositiones de inesse*: nam de conuersione modalium agit cap. sequenti.

he intent of Aristotle is to explain the mode in which 7 T propositions de inesse are converted. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he divides the proposition into the one he calls de inesse and another, which is called Modal. In the second he teaches in what way propositions de inesse are converted; for he treats of the conversion of modals in the following chapter.

> Diuisio est hæc, *propositio, alia est*, in qua simpliciter prædicatur vnum de altero: aut negatur de illo, absque modo aliquo necessario, aut contingenti adiuncto, & hæc vocatur propositio *de inesse*: quia prædicatum, dicitur de subiecto, secundùm esse, quod habet in eo non secundùm hunc vel illum modum, quo ei conuenit, videlicet secundùm modum necessitatis, aut contingentiæ: vt homo est animal. *Alia est propositio modalis*: in qua prædicatum dicitur, vel negatur de subiecto cum aliquo modo necessitatis, aut contingentiæ adiuncto: vt homo necessariò est animal: paries contingenter est albus. Acturus igitur Arist. de conuersione propositionum, priùs agit de conuersione modalis: quia propositio de inesse prior est, & quasi fundamentum modalis.

The division is this: one proposition is that in which one thing is simply predicated of another, or denied of it, without any mode of necessity or contingency adjoined; and this is called a proposition de inesse, because the predicate is said of the subject according to the being it has in it, not according to this or that mode in which it belongs to it, namely according to the mode of necessity or of contingency: as man is an animal. Another is the modal proposition, in which the predicate is said or denied of the subject with some mode of necessity or contingency adjoined: as man is necessarily an animal; the wall is contingently white. Aristotle, therefore, being about to treat of the conversion of propositions, first treats of the conversion of the proposition de inesse before that of the modal, because the proposition de inesse is prior to the modal and as it were its foundation.

> 8 Propositio de inesse quadruplex est. *Vniuersalis negatiua, Vniuersalis affirmatiua: Particularis affirmatiua, & Particularis negatiua*: quam hoc modo diuidit: quia diuersum modum conuersionis habent affirmatiuæ, & negatiuæ: *Indefinita* verò, eundem modum conuersionis habet, ac particularis.

8 The proposition de inesse is fourfold: Universal negative, Universal affirmative, Particular affirmative, and Particular negative. He divides it in this way because affirmatives and negatives have a different mode of conversion; but the Indefinite has the same mode of conversion as the particular.

> Quatuor igitur assignat regulas pro conuersione harũ quatuor propositionum.
