Primam, pro conuersione *Vniuersalis negatiuæ*, quam dicit conuerti in seipsam: vt nullus homo est animal, in hanc, nullum animal est homo. Secundam, pro *Vniuersalis affirmatiua*, quam dicit, non conuerti in seipsam, hoc est, non in aliam vniuersalem, sed in partem, hoc est, in particularem: vt Omnis homo est animal, in hanc, Aliquod animal est homo. Tertiam, pro *Particulari affirmatiua*, quam dicit conuerti in seipsam [p. 563]: vt aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquod animal est homo. Vltimam regulam, pro conuersione *Particularis negatiuæ*, quam dicit nullo modo conuerti. Vt hæc propositio, Aliquod animal non est homo: non conuertitur in hanc, Aliquis homo non est animal.

He assigns, therefore, four rules for the conversion of these four propositions. The first, for the conversion of the Universal negative, which he says is converted into itself: as No man is an animal into this, No animal is a man. The second, for the Universal affirmative, which he says is not converted into itself, that is, not into another universal, but into part, that is, into a particular: as Every man is an animal into this, Some animal is a man. The third, for the Particular affirmative, which he says is converted into itself [p. 563] as Some man is an animal; therefore some animal is a man. The last rule, for the conversion of the Particular negative, which he says is in no way converted: as this proposition, Some animal is not a man, is not converted into this, Some man is not an animal.

### Notabile circa literam — Note on the Letter.

> 9 Quædam sunt notanda circa hoc cap. vt meliùs intelligatur doctrina Arist. primum, *Quid conuersio sit?* Et licèt à pluribus sic definiatur, Conuersio propositionis est, *Transmutatio prædicati in subiectum*: tamen insufficiens est hæc definitio: quia conuersio, argumentatio quædam est, ab vna propositione, in alteram, per transmutationem extremorum, & bona conuersio illa debet appellari, quæ bona consequentia est: quia in ea, repugnat dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum. Mala verò, in qua id dari potest. Ita ergo definienda est: Conuersio propositionis est, *Argumentatio, in qua per transmutationem prædicati in subiectum, colligimus vnam propositionem ex altera*, vt si sic dicamus, Nullus homo est animal: ergo nullum animal est homo. Transmutatio autem extremorum, sic debet fieri in conuersione, vt non solùm non varientur termini, sed nec significatio eorum, nec suppositio, nec distributio.

9 Certain things should be noted concerning this chapter, so that the doctrine of Aristotle may be better understood. First, what conversion is. And although it is defined by many thus: The conversion of a proposition is the transposition of the predicate into the subject, this definition is nevertheless insufficient: because conversion is a certain argumentation from one proposition to another through the transposition of the extremes; and that conversion ought to be called good which is a good consequence, because in it it is impossible for the antecedent to be true and the consequent false; and bad, that in which this can be the case. It must therefore be defined thus: The conversion of a proposition is an argumentation in which, through the transposition of the predicate into the subject, we gather one proposition from another: as if we say thus, No man is an animal; therefore no animal is a man. Moreover, the transposition of the extremes in conversion ought to be made in such a way that not only the terms are not varied, but neither their signification, nor their supposition, nor their distribution.

> *Secundum notabile.*

Second Note.

> 10 Secundò notandum est: *Duplicem esse conuersionem*: Vna est, *Quæ fit per simplicem transmutationem extremorum*: Alia, *Quæ fit per contrapositionem eorum*: & prima, satis per se est manifesta. Secunda verò, fit per transmutationem quidem extremorum, sed additis eis duabus negationibus infinitantibus: & huius conuersionis non est vsus, nisi in propositionibus affirmatiuis, quia negationes non possunt addi supra alias negationes, sine magna confusione. Vniuersalis igitur affirmatiua, conuerti potest in seipsam, per contrapositionem, hoc modo: Omnis homo est animal: ergo omne non animal, est non homo. Et particularis etiam affirmatiua, vt aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquod non animal, est non homo. Huius autem conuersionis non fecit mentionem Aristot. quia non est propriè cõuersio: nam cùm extremis addantur negationes, non videntur eadem manere, sed variari: quod tamen ad veram conuersionem necessarium esse diximus: vnde non [p. 564] tam est conuersio secundùm formam propositionis, quàm secundùm sensum. Præterea, quia ad constitutionem syllogismorum inutilis etiam est, propter negationes, quibus obscura redditur forma syllogistica. Alij addunt, hanc conuersionem solùm posse fieri in terminis existentibus: quia si non existant, dabitur antecedens verum, & consequens falsum: vt patet in hac conuersione: Omnis homo est ens: ergo omne non ens, est non homo, in qua antecedens est verum, & consequens falsum, cùm sit propositio affirmatiua, de subiecto non supponente. Mihi tamen videtur, etiam in terminis non existentibus fieri posse: neque vnquam dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum: quare nec datur in eodem exemplo. Sed negandum est, quòd consequens sit propositio affirmatiua, de subiecto non supponente: nam terminus infinitus, etiam de non entibus, & de quibuscunque non existentibus dicitur: vt in 1. lib. de interpretatione probauimus: quare non efficit propositiones de subiecto non supponente, sed similes essentialibus, in quibus copula absoluitur à tempore: & ideo non est necessaria existentia extremorum ad suppositionem.

10 Second, it should be noted that conversion is twofold: one, which takes place through the simple transposition of the extremes; the other, which takes place through their contraposition. And the first is sufficiently manifest of itself. The second takes place through the transposition of the extremes indeed, but with two infinitizing negations added to them; and this conversion has no use except in affirmative propositions, because negations cannot be added on top of other negations without great confusion. The universal affirmative, therefore, can be converted into itself by contraposition in this way: Every man is an animal; therefore every non-animal is a non-man. And also the particular affirmative, as: Some man is an animal; therefore some non-animal is a non-man. But Aristotle made no mention of this conversion, because it is not properly conversion: for since negations are added to the extremes, they do not seem to remain the same but to be varied; which, however, we said is necessary for true conversion. Whence it is not Nn ij [p. 564] so much a conversion according to the form of the proposition as according to the sense. Moreover, because it is also useless for the construction of syllogisms, on account of the negations, by which the syllogistic form is rendered obscure. Others add that this conversion can be made only in existing terms: because if they do not exist, the antecedent will be true and the consequent false, as is plain in this conversion: Every man is a being; therefore every non-being is a non-man, in which the antecedent is true and the consequent false, since it is an affirmative proposition about a subject that does not supposit. To me, however, it seems that it can be made even in non-existing terms, and that the antecedent is never true and the consequent false; wherefore neither is this the case in the same example. Rather, it must be denied that the consequent is an affirmative proposition about a subject that does not supposit: for an infinite term is said even of non-beings and of any non-existing things whatever, as we proved in bk. 1 of On Interpretation; wherefore it does not make propositions about a subject that does not supposit, but ones similar to essential propositions, in which the copula is absolved from time; and therefore the existence of the extremes is not necessary for supposition.

> *Tertium notabile.*

Third Note.

> 11 Circa conuersionem particularis negatiuæ, notandum est, *ideo non conuerti*: quia dari potest aliquando in conuersione eius antecedens verum, & consequens falsum, quod sufficit, vt conuersio non sit legitima: cùm de ratione conuersionis sit argumentatio: & hæc euidenter probetur vitiosa, ex eo tantùm, quòd semel dari possit antecedens verum, & consequens falsum, in simili forma arg. Ratio autem fundamentalis, propter quam in tali conuersione, datur antecedens verum, & consequens falsum est: quia fit argumentum à termino non distributo in antecedente, ad eundem distributum in consequente: vt fit manifestum, si dicamus: Aliquod animal, non est homo: ergo Aliquis homo, non est animal. Animal enim non distribuitur in antecedente, cùm sit subiectum propositionis particularis, & distribuitur in consequente, cùm sit prædicatum propositionis negatiuæ. Et ideo, non est bona consequentia, à conuersa ad conuertentem: nec proinde legitima conuersio, & hoc vult dicere Aristoteles, dum particularem negatiuam, non conuerti docet: quia mala conuersio, non est conuersio, sicut mala consequentia, non est consequentia.

11 Concerning the conversion of the particular negative, it should be noted that it is not converted for this reason: because in its conversion the antecedent can sometimes be true and the consequent false, which suffices for the conversion not to be legitimate, since it belongs to the ratio of conversion that it be an argumentation; and an argumentation is evidently proved faulty from this alone, that the antecedent can once be true and the consequent false in a similar form of argument. And the fundamental reason why in such a conversion the antecedent is true and the consequent false is that the argument is made from a term not distributed in the antecedent to the same term distributed in the consequent, as becomes manifest if we say: Some animal is not a man; therefore some man is not an animal. For animal is not distributed in the antecedent, since it is the subject of a particular proposition, and it is distributed in the consequent, since it is the predicate of a negative proposition. And therefore it is not a good consequence from the converted to the converting proposition, nor consequently a legitimate conversion; and this is what Aristotle means when he teaches that the particular negative is not converted: because a bad conversion is not a conversion, just as a bad consequence is not a consequence.

[p. 565]

## CHAPTER III

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Eodem autem modo se habebit, & in necessariis propositionibus, &c.*

And it will be in the same way also in necessary propositions, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 12 Intentum Arist. in hoc capite est, tradere regula conuertendi propositiones modales. Diuiditur autem cap. in duas partes. In prima tradit regulas *Conuertendi propositiones de necesse*. In secunda verò, regulas *conuertendi propositiones, de modo contingenti*.

he intent of Aristotle in this chapter is to hand down the 12 T rules for converting modal propositions. And the chapter is divid‐ ed into two parts. In the first he hands down the rules for converting propositions de necesse; in the second, the rules for converting propositions of the contingent mode.

> Pro conuersione igitur Propositionum de necesse, easdem regulas tradit, quas capite præcedenti tradiderat, pro conuersione propositionum de inesse. Prima regula est, *Quòd vniuersalis negatiua de necesse conuertitur simpliciter.* Quam probat arg. ducente ad impossibile, in terminis non significantibus. Sed vt meliùs intelligatur, illud constituemus in terminis significantibus, hoc modo: Si vniuersalis negatiua, non conuertitur simpliciter: ergo hæc non est bona consequentia, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: ergo necesse est, nullum equum esse hominem: poterit ergo dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum. Sit igitur verum illud antecedens, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: & hoc consequens falsum, Necesse est nullum equum esse hominem; & si hoc consequens falsum est, verum erit istud: Contingit aliquem equum esse hominem: ex quo bene sequitur: ergo contingit aliquem hominem, esse equum, per conuersionem simplicem: sed hæc est contradictoria primi antecedentis malæ conuersionis, quod concessum est esse verum: nempe, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: ergo concedendum est, vniuersalem negatiuam de necesse, conuerti simpliciter, vel dari duas contradictorias simul veras.

For the conversion of propositions de necesse, then, he hands down the same rules that he had handed down in the preceding chapter for the conversion of propositions de inesse. The first rule is that the universal negative de necesse is converted simply. This he proves by an argument leading to the impossible, in non-significative terms. But so that it may be better understood, we shall set it out in significative terms, in this way: If the universal negative is not converted simply, then this is not a good consequence: It is necessary that no man be a horse; therefore it is necessary that no horse be a man; the antecedent, then, can be true and the consequent false. Let, therefore, that antecedent be true, It is necessary that no man be a horse, and this consequent false, It is necessary that no horse be a man. And if this consequent is false, this will be true: It is contingent that some horse is a man; from which it follows well: therefore it is contingent that some man is a horse, by simple conversion. But this is the contradictory of the first antecedent of the bad conversion, which was granted to be true, namely, It is necessary that no man be a horse. Therefore it must be granted either that the universal negative de necesse is converted simply, or that two contradictories are true at the same time.

> Secunda regula est: *Vniuersalem affirmatiuam de necesse, conuerti in partem: & particularem affirmatiuam conuerti simpliciter.* Quam probat simili alio argumento, ducente ad impossibile quod non est necessarium repetere. Tertia regula: *Particularis negatiua de esse conuertitur.* Hanc probat hac ratione: Quia sicut hæc est mala consequentia, Aliquod animal non est homo: ergo aliquis homo non est animal, in conuersione particularis negatiuæ de inesse: quia datur antecedens verum, & [p. 566] consequens falsum: ita in particulari negatiua de necesse, Aliquod animal non esse hominem, est necesse: ergo aliquem hominem esse animal, non est necesse.

The second rule is: The universal affirmative de necesse is converted into part, and the particular affirmative is converted simply. This he proves by another, similar argument leading to the impossible, which it is not necessary to repeat. The third rule: The particular negative de necesse is not converted. This he proves by this reason: Because, just as this is a bad consequence, Some animal is not a man; therefore some man is not an animal, in the conversion of the particular negative de inesse, because the antecedent is true and Nn iij [p. 566] the consequent false, so in the particular negative de necesse: That some animal is not a man is necessary; therefore that some man is not an animal is necessary.

> In secunda parte cap. agit de conuersione propositionum de contingenti: quod duobus modis sumi posse ait, Primò, prout est idem, quod possibile: & hoc modo etiam conuenit rebus necessariis: quia si necesse est hominem esse animal: ergo etiam est possibile, & consequenter contingens, sumpto contingenti pro possibili. Sed hanc acceptionem contingentis, impropriam esse docet. Ideo secundo modo, sumitur propriè, pro eo, *quod potest esse, & potest non esse.*

In the second part of the chapter he treats of the conversion of propositions de contingenti, which he says can be taken in two ways. First, as it is the same as possible; and in this way it belongs even to necessary things: because if it is necessary that man be an animal, then it is also possible, and consequently contingent, taking contingent for possible. But he teaches that this acceptation of contingent is improper. Therefore, in the second way, it is taken properly for that which can be and can not be.

> Hoc supposito, prima regula est: *Quòd omnes propositiones de contingenti, Primo modo, eadem prorsus ratione conuertantur, ac propositiones de inesse, & de modo necesse.* quam nec oportet probare, nec exemplis ostendere, cùm sit satis manifesta.

This supposed, the first rule is: That all propositions de contingenti in the first way are converted in altogether the same manner as propositions de inesse and of the mode de necesse. This needs neither to be proved nor shown by examples, since it is sufficiently manifest.

> Secunda regula: *Omnes propositiones affirmatiuæ de contingenti, Secundo modo accepto, conuertuntur, etiam eisdem modis: nempe, Vniuersalis affirmatiua in partem*: vt contingit omnem hominem esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album esse hominem, & particularis affirmatiua simpliciter, vt contingit aliquem hominem esse album: ergo cõtingit aliquod album esse hominẽ. Quæ etiam regula non probatur ab Arist. quia manifesta est.

The second rule: All affirmative propositions de contingenti, taken in the second way, are converted also in the same modes: namely, the universal affirmative into part, as: It is contingent that every man is white; therefore it is contingent that something white is a man; and the particular affirmative simply, as: It is contingent that some man is white; therefore it is contingent that something white is a man. This rule too is not proved by Aristotle, because it is manifest.

> Tertia: *Vniuersalis negatiua, non conuertitur, particularis verò negatiua conuertitur simpliciter*: & in hoc differunt propositiones de contingenti, ab omnibus aliis. Hanc regulam probat alia ratione, nisi quia negatiuæ de modo contingenti propriè sumpto, affirmatiuam habent figuram: quid autem hoc sit, statim explicabitur.

The third: The universal negative is not converted, but the particular negative is converted simply; and in this propositions de contingenti differ from all the others. He proves this rule by no other reason than that negatives of the contingent mode, properly taken, have an affirmative figure; but what this is will be explained presently.

> Dubium primum circa conuersionem propositionum de necesse.

F I R S T D O U B T, C O N C E R N I N G T H E C O N V E R S I O N O F P RO P O S I T I O N S D E NECESSE

> *An vera sit secunda regula conuersionis, vniuersalis affirmatiuæ, & particularis affirmatiuæ, de necesse.*

Whether the second rule of conversion, of the universal affirmative and the particular affirmative de necesse, is true.

> 14 Primò agendum est *de cõuersione propositionum de necesse*, vt ordinem Arist. sequamur. Deinde *de conuersione propositionum de cõtingenti*: & tandem dicemus, quid sentiendum sit, de propositionibus de possibili, & impossibili. Est ergo primũ dubium: Quia secundùm hanc regulam, propositio vniuersalis affirmatiua de necesse, conuertitur in particularem, & particularis affirmatiua simpliciter: sed probatur vtrumque falsum: quia in vtraque conuersione datur antecedens verum, & cõsequens falsum: ergo vtraq; est mala conuersio. Probatur [p. 567] antecedens in his: Necesse est omnem grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est aliquem hominem, esse grammaticum: & rursus, Necesse est aliquem grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum. Aliqui respondent, has propositiones modales, duobus modis sumi posse. Primo in sensu composito: ita, vt significatio modi, cadat supra totum illud concretum, vt compositum ex homine, & grammatica: & sensus sit, Necesse est omne quod necessariò est grammaticum, esse hominem: & tunc antecedens est falsum, sicut & consequens: quare non probatur malam esse conuersionem. Si verò sumantur *in sensu diuiso*: ita vt modus non componat grammaticam cum homine, sed naturæ suæ relinquat: verbi gratia, si talis sensus sit, Omnem grammaticum, non posse nõ esse hominem, non possunt conuerti iuxta traditas regulas: quas solùm in sensu composito intellexit Arist. Hæc solutio non placuit Villalpandeo in Commentariis huius capitis: quia verè diminuta est. Nam cùm in vtroque sensu, possit sumi modus, & meliùs atque frequentiùs sumatur in sensu diuiso, vt per se est manifestum, satis diminutus esset Arist. si regulas conuersionis non assignaret iuxta communem, & magis proprium sensum propositionum. Propterea respondet ipse: Veram esse eandem regulam, etiam exemplo allato, si seruetur idem sensus vtriusque propositionis Quod in conuersione vniuersalis negatiuæ probat, Videlicet Necesse est nullum grammaticum esse hominem: ergo necesse est nullum hominem esse grammaticum, nam vtraque in eodem sensu accepta, est falsa.

14 First we must treat of the conversion of propositions de necesse, so as to follow Aristotle’s order; then of the conversion of propositions de contingenti; and finally we shall say what is to be held concerning propositions de possibili and de impossibili. The first doubt, then, is this: According to this rule the universal affirmative proposition de necesse is converted into a particular, and the particular affirmative simply; but each is proved false, because in each conversion the antecedent is true and the consequent false; therefore each is a bad conversion. This is proved [p. 567] the antecedent in these: It is necessary that every grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that some man be a grammarian; and again: It is necessary that some grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that some man be a grammarian. Some reply that these modal propositions can be taken in two ways. First, in the composite sense, so that the signification of the mode falls upon the whole of that concrete as composed of man and grammar, and the sense is: It is necessary that everything that is necessarily a grammarian be a man; and then the antecedent is false, as is the consequent, wherefore it is not proved that the conversion is bad. But if they are taken in the divided sense, so that the mode does not compound grammar with man but leaves it to its own nature (for example, if the sense is: That every grammarian cannot not be a man), they cannot be converted according to the rules handed down, which Aristotle understood only in the composite sense. This solution did not please Villalpando in his Commentaries on this chapter, because it is truly defective. For since the mode can be taken in either sense, and is better and more frequently taken in the divided sense, as is manifest of itself, Aristotle would be quite defective if he did not assign the rules of conversion according to the common and more proper sense of the propositions. Therefore he himself replies that the same rule is true even with the example adduced, if the same sense of each proposition is preserved. This he proves in the conversion of the universal negative, namely: It is necessary that no grammarian be a man; therefore it is necessary that no man be a grammarian: for each, taken in the same sense, is false.

> Sed hæc solutio minùs satisfacit, quàm prima: nam regula non habet difficultatem in conuersione vniuersalis negatiuæ, sed in solis affirmatiuis: quæ etiam si in eodem sensu accipiantur, necesse est dari aliquando in earum conuersione, antecedens verum, & consequens falsum. Vt exemplum datum probat euidenter.

But this solution satisfies less than the first: for the rule has no difficulty in the conversion of the universal negative, but only in the affirmatives; and these, even if they are taken in the same sense, must sometimes have in their conversion a true antecedent and a false consequent, as the example given proves evidently.

> Ideo respondemus: Propositiones de modo Necesse, vniuersaliter loquendo accipiendas esse, supposita existentia extremorum: vt in eis vera esse possit regula conuersionis tradita ab Aristo. Vt in exempli argumento, supposito, quòd homines, & grammatica sint in rerum natura, tunc verum est antecedens: Necesse est omnem grammaticum esse hominem: quia sensus est, existente homine, & grammatica, necesse est omnem grammaticam esse in homine. Et etiam verum est consequens, Necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum; quia sensus est, homine, & grammatica existentibus [p. 568] in rerum natura, necesse est aliquem hominem esse grammaticum: quamuis non supposita existentia extremorum, sed absolutè accepta, sine tali suppositione, falsa esset propositio.

Therefore we reply: Propositions of the mode de necesse, speaking universally, are to be taken with the existence of the extremes supposed, so that in them the rule of conversion handed down by Aristotle may be true. As in the argument of the example: supposing that men and grammar exist in the nature of things, then the antecedent is true, It is necessary that every grammarian be a man, because the sense is: man and grammar existing, it is necessary that all grammar be in a man. And the consequent is also true, It is necessary that some man be a grammarian, because the sense is: man and grammar existing, Nn iiij [p. 568] in the nature of things, it is necessary that some man be a grammarian; although, without the existence of the extremes being supposed, but taken absolutely, without such a supposition, the proposition would be false.

> Dubium secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

> *An bene probauerit Aristoteles regulas conuersionis propositionum de necesse.*

Whether Aristotle proved well the rules for the conversion of propositions de necesse.

> 15 Videtur non bene id probasse, propter hoc arg. quia non bene probatur res aliqua per medium minùs notum, quàm ipsa sit: sed Arist. probauit regulas conuertendi propositiones de necesse, per conuersionem particularis de contingenti, de qua nihil adhuc dixerat: ergo minùs bene id probauit. Minor patet ex litera Aristotelis. Respondetur, quòd si bene intelligatur ratio Aristotelis, non vtitur conuersioné propositionis de modo contingenti, sed propositionis de inesse: ex qua postea colligit, propositionem particularem de contingenti hoc modo: Si non conuertitur simpliciter vniuersalis negatiua de necesse: ergo potest dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum: sit ergo verum hoc antecedens, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: & consequens falsum, Necesse est nullum equum esse hominem. Et si hoc consequens falsum est, benè sequitur ex eo, veram esse hanc propositionem: Contingit aliquem equum esse hominem, quæ est eius contradictoria. Et quia contingens, sumptum pro possibili, significat id, quod potest esse: ex propositione particulari de contingenti, hoc modo sumpto, infert Aristotel. propositionem particularem de inesse, per illam regulam, Possibili posito in esse, nullum sequitur inconueniens hoc modo: Contingit aliquem equum esse hominem: ponatur ergo in esse: Quòd aliquis equus sit homo: & tunc propositio hæc de inesse, Aliquis equus est homo, conuertitur simpliciter in hanc: ergo aliquis homo est equus, per regulas conuertendi propositiones de inesse, iam traditas ca. præcedenti: ex qua colligit hanc modalem de contingenti pro possibili, Contingit aliquem hominem esse equum: quia ex propositione de inesse, euidenter colligitur propositio de possibili sicut ex actu, colligitur bene potentia. Et hæc vltima, est contradictoria illius antecedentis malę conuersionis, quod verum esse concedebatur videlicet, Necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: & ideo colligit duas contradictorias simul esse veras, sine vlla conuersione propositionis de contingenti, per [p. 569] solam conuersionem propositionis de inesse, & per regulam contradictoriæ oppositionis, traditam lib. 2. de interpretatione quòd si vna est falsa, altera debet esse vera: & quòd propositiones de necesse, habeant oppositionem cum propositionibus de contingenti, etiam sumpto pro possibili, modo, quo explicatur.

15 It seems that he did not prove it well, on account of this argument: because a thing is not well proved through a middle less known than the thing itself; but Aristotle proved the rules for converting propositions de necesse through the conversion of the particular de contingenti, of which he had as yet said nothing; therefore he proved it less well. The minor is plain from the letter of Aristotle. The reply is that, if Aristotle’s reasoning is well understood, he does not use the conversion of a proposition of the contingent mode but of a proposition de inesse, from which he afterwards gathers the particular proposition de contingenti, in this way: If the universal negative de necesse is not converted simply, then the antecedent can be true and the consequent false. Let, then, this antecedent be true, It is necessary that no man be a horse, and the consequent false, It is necessary that no horse be a man. And if this consequent is false, it follows well from it that this proposition is true: It is contingent that some horse is a man, which is its contradictory. And since contingent, taken for possible, signifies that which can be, from the particular proposition de contingenti taken in this way Aristotle infers the particular proposition de inesse by that rule, When the possible is posited as being, nothing impossible follows, in this way: It is contingent that some horse is a man; let it then be posited as being: That some horse is a man. And then this proposition de inesse, Some horse is a man, is converted simply into this: therefore some man is a horse, by the rules for converting propositions de inesse already handed down in the preceding chapter. From this he gathers this modal de contingenti taken for the possible: It is contingent that some man is a horse; because from a proposition de inesse a proposition de possibili is evidently gathered, just as potency is well gathered from act. And this last is the contradictory of that antecedent of the bad conversion which was granted to be true, namely, It is necessary that no man be a horse; and therefore he gathers that two contradictories are true at the same time, without any conversion of a proposition de contingenti, through [p. 569] the sole conversion of a proposition de inesse, and through the rule of contradictory opposition handed down in bk. 1 of On Interpretation, that if one is false the other must be true; and that propositions de necesse have opposition with propositions de contingenti, even taken for the possible, in the way that is explained.

### Circa conuersionem propositionum de modo contingenti — On the Conversion of Propositions of the Contingent Mode.

> *Primum notabile.*

First Note.

> Duobus modis docuit Arist. sumi contingens. Primo, *Impropriè*. Secundò, *Propriè, Impropriè* quidem pro possibili, & ita sumpto, eisdem modis conuerti propositiones eius, ac conuertuntur propositiones de necesse & eisdem argumentis probandæ sunt, atque etiam, vt regulæ veræ esse possint, intelligi debent propositiones, supposita existentia extremorum; vt dictum est in eisdem propositionibus de necesse. Et tandem in cõuersione omnium modalium, intelligendum est, solùm agere Arist. de propositionibus, de modo affirmato: sed variatis ex parte dicti, secundùm quantitatem, & qualitatem. Hoc est de vniuersalibus, & particularibus, affirmatiuis, & negatiuis.

Aristotle taught that contingent is taken in two ways: first, improperly; second, properly. Improperly, indeed, for the possible; and taken in this way, its propositions are converted in the same modes as propositions de necesse are converted, and are to be proved by the same arguments; and also, so that the rules may be true, the propositions must be understood with the existence of the extremes supposed, as was said in the case of those same propositions de necesse. And finally, in the conversion of all modals, it must be understood that Aristotle treats only of propositions of an affirmed mode, but varied on the part of the dictum according to quantity and quality; that is, of universals and particulars, affirmatives and negatives.

> *Secundum notabile.*

Second Note.

> Circa propositiones verò de contingenti, secundo modo sumpta, notandum est, *Omnes propositiones eius efficere sensum copulatiuum*, vt hæc propositio: Contingit hominem esse album, efficit hunc sensum, Possibile est hominem esse album, & hominem non esse album: sicque de reliquis: cuius ratio euidens est, significatio ipsius modi: quæ est, rem posse esse, & posse non esse: & propterea contingens hoc modo sumptum, vocatur ad vtrumlibet, quasi vtrumque partem possibilem significet. Vnde sequitur ex affirmatiua inferri negatiuam, & ex negatiua, affirmatiuam. Bene enim sequitur, Contingit hominem esse album: ergo contingit hominem non esse album: atque etiam, Contingit hominem non esse album: ergo contingit hominem esse album. Et ideo propositionibus de modo contingenti, opponũtur propositiones de modo necesse, & de modo impossibili: quia ex duobus potest prouenire, quòd aliquid non sit cõtingens: nempe, ex eo, quòd sit necessarium, & ex eo, quòd sit impossibile: vnde vtraque hæc est falsa, Contingit hominem esse animal: atq; etiam, Contingit hominẽ esse equum [p. 570] Prima: quia necessaria. Secunda, quia impossibilis. Et ex hoc procedit, tam diuersum modum conuersionis habere propositiones de contingenti, ab aliis omnibus aliorum modorum. Nam cùm vniuersalis negatiua aliorum modorum, conuertatur simpliciter, de modo tamen contingenti, non conuertitur simpliciter. Et cùm particularis negatiua aliorum modorum, non conuertatur, si sit de modo contingenti, conuertitur simpliciter: & hæc est sententia Aristotelis.

Concerning propositions de contingenti taken in the second way, it should be noted that all its propositions produce a copulative sense: as this proposition, It is contingent that a man is white, produces this sense: It is possible that a man is white and that a man is not white; and so of the rest. The evident reason for this is the signification of the mode itself, which is that a thing can be and can not be; and for this reason contingent taken in this way is called ad utrumlibet, as if it signified each part as possible. Whence it follows that from the affirmative the negative is inferred, and from the negative the affirmative. For it follows well: It is contingent that a man is white; therefore it is contingent that a man is not white; and also: It is contingent that a man is not white; therefore it is contingent that a man is white. And therefore to propositions of the contingent mode are opposed propositions of the mode de necesse and of the mode de impossibili, because it can come about from two things that something is not contingent: namely, from its being necessary and from its being impossible. Whence each of these is false: It is contingent that a man is an animal; and also, It is contingent that a man is a horse [p. 570] the first because it is necessary, the second because it is impossible. And from this it comes about that propositions de contingenti have a mode of conversion so different from all the others of the other modes. For whereas the universal negative of the other modes is converted simply, in the contingent mode it is not converted simply. And whereas the particular negative of the other modes is not converted, if it is of the contingent mode it is converted simply; and this is the opinion of Aristotle.

> *Tertium notabile.*

Third Note.

> 17 Sed vt eam intelligamus, notandum est Tertiò, quòd vt *aliqua propositio conuertatur*, necesse est, secundùm omnia quæ includit conuerti: nam si secundùm aliquid non conuertatur, non fiet conuersio secundùm integrum sensum eius: nec dicetur ipsa conuerti, sed aliquid eius: quare talis conuersio, fiet secundùm vocem tantùm, & non secundùm sensum, & veritatem: & ideo non erit vera, sed apparens tantùm. Ex quo præsupposito certissimo, non erit difficile intelligere, verum esse vtrumque assertum ab Aristo. Primum quidem, quòd vniuersalis negatiua de contingenti, non conuertatur simpliciter. Exempli gratia: Contingit nullum hominem esse album: non conuertitur in hanc, Contingit nullum album esse hominem: quia includit has duas propositiones, de possibili, Nullum hominem esse album, est possibile: & Possibile est omnem hominem esse album: sed hæc secunda non conuertitur simpliciter, vt per se est manifestum: ergo nec vniuersalis negatiua eam includens poterit simpliciter conuerti.

17 But in order that we may understand it, it should be noted, third, that for some proposition to be converted it is necessary that it be converted according to everything it includes: for if it is not converted according to something, the conversion will not take place according to its whole sense, nor will it itself be said to be converted, but something of it; wherefore such a conversion will take place according to the word only, and not according to the sense and truth, and therefore it will not be true but only apparent. From this most certain presupposition it will not be difficult to understand that both of Aristotle’s assertions are true. The first, indeed, that the universal negative de contingenti is not converted simply. For example: It is contingent that no man is white is not converted into this, It is contingent that nothing white is a man; because it includes these two propositions de possibili: That no man is white is possible, and It is possible that every man is white; but this second is not converted simply, as is manifest of itself; therefore neither can the universal negative that includes it be converted simply.

> Quòd verò secunda regula, de conuersione particularis negatiuæ vera sit, hoc modo probatur: Propositio particularis negatiua, propter significationem modi, infert affirmatiuam: vt probauimus: ergo hæc est bona consequentia, Contingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquem hominem esse album: ex qua sequitur per conuersionem simplicem iam traditam: ergo contingit aliquod album esse hominem: & ex hac sequitur etiam, propter significationem modi, negatiua, nempe, Contingit aliquod album non esse hominem, quæ est conuertens negatiuæ particularis in principio sumptæ: ergo euidenter probatur, conuertendam esse simpliciter. Sed vt hæc regula vera sit, propositiones habent sumi supposita existentia extremorum: vt in propositionibus de possibili, & necesse diximus, alioqui dabitur antecedẽs verum, [p. 571] & consequens falsum: vt in hoc exemplo: Cõtingit hominem non esse ridentem: ergo contingit ridentem non esse hominem: atque etiam, Contingit hominem non esse grammaticum: ergo contingit grammaticum non esse hominem. Supposita autem existentia extremorum, nempe, risus, & hominis, aut Grammaticæ, & hominis, sicut consequens est falsum, ita & antecedens: nam homine, & Grammatica existentibus, non est contingens, quòd Grammaticum sit homo: sed necessarium ex suppositione: nam si Grammatica est in rerum natura, non potest esse nisi in homine, seu non esse in homine: ergo necesse est eam in homine esse: quare falsum erit, quòd contingat Grammaticum esse hominem.

That the second rule, on the conversion of the particular negative, is true is proved in this way: The particular negative proposition, on account of the signification of the mode, infers the affirmative, as we proved; therefore this is a good consequence: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that some man is white. From this there follows, by the simple conversion already handed down: therefore it is contingent that something white is a man; and from this there follows also, on account of the signification of the mode, the negative, namely, It is contingent that something white is not a man, which is the converse of the particular negative taken at the beginning; therefore it is evidently proved that it is to be converted simply. But in order that this rule may be true, the propositions have to be taken with the existence of the extremes supposed, as we said in the case of propositions de possibili and de necesse; otherwise the antecedent will be true [p. 571] and the consequent false, as in this example: It is contingent that a man is not laughing; therefore it is contingent that something laughing is not a man; and also: It is contingent that a man is not a grammarian; therefore it is contingent that a grammarian is not a man. But supposing the existence of the extremes, namely of laughter and of man, or of grammar and of man, just as the consequent is false, so is the antecedent; for when man and grammar exist, it is not contingent that a grammarian is a man, but necessary by supposition: for if grammar is in the nature of things, it cannot be except in a man, or cannot not be in a man; therefore it is necessary that it be in a man; wherefore it will be false that it is contingent that a grammarian is a man.

> 18 Sed aduersus hanc conuersionem particularis negatiuæ, est arg. satis difficile. Nam ideo dictum est ab Arist. *particularem negatiuam de inesse non conuerti simpliciter*: quia datur antecedens verum & consequens falsum: & hoc ideo, quia fit argumentum à termino non distributo, ad terminum distributum, ex parte subiecti propositionis conuertendæ: vt patet in hac, Aliquod animal non est homo: ergo aliquis homo non est animal, Animal enim non est distributum in antecedente: & tamen distribuitur in consequente, ratione negationis supra illud cadentis: sed idem defectus contingit in conuersione particularis negatiuæ de contingenti: ergo falsum erit, quòd conuertatur, Et hæc regula erit contraria illi, quæ negat particularem negatiuam de inesse conuerti. Probatur minor: quia dum sic procedimus, Contingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album non esse hominem, homo, qui est subiectum in antecedente, non distribuitur, sed solùm afficitur signo particulari: & tamen distribuitur in consequente, ratione negationis cadentis supra illum: ergo ex parte eius erit talis conuersio, argumenti à termino non distributo, ad terminum distributum, sicut conuersio particularis negatiuæ de inesse: & consequenter, erit vitiosa, & nulla, sicut est illa.

18 But against this conversion of the particular negative there is a rather difficult argument. For Aristotle said that the particular negative de inesse is not converted simply for this reason, that the antecedent is true and the consequent false; and this because the argument is made from a term not distributed to a term distributed, on the part of the subject of the proposition to be converted, as is plain in this: Some animal is not a man; therefore some man is not an animal. For animal is not distributed in the antecedent, and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it. But the same defect occurs in the conversion of the particular negative de contingenti; therefore it will be false that it is converted. And this rule will be contrary to the one that denies that the particular negative de inesse is converted. The minor is proved: because when we proceed thus, It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man, man, which is the subject in the antecedent, is not distributed, but is only affected by a particular sign; and yet it is distributed in the consequent, by reason of the negation falling upon it; therefore on its part such a conversion will be an argument from a term not distributed to a term distributed, like the conversion of the particular negative de inesse; and consequently it will be faulty and null, as that one is.

> Respondetur, Distinguendo minorem, quòd in conuersione negatiuæ de contingenti: fiat argumentum à non distributo ad distributum: quia diuerso modo fit, atque in propositione de inesse; nam in hac fit, ex parte totius, atque integri extremi, sed in modali de contingenti, tantùm ex parte extremi partialis, cùm tamen ex alia parte maneat extremum sine distributione, nam extremum propositionis modalis est dictum: & cùm propositio de modo contingente negatiua, contineat etiam affirmatiuam, duas habet partes dictum eius: [p. 572] vnam negatam, & alteram affirmatam. Et ideo vnam distributam, & alteram sine distributione. Gratia exempli, dum sic procedimus, in eodem exempli loco allato arg. Cõtingit aliquem hominem non esse album: ergo contingit aliquod album, non esse hominem: hoc consequens negatiuum, continet etiam affirmatiuum, nempe, Contingit aliquod album esse hominem: in quo patet hominem non distribui, licèt distribuatur in alia parte eiusdem dicti negatiua: ex affirmatiua autem, sequitur iterum alia pars negatiua: nempe, Contingit aliquod album, non esse hominem: quæ est conuertens eiusdem particularis negatiuæ. Vnde sequitur, non impedire conuersionem, nec vitiosam eam reddere argumentationem, à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte extremi partialis, manentis sine distritione in alia parte affirmatiua eiusdem.

The reply is by distinguishing the minor: that in the conversion of the negative de contingenti an argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed, because it is made in a different way than in the proposition de inesse; for in the latter it is made on the part of the whole and entire extreme, but in the modal de contingenti only on the part of a partial extreme, while on the other side the extreme nevertheless remains without distribution; for the extreme of a modal proposition is the dictum; and since a negative proposition of the contingent mode also contains the affirmative, its dictum has two parts; [p. 572] one negated and the other affirmed, and therefore one distributed and the other without distribution. For example, when we proceed thus, in the same argument adduced as an example: It is contingent that some man is not white; therefore it is contingent that something white is not a man: this negative consequent also contains the affirmative, namely, It is contingent that something white is a man, in which it is plain that man is not distributed, although it is distributed in the other, negative part of the same dictum; and from the affirmative there follows in turn the other, negative part, namely, It is contingent that something white is not a man, which is the converse of that same particular negative. Whence it follows that argumentation from the non-distributed to the distributed, on the part of a partial extreme that remains without distribution in the other, affirmative part of the same, does not impede conversion nor render it faulty.

> Sed aduersus hanc solutionem, est argum. adhuc difficilius: Quia ex eo sequitur vniuersalem negatiuam eiusdem modi contingentis, conuerti simpliciter, contra aliam regulam negantem conuersionem eius. Probatur id sequi, quia ex eo tantùm non potest conuerti vniuersalis negatiua simpliciter, quia includit vniuersalem affirmatiuam, non conuertibilem simpliciter, sed vniuersalis affirmatiua, ex eo solùm non potest conuerti simpliciter: quia talis conuersio erit argumentum à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte prædicati eius: quod cùm non sit in ea distributum, distribuitur in conuertente, vt patet, dum sic procedimus: Contingit omnem hominem esse album: ergo contingit, omne album esse hominem. Constat verò vniuersalem affirmatiuam, solùm esse partem dicti vniuersalis negatiuæ, eam includentis: & ideo solùm esse extremum partiale eius: ergo si non reddit vitiosam conuersionem, quòd in ea fiat argumentum, à non distributo ad distributum, ex parte extremi partialis: vt dictum est in conuersione particularis negatiuæ, nec igitur efficietur vitiosa conuersio vniuersalis negatiuæ. Respondetur, Esse diuersam rationem in vniuersali negatiua, includente vniuersalem affirmatiuam, ac in particulari negatiua: nam in conuersione huius duo sunt: Primum, quòd idem terminus, qui non est distributus in subiecto antecedens, non distribuitur in vtraque parte consequentis, sed in altera tantùm: in alia verò, sine distributo manet, cùm sit particularis affirmatiua.

But against this solution there is a still more difficult argument: Because from it it follows that the universal negative of the same contingent mode is converted simply, against the other rule denying its conversion. That this follows is proved: because the universal negative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that it includes the universal affirmative, which is not convertible simply; but the universal affirmative cannot be converted simply only for this reason, that such a conversion would be an argument from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of its predicate, which, since it is not distributed in it, is distributed in the converse, as is plain when we proceed thus: It is contingent that every man is white; therefore it is contingent that everything white is a man. But it is certain that the universal affirmative is only part of the dictum of the universal negative that includes it, and therefore only its partial extreme; therefore, if it does not render the conversion faulty that an argument is made in it from the non-distributed to the distributed on the part of a partial extreme, as was said in the conversion of the particular negative, then neither is the conversion of the universal negative rendered faulty. The reply is that the reason is different in the universal negative, which includes the universal affirmative, and in the particular negative: for in the conversion of the latter there are two things. First, that the same term which is not distributed in the subject of the antecedent is not distributed in both parts of the consequent, but in one only, while in the other it remains without distribution, since it is a particular affirmative.

> Secundum est, quòd eadem pars affirmatiua conuertitur simpliciter: & per talem conuersionem, colligitur euidenter ex ea particularis negatiua: quæ est conuertens particularis negatiuæ, in principio assumptæ ad conuersionem: & ideo à [p. 573] primo ad vltimum, sequitur euidenter particulam negatiuam conuerti. In vniuersali verò affirmatiua, inclusa in negatiua vniuersali, neutrum horum reperitur. Non primum: quia sic argumentum à non distributo ad distributum, dum eam conuertimus: vt terminus qui non distribuitur in antecedenti, semper in consequenti distribuatur: hoc est, tam in conuertente affirmatiua, vt patet, cùm sit vniuersalis quàm in negatiua vniuersali, quam includit, cuius omnes terminos patet esse distributos. Ideo omni ex parte est argumentatio à non distributo ad distributum: & plus infertur in consequenti, quàm contineatur in antecedenti. Sed nec reperitur secundùm: quia vniuersalis affirmatiua, in quam conuertitur, non includit propositionem conuertibilem, ex qua possit deduci conuertens vniuersalis negatiuæ, sed solùm vniuersalem negatiuam non conuertibilem, vel de qua disputatio est, an conuertatur: quare non possumus vti conuersione eius in eadem argumentatione, sicut possumus vti conuersione particularis affirmatiuæ inclusæ in alia particulari negatiua, ideo nunquam possumus colligere ex conuersione vniuersalis affirmatiuæ, quam includit, vniuersalem negatiuam, quæ sit conuertens alterius vniuersalis negatiuæ: de cuius conuersione agitur. Ex his igitur duabus differentiis, tanquam à signo euidenti colligimus, propositionem particularem negatiuam, continere virtualiter suam conuertentem: cùm per euidentes consequentias ex ea deducatur: & ideo conuerti posse, vt docuit Arist. Vniuersalem verò negatiuam, non continere suam conuertentem vllo modo, cùm ex ea non possit deduci: sed solùm affirmatiuam vniuersalem, quæ impedimento est ei, ne possit simpliciter conuerti.

The second is that the same affirmative part is converted simply, and through such a conversion the particular negative is evidently gathered from it, which is the converse of the particular negative assumed at the beginning for conversion; and therefore from [p. 573] first to last it follows evidently that the particular negative is converted. But in the universal affirmative, included in the universal negative, neither of these is found. Not the first: because when we convert it, the argument is made from the non-distributed to the distributed in such a way that the term which is not distributed in the antecedent is always distributed in the consequent; that is, both in the converse affirmative, as is plain, since it is universal, and in the universal negative which it includes, all of whose terms are plainly distributed. Therefore the argumentation is in every respect from the non-distributed to the distributed, and more is inferred in the consequent than is contained in the antecedent. But neither is the second found: because the universal affirmative into which it is converted does not include a convertible proposition from which the converse of the universal negative could be deduced, but only the universal negative, which is not convertible, or about which the dispute is whether it is converted; wherefore we cannot use its conversion in the same argumentation, as we can use the conversion of the particular affirmative included in the other, particular negative; and therefore we can never gather, from the conversion of the universal affirmative which it includes, the universal negative that would be the converse of the other universal negative whose conversion is in question. From these two differences, then, as from an evident sign, we gather that the particular negative proposition virtually contains its converse, since it is deduced from it through evident consequences, and therefore that it can be converted, as Aristotle taught; but that the universal negative in no way contains its converse, since it cannot be deduced from it, but only the universal affirmative, which is an impediment to it, so that it cannot be converted simply.

> Et si tandem dicatur, hinc sequi, quòd vniuersalis negatiua saltem possit conuerti in partem: cùm vniuersalis affirmatiua, quam includit, & propter quam solam non potest conuerti, in particularem conuertatur: quod tamen videtur esse contra regulam Arist. negantem vllo modo conuerti, Respondeo: Necessariò concedendum esse, quòd vniuersalis negatiua conuertatur in particularem: quia id conuincit argumentum: quia hoc nunquam Arist. negauit: quia nullum est fundamentum, propter quod negari possit, sed solùm negauit conuerti, vt petit propria natura: hoc est conuersione simplici, sicut conuertitur in aliis modis, atque in propositionibus de inesse. Et hæc de conuersione propositionum de modo contingenti.

And if, finally, it is said that it follows from this that the universal negative can at least be converted into part, since the universal affirmative which it includes, and on account of which alone it cannot be converted, is converted into a particular (which nevertheless seems to be against the rule of Aristotle denying that it is converted in any way), I reply: It must necessarily be granted that the universal negative is converted into a particular, because the argument convinces of it; because Aristotle never denied this; because there is no foundation on account of which it could be denied. He denied only that it is converted as its own nature demands, that is, by simple conversion, as it is converted in the other modes and in propositions de inesse. And this concerning the conversion of propositions of the contingent mode.

[p. 574]

> Notabile vnicum.

Single Note.

### Notabile vnicum circa conuersionem propositionum de possibili, & impossibili — On the Conversion of Propositions de Possibili and de Impossibili.

> 12 Vltimò notandum est, *circa conuersionem propositionum de possibili: & impossibili*: non esse locutum Arist. expressè, & non in particulari de illis: quia eisdem modis conuertuntur, secundùm sensum, & æquipollentiam, ac propositiones de necesse: licèt aliquando diuersæ appareant ab eis, præsertim propositiones de impossibili, Et de propositionibus de possibili, res est manifesta, cùm sint de contingenti in impropriè sumpto, de quibus suprà diximus, eodem modo conuerti posse, ac propositiones de necesse. Sed de propositionibus de impossibili, intelligetur facile, si consideremus propositiones de impossibili affirmato, æquipollere propositionibus de necesse, habentibus oppositum dictum, vt hæc propositio: Impossibile est aliquem hominem esse equum, æquipollet huic, necesse est nullum hominem esse equum: quare sicut illa conuertenda est: & sic de cæteris de impossibili, affirmato modo: nam de his solis loquitur Arist. in his conuersionibus: vt diximus. Solùm est repetendum in hac parte, quod intelligitur semper, supposita existentia extremorum.

12 Lastly, it should be noted that, concerning the conversion of propositions de possibili and de impossibili, Aristotle did not speak expressly and in particular of them, because they are converted in the same modes, according to sense and equipollence, as propositions de necesse, although they sometimes appear different from them, especially propositions de impossibili. And as for propositions de possibili, the matter is manifest, since they are of the contingent improperly taken, of which we said above that they can be converted in the same way as propositions de necesse. But as for propositions de impossibili, it will be easily understood if we consider that propositions of an affirmed de impossibili are equipollent to propositions de necesse having the opposite dictum: as this proposition, It is impossible that some man is a horse, is equipollent to this, It is necessary that no man be a horse; wherefore it is to be converted as that one is; and so of the others of the affirmed de impossibili mode, for of these alone Aristotle speaks in these conversions, as we said. It need only be repeated in this part that this is always understood with the existence of the extremes supposed.

## CHAPTER IIII

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Determinatis verò his. Dicamus iam per quæ, & quando, & quomodo fiat omnis syllogismus, &c.*

These things having been determined, let us now say through what things, and when, and how every syllogism comes about, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 22 Intentum Arist. cap. præsenti est, explicare *naturam, & rationem primæ figuræ.* Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima, Explicat modos vniuersales, quibus syllogismi fieri possunt: ex quibus alios omnes inutiles, qui videntur eis similes, reijcit. In secunda: Explicat duos alios modos particulares vtiles, & ex eis tanquam inutiles, omnes alios, qui in simili dispositione fieri possunt, etiam reiicit.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na22 T ture and ratio of the first figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he explains the universal moods in which syllogisms can be made, and from them he rejects all the other, useless ones that seem similar to them. In the second he explains two other, particular useful moods, and from them he likewise rejects as useless all the others that can be made in a similar disposition.

> Modos vniuersales explicat his verbis: *Quando tres termini sic se habent, vt postremus sit in toto medio, & medius in toto primo, sic, vel non sit, extremorum fieri syllogismum necesse est, &c.* Per medium terminum intelligit eum, qui bis sumitur in præmissis. Per postremum terminum, minorem extremitatem [p. 575]: & per primum, maiorem extremitatem. Sensus igitur verborum eius talis est: Quando tres termini, ita sunt dispositi, vt medium subiiciatur vniuersaliter maiori extremitati, in prima propositione: in secunda verò, minor extremitas subiiciatur vniuersaliter medio, affirmatiuè quidem fit syllogismus in primo modo, qui vocatur, *Barbara*: quia constat tribus propositionibus affirmatiuis, & est talis: Omne animal est substantia: omnis homo est animal: ergo omnis homo est substantia. Negatiuè verò, in secundo modo, qui vocatur *Celarent*: quia constat minori affirmatiua, & maiori, & conclusione negatiuis: & ita constituitur: Nullum animal est lapis: omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis. Quomodocunque autem aliter disponantur medium, & extremitates in propositionibus vniuersalibus, modos inutiles, ac vitiosos efficiunt: in quibus tam propositiones vniuersales affirmatiuæ, quàm negatiuæ, indifferenter sequuntur: vel, vt alij dicunt: dantur termini, in quibus Omni, & etiam termini, in quibus Nulli, & probatur vitiosas esse consequentias, v. g. dari duas contradictorias simul veras. Itaque, ex dispositione vniuersali terminorum solùm duo producti modi vtiles resultant, in quibus perfecti efficiuntur syllogismi. Quod probatur euidenter, quia in primo, dicitur de omni: hoc est prædicatum maioris quod vniuersaliter dicitur de subiecto in maiori, dicitur necessariò de aliquo contento, & sumpto sub eo in conclusione. In secundo verò, dicitur de nullo: nam prædicatum maioris negatur vniuersaliter de subiecto eiusdem: & ideo negatur etiam necessariò de subiecto minoris in conclusione.

He explains the universal moods in these words: When three terms are so related that the last is in the whole middle, and the middle is or is not in the whole first, there must be a syllogism of the extremes, etc. By the middle term he understands the one that is taken twice in the premises. By the last term, the minor extreme [p. 575] and by the first, the major extreme. The sense of his words, then, is this: When three terms are so disposed that the middle is subjected universally to the major extreme in the first proposition, and in the second the minor extreme is subjected universally to the middle, there comes about, affirmatively, a syllogism in the first mood, which is called Barbara, because it consists of three affirmative propositions; and it is this: Every animal is a substance; every man is an animal; therefore every man is a substance. Negatively, in the second mood, which is called Celarent, because it consists of an affirmative minor and of a negative major and conclusion; and it is constructed thus: No animal is a stone; every man is an animal; therefore no man is a stone. But however else the middle and the extremes are disposed in universal propositions, they produce useless and faulty moods, in which universal propositions, affirmative as well as negative, follow indifferently; or, as others say, terms are given in which “all” follows and also terms in which “none” follows; and the consequences are proved to be faulty, for example by two contradictories being given true at the same time. And so from the universal disposition of the terms only the two moods produced result as useful, in which perfect syllogisms are made. This is proved evidently: because in the first, said of all holds, that is, the predicate of the major, which is said universally of the subject in the major, is necessarily said of something contained and taken under it in the conclusion. In the second, said of none holds: for the predicate of the major is denied universally of its subject, and therefore it is also necessarily denied of the subject of the minor in the conclusion.

> In secunda part. cap. Explicat duos alios modos vtiles eiusdem figuræ, quos vocat particulares: quia altera præmissarum particularis est, & vniuersalis altera. Si ergo inquit vtraque præmissa sit particularis, inutiles fiunt omnes modi: Si verò particularis vna, & vniuersalis altera: vel maior est vniuersalis, in qua maior extremitas dicitur vniuersaliter de medio: & minor particularis, in qua medium dicitur de minori extremitate, modo particulari: fit tertius modus perfecti syllogismi, qui dicitur *Darij*, quia constat maiori vniuersali affirmatiua, & minori, & conclusione, particularibus etiam affirmatiuis. Et talis est modus is, Omne animal rationale, est risibile: Aliquis homo est animal rationale: ergo aliquis homo est risibilis. Si verò maior sit vniuersalis negatiua in qua maior extremitas negetur vniuersaliter de medio: & minor particularis affirmatiua, in qua medium dicatur de [p. 576] minori extremitate, modo particulari, fit modus vtilis quartus primæ figuræ, qui vocatur *Ferio*, & est talis: Nullum animal est lapis: Aliquis homo est animal: ergo aliquis homo non est lapis. Quòd verò duo isti syllogismi perfecti sint, euidens est, ex duobus aliis prioribus: à quibus solùm differunt ex parte minoris propositionis, quæ in illis est vniuersalis, & in his particularis: & consequenter conclusiones eorum sunt particulares. Cùm ergo particulares propositiones eorum, contineantur sub vniuersalibus aliorum, si illi euidentes sunt, & in eis dicitur de omni, & de nullo, idem prorsus habebunt isti. Cæteri verò modi, quibus disponi possunt præmissæ vniuersalis, & particularis: inutiles sunt: & in quibus dantur termini, in quibus Omni, & in quibus Nulli. Hæc Arist.

In the second part of the chapter he explains two other useful moods of the same figure, which he calls particular, because one of the premises is particular and the other universal. If, then, he says, each premise is particular, all the moods become useless. But if one is particular and the other universal: either the major is universal, in which the major extreme is said universally of the middle, and the minor particular, in which the middle is said of the minor extreme in a particular mode, and there comes about the third mood of perfect syllogism, which is called Darij, because it consists of a universal affirmative major and of a minor and conclusion that are particular and also affirmative. And this mood is such: Every rational animal is risible; some man is a rational animal; therefore some man is risible. Or if the major is a universal negative, in which the major extreme is denied universally of the middle, and the minor a particular affirmative, in which the middle is said of [p. 576] the minor extreme in a particular mode, there comes about the fourth useful mood of the first figure, which is called Ferio; and it is this: No animal is a stone; some man is an animal; therefore some man is not a stone. That these two syllogisms are perfect is evident from the two other, prior ones, from which they differ only on the part of the minor proposition, which in those is universal and in these particular; and consequently their conclusions are particular. Since, then, their particular propositions are contained under the universals of the others, if those are evident and in them said of all and said of none hold, these will have altogether the same. But the other moods in which a universal and a particular premise can be disposed are useless, and in them terms are given in which “all” follows and in which “none” follows. Thus far Aristotle.

### Quid sit figura, & quotuplex, & qui modus — What a figure is, and how many kinds, and what a mood is, is explained.

> *Figura syllogismorum, nihil aliud est quàm debita dispositio trium terminorum*: hoc est, medij, & extremitatum, *secundùm debitum modum prædicationis, & subiectionis.* Dicitur autem per metaphoram, ex similitudine figuræ geometricæ: nam sicut hæc resultat ex lineis terminatis per puncta, ita dispositis, eodem modo figura syllogistica, ex propositionibus, quæ sunt quasi lineæ terminatæ extremis punctis, hoc est, subiecto, & prædicato: quæ vocantur termini propositionum, quia sunt extrema eius.

The figure of syllogisms is nothing other than the due disposition of three terms, that is, of the middle and the extremes, according to the due mode of predication and subjection. It is so called by metaphor, from its likeness to a geometrical figure: for just as the latter results from lines terminated by points and so disposed, in the same way the syllogistic figure results from propositions, which are as it were lines terminated by extreme points, that is, by the subject and the predicate, which are called the terms of propositions because they are their extremes.

> *Figura triplex est*: quia tribus tantùm modis disponi possunt media, & extremitates. Nam vel medium in prima est subiectum, & in secunda prædicatum: & vocatur prima figura propter tria. Primò, Quia medium in hac dispositione, non solùm rationem habet medij, quod per id coniungantur extremitates: sed etiam proprium situm medio debitum, cùm sit inter extremitates collocatum: ita vt sit subiectum vnius, & prædicatum alterius. Secundò, Quia in hac figura, omne genus propositionis colligitur, nempe vniuersalis affirmatiua, vniuersalis negatiua, particularis affirmatiua, & particularis negatiua. Tertiò, Quia ex hac figura deriuantur aliæ: nam vel medium est prædicatum vtriusque præmissæ, & sic est secunda figura: vel est subiectum vtriusque, & sic est tertia. Cuius ratio satis congruens est: quia prædicatum est nobilius subiecto: & ideo nobiliorem rationem, & locum habet medium: & nobilior ex consequenti est dispositio ipsa, in qua semper est prædicatum ea, in qua semper est subiectum: & [p. 577] propterea dispositio illa, Secundam, hæc verò figuram Tertiam meritò constituit,

The figure is threefold: because the middle and the extremes can be disposed in only three ways. For either the middle is the subject in the first and the predicate in the second, and this is called the first figure, for three reasons. First, because the middle in this disposition not only has the ratio of a middle, in that the extremes are conjoined through it, but also the proper position due to a middle, since it is placed between the extremes, so as to be the subject of one and the predicate of the other. Second, because in this figure every kind of proposition is concluded, namely the universal affirmative, the universal negative, the particular affirmative, and the particular negative. Third, because the others are derived from this figure: for either the middle is the predicate of both premises, and so it is the second figure; or it is the subject of both, and so it is the third. The reason for this order is quite fitting: because the predicate is nobler than the subject, and therefore the middle has a nobler ratio and place, and consequently the disposition itself in which it is always the predicate is nobler than that in which it is always the subject; and [p. 577] therefore that disposition rightly constitutes the Second figure, and this one the Third.

> *Modus est, debita dispositio præmissarum, secundùm debitam qualitatem, & quantitatem* hoc est, secundùm rationem vniuersalis, & particularis: in qua consistit quantitas propositionis: & secundùm affirmationem, & negationem, in quibus consistit qualitas.

A mood is the due disposition of the premises according to due quality and quantity, that is, according to the ratio of universal and particular, in which the quantity of a proposition consists, and according to affirmation and negation, in which its quality consists.

> 25 *Modi primæ igitur*, quatuor tantùm enumerati sunt, nempe, *duo vniuersales, & duo particulares.* Quia his tantùm quatuor modis, debito modo disponi possunt præmissæ: vt ex eis euidenter inferatur conclusio: cæteri verò omnes modi, inutiles sunt vt dictum est.

25 Of the first, then, only four moods have been enumerated, namely two universal and two particular, because only in these four moods can the premises be disposed in the due manner so that the conclusion is evidently inferred from them; but all the other moods are useless, as has been said.

> Dubium Secundum.

S E C O N D D O U B T.

### An præter tres figuras enumeratas ab Arist. addenda sit quarta — Whether, besides the three figures enumerated by Aristotle, a fourth is to be added.

> Prima opinio tenet, *Addendam esse quartam*: quam tribuunt Galeno medicorum principi. Et probatur hoc arg. *Figura est debita dispositio medij, & extremitatum, secundùm debitam subiectionem, & prædicationem*: sed præter tres modos: quibus disponuntur ab Arist. possunt quarto alio modo ab eis diuerso disponi: ergo ex tali dispositione efficietur diuersa figura, quæ sit quarta. Probatur minor: quia dispositio primæ figuræ est, in qua medium est subiectum maioris, & prædicatum minoris: dispositio secundæ, in qua medium est prædicatum vtriusque præmissæ: & dispositio tertiæ, in qua medium est vtriusque subiectum, sed possunt etiam quarto modo disponi, ita vt medium sit prædicatum maioris, & subiectum minoris: scilicet vt ex tali dispositione non minùs euidenter sequatur conclusio, quàm ex tribus prioribus: ergo resultabit ex tali dispositione quarta figura, distincta à tribus. Minor probatur hoc exemplo: Omne risibile est homo: omnis homo est animal rationale: ergo omne animal rationale, est risibile.

The first opinion holds that a fourth is to be added; they attribute it to Galen, the prince of physicians. And it is proved by this argument: A figure is the due disposition of the middle and the extremes according to due subjection and predication; but besides the three modes in which they are disposed by Aristotle, they can be disposed in a fourth mode different from them; therefore from such a disposition a different figure will be produced, which is the fourth. The minor is proved: because the disposition of the first figure is that in which the middle is the subject of the major and the predicate of the minor; the disposition of the second, that in which the middle is the predicate of each premise; and the disposition of the third, that in which the middle is the subject of each; but they can also be disposed in a fourth mode, so that the middle is the predicate of the major and the subject of the minor, namely in such a way that from such a disposition the conclusion follows no less evidently than from the three prior ones; therefore from such a disposition there will result a fourth figure, distinct from the three. The minor is proved by this example: Everything risible is a man; every man is a rational animal; therefore every rational animal is risible.

> 26 Communis tamen consensus totius scholæ, *tres tantùm figuras ponit* cum Arist. Et ita nobis sentiendum est. & probatur hac ratione: Quia figura propriè loquendo, est quasi forma syllogismi: in qua formaliter disponuntur propositiones: hoc est secundùm modum naturalem, ac debitum formæ earum. Debitus autem modus, in eo consistit, vt id quod se habet, vt forma, sit prædicatum, & quod se habet vt materia, sit subiectum: sed tribus tantùm modis ita possunt propositiones disponi [p. 578], ergo tres tantùm erunt figuræ enumeratæ ab Aristot. Minorem sic probo: Non possunt disponi quarto illo modo, nisi in maiori prædicetur, id, quod verè se habet vt materia, & subiiciatur, quod se habet vt forma: atqui hæc dispositio præter naturam, & formam propositionis est, vt idem exemplum assignatum probat: ergo ex illa dispositione nõ potest propria aliqua figura resultare: quare rarò, vel nunquam in disputationibus tali dispositione syllogismorum vtimur. Talis ergo dispositio, si aliquid simile figuræ habere potest, imperfectum quiddam est, & dispositioni primæ figuræ, quodammodo affine, ad quam reduci debet. Ad argum. verò: Distinguenda est minor: quia disponi possunt, sed non modo debito ad efficiendam figuram, vt probatum est: & ideo talis dispositio, figuram distinctam non efficit, sed propter quandam similitudinem, reducitur ad primam.

26 The common consensus of the whole school, however, posits only three figures with Aristotle. And so we must hold; and it is proved by this reason: Because a figure, properly speaking, is as it were the form of the syllogism, in which the propositions are formally disposed, that is, according to the natural mode and that due to their form. But the due mode consists in this, that what stands as form be the predicate, and what stands as matter be the subject; but only in three modes can propositions be disposed Oo [p. 578] in this way; therefore there will be only the three figures enumerated by Aristotle. The minor I prove thus: They cannot be disposed in that fourth mode unless in the major that which truly stands as matter is predicated, and that which stands as form is subjected; but this disposition is against the nature and form of the proposition, as the same example assigned proves; therefore no proper figure can result from that disposition; wherefore we rarely or never use such a disposition of syllogisms in disputations. Such a disposition, then, if it can have anything like a figure, is something imperfect, and in a certain way akin to the disposition of the first figure, to which it ought to be reduced. To the argument: the minor must be distinguished, because they can be disposed, but not in the due manner for producing a figure, as has been proved; and therefore such a disposition does not produce a distinct figure, but on account of a certain likeness it is reduced to the first.

> 27 Et si aliquis obiiciat ex opposito, primam solam sufficere, cùm per eam inferatur omne genus propositionis: & ideo, secundam, & tertiam non fuisse addendas. Respondeo, Necessarias esse secundam, & tertiam: quia licèt in prima colligi possit omne genus propositionis, non tamen semper ea vti possumus in disputationibus: quia non semper tam manifesta cõsequentia constitui potest, vt omnibus euidens appareat: sed necesse est, aliis minus euidentibus sæpe vti, vt per eas ad euidentiores primæ figuræ perueniamus. Necessariæ præterea sunt, vt copiam syllogismorum habeamus, ad instituendas disputationes: quam per solam primam figuram non haberemus.

27 And if someone objects from the opposite side that the first alone suffices, since every kind of proposition is inferred through it, and therefore that the second and third ought not to have been added, I reply that the second and third are necessary: because, although every kind of proposition can be concluded in the first, we cannot nevertheless always use it in disputations, because a consequence cannot always be constructed so manifest that it appears evident to all; but it is necessary often to use others, less evident, so that through them we may arrive at the more evident ones of the first figure. Moreover, they are necessary so that we may have an abundance of syllogisms for conducting disputations, which we should not have through the first figure alone.

> CAPVT V.

C H A P T E R V.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Quando vero huic quidem omni, illi autem nulli insit, aut vtrique omni, aut nulli, figuram quidem talem voco secundam.*

But when the same belongs to all of one and to none of the other, or to all of each, or to none, such a figure I call the second.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 28 Intentum Arist. cap. præsenti est, explicare *naturam secundæ figuræ*. Diuiditur autem in duas partes: In prima, Explicat dispositionem secundæ figuræ, In secunda: Modos omnes vtiles syllogizandi in ea, refutatis inutilibus, percenset.

he intent of Aristotle in the present chapter is to explain the na28 T ture of the second figure. And it is divided into two parts. In the first he explains the disposition of the second figure; in the second he reviews all the useful moods of syllogizing in it, the useless ones having been refuted.

> Secunda figura efficitur, (inquit Arist.) *quando sic disponuntur [p. 579] præmissæ: vt medium sit prædicatum vniuersale de extremitatibus, in vtraque*: ita vt affirmetur in vna, & negetur in alia: indifferenter quidem, quia siue maior sit negatiua, siue minor, dum modo non sit vtraque affirmatiua, aut negatiua, bona est dispositio, vt his duobus exemplis ostenditur: Nullus lapis est animal: Omnis homo est animal: ergo nullus homo est lapis, & rursus: Omnis homo est viuens: Nullus lapis est viuens: ergo nullus lapis est homo. Ideo medium in hac figura, ait Aristot. esse, *quod omni, vel nulli extremitati inest*: Extremitates verò, quibus inest medium: & vt vtramque distinguat, asserit maiorem extremitatem esse eam, quæ iuxta medium posita est: esse autem iuxta medium positam dicit, quia sicut medium est prædicatum in præmissis, ita maior extremitas in conclusione.
