Likewise in human faith, whose formal objective ratio is the testimony of one worthy of credence, and therefore it is efficient of the act of believing; but the formal objective ratio on account of which the intellect assents to the conclusion is the assent of the principles, as Aristotle expressly teaches in the following chapter. And an evident reason proves it: because it is on account of the principles that the intellect assents to the conclusion; therefore it will be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion.

> Ad primum arg. Durandi: Neganda est minor: quòd dum intellectus assentitur conclusioni, non permaneant assensus principiorum. Et cùm dicitur, intellectum non posse simul habere plures assensus: distinguendum est: quia duobus modis possunt se habere plures assensus, vel per modum plurium, quando non sunt inter sese ordinati, vel per modum vnius, quando sunt ordinati. Intellectus ergo non potest habere plures assensus per modum pluriũ, bene tamen per modum vnius & ita se habent assensus principiorum & conclusionis, qui ordinati sunt, cùm ille sit ratio formalis assentiendi huius. Dum ergo intellectus assentitur conclusioni, perseuerare potest, & perseuerat in assensibus principiorum, quasi continuans eos: & ideo possunt esse causa efficiens assensus conclusionis. Quòd verò vnus actus intellectus, non possit esse causa alterius, negandum est: nam saltem potest esse causa, *Qua*, licèt non sit causa, *Quæ*: hoc est, ratio formalis causandi, licèt non sit id quod causat: & ita assensus principiorum, est ratio formalis assentiendi, licèt non sit causa, quæ efficiat assensum conclusionis: sed hoc solus intellectus habet, ratione eiusdem assensus principiorum: & ideo assensus iste est efficiens, Quo assensus conclusionis, non efficiens, *Quod*: sicus veritas rei, est causa efficiens intellectionis eius, tanquam *Quo*, non tanquam *Quod*.

To the first argument of Durandus: the minor must be denied, namely that while the intellect assents to the conclusion the assents of the principles do not remain. And when it is said that the intellect cannot have several assents at the same time, a distinction must be made: because several assents can be related in two ways, either by way of many, when they are not ordered among themselves, or by way of one, when they are ordered. The intellect, then, cannot have several assents by way of many, but it can indeed by way of one; and so are related the assents of the principles and of the conclusion, which are ordered, since the former is the formal ratio of assenting to the latter. While, then, the intellect assents to the conclusion, it can persevere, and does persevere, in the assents of the principles, as it were continuing them; and therefore they can be the efficient cause of the assent of the conclusion. But that one act of the intellect cannot be the cause of another must be denied: for at least it can be a cause Quo [by which], although it is not a cause Quod [which], that is, the formal ratio of causing, although it is not that which causes. And so the assent of the principles is the formal ratio of assenting, although it is not the cause which effects the assent of the conclusion; but the intellect alone has this, by reason of that same assent of the principles; and therefore this assent is efficient Quo of the assent of the conclusion, not efficient Quod: as the truth of a thing is the efficient cause of the understanding of it as a cause Quo, not as a cause Quod.

> 29 Ad secundùm: Concedenda est prima cõsequentia, quòd assensus principiorum sit causa æquiuoca assensus conclusionis: quia specie distinctus ab eo, sed minor neganda, quòd sola causa vniuersalis, & remota sit æquiuoca: nam omnis causa, siue vniuersalis, siue particularis: proxima, vel remota, verè est æquiuoca: quia ratio causæ æquiuocæ, non consistit in eo quòd particularis sit, vel vniuersalis, proxima, vel remota, sed solùm in eo, quòd sit distincta specie à suo effectu: quod patet: quia eo ipso, quòd est eiusdem speciei, est vniuoca

29 To the second: the first consequence is to be granted, namely that the assent of the principles is an equivocal cause of the assent of the conclusion, because it is distinct in species from it; but the minor is to be denied, namely that only a universal and remote cause is equivocal: for every cause, whether universal or particular, proximate or remote, is truly equivocal, because the ratio of an equivocal cause does not consist in its being particular or universal, proximate or remote, but only in its being distinct in species from its effect: which is plain, because by the very fact that it is of the same species, it is univocal.

[p. 611]

## QUESTION VI

> *An assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in assensu conclusionis.*

Whether the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

> 30 CErtum est, quòd intellectus diuerso actu, atque priori assentitur præmissis, deinde conclusioni: & diuerso quidem numero, atque specie: quia principiis assentitur propter se: hoc est, sine aliquo medio: sed habita solùm significatione terminorum. Conclusioni verò non propter se: sed propter principia, quorum accedit, præsupponitur assensui conclusionis: Quæstio igitur est, An postquam intellectus habuit assensum principiorum, & accedit ad assentiendum conclusioni, sic ei assentiatur propter principia, vt assensum eorum iterum repetat: vel satis sit, vt dicatur assentire conclusioni propter principia, quòd assensum eorum immediatè habuerit absque eius repetitione: nam si primo modo fiat, includetur formaliter assensus principiorum in assensu conclusionis: si verò secundo modo, non includetur formaliter, sed solùm præsuppositiuè: quod est verè non includi formaliter, sed præsupponi.

30 It is certain that the intellect assents by a different and prior act to the premises, and then to the conclusion; and by one different indeed in number and in species: because it assents to the principles on account of themselves, that is, without any middle, but having only the signification of the terms; but to the conclusion not on account of itself, but on account of the principles, the assent to which is presupposed to the assent of the conclusion. The question, then, is whether, after the intellect has had the assent of the principles and comes to assent to the conclusion, it assents to it on account of the principles in such a way that it repeats the assent to them again; or whether it is enough, for it to be said to assent to the conclusion on account of the principles, that it has had the assent to them immediately before, without its repetition: for if it comes about in the first way, the assent of the principles will be formally included in the assent of the conclusion; but if in the second way, it will not be included formally, but only presuppositively: which is truly not to be included formally, but to be presupposed.

> Et prima opinio, quam sequuntur moderni quidam, tenet, *necessariò quidem præsupponi*, sed cùm sit prior, realiter atque specie distinctus ab assensu conclusionis, non posse in eo includi formaliter. Probat testimonio Aristo. Et duplici argum. Aristo. enim in libris priorum, agens de forma syllogistica, asserit, *Medium bis sumendum esse in præmissis*: & ideò non esse repetendum in conclusione, sed in ea vnam extremitatem prædicari de altera. Peccaret igitur syllogismus in forma: si medium ingrederetur conclusionem: sed hoc est necessariò concedendum, si assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in conclusione: ergo non potest includi. Minorem sic probo: Præmissæ componuntur ex medio, & extremitatibus: ergo si repetantur in assensu conclusionis, medium erit necessariò in conclusione repetendum: sed non potest includi formaliter, nisi repetatur, vt per se est manifestum: ergo falsum est, quòd formaliter includatur. Asserit etiam Aristoteles cap. præsenti, agens de modo demonstrandi, notitiam conclusionis fieri ex præexistenti notitia principiorum: si ergo assensus principiorum præexistens, est respectu assensus conclusionis, erit præsuppositus: & consequenter, non inclusus formaliter in eo: nam si formaliter includeretur, simul haberetur, & non prius.

And the first opinion, which certain moderns follow, holds that it is indeed necessarily presupposed, but that, since it is prior, and really and in species distinct from the assent of the conclusion, it cannot be formally included in it. It proves this by the testimony of Aristotle and by a twofold argument. For Aristotle, in the books of the Prior Analytics, treating of the form of the syllogism, asserts that the middle is to be taken twice in the premises, and therefore is not to be repeated in the conclusion, but in it one extreme is to be predicated of the other. The syllogism would therefore sin in form if the middle entered the conclusion; but this must necessarily be granted if the assent of the principles is formally included in the conclusion; therefore it cannot be included. I prove the minor thus: the premises are composed of the middle and the extremes; therefore if they are repeated in the assent of the conclusion, the middle will necessarily have to be repeated in the conclusion; but it cannot be included formally unless it is repeated, as is manifest of itself; therefore it is false that it is formally included. Aristotle also asserts in the present chapter, treating of the mode of demonstrating, that the cognition of the conclusion comes about from the preexisting cognition of the principles: if, then, the assent of the principles is preexisting with respect to the assent of the conclusion, it will be presupposed, and consequently not formally included in it: for if it were formally included, it would be had at the same time, and not before. Q q ij

[p. 612]

> 31 Primum arg. eiusdem sententiæ est: quia si principia includuntur formaliter in conclusione, ergo eodem actu, quo assentitur intellectus conclusioni, assentitur etiam principiis: sed assensus conclusionis, est scientificus, procedens ab habitu scientiæ: ergo per actum & habitum scientiæ assentiremus principiis: consequens autem est falsum: quia assensus conclusionis est notitia discursiua, assensus verò principiorum intuitiua, & sine discursu: ergo non potest iste formaliter in illo includi. Quod etiam probatur impossibile: quia assensus principiorum, numero, & specie distinctus est, ab assensu conclusionis: ergo non potest includi in eo formaliter. Probatur consequentia, quia quæ sic distincta sunt: non possunt formaliter se includere.

31 The first argument of the same opinion is: because if the principles are formally included in the conclusion, then by the same act by which the intellect assents to the conclusion it assents also to the principles; but the assent of the conclusion is scientific, proceeding from the habit of science; therefore we would assent to the principles through an act and habit of science; but the consequent is false, because the assent of the conclusion is a discursive cognition, whereas the assent of the principles is intuitive and without discursive reasoning; therefore the latter cannot be formally included in the former. This is also proved to be impossible: because the assent of the principles is distinct in number and in species from the assent of the conclusion; therefore it cannot be formally included in it. The consequence is proved: because things that are thus distinct cannot formally include one another.

> Probatur secundò: Quia in syllogismo euidenti infertur aliquando conclusio vera, ex pręmissis falsis. Vt patet in hoc: Omnis arbor est animal: Omnis homo est arbor: ergo, Omnis homo est animal: Si ergo præmissæ includuntur in conclusione formaliter, falsum includetur formaliter in vero: quod repugnat. Confirmari etiam potest experientia: quia in conclusione solùm coniungitur vna extremitas cum altera, nulla ibi facta mentione medij: coniungitur ergo propter medium pręsuppositum, non formaliter inclusum, sed ad summum virtualiter. Probatur consequentia: quia formalis inclusio impossibilis est, sine formali mentione, aut repetitione.

It is proved second: because in an evident syllogism a true conclusion is sometimes inferred from false premises, as is plain in this one: Every tree is an animal; every man is a tree; therefore every man is an animal. If, then, the premises are formally included in the conclusion, the false will be formally included in the true: which is repugnant. It can also be confirmed by experience: because in the conclusion only one extreme is joined with the other, no mention being made there of the middle; it is joined, therefore, on account of the middle as presupposed, not as formally included, but at most virtually. The consequence is proved: because formal inclusion is impossible without formal mention or repetition.

> Secunda opinio, Affirmat *assensum principiorum, non solùm præsupponi assensui conclusionis, sed formaliter includi in eo.* Ita D. Tho. 1. 2. qu. 8. art. 3. his verbis: *Primò aliquis intelligit, ipsa principia secundùm se: postmodum autem intelligit ea in ipsis conclusionibus, secundùm quod assentit conclusionibus, propter principia.* Idem etiam tenet, q. 12. art. 4. D. Tho. sequuntur Capr. in 1. d. 2. q. 1. in solutione ad arg. contra 4. conclus. Ferra. 1. lib. contra gentes, ca. 57. Soncin. 6. Meta. q. 10. Duran. in 2. d. 38. q. 3. ad 3. qui omnes docent, intellectum eodem actu ferri in conclusionem, & principia, cùm ei propter principia assentiatur: quod aliter fieri repugnat, nisi assensus principiorum includatur formaliter in assensu concl.

The second opinion affirms that the assent of the principles is not only presupposed to the assent of the conclusion, but formally included in it. So St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 8, a. 3, in these words: First someone understands the principles themselves according to themselves; but afterwards he understands them in the conclusions themselves, inasmuch as he assents to the conclusions on account of the principles. He holds the same also in q. 12, a. 4. St. Thomas is followed by Capreolus in 1, d. 2, q. 1, in the solution to the arguments against the 4th conclusion; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 1, ch. 57; Soncinas, Metaph. 6, q. 10; Durandus in 2, d. 38, q. 3, ad 3; who all teach that the intellect is borne by the same act to the conclusion and to the principles, since it assents to it on account of the principles: which cannot come about otherwise unless the assent of the principles is formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

> 32 Deinde probatur hoc arg. satis efficaci: Eodem actu fertur potentia quælibet in obiectum, & in rationem formalem eius, vt visus eodem actu fertur in colorem, & in rationem visibilitatis: aut in colorem, & lucem, si lux se teneat ex parte obiecti in visione coloris. Et ratio huius euidens est: quia ex obiecto, quod percipitur, & ex ratione formali illud percipiendi, constituitur vnum obiectum totale, atque completum, tanquam [p. 613] ex Quo, & Quod, sed assensus principiorum, est ratio formalis obiectiua assentiendi conclusioni: ergo eodem actu fertur intellectus in conclusionem, quæ est obiectum, cui assentitur, & in principia, quæ sunt rationes essentiendi: sed non potest ferri in principia eodem actu, nisi in obiecto eiusdem actus includantur formaliter: ergo necessarium est formaliter includi præsertim cùm assensus conclusionis distinguatur specie, à fide humana, & opinione, solùm propter diuersam rationem formalẽ assentiendi: quæ in opinione est, ratio probabilis, in fide humana, testimonium fide digni, in assensu scientifico, principia per se euidentia.

32 Next, this is proved by a quite efficacious argument: any power is borne by the same act to its object and to its formal ratio, as sight is borne by the same act to color and to the ratio of visibility; or to color and light, if light stands on the side of the object in the vision of color. And the reason for this is evident: because from the object which is perceived and from the formal ratio of perceiving it there is constituted one total and complete object, as [p. 613] from a Quo and a Quod; but the assent of the principles is the formal objective ratio of assenting to the conclusion; therefore the intellect is borne by the same act to the conclusion, which is the object to which it assents, and to the principles, which are the rationes of assenting; but it cannot be borne to the principles by the same act unless they are formally included in the object of that same act; therefore it is necessary that they be formally included; especially since the assent of the conclusion is distinguished in species from human faith and from opinion solely on account of the different formal ratio of assenting: which in opinion is a probable reason, in human faith the testimony of one worthy of credence, in scientific assent principles evident per se.

> 34 Probatur secundò, Inductione, in actibus intellectus, & voluntatis: nam in actu fidei, formaliter includitur testimonium fide digni: quia est ratio formalis credendi: vt in actu voluntatis, per quem volumus media, includitur voluntas finis, tanquam ratio volendi media: vt in actu, quo volumus sumere potionem propter sanitatem, includitur formaliter actus intentionis, quo volumus sanitatem: sed assensus principiorum est ratio formalis, & actualis propter quem assentimus conclusioni: ergo actu & formaliter includitur in assensu conclusionis.

34 It is proved second by induction in the acts of the intellect and of the will: for in the act of faith the testimony of one worthy of credence is formally included, because it is the formal ratio of believing; as in the act of the will by which we will the means the willing of the end is included, as the ratio of willing the means; as in the act by which we will to take a potion for the sake of health the act of intention by which we will health is formally included; but the assent of the principles is the formal and actual ratio on account of which we assent to the conclusion; therefore it is actually and formally included in the assent of the conclusion.

> Sed vt veritas nostræ sententiæ intelligatur, & arg. oppositæ meliùs soluantur. Notandum est: *Principia, & conclusionem, & assensus vtriusque duobus modis considerari posse. Primò*, in quantum intellectus assentitur Principiis per se, & ex sola cognitione terminorum & conclusioni, tanquam alteri obiecto distincto: non considerando: quòd ei assentiatur propter principia: cùm constet posse ei assentire propter aliam rationem, vt propter testimonium fide digni, aut propter argumentum probabile. Et hoc modo, nec præmissæ includuntur in conclusione, nec assensu eorum. Secundo modo considerantur, *in quantum habent ordinem, ac dependentiam inter sese*: nempe conclusio, vt ei assentitur intellectus, propter principia: & principia, vt sunt causa conclusionis, tanquam formalis ratio assentiendi: & hæc dependentia, & hic ordo, essentialis est assensui conclusionis. Sicut ordo, ac dependentia assensus fidei ex testimonio, intrinsecus est ei. Euidens igiter est, assensum conclusionis, essentialiter includere ordinem dependentiæ, ad assensum principiorum, tanquam ad rationem formalem obiectiuam.

But in order that the truth of our view may be understood, and the opposing arguments better solved, it should be noted that the principles and the conclusion, and the assent of each, can be considered in two ways. First, insofar as the intellect assents to the principles per se and from the cognition of the terms alone, and to the conclusion as to another, distinct object, not considering that it assents to it on account of the principles: since it is established that it can assent to it on account of another reason, as on account of the testimony of one worthy of credence, or on account of a probable argument. And in this way neither are the premises included in the conclusion, nor the assent to them. In the second way they are considered insofar as they have order and dependence among themselves: namely the conclusion, as the intellect assents to it on account of the principles; and the principles, as they are the cause of the conclusion, as the formal ratio of assenting; and this dependence and this order is essential to the assent of the conclusion, just as the order and dependence of the assent of faith on testimony is intrinsic to it. It is evident, then, that the assent of the conclusion essentially includes the order of dependence on the assent of the principles, as on the formal objective ratio.

> 35 Sed vbi clauditur formaliter ordo, clauditur ex consequenti illud, ad quod ordo ipse terminatur: ergo in assensu conclusionis, clauditur etiam ex consequenti assensus principiorum tanquam terminus dependentiæ essentialis: quam habet [p. 614] ab eo assensus conclusionis. Itaque assensus, non clauditur formaliter, aut essentialiter in assensu, cùm distinguantur specie, & numero: sed ordo dependentiæ vnius ab altero, clauditur formaliter: & consequenter, assensus ipse, à quo essentialiter dependet. Vnde ordo dependentiæ, tanquam quid intrinsecum, & formale includitur; assensus verò, tanquam extrinsecum, à quo dependet, & sine quo idem ordo dependentiæ essentialis, nec esse, nec intelligi potest. Verùm actu includitur: quia actualis est ordo: nec includitur vt Quod, sed solùm vt Quo: quia solùm, vt ratio assentiendi. Exemplum huius possumus adducere in visione coloris, supposito quòd lux sit necessaria ex parte obiecti ad videndum: tunc enim eodem actu fertur visus, in colorem, & lucem: non ita, vt lux sit, quod videtur, sed ratio formalis videndi: nec lux ipsa includitur in colore ipso, qui videtur: imò nec in obiecto actus videndi, tanquam aliquid intrinsecum: sed quia color, vt in obiectum visus, habet essentialem ordinem dependentiæ à luce: quia nec esse potest, nec intelligi sine illa, propterea lux etiam actu includitur in obiecto visionis: per quam videtur color, tanquam terminus actualis dependentiæ obiectiuæ. Sic ergo intelligendum est, principia, & eorum assensus, includi in conclusione, & assensu eius: quia essentialis est ordo dependentiæ ab eis, assensui conclusionis, & quia ordo iste actu formaliter, & essentialiter includitur in assensu conclusionis, necesse est, principia etiam, & eorum assensum, actu, & formaliter includi: non, tanquam ei intrinseca, sed tanquam id, sine quo essentialis ipse ordo, nec esse potest, nec intelligi.

35 But where an order is formally contained, that at which the order itself terminates is consequently contained; therefore in the assent of the conclusion the assent of the principles is also consequently contained, as the term of the essential dependence which it has Q q iij [p. 614] on it, the assent of the conclusion. Thus the assent is not contained formally or essentially in the assent, since they are distinguished in species and in number; but the order of dependence of the one on the other is contained formally, and consequently the assent itself on which it essentially depends. Hence the order of dependence is included as something intrinsic and formal; but the assent as something extrinsic, on which it depends, and without which that same essential order of dependence can neither be nor be understood. It is, however, actually included, because the order is actual; nor is it included as Quod, but only as Quo, because only as the ratio of assenting. We can adduce an example of this in the vision of color, supposing that light is necessary on the side of the object for seeing: for then sight is borne by the same act to the color and to the light; not in such a way that the light is that which is seen, but the formal ratio of seeing; nor is the light itself included in the color itself which is seen, nor indeed in the object of the act of seeing as something intrinsic; but because color, as the object of sight, has an essential order of dependence on light, since it can neither be nor be understood without it, therefore light too is actually included in the object of vision, through which the color is seen, as the term of the actual objective dependence. Thus, then, it is to be understood that the principles and the assent to them are included in the conclusion and in the assent to it: because the order of dependence on them is essential to the assent of the conclusion; and because this order is actually, formally, and essentially included in the assent of the conclusion, it is necessary that the principles too, and the assent to them, be actually and formally included: not as intrinsic to it, but as that without which the essential order itself can neither be nor be understood.

> 36 Ex hac ergo doctrina: Respondetur ad testimonia Aristo. Ad primum quidem: Concedendo, quòd medium non debet ingredi conclusionem: nec id sequitur ex nostra sententia, quòd formaliter ingrediatur: quia principia non ingrediũtur, vt Quod: id est, vt quibus assentitur intellectus, sed solùm, vt Quo. Ideo non sunt formaliter exprimenda, aut repetenda in conclusione: sed sufficit extremitates formaliter exprimere, aut repetere, atque coniungere, cum actuali dependentia à principiis: & consequenter à medio, vt formaliter includantur, licèt non exprimantur: sicut in actu fidei non exprimimus testimonium, dicentes, nos credere propter testimonium fidedigni, sed solùm exprimitur illud, quod creditur: ratione tamen actualis dependentiæ ab eodem testimonio, inclusum censetur testimonium, licèt non exprimatur. Ad secundum [p. 615] testimonium. Respondemus: Notitiam conclusionis fieri ex præexistenti notitia principiorum: præsupposita quidem, vt Quod, sed inclusa in ea, vt Quo. Hoc est, vt ratio assentiendi, eidem conclusioni.

36 From this doctrine, then, the reply is made to the testimonies of Aristotle. To the first, indeed: by granting that the middle ought not to enter the conclusion; nor does it follow from our view that it enters formally: because the principles do not enter as Quod, that is, as that to which the intellect assents, but only as Quo. Therefore they are not to be formally expressed or repeated in the conclusion; but it suffices to express or repeat the extremes formally, and to join them with an actual dependence on the principles, and consequently on the middle, so that they are formally included although they are not expressed: just as in the act of faith we do not express the testimony by saying that we believe on account of the testimony of one worthy of credence, but only that which is believed is expressed; yet by reason of the actual dependence on that same testimony the testimony is deemed included, although it is not expressed. To the second [p. 615] testimony, we reply: the cognition of the conclusion comes about from the preexisting cognition of the principles, presupposed indeed as Quod, but included in it as Quo; that is, as the ratio of assenting to that same conclusion.

> Ad primum argum. Concedendum est, quidquid assumit: & concludit præter vltimam consequentiam, quam hoc modo infert: ergo per actum, & habitum scientiæ assentiretur intellectus principiis. Hæc enim neganda est: quia principia, vel eorum assensus, non includuntur in assensu conclusionis, tanquam id cui assentitur intellectus: sed tanquam ratio assentiendi: vnde solùm sequitur, quòd per actum, & habitum scientiæ assentitur intellectus conclusioni, propter principia.

To the first argument: everything it assumes and concludes is to be granted except the last consequence, which it infers in this way: therefore the intellect would assent to the principles through an act and habit of science. For this is to be denied: because the principles, or the assent to them, are not included in the assent of the conclusion as that to which the intellect assents, but as the ratio of assenting; whence it follows only that the intellect assents to the conclusion through an act and habit of science on account of the principles.

> Quod verò dicitur, Assensum principiorum specie, & numero distingui, ab assensu conclusionis, Verum est: sed ex hoc solùm sequitur, quòd non possit in eo includi, tanquam aliquid ei intrinsecum, sed tanquam extrinsecum: sine quo nec esse, nec intelligi potest essentialis ordo dependentiæ, quem includit assensus conclusionis, ab eo. Hunc enim modum inclusionis, non tollit differentia numerica, nec specifica, vt per se est manifestum.

But as for what is said, that the assent of the principles is distinguished in species and in number from the assent of the conclusion: it is true; but from this it follows only that it cannot be included in it as something intrinsic to it, but as something extrinsic, without which the essential order of dependence on it, which the assent of the conclusion includes, can neither be nor be understood. For numerical or specific difference does not take away this mode of inclusion, as is manifest of itself.

> Ad secundum: Concedendum est antecedens, neganda consequentia, quòd falsum includatur in vero: quia conclusio vera, non sequitur ex præmissis, vt falsis, sed vt sic dispositis in forma syllogistica: quare solùm infertur: quòd illæ, vt sic dispositæ, includantur in assensu conclusionis, tanquam, Quo, modo iam explicato.

To the second: the antecedent is to be granted, and the consequence denied, namely that the false is included in the true: because a true conclusion does not follow from the premises as false, but as so disposed in syllogistic form; wherefore it is inferred only that they, as so disposed, are included in the assent of the conclusion as Quo, in the manner already explained.

> Ad confirmationem, Concedendum est antecedens, quòd solùm in conclusione coniungantur extremitates, nulla facta mentione medij: sed quia coniunguntur per medium: hoc est, cum actuali, & formali dependẽtia ab eo, necesse est, medium includi formaliter in tali coniunctione, quæ est assensus ipse conclusionis: veruntamen: quia non includitur tanquam Quod, hoc est, tanquam id cui assentiatur intellectus, per assensum conclusionis: sed tanquam Quo, id est tanquam ratio formalis, & actualis assentiatur eidem conclusioni: ideo non exprimitur, nec expressa mentio eius fit, sed nec exprimi potest, absque peccato contra formam syllogisticam.

To the confirmation: the antecedent is to be granted, that in the conclusion only the extremes are joined, no mention being made of the middle; but because they are joined through the middle, that is, with an actual and formal dependence on it, it is necessary that the middle be formally included in such a conjunction, which is the very assent of the conclusion; nevertheless, because it is not included as Quod, that is, as that to which the intellect assents through the assent of the conclusion, but as Quo, that is, as the formal and actual ratio by which it assents to that same conclusion, therefore it is not expressed, nor is express mention made of it; nor indeed can it be expressed without a sin against syllogistic form.

### Quæstio 7. An habito assensu præmissarum, assentiatur intellectus conclusioni in eodem instanti — QUESTION VII. Whether, once the assent of the premises is had, the intellect assents to the conclusion in

> QVÆSTIO VII.

[…]

> *An habito assensu præmissarum, assentiatur intellectus conclusioni in eodem instanti.*

the same instant.

> SI præmissæ disponantur debito ordine, quem postulat eis syllogistica, ac demonstratiua: *Certum est assensum maioris, [p. 616] priùs tempore haberi posse, quàm assensus minoris, & conclusionis habeatur.* Quia vniuersalis propositio est, sub qua subsumenda est minor, tanquam particularis; & ex vtraque inferenda conclusio: ideo non dependet ab assensu minoris, & conclusionis.

If the premises are disposed in the due order which the syllogistic and demonstrative form requires of them, it is certain that the assent of the major, Q q iiij [p. 616] can be had prior in time to the assent of the minor and of the conclusion. Because it is the universal proposition, under which the minor is to be subsumed as a particular, and from both of which the conclusion is to be inferred, therefore it does not depend on the assent of the minor and of the conclusion.

> 38 Certum est etiam, *quòd si non seruetur ordo disponendi præmissas, etiam assensus minoris poterit haberi prius tempore, quàm assensus maioris, & conclusionis*: quia dum minor non subordinatur maiori: sine illa esse potest: & si ita habeatur, non est necessarium, quòd statim ex ea inferatur conclusio. Gratia exempli: Priùs tempore habere potest intellectus, hunc assensum maioris, Omne animal rationale est risibile, quàm habeat assensum minoris, Homo est animal rationale: & hunc assensum conclusionis, Omnis homo est risibilis. Potest etiam nullo ordine seruato, priùs tempore habere secundum quàm primum & tertium: de his igitur non potest esse dubium.

38 It is certain also that if the order of disposing the premises is not observed, the assent of the minor too can be had prior in time to the assent of the major and of the conclusion: because while the minor is not subordinated to the major, it can be without it; and if it is had in this way, it is not necessary that the conclusion be immediately inferred from it. For example: the intellect can have this assent of the major, Every rational animal is risible, prior in time to having the assent of the minor, Man is a rational animal, and this assent of the conclusion, Every man is risible. It can also, no order being observed, have the second prior in time to the first and the third: about these, then, there can be no doubt.

> Sed solùm, *An habitis assensibus, maioris, & minoris, dispositis, & ordinatis, necesse sit simul habere assensum conclusionis: vel priùs haberi possint illi, quàm habetur iste.* Et de proprietate naturæ, certum est, priùs illos haberi: quia sunt causa assensus conclusionis: causa autem prior est natura suo effectu. Quæstio ergo procedit, de prioritate temporis, An possit intellectus habere assensum maioris, & minoris, dispositis in hoc instanti & non habere in eodem assensum conclusionis: vel necesse sit, quòd in eodem instanti sequatur ex eis, & cum eis simul tempore habeatur.

But only whether, the assents of the major and minor being had, disposed and ordered, it is necessary to have the assent of the conclusion at the same time; or whether those can be had prior to the having of this one. And with respect to priority of nature it is certain that those are had first, because they are the cause of the assent of the conclusion, and a cause is prior by nature to its effect. The question therefore proceeds concerning priority of time: whether the intellect can have the assent of the major and minor, disposed in this instant, and not have the assent of the conclusion in the same instant; or whether it is necessary that it follow from them in the same instant and be had simultaneously in time with them.

> Et videtur non esse necessarium, quòd habeatur in eodem instanti: quia intellectus non potest simul plura intelligere, vt docet Arist. 2. lib. Top. cap 3. loco 33. his verbis, *Contingit enim plura scire, cogitare autem non.* Per cogitationem, intelligens actualem cognitionem: sed præmissæ, & conclusio sunt plura: ergo non poterit ea simul hoc est, in eodem instanti intelligere. Et, si dicas plura quidem esse, sed habere modum vnius; in quantùm ordinata sunt in eodem syllogismo. Adhuc duplex est aliud impedimentum.

And it seems that it is not necessary that it be had in the same instant: because the intellect cannot understand many things at the same time, as Aristotle teaches in Topics 2, ch. 3, place 33, in these words: For it happens that one knows many things, but does not think of them, understanding by thinking actual cognition; but the premises and the conclusion are many; therefore it will not be able to understand them at the same time, that is, in the same instant. And if you say that they are indeed many, but have the mode of one, inasmuch as they are ordered in the same syllogism: there is still a twofold further impediment.

> 39 Primum: quia potest habere errorem contrarium conclusioni, & nimis radicatum in subiecto, per plures actus: tunc ergo non poterit statim eum expellere per assensum conclusionis: & ideò, nec statim ei assentire. Secundum: quia capacitas intellectus, per quam potest multa simul intelligere, finita est: ergo si numerus eorum quæ potest actu considerare, impleatur per assensus præmissarum, non poterit simul habere assensum conclusionis, quousque alium dimittat.

39 The first: because it can have an error contrary to the conclusion, too deeply rooted in the subject through many acts; then, therefore, it will not be able to expel it immediately through the assent of the conclusion, and therefore not to assent to it immediately either. The second: because the capacity of the intellect, by which it can understand many things at the same time, is finite; therefore if the number of the things it can actually consider is filled by the assents of the premises, it will not be able to have the assent of the conclusion at the same time until it lets another go.

[p. 617]

> Vera tamen sententia est, *Assensum conclusionis in eodem instanti sequi, ex assensibus præmissarum.* Cuius ratio est: Quia vt Arist. docuit, cap. præsenti, ex terminis eorum fit, & in eis continetur virtualiter, tanquam in causa, aut tanquam arbor in semine: ideo nullum potest esse impedimentum: quin statim ex eis sequatur.

The true opinion, however, is that the assent of the conclusion follows in the same instant from the assents of the premises. The reason for this is: because, as Aristotle taught in the present chapter, it comes about from their terms and is contained in them virtually, as in a cause, or as a tree in its seed; therefore there can be no impediment to its following from them immediately.

> Ad testimonium Arist. Respondetur, intelligendum esse de pluribus, vt plura sunt, hoc est, diuersa, & nullo modo inter se, vel ad tertium ordinata: nam quæ per modum vnius intelliguntur, non dicuntur plura simpliciter, sed vnum: assensus autem præmissarum, & conclusiones, per modum vnius se habent: quia in eodem syllogismo ordinati sunt, ideo simul possunt haberi ab intellectu. Cui non obstat impedimentum erroris: nam cùm fortior causa sit demonstratio, statim illũ vincit atque expellit: & etiam si nimis sit radicatus, non impediet assensum conclusionis, neque habitum scientiæ: qui per illam producitur in eodem instanti, sed permanebit simul cum eo, quousque multiplicatis demonstrationibus omnino expellatur. Non enim repugnat, contrarios habitus remissos, simul permanere in eodem subiecto: sicut neque contrarias qualitates remissas, vt calorem, & frigus. Aliud denique impedimentum, de capacitate intellectus finita (circa quòd multa verba consumit Sotus, cap. præsenti) difficultate caret: nã licèt intellectus, duo, vel quatuor tantùm diuersa simul possit intelligere, & vnum vel tria actu consideret: dum accedit ad constituendam demonstrationem, poterit assensus præmissarum, & conclusionis simul habere, cùm modum vnius habeant, licèt sint tres.

To the testimony of Aristotle the reply is that it is to be understood of many things as they are many, that is, diverse, and in no way ordered among themselves or to a third: for things that are understood by way of one are not said to be many simply, but one; but the assents of the premises and the conclusions are related by way of one, because they are ordered in the same syllogism; therefore they can be had by the intellect at the same time. Nor does the impediment of error stand in the way of this: for since demonstration is the stronger cause, it immediately overcomes and expels it; and even if it is too deeply rooted, it will not impede the assent of the conclusion, nor the habit of science, which is produced through that demonstration in the same instant; but it will remain together with it until it is altogether expelled by multiplied demonstrations. For it is not repugnant that contrary habits, remiss, should remain together in the same subject, just as neither are contrary qualities, remiss, such as heat and cold. The other impediment, finally, concerning the finite capacity of the intellect (about which Soto spends many words on the present chapter), is without difficulty: for although the intellect can understand only two or four different things at the same time, and actually considers one or three, when it comes to constitute a demonstration it will be able to have the assents of the premises and of the conclusion at the same time, since they have the mode of one, although they are three.

## QUESTION VIII

> QVÆSTIO VIII.

[…]

> *An habitis assensibus præmissarum, liberum sit intellectui assentire conclusioni: vel necesse sit assensum eius habere in eodem instanti.*

Whether, once the assents of the premises are had, the intellect is free to assent to the conclusion, or whether it is necessary to have the assent to it in the same instant.

> 40 DVplex est libertas voluntatis, *Contrarietatis, & Contradictionis*: & illa vocatur etiam libertas, quoad specificationem, hæc verò libertas quoad exercitium. *Libertas contrarietatis* est posse voluntatem actum bonum, & malum habere, aut intellectum assensum, vel dissensum. Et dicitur contrarietatis: quia actus bonus, & malus contrarij sunt, atque etiam assensus, & dissensus intellectus. Specificationis verò: quia ab obiecto speciem accipiunt actus. *Libertas* verò *contradictionis* est posse voluntatem, vel intellectum exercere actum, vel eum [p. 618] suspendere: quia habere actum, & non habere, contradictoriè opponuntur. Et exercere actum, vel non exercere, denotat exercitium potentiæ. Intellectus autem, licèt radicalem quandam rationem libertatis habeat: in quantum formalis libertas voluntatis originem habeat ab eo, quòd intellectus plura potest ei obiecta proponere, & ideo ipsa operari valet, circa vnũ, vel alterum: vt sibi placuerit nihilominus formalem libertatem, quæ consistit in eo, quòd est velle se applicare ad operandum, vel nolle operari, sola voluntas habet: à qua eam participat intellectus, in quantum potest applicari ad intelligendum: non à se, sed à voluntate, & etiam potest ab intelligendo diuerti, aut remoueri.

he freedom of the will is twofold, of Contrariety and of 40 T Contradiction: and the former is also called freedom as to specification, the latter freedom as to exercise. Freedom of contrariety is that the will can have a good and a bad act, or the intellect assent or dissent. And it is called of contrariety because a good and a bad act are contraries, and so too are the assent and dissent of the intellect. But of specification, because acts receive their species from the object. Freedom of contradiction is that the will or the intellect can exercise an act, or [p. 618] suspend it: because to have an act and not to have it are contradictorily opposed. And to exercise an act or not to exercise it denotes the exercise of the power. Now the intellect, although it has a certain radical ratio of freedom, inasmuch as the formal freedom of the will has its origin from the fact that the intellect can propose several objects to it, and therefore the will is able to operate about one or the other as it pleases, nevertheless the will alone has formal freedom, which consists in this, that it wills to apply itself to operating or wills not to operate: from which the intellect participates it, inasmuch as it can be applied to understanding, not by itself but by the will, and can also be diverted or removed from understanding.

> Quia supposito, quærimus: *An habitis assensibus euidentibus maioris, & minoris, possit intellectus per dependentiam à voluntate assensum conclusionis suspendere: Ita vt in eodem instanti, vel non operetur, vel a voluntate diuertatur ad operandum circa aliud obiectum diuersum ab assensu conclusionis, vel omnino necessitetur ad assentiendum eidem conclusioni.*

Which supposed, we ask: Whether, the evident assents of the major and minor being had, the intellect can, through dependence on the will, suspend the assent of the conclusion, so that in the same instant it either does not operate, or is diverted by the will to operating about another object different from the assent of the conclusion; or whether it is altogether necessitated to assent to that same conclusion.

> 41 Certum est autem necessitati, quantùm pertinet ad specificationem: ita vt non sit ei liberum assentire, aut dissentire: sed si operetur circa obiectum propositum, assentire debeat conclusioni, dissentire verò nullo modo possit: quia ex assensibus principiorum veris & necessariis, non potest, nisi assensus verus ac necessarius procedere: ergo si procedat aliquis, assensus debet esse, dissensus esse non potest. Nam sicut voluntas non potest odio prosequi bonum: vt bonum sibi repræsentatum: ita intellectus, non potest dissentire vero ac necessario, vt tali sibi proposito. Quæstio igitur: *An possit non assentire conclusioni, vel quod idem est, assensum suspendere, cessando omnino ab operatione, vel operando circa aliud.*

41 Now it is certain that it is necessitated as far as pertains to specification, so that it is not free for it to assent or dissent; but if it operates about the proposed object, it must assent to the conclusion, and can in no way dissent: because from true and necessary assents of the principles nothing but a true and necessary assent can proceed; therefore if any proceeds, it must be assent; dissent cannot be. For just as the will cannot pursue the good, as good represented to it, with hatred, so the intellect cannot dissent from the true and necessary as proposed to it as such. The question, then, is: whether it can not assent to the conclusion, or, what is the same, suspend the assent, by ceasing altogether from operation or by operating about something else.

> Et est prima opinio quorundam modernorum, asserentium: *Nullo modo posse intellectum suspendere assensum conclusionis, sed necessariò eum elicere.* Probant primò: Quia assensus principiorum sunt per se euidentes, & necessarij, & continent virtualiter assensum conclusionis: & continentia quidem naturali: sicut semen continet virtualiter arborem & arbor fructum: ergo conuincitur ab eis intellectus naturaliter: vt assentiat conclusioni: sed necessitas naturalis, non subditur libertati voluntatis, vt patet in actu potentiæ nutritiuæ, quem non potest suspendere voluntas, quin cibum sibi applicatum conuertat in substantiam viuentis: ergo non poterit voluntas suspendere actum intellectus, quin statim assentiatur conclusioni.

And the first opinion is that of certain moderns, who assert that the intellect can in no way suspend the assent of the conclusion, but necessarily elicits it. They prove it first: because the assents of the principles are per se evident and necessary, and contain virtually the assent of the conclusion, and indeed by a natural containment, as a seed virtually contains a tree and a tree its fruit; therefore the intellect is convinced by them naturally to assent to the conclusion; but natural necessity is not subject to the freedom of the will, as is plain in the act of the nutritive power, which the will cannot suspend so as to keep it from converting the food applied to it into the substance of the living thing; therefore the will will not be able to suspend the act of the intellect so as to keep it from assenting immediately to the conclusion.

[p. 619]

> Secundò: Quia sicut se habet in voluntate intentio finis ad electionem mediorum, sic se habet in intellectu assensus principiorum, ad assensum conclusionis, vt D. Tho. docet, 1. 2. q. 8. art. 3. & cum eo tota schola: sed certum est apud omnes: quòd posita efficaci intentione finis & perseuerante voluntate in ea, non potest suspendere actum electionis, sed necessitatur omnino ad eligendum aliquod medium, pro consecutione eius: ergo habito assensu principiorum, & perseuerante in eo intellectu, non potest vllo modo suspendere actum conclusionis.

Second: because as the intention of the end is related in the will to the choice of the means, so the assent of the principles is related in the intellect to the assent of the conclusion, as St. Thomas teaches, 1-2, q. 8, a. 3, and with him the whole school; but it is certain among all that, given an efficacious intention of the end and the will persevering in it, it cannot suspend the act of choice, but is altogether necessitated to choose some means for attaining it; therefore, the assent of the principles being had and the intellect persevering in it, it cannot in any way suspend the act of the conclusion.

> Secunda opinio est opposita, quòd adhuc *positis assensibus præmissarum possit intellectus suspendere assensum conclusionis, ita vt à voluntate diuertatur ad operandum circa aliud obiectum.* Hanc sequitur iam maior pars modernorum, & continetur in doctrina D. Tho. & ideo à nobis tenenda est.

The second opinion is the opposite: that even given the assents of the premises, the intellect can suspend the assent of the conclusion, so that it is diverted by the will to operating about another object. This is now followed by the greater part of the moderns, and it is contained in the doctrine of St. Thomas, and therefore is to be held by us.

> Sed vt eam explicemus simul, & probemus, duo sunt notanda, ex doctrina D. Tho. ab omnibus iam recepta Primum est, quòd *intellectus subditur voluntati*, quantum ad exercitium actus: hoc est, quantùm ad applicationem eius ad operandum, vel remotionem ad operatione hac, vel illa: ita docet D. Tho. 1. 2. qu. 9. art. 1. ad 3. his verbis: *Voluntas mouet intellectum, quantùm ad exercitium actus: quia & ipsum verum, quod est perfectio intellectus, continetur sub vniuersali bono, vt quoddam bonum particulare.*

But in order that we may explain it and prove it at the same time, two things are to be noted from the doctrine of St. Thomas, now received by all. The first is that the intellect is subject to the will as to the exercise of its act, that is, as to its application to operating, or its removal from this or that operation: so St. Thomas teaches, 1-2, q. 9, a. 1, ad 3, in these words: The will moves the intellect as to the exercise of its act: because the true itself, which is the perfection of the intellect, is contained under the universal good, as a certain particular good.

> 43 Ex quibus deducitur hæc distinctio: *Sicut bonum est duplex, Summum & perfectissimum*, in quo continetur omnis ratio boni, quale est Deus, & *Particulare, ac limitatum*, quale est quodlibet bonum creatum. Eodem modo *duplex est verum, Summum, & perfectissimum*, continens omnem rationem veri, vt idemmet Deus: & *Particulare, ac limitatum*, quale est quodlibet verum creatum: siue sit principium euidens siue conclusio ex eo deducta. Præterea, sicut voluntas libera est circa quodcunque bonum particulare, siue sit finis, siue medium, ita vt possit operari, & nõ operari circa illud: circa bonum verò summum, perfectè, cognitum: quale est Deus clarè visus à beatis, nullam habet libertatem, sed omnino necessitatur ad illud diligendum. Eodem modo intellectus, circa quodlibet verum particulare, liber est, per dependentiam à voluntate: ita vt possit applicari à voluntate, ad operandum circa illud, & diuerti ab operatione: sed circa summum verum clarè sibi ostensum, nullam habet libertatem, nec potest diuerti à voluntate, quin operetur circa illud. Et rationem huius reddit D. Tho. Quia quodlibet verum particulare, & operatio intellectus circa illud, est etiam particulare bonum: sed circa particulare bonum quodcunque, [p. 620] non necessitatur voluntas, sed potest velle, & non velle illud, ergo liberum est voluntati, velle applicare intellectum ad operandum, circa quodcunque verum particulare, vel diuertere illũ ab operando circa illud: non tamen circa verum vniuersale, ad perfectissimum clarè ei ostensum, quale est Deus in patria. Quia omnis potentia, naturaliter determinata est ad operandum circa illud, quod perfectissimè continet omnem rationem sui obiecti: ita vt dum sibi offertur, non possit suspendere operationem: sed Deus clarè visus continet perfectissimè omnem rationem veri: ergo nec voluntas potest suspendere actum propositum circa illud sibi ab intellectu, nec intellectus circa illud sibi clarè ostensum. Quia sicut est vniuersale bonum, sic operari circa illud est vniuersale bonum potentiæ: & ideo clarè illud videre intellectum, summum bonum eius est, & summum bonum voluntatis, & ita nec ipsa potest eum non diligere, nec diuertere intellectum à visione clara eiusdem.

43 From which this distinction is deduced: Just as the good is twofold, the Highest and most perfect, in which every ratio of good is contained, such as God is, and the Particular and limited, such as is any created good; in the same way the true is twofold, the Highest and most perfect, containing every ratio of the true, as God likewise is, and the Particular and limited, such as is any created truth, whether it be an evident principle or a conclusion deduced from it. Moreover, just as the will is free about any particular good whatever, whether it be an end or a means, so that it can operate or not operate about it, but about the highest good perfectly known, such as is God clearly seen by the blessed, it has no freedom, but is altogether necessitated to love it: in the same way the intellect is free about any particular truth through its dependence on the will, so that it can be applied by the will to operating about it and diverted from operation; but about the highest truth clearly shown to it, it has no freedom, nor can it be diverted by the will from operating about it. And St. Thomas gives the reason for this: because any particular truth, and the operation of the intellect about it, is also a particular good; but about any particular good whatever, [p. 620] the will is not necessitated, but can will it and not will it; therefore the will is free to will to apply the intellect to operating about any particular truth whatever, or to divert it from operating about it: not, however, about the universal and most perfect truth clearly shown to it, such as God is in the fatherland. Because every power is naturally determined to operate about that which most perfectly contains every ratio of its object, so that while it is offered to it, it cannot suspend its operation; but God clearly seen most perfectly contains every ratio of the true; therefore neither can the will suspend the act proposed to it by the intellect about him, nor the intellect its act about him clearly shown to it. Because, just as he is the universal good, so to operate about him is the universal good of the power; and therefore for the intellect to see him clearly is its highest good, and the highest good of the will; and so neither can the will fail to love him, nor divert the intellect from the clear vision of him.

> 45 Ex tota hac doctrina colligitur hæc ratio efficaciter probans nostram sententiam: Voluntas non necessitatur ad operandum circa aliquod particulare bonum: ergo nec intellectus circa particulare verum. Probatur consequentia, supposito, quòd intellectus subditur voluntati, quantùm ad applicationem, seu exercitium operandi: quia intellectum operari circa particulare verum, est bonum particulare eius, atque etiam bonum particulare voluntatis: ergo non necessitat voluntatem ad applicandum intellectum vt operetur circa illud, sed liberum est ei eum applicare, aut diuertere. Conclusio autem demonstrationis, verum quoddam particulare: ergo etiam habito assensu principiorum, non necessitatur voluntas ad applicandum intellectum, vt assentiatur conclusioni, sed potest eum diuertere ab assentiendo.

45 From this whole doctrine is gathered this reason, which efficaciously proves our view: the will is not necessitated to operate about any particular good; therefore neither is the intellect about a particular truth. The consequence is proved, supposing that the intellect is subject to the will as to application, or the exercise of operating: because for the intellect to operate about a particular truth is its particular good, and also a particular good of the will; therefore it does not necessitate the will to apply the intellect so that it operates about it, but the will is free to apply it or divert it. But the conclusion of a demonstration is a certain particular truth; therefore, even when the assent of the principles is had, the will is not necessitated to apply the intellect so that it assents to the conclusion, but it can divert it from assenting.

> 46 Secundò notandum est ex doctrina eiusdem D. Tho. 1. 2. q. 50. art. 1. & 3. deducta ex Arist. & recepta etiam ab omnibus: *Quòd potentia non est capax habitus*, nisi in ordine ad obiectum, circa quod potest operari liberè: vnde potentia omnino naturalis, nullam habens libertatem in suis operationibus, saltem ex participatione voluntatis non est capax habitus: nec potest eum acquirere, quantumuis frequenter operetur vt patet in potentia visiua, quæ non est capax habitus ad videndum, neque potest illum acquirere, per frequentes actus visionis. Sed intellectus, per assensus principiorum, acquirit habitum, qui vocatur intellectus: & habitis assensibus principiorum, etiam acquirit habitum scientiæ, per assensum conclusionis, [p. 621] secundùm communem sententiam totius. Scholæ ergo aliquam habet libertatem in assensu principiorum: & eo habito, in assensu conclusionis: minima autem libertas est, posse assentire, & assensum suspendere: ergo negari non potest, quin hanc habeat.

46 Second, it should be noted from the doctrine of the same St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 50, a. 1 and 3, deduced from Aristotle and also received by all, that a power is not capable of a habit except in order to an object about which it can operate freely: whence a wholly natural power, having no freedom in its operations, at least by participation in the will, is not capable of a habit, nor can it acquire one, however frequently it operates: as is plain in the visive power, which is not capable of a habit for seeing, nor can it acquire one through frequent acts of vision. But the intellect acquires through the assents of the principles a habit, which is called understanding; and, the assents of the principles being had, it also acquires the habit of science through the assent of the conclusion, [p. 621] according to the common opinion of the whole School. Therefore it has some freedom in the assent to the principles, and, having had that, in the assent to the conclusion. But the least freedom is to be able to assent and to suspend assent; therefore it cannot be denied that it has this.

> 47 Ad primum arg. oppositæ sententiæ, Concedendum est antecedens, cum consequentia, sed distinguendum consequẽs, quòd conuincatur intellectus per assensum principiorum, ad assentiendum conclusioni: nam licèt conuincatur quantum ad specificationem actus: quia non est liberum, si operatur circa conclusionem, elicere actum dissensus sed necessariò assentiendum est ei: quantum ad exercitium tamen non conuincitur: quia intellectus non est potentia purè naturalis, sicut visus, nec operatur omnino ex determinatione ad vnum, sicut ille: sed subditur imperio voluntatis, circa quodcunque particulare verum, quantum ad applicationem, vel exercitium: & ita potest à voluntate applicari ad assentiendum principiis, & conclusioni (quæ vera particularia sunt) & diuerti ab assensu eorum.

47 To the first argument of the opposite opinion: The antecedent is to be granted together with the consequence, but the consequent is to be distinguished, namely that the intellect is compelled by the assent to the principles to assent to the conclusion. For although it is compelled as to the specification of the act (because, if it operates about the conclusion, it is not free to elicit an act of dissent, but it must necessarily assent to it), yet as to the exercise it is not compelled: because the intellect is not a purely natural power, as sight is, nor does it operate altogether from determination to one, as that does; but it is subject to the command of the will, about any particular truth whatever, as to application or exercise. And so it can be applied by the will to assenting to the principles and to the conclusion (which are particular truths), and diverted from assent to them.

> Ad secundum, Distinguendum est antecedens: quia sic habet in intellectu assensus principiorum, ad assensum cõclusionis, sicut in voluntate intentio finis, ad electionem mediorum, quantum ad aliquid, sed quantum ad aliud, se habet diuerso modo.

To the second: The antecedent is to be distinguished: because the assent to the principles stands in the intellect, with respect to the assent to the conclusion, as the intention of the end stands in the will with respect to the election of the means, as to one thing, but as to another it stands in a different manner.

> 48 Conueniunt namque in eo, quòd sicut voluntas, per se primò tendit in finem, & ex intentione finis mouetur ad media, sic intellectus, per se primò mouetur ad assensum principiorum, & ex assensu principiorum mouetur ad assensum conclusionis. Differunt tamen, quòd voluntas non eligit media, propter finem vtcunque spectatum, sed propter consecutionem eius: & ex hoc prouenit, quòd si velit perseuerare in intentione finis, non possit suspendere actum electionis, sed quamuis liberum sit ei, vnum aut alterum medium eligere, non possit non eligere aliquod. In intellectu verò hoc non reperitur quia assensus conclusionis, non ordinatur ad consequutionem alicuius finis, sed solùm habet necessitatem consequentiæ: quia virtualiter continetur in principiis, ex quibus procedit per euidentem consequentiam. Sed procedere, aut non procedere, dependet ex applicatione voluntatis ad assensum eliciendum: quæ applicatio libera est, vt probauimus, cùm sit circa verum quoddam particulare, & distinctum ab ipsismet principiis. Vnde liberum est voluntati applicare, aut diuertere intellectum ab assentiendo.

48 For they agree in this: that just as the will per se primarily tends to the end, and from the intention of the end is moved to the means, so the intellect per se primarily is moved to the assent to the principles, and from the assent to the principles is moved to the assent to the conclusion. They differ, however, in that the will does not elect the means on account of the end regarded in any way whatever, but on account of attaining it; and from this it comes about that, if it wishes to persevere in the intention of the end, it cannot suspend the act of election, but, although it is free for it to elect one means or another, it cannot fail to elect some one. But in the intellect this is not found, because the assent to the conclusion is not ordered to the attainment of some end, but has only the necessity of the consequence: because it is virtually contained in the principles, from which it proceeds through an evident consequence. But to proceed or not to proceed depends on the application of the will to eliciting the assent; which application is free, as we have proved, since it is about some particular truth, distinct from the principles themselves. Whence the will is free to apply the intellect or to divert it from assenting.

[p. 622]

## CHAPTER II

> CAPVT II.

[…]

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> TEXTVS ARIST.

[…]

> *Scire autem arbitramur vnumquodque simpliciter, & non sophistico more, &c.*

We think, moreover, that we know each thing simply, and not in the sophistical manner, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 1 CApite præcedenti, docuit Arist. *Scientiam esse, & de nouo acquiri per demonstrationem, ex præexistenti cognitione principiorum.* In hoc autem secundo ca. intendit docere, quid *Scientia; & quid demonstratio sit.* Diuiditur autem in tres partes. In prima, *Vnam definitionem scientiæ*, & *duplicem demonstrationis.* tradit. In secunda. *Definit principium*, illudque duplici diuisione diuidit. Et in tertia, *Docet, & probat principia*, seu præmissas notiores esse conclusione.

n the preceding chapter Aristotle taught that science exists, and is acquired 1 I        anew through demonstration, from preexisting cognition of the principles. In this second chapter, however, he intends to teach what science is and what demonstration is. And it is divided into three parts. In the first he hands down one definition of science and a twofold one of demonstration. In the second he defines principle, and divides it by a twofold division. And in the third he teaches and proves that the principles, or premises, are better known than the conclusion.

> Pluribus verbis definit *scire*, hoc est scientiam in concreto ex quibus pauca hæc sumenda sunt, quibus breuis definitio assignatur, *Scire est cognoscere causam rei: & quod illius est causa & quòd non contingit aliter se habere.* Per quam solùm definit Aristo. perfectissimam scientiam, quam vocat scientiam. *Propter quid*: (nam de sciẽtia Quia, minùs perfecta, c. 10. huius libri se acturum promittit) ad quam habendam, triplicem conditionem requiri affirmat. Prima est, vt *causam conclusionis cognoscamus.* Secunda, vt *cognoscamus talem causam, non solùm secundùm cognitionem nostram esse causam, sed etiam secundùm rem*: nam dum probamus hominem esse rationalem, quia est risibilis, risibile priùs est in nostro intellectu: & ideo causa cognoscendi rationale, sed non est causa essendi eius, verùm potiùs est effectus. Et ideo non habemus scientiam Propter quid, de rationali, sed solùm. Quia, Tertia conditio est, vt *cognoscamus, non solùm esse causam essendi, sed causam necessariam*: ita vt ea posita, necessariò sequatur effectus: hoc enim significatur illo verbo, *Et quod contingit aliter se habere.* Integram definitionem breuissimè explicat Arist. dicens: *Scire esse, per demonstrationem intelligere*, quia si vera sit demonstratio Propter quid, tres illæ conditiones reperiuntur in præmissis respectu conclusionis.

He defines to know, that is, science in the concrete, in many words, from which these few are to be taken, by which a brief definition is assigned: To know is to cognize the cause of the thing, and that it is the cause of that, and that it cannot be otherwise. By which Aristotle defines only the most perfect science, which he calls science Propter quid (for he promises to treat of science Quia, which is less perfect, in ch. 10 of this book), for having which he affirms that a threefold condition is required. The first is that we cognize the cause of the conclusion. The second, that we cognize such a cause to be the cause not only according to our cognition but also according to the thing: for when we prove that man is rational because he is risible, risible is prior in our intellect, and therefore it is the cause of cognizing rational, but it is not the cause of its being; rather it is its effect. And therefore we do not have science Propter quid of rational, but only Quia. The third condition is that we cognize it to be not only a cause of being, but a necessary cause, so that, it being posited, the effect necessarily follows: for this is signified by those words, And that it cannot be otherwise. Aristotle explains the whole definition most briefly, saying: To know is to understand through demonstration; because, if the demonstration is truly Propter quid, those three conditions are found in the premises with respect to the conclusion.

> 2 Definit deinde demonstrationem, duplici definitione, quarum prima ita habet: *Demonstratio, est syllogismus scientialis siue syllogismus faciens scire*: & est definitio finalis: quia finis demonstrationis est, generare scientiam: & hæc scientia genita per demonstrationem, est assensus conclusionis eius, genitus ex præmissis.

2 Next he defines demonstration by a twofold definition, the first of which runs thus: Demonstration is a scientific syllogism, or a syllogism producing knowledge; and it is a final definition, because the end of demonstration is to generate science; and this science generated through demonstration is the assent to its conclusion, generated from the premises.

[p. 623]

> 3 Secunda definitio, *Materialis est.* Nam sicut ex fine, propter quem efficitur domus, nempe, vt à pluuiis, aliísve temporum iniuriis nos defendat, colligimus ex quibus partibus materialibus constare debeat, nempe ex lignis, lapidibus aliisque partibus tali modo dispositis: ita Arist. ex fine demonstrationis, colligit, quibus partibus dispositis, & ordinatis, constare debeat demonstratio: quasi ita arguens: Demonstratio ordinatur ad generandam scientiam, tanquam ad finem: ergo talis debet esse: *Vt procedat ex veris, primis, immediatis, notioribus, & prioribus, causisque conclusionis.* Probat singulas particulas definitionis: & primò, quòd *demonstratio procedat* ex veris, hoc modo: Obiectum scientiæ debet habere esse: ergo quod non est, non scitur: sed falsum nihil est: ergo non potest de illo esse scientia: veram igitur esse oportet conclusionem demonstrationis, cuius assensus est scientia: ergo debet procedere ex præmissis veris, tanquam ex causa. Probatur consequentia: quia falsum cùm nihil sit, non potest esse causa veri. Quòd verò demonstratio procedat *ex primis*, probat secundò: quia nisi præmissæ sint principia per se euidentia formaliter: hoc est, quibus cognita significatione terminorum, statim assentiatur intellectus: vel saltem virtualiter: si is qui demonstrationem facit, sciat ea reducere ad principia per se nota, per alias demonstrationes, non habebit scientiam conclusionis: nec proinde veram demonstrationem, sed Dialecticum tantùm syllogismum, & assensum opinionis de conclusione. Probat tandem tertiò quòd *notioribus, prioribus, & causis conclusionis procedat.* Quia *Scire*, est rem per causam cognoscere: ergo præmissæ debent esse vera causa conclusionis, sed causa est prior & notior effectu, ergo debent esse priores & notiores: non solùm quo ad nos: quo pacto illud est prius, quod notius est nobis, licèt secundùm naturam sit posterius, vt effectus notior nobis est causa: & ideo prior quoad nostram cognitionem: sed præmissæ debent esse priores, & notiores conclusione, ex natura rei, quod habebunt, si secundùm rem sint causæ eius, vt expositum est.

3 The second definition is material. For just as from the end for the sake of which a house is made, namely that it may defend us from rains and other injuries of the weather, we gather of what material parts it ought to consist, namely of timbers, stones, and other parts disposed in such a way: so Aristotle, from the end of demonstration, gathers of what parts, disposed and ordered, demonstration ought to consist, as if arguing thus: Demonstration is ordered to generating science as to its end; therefore it ought to be such that it proceeds from things true, first, immediate, better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. He proves the single parts of the definition; and first, that demonstration proceeds from things true, in this way: The object of science ought to have being; therefore what is not is not known; but the false is nothing; therefore there cannot be science of it. Therefore the conclusion of a demonstration, whose assent is science, must be true; therefore it ought to proceed from true premises as from a cause. The consequence is proved: because the false, since it is nothing, cannot be the cause of the true. That demonstration proceeds from first things he proves second: because unless the premises are principles evident per se formally, that is, such that, once the signification of the terms is cognized, the intellect at once assents to them, or at least virtually, if he who makes the demonstration knows how to reduce them to principles known per se through other demonstrations, he will not have science of the conclusion, nor consequently a true demonstration, but only a Dialectical syllogism and an assent of opinion concerning the conclusion. He proves finally, third, that it proceeds from things better known, prior, and causes of the conclusion. Because to know is to cognize a thing through its cause; therefore the premises ought to be the true cause of the conclusion; but a cause is prior to and better known than its effect; therefore they ought to be prior and better known: not only as regards us, in which way that is prior which is better known to us, although according to nature it is posterior, as an effect is better known to us than the cause, and therefore prior as regards our cognition; but the premises ought to be prior to and better known than the conclusion from the nature of the thing, which they will be if according to the thing they are its causes, as has been explained.

> 4 In secunda part. c. 2. Quia dixerat demonstrationem debere procedere ex primis: hoc est, ex præmissis, quæ sint principia indemonstrabilia: definit principium indemonstrabile: hoc modo, *Principium est, propositio immediata demonstrationis.* Explicat autem, quid sit esse propositionem demonstrationis, vel demonstratiuam: & quid sit esse immediatam. *Propositio, inquit, est altera pars enunciationis, vno complens.* Nam enunciatio diuiditur in *affirmatiuam, & negatiuam.* Esse igitur propositionem [p. 624] demonstrationis idem est ac esse enunciationem affirmatiuam, aut negatiuam: quæ tanquam præmissa ponitur in demonstratione, ad inferendam conclusionem: & ideo debet esse vera, ac necessaria: vt distinguatur à propositione Dialectica, quæ solùm est probabilis: & ideo potest esse falsa. *Immediata verò propositio est qua non est alia prior.* Hoc est, quæ non habet aliam, per quam demonstrari possit, sed qui intellectus, ex sola notitia terminorum assentitur.

4 In the second part of ch. 2: Because he had said that demonstration ought to proceed from first things, that is, from premises which are indemonstrable principles, he defines indemonstrable principle in this way: A principle is an immediate proposition of demonstration. And he explains what it is to be a proposition of demonstration, or demonstrative, and what it is to be immediate. A proposition, he says, is one part of an enunciation, stating one thing. For an enunciation is divided into affirmative and negative. Therefore to be a proposition [p. 624] of demonstration is the same as to be an affirmative or negative enunciation which is posited in the demonstration as a premise, for inferring the conclusion; and therefore it ought to be true and necessary, so that it may be distinguished from a Dialectical proposition, which is only probable and therefore can be false. But an immediate proposition is one to which there is no other prior; that is, which does not have another through which it could be demonstrated, but to which the intellect assents from the cognition of the terms alone.

> 5 Diuidit deinde principium in duo membra: nempe in *Dignitatem, & Positionem. Dignitas*, seu ἀξίωμα, est propositio immediata, atque indemonstrabilis, adeo vniuersalis, & manifesta, vt eius veritas omnibus pateat: & hac fortè ratione vocatur Dignitas, quia dignum est, cui assentiantur omnes. Et hac etiam de causa inquit, Arist. *Dignitates cognoscere debere omnes: qui scientiam aliquam acquirere volunt, priusquam ad eam addiscendam accedant.* Tales sunt: *Quodlibet est, vel non est: Totum est maius sua parte*, & similes. *Positio* verò, seu, θέσις, est propositio per se nota, & indemonstrabilis, sed nec vniuersalis adeò, vt ἀξίωμα nec cuius veritas, omnibus sit manifesta: & ideo, quam non est necessarium, vt cognoscat prius, qui aliquam scientiam addiscere incipit, sed tunc potest per se, vel à magistro eam accipere: & talia sunt omnia principia particularium sciẽtiarum, vt definitiones. Est autem alia differentia, inter *Dignitatem, & Positionem*, quòd *Dignitates* vix, aut nunquam ingrediuntur demonstrationem, sed omnibus scientiis præsupponuntur. *Positiones* verò præmissæ demonstrationis sunt: & ideo *positiones* vocantur, quia ponuntur in demonstratione ad inferendam conclusionem.

5 Next he divides principle into two members, namely into dignity and position. A dignity, or ἀξίωμα, is an immediate and indemonstrable proposition so universal and manifest that its truth is plain to all; and perhaps it is called a dignity for this reason, because it is worthy that all should assent to it. And for this cause also Aristotle says that all who wish to acquire any science ought to cognize the dignities before they approach to learning it. Such are: Anything whatever is or is not; The whole is greater than its part; and the like. But a position, or θέσις, is a proposition known per se and indemonstrable, but neither so universal as an ἀξίωμα, nor one whose truth is manifest to all; and therefore it is not necessary that he who begins to learn some science should cognize it beforehand, but he can then receive it by himself or from a master. And such are all the principles of the particular sciences, such as definitions. And there is another difference between dignity and position: that dignities scarcely or never enter a demonstration, but are presupposed by all sciences, whereas positions are the premises of a demonstration; and therefore they are called positions, because they are posited in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion.

> Positionem rursus diuidit, in eam quæ *verum*, vel *falsum* continet: & hæc est propositio, quam appellant *Suppositionem*: quia sub tali dispositione ponitur in demonstratione ad inferendam conclusionem. Et in eam, quo non continet, *verum, nec falsum*, sed ex illa potest suppositio fieri, & dicit esse definitionem, vt animal rationale, est principiũ, quod vocatur definitio, ex qua potest fieri aliud principium, quod sit suppositio: vt si dicamus, Homo est animal rationale, Suppositio est: quia verum, vel falsum continet.

He divides position again into that which contains the true or the false; and this is the proposition which they call a supposition, because it is posited under such a disposition in the demonstration for inferring the conclusion. And into that which contains neither the true nor the false, but from which a supposition can be made; and he says it is a definition: as rational animal is a principle which is called a definition, from which another principle can be made which is a supposition: as if we say, Man is a rational animal, it is a supposition, because it contains the true or the false.

> 6 In tertia parte, Docet, *principia, vel præmissas demonstrationis*, magis euidentes, magisque certas esse debere, quàm conclusionem eiusdem demonstrationis. Quod probat, ex communi illo axiomate: *Propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis.* Vt si Petrum diligo propter Ioannem, magis diligo Ioannem, quàm Petrum: sed conclusioni demonstrationis [p. 625] assentitur intellectus propter præmissas: ergo fortiùs ac certiùs assentitur præmissis: quare certiores & notiores esse debent conclusione.

6 In the third part he teaches that the principles, or premises of a demonstration, ought to be more evident and more certain than the conclusion of the same demonstration. Which he proves from that common axiom: That on account of which each thing is such is itself more so. As, if I love Peter on account of John, I love John more than Peter. But to the conclusion of the demonstration the [p. 625] On Book 1 of the Posterior Analytics, Chap. 2, Quest. 1.  625 the intellect assents on account of the premises; therefore it assents more strongly and more certainly to the premises; wherefore they ought to be more certain and better known than the conclusion.

## QUESTION I

> QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

> *An secunda definitio demonstrationis sit bona.*

Whether the second definition of demonstration is good.

> QVæstio hæc, non tam proponitur ad rei difficultatem discutiendam, quàm ad elucidandam definitionem Aristo. atque ostendendum exactam esse. Quod vt fiat, duo argu. aduersus eam proponemus, ex quorum solutione id fiat manifestum.
