Which can be proved more firmly in [p. 640] Theological demonstrations, in which the conclusion proceeds from one premise pertaining to divine faith and from another pertaining to natural Philosophy, as is shown in this one: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible. Then, therefore, the conclusion pertains either to divine faith or to the habit of Theological science; and in either way it is more certain than the evident premise. Because divine faith is more certain than science; therefore that too which is derived from divine faith will be more certain. That conclusion, therefore, Christ is risible, in whatever way it is taken, is more certain than the major premise, namely Every man is risible. Wherefore the conclusion can have not only equal certitude with one of the premises, but sometimes greater.

> Nostra sententia est: *Vtramque præmissam semper, & necessariò esse certiorem conclusione: ita, vt nullo casu possit habere æqualem certitudinem cum aliqua earum.* Et hæc est magis communis inter modernos.

Our view is: Each premise is always and necessarily more certain than the conclusion, so that in no case can it have equal certitude with either of them. And this is the more common view among the moderns.

> Probatur duplici arg. Primo: Quia in demonstratione propter quid (de qua loquimur) præmissa demonstrabilis agit in virtute principiorum, à quibus proximiùs deriuatur, quàm conclusio: cùm hæc deriuetur mediante illa: ergo maiorem habebit certitudinem. Probatur euidenter consequentia: quia quo effectus proximus deriuatur à causa, eò perfectiùs participat virtutem eius: pręsertim comparatione alterius effectus: à quo non nisi vllo mediante participatur.

It is proved by a twofold argument. First: Because in a demonstration propter quid (of which we are speaking) the demonstrable premise acts in virtue of the principles, from which it is derived more proximately than the conclusion, since the latter is derived by means of it; therefore it will have greater certitude. The consequence is evidently proved: because the more proximately an effect is derived from a cause, the more perfectly it participates its virtue, especially in comparison with another effect, by which it is participated only through some medium.

> Secundo. Quia præmissæ, quæcunque illæ sint, continent vnionem extremitatum cum medio: conclusio verò continet vnionem earundem extremitatum inter sese, media vnione earum cum medio, tãquam ratione formali, ac totali: propter quàm vniuntur inter se: ergo prior vnio, à quo totaliter dependet secunda fortior est, cùm sit immediatior: sed fortioré esse vnionem extremitatum cum medio, est certiores esse præmissas, ergo maior certitudo prouenit eis, ex natura demonstrationis. Quare repugnat conclusionem, habere æqualem certitudinem, cum aliqua earum.

Second: Because the premises, whatever they may be, contain the union of the extremes with the middle; but the conclusion contains the union of the same extremes with each other, by means of their union with the middle, as the formal and total ratio on account of which they are united with each other; therefore the prior union, on which the second totally depends, is stronger, since it is more immediate. But for the union of the extremes with the middle to be stronger is for the premises to be more certain; therefore greater certitude comes to them from the nature of demonstration. Wherefore it is repugnant that the conclusion should have equal certitude with either of them.

> Ad testimonium Arist. Respondet D. Thom in Commentariis illius, non dixisse, *omnia principia certiora esse conclusione sed saltem aliqua*: quia licet ex virtute demonstrationis semper sit vtraque pręmissa certior, contingit tamen aliquando conclusionem habere aliam certitudinem experientiæ, præter eã, quam à præmissis participat, ratione cuius habebit æqualem certitudinem cum aliqua præmissarum: vt dum quòd luna nunc eclipsetur, experientia sensuum cognoscimus: & ideo non est minus nobis certa, quã quòd terra interponatur inter [p. 641] eam, & solem, per quam demonstratur à priori: tamen per accidens contingit hoc: & ideo non tollit, quin per se, & ex virtute demonstrationis semper sit vtraque præmissa certior conclusione.

To the testimony of Aristotle, St. Thomas replies, in his Commentary on that passage, that he did not say that all the principles are more certain than the conclusion, but at least some: because, although by the force of the demonstration each premise is always more certain, it nevertheless happens sometimes that the conclusion has another certitude, of experience, besides that which it participates from the premises, by reason of which it will have equal certitude with one of the premises: as when we cognize by the experience of the senses that the moon is now eclipsed; and therefore it is not less certain to us than that the earth is interposed between [p. 641] it and the sun, through which it is demonstrated a priori. Yet this happens per accidens, and therefore it does not prevent each premise from always being, per se and by the force of the demonstration, more certain than the conclusion.

> 35 Primum arg. petit expositionem illius vniuersalis axiomatis: *Propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis*. Vt constet in quo sensu verum sit: & cur ab Arist. adductum, ad probandum pręmissas debere esse certiores conclusione. Et an ex illo efficaciter probetur. Plures ac variæ expositiones eius adducuntur à diuersis interpretibus. Plures etiam, & diuersas conditiones requirunt, ad veritatem eius quas molestum esset referre. Nos igitur tres conditiones requisitas esse dicimus, vt verum sit: quarum duas posuit ipsemet Arist. 4. lib. Meta. tex. 4. idemmet axioma referens his verbis: *Vnumquodque autem maximè tale est, præ cæteris, cuius causa nomine & ratione idem conuenit: sic ignis est calidissimus, quòd cæteris caloris causa sit*. Quibus, Primò, asserit, *prædicatum debere conuenire pluribus formaliter*: & vni eorum per se primò, aliis verò per participationem eius, & non aliundo. Secundò: *Eidem primo & cæteris nomine, & ratione*, hoc est vniuocè: & ideo essentialiter. Tertiam conditionem posuit D. Th. 1. part. q. 87 art. 2. ad 3. quòd in eodem ordine causarum contineantur, hoc est, in eodem genere causæ efficientis, vel finalis, aut quouis alio. Ita, vt si illud cui per se primò prædicatum conuenit, sit finis, cætera sint media ad ipsum ordinata: & si illud sit efficiens, cætera sint quasi effectus ab ipso procedentes. His igitur tribus conditionibus concurrentibus verum est, ac necessarium illud axioma. *Propter quod vnumquodque tale, & illud magis tale*. Cuius sensus est: Si aliquid conuenit multis, & vni eorum per se primò: quòd ideo dicitur maximè, tale, aliis verò propter ipsum, necesse est magis conuenire primo, quàm cæteris. Nec potest dari aliquis casus, in quo oppositum contingat.

35 The first argument asks for an exposition of that universal axiom, That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more so: so that it may be clear in what sense it is true, and why it was adduced by Aristotle to prove that the premises must be more certain than the conclusion, and whether it is proved efficaciously from it. Many and various expositions of it are brought forward by different interpreters. They also require many and diverse conditions for its truth, which it would be tedious to report. We, then, say that three conditions are required for it to be true. Two of them Aristotle himself laid down in Metaph. 4, text 4, reporting this same axiom in these words: Each thing is most of all such, in preference to the others, to which, as cause, the same thing belongs in name and in ratio: thus fire is hottest, because it is the cause of heat to the others. By which he asserts, first, that the predicate must belong to several formally, and to one of them per se primarily, but to the others through participation in it, and not from elsewhere. Second, that it belongs to the same one first and to the others in name and in ratio, that is, univocally, and therefore essentially. The third condition St. Thomas laid down in 1 p., q. 87, a. 2, ad 3: that they be contained in the same order of causes, that is, in the same genus of efficient or final cause, or any other whatever; so that, if that to which the predicate belongs per se primarily is the end, the others are means ordered to it; and if it is the efficient, the others are as it were effects proceeding from it. When these three conditions concur, then, that axiom is true and necessary: That on account of which each thing is such, is itself more such. Its sense is: If something belongs to many, and to one of them per se primarily (which is therefore said to be most of all such), but to the others on account of it, it must belong more to the first than to the others. Nor can any case be given in which the opposite happens.

> Ex eodem axiomate, efficax deduxit arg. Arist. ad probandum, certiores, euidentiores, magis necessarias esse, perfectiorémque veritatem continere præmissas, quàm conclusionem: quia tam illis, quàm huic conuenit formaliter certitudo, euidentia, necessitas, atque veritas: & omnes continentur in eodem ordine causæ efficientis: præmissis etiam conueniunt hęc, per se primò: conclusioni verò, vt conclusio demonstrationis est solùm propter pręmissas, & non aliunde: ideo euidenter infertur, quòd magis aut perfectiùs eis conueniant.

From this axiom Aristotle drew an efficacious argument to prove that the premises are more certain, more evident, more necessary, and contain a more perfect truth than the conclusion: because certitude, evidence, necessity, and truth belong formally both to them and to it, and all are contained in the same order of efficient cause; and these belong to the premises per se primarily, but to the conclusion, as the conclusion of a demonstration, only on account of the premises and not from elsewhere. Therefore it is evidently inferred that they belong to the premises more, or more perfectly.

> Ad formam etiam arg. Neganda est consequentia, quòd solùm teneat verum, prædictum axioma in causis æquiuocis: [p. 642] negandum est, quòd solùm probet de præmissis immediatis, & non de demonstrabilibus. Nam licèt primò probet de illis, consequenter tamen etiam probat de his: quia præmissæ demonstrabiles, non sunt causa conclusionis ex propria virtute, aut secundùm se, sed virtute principiorum, à quibus deriuantur, & vt ab eis deriuantur: cuius euidens signum est, quòd si is qui demonstrationem constituit, nesciat eas reducere ad prima principia, per euidentes demonstrationes: non efficiet demonstrationem, nec habebit scientiam conclusionis: sed efficiet argumentum probabile, generans opinionem. Vnde sequitur, prima principia: virtualiter, & vt talia, esse causam conclusionis. Et ideo per se primò, secundùm eandem rationem virtualem, conuenire eis veritatem, necessitatem, certitudinem, & euidentiam, conclusioni verò solùm propter illa: & propterea illis perfectiùs.

To the form of the argument, too: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the aforesaid axiom holds true only in equivocal causes; Ss [p. 642] it is to be denied that it proves only of immediate premises and not of demonstrable ones. For although it proves first of the former, it consequently proves of the latter as well: because demonstrable premises are not the cause of the conclusion by their own power, or according to themselves, but by the power of the principles from which they are derived, and as derived from them. Of this there is an evident sign: if the one who constructs a demonstration does not know how to reduce them to the first principles through evident demonstrations, he will not produce a demonstration, nor will he have science of the conclusion, but he will produce a probable argument, generating opinion. Whence it follows that the first principles, virtually and as such, are the cause of the conclusion. And therefore truth, necessity, certitude, and evidence belong to them per se primarily, according to the same virtual ratio, but to the conclusion only on account of them; and for this reason more perfectly to them.

> Ad secundum: neganda est consequentia, quòd æqualem habeat certitudinem conclusio, cum præmissis demonstrabilibus, quia omnes deriuantur ab eisdem principiis, nam non deriuantur æquè proximè: ideo non æqualiter non participant certitudinem principiorum, sed perfectiùs illæ: quia magis propriè deriuantur

To the second: the consequence is to be denied, namely that the conclusion has equal certitude with the demonstrable premises because all are derived from the same principles; for they are not derived equally proximately. Therefore they do not participate equally in the certitude of the principles, but the premises more perfectly, because they are derived more properly.

> 37 Vltimum quod additur in eo secundo arg tangit demonstrationes scientiæ Theologicæ, quæ procedunt ex vna præmissa diuinæ fidei, & ex altera euidenti: & aliquando ex vtraque de fide, per consequentiam euidentem. In quibus dicimus conuincere rationem Aristot. quòd *ambæ præmissæ sint certiores conclusione*. Quod pręterea probatur, ex cõmuni alio axiomate in scholis recepto: *Cõclusio sequitur debiliorem partem præmissarum*: ergo si vna, vel ambę sint fidei diuinę, cùm diuina fides sit obscura, non poterit esse euidens conclusio: imò neque habere eandem certitudinem fidei, sed obscura quoque erit. Et si vtraque pręmissa sit diuinę fidei, conclusio obscura erit, & minùs certa vtraque pręmissa. Cuius ratio est: quia pręmissæ fidei non concurrunt in demonstratione Theologica ad inferendã conclusionem, nisi media demonstratione: ergo certitudo earum modificatur per certitudinem consequentiæ quę non potest esse, nisi naturalis: vnde nec poterunt producere conclusionem perfectiorem in certitudine quàm sit perfectio certitudinis naturalis. Sed hęc est minor certitudine diuinæ fidei: ergo minorem habebit certitudinem conclusio, quàm pręmissæ. Et si altera pręmissarum sit certa, certitudine Philosophica minorem habebit certitudinem conclusio. Et si contingeret, quòd altera præmissarum esset solùm probabilis, non posset [p. 643] esse certa conclusio, sed probabilis tantùm. Probantur hæc omnia, duabus illis rationibus: quibus probatum est, præmissas perfectiores esse debere conclusione, in veritate, in certitudine, necessitate, atque euidentia, & in cæteris omnibus. Ex quo deductum est hoc idem axioma: Conclusio sequitur debiliorem partem præmissarum cuius sensus est, nullam posse habere perfectionem æqualem, cum præmissis, sed quicquid imperfectionis est in eis, manifestari debet in conclusione.

37 The last point added in that second argument touches the demonstrations of the science of Theology, which proceed from one premise of divine faith and from another that is evident, and sometimes from both of faith, through an evident consequence. In these we say that Aristotle’s reasoning holds conclusively, namely that both premises are more certain than the conclusion. This is further proved from another common axiom received in the schools: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises. Therefore, if one or both are of divine faith, since divine faith is obscure, the conclusion cannot be evident; indeed, it cannot even have the same certitude as faith, but will be obscure as well. And if both premises are of divine faith, the conclusion will be obscure, and less certain than either premise. The reason for this is that the premises of faith do not concur in a Theological demonstration to infer the conclusion except by means of the demonstration; therefore their certitude is modified by the certitude of the consequence, which can be no other than natural. Whence they cannot produce a conclusion more perfect in certitude than is the perfection of natural certitude. But this is less than the certitude of divine faith; therefore the conclusion will have less certitude than the premises. And if one of the premises is certain with philosophical certitude, the conclusion will have less certitude. And if it should happen that one of the premises were only probable, the conclusion could not [p. 643] be certain, but only probable. All these things are proved by those two reasons by which it was proved that the premises must be more perfect than the conclusion in truth, in certitude, necessity, and evidence, and in all other respects. From which this same axiom was deduced: The conclusion follows the weaker part of the premises; whose sense is that it can have no perfection equal to the premises, but whatever imperfection is in them must be manifested in the conclusion.

> 38 Ex quibus infero: Conclusionem demonstrationis Theologicæ, non pertinere ad habitum fidei diuinæ, vt quibusdam modernis placuit: sed ad habitum scientiæ Theologicæ. Quod hac ratione probo: Habitus fidei diuinæ, solùm innititur testimonio, aut reuelationi diuinæ: & immediatè ei innititur, non discursui aut ratiocinationi, seu demonstrationi: sed conclusio demonstrationis Theologicæ, innititur immediatè discursui, aut demõstrationi, per quam deducitur ex præmissis, & non testimonio, aut reuelationi immediatè: ergo non pertinet ad habitum diuinæ fidei, sed scientiæ Theologicæ. Minorem licèt satis per se certam, probo: quia si vtraque præmissa syllogismi sit diuinæ fidei, vel altera euidens euidentia naturali, & syllogismus solùm probabilis, certum est, conclusionem solùm esse probabilem hoc est nec scientiam, nec fidem diuinam, sed opinionem: ergo non causatur à præmissis secundùm se, sed vt modificatis per certitudinem demonstrationis: huic ergo innititur proximè conclusio, & non testimonio, aut reuelationi diuinæ.

38 From these things I infer that the conclusion of a Theological demonstration does not pertain to the habit of divine faith, as some moderns have held, but to the habit of the science of Theology. This I prove by the following reason: The habit of divine faith rests only on testimony, or divine revelation, and rests on it immediately, not on discourse or reasoning or demonstration; but the conclusion of a Theological demonstration rests immediately on discourse or demonstration, through which it is deduced from the premises, and not immediately on testimony or revelation; therefore it does not pertain to the habit of divine faith, but to that of the science of Theology. The minor, though certain enough of itself, I prove: because, if both premises of a syllogism are of divine faith, or one is evident with natural evidence, and the syllogism is only probable, it is certain that the conclusion is only probable, that is, neither science nor divine faith, but opinion; therefore it is not caused by the premises according to themselves, but as modified by the certitude of the demonstration; on this, then, the conclusion rests proximately, and not on testimony or divine revelation.

> 39 Et ex his respondetur ad argumentum: conclusionem demonstrationis Theologicę, nec pertinere ad fidem diuinam, neque ad scientiam naturalem, sed ad scientiam Theologicam, imperfectam, & obscuram: vnde fit, imperfectiorem esse, & minùs certam vtraque præmissa. Concedimus ergo: quòd fides diuina sit certior scientia: negamus tamen, quòd conclusio ab ea deriuata, sit etiam certior scientia: nam conclusio ab ea deriuata, non habet maiorem certitudinem, quàm sit certitudo consequentiæ, vel illationis per quam modificantur pręmissæ ad inferendam conclusionem: in illatione verò, aut syllogismo, perfectiùs esse habent præmissæ, quàm conclusio in certitudine, euidentia, necessitate, ac veritate, vt probauimus, & ideo, impossibile est, conclusionem esse æqualem in his, cum altera præmissarum.

39 And from these things the reply to the argument is given: the conclusion of a Theological demonstration pertains neither to divine faith nor to natural science, but to the science of Theology, imperfect and obscure; whence it comes about that it is more imperfect and less certain than either premise. We grant, therefore, that divine faith is more certain than science; but we deny that the conclusion derived from it is also more certain than science. For the conclusion derived from it has no greater certitude than is the certitude of the consequence or illation by which the premises are modified for inferring the conclusion; and in the illation or syllogism the premises have being more perfectly than the conclusion in certitude, evidence, necessity, and truth, as we have proved; and therefore it is impossible for the conclusion to be equal in these respects with either of the premises. Ss ij

[p. 644]

> CAPVT IV.

C H A P T E R I V.

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> TEXTVS ARIST.

[…]

> *Quoniam autem impossibile aliter se habere, cuius est scientia simpliciter, necessarium vtique fuerit scibile, &c.*

But since it is impossible for that of which there is science simply to be otherwise, what is knowable will surely be necessary, etc.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> 1 INtentum Arist. in præsenti cap. est, docere quales debeant esse propositiones, ex quibus demonstratio componitur. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima proponit hanc conclusionem vniuersalem, *Scientiam, quæ per demonstrationem generatur, esse de rebus necessariis*: & ex ea colligit, demonstrationem debere procedere, aut componi, ex propositionibus necessariis. In secunda parte: Ponit *tres conditiones, quas habere debent propositiones*, vt ita sint necessariæ, quòd ex eis possit componi demonstratio. Conclusio, quam proponit, est, *Scientia, quæ est conclusio demonstrationis, debet esse de rebus necessariis*. Quam sic probat: Conclusionem demonstrationis, scimus ex principiis, quæ sunt propositiones immediatæ: ergo non potest aliter se habere: sed quod non potest aliter se habere, est necessarium: ergo conclusio demonstrationis est necessaria. Probatur prima cõsequentia: nam cætera per se patent. *Scire*, est rem per causam cognoscere: & quod illius est causa: & non potest aliter se habere: ergo non solùm scientia, sed id, quod scitur, nempe obiectum, circa quod versatur, non possunt aliter se habere, quod est esse necessaria: cùm necessariũ sic definiatur, quod non potest aliter se habere.

ristotle’s intent in the present chapter is to teach what kind of 1 A propositions demonstration ought to be composed of. It is divid‐ ed into two parts. In the first he proposes this universal conclusion, that science, which is generated through demonstration, is of necessary things; and from it he gathers that demonstration must proceed from, or be composed of, necessary propositions. In the second part he lays down three conditions which propositions must have, in order to be necessary in such a way that demonstration can be composed of them. The conclusion he proposes is: Science, which is the conclusion of demonstration, must be of necessary things. This he proves thus: We know the conclusion of demonstration from principles, which are immediate propositions; therefore it cannot be otherwise; but what cannot be otherwise is necessary; therefore the conclusion of demonstration is necessary. The first consequence is proved, for the rest are plain of themselves. To know scientifically is to cognize a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of it, and that it cannot be otherwise; therefore not only science, but that which is known, namely the object with which it is concerned, cannot be otherwise. And this is to be necessary, since the necessary is defined thus: that which cannot be otherwise.

> Ex hoc infert, quòd demonstratio debeat componi, aut procedere ex propositionibus necessariis. Quod sic potest probari: Conclusio demonstrationis, quæ est scientia, est necessaria, & de rebus necessariis, & procedit ex præmissis, tanquam ex causis: ergo præmissæ, ex quibus componitur demonstratio, non solùm veræ, sed necessariæ debent esse. Probatur consequentia: quia licèt ex præmissis falsis contingat colligi conclusionem veram, & ex non necessariis necessariam, tamen id fit, non tanquam ex causis, sed virtute dispositionis syllogisticæ: alioqui effectus esset nobilior sua causa, quod est impossibile.

From this he infers that demonstration must be composed of, or proceed from, necessary propositions. This can be proved thus: The conclusion of demonstration, which is science, is necessary and of necessary things, and proceeds from the premises as from causes; therefore the premises of which demonstration is composed must be not only true but necessary. The consequence is proved: because, although it happens that a true conclusion is gathered from false premises, and a necessary one from non-necessary premises, yet this comes about not as from causes, but by virtue of the syllogistic disposition; otherwise the effect would be nobler than its cause, which is impossible.

> 2 In secunda parte: *Proponit tres conditiones, quas habere debent propositiones*, vt ita sint necessariæ, quòd ex eis componi possit demonstratio. Quarum prima est, vt *sint de omni*. Hoc est, vt [p. 645] prædicatum in eis dicatur de quolibet contento sub subiecto, & pro quolibet tempore. Defectu primi, hæc propositio non est de omni: Omnis homo disputat: quia plures sunt, de quibus non verificatur prædicatum. Defectu secundi, neque ista est de omni: Omnis homo vigilat: quia licèt prædicatum dicatur de quolibet contento sub subiecto, non tamen pro quolibet tempore: sed pro certo quodam ac determinato. Hæc verò: Omnis homo est coloratus, est de omni: quia habet vtrumque, vt per se patet.

2 In the second part he proposes three conditions which propositions must have, in order to be necessary in such a way that demonstration can be composed of them. The first of these is that they be said of every. That is, that [p. 645] the predicate in them be said of anything whatever contained under the subject, and for any time whatever. For want of the first, this proposition is not said of every: Every man is disputing, because there are many of whom the predicate is not verified. For want of the second, neither is this one said of every: Every man is awake, because, although the predicate is said of anything whatever contained under the subject, yet not for any time whatever, but for a certain fixed and determinate time. But this one, Every man is colored, is said of every, because it has both, as is plain of itself.

> Secunda conditio est: *Quòd propositiones sint per se*: ideo, vt eam explicet: diuidit *per se* in quatuor modos. Primus modus, *per se* est, quando *prædicatum ad essentiam subiecti*: quia vel est definitio eius, vel pars definitionis: vnde istæ omnes propositiones, sunt in primo modo per se: homo est animal: homo est rationalis: homo est animal rationale.

The second condition is: That the propositions be per se; therefore, in order to explain it, he divides per se into four modes. The first mode is per se when the predicate belongs to the essence of the subject, because it is either its definition or a part of its definition: whence all these propositions are in the first mode per se: Man is an animal; Man is rational; Man is a rational animal.

> Secundus modus est, *quando ex exposito, Subiectum pertinet ad definitionem prædicati*, vt homo est admiratiuus, homo est risibilis.

The second mode is when, conversely, the subject pertains to the definition of the predicate, as Man is capable of wonder, Man is risible.

> 3 Tertius modus, *non est prædicandi sed essendi*. & illud dicitur per se hoc modo, quod per se subsistit, & non inhæret alteri, tanquam accidens: & iste est modus proprius prædicamenti substantiæ. Quartus modus est, *per se causandi*, quando prædicatur effectus de sua causa per se. *Effectus per se* dicitur, qui sequitur ex propria virtute causæ: & non aliunde: hoc est, non casu, aut fortuna: quia effectus casuales, & fortuiti, qui non sequuntur ex virtute causæ, sed ex quodam concursu casuali, aut per accidens, non dicuntur effectus per se, sed per accidens: vnde propositio hæc: Fodiens terram inuenit thesaurum non est per se. At verò per se sunt istæ, in hoc quarto modo: Iugulatus interiit: Ædificator ædificat. Ex his igitur quatuor modis per se, duo priores sunt per se prædicandi, tertius per se essendi: quartus per se causandi: & vt propositiones sint aptæ ad demonstrationem, necesse est, sint per se in primo, secundo, aut quarto modo.

3 The third mode is not of predicating but of being; and that is said to be per se in this mode which subsists per se and does not inhere in another as an accident: and this is the mode proper to the category of substance. The fourth mode is per se of causing, when an effect is predicated of its cause per se. That effect is said to be per se which follows from the proper power of the cause, and not from elsewhere, that is, not by chance or fortune: for chance and fortuitous effects, which do not follow from the power of the cause but from some chance concurrence, or per accidens, are not called effects per se but per accidens. Whence this proposition, The one digging the earth found a treasure, is not per se. But these are per se in this fourth mode: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds. Of these four modes per se, then, the first two are per se of predicating, the third per se of being, the fourth per se of causing; and in order that propositions be apt for demonstration, they must be per se in the first, second, or fourth mode.

> Tertia conditio est seu terminus, *vt vniuersaliter prædicetur*: quod sic definit Arist. *Vniuersaliter autem dico, quod vtique, & de omni sit, & per se, & secundùm quod ipsum*. Quæ definitio triplicem conditionem continet, quam habere debet propositio, vt in ea prædicatum dicatur vniuersaliter de subiecto. Prima est, *quòd dicatur de omni*: & defectu huius conditionis, in hac, non dicitur prædicatum vniuersaliter, homo vigilat, quia non dicitur de omni. Defectu secundæ conditionis, neque in hac dicitur vniuersaliter prædicatum de subiecto: Homo est coloratus: quia nec dicitur per se. Defectu quoque tertiæ, non dicitur in [p. 646] hac vniuersaliter, homo est sensibilis: quia sensibile, non conuenit homini secundùm quod ipsum: hoc est, in quantum homo est, sed, in quantum est animal: Conuenire enim prædicatum subiecto, secundùm quod ipsum, idem videtur esse, ac conuenire illi, in quantum tale est: hoc est, non secundùm rationem communem, sed secundùm propriam.

The third condition, or term, is that it be predicated universally, which Aristotle defines thus: But I call universal that which is both said of every, and per se, and according as it is itself. This definition contains a threefold condition which a proposition must have in order that in it the predicate be said universally of the subject. The first is that it be said of every; and for want of this condition the predicate is not said universally in this one, Man is awake, because it is not said of every. For want of the second condition, neither is the predicate said universally of the subject in this one, Man is colored, because it is not said per se. For want of the third as well, it is not said in Ss iij [p. 646] this one universally: Man is sensible, because sensible does not belong to man according as he is himself, that is, inasmuch as he is man, but inasmuch as he is an animal. For a predicate’s belonging to a subject according as it is itself seems to be the same as belonging to it inasmuch as it is such, that is, not according to a common ratio, but according to its proper one.

## QUESTION I

> QVÆSTIO I.

[…]

> *An demonstratio debeat procedere ex necessariis.*

Whether demonstration must proceed from necessary things.

> TRia proponam argu. quibus videtur probari non omnem demonstrationem procedere ex necessariis. Primum sit: Hæc est vera demonstratio propter quid: Quotiescunque terra interponitur inter solem, & lunam, & sequitur eclipsis: sed dum duo hæc astra, ad talem punctum perueniunt, interponitur terra inter vtrumque: ergo eclipsis sequitur. Minor verò non est necessaria, sed contingens. Quia, quòd ad talem punctum perueniant, vel non, accidentale omnino est naturæ eorum, cùm possit eis adesse, & abesse præter corruptionem: ergo non omnis demonstratio constat ex propositionibus necessariis.

I shall propose three arguments by which it seems to be proved that not every demonstration proceeds from necessary things. Let the first be: This is a true demonstration propter quid: Whenever the earth is interposed between the sun and the moon, an eclipse also follows; but when these two heavenly bodies arrive at such a point, the earth is interposed between them; therefore an eclipse follows. But the minor is not necessary but contingent: because whether they arrive at such a point or not is altogether accidental to their nature, since it can be present to them and absent from them without their corruption; therefore not every demonstration consists of necessary propositions.

> Secundùm, Quia hæc etiam est vera, & propria demonstratio: Omne album est disgregatiuum visus: sed corpus habens albedinem est album: ergo est disgregatiuum visus. Et tamen minor non est necessaria, sed contingens: quia contingens est, quòd corpus habeat albedinem, & quòd sit album: vnde neque etiam conclusio necessaria est: quia sicut non est necessarium, corpus esse album, ita neque est necesse, quòd cùm sit album, sit etiam disgregatiuum visus: ergo non omnis demonstratio procedit ex necessariis.

Second, because this too is a true and proper demonstration: Everything white is disgregative of sight; but a body having whiteness is white; therefore it is disgregative of sight. And yet the minor is not necessary but contingent: because it is contingent that a body have whiteness and that it be white; whence neither is the conclusion necessary, because, just as it is not necessary that a body be white, so neither is it necessary that, since it is white, it be also disgregative of sight; therefore not every demonstration proceeds from necessary things.

> Tertium, Quia *necessarium est, quod non potest aliter se habere*: sed in Philosophia naturali, & morali, dantur multæ propositiones demonstratiuæ, multæ etiam conclusiones demonstratæ, quæ possunt aliter se habere: & aliquando aliter se habent: vt quòd futuræ sint pluuiæ in hyeme, & calores vigebunt æstate: ergo non omnes demonstrationes procedere debent ex necessariis.

Third, because the necessary is that which cannot be otherwise; but in natural and moral Philosophy there are many demonstrative propositions, and many demonstrated conclusions too, which can be otherwise, and sometimes are otherwise: as that there will be rains in winter, and heat will prevail in summer; therefore not all demonstrations must proceed from necessary things.

> Sententia tamen Aristot. vniuersaliter vera est, & tenenda, *quòd non possit vlla demonstratio procedere, ex propositionibus contingentibus, aut non necessariis*. Quod hac ratione, deducta ex doctrina eius, euidenter probatur: Conclusio cuiuslibet demonstrationis, est scientia: sed scientia habetur per causam necessariam, vt constat ex definitione eius: quæ talis est: *Scire, [p. 647] est rem per causam cognoscere: & quòd illius est causa: & quod non potest aliter se habere, quin ea posita sequatur effectus*: ergo debet procedere ex necessariis. Probatur consequentia: quia præmissæ ex quibus procedit, sunt causa per se, & necessaria conclusionis: ergo debent esse necessariæ.

Nevertheless Aristotle’s view is universally true and to be held, that no demonstration can proceed from contingent or non-necessary propositions. This is evidently proved by the following reason, deduced from his doctrine: The conclusion of any demonstration whatever is science; but science is had through a necessary cause, as is clear from its definition, which is this: To know [p. 647] scientifically is to cognize a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of it, and that it cannot be otherwise, but that when it is posited the effect follows; therefore it must proceed from necessary things. The consequence is proved: because the premises from which it proceeds are the per se and necessary cause of the conclusion; therefore they must be necessary.

> Ad primam arg. diuersis modis respondetur. Nam Venetus cap. pręsenti respondet, non demonstrari lunam eclipsari actu, sed potentia, vel aptitudine: hoc est, non demonstrari, quòd eclipsetur, sed quòd sit eclipsabilis. Et licèt actu eclipsari non sit necessarium, esse tamen eclipsabilem necessarium est: & pari ratione, licèt non sit necessarium, quòd ad talem punctum ipsa, & Sol perueniant, tamen quòd peruenire possint, necessarium est. Vnde propositiones illius demonstrationis ita sumptæ, necessariæ sunt. Hęc tamen solutio falsa est propter duo.

To the first argument the reply is made in different ways. For Paul of Venice, on the present chapter, replies that it is not demonstrated that the moon is eclipsed in act, but in potency or aptitude; that is, it is not demonstrated that it is eclipsed, but that it is eclipsable. And although to be eclipsed in act is not necessary, yet to be eclipsable is necessary; and by like reasoning, although it is not necessary that the moon itself and the sun arrive at such a point, yet that they can arrive there is necessary. Whence the propositions of that demonstration, taken thus, are necessary. This solution, however, is false, for two reasons.

> Primum: quia Astrologi non solùm demonstrant lunam esse eclipsabilem, sed tali die, tali hora, & tali puncto eclipsandam esse: ergo secundùm actum accipi debent propositiones illius demonstrationis. Secundum: quia causa per se, & effectus per se, non solùm secundùm aptitudinem, sed etiam secundùm actum constituunt propositionem per se, in quarto modo: ergo secundùm actum constituunt propositionem necessariam. Probatur consequentia: quia omnis propositio per se, est necessaria apud Arist. & apud omnes.

First, because Astrologers demonstrate not only that the moon is eclipsable, but that it is to be eclipsed on such a day, at such an hour, and at such a point; therefore the propositions of that demonstration must be taken according to act. Second, because a per se cause and a per se effect, not only according to aptitude but also according to act, constitute a proposition per se in the fourth mode; therefore according to act they constitute a necessary proposition. The consequence is proved: because every proposition per se is necessary according to Aristotle and according to all.

> 6 Ideo est secunda solutio aliorum modernorum: Quòd demonstratio illa non procedit de hac luna, & de hoc sole, vt singularibus, sed secundùm rationem communem, & specificam, aut genericam eorum: quam constat multis possibilibus esse communem: nam plures possunt soles, plures etiam lunæ à Deo fieri. Licèt ergo contingens sit, quòd Sol iste, & hæc Luna, ad talem punctum perueniant, tamen quòd Soli, & Lunæ: vt sic conueniat, non est contingens, sed necessarium. Sed hæc etiam solutio, aut nihil dicit, aut non est minùs falsa quàm præcedens. Quod ita probo: quia vel ad talem punctum peruenire, & eclipsari, accipiuntur secundùm actum, vel secundùm potentiam, si secundùm actum, eo ipso, quòd sunt prędicata accidentalia, & contingentia, respectu horum indiuiduorum, euidenter probatur esse accidentalia respectu speciei: nam si albedo contingenter inest Petro, euidenter sequitur, contingenter inesse homini, & animali: ergo si prædicata illa contingenter insunt isti soli, & huic lunæ: contingenter etiam conuenire debent soli, & lunæ, sub ratione communi, aut specifica acceptis. Et prætereà effectus per se, non solùm in communi sed etiã in singulari prædicatur per se, & necessariò de sua causa [p. 648] etiam in singulari, & actu accepta, vt ostendunt propositiones istæ: Iugulatus interiit: Ædificator ædificat.

6 Therefore there is a second solution, of other moderns: that that demonstration does not proceed concerning this moon and this sun as singulars, but according to their common and specific, or generic, ratio, which is certainly common to many possibles: for several suns, and several moons too, can be made by God. Although, then, it is contingent that this Sun and this Moon arrive at such a point, yet that this belongs to the Sun and the Moon as such is not contingent but necessary. But this solution too either says nothing or is no less false than the preceding one. This I prove thus: because to arrive at such a point and to be eclipsed are taken either according to act or according to potency. If according to act, by the very fact that they are accidental and contingent predicates with respect to these individuals, they are evidently proved to be accidental with respect to the species: for if whiteness inheres contingently in Peter, it evidently follows that it inheres contingently in man and in animal; therefore, if those predicates inhere contingently in this sun and this moon, they must also belong contingently to the sun and the moon taken under the common or specific ratio. And moreover, an effect per se is predicated per se and necessarily of its cause not only in common but also in the singular Ss iiij [p. 648] and taken in act, as these propositions show: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds.

> Nostra igitur sententia duo asserit, Primum: Demonstrationem illam, per se primò procedere de sole, & luna secundùm rationem communem: vel certè de communi ipsa ratione, & specifica. Nihilominus etiam de hoc sole & hac luna, per applicationem. Quemadmodum passio demonstrata de specie, applicari potest ad hoc, vel illud indiuiduum: & si de homine demonstramus, quòd sit risibilis, eandem demonstrationem possumus applicare Petro, sumpto pro minori extremitate, ac dicere: Omne animal rationale est risibile; Petrus est animal rationale: ergo Petrus est risibilis. Ita ergo, quòd ad talem punctum perueniant sol, & luna, & hæc eclipsetur per interpositionem terrę, de ratione eorum communi demonstratur primò, at per applicationem, de his singularibus.

Our view, then, asserts two things. First: that demonstration proceeds per se primarily concerning the sun and the moon according to their common ratio, or rather concerning that common and specific ratio itself; nevertheless also concerning this sun and this moon, by application. Just as an attribute demonstrated of a species can be applied to this or that individual: and if we demonstrate of man that he is risible, we can apply the same demonstration to Peter, taken for the minor extreme, and say: Every rational animal is risible; Peter is a rational animal; therefore Peter is risible. Thus, then, that the sun and the moon arrive at such a point, and that the latter is eclipsed through the interposition of the earth, is demonstrated primarily of their common ratio, but by application of these singulars.

> 7 Secundò dicimus: Non secundùm potentiam, sed secũdùm actum demonstrari eclipsim, per actualem interpositionem terræ: & nihilominus vtramque propositionem esse per se. Non quidem in primo, aut secundo modo, sed in quarto: & ideo sicut sunt per se, perseitate causalitatis, sic etiam sunt necessariæ, necessitate causalitatis. Nam prędicatum, duobus modis potest comparari ad subiectum, vel prędicari de illo, atque ei conuenire, aut secundùm rationem essendi, vel inhærendi, aut secundùm rationem causandi. Et secundùm primam rationem, sumuntur in propositionibus primi, & secundi modi per se. Iuxta secundam verò, in propositionibus quarti modi: quia primus, & secundus modus, sunt modi per se prędicandi, tertius per se essendi, & quartus per se causandi: vt docet Arist. Vnde intelligitur, quòd si propositiones quarti modi accipiantur in ratione prædicandi, nulla ferè erit per se, sed omnes erunt per accidens: vt patet in his: Iugulatus interiit: Ædificator ædificat. Actu enim ædificare, accidit planè ædificatori, & de illo prędicatur prędicatione quinti prędicabilis, vt constat: sed in ratione causandi, per se sunt: quia effectus per se, etiam secundùm actum, per se prædicatur de sua causa, actu causante, perseitate causandi.

7 Second, we say that the eclipse is demonstrated not according to potency but according to act, through the actual interposition of the earth; and nevertheless that both propositions are per se: not indeed in the first or second mode, but in the fourth. And therefore, just as they are per se with the perseity of causality, so too they are necessary with the necessity of causality. For a predicate can be compared to a subject, or be predicated of it and belong to it, in two ways: either according to the ratio of being, or of inhering, or according to the ratio of causing. And according to the first ratio they are taken in propositions of the first and second mode per se; but according to the second, in propositions of the fourth mode: because the first and second modes are modes per se of predicating, the third per se of being, and the fourth per se of causing, as Aristotle teaches. Whence it is understood that, if propositions of the fourth mode are taken in the ratio of predicating, hardly any will be per se, but all will be per accidens, as is plain in these: The one whose throat was cut perished; The builder builds. For to build in act is plainly accidental to the builder, and is predicated of him with the predication of the fifth predicable, as is clear; but in the ratio of causing they are per se, because an effect per se, even according to act, is predicated per se of its cause actually causing, with the perseity of causing.

> 8 Ad formam igitur arg. Distinguenda est minor: Quia solem & lunam ad talem punctum peruenire, vt interpositio terræ sequatur: per se eis conuenit perseitate causandi: & eodem modo, per se sequitur ex interpositione eclipsis: nam impossibile est rem aliter se habere, quin ex motu horum astrorum sequatur, quòd ad talem punctum non perueniant, & vbi peruenerint quòd non eueniat eclipsis lunæ. Si ergo in ratione [p. 649] causandi sumantur, necessariæ sunt propositiones: & ita sumuntur hîc: Si verò in ratione essendi, vel prędicandi, nõ sunt necessariæ, sed accidentales, & contingentes. Verùm non accipiuntur hoc modo. Pro solutione aliorum argum. notandum est, propositionem necessariam esse, quæ enunciat rem necessariam: hoc est, quæ non potest aliter se habere. Sed rem esse necessariam, duobus modis contingit: *Simpliciter*, vel *ex suppositione*. *Necessarium simpliciter* est illud, quòd ex propria natura tale est, vt non possit non esse: vt quòd homo sit animal, vel rationalis. *Necessarium verò ex suppositione*, quòd ex propria natura potest non esse, aut non esse tale: vt corpus disgregare visum, non esse necessarium secundùm naturam corporis, sed contingens: ex suppositione verò, quòd sit album, necessarium est. Prętereà *necessarium simpliciter*, adhuc est triplex.

8 To the form of the argument, then: the minor is to be distinguished. For that the sun and the moon arrive at such a point, so that the interposition of the earth follows, belongs to them per se with the perseity of causing; and in the same way the eclipse follows per se from the interposition: for it is impossible for the thing to be otherwise, so that it should follow from the motion of these heavenly bodies that they do not arrive at such a point, and that, when they have arrived, an eclipse of the moon does not occur. If, then, in the ratio [p. 649] of causing they are taken, the propositions are necessary; and so they are taken here. But if in the ratio of being or of predicating, they are not necessary, but accidental and contingent. But they are not taken in this way. For the solution of the other arguments, it should be noted that a necessary proposition is one which enunciates a necessary thing, that is, one which cannot be otherwise. But a thing happens to be necessary in two ways: simply, or on a supposition. Necessary simply is that which is such from its own nature, so that it cannot not be: as that man is an animal, or rational. Necessary on a supposition is that which by its own nature can not be, or not be such: as that a body disgregates sight is not necessary according to the nature of the body, but contingent; but on the supposition that it is white, it is necessary. Moreover, the necessary simply is in turn threefold.

> Primum, *quod nullo modo potest non esse, sed implicat contradictionem quod non sit*, vt hominem esse animal, vel rationale. Secundum *quod non potest non esse, per virtutem naturalem causarũ, benè tamen potest, per supernaturalem Dei*: vt quòd ignis sit calidus, vel homo sit risibilis. Nam per potentiam supernaturalem Dei, separari potest calor ab igne, & risibilitas ab homine. Tertium *quod non potest non esse, per virtutem naturalem causarum, vt plurimum, quamuis raro possit per eandem virtutem non esse*.

The first, that which can in no way not be, but it implies a contradiction that it not be: as that man is an animal, or rational. The second, that which cannot not be by the natural power of causes, but can well not be by the supernatural power of God: as that fire is hot, or man is risible. For by the supernatural power of God heat can be separated from fire, and risibility from man. The third, that which cannot not be by the natural power of causes for the most part, although rarely it can, by the same power, not be.

> 9 Et secundùm hos quatuor modos necessarij, distinguendi sunt quatuor alij modi, propositionũ necessariarũ: dicendumque, demonstrationem debere procedere ex necessariis propositionibus, vno, vel alio modo: sed perfectior erit, si procedat ex propositionibus necessariis simpliciter, quàm si solùm procedat ex propositionibus necessariis ex suppositione: & perfectissima, si procedat ex necessariis simpliciter, iuxta primum modum: minùs perfecta, si iuxta secundum: imperfectissima verò, si iuxta tertium. Et ideo demonstrationes Philosophiæ naturalis, & motalis ex quibus plures constat propositionibus, quæ solùm, vt plurimùm veræ sunt, imperfectissimæ censentur: & scientiæ ipsæ, infimum locum certitudinis inter omnes tenent.

9 And according to these four modes of the necessary, four other modes of necessary propositions are to be distinguished; and it must be said that demonstration must proceed from necessary propositions in one mode or another. But it will be more perfect if it proceeds from propositions necessary simply than if it proceeds only from propositions necessary on a supposition; and most perfect if it proceeds from things necessary simply according to the first mode; less perfect if according to the second; but most imperfect if according to the third. And therefore the demonstrations of natural and moral Philosophy, which consist of many propositions that are true only for the most part, are reckoned most imperfect, and these sciences themselves hold the lowest place of certitude among all.

> Ex his ergo solutum est secundum, & tertium arg. Nam licèt demonstrationes illæ, non procedant ex necessariis, simpliciter, tamen procedunt ex talibus ex suppositione: vt ea quæ adducitur in secundo argumento: vel si ex necessariis simpliciter, non tamen semper euenientibus, sed vt plurimùm tantùm. Sufficit autem aliquo modorum istorum, procedere ex necessariis. Et quòd sufficiat procedere ex necessariis, vt plumùm euenientibus, docuit expresè Arist. cap. 24. huius primi [p. 650] libri, & recipiunt id omnes: Quia omnes recipiunt vtramque Philosophiam pro vera scientia: & meritò: quia necessarium reputatur, quòd vt plurimùm euenit, necessitate naturali, aut morali, ergo obiectum scientię esse potest. Nec est periculum errandi, in tali modo demonstrandi: quia non demonstratur effectum semper euenire, sed vt substat virtuti, aut modo operandi causarum: hoc autem deficere non potest: ideo nec erroris periculo se exponit, ita procedens. Quòd verò sufficiat propositiones esse necessarias, ex suppositione, probatur: Quia sic acceptæ, non possunt aliter se habere: quare cùm in tali processu demonstrandi sic accipiantur, conclusionem euidenter inferunt: quæ vt substat præmissis, non potest aliter se habere: & ideo scientifica est, atque necessaria.

From these things, then, the second and third arguments are solved. For although those demonstrations do not proceed from things necessary simply, yet they proceed from things such on a supposition, like the one adduced in the second argument; or, if from things necessary simply, yet not always occurring, but only for the most part. And it suffices to proceed from necessary things in some one of these modes. And that it suffices to proceed from necessary things that occur for the most part, Aristotle expressly taught in ch. 24 of this first [p. 650] book, and all accept this: because all accept both Philosophies as true science, and rightly so; because what occurs for the most part is reckoned necessary, with natural or moral necessity, and therefore it can be the object of science. Nor is there any danger of erring in such a mode of demonstrating: because it is not demonstrated that the effect always occurs, but as it stands under the power or mode of operating of the causes; and this cannot fail; therefore one who proceeds thus does not expose himself to the danger of error either. And that it suffices for the propositions to be necessary on a supposition is proved: because, taken thus, they cannot be otherwise; wherefore, since in such a process of demonstrating they are taken thus, they evidently infer the conclusion, which, as it stands under the premises, cannot be otherwise, and is therefore scientific and necessary.

## QUESTION II

> QVÆSTIO II.

[…]

### Quæst. 2. An demonstratio debeat constare ex propositionibus de omni, per se, & vniuersaliter — Whether demonstration must consist of propositions said of every, per se, and universally.

> *An demonstratio debeat constare ex propositionibus, de omni, per se, & vniuersaliter.*

[…]

> 11 TRia propono argumenta aduersus hos tres terminos, vt eorum occasione explicentur singuli, Primum erit, *aduersus primum terminum de omni*. Quod propositiones singulares, necessariæ, atque per se, possunt demonstrationem componere, & tamen non sunt de omni: ergo non omnes propositiones demonstratiuæ debent esse de omni. Maior satis est per se manifesta, cùm in Philosophia demonstretur de Deo, quòd sit, & quòd sit vnus; nec solùm à posteriori, vel demonstratione, Quia, sed etiam demonstratione Propter quid, demonstrare possumus de eo, quòd sit æternus: quia est immutabilis. Et de Christo Domino demonstrantur plura in Theologia, suppositis principiis fidei: quæ omnia non possunt, nisi per propositiones singulares demonstrari. Nam cùm Deus & Christus sint termini singulares, non possunt ex eis fieri: nisi propositiones singulares. Minor verò, quòd tales propositiones non sint de omni, euidens est, cùm repugnet propositionem esse de omni, & non esse vniuersalem: quomodo enim in propositione singulari conuenire potest prædicatum, cuilibet contento sub subiecto, & pro quolibet tempore, cùm nihil sub subiecto singulari contineatur.

11 I propose three arguments against these three terms, so that on their occasion each may be explained. The first will be against the first term, “of every.” Singular propositions, necessary and per se, can compose a demonstration, and yet they are not said of every; therefore not all demonstrative propositions must be said of every. The major is manifest enough of itself, since in Philosophy it is demonstrated of God that he exists and that he is one; and not only a posteriori, or by a demonstration quia, but also by a demonstration propter quid we can demonstrate of him that he is eternal, because he is immutable. And many things are demonstrated of Christ the Lord in Theology, the principles of faith being supposed; all of which can be demonstrated only through singular propositions. For since God and Christ are singular terms, nothing but singular propositions can be made from them. The minor, that such propositions are not said of every, is evident, since it is repugnant for a proposition to be said of every and not be universal: for how in a singular proposition can the predicate belong to anything whatever contained under the subject, and for any time whatever, when nothing is contained under a singular subject?

> Secundum arg. *Contra primum & secundum modum per se*, hac ratione: Primus modus per se est, quando prædicatum est definitio, aut pars definitionis subiecti: ergo hæc propositio, Risibile est homo, & similes, erunt in secundo modo per [p. 651] se, quod est falsum: quia indirectæ sunt, & ex quibus demonstrationes, saltem propter quid, non possunt componi. Prætereà, secundus modus per se est, quando subiectum pertinet ad definitionem prædicati; sed omnia accidentia definiuntur per subiectum aliquo modo, cùm habeant intrinsecum ordinem aptitudinalis inhærentiæ ad illud qui non potest explicari, nisi posito eodem subiecto in definitione accidentium: ergo omnia accidentia prædicabuntur de subiectis in secundo modo per se. Et ita, hæc propositio, corpus est album, & similes, erunt in secundo modo: cùm album definiatur per corpus, quòd tamen patet esse falsum: Quia omnes sunt accidentales, & contingentes, ex quibus demonstrationem componi repugnat: ergo secundus modus per se, falsus est, & ad demonstrationem ineptus.

The second argument, against the first and second mode per se, by this reasoning: The first mode per se is when the predicate is the definition, or part of the definition, of the subject; therefore this proposition, The risible is man, and the like, will be in the second mode per [p. 651] se; which is false, because they are indirect, and demonstrations, at least propter quid, cannot be composed of them. Moreover, the second mode per se is when the subject pertains to the definition of the predicate; but all accidents are defined in some way through the subject, since they have an intrinsic order of aptitudinal inherence to it, which cannot be explained unless that same subject is placed in the definition of accidents; therefore all accidents will be predicated of their subjects in the second mode per se. And so this proposition, Body is white, and the like, will be in the second mode, since white is defined through body; which, however, is plainly false, because they are all accidental and contingent, and it is repugnant for demonstration to be composed of them; therefore the second mode per se is false, and inept for demonstration.

> Tertium arg. est *contra modum vniuersaliter*, quem sic exponit Arist. *Vniuersaliter dicitur prædicatum de subiecto, si ei conueniat secundùm quod ipsum*: hoc secundùm rationem propriam, vel vt tale est: quod patet non habere, nisi conuertatur cum eo: ergo nulla propositio superioris prædicati, quales sunt istæ, Homo est animal, Homo est corpus, erunt vniuersales: sed constat esse has in primo modo per se, & ex eis posse demonstrationem Propter quid componi: ergo modus vniuersaliter diminutus est, non comprehendens omnes propositiones, ex quibus perfectissima demonstratio potest procedere.

The third argument is against the mode “universally,” which Aristotle expounds thus: A predicate is said universally of a subject if it belongs to it according as it is itself: that is, according to its proper ratio, or as it is such; which plainly it does not have unless it is convertible with it. Therefore no proposition with a superior predicate, such as these, Man is an animal, Man is a body, will be universal; but it is certain that these are in the first mode per se, and that a demonstration propter quid can be composed of them; therefore the mode “universally” is defective, not comprehending all the propositions from which the most perfect demonstration can proceed.

> 12 Circa ordinem horum trium terminorum, D. Thom. ca. pręsenti, & cum eo Sotus, & iam ferè omnes moderni, asserunt, *ita se habere, tanquam prædicata superiora, & inferiora*: ita vt *Vniuersaliter*, sit inferior cæteris, & post ipsum sequatur *Per se*: tandem *De omni*. Itaque se habẽt hoc modo, sicut Homo, Animal, & Viuens. Nam quidquid dicitur vniuersaliter, est per se, & de omni: & quidquid est per se, est etiam de omni: non tamen quidquid est de omni, est per se, nec omne per se est vniuersaliter. Quod colligitur ex Arist. definiente *Vniuersaliter, quòd sit de omni, & per se, & quòd conueniat prædicatum subiecto secundùm quod ipsum*, vel vt tale est: quibus apertè satis significat: Per se, aliquid addere supra Vniuersaliter: sicut Vniuersaliter, aliquid addit suprà per se, & de omni: quod non potest esse verum, nisi tanquam quid superius, & inferius se habeant, modo explicato. Et hæc est vera sententia, & tenenda.

12 Concerning the order of these three terms, St. Thomas on the present chapter, and with him Soto, and now almost all the moderns, assert that they stand to one another as superior and inferior predicates, so that universally is inferior to the others, and after it follows per se, and finally of every. Thus they stand in the same way as Man, Animal, and Living. For whatever is said universally is per se and of every; and whatever is per se is also of every; but not everything that is of every is per se, nor is everything per se universally. This is gathered from Aristotle, who defines universally as that which is of every, and per se, and in which the predicate belongs to the subject according as it is itself, or as it is such: by which he signifies quite openly that per se adds something over of every, just as universally adds something over per se and of every: which cannot be true unless they stand to one another as something superior and inferior, in the manner explained. And this is the true view, and to be held.

> Licèt contrarium teneat Toletus, quantum ad modum Per se, & De omni: affirmans plures propositiones esse per se, quæ non sunt de omni: vt hominem esse grammaticum est, in secundo modo, per se, & non est, de omni: cùm non conueniat [p. 652] omni homini actu habere grammaticam. Nam de aptitudine, euidens est conuenire omnibus, & curuitas etiam conuenit naso, Per se, non tamen omni. Falsum est enim, quòd propositiones istæ sint per se. Nam neque grammatica, proximè ac per se definitur per hominem, sicut nec reliquæ scientiæ, aut artes: neque curuitas definitur per nasum adæquatè & per se: cùm constet aliis etiam subiectis conuenire eam posse, præter nasum, & hominem: vnde ad quintum prędicabile pertinent similes propositiones, tanquam purè accidentales.

Although Toledo holds the contrary as regards the mode per se and of every, affirming that many propositions are per se which are not of every: as that man is grammatical is per se in the second mode, and is not of every, since it does not belong [p. 652] to every man to have grammar in act. For as regards aptitude, it is evident that it belongs to all; and curvature too belongs to the nose per se, yet not to every one. But it is false that these propositions are per se. For neither is grammar defined proximately and per se through man, just as neither are the other sciences or arts; nor is curvature defined adequately and per se through the nose, since it is certain that it can belong to other subjects as well, besides the nose and man. Whence such propositions pertain to the fifth predicable, as purely accidental.

> 13 Circa terminum, *De omni*, notandum est, cum D. Tho. lect. 9. horum Commentar. Themistio ca. 9. suæ Paraphrasis, & Soto, c. præsenti. Quòd *dici de omni*, duplex est, *Prioristicum & Posterioristicum*. *Prioristicum* vocatur in eo sensu, quo adducitur ab Arist. in lib. priorum, & à Summulistis in 4. lib. Summularum, & significatio eius est: quòd nihil sit sumere sub Subiecto, de quo non dicatur Prædicatum, non quidem secundùm veritatem propositionis, sed secundùm modum enunciandi. Nam ad formam syllogisticam impertinens est, quòd propositiones sint veræ, vel falsæ, & solùm per se requiritur forma aut modus enunciandi vniuersalis: ex quo habetur, vt si prædicatum dicitur de subiecto distributo, necesse sit dici de quolibet assumpto sub eo: cùm pro omnibus distribuatur. *Dici verò de omni, Posterioristicum* vocatur, in eo sensu, quo adducitur ab Arist. in hoc opere, nempe in ordine ad demonstrationem: quæ cùm ex veris propositionibus constare debeat, necesse est, vt Prædicatum de omni, dicatur de quolibet contento sub Subiecto: non solùm secundùm modum enunciandi, sed etiam secundùm veritatem propositionis. Et in eodem sensu accipiendum est, *Dici de nullo*: de quo non fecit mentionem Aristo. in hoc cap. quia facilè intelligi potest, idem esse in propositionibus negatiuis, prædicatum negari de omni subiecto, ac in affirmatiuis dici. Vnde negatiuæ omnes propositiones, in quibus prædicatum negatur de omni subiecto, & quolibet contento sub eo, & pro quolibet tempore, etiam sunt de omni modo negatiuo.

13 Concerning the term of every, it should be noted, with St. Thomas, lect. 9 of these Commentaries, Themistius, ch. 9 of his Paraphrase, and Soto on the present chapter, that being said of every is twofold: Prioristic and Posterioristic. It is called Prioristic in the sense in which it is adduced by Aristotle in the books of the Prior Analytics, and by the Summulists in book 4 of the Summulae; and its signification is that nothing can be taken under the Subject of which the Predicate is not said: not indeed according to the truth of the proposition, but according to the mode of enunciating. For it is irrelevant to the syllogistic form whether the propositions are true or false, and only the universal form or mode of enunciating is required per se: from which it results that, if the predicate is said of a distributed subject, it must be said of anything whatever taken under it, since it is distributed for all. But being said of every is called Posterioristic in the sense in which it is adduced by Aristotle in this work, namely in relation to demonstration: which, since it must consist of true propositions, requires that the Predicate, of every, be said of anything whatever contained under the Subject, not only according to the mode of enunciating but also according to the truth of the proposition. And in the same sense being said of none is to be taken, of which Aristotle made no mention in this chapter, because it can easily be understood that in negative propositions the predicate’s being denied of every subject is the same as its being said of it in affirmative ones. Whence all negative propositions in which the predicate is denied of every subject, and of anything whatever contained under it, and for any time whatever, are also of every in the negative mode.

> 14 *Circa terminum Per se*: notanda est ratio, propter quam, in quatuor modos diuiditur ab Arist. ita vt nec sint plures, nec pauciores: & est hæc: Res de qua aliquid demonstramus, quatuor tantùm potest habere considerationes. Primam, *vt est in se, & per se*. Secundam, *In ordine ad prædicata essentialia*. Tertiam, *In ordine ad proprias passiones*. Quartam, *In ordine ad propriam operationem, cuius est causa per se*. Et prima consideratio, constituit tertium modum, qui non est prædicandi, sed essendi, [p. 653] Secunda consideratio, constituit primum: & Tertia constituit secundum: qui sunt modi prædicandi: Quarta verò, constituit quartum: qui nec est modus essendi, nec prædicandi, sed per se causandi. De termino verò *Vniuersaliter*, dicemus quæstione sequenti.

14 Concerning the term per se: the reason should be noted why it is divided by Aristotle into four modes, so that there are neither more nor fewer; and it is this: The thing of which we demonstrate something can have only four considerations. The first, as it is in itself and per se. The second, in relation to essential predicates. The third, in relation to proper attributes. The fourth, in relation to its proper operation, of which it is the per se cause. And the first consideration constitutes the third mode, which is not of predicating but of being; [p. 653] the second consideration constitutes the first, and the third constitutes the second, which are modes of predicating; but the fourth constitutes the fourth, which is neither a mode of being nor of predicating, but per se of causing. Of the term universally we shall speak in the following question.

> His suppositis: Sententia Arist. est, quam sequuntur omnes expositores: *Quòd omnis demonstratio Propter quid, debet constare propositionibus, de omni, & per se: sed non omnis debet constare propositionibus, quæ sint vniuersaliter: sed solùm perfectissima inter has*: illa, inquam, quæ procedit ex causa adæquata conuertibili cum effectu, & vtrumque probari potest efficaciter. Primum quidem hoc arg. *Omnis demonstratio debet procedere ex necessariis*, vt asseruit, & probauit Arist. in principio huius c. sed omnis propositio necessaria, debet esse aliquo modo de omni, atque etiam per se: ergo omnis demonstratio debet constare propositionibus de omni, & per se. Quòd verò non omnis demonstratio Propter quid, procedere debeat ex propositionibus, in quibus prædicatum dicatur vniuersaliter de subiecto, in sequentibus erit manifestum.

These things being supposed: Aristotle’s view, which all the expositors follow, is that every demonstration propter quid must consist of propositions of every and per se; but not every one must consist of propositions that are universally, but only the most perfect among them: that one, I mean, which proceeds from an adequate cause convertible with the effect. And both can be proved efficaciously. The first indeed by this argument: Every demonstration must proceed from necessary things, as Aristotle asserted and proved at the beginning of this chapter; but every necessary proposition must in some way be of every, and also per se; therefore every demonstration must consist of propositions of every and per se. But that not every demonstration propter quid must proceed from propositions in which the predicate is said universally of the subject will be manifest in what follows.

> 15 Circa solutionem primi arg. *Distinguenda sunt diuersa singularia*: nam quædam sunt, in quibus indiuidualis differentia non distinguitur à specifica, vt plures tenent de angelis: vel certè à prædicatis essentialibus, vt in Deo: in quo sicut esse, & essentia, non distinguuntur, eadem ratione, nec distinguuntur prædicata essentialia ab indiuidualibus. Alia sunt singularia, in quibus certum est distingui indiuidualem differentiam aliquo modo, à specifica, cùm indiuidua multiplicentur sub eadem specie Sic autem & in angelis etiam apud alios distinguitur: & in his indiuiduis in quibus non distinguitur, dantur propositiones singulares, quæ sint per se, & ex quibus demonstratio componi potest: & istæ æquiualent vniuersalibus, quia essentiales sunt, & si plura darentur indiuidua illius essentiæ, essent de prædicato communi. Vnde virtute saltem sunt de omni: & hoc sufficit, vt verum sit, omnem propositionem demonstratiuam esse de omni. In indiuiduis verò, in quibus differentia indiuidualis distinguitur à specifica, nulla potest dari propositio, ex qua possit fieri demonstratio propter quid: quia de his indiuiduis, sub ratione talium indiuiduorum acceptis, vt de Petro, vt Petrus est, non potest dari demonstratio, nec scientia propter quid: vt expresè docet Arist. 7. lib. Meta. cap. 24. & pluribus aliis locis. Et D. Tho. qu. 9. de potentia, art. 2. ad 1. & 1. p. q. 29. ar. 1. ad 5. negat singularia posse definiri, & proinde esse obiectum scientiæ: quia definitio est medium demonstrationis [p. 654], & scientiæ. Vnde sequitur, nec in his dari propositionem, quæ propriè sit, per se, neque de omni: sed dum aliquid demonstratur de eis, demonstratione propter quid, solùm demonstrantur passiones communes speciei, per essentiam quoque communem: & hoc est de illis demonstrari: in quantum participant naturam speciei, non ratione differentię indiuidualis: & est quasi applicatio scientiæ de specie, ac illa.

15 Concerning the solution of the first argument: different singulars are to be distinguished. For there are some in which the individual difference is not distinguished from the specific, as many hold of angels; or rather, not from the essential predicates, as in God: in whom, just as being and essence are not distinguished, so by the same reason the essential predicates are not distinguished from the individual ones. There are other singulars in which it is certain that the individual difference is distinguished in some way from the specific, since the individuals are multiplied under the same species. Thus, however, it is distinguished also in angels according to others. And in those individuals in which it is not distinguished there are singular propositions which are per se, and from which a demonstration can be composed; and these are equivalent to universals, because they are essential, and if several individuals of that essence were given, they would be of a common predicate. Whence they are at least virtually of every; and this suffices for it to be true that every demonstrative proposition is of every. But in individuals in which the individual difference is distinguished from the specific, no proposition can be given from which a demonstration propter quid could be made: because of these individuals, taken under the ratio of such individuals, as of Peter as he is Peter, no demonstration can be given, nor any science propter quid, as Aristotle expressly teaches in Metaph. 7, ch. 24, and in many other places. And St. Thomas, q. 9 On Power, a. 2, ad 1, and 1 p., q. 29, a. 1, ad 5, denies that singulars can be defined, and consequently that they are the object of science, because the definition is the middle of demonstration [p. 654] and of science. Whence it follows that in these no proposition is given which is properly per se, nor of every; but when something is demonstrated of them by a demonstration propter quid, only the common attributes of the species are demonstrated, through the essence, likewise common; and this is to demonstrate them of those individuals inasmuch as they participate in the nature of the species, not by reason of the individual difference: and it is as it were an application of the science of the species, and the same science.

> 16 Et hoc modo demonstrantur in Theologia de Christo, passiones hominis: & etiam diuina attributa & proprietates, inquantum habet vtramque naturam, Diuinam & Humanam, quasi per applicationem scientiæ de Deo, & homine, illi personæ, illique indiuiduo esse habenti vtramque naturam. Et hoc esse verum, ostendunt demonstrationes ipsæ: quod certè, non est dari scientiam, vel demonstrationem, propter quid, de singulari naturæ corruptibilis, vt talis, sed vt habente naturam specificam, vel etiam simul diuinam de qua vera scientia esse potest vt explicatum est.

16 And in this way the attributes of man are demonstrated of Christ in Theology, and also the divine attributes and properties, inasmuch as he has both natures, the Divine and the Human: as it were by an application of the science of God and of man to that person, and to that individual having both natures. And the demonstrations themselves show that this is true: which is that, certainly, there is no science or demonstration propter quid of a singular of a corruptible nature as such, but as having the specific nature, or also at the same time the divine nature, of which there can be true science, as has been explained.

> De his tamen indiuiduis potest dari scientia à posteriori, quę vocatur scientia, *Quia*, atque etiam demonstratio, *Quia*: ex effectibus per experientiam cognitis procedens: & ideo tam scientia ipsa, quàm demonstratio *Experimentalis* vocatur. Qualis de Petro daretur, etiam si de homine nullam scientiam à priori haberemus: quia per experientiam cognoscimus, Petrum, & Ioannem esse capaces disciplinæ: & consequenter per eandem experientiam, quòd homo, sit capax disciplinæ, quòd admiratiuus, atque risibilis: talem ergo demonstrationem possumus constituere de Petro: Omne illud, quod assequitur notitiam alicuius rei, est capax disciplinæ: Petrus consequitur notitiam huius, aut illius rei: ergo est capax disciplinæ, & etiam Quidquid admiratur, est admiratiuum: Petrus admiratur: ergo est admiratiuus. Et pariter probare possumus, quòd sit risibilis, & rationalis. Sed demonstrationes istæ nimis sunt imperfectæ, vt ca. 10. ostendit Arist. Quare non est necessarium constare eas propositionibus per se, aut de omni, sed satis est, constare propositionibus vtcumque necessariis. Quia hos tres terminos, de omni, per se, & vniuersaliter, solùm adduxit Arist. pro demonstrationibus perfectis, quæ vocantur propter quid. Et ex his constat solutum esse primum arg.

Of these individuals, however, there can be science a posteriori, which is called science quia, and also demonstration quia, proceeding from effects known through experience; and therefore both the science itself and the demonstration are called experimental. Such would be had of Peter even if we had no science a priori of man: because we know through experience that Peter and John are capable of learning, and consequently, through the same experience, that man is capable of learning, capable of wonder, and risible. We can therefore construct such a demonstration of Peter: Everything that attains the knowledge of some thing is capable of learning; Peter attains the knowledge of this or that thing; therefore he is capable of learning. And also: Whatever wonders is capable of wonder; Peter wonders; therefore he is capable of wonder. And in like manner we can prove that he is risible and rational. But these demonstrations are very imperfect, as Aristotle shows in ch. 10. Wherefore it is not necessary that they consist of propositions per se or of every, but it is enough that they consist of propositions necessary in whatever way. For Aristotle adduced these three terms, of every, per se, and universally, only for perfect demonstrations, which are called propter quid. And from these things it is clear that the first argument has been solved.

> 17 *Circa propositiones indirectas*, de quibus procedit prima pars secundo argu. diuersæ sunt opiniones. Prima, Caiet. cap. præsenti, qui dicit, *esse per se in secundo modo*, cùm conueniat eis definitio: nam prædicatum est de definitione subiecti, vt in hac: Risibile est homo: aut rationale est homo. Alij [p. 655] verò, negant omnino, vllam propositionem indirectam esse per se, aut ex ea posse fieri demonstrationem, propter quid. Et hoc mihi videtur probabilius: Quia propositiones indirectæ, carent forma, & modo naturali propositionum: in quibus prædicatum habet modum formæ, subiectum verò modum materiæ. In indirectis verò, oppositum videmus, cùm illud habeat locum prædicati: quòd verè subiectum est: & ideo sunt quasi propositiones contra naturam: ergo non conuenit illis ratio, per se, vel de omni: qui modi cùm pro demonstrationibus, Propter quid, traditi sint ab Arist. non conueniunt, nisi propositionibus naturalibus, & habentibus veram formam propositionum: ex quibus demonstratio, propter quid fieri potest. Nihilominus quandam habent similitudinem cum propositionibus, per se, & de omni.

17 Concerning the indirect propositions, from which the first part of the second argument proceeds, there are different opinions. The first, of Cajetan on the present chapter, who says that they are per se in the second mode, since the definition belongs to them: for the predicate is of the definition of the subject, as in this one: The risible is man, or The rational is man. Others [p. 655] deny altogether that any indirect proposition is per se, or that a demonstration propter quid can be made from it. And this seems to me more probable: because indirect propositions lack the natural form and mode of propositions, in which the predicate has the mode of form, but the subject the mode of matter.
