Sed assensum vtriusque demonstrationis, esse inadæquatum, respectu eiusdem habitus: & solùm differre ab alio, quasi specie partiali, & inadæquata, ideo posse procedere ab eodem habitu scientiæ, secundùm speciem. Quia habitus solùm distinguuntur specie, per actus adæquatos, sicut etiam per adæquata obiecta: & non per inadæquatos.

The second thing which the same argument asked is whether through these demonstrations there are generated not only diverse assents, which are called diverse actual sciences, but also diverse habits, which are called absolutely diverse sciences. On which there is the first opinion of many of those who hold with us that the assents of each demonstration are diverse, asserting that they do not generate a habit of science diverse according to species, if such demonstrations are concerned with the same thing, as with man, or with natural being, which is the object of natural Philosophy; but that the assent of each demonstration is inadequate with respect to the same habit, and differs from the other only by a partial and as it were inadequate species, and therefore can proceed from the same habit of science according to species. Because habits are distinguished in species only by adequate acts, just as also by adequate objects, and not by inadequate ones.

> 17 Probatur testimonio Arist. qui cap. præsenti docet, *demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, differre, in eadem scientia atque in diuersis*. Quod non potest esse verum, nisi pertineant aliquando ad eandem scientiam: sed eadem scientia est, idem habitus: ergo nec verum esse potest, nisi pertineant ad eundem habitum. Quare non potest defendi in doctrina. Arist. quòd per demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, circa eandem rem, generentur diuersi habitus scientiæ: alioqui de eodem homine habebit quia plures scientias: & de eodem ente naturali, plures philosophias, si per demonstrationes, quia, & propter quid, naturam & proprietates eorum cognoscat: quod inauditum est in scholis.

17 It is proved by the testimony of Aristotle, who in the present chapter teaches that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in the same science and in diverse ones. Which cannot be true unless they sometimes pertain to the same science; but the same science is the same habit; therefore neither can it be true unless they pertain to the same habit. Wherefore it cannot be defended in the doctrine of Aristotle that through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing diverse habits of science are generated; otherwise one will have several sciences of the same man, and several philosophies of the same natural being, if he knows their nature and properties through demonstrations quia and propter quid: which is unheard of in the schools.

> Probant deinde ratione: quia sicut potentia habet maiorem extensionem, quàm habitus, & ideo potest eadem secundùm speciem, intra latitudinem sui obiecti, habere plures habitus, specie distinctos, qui sint quasi inadæquati respectu illius: eodem modo habitus, habet maiorem extensionem, quàm actus, cùm videamus eundem habitum scientiæ, plures atque diuersas habere demonstrationes: & ideo plures [p. 671] assensus diuersos, qui sunt plures actus: etiam si solùm procedat à causa, vel solùm ab effectu: ergo poterit habere plures actus, vel assensus, quorum quidam procedant à causa, per demonstrationem, propter quid, alii verò ab effectu, per demonstrationem, quia.

They prove it next by reason: because just as a power has a greater extension than a habit, and therefore one and the same according to species can, within the latitude of its object, have several habits distinct in species, which are as it were inadequate with respect to it, in the same way a habit has a greater extension than an act, since we see the same habit of science have many and diverse demonstrations; and therefore several [p. 671] diverse assents, which are several acts, even if they proceed only from the cause or only from the effect; therefore it will be able to have several acts or assents, of which some proceed from the cause through demonstration propter quid, and others from the effect through demonstration quia.

> 18 Et sicut demonstrationes, ita assensus erunt inadæquati, respectu eiusdem habitus. Non est ergo necessarium, plures multiplicare habitus, circa idem obiectum, propter demonstrationes, quia, & propter quid, & assensus earum specie distinctos: sed idem habitus poterit se extendere ad illos, tanquam ad diuersos, sed inadæquatos.

18 And just as the demonstrations, so the assents will be inadequate with respect to the same habit. It is not necessary, then, to multiply several habits concerning the same object on account of demonstrations quia and propter quid and their assents distinct in species; but the same habit will be able to extend itself to them as to diverse but inadequate ones.

> Nostra sententia est, *Per has demonstrationes, non solùm generari diuersos assensus secundùm speciem, sed etiam diuersos habitus scientiæ*. Quod est distinctione specifica assensuum vel actuum (quam amittit opposita scientia) sic probo: Habitus generantur ex actibus, & ab eisdem sumunt vnitatem, & distinctionem specificam: sed assensus conclusionum vtriusque demonstrationis, qui sunt proprij actus, ex quibus generantur habitus, distinguuntur specie: ergo generant habitus distiuctos. Et si dicas, Esse partiales actus, & inadæquatos. Ex hoc inprimis sequitur euidenter, generare habitus distinctos specie partiali: vnde iam teneris concedere, circa idem obiectum plures habitus, & plures scientias partiales: quod falsum probauimus in quæst. proœmialibus. Idem præterea probo, Quòd non solùm assensus distinguantur specie partiali, sed etiam totali.

Our view is that through these demonstrations not only diverse assents according to species are generated, but also diverse habits of science. This, given the specific distinction of the assents or acts (which the opposing view admits), I prove thus: Habits are generated from acts, and take their specific unity and distinction from them; but the assents to the conclusions of each demonstration, which are the proper acts from which the habits are generated, are distinguished in species; therefore they generate distinct habits. And if you say that they are partial and inadequate acts: from this, first of all, it evidently follows that they generate habits distinct by a partial species; whence you are now bound to grant several habits and several partial sciences concerning the same object, which we proved false in the proemial questions. I prove besides that the assents are distinguished not only by a partial species, but also by a total one.

> Quia ea quæ distinguuntur partialiter, debent esse partes alicuius totius: ergo si assensus distinguuntur partialiter, & inadæquatè, cùm distingui debeant per rationem formalem obiectiuam, dabitur aliqua ratio obiectiua totalis, atque communis, cuius sint partes: sed hæc est impossibilis: ergo impossibile est, quòd distinguantur specie partiali. Probatur minor: quia principia sunt ratio obiectiua assensuum, sicut sunt ratio assentiendi conclusionibus: sed principia quæ continent causam, & quæ continent effectum, sunt quasi opposita, & omnino diuersa nec dantur alia superiora, vel inferiora, quorum sint partes: ergo non possunt distingui specie partiali, sed totali debent distingui: & ex consequenti non possunt generare habitus specie partiali distinctos, sed totali.

Because things that are distinguished partially must be parts of some whole; therefore if the assents are distinguished partially and inadequately, since they must be distinguished by the objective formal ratio, there will be some total and common objective ratio of which they are parts; but this is impossible; therefore it is impossible that they be distinguished by a partial species. The minor is proved: because the principles are the objective ratio of the assents, as they are the ratio of assenting to the conclusions; but the principles that contain the cause and those that contain the effect are as it were opposed and altogether diverse, nor are there any other superior or inferior ones of which they are parts; therefore they cannot be distinguished by a partial species, but must be distinguished by a total one; and consequently they cannot generate habits distinct by a partial species, but by a total one.

> Sed vt testimonium Arist. explicemus & argu. soluere possimus, notandum est, *Vtrumque genus demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, versari aliquando circa eandem rem, aliquando circa [p. 672] diuersas*. Res autem circa quam versatur scientia, solùm est obiectum materiale: formale verò sunt principia, per quæ demonstrantur passiones de illo: vnde licèt versantur aliquando circa idem obiectum materiale, semper habent diuersa obiecta formalia. Neque hoc vllam continet repugnantiam, cùm circa idem obiectum materiale, versari etiam possint scientia, & opinio, per diuersa media, aut principia: quæ sunt rationes assentiendi, & quasi obiecta formalia. Non est ergo nouum, circa eandem rem ponere diuersos habitus scientiæ, cùm plus differant scientia, & opinio: & tamen sint aliquando etiam de eadem re. Isti autem diuersi habitus, geniti per demonstrationem, quia, & propter quid, circa eandem rem, sub nomine eiusdem scientiæ comprehenduntur propter identitatem obiecti materialis, & abstractionis à materia. Et hoc est, quod voluit Arist. significare, dum dixit, *Scire, quia, & propter quid*, & ex consequenti, demonstrationes differre in eadem scientia, & in diuersis: per eandem scientiam vtrumque habitum intelligens, qui intra latitudinem eiusdem obiecti materialis, & eodem modo abstrahentis à materia, continentur: per scientias verò diuersas, eas etiam intelligens, quæ versantur circa res diuersas, & diuerso modo, abstrahentes à materia, vt exempla eius ostendunt. Itaque non est sensus eius, quòd scire quia, & propter quid, differant intra eundem habitum, sed intra cognitionem scientificam eiusdem rei, circa quam versari solent, & quam nomine eiusdem scientiæ intelligit. Et eadem ratione, sub nomine eiusdem Philosophiæ, intelligitur vterque habitus: quia Philosophiam naturalem vocamus, in communi modo loquendi, cognitionem scientificam entis naturalis: siue per plures assensus, vel habitus distinguatur scire quia, & scire propter quid, siue non.

But in order that we may explain the testimony of Aristotle and be able to answer the argument, it should be noted that each kind of demonstration, quia and propter quid, is sometimes concerned with the same thing, sometimes with [p. 672] diverse ones. Now the thing with which a science is concerned is only the material object; the formal object is the principles through which the attributes are demonstrated of it. Whence, although they are sometimes concerned with the same material object, they always have diverse formal objects. Nor does this contain any repugnance, since science and opinion too can be concerned with the same material object through diverse media or principles, which are the rationes of assenting and as it were the formal objects. It is nothing new, then, to posit diverse habits of science concerning the same thing, since science and opinion differ more, and yet are sometimes also of the same thing. These diverse habits, then, generated through demonstration quia and propter quid concerning the same thing, are comprised under the name of the same science, on account of the identity of the material object and of the abstraction from matter. And this is what Aristotle meant to signify when he said that knowing quia and propter quid, and consequently the demonstrations, differ in the same science and in diverse ones: by the same science understanding both habits, which are contained within the latitude of the same material object, abstracting from matter in the same way; but by diverse sciences understanding those also which are concerned with diverse things, and abstract from matter in a diverse way, as his examples show. And so his sense is not that knowing quia and propter quid differ within the same habit, but within the scientific cognition of the same thing, with which they are wont to be concerned, and which he understands by the name of the same science. And by the same reasoning both habits are understood under the name of the same Philosophy: for in the common way of speaking we call natural Philosophy the scientific cognition of natural being, whether knowing quia and knowing propter quid are distinguished through several assents or habits or not.

> 20 Ad argu. verò, Concedimus primum, quod in antecedenti assumitur: nempe maiorem habere extensionem potentiam, quàm habitum: sed negamus secundum: quòd habitus maiorem habeat extensionem, quàm actus, vel assensus. Et huius ratio est, quia habitus proximè specificatur ab actu, secundùm rationem formalem, quia per illum attingit obiectum: & cùm hæc sit limitata, non habet maiorem extensionem habitus, quàm actus. Potentia verò vniuersalior est: & sub vniuersaliori ratione attingit obiectum: & ideo per actus & habitus diuersæ speciei id fit. Vnde sequitur non esse superfluum multiplicare habitus, vbi actus distinguuntur specie, sed omnino necessarium, vt iam probauimus.

20 To the argument, then: we grant the first thing that is assumed in the antecedent, namely that a power has a greater extension than a habit; but we deny the second, that a habit has a greater extension than an act or assent. And the reason for this is that the habit is proximately specified by the act according to the formal ratio, because through it it attains the object; and since this is limited, the habit does not have a greater extension than the act. But the power is more universal, and attains the object under a more universal ratio; and therefore it happens through acts and habits of diverse species. Whence it follows that it is not superfluous to multiply habits where the acts are distinguished in species, but altogether necessary, as we have already proved. Treatise

[p. 673]

### TRACT. De subalternatione scientiarum — T R E AT I S E O N T H E S U B A L -ternation of Sciences.

> TRACTATVS DE SVBALternatione scientiarum.

[…]

#### Quid nomine scientiæ subalternantis, & subalternatæ intelligatur — What is understood by the name of subalternating and subalternated science.

> *Quid nomine scientiæ subalternantis, & subalternatæ intelligatur.*

[…]

> 21 In secunda part. cap. docuit Arist *Scire quia, & propter quid*: & consequenter, *demonstrationes differre in diuersis scientiis, non subordinatis, sed totaliter diuersis, & quasi disparatis*. Atque etiam idem fieri in diuersis scientiis subordinatis tamen, quas vocat subalternatas, in eodem sensu, quo propositiones docuit, 2. lib. de interpretatione, quandam habere oppositionem: quasi Subalternam: quando fiunt ex eodem prædicato, & subiecto, sed vna collocatur sub altera, vna est vniuersalis, & particularis altera. Tales igitur asserit esse quasdam scientias, quarum vna versatur circa rem aliquam vniuersalem, alia verò circa rem particularem, sub ea contentam, vt Geometria, quæ versatur circa lineam, & perspectiua, circa lineam visualem, sic Arithmetica circa numerum, Musica verò circa numerũ sonorum. Et vniuersalem vocat *Subalternantem*: particularem verò *Subalternatam*: aut illam *continẽtem*, & hanc *contentam*. De natura igitur, & ratione harum scientiarum, nobis est, de qua agunt oẽs interpretes Arist. c. præsenti, agendum, differentiam demonstrationis, quia, & propter quid, in eis designatam intelligamus. Nam quæ sint scientiæ totaliter diuersæ, & quomodo in eis differant, satis notum est.

n the second part of the chapter Aristotle taught that knowing 21 I        quia and propter quid, and consequently demonstrations, differ in diverse sciences that are not subordinated, but totally diverse, and as it were disparate; and also that the same happens in diverse sciences that are, however, subordinated, which he calls subalternated, in the same sense in which, in bk. 1 of On Interpretation, he taught that propositions have a certain opposition, as it were Subaltern, when they are made of the same predicate and subject, but one is placed under the other, one being universal and the other particular. He asserts, then, that there are certain sciences of which one is concerned with some universal thing, and another with a particular thing contained under it: as Geometry, which is concerned with the line, and Perspective, with the visual line; so Arithmetic with number, but Music with sonorous number. And the universal he calls Subalternating, but the particular Subalternated; or the former containing and the latter contained. Of the nature and ratio of these sciences, then, we must treat (which all the interpreters of Aristotle treat in the present chapter), in order that we may understand the difference of demonstration quia and propter quid designated in them. For what sciences are totally diverse, and how they differ in them, is well enough known.

> Expositis nominibus *Subalternantis & subalternatæ scientiæ*, quatuor de illis explicanda sunt. Primum, *Quidnam sit, vnam scientiam esse subalternatam alteri?* Secundum, *An talis subalternatio sit possibilis?* Tertium, *Quonam modo dependeat scientia subalternata à subalternante, & an sine illa esse possit, & veram habere rationem scientiæ?* Quartum, *An subalternata intra proprios limites, demonstret, propter quid, suarum conclusionum.*

Having expounded the names of subalternating and subalternated science, four things must be explained about them. First, what it is for one science to be subalternated to another. Second, whether such subalternation is possible. Third, in what way the subalternated science depends on the subalternating, and whether it can exist without it and have the true ratio of science. Fourth, whether the subalternated science, within its own limits, demonstrates the propter quid of its conclusions.

#### Quidnam sit subalternatio scientiarum — What the subalternation of sciences is.

> *Quidnam sit subalternatio scientiarum.*

[…]

> 22 Circa conditiones requisitas, & sufficientes ab subalternationem scientiarum, diuerso modo loquuntur authores: nam quidam plures: alij verò pauciores assignant: quidam easdem, alij diuersas. Inter omnes verò, optimè eas videtur enumerasse Caie. in tract. de subalternatione scientiarum, vbi ad 4. aut 5. præcipuas reduxit omnes. Prima est, *Quòd subiectum vnius, contineatur sub subiecto alterius*: cuius defectu Medicina [p. 674] nõ subalternatur geometriæ: nam corpus sanabile, non continetur sub linea, sed disparata sunt. Secunda, *Quòd subiectũ inferioris, includat subiectum superioris*: & addat supra illud aliquam differentiam accidentalem. Cuius defectu scientia de specie, non subalternatur scientię de genere. Nam licèt species sub genere, non addit tamen supra genus conditionem accidentalem: sed essentialem differentialem: vnde ferè semper eadem est scientia de vtroque. Tertia conditio est, *Quòd differentia, quam addit, nõ sit propria passio eiusdem subiecti*: Quia licèt passio sit differẽtia quodammodo accidentalis: non est tamen purè accidentalis: & ideo non pertinet ad distinctam scientiam, ac subiectum: sed ad eandem, in qua demonstratur de illo. Quarta conditio est, *Quòd principia scientiæ inferioris, probentur à priori, & per causam à scientia superiori*. Principia autem, quæ assumit scientia subalternata ad probandum suas conclusiones, sunt in duplici differentia: quædam enim sumit ex subiecto scientiæ subalternantis: alia verò ex materia alterius scientiæ, ad quam per se pertinet conditio accidentalis, quam addit obiectum eius supra obiectum scientiæ subalternantis.

22 Concerning the conditions required and sufficient for the subalternation of sciences, authors speak in diverse ways: for some assign more, others fewer; some the same, others diverse ones. But among all, Cajetan seems to have enumerated them best, in his treatise On the Subalternation of Sciences, where he reduced them all to four or five chief ones. The first is that the subject of one be contained under the subject of the other; for lack of which Medicine Vu [p. 674] is not subalternated to geometry: for curable body is not contained under line, but they are disparate. The second, that the subject of the inferior include the subject of the superior, and add over and above it some accidental difference; for lack of which the science of the species is not subalternated to the science of the genus. For although the species is under the genus, it does not add over and above the genus an accidental condition, but an essential differential one; whence the science of both is nearly always the same. The third condition is that the difference which it adds be not a proper attribute of the same subject: because, although an attribute is in a certain way an accidental difference, it is not purely accidental; and therefore it does not pertain to a distinct and subalternated science, but to the same one in which it is demonstrated of that subject. The fourth condition is that the principles of the inferior science be proved a priori and through the cause by the superior science. Now the principles which the subalternated science assumes for proving its conclusions are of two kinds: for some it takes from the subject of the subalternating science, and others from the matter of another science, to which the accidental condition belongs per se which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating science.

> 23 Et illa omnia, & sola, debet probare à priori scientia subalternans, non alia. Quia cùm ad materiam alterius scientiæ pertineant, non possunt ab illa probari. Exempli gratia: Perspectiua, assumit vnum principium, quasi geometricum ex materia lineæ, quæ obiectum geometriæ est, & aliud philosophicum, ex materia visualis: nam visuale ad philosophiam naturalem pertinet. Geometria igitur, cui subalternatur: solùm probare debet illa, quæ ex eius materia, aut obiecto deriuantur: non, quæ pertinent ad philosophiam naturalem. Ex his conditionibus vna, vel altera reperietur aliquo modo in diuersis scientiis, non subalternatis, sed omnes simul in solis subalternatis reperiri possunt, & ideo omnes simul sunt requisitæ, & sufficienter, ad veram, & propriam subalternationem. Ita, vt solùm illæ scientiæ, & omnes in quibus reperiuntur, veræ, & propriæ sint subalternatæ. Et sic est explicatum, quid sit subalternatio scientiarum.

23 And all of the former, and they alone, the subalternating science must prove a priori, and not the others: because, since they pertain to the matter of another science, they cannot be proved by it. For example, Perspective assumes one principle that is as it were geometrical, from the matter of the line, which is the object of geometry, and another that is philosophical, from the matter of the visual: for the visual pertains to natural philosophy. Geometry, then, to which it is subalternated, must prove only those that are derived from its own matter or object, not those that pertain to natural philosophy. Of these conditions one or another will be found in some way in diverse sciences that are not subalternated, but all together can be found only in subalternated sciences; and therefore all together are required, and sufficient, for true and proper subalternation, so that only those sciences, and all those in which they are found, are truly and properly subalternated. And thus it has been explained what the subalternation of sciences is.

#### An subalternatio scientiarum explicata sit possibilis, vel sola imaginatione excogitata — Whether the subalternation of sciences explained above is possible, or devised by the imagination alone.

> 24 Tria arg. proponemus, quę videtur probare subalternationem scientiarum nõ esse possibilẽ, & est primũ tale: *Quia si obiectũ scientiæ subalternatæ, addit conditionẽ accidentalẽ, supra obiectũ sciẽtiæ subalternãtis, sequitur subalternatã non esse vnã scientiã per se.* Probatur consequentia: quia scientia sumit suam [p. 675] vnitatem per se ab obiecto: sed obiectum eius non est vnũ per se, sed per accidens, cũ constet ex duplici ente in actu, vt ostendit linea visualis, aut numerus sonorus: ergo nec ipsa erit vna scientia per se, sed per accidens. Secundum: *Scientia subalternans, & subalternata, debent esse distinctæ specie*: sed nõ possunt distingui specie, si vera est eadem conditio: ergo nec erit possibilis subalternatio. Probatur minor: quia scientiæ distinguuntur specie per obiecta: sed obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, solùm distinguitur accidentaliter, ab obiecto scientiæ subalternantis: cùm solùm addit supra ipsum differentiam accidentalem, vt linea visualis, solũ distinguitur accidentaliter à linea, ergo scientia ipsa subalternata, solummodo distinguetur accidentaliter à scientia subalternante. Quod etiam videtur probari, ex vltima conditione subalternationis, quòd subalternans debeat probare à priori principia scientiæ subalternatæ: nam si hoc verum est: principia subalternatæ erunt conclusiones subalternantis: sed conclusiones pertinent ad eandem scientiam, in qua probantur à priori: ergo eandem scientiã efficiet subalternata cum subalternante. Tertium: *Si subalternata addit in suo subiecto conditionem accidentalem supra obiectum subalternantis, sequitur obiectum eius habere duplicem partem*: vna erit obiectum subalternantis, alia verò accidentalis conditio, addita supra illud, & pertinens quidem ad aliam scientiam, quo supposito, non erit maior ratio, quare dicatur magis subalternata vni, quàm alteri: & ideo nec vni, nec alteri subalternata erit, sed subalternatio ipsa impossibilis reputabitur. Gratia exempli: Obiectum perspectiuæ, quod est linea visualis, includit, duplicem partem: nempe lineam, pertinentem ad Geometriam, & conditionem accidentalem visualis, pertinentem ad Philosophiam naturalem: ideo non erit maior ratio, ob quam vni earum quàm alteri subalternetur, & ita non erit alicui earum subalternata.

24 We shall propose three arguments which seem to prove that the subalternation of sciences is not possible; and the first is this: Because if the object of the subalternated science adds an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating science, it follows that the subalternated science is not one science per se. The consequence is proved: because a science takes its [p. 675] unity per se from its object; but its object is not one per se but per accidens, since it consists of a twofold being in act, as visual line or sonorous number shows; therefore neither will it be one science per se, but per accidens. Second: The subalternating and the subalternated science must be distinct in species; but they cannot be distinguished in species if the same condition is true; therefore neither will subalternation be possible. The minor is proved: because sciences are distinguished in species by their objects; but the object of the subalternated science is distinguished only accidentally from the object of the subalternating science, since it adds over and above it only an accidental difference, as visual line is distinguished only accidentally from line; therefore the subalternated science itself will be distinguished only accidentally from the subalternating science. This also seems to be proved from the last condition of subalternation, that the subalternating science must prove a priori the principles of the subalternated science: for if this is true, the principles of the subalternated science will be conclusions of the subalternating; but conclusions pertain to the same science in which they are proved a priori; therefore the subalternated science will make one and the same science with the subalternating. Third: If the subalternated science adds in its subject an accidental condition over and above the object of the subalternating, it follows that its object has a twofold part: one will be the object of the subalternating science, but the other the accidental condition added over and above it, and pertaining indeed to another science; which supposed, there will be no greater reason why it should be called subalternated to one rather than to the other; and therefore it will be subalternated neither to one nor to the other, but subalternation itself will be reckoned impossible. For example: the object of perspective, which is the visual line, includes a twofold part, namely line, pertaining to Geometry, and the accidental condition of visual, pertaining to natural Philosophy; therefore there will be no greater reason for which it should be subalternated to one of them rather than to the other, and so it will not be subalternated to either of them.

> 25 His tamen non obstantibus, omnes tenent cum Arist. *possibilem esse subalternationem scientiarũ, & quasdam esse scientias subalternatas aliis.* in quibus quatuor illæ conditiones concurrunt, vt perspectiua subalternatur geometriæ, & musica arithmeticæ.

25 Notwithstanding these things, however, all hold with Aristotle that the subalternation of sciences is possible, and that there are some sciences subalternated to others, in which those four conditions concur, as perspective is subalternated to geometry, and music to arithmetic.

> Sed circa solutionẽ primi arg. est prima opinio Sonc. 4. Met. q. 9. asserentis, *Scientiam subalternatam, esse vnam per se, atque distinctam à subalternante*: quia differentia, quam obiectũ eius addit, supra obiectum subalternantis, non est accidens commune, sed propria passio eiusdem obiecti subalternantis: vt visuale, inquit, non est accidens commune lineæ, sed propria passio eius: quia linea est quantitatis: & quantitas est per se sensibilis, vt docet Aristot. 2. lib. de anima: ergo linea est per se visibilis, [p. 676] ita vt visibilitas sit propria eius passio, ex subiecto autem, & propria passione, fit vnum per se, & non per accidens: sicut fit ex subiecto, & accidenti communi, vt ex corpore, & albedine.

But concerning the solution of the first argument there is the first opinion, of Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9, who asserts that the subalternated science is one per se and distinct from the subalternating: because the difference which its object adds over and above the object of the subalternating is not a common accident, but a proper attribute of that same object of the subalternating: as visual, he says, is not a common accident of line, but a proper attribute of it; because line belongs to quantity, and quantity is per se sensible, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul 2; therefore line is per se visible, V v ij [p. 676] so that visibility is its proper attribute; and from a subject and a proper attribute there comes about something one per se and not per accidens, as there does from a subject and a common accident, as from body and whiteness.

> 26 Hæc tamen sententia falsa est: & vt talis refutatur à Caie. c. præsenti. Probatur euidenter, quia duo quæ asserit, sunt apertè falsa. Primum: quòd *visuale sit propria passio lineæ*, vt est obiectum geometriæ. Nam geometria est scientia mathematica, abstrahens à materia sensibili: ergo agit de linea, vt abstrahit à materia sensibili: sed visuale est conditio per se sensibilis, cùm dicat respectum ad visum: ergo euidens est non conuenire lineæ, vt est obiectum geometriæ: quare falsum erit, quòd conditio, quam addit perspectiua supra geometriam, sit propria passio obiecti geometriæ Imò etiamsi concederemus, esse propriam passionem eius, falsum est. Secundum, quod asserit, *efficere vnum per se cum linea*: quia propria passio verum accidens est, & extra essentiam subiecti: ergo si accidens commune non potest facere vnum per se cum subiecto, nec poterit accidens proprium efficere vnum per se cum eo. Quia non minùs risibile, constabit duplici ente in actu, nempe subiecto, & accidente, quàm album. Et tandem: Si conditio addita obiecto scientiæ subalternatæ, sit propria passio obiecti subalternantis, ad eandem scientiam pertinebit cum eo. Probatur consequentia: quia propria passio obiecti alicuius scientiæ, probatur de illo in eadem scientia cuius est obiectum.

26 This view, however, is false, and is refuted as such by Cajetan in the present chapter. It is proved evidently, because the two things it asserts are openly false. The first: that visual is a proper attribute of line as it is the object of geometry. For geometry is a mathematical science, abstracting from sensible matter; therefore it deals with line as it abstracts from sensible matter; but visual is a per se sensible condition, since it implies a relation to sight; therefore it is evident that it does not belong to line as it is the object of geometry. Wherefore it will be false that the condition which perspective adds over and above geometry is a proper attribute of the object of geometry. Indeed, even if we granted that it is its proper attribute, the second thing it asserts is false, that it makes something one per se with line: because a proper attribute is a true accident, and outside the essence of the subject; therefore if a common accident cannot make something one per se with its subject, neither will a proper accident be able to make something one per se with it. For risible no less than white is composed of a twofold being in act, namely of subject and accident. And finally: if the condition added to the object of the subalternated science is a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, it will pertain to the same science with it. The consequence is proved: because the proper attribute of the object of any science is proved of it in the science whose object it is.

> 27 Nostra igitur sententia in primis asserit: *Conditionem, quam addit obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, non esse propriam passionem obiecti subalternantis, sed accidens commune.* Obiectum tamen includens talem conditionem, vt lineam visualem, dupliciter sumi posse. *Vnum modum, prout includit vtrumque, per modum aggregationis.* Et hoc modo euidens est, quòd sit vnum per accidens: & non possit esse obiectum scientiæ. Quia vt sit sumptum, non habet vnam naturam, vel essentiam, sed duplicem essentiam: nec vnam definitionem, nec determinatas passiones, quæ de eo probari possint. *Alio modo sumitur prout includit vnum cum ordine ad aliud*: vel vt determinatum per illud, aliud verò vt determinans. Et ita est vnum per se, non entitate, sed ordine, quæ vnitas sufficit vt definiri possit, & per se considerari ab vna scientia, & vt determinatæ passiones de eo probari possint in ea Et hoc modo consideratur obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ ab eadem: quare vt vnum per se, ex quo habebit illa, quòd sit vna scientia per se. Et ideo ex hac parte, non erit impossibilis subalternatio scientiarum.

27 Our view, therefore, asserts first of all that the condition which the object of the subalternated science adds is not a proper attribute of the object of the subalternating, but a common accident. The object, however, that includes such a condition, as visual line, can be taken in two ways. One way, as it includes both by way of aggregation. And in this way it is evident that it is one per accidens and cannot be the object of a science: because, as so taken, it does not have one nature or essence, but a twofold essence; nor one definition, nor determinate attributes that could be proved of it. In another way it is taken as it includes one with order to the other, or the one as determined by the other, and the other as determining. And so it is one per se, not in entity but in order; which unity suffices for it to be able to be defined and considered per se by one science, and for determinate attributes to be able to be proved of it in that science. And in this way the object of the subalternated science is considered by it: wherefore as one per se, from which that science will have it that it is one science per se. And therefore on this side the subalternation of sciences will not be impossible.

> Secundum argumentum soluitur alia distinctione: Nam [p. 677] conditio, quam addit obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, duobus modis sumi potest: vel, *vt est accidens obiecti* subalternantis, ei inhærens, vel, *vt per se consideratur*, à tali scientia, & primo modo, solùm accidentaliter illud determinat, vel contrahit, sicut quodlibet aliud accidens subiectum, cui inhæret. Secundo verò modo, contrahit illud per se, ad considerationem talis scientiæ: quia linea per se consideratur à perspectiua, vt visualis est. Itaque, licèt visuale sit accidens lineæ, vt sumitur secundùm propriam entitatem, vel essentiam: tamen vt ad obiectum perspectiuæ pertinet, per se coniungitur cum visuali: quia per se consideratur à scientia, in ordine ad visuale: vel vt per talem conditionem determinatur. Vnde quamuis linea, quæ est obiectum geometriæ secundùm entitatem, solùm distinguatur à linea visuali quæ est obiectum perspectiuæ, etiam secundum, entitatem sumptæ, accidentaliter: nihilominus si vtraque sumatur, vt per se consideratur à sua scientia, per se, & essentialiter distinguuntur: vel vt vno verbo dicatur, solùm distinguuntur accidentaliter in esse rei: in esse verò obiecti essentialiter, & per: & ideo possunt distinguere scientias specie.

The second argument is answered by another distinction: for [p. 677] the condition which the object of the subalternated science adds can be taken in two ways: either as it is an accident of the object of the subalternating science, inhering in it, or as it is considered per se by such a science. And in the first way it determines or contracts that object only accidentally, as any other accident [determines] the subject in which it inheres. But in the second way it contracts it per se to the consideration of such a science: because line is considered per se by perspective as it is visual. And so, although visual is an accident of line as line is taken according to its own entity or essence, nevertheless, as it pertains to the object of perspective, it is joined per se with visual: because it is considered per se by the science in order to the visual, or as determined by such a condition. Whence, although line, which is the object of geometry according to entity, is distinguished only accidentally from visual line, which is the object of perspective, also taken according to entity, nevertheless, if each is taken as it is considered per se by its own science, they are distinguished per se and essentially; or, to put it in one word, they are distinguished only accidentally in the being of a thing, but in the being of an object essentially and per se; and therefore they can distinguish sciences in species.

> 29 Ad formam ergo secundi arg. distinguenda est minor secundi syllogismi, quòd obiectum scientiæ subalternatæ, solùm distinguatur accidentaliter ab obiecto subalternantis: nam in esse rei accidentaliter solùm distinguitur, sed in esse obiecti scibilis, per talem scientiam, essentialiter. Et ideo scientia subalternata non accidentaliter: sed essentialiter distinguitur à subalternante.

29 To the form of the second argument, then, the minor of the second syllogism must be distinguished, namely that the object of the subalternated science is distinguished only accidentally from the object of the subalternating: for in the being of a thing it is distinguished only accidentally, but in the being of an object knowable through such a science, essentially. And therefore the subalternated science is distinguished from the subalternating not accidentally but essentially.

> Pro solutione tertij notandum est: Quòd ex duobus, quæ includit obiectum subalternatæ scientiæ, nempe, obiectum subalternantis, & accidentalem conditionem superadditam, primum ac præcipuum est obiectum: conditio verò quasi limitatio eius est, per quam determinatur: & imperfectior quidem, quia materialis, atque sensibilis: obiectum verò subalternantis, vt magis à materia abstractum, perfectius est. Et ex hoc sequitur ratione eius: eandem scientiam esse subordinatam superiori, & vocari subalternatam, & non ratione conditionis: quod ex alia conditione colligitur euidenter: quia principia subalternatæ scientiæ, superior probat à priori potius, quàm illa scientia, ad quem conditio pertinet. Et ideo potiùs illi subalternatur, quàm huic. Gratia exempli: Obiectum perspectiuæ includit lineam & conditionem visualis: ex quibus linea est primum, & principale, ratione cuius subordinatur geometriæ: est etiam magis abstracta à materia, & quia demonstrare, propter quid, conclusionum, potiùs pertinet ad illam scientiam, [p. 678] quæ magis abstrahit à materia sensibili: cùm scientiæ respicientes materiam sensibilem, ab effectu potiùs demonstrare soleant: hinc est, quòd perspectiua potiùs subalternatur geometriæ, quàm philosophiæ naturali.

For the solution of the third it should be noted that of the two things which the object of the subalternated science includes, namely the object of the subalternating and the accidental condition superadded, the first and chief is the object, while the condition is as it were its limitation, by which it is determined; and it is more imperfect, because material and sensible, whereas the object of the subalternating, as more abstracted from matter, is more perfect. And from this it follows that it is by reason of the former that the same science is subordinated to the superior and called subalternated, and not by reason of the condition: which is evidently gathered from another condition, because the superior science proves the principles of the subalternated science a priori rather than does that science to which the condition pertains. And therefore it is subalternated to the former rather than to the latter. For example: the object of perspective includes line and the condition of visual; of which line is the first and principal, by reason of which it is subordinated to geometry; it is also more abstracted from matter, and because demonstrating the propter quid of the conclusions pertains rather to that science, V v iij [p. 678] which abstracts more from sensible matter: since the sciences that regard sensible matter are wont rather to demonstrate from the effect, hence it is that perspective is subalternated to geometry rather than to natural philosophy.

> 30 Hoc est enim principium perspectiuæ, *Visio facta secundùm lineam rectam, est perfectissima*: quod licèt præsupponat aliud, per se notum in philosophia, nempe agens naturale fortiùs agit in proximum, quàm in remotum: tamen à priori demonstratur à geometria: quia linea recta est perfectissima, & breuissima.

30 For this is a principle of perspective: Vision effected along a straight line is most perfect; which, although it presupposes something known per se in philosophy, namely that a natural agent acts more strongly on what is near than on what is remote, is nevertheless demonstrated a priori by geometry, because the straight line is the most perfect and the shortest.

> Ad formam igitur arg. neganda est consequentia, quòd non sit maior ratio, propter quam scientia inferior magis dicatur subalternata vni, quam alteri scientiæ: quia cùm obiectum superioris scientiæ sit primum, quod includit, & ratione cuius subordinatur scientiæ superiori, agenti de illo, ad quam etiam pertinet probare à priori principia eiusdem scientiæ inferioris: potiùs quàm ad aliam scientiam, ad quam conditio pertinet: ideo potiùs illi, quàm huic subalternatur.

To the form of the argument, then, the consequence must be denied, namely that there is no greater reason why the inferior science should be said to be subalternated to one science rather than to the other: because, since the object of the superior science is the first thing it includes, and that by reason of which it is subordinated to the superior science which deals with that object, to which it also pertains to prove a priori the principles of that same inferior science, rather than to the other science to which the condition pertains, therefore it is subalternated to the former rather than to the latter.

#### An subalternata scientia, existens sine subalternante, sit vera scientia: vel potiùs opinio — Whether a subalternated science, existing without the subalternating, is true science, or rather opinion.

> PRæsupponit titulus quæstionis tanquam certum, quòd *scientia subalternata, possit esse separata à scientia subalternante*, & omnino sine ea esse: quod constat experientia, cùm plures cognoscamus musicos, ignorantes Arithmeticam. Quærit autem hoc supposito, *An musica in his sit vera scientia, vel solùm opinio*.

The title of the question presupposes as certain that the subalternated science can be separated from the subalternating science, and exist altogether without it: which is established by experience, since we know many musicians ignorant of Arithmetic. But, this supposed, it asks whether music in them is true science, or only opinion.

> 31 Et prima sententia tenet. *Non esse scientiam, sed opinionem*: ita Soncinas 4. Meta. quæst. 9. quem sequuntur plures moderni: quorum hæc est ratio: Quia vt docuit Arist. 2. cap. huius libri, aliquis habeat scientiam alicuius conclusionis, necesse est, quòd principia sint ei certa, ita, vt ex terminis ea cognoscat vel si demonstrabilia sint, sciat ea reducere ad prima indemonstrabilia: & qui hoc non scit, (inquit Aristot.) non habet demonstrationem, nec scientiam conclusionis: atqui principia scientiæ subalternatæ non sunt immediata, sed demonstrabilia, per scientiam subalternantem, quam cùm non habeat musicus, nescit ea reducere ad immediata, sed solùm ea credit propter testimonium Arithmeticorum: ergo non habet scientiam conclusionum eius, sed opinionem.

31 And the first view holds that it is not science but opinion: so Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9, whom many moderns follow; whose reason is this: because, as Aristotle taught in ch. 2 of this book, for someone to have science of some conclusion it is necessary that the principles be certain to him, so that he knows them from the terms, or, if they are demonstrable, that he know how to reduce them to the first indemonstrable ones; and he who does not know this (says Aristotle) does not have demonstration, nor science of the conclusion; but the principles of the subalternated science are not immediate, but demonstrable through the subalternating science, which, since the musician does not have it, he does not know how to reduce them to the immediate ones, but only believes them on account of the testimony of the Arithmeticians; therefore he does not have science of its conclusions, but opinion.

> Secunda opinio est aliorum, *Quòd vera sit scientia, quamuis imperfecta*. Et ratio horum est opposita: quia si non esset scientia [p. 679] sed opinio, maximè hoc esset propterea, quia is qui eam habet sine subalternante, non habet certitudinem principiorum, sed fides humana potest esse certa, propter frequentia testimonia: vt patet in hac propositione, Roma est: cui, licèt multi assentiantur, solùm propter testimonium eorum, qui eam viderunt, tot tamen testimonia multiplicantur: vt certum efficiant assensum eorum: cuius signum est: quia nemo est qui dubitet de veritate eius.

The second opinion is that of others, that it is true science, although imperfect. And their reason is the opposite: because if it were not science [p. 679] but opinion, this would be chiefly because he who has it without the subalternating science does not have certitude of the principles; but human faith can be certain on account of the frequency of testimonies, as is plain in this proposition, Rome exists: to which, although many assent only on account of the testimony of those who have seen it, yet the testimonies are so multiplied as to make their assent certain; a sign of which is that there is no one who doubts its truth.

> 32 Pro explicatione nostræ sententię, notandum est *Duobus modis posse cõtingere, quòd scientia subalternata sit sine subalternãte.* Primò, Ita, vt principia eius solùm sint accepta, per testimoniũ habentium scientiam subalternantem. Secundò: Ita vt etiam ab eo, qui habet eam sine subalternante nota, per experientiam euidentem multorum singularium: ex quibus colligitur euidenter, experimentum vniuersale principiorum.

32 For the explanation of our view it should be noted that it can happen in two ways that the subalternated science exists without the subalternating. First, so that its principles are only accepted through the testimony of those who have the subalternating science. Second, so that they are known also by him who has it without the subalternating, through evident experience of many singulars, from which the universal experiential knowledge of the principles is evidently gathered.

> Hoc supposito: Tria asserit nostra sententia. Primum est: *Siue subalternata scientia, sine subalternante existens, sit vera scientia siue non, certum est, non esse actu, & formaliter scientiam subalternatam: prout sic habetur, sed solùm materialiter.* Quod sic probo: Scientia dicitur subalternata, quia subordinatur subalternanti, à qua principia eius accipiunt certitudinem, & euidentiam requisitam ad veram scientiam: sed scientia inferior existens, sine superiori, vt sic existens, non subordinatur actu superiori scientiæ, nec ab ea participat euidentiam suorum principiorum: ergo non est actu, & formaliter scientia subalternata: sed solùm materialiter, & quasi in potentia: in quantum cum ea coniungi potest, in eo, qui vtramque habeat.

This supposed, our view asserts three things. The first is: Whether the subalternated science existing without the subalternating is true science or not, it is certain that it is not actually and formally a subalternated science as it is so had, but only materially. This I prove thus: A science is called subalternated because it is subordinated to the subalternating science, from which its principles receive the certitude and evidence required for true science; but an inferior science existing without the superior, as so existing, is not actually subordinated to the superior science, nor does it participate from it the evidence of its principles; therefore it is not actually and formally a subalternated science, but only materially and as it were in potency, inasmuch as it can be joined with it in one who has both.

> 33 Secundum, quod asserit, *Quòd scientia subalternata, sine subalternante, erit vera scientia (licèt imperfecta,) si ei, qui eam habuerit, nota sint principia per experientiam.* Probatur hoc: Quia tunc erunt certa, atque euidentia principia: ex quibus per demõstrationem à posteriori, colligitur euidenter conclusio: quæ ex sequenti erit certa, & euidens, & per consequens, verè sciẽtifica.

33 The second thing it asserts is that a subalternated science without the subalternating will be true science (although imperfect) if the principles are known through experience to him who has it. This is proved: because then the principles will be certain and evident, from which through demonstration a posteriori the conclusion is evidently gathered; which consequently will be certain and evident, and consequently truly scientific.

> Tertiò dicimus: *Quòd si principia eius solùm cognoscantur per testimonium eorum, qui habent subalternantem scientiam, non erit vera scientia, sed opinio.* Et hoc probat efficaciter argum. primæ opinionis, quam in hoc sensu veram esse existimamus. Argu. verò secundæ opinionis nihil probat: Quia testimonium humanum, per se loquendo, nõ potest generare assensum certum cùm non repugnet ei subesse falsum. Quòd verò per frequentiam testimoniorum, sublatum sit actuale dubium, per accidẽs est: quia hoc non obstante, assensus illius propositionis, Roma est, ab intrinseco est incertus: & cui potest subesse falsum. [p. 680] Et eo igitur non potest per se colligi certa conclusio, nisi ratione quadam materiali, & accidẽtali. Per se autem, est incerta: quod repugnat scientiæ. Quemadmodum dicimus, Conclusionem nõ esse per se, & formaliter certam nec scientificam, quæ colligitur per aliquam consequentiam, solùm necessariam in his, aut illis terminis: quod est, esse necessariam solùm materialiter, formaliter verò, & per se incertam: cùm in simili forma, possit dari antecedens verum, & consequens falsum.

Third, we say that if its principles are known only through the testimony of those who have the subalternating science, it will not be true science, but opinion. And this the argument of the first opinion proves effectively, which we judge to be true in this sense. But the argument of the second opinion proves nothing: because human testimony, speaking per se, cannot generate certain assent, since it is not repugnant that falsity underlie it. And that through the frequency of testimonies actual doubt is removed is per accidens: because, notwithstanding this, the assent to that proposition, Rome exists, is intrinsically uncertain, and falsity can underlie it. V u iiij [p. 680] From it, therefore, a certain conclusion cannot be gathered per se, except by a certain material and accidental reason. Per se, however, it is uncertain: which is repugnant to science. Just as we say that a conclusion is not per se and formally certain, nor scientific, which is gathered through some consequence that is necessary only in these or those terms; that is, necessary only materially, but formally and per se uncertain, since in a similar form there can be given a true antecedent and a false consequent.

#### An subalternata scientia, inter proprios limites, demonstret propter quid, vel solùm quia — Whether a subalternated science, within its own limits, demonstrates propter quid, or only quia.

> IAm hoc intelligitur de scientia subalternata, non sine subalternãte: sed illi actu coniuncta in eo, qui habet vtramque: & tunc habet statum scientiæ subalternatæ, de qua quærimus, *An intra proprios limites*, hoc est, in quantum solùm se extendit, vsque ad principia à se indemonstrabilia: sed quæ possunt demonstrari à priori, & verè demonstrantur, à subalternante: cui quasi continuantur: an, inquam, intra hos limites, *veras habeat demonstrationes, propter quid*, per quas demonstret à priori suas conclusiones, ex propriis principiis: vel solùm dicatur demonstrare ea, quasi per demonstrationes, quia. Exempli gratia: Hęc est conclusio perspectiuæ scientiæ, *Res ad maiorem distantiã visa minor apparet, quam ipsamet existat in se.* Perspectiua eam demõstrat per hanc, Res à longè visa, minori, aut acutiori angulo mouet potentiam: & ideo apparet minor. Sed illius secundæ propositionis, per quã probat primam, nescit reddere causam: eam verò reddit geometria: quia angulus eo est acutior, quo magis protrahitur: esse verò acutiorem est esse minorem.

This is now understood of the subalternated science not without the subalternating, but actually joined to it in one who has both; and then it has the status of a subalternated science, about which we ask whether within its own limits, that is, inasmuch as it extends only as far as the principles that are indemonstrable by itself, but can be demonstrated a priori, and are in fact demonstrated, by the subalternating science, to which it is as it were continued: whether, I say, within these limits it has true demonstrations propter quid, through which it demonstrates its conclusions a priori from its own principles; or whether it is said to demonstrate them only as it were through demonstrations quia. For example: this is a conclusion of the science of perspective: A thing seen at a greater distance appears smaller than it exists in itself. Perspective demonstrates it through this: A thing seen from afar moves the power at a smaller or more acute angle, and therefore appears smaller. But it does not know how to give the cause of that second proposition, through which it proves the first; geometry, however, gives it: because the angle is the more acute the more it is drawn out; and to be more acute is to be smaller.

> 35 Et ideo res visa ad maiorem distãtiam, minori angulo mouet potentiam. Quærimus ergo, *An demonstratio illa*, per quam perspectiua probat, quòd res à longè visa minor apparet: quia minori angulo mouet potentiam, (hoc est enim intra proprios limites demonstrare suas conclusiones sit demonstratio propter quid, & à priori: vel solùm demonstratio, quia.

35 And therefore a thing seen at a greater distance moves the power at a smaller angle. We ask, then, whether that demonstration through which perspective proves that a thing seen from afar appears smaller because it moves the power at a smaller angle (for this is to demonstrate its conclusions within its own limits) is demonstration propter quid and a priori, or only demonstration quia.

> Prima opinio est Soti, & Veneti cap. præsenti, asserentium, *verè demonstrare, propter quid, intra latitudinem propriam*: quam tamen sine limitatione, videtur tenuisse Albertus Mag. tract. 2. de vsu principiorum, c. 7. vbi negare omnino videtur quòd propria principia subalternatæ scientię, demonstrentur à scientia subalternante. Quia cùm subalternans abstrahat à materia sensibili, & principia subalternatæ respiciant materiam sensibilem, non potest se extendere, aut descendere ad illa demon- [p. 681] stranda. Quod verum est non solùm intra proprios limites demonstrabit, propter quid, suarum conclusionum, scientia subalternata, sed omnino. Nam si principia eius non demonstrantur à subalternante, neque ab alia, erunt prorsus indemonstrabilia: ex quibus perinde demonstrabit subalternata proprias conclusiones, atque quælibet alia scientia etiam subalternans.

The first opinion is that of Soto and Paul of Venice in the present chapter, who assert that it truly demonstrates propter quid within its own latitude; which, however, Albert the Great seems to have held without limitation, tract. 2 On the Use of Principles, ch. 7, where he seems altogether to deny that the proper principles of the subalternated science are demonstrated by the subalternating science: because, since the subalternating science abstracts from sensible matter, and the principles of the subalternated regard sensible matter, it cannot extend itself or descend to demonstrating them [p. 681] Which is true: the subalternate science will demonstrate its conclusions propter quid not only within its own limits, but absolutely. For if its principles are not demonstrated by the subalternating science, nor by another, they will be altogether indemonstrable; and from them the subalternate science will demonstrate its own conclusions just as any other science does, even a subalternating one.

> Probatur hæc sententia. Primò: Quia scientia subalternata, licèt non reddat causam primam suę conclusionis: nec demonstret illam: vsque ad principium primum, reddit tamen causam proximam eius: ergo eam demonstrat à priori, per causam proximam: vt patet in exemplo designato.

This opinion is proved. First, because the subalternate science, although it does not render the first cause of its conclusion, nor demonstrate it up to the first principle, nevertheless renders its proximate cause: therefore it demonstrates it a priori through the proximate cause, as is plain in the example indicated.

> 36 Et certè si sola scientia subalternans demonstraret à priori, conclusiones scientiæ subalternatæ, solus Arithm. diceretur Musicus: & solus Geometra, perspectiuus, Quod patet esse falsum. Probatur consequentia: quia sciens, & scientia, denominationem accipiunt à conclusionibus, quas demonstrant: cùm in eis consistat, vera, & propria ratio scientiæ: ergo sicut dicitur philosophus, qui scit demonstrare conclusiones philosophiæ: ita dicitur perspectiuus, qui scit demonstrare conclusiones perspectiuæ: præsertim si à nullo alio demonstrentur, sed ab eo solo.

36 And certainly, if the subalternating science alone demonstrated a priori the conclusions of the subalternate science, the Arithmetician alone would be called a Musician, and the Geometer alone a Perspectivist; which is plainly false. The consequence is proved: because the knower and the science receive their denomination from the conclusions which they demonstrate, since the true and proper ratio of science consists in them: therefore, just as he is called a philosopher who knows how to demonstrate the conclusions of philosophy, so he is called a perspectivist who knows how to demonstrate the conclusions of perspective; especially if they are demonstrated by no other science, but by it alone.

> Secundò: Quia si scientia subalternata non demonstrat à priori suas conclusiones, maximè id facit, quia non reddit causam earum, vsque ad primam, sed solùm reddit proximam, relinquens primam reddendam à subalternante: sed hoc est impossibile: ergo non est negandum, quòd demonstret à priori suas conclusiones. Probatur minor: quia si hoc ita esset, sequeretur subalternantem demonstrare à priori principia subalternatæ: & ideo principia subalternatę esse conclusiones subalternantis. Quod repugnat fieri propter duo. Primum, *Quia subalternans abstrahit à materia sensibili*: principia verò subalternatæ, respiciunt materiam sensibilem: ergo repugnat: quòd hæc illis coniungantur, in eadem demonstratione coniungi autem necessarium est, si sunt conclusiones per illa demonstratæ.

Second, because if the subalternate science does not demonstrate its conclusions a priori, it is chiefly because it does not render their cause up to the first, but renders only the proximate cause, leaving the first to be rendered by the subalternating science; but this is impossible: therefore it must not be denied that it demonstrates its conclusions a priori. The minor is proved: because if this were so, it would follow that the subalternating science demonstrates a priori the principles of the subalternate, and therefore that the principles of the subalternate are conclusions of the subalternating science. Which cannot be the case, for two reasons. First, because the subalternating science abstracts from sensible matter, whereas the principles of the subalternate regard sensible matter: therefore it is repugnant that the latter be joined with the former in the same demonstration; yet it is necessary that they be joined, if they are conclusions demonstrated through them.

> Secundum: Quia principia inferioris essent conclusiones superioris, non essent distinctæ scientiæ, superior & inferior, sed eandem efficerent. Probatur consequentia: Nam conclusiones ad eam sententiam pertinent, in qua demonstrantur: sed principia inferioris, sunt conclusiones demonstratæ à superiori: ergo ad hanc pertinebunt, & non efficient scientiam subalternatam distinctam.

Second, because if the principles of the inferior were conclusions of the superior, the superior and the inferior would not be distinct sciences, but would make up one and the same. The consequence is proved: for conclusions pertain to that science in which they are demonstrated; but the principles of the inferior are conclusions demonstrated by the superior: therefore they will pertain to it, and will not make up a distinct subalternate science.

> Secunda opinio: *Negat subalternatam, aut simpliciter demonstrare proprias conclusiones priori, aut etiam intra proprios limites*: [p. 682] sed solùm auxilio superioris, & vt continuatur cum illa, veras demonstrationes efficere posse. Hæc est communis, quam tenent D. Th. in Comment. huius cap Soncinas 4. Meta. qu. 9. Caiet. tract. de subalternatione scientiarum circa finem, Louanienses, & Tolet. in expositione huius cap. Et videtur nobis in doctrina Arist. necessaria, & in ratione vera.

The second opinion denies that the subalternate science demonstrates its own conclusions a priori, either absolutely or even within its own limits: [p. 682] but holds that it can produce true demonstrations only with the help of the superior science, and as it is continued with it. This is the common opinion, which is held by St. Thomas in his Commentary on this chapter; Soncinas, Metaph. 4, q. 9; Cajetan, in his treatise on the subalternation of sciences, toward the end; the Louvain commentators; and Toledo in his exposition of this chapter. And it seems to us necessary in the doctrine of Aristotle, and true in reason.

> Probatur primum: Quia Arist cap. pręsenti in principio, docet expressè, *differre demonstrationem quia, & propter quid, in diuersis scientiis subalternatis*: quia demõstratio, propter quid, pertinet ad scientiam subalternantem: demonstratio verò, quia, ad subalternatam. Quæ differentia, non potest esse vera, si scientia subalternata demõstrat proprias conclusiones demõstratione, propet quid, etiam intra proprios limites: vel etiam reddens causam proximam earum, licèt non primam. Nam si hoc verum est, ad eam pertinebit demonstratio propter quid, & non quia. Præterea loquens Arist. de vtraque scientia in particulari, & vocans subalternantem Mathematicam, & subalternatam sensibilem, quia illa abstrahit à materia sensibili, hæc verò respicit illam, expressè docet: subalternatam solùm demonstrare, quia: ad subalternantem verò pertinere demonstrationem, propter quid, his verbis: *Hic enim, ipsum quidem sensitiuorum est scire, ipsum vero, propter quid, Mathematicorum.*

The first is proved: because Aristotle, at the beginning of the present chapter, teaches expressly that demonstration quia and propter quid differ in diverse subalternate sciences: because demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, but demonstration quia to the subalternate. Which difference cannot be true if the subalternate science demonstrates its own conclusions by demonstration propter quid, even within its own limits, or even by rendering their proximate cause, though not the first. For if this is true, demonstration propter quid will pertain to it, and not demonstration quia. Moreover, Aristotle, speaking of each science in particular, and calling the subalternating science Mathematical and the subalternate sensible, because the former abstracts from sensible matter while the latter regards it, teaches expressly that the subalternate science only demonstrates quia, but that demonstration propter quid pertains to the subalternating science, in these words: For here to know the that belongs to those who deal with sensibles, but to know the propter quid belongs to the Mathematicians.

> Secundum verò, quòd vera sit nostra sententia, probatur hoc arg. Vt aliquis habeat scientiam alicuius conclusionis, & veram demonstrationem eius, necesse est, quòd præmissis assentiatur ex sola notitia terminorum: vel si demonstrabiles sint, eas sciat reducere vsque ad principia omnino indemonstrabilia: alioqui si sic eas reducere nesciat, non habebit veram demonstrationem conclusionis, nec veram scientiam eius. Sed principia propria scientiæ subalternatæ, per quæ demonstrat suas conclusiones, non sunt immediata, sed demonstrabilia: cùm possint demonstrari à scientia subalternante: ergo non fiet vera demonstratio alicuius conclusionis ex eis, nisi ab eo, qui sciat ea reducere vsque ad prima omnino indemonstrabilia, per veras demonstrationes. Atqui subalternata scientia, intra proprios limites, nescit ea sic reducere, vt patet, à solaque subalternante reduci possunt: ergo subalternata intra proprios limites, non potest veram demonstrationem, propter quid, suarum conclusionum efficere, nisi auxilio scientiæ subalternantis aut in quantum cum ea continuatur.

That the second part, namely that our view is true, is proved by this argument. For someone to have science of some conclusion, and a true demonstration of it, it is necessary that he assent to the premises from the sole cognition of the terms; or, if they are demonstrable, that he know how to reduce them up to altogether indemonstrable principles: otherwise, if he does not know how to reduce them in this way, he will not have a true demonstration of the conclusion, nor true science of it. But the proper principles of the subalternate science, through which it demonstrates its conclusions, are not immediate but demonstrable, since they can be demonstrated by the subalternating science: therefore there will be no true demonstration of any conclusion from them, except by one who knows how to reduce them up to the first, altogether indemonstrable, principles through true demonstrations. But the subalternate science within its own limits does not know how to reduce them in this way, as is plain, and they can be reduced by the subalternating science alone: therefore the subalternate science within its own limits cannot produce a true demonstration propter quid of its conclusions, except with the help of the subalternating science, or inasmuch as it is continued with it.

> 39 Sed vt explicemus, quonã modo fiat cõtinuatio hæc, quo etiam modo demonstrentur à subalternante: notandum est, Quòd *in quacunque demonstratione, necessarium est medium con- [p. 683] iungi cum extremitatibus in præmissis, vt ratione* talis coniunctionis extremitates ipsæ coniungantur in conclusione: & hoc est fundamentum totius artis demonstratiuæ. Vt ostenditur in hac demonstratione: Omne animal rationale est risibile: Omnis homo est animal rationale, ergo Omnis homo est risibilis. In qua animal rationale, quod est medium, coniungitur in præmissis cum homine, qui est maior extremitas, & cum risibilitate, quæ est minor: & virtute huius coniunctionis, coniunguntur homo, & risibile in conclusione.

39 But in order to explain in what way this continuation takes place, and in what way also they are demonstrated by the subalternating science, it should be noted that in any demonstration whatever it is necessary that the middle [p. 683] be joined with the extremities in the premises, so that by reason of such a conjunction the extremities themselves are joined in the conclusion: and this is the foundation of the whole demonstrative art. As is shown in this demonstration: Every rational animal is risible; Every man is a rational animal; therefore Every man is risible. In which rational animal, which is the middle, is joined in the premises with man, which is the major extremity, and with risibility, which is the minor; and by virtue of this conjunction man and risible are joined in the conclusion.

> Secundò notandũ, *Medium in demonstratione propter quid continere causam conclusionis.* Vnde sequitur non posse scientiam subalternantem demonstrare à priori principium scientiæ subalternatæ, per medium sibi proprium nudè acceptum: hoc est, in propria abstractione à materia sensibili consideratum, sed necesse est, vt tale medium coniungatur extremitatibus, ex quibus constat principium eiusdem subalternatæ scientiæ demonstrandum, tanquam conclusio, alioqui non erit medium.

It should be noted, second, that the middle in a demonstration propter quid contains the cause of the conclusion. Whence it follows that the subalternating science cannot demonstrate a priori a principle of the subalternate science through a middle proper to itself taken barely, that is, considered in its own abstraction from sensible matter; but it is necessary that such a middle be joined with the extremities of which the principle of that same subalternate science, to be demonstrated as a conclusion, is composed; otherwise it will not be a middle.

> 40 Sed extremitates eius respiciunt materiam sensibilem: ergo necesse est medium scientiæ subalternantis quasi descendere ad materiam sensibilem, ad eamque determinari, vt per talem coniunctionem cum extremitatibus in præmissis, efficiat, vt coniungantur extremitates ipsæ in conclusione: & ita conclusio ipsa, quæ principium est subalternatæ scientiæ, à priori demonstretur. Et talis coniunctio medii cum extremitatibus, ex quibus constat principium scientiæ subalternatæ demonstrandum, est continuatio inferioris scientiæ cum superiori: in qua cõtinuatione cõsistit formalis ratio subalternationis. Quæ omnia hoc exemplo fiunt manifesta. Principium sciẽtię subalternatæ, nempe perspectiuæ: quod ipsa nec scit, nec potest demonstrare intra proprios limites, est hoc: Res à longè videtur sub minori, vel acutiori angulo. Demõstratur autem sic, à sciẽtia subalternante, nempe à geometria: Res quæ videtur sub angulo magis protracto, videtur sub angulo minori, (nam angulus magis protractus acutior est, & ideo minor: ) sed res visa à longè videtur per angulum magis protractum, aut longiorem vt est manifestum, ergo videtur sub angulo minori. Ecce medium geometricũ, nempe angulum magis protractum, esse minorem, quod nõ posset demõstrare principium illud perspectiuæ nisi coniungeretur cum extremitatibus, ex quibus componitur, videlicet cum re à longè visa, & cum minori angulo: & nisi ita coniunctum efficeret cum eis vtraque pręmissam eiusdem demonstrationis per quam demonstraretur idem principium, tanquam conclusio composita ex eisdem extremitatibus,

40 But its extremities regard sensible matter: therefore it is necessary that the middle of the subalternating science descend, as it were, to sensible matter and be determined to it, so that through such a conjunction with the extremities in the premises it may bring it about that the extremities themselves are joined in the conclusion; and thus the conclusion itself, which is a principle of the subalternate science, is demonstrated a priori. And such a conjunction of the middle with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science to be demonstrated is composed is the continuation of the inferior science with the superior; and in this continuation consists the formal ratio of subalternation. All of which is made manifest by this example. A principle of the subalternate science (namely of perspective), which it neither knows nor can demonstrate within its own limits, is this: A thing far off is seen under a smaller, or more acute, angle. And it is demonstrated thus by the subalternating science, namely by geometry: A thing which is seen under a more protracted angle is seen under a smaller angle (for a more protracted angle is more acute, and therefore smaller); but a thing seen from far off is seen through a more protracted, or longer, angle, as is manifest; therefore it is seen under a smaller angle. Behold the geometrical middle, namely that a more protracted angle is smaller, which could not demonstrate that principle of perspective unless it were joined with the extremities of which it is composed, namely with the thing seen from far off and with the smaller angle; and unless, so joined with them, it produced each premise of the same demonstration through which that same principle would be demonstrated, as a conclusion composed of the same extremities,

[p. 684]

> Et ecce continuatam scientiam subalternatam, cum subalternante, in eadem demonstratione, per tales coniunctiones. Continuatiuum autem, est medium scientiæ subalternantis, vt coniunctum in præmissis cum extremitatibus, ex quibus componitur, principium scientiæ subalternatæ, per illud demonstratum.

And behold the subalternate science continued with the subalternating science in the same demonstration, through such conjunctions. And that which effects the continuation is the middle of the subalternating science, as joined in the premises with the extremities of which the principle of the subalternate science, demonstrated through it, is composed.

> Et continuatio hæc, non tollit distinctionem vtriusque scientiæ, vt statim probabitur.

And this continuation does not take away the distinction of the two sciences, as will be proved presently.

> 42 Ex his intelligitur, primò quomodo sit possibile, quòd scientia subalternans probet per demonstrationẽ à priori, principia scientiæ subalternatæ, etiam si abstrahat à materia sensibili, & principia probanda eam respiciant, id enim facit, per vnionem proprij medij, cum extremitatibus principij probandi, cum quibus coniungitur in pręmissis & per coniunctionem, quasi descendit, & contrahitur per eas, ad materiam sensibilem: & per talem contractionem continuatur cum ea.

42 From these things it is understood, first, how it is possible that the subalternating science should prove the principles of the subalternate science by demonstration a priori, even though it abstracts from sensible matter and the principles to be proved regard that matter: for it does this through the union of its own middle with the extremities of the principle to be proved, with which it is joined in the premises; and through that conjunction it descends, as it were, and is contracted through them to sensible matter; and through such contraction it is continued with it.

> 43 Iam ergo soluuntur facilè arg. oppositæ opinionis. *Nam ad primum*, Concedimus antecedens, quòd subalternata scientia reddat causam proximam suæ conclusionis: sed negamus consequentiam, quòd demonstret eas intra proprios limites. Nam ad veram demonstrationem, non sufficit reddere causam, sed requiritur reddere omnes causas, vsque ad primam: alioqui nõ habebit certum assensum præmissarum, cùm nesciat eas reducere vsque ad principia per se nota, & indemonstrabilia: & ideo nec habebit veram scientiam conclusionis, nec veram demonstrationem eius.

43 Now, therefore, the arguments of the opposite opinion are easily solved. To the first: we grant the antecedent, that the subalternate science renders the proximate cause of its conclusion; but we deny the consequence, that it demonstrates them within its own limits. For to a true demonstration it is not enough to render the cause; rather it is required to render all the causes up to the first: otherwise it will not have a certain assent to the premises, since it does not know how to reduce them up to principles known per se and indemonstrable; and therefore it will have neither true science of the conclusion nor a true demonstration of it.

> Ad aliud verò, quod additur in eodem arg nempe, solum Arithmeticum esse musicum, & solum geometram, perspectiuum: si hi soli demonstrare dicuntur à priori conclusiones musicæ, perspectiuæ, negandum est, quia principia alicuius scientiæ, per quæ demonstrantur conclusiones eius, non pertinent ad habitum talis scientiæ, sed ad alium distinctum, qui dicitur habitus principiorum: & ideo nec suscipiunt denominationem sciẽtiæ: nec ea habent denominationem à scientiis. Principia autem scientiæ subalternatæ, quæ demonstrantur à scientia subalternante, comparantur ad principia eius, per quæ demonstrantur, tanquam conclusiones eorum: & ideo non pertinent ad eam, sed ad alium habitum inferiorem, qui est scientia subalternata.

But to the other point which is added in the same argument, namely that the Arithmetician alone would be a musician, and the geometer alone a perspectivist, if these alone are said to demonstrate a priori the conclusions of music and of perspective, it must be denied: because the principles of any science, through which its conclusions are demonstrated, do not pertain to the habit of such a science, but to another distinct habit, which is called the habit of principles; and therefore they do not receive the denomination of the science, nor do they have a denomination from the sciences. But the principles of the subalternate science, which are demonstrated by the subalternating science, are related to its principles, through which they are demonstrated, as their conclusions; and therefore they do not pertain to it, but to another, inferior habit, which is the subalternate science.

> 44 Quare nec Geometra denominatur perspectiuus, nec Arithmeticus denominatur musicus, sicut nec conclusiones musicæ, dicuntur geometria, quamuis verum sit, non denominari musicum verè scientem, nisi simul sit Arithmeticus: nec scientem perspectiuum, nisi simul sit geometra,

44 Wherefore neither is the Geometer denominated a perspectivist, nor the Arithmetician denominated a musician; just as neither are the conclusions of music called geometry; although it is true that one is not denominated a musician truly knowing unless he is at the same time an Arithmetician, nor a perspectivist knowing unless he is at the same time a geometer,

[p. 685]
