> Ad secundum, Concedimus primam & secundam consequentiam: quòd principia subalternatæ, sunt conclusiones subalternantis, negamus tamen, quòd non possint eis coniungi in eadem demonstratione. Nam licèt principia subalternantis, abstrahant à materia sensibili, determinari tamen possunt, & quasi contrahi, per principia subalternatæ, ad conficiendam eandem demonstrationem: vt explicatum est. Per hanc autem vnionem principiorum vnius, cum principiis alterius, vt conclusionibus eorum, non tollitur distinctio vtriusque scientiæ: sicut per vnionem principiorum cuiuslibet scientiæ, cum conclusionibus eiusdem, in eisdem demonstrationibus, non tollitur distinctio habitus scientiæ, ab habitu principiorum. Præsertim cùm semper scientia subalternata, & subalternans, habeant diuersa obiecta, & diuerso modo à materia abstrahentia, ex quibus distinctio habituum apertè colligitur. Et si aliquis quęrat, Quid ergo, aut quomodo dicendum est, demonstrare scientiam subalternatam, intra proprios limites, aut quomodo loquendum. Respõdeo, Si intra proprios limites, accipiatur præcisè, nullam demonstrationem propter quid, habere posse, neque etiam, quia, neque aliquam posse demonstrare conclusionem. Vnde neque esse scientiam, hoc modo sumptam: quia sub hac præcisione accepta, nescit demonstrare propria principia, verè demonstrabilia: ergo non habebit certum assensum eorum: & ideò, non poterit certam cõclusionem, aut scientificam colligere. De demonstratione verò, quia certum est, eam non habere, sub ratione formali scientiæ subalternatæ, quia vt talis est, non procedit ab effectu, sed à causa: Solùm igitur demonstrat suas conclusiones: demonstratione propter quid, auxilio subalternantis, vt continuatur cum ea, quare solùm hoc modo est vera scientia subalternata.

To the second, we grant the first and the second consequence, namely that the principles of the subalternate science are conclusions of the subalternating science; we deny, however, that they cannot be joined to them in the same demonstration. For although the principles of the subalternating science abstract from sensible matter, they can nevertheless be determined, and as it were contracted, through the principles of the subalternate science, so as to construct the same demonstration, as has been explained. And through this union of the principles of the one with the principles of the other, as their conclusions, the distinction of the two sciences is not taken away; just as, through the union of the principles of any science with its conclusions in the same demonstrations, the distinction of the habit of science from the habit of principles is not taken away. Especially since the subalternate and the subalternating science always have diverse objects, abstracting from matter in a diverse manner, from which the distinction of the habits is plainly gathered. And if anyone should ask what, then, or in what manner it must be said that the subalternate science demonstrates within its own limits, or how one must speak of it, I reply: if within its own limits is taken precisely, it can have no demonstration propter quid, nor even quia, nor can it demonstrate any conclusion. Whence, taken in this way, it is not a science either: because, taken under this precision, it does not know how to demonstrate its own principles, which are truly demonstrable; therefore it will not have a certain assent to them; and therefore it will not be able to infer a certain or scientific conclusion. As for demonstration quia, it is certain that it does not have it under the formal ratio of subalternate science, because as such it does not proceed from the effect but from the cause. It demonstrates its conclusions, therefore, only by demonstration propter quid, with the help of the subalternating science, as it is continued with it; wherefore only in this manner is it a true subalternate science.

## CHAPTER XXVI

## TEXT OF ARISTOTLE

> *Scibile autem, & scientia differunt ab opinabili, & opinione, quoniam scientia quidem vniuersalis.*

But the knowable and science differ from the opinable and opinion, since science is universal.

> *Breuis expositio textus.*

B R I E F E X P O S I T I O N O F T H E T E X T.

> INtentum Arist. in hoc cap. est, *distinguere scientiam ab opinione*, postquam scientias distinxit inter sese, in his capitibus intermediis, à decimo vsque ad hoc vigesimum sextum. Diuiditur autem in duas partes. In prima, Asserit, & probat scientiam, & scibile, distingui ab opinio- [p. 686] ne & opinabili. In secunda, Duo proponit dubia in contrarium solui.

he intention of Aristotle in this chapter is to distinguish science from T         opinion, after he has distinguished the sciences from one another in these intermediate chapters, from the tenth up to this twenty-sixth. And it is divided into two parts. In the first, he asserts and proves that science and the knowable are distinguished from opinion [p. 686] and the opinable. In the second, he proposes two doubts to be solved in the contrary sense.

> Conclusio, Arist. est hæc: *Scientia, & scibile, ex vna parte, differunt ab opinione, & opinabili, ex altera.* Quam probat hac ratione: Scientia versatur circa vniuersale, & necessarium: ergo scibile est vniuersale, & necessarium: opinio verò circa contingens, & sæpe particulare, aut etiam singulare: ergo opinabile est contingens, & particulare: ergo diuersa est scientia ab opinione: & scibile ab opinabili. Antecedens probat, ex parte scientiæ, quia vt cap. 2. dictum est, *Scientia est de his, quæ non possunt aliter se habere*: ergo de necessariis, quia necessarium est, quod non potest aliter se habere. Præterea: *Scientia est de his, quæ sunt de omni, per se, & vniuersaliter, aut secundùm quod ipsum*: ergo est de vniuersalibus. Probat deinde idem antecedens, de opinione, & opinabili. Nam quædam ait vera sunt in existimatione, quæ in re possunt esse vera, aut falsa: de quibus non est scientia, neque intellectus, qui est notitia principiorum: ergo de his erit opinio, & cùm possint aliter se habere, quod est esse contingentia: erit de contingenti: & ideo opinabile erit contingens.

Aristotle’s conclusion is this: Science and the knowable, on the one side, differ from opinion and the opinable, on the other. Which he proves by this argument: Science is concerned with the universal and necessary: therefore the knowable is universal and necessary; but opinion is concerned with the contingent, and often with the particular, or even the singular: therefore the opinable is contingent and particular: therefore science is diverse from opinion, and the knowable from the opinable. He proves the antecedent, on the side of science, because, as was said in ch. 2, science is of things which cannot be otherwise: therefore it is of necessary things, because the necessary is that which cannot be otherwise. Moreover, science is of things which are said of all, per se, and universally, or according as it is itself: therefore it is of universals. Next he proves the same antecedent on the side of opinion and the opinable. For certain things, he says, are true in estimation which in reality can be true or false: of these there is no science, nor understanding, which is the cognition of principles: therefore of these there will be opinion; and since they can be otherwise, which is to be contingent, it will be of the contingent; and therefore the opinable will be contingent.

> 2 Probatur antecedens, Quòd de his, quæ possunt aliter se habere, non sit scientia, neque intellectus, quia scientia, est de his, quæ non possunt aliter se habere: intellectus verò, quasi scientia quædam immediata est: & sic definiri potest, *Intellectus est certa cognitio immediatæ propositionis* quod est, esse certam cognitionem, ex sola significatione terminorum habita, sed certa cognitio ex terminis habita, non potest esse de re contingenti, nisi tantùm de necessaria: ergo repugnat, quòd intellectus, & scientia sint de re contingenti. Consequentiam verò, quod de re contingenti sit opinio, probat, quia si certa cognitio dari non potest, de re contingenti, dabitur incerta, & fallibilis. Hoc est talis, quæ licèt vera esse existimetur, tamen non repugnet ei subesse falsum.

2 The antecedent is proved, namely that of things which can be otherwise there is neither science nor understanding: because science is of things which cannot be otherwise; and understanding is as it were a certain immediate science, and can be defined thus: Understanding is the certain cognition of an immediate proposition; that is, it is a certain cognition had from the sole signification of the terms. But a certain cognition had from the terms cannot be of a contingent thing, but only of necessary things: therefore it is repugnant that understanding and science be of a contingent thing. And the consequence, namely that opinion is of a contingent thing, he proves because, if a certain cognition cannot be had of a contingent thing, there will be an uncertain and fallible one. This is such that, although it is thought to be true, nevertheless it is not repugnant to it that falsity underlie it.

> Vnde infert, sic esse definiendam opinionem: *Opinio est acceptio, vel existimatio, seu assensus immediatæ propositionis, & non necessariæ.* Et per primam particulam, *Immediatæ propositionis*, distinguitur opinio à scientia, quæ est cognitio propositionis mediatæ: & conuenit cum intellectu. Per secundam verò, nempè, *Non necessariæ*, distinguitur ab vtroque, videlicet intellectu, & scientia: quia vtrumque est de necessariis, vt probatum est.

Whence he infers that opinion should be defined thus: Opinion is the acceptance, or estimation, or assent of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. And by the first particle, of an immediate proposition, opinion is distinguished from science, which is the cognition of a mediate proposition, and it agrees with understanding. But by the second, namely non-necessary, it is distinguished from both, that is, from understanding and from science, because both are of necessary things, as has been proved.

> 3 Sed hæc definitio opinionis, non traditur ab Arist. de omni opinione, sed solùm de immediata. Datur enim mediata [p. 687] opinio, quæ ex immediata colligitur, per euidentem, aut probabilem consequentiam: vel ex propositione euidenti, per consequentiam non necessariam, vt Arist. docet in hoc eodem cap. Sed solùm voluit immediatam definire, vt cùm notum sit dari opinionem mediatam, definitione ipsa ostenderet, dari etiam opiniones immediatas, quibus assentitur intellectus probabiliter, ex sola notitia terminorum: sicut dantur propositiones necessariæ, quibus ex sola notitia terminorum assentitur, assensu certo, ac necessario.

3 But this definition of opinion is not delivered by Aristotle of every opinion, but only of the immediate one. For there is also a mediate [p. 687] opinion, which is inferred from an immediate opinion through an evident or probable consequence, or from an evident proposition through a non-necessary consequence, as Aristotle teaches in this same chapter. But he wished to define only the immediate one, so that, since it is known that a mediate opinion is given, he might show by the definition itself that immediate opinions are also given, to which the intellect assents probably from the sole cognition of the terms; just as there are necessary propositions to which it assents from the sole cognition of the terms with a certain and necessary assent.

> Sed contra differentiam probatam, inter scibile, & scientiam, & opinabile, & opinionem, proponit duo dubia in secunda parte capitis. Primum est, ad probandum: *quod non differant scibile, & opinabile*: quia sæpe contingit, vt quod vnus scit, alter opinetur: ergo idem erit scibile, & opinabile. Respondet, quòd de eadem re simplici, aut incomplexa, possunt esse scientia, & opinio, vt de homine. Non tamen de eadem re complexa: vt de propositione. Nam de homine, potest esse scientia, & opinio, sed non de propositione: vt de hac, *Quod diameter sit commensurabilis, aut æqualis costæ*: opinio fortè esse poterit, non scientia.

But against the difference proved between the knowable and science, and the opinable and opinion, he proposes two doubts in the second part of the chapter. The first is for proving that the knowable and the opinable do not differ: because it often happens that what one man knows, another opines: therefore the same thing will be knowable and opinable. He replies that of the same simple or incomplex thing there can be science and opinion, as of man; not, however, of the same complex thing, as of a proposition. For of man there can be science and opinion, but not of a proposition: as of this one, That the diagonal is commensurable, or equal to the side, there could perhaps be opinion, not science.

> 4 Secundum dubium est: Quia sicut scientia procedit ex immediatis principiis, ad mediatam conclusionem, ita opinio potest procedere, ex propositione immediata probabili, ad mediatam, quam de ea colligit. Præterea: Sicut demonstratio, si procedat à causa, erit propter quid: & si ab effectu, erit quia: eadem ratione opinio, si procedat ab immediata, continente causam conclusionis, dicitur, propter quid: si verò ab ea, quæ continet effectum, dicitur, quia: ergo conueniunt in his duobus, scientia, & opinio: quare non distinguentur. Respondet, Verum esse antecedens, sed negandum esse consequentiam. quia diuersus est modus procedendi vtriusque. Nam scientia procedit per medium necessarium, hoc est, ex necessariis principiis, & per necessariam consequentiam: opinio verò, per medium contingens, hoc est, vel ex principiis non necessariis, vel per consequentiam non necessariam, sed probabilem: & hoc est, distingui essentialiter, per diuersa media assentiendi. Vnde sequitur, scientiæ non posse subesse falsum, opinionem verò falsam esse posse.

4 The second doubt is: because just as science proceeds from immediate principles to a mediate conclusion, so opinion can proceed from an immediate probable proposition to a mediate one, which it infers from it. Moreover, just as demonstration, if it proceeds from the cause, will be propter quid, and if from the effect, will be quia, by the same reasoning opinion, if it proceeds from an immediate proposition containing the cause of the conclusion, is called propter quid; but if from one which contains the effect, it is called quia: therefore science and opinion agree in these two things; wherefore they will not be distinguished. He replies that the antecedent is true, but that the consequence must be denied, because the mode of proceeding of each is diverse. For science proceeds through a necessary middle, that is, from necessary principles and through a necessary consequence; but opinion through a contingent middle, that is, either from non-necessary principles, or through a consequence that is not necessary but probable: and this is to be distinguished essentially, through diverse middles of assenting. Whence it follows that falsity cannot underlie science, but that opinion can be false.

> TRACTATVS I.

T R E AT I S E I .

> De habitu principiorum.

On the Habit of Principles.

> 5 DE tribus agit Arist. cap. præsenti, *De Intellectu*, qui est notitia principiorum. *De Scientia*, quæ est notitia [p. 688] conclusionum: quæ demonstrantur ex principiis. Et de *Opinione*: quam ab his differre docet. De quibus eodem ordine agendum nobis est, & de singulis singulos tractatus instituimus: in quibus ea, quæ necessaria sunt ad intelligendam eorum naturam, & rationem, breuissimè explicamus. Vt sic meliùs possimus intelligere, differentiam, quam inter ea posuit Aristot. Et primò de habitu principiorũ quatuor explicabuntur. Primum, *An sit*, hoc est, an pręter potentiam intellectiuam, & species intelligibiles, per quas principia, hoc est, propositiones immediatas apprehendimus, ponendus sit habitus, per quem facilè possit intellectus iudicare de veritate eorum, eisdemque assensum præstare. Secundum, *Quid sit habitus iste.* Tertium, *An sit naturalis*: Ita, vt illum receperit anima, simul cùm potentia intellectiua, dum creata fuit à Deo: vel an acquisitus per proprios actus. Quartum, *An sit vnus secundùm speciem, pro principiis omnium scientiarum, vel diuersus pro diuersis principiis.*

Of three things Aristotle treats in the present chapter: of Understanding, which is the cognition of principles; of Science, which is the cognition [p. 688] of conclusions, which are demonstrated from principles; and of Opinion, which he teaches differs from these. Of which we must treat in the same order, and we institute a separate treatise on each: in which we explain very briefly the things that are necessary for understanding their nature and ratio, so that in this way we may better understand the difference which Aristotle posited among them. And first, concerning the habit of principles four things will be explained. First, whether it exists: that is, whether, besides the intellective power and the intelligible species through which we apprehend principles, that is, immediate propositions, a habit must be posited through which the intellect may easily judge of their truth and give them its assent. Second, what this habit is. Third, whether it is natural, so that the soul received it together with the intellective power when it was created by God; or whether it is acquired through its own acts. Fourth, whether it is one in species for the principles of all the sciences, or diverse for diverse principles.

### An præter intellectum, & species intelligibiles detur habitus principiorum — Whether, besides the intellect and the intelligible species, there is a habit of principles.

> 6 PRimò præsupponendum est, tanquam certum in doctrina Arist. & in schola Peripatetica, *Quòd in intellectu, & voluntate, dantur habitus virtutum moralium, & intellectualium.*

6 First, it must be presupposed, as certain in the doctrine of Aristotle and in the Peripatetic school, that in the intellect and the will there are habits of the moral and of the intellectual virtues.

> Secundò præsupponendum est, *Hos habitus ponendos esse in intellectu, distinctos à speciebus intelligibilibus.* Quod eorum, & illarum officium efficaciter probat. Nam officium speciei intelligibilis, solũ est vnire obiectum intelligendũ, cum potentia intellectiua, ex qua vnione sequitur apprehensio eius, quæ est prima operatio (Intellectus) vel vnio ipsa est apprehensio. Vnde sequitur, species intelligibiles, solùm ad apprehendendum obiecta proximè deseruire. Sed cùm post apprehensionem, sequatur iudiciũ de veritate, aut falsitate propositionum: in qua principaliter consistit secunda operatio intellectus: & in quo potest esse aliqua indifferentia, aut etiam difficultas, ad iudicandum, additur alius habitus ab Arist. & omnibus (solis exceptis nominalibus) qui species ipsas intelligibiles, dicũt esse habitus: & ideo, nihil aliud præter illas ad iudicandum ponunt.

Second, it must be presupposed that these habits are to be posited in the intellect as distinct from the intelligible species. Which the office of the former and of the latter effectively proves. For the office of the intelligible species is only to unite the object to be understood with the intellective power, from which union follows the apprehension of it, which is the first operation of the intellect; or the union itself is the apprehension. Whence it follows that intelligible species serve proximately only for apprehending objects. But since after apprehension there follows the judgment of the truth or falsity of propositions, in which the second operation of the intellect principally consists, and in which there can be some indifference, or even difficulty, in judging, another habit is added by Aristotle and by all (the Nominalists alone excepted), who say that the intelligible species themselves are habits, and therefore posit nothing besides them for judging.

> His suppositis, Primum dubium est: *An præter species intelligibiles, per quas principia apprehendimus, necessarius sit habitus principiorum, ad iudicandum de veritate eorum*: quod est eis assentire. Et est prima opinio Duran. in 3. d. 33. q. 1 ad finem. & Soti 1. li. de Iustitia, & iure, q. 4. art. 2. qui licèt habitus scientiarum, in intellectu ponant, præter species intelligibiles, ad assensum [p. 689] cõclusionum: nihilominus ad assentiendum principiis, nullum habitum esse ponendum asserunt: sed sufficere aiunt lumen naturale, quod est potentia ipsa intellectiua.

These things supposed, the first doubt is: whether, besides the intelligible species through which we apprehend principles, a habit of principles is necessary for judging of their truth, which is to assent to them. And the first opinion is that of Durandus, in 3, d. 33, q. 1, toward the end, and of Soto, On Justice and Right bk. 1, q. 4, a. 2, who, although they posit habits of the sciences in the intellect, besides the intelligible species, for assent to [p. 689] conclusions, nevertheless assert that no habit is to be posited for assenting to principles; rather, they say, the natural light suffices, which is the intellective power itself.

> 7 Probant hoc arg. Ad operationes naturales, in quibus nulla est indifferentia, vel libertas, non ponuntur habitus, vt in potentia visiua: imò nec in volũtate, respectu vltimi finis, in quem naturaliter tendit, per amorem, sed intellectus, naturaliter assentitur principiis, cùm sint veritates immediatæ ac necessariæ: ita vt eis propositis, non possit non assentire: ita enim se habet ad illa: sicut voluntas ad vltimum finem, vel visus ad colores: ergo nullo indiget habitu, ad eis assentiendem.

7 They prove it by this argument. For natural operations, in which there is no indifference or liberty, habits are not posited: as in the visual power; nay, not even in the will with respect to the ultimate end, to which it tends naturally through love. But the intellect assents naturally to principles, since they are immediate and necessary truths, so that, once they are proposed, it cannot fail to assent to them; for it is related to them as the will is to the ultimate end, or sight to colors: therefore it needs no habit in order to assent to them.

> Opposita sententia tenet, *præter intellectum, & species intelligibiles, ponendum esse habitum, ad assentiendum primis principiis indemonstrabilibus.* Hæc est expressa apud Arist. 6. lib. Ethic. cap. vbi inter virtutes intellectuales, quæ sunt habitus superadditi potentiis, enumerat intellectum, qui est habitus principiorum. Et D. Tho. in Commentariis eiusdem loci, declarat non de intellectu pro potentia, sed pro habitu superaddito potentiæ, loqui Arist. his verbis: *Accipitur autem hic intellectus, non pro ipsa intellectiua potentia, seu pro habitu quodam quo homo ex virtute luminis intellectus agentis, naturaliter cognoscit principia indemonstrabilia.* Et 1. 2. q. 94. art. 1. inquit, *Principia indemonstrabilia in speculatiuis, non sunt ipse habitus principiorum, sed sunt principia, quorum est habitus*: quam sententiam sequuntur, Henricus quodlib. 5. 28. Caiet. 1. 2. q. 51. art. 1. & ibidem Conradus Ferr. 1. li. contra gentes, ca. 94. Medina 1. 2. q. 49. & moderni omnes. Et videtur nobis vera, & tenenda.

The opposite opinion holds that, besides the intellect and the species intelligible, a habit is to be posited for assenting to the first indemonstrable principles. This is express in Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch., where among the intellectual virtues, which are habits superadded to the powers, he enumerates understanding, which is the habit of principles. And St. Thomas, in his Commentary on the same passage, declaring that Aristotle speaks of understanding not as a power but as a habit superadded to the power, in these words: But understanding is taken here not for the intellective power itself, but for a certain habit by which man, by virtue of the light of the agent intellect, naturally knows indemonstrable principles. And in 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, he says: Indemonstrable principles in speculative matters are not the habit of principles itself, but are the principles of which there is the habit. This opinion is followed by Henry of Ghent, Quodlibet 5, 28; Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, and Conrad in the same place; Ferrara, Contra Gentiles bk. 1, ch. 94; Medina, 1-2, q. 49; and all the moderns. And it seems to us true and to be held.

> 8 Probatur primò: Necessitas ponendi habitum in potentia: circa aliquod obiectum, est indifferentia eius, ad bene, vel malè operandum, circa illud: vt cùm vtroque modo possit operari, determinetur ad bene operandum, per habitum: *Nam habitus*, vt vidimus apud Arist. in prædicamento qualitatis, *est dispositio subiecti*, per quam bene vel malè se habet in ordine ad propriam naturam, vel operationem: sed intellectus circa prima principia, potest bene vel malè operari, cùm possit errare circa illa: ergo indiget habitu ad bene operandum: & ideo necesse est eum ponere.

8 It is proved, first: the necessity of positing a habit in a power with respect to some object is its indifference to operating well or badly with respect to it, so that, since it can operate in either way, it may be determined to operating well through the habit. For a habit, as we saw in Aristotle in the category of quality, is a disposition of the subject by which it is well or badly disposed in order to its proper nature or operation. But the intellect can operate well or badly with respect to the first principles, since it can err about them: therefore it needs a habit for operating well; and therefore it is necessary to posit it.

> Secundò: Quia si intellectus non indiget habitu ad assentiendum principiis: quia sicut euidentia, & naturaliter eum mouent: sequitur nec indigere habitu, ad assentiendum cõclusionibus. Probatur consequentia: quia habito assensu principiorum, euidentem veritatem continet conclusio in eis contenta, & etiam naturaliter mouet intellectum: sed opposita [p. 690] opinio ponit habitum pro conclusionibus: ergo necessariò debet eum ponere circa principia.

Second: because if the intellect does not need a habit for assenting to principles, because they are evident and move it naturally, it follows that neither does it need a habit for assenting to conclusions. The consequence is proved: because, once assent to the principles is had, the conclusion contained in them contains evident truth, and also moves the intellect naturally; but the opposite Xx [p. 690] opinion posits a habit for conclusions: therefore it must necessarily posit one with respect to principles.

> 9 Et ad arg. eius: Distinguenda est minor, quòd intellectus naturaliter assentiatur primis principiis. Nam quantum ad specificationem, verum est: quia supposita debita apprehensione eorum: si iudicium ferat circa illa, non potest esse iudicium dissensus, sed assensus debet esse: quantum verò attinet ad exercitium, libertatem habet circa illa, dependenter à voluntate: & ideo potest assensum suspendere, vt superiùs probauimus, quam libertatem non habent sensus, nec voluntas circa bonum in communi: ideo non sunt capaces habitus.

9 And to its argument: the minor must be distinguished, namely that the intellect assents naturally to the first principles. For as regards specification, it is true: because, given the due apprehension of them, if it passes judgment on them, it cannot be a judgment of dissent, but must be one of assent. But as regards exercise, it has liberty with respect to them, dependently on the will; and therefore it can suspend its assent, as we proved above. Which liberty the senses do not have, nor the will with respect to the good in general: therefore they are not capable of a habit.

### Quidnam sit habitus principiorum — What the habit of principles is.

> 10 NAtura & essentia habitus, ex proprio actu, & obiecto, circa quod natus est, operari intelligenda est. Nam ab his sumunt speciem potentiæ, & habitus, vt docet Arist. lib. 2. de Anima, c. 4. Explicare igitur oportet: *Quodnam sit proprium obiectum huius habitus, & quem habeat actum circa illud.* *Obiectum*, proprium habitus, est euidens, & immediata veritas: siue vniuersalis sit illa, siue particularis. Proprius modus tendendi in obiectum, à quo formalis, & vltima ratio habitus desumitur, est per immediatam comparationem ad ipsam veritatem euidentem, quam sine vllo medio respicit. Vnde, sicut alij habitus intellectus, constituuntur, & distinguuntur specie, per tale, vel tale medium assentiendi: vt scientia, per medium demonstratiuum: opinio, per medium probabile, & fides per testimonium: ita habitus principiorum, qui dicitur intellectus, talis est in propria specie, & à cæteris habitibus distinguitur, quia per se immediatè comparatur ad euidentiam veritatis. Vnde proprius actus eius est, *sine vllo medio ei assentire*, sicut actus scientiæ, assentire per medium demonstratiuum, Definitio igitur eius talis erit: *Habitus principiorum, est virtus intellectualis, per quam potentia intellectiua, determinatur ad assensum principiorum per se euidentem, & facile eundem eliciendum.* In quo autem consistat hæc facilitas, dicemus inferiùs.

10 The nature and essence of a habit are to be understood from its proper act and from the object with respect to which it is apt to operate. For from these powers and habits take their species, as Aristotle teaches in On the Soul bk. 2, ch. 4. It is necessary, therefore, to explain what the proper object of this habit is, and what act it has with respect to it. The proper object of the habit is evident and immediate truth, whether it be universal or particular. Its proper mode of tending to its object, from which the formal and ultimate ratio of the habit is taken, is through an immediate comparison to the evident truth itself, which it regards without any middle. Whence, just as the other habits of the intellect are constituted and distinguished in species through this or that middle of assenting (as science through a demonstrative middle, opinion through a probable middle, and faith through testimony), so the habit of principles, which is called understanding, is such in its proper species, and is distinguished from the other habits, because it is compared per se and immediately to the evidence of truth. Whence its proper act is to assent to it without any middle, just as the act of science is to assent through a demonstrative middle. Its definition, therefore, will be this: The habit of principles is an intellectual virtue through which the intellective power is determined to the assent to principles evident per se, and to eliciting that assent easily. And in what this facility consists we shall say below.

### An habitus principiorum sit naturalis, vel acquisitus ab intellectu, per proprios actus — Whether the habit of principles is natural, or acquired by the intellect through its own acts.

> 11 HAbito iam quòd habitus intellectus sit, & quid sit: sequitur tertium explicandum: *Quoniam modo generetur, aut fiat in nobis.* Videlicet, an eum accipiat anima simul cum propria natura, & intellectu, dum creatur à Deo: vel sicut [p. 691] in ipsa creatione, accipit intellectum sine vlla specie intelligibili, sed tanquam tabulam rasam: in qua nihil depictum est, vt asseruit Arist. eodem modo eum accipiat, sine vllo habitu principiorum. Nam de cæteris habitibus scientiarum, & virtutum, certum est, nullum habere intellectum à principio tales tum, certum est, nullum habere intellectum à principio tales habitus: & ita sicut eos acquirit successu temporis, per proprios actus pari ratione acquirat habitum principiorum. Nam si cum intellectu eum accipiat anima, naturalis dicetur: hoc est à natura inditus, si verò per actus eum acquirat: non naturalis, sed acquisitus dicetur, sicut cæteri.

11 Having now explained that the habit of understanding exists, and what it is, there follows the third thing to be explained: in what manner it is generated, or comes to be in us; namely, whether the soul receives it together with its own nature and intellect when it is created by God, or whether, just as [p. 691] in its very creation it receives the intellect without any intelligible species, but as a blank tablet in which nothing is painted, as Aristotle asserted, it receives it in the same manner, without any habit of principles. For concerning the other habits, of the sciences and of the virtues, it is certain that the intellect has no such habits from the beginning; and thus, just as it acquires these in the course of time through its own acts, by parity of reasoning it would acquire the habit of principles. For if the soul receives it together with the intellect, it will be called natural, that is, implanted by nature; but if it acquires it through acts, it will be called not natural but acquired, like the others.

> Prima opinio affirmat, *Esse naturalem, & non acquisitum*, Ita Cõradus 1. 2. q. 94. art. 1. & Bãnes 1. par. q. 1. art. 6. notabili 3. & videtur expressa apud D. Th. 1. 2. q. 49. art. 1. ad 3. vbi sic ait: 12 *Puer non potest vti habitu intellectus principiorum, vel etiam lege naturali, quæ ei habitualiter inest propter defectum ætatis.* Quibus verbis, habitum principiorum ponit in puero, nondum habente vsum rationis, & addit, non posse eo vti, propter defectum ætatis: ergo sentit inesse ei à natura, & non esse acquisitum per actus, & in 2. d. 24. q. 2. art 3. ad 3. Vocat eum *naturalem*, his verbis: *Habitus naturalis nunquam amittitur, sicut patet de habitu principiorum.*

The first opinion affirms that it is natural and not acquired. So Conrad, 1-2, q. 94, a. 1, and Báñez, 1 p., q. 1, a. 6, notable 3, etc.; and it seems to be express in St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 49, a. 1, ad 3, where he says: 12 A child cannot use the habit of the understanding of principles, or even the natural law, which is in him habitually, on account of the defect of age. In which words he posits the habit of principles in a child who does not yet have the use of reason, and adds that he cannot use it on account of the defect of age: therefore he thinks that it is in him from nature, and is not acquired through acts. And in 2, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3, ad 3, he calls it natural, in these words: A natural habit is never lost, as is plain of the habit of principles.

> Et ratione probatur: Quia habitus acquisiti, sunt facilitates quædam: & ideo ponuntur, ad vincendam difficultatem: quam habet potentia ad operandum, circa tale obiectum, sed intellectus nullam habet difficultatem, in assentiendo primis principiis, pręsertim vniuersalissimis, vt his, Quodlibet est, vel non est. Totum est maius sua parte: ergo neque aliquam acquirit facultatem in assensu frequenti eorum: imò neque ea indiget. Probatur consequentia: Quia facilitas difficultati opponitur, & ad eam superandam ordinatur, vnde sequitur: vel non esse ponendum talem habitum, vel esse naturalem, & non acquisitum. Et talem eum appellat communis modus loquendi, fundatus fortè in nomine ipso: quia intellectus vocatur: sicut potentia ipsa, in qua recipitur: quia naturalis est ei.

And it is proved by reason: because acquired habits are certain facilities, and therefore they are posited for overcoming the difficulty which the power has in operating with respect to such an object. But the intellect has no difficulty in assenting to the first principles, especially the most universal ones, such as these: Anything whatever either is or is not; The whole is greater than its part: therefore it does not acquire any facility in the frequent assent to them; nay, it does not even need one. The consequence is proved: because facility is opposed to difficulty, and is ordered to overcoming it; whence it follows either that such a habit is not to be posited, or that it is natural and not acquired. And the common manner of speaking calls it such, founded perhaps on the very name: because it is called understanding, like the power itself in which it is received, because it is natural to it.

> 13 Secunda opinio est, Caiet. 1. 2. qu. 51. art. 1. d. 1. *Vbi negat esse acquisitum*: sic autem esse naturalem docet, vt eum non accipiat anima à principio, cum ipso intellectu: sed sicut intellectus nullam accipit speciem intelligibilem, dum creatur anima & infunditur corpori: ita nullum accipit habitum: sed acquisitis speciebus primorum principiorum, per abstractionem intellectus agentis, statim ait, profluere naturaliter habitum principiorum ac ipsa natura intellectus passibilis: cui tribui- [p. 692] tur, vt statim per ipsum assentiatur eiusdem principiis, apprehensis per species. Et hoc modo, ait, vocandum esse *naturalem*.

13 The second opinion is that of Cajetan, 1-2, q. 51, a. 1, d. 1, where he denies that it is acquired; but he teaches that it is natural in such a way that the soul does not receive it from the beginning together with the intellect itself; rather, just as the intellect receives no intelligible species when the soul is created and infused into the body, so it receives no habit; but once the species of the first principles have been acquired through the abstraction of the agent intellect, the habit of principles, he says, immediately flows forth naturally from the very nature of the passive intellect, to which it is attributed X x ij [p. 692] so that through it the intellect immediately assents to the same principles, once they are apprehended through the species. And in this way, he says, it is to be called natural.

> Tertia sententia, asserit: *Habitum principiorum cum natura, neque ab eadem natura intellectus fluere, eo ipso, quòd habet species principiorum, per quas ea apprehendit: sed esse acquisitum per actus ipsos: quibus intellectus assentitur principiis.* Sicut habitus scientiæ, & virtutum, acquiruntur per proprios actus: ita Ferrar. 2. contra gentes, c. 78. Et est communis modernorum: & videtur nobis vera, & tenenda. Probatur primò, expresso testimonio Arist. cap. vlt. huius 1. lib. vbi explicans modum, quo habitus iste generatur in nobis, ita ait, *Neque itaque insunt determinati habitus, neque ab aliis habitibus fiunt notioribus, sed assensu.* Quibus verbis, docet non inesse nobis à natura: neque ex aliis notioribus notitiis fieri, sicut habitus scientiæ, sed per assensum immediatum veritatis per se notæ. Quod est acquiri per proprios actus.

The third opinion asserts that the habit of principles neither comes with nature, nor flows from that same nature of the intellect by the very fact that it has the species of the principles through which it apprehends them; but that it is acquired through the very acts by which the intellect assents to the principles, just as the habits of the sciences and of the virtues are acquired through their own acts. So Ferrara, Contra Gentiles 2, ch. 78; and it is the common opinion of the moderns, and seems to us true and to be held. It is proved, first, by the express testimony of Aristotle in the last chapter of this book 1, where, explaining the manner in which this habit is generated in us, he speaks thus: Therefore the determinate habits are neither innate in us, nor do they come to be from other, better-known habits, but from assent. In which words he teaches that it is not in us from nature, nor does it come to be from other, better-known cognitions, as the habit of science does, but through the immediate assent to truth known per se. Which is to be acquired through its own acts.

> Probatur deinde ratione: Quia natura non concedit rebus, nisi ea quæ necessaria sunt ad essendum, & operandum simpliciter: quæ verò ad meliùs vel faciliùs operandum seruiunt, acquirenda eis relinquit propria industria, & labore tribuens principia, quibus possint operari, & operando ea acquirere: & hac de causa non concessit hominibus habitus virtutum: quia non requiruntur ad operandum simpliciter bona opera, sed ad meliùs, hoc est, cum facilitate & promptitudine operandum. At habitus principiorum, non est necessarius ad assentiendum simpliciter, primis principiis: sed solùm ad assentiendum cum facilitate: ergo non est nobis à natura datus: sed propria industria, & labore acquisitus. Probatur minor: quia assensus principiorum, non excedit facultatem intellectus: sed is informatus per species intelligibiles, per quas apprehendit terminos, ex quibus principia fiunt, dum cognoscit significationem eorum: potest ipse propria virtute iudicare de veritate eorum, quòd est eis assentire: ergo ad assentiendum simpliciter, non indiget habitu. Probatur antecedens: quia principia sunt veritates quædam naturales, per se euidentes: ergo sunt proportionatæ lumini naturali, eiusdem intellectus: quare per propriam virtutem potest circa eas operari, per assensum.

It is proved next by reason: because nature does not grant to things anything but what is necessary for being and for operating simply; but the things which serve for operating better or more easily it leaves to be acquired by their own industry and labor, granting them principles by which they can operate and, by operating, acquire them. And for this reason it did not grant to men the habits of the virtues: because they are not required for doing good works simply, but for doing them better, that is, for operating with facility and promptness. But the habit of principles is not necessary for assenting to the first principles simply, but only for assenting with facility: therefore it is not given to us by nature, but acquired by our own industry and labor. The minor is proved: because the assent to principles does not exceed the faculty of the intellect; rather, informed by the intelligible species through which it apprehends the terms of which the principles are made, while it knows their signification, it can by its own power judge of their truth, which is to assent to them: therefore for assenting simply it does not need a habit. The antecedent is proved: because principles are certain natural truths, evident per se: therefore they are proportioned to the natural light of the same intellect; wherefore by its own power it can operate with respect to them through assent.

> 15 Sed vt hæc nostra sententia meliùs intelligatur, & vt testimonia D. Th. iuxta mentem eius explicentur: notandum est: *Quòd licet habitus principiorum, non sit nobis à natura datus*, maximum tamen habet principium in natura ipsa, ratione cuius naturalis etiam aliquo modo dici potest. Quod non habent alij habitus. Vt enim superiùs dicebamus, propria ratio huius [p. 693] habitus sumitur, per immediatam comparationem, ad ipsam veritatem per se euidentem: quam nec respicit, neque attingit per aliquod medium, sed solùm indiget notitia terminorum: quam item habet per species terminorum, ex quibus principia ipsa componuntur. Istæ autem species, producuntur ab intellectu agente, & imprimuntur intellectui passibili, mediis speciebus sensibilibus obiectorum: quæ vocantur phanthasmata. Operatio porrò sensuum, & eiusdem intellectus agentis: per quam efficiuntur species, naturalis est, & sine habitu efficitur. Informatus autem intellectus patiens per has species principiorum, & intellecta per eas significatione terminorum, sine vlla arte, vel industria, sine vllo medio, vel discursu, assentitur principiis: & per talem assensum, generatur habitus principiorum: qui postea intenditur, & perficitur, per frequentem repetitionem eiusdem assensus. Et ideo, tam ex parte specierum, naturaliter productarum: quàm ex parte assensus principiorum, dicitur habitus iste naturalis: quamuis liber assensus, & ex consequenti, liberè producatur habitus per eum. Et tandem, quia assensus principiorum, & habitus ipse, producuntur sine medio, sine discursu, sine arte, solùm per naturale lumen eiusdem intellectus: ideo non est nomen aliud ei inditum, sed nomine eiusdem intellectus significatur: dum dicimus, esse intellectum principiorum.

15 But in order that this view of ours may be better understood, and that the testimonies of St. Thomas may be explained according to his mind, it should be noted that, although the habit of principles is not given to us by nature, it nevertheless has its greatest principle in nature itself, by reason of which it can also in some manner be called natural. Which the other habits do not have. For, as we were saying above, the proper ratio of this [p. 693] habit is taken from its immediate comparison to truth itself evident per se, which it neither regards nor attains through any middle, but needs only the cognition of the terms; which, again, it has through the species of the terms of which the principles themselves are composed. And these species are produced by the agent intellect and impressed on the passive intellect, by means of the sensible species of the objects, which are called phantasms. Now the operation of the senses, and of the same agent intellect, through which the species are produced, is natural, and is performed without a habit. And the patient intellect, informed through these species of the principles, and having understood through them the signification of the terms, assents to the principles without any art or industry, without any middle or discursive reasoning; and through such assent the habit of principles is generated, which is afterwards intensified and perfected through frequent repetition of the same assent. And therefore, both on the side of the species, which are produced naturally, and on the side of the assent to the principles, this habit is called natural; although the assent is free, and consequently the habit is freely produced through it. And finally, because the assent to principles and the habit itself are produced without a middle, without discursive reasoning, without art, solely through the natural light of the same intellect, therefore no other name has been given to it, but it is signified by the name of the same intellect, when we say that it is the understanding of principles.

> 16 Hæc autem non habent alij habitus intellectuales, vt habitus scientię. Is enim præter operationem intellectus agentis, præter species conclusionis, quas imprimit intellectui patienti, prærequirit artem, per quam disponantur principia: prærequirit assensum eorum, tanquam medium formale, quo intellectus assentitur conclusioni: & per talem assensum generatur. Et ideo neque habitus scientiæ, neque alij similes dicuntur naturales.

16 But the other intellectual habits do not have these features, as the habit of science. For besides the operation of the agent intellect, and besides the species of the conclusion, which it impresses on the patient intellect, it prerequires art, through which the principles are disposed; it prerequires the assent to them, as the formal middle by which the intellect assents to the conclusion; and through such assent it is generated. And therefore neither the habit of science nor other similar habits are called natural.

> Ex quibus intelligitur: Vtrumque habere habitum principiorum: & quòd naturalis sit, & quòd sit acquisitus per proprios actus: non tamen sicut acquiruntur cæteri habitus: sed sine vllo medio, sine vlla arte, vel industria, per solam virtutem naturalem vtriusque intellectus, agentis, & patientis, ac sensuum, quorum naturales operationes præsupponuntur. Et in hoc sensu loquitur D. Tho. dum vocat naturalem hunc habitum: vel dum dicit à natura haberi: non negans per hos modos loquendi, quòd sit acquisitus per proprios actus: quia vterque sensus verus est, & neuter contradicit alteri. Hunc autem esse sensum eius, colligitur euidenter ex proprio loco, vbi ex professo agit D. Th. de hoc habitu inquirens, *An sit naturalis*, [p. 694] nempe 1. 2. q. 1. art. 1. asseritque esse naturalem secundùm inchoationem, quod non habent cæteri habitus: & nihilominus esse acquisitum, per operationem intellectus agentis, & sensuum, præsuppositam assensui intellectus passibilis, per quem proximè acquiritur. In quo etiam sensu, dixit Arist. *ex sensibus, & non à natura haberi hunc habitum.*

From which it is understood that the habit of principles has both features: both that it is natural and that it is acquired through its own acts; not, however, as the other habits are acquired, but without any middle, without any art or industry, solely through the natural power of both intellects, the agent and the patient, and of the senses, whose natural operations are presupposed. And it is in this sense that St. Thomas speaks when he calls this habit natural, or when he says that it is had from nature; not denying, by these ways of speaking, that it is acquired through its own acts, because each sense is true and neither contradicts the other. And that this is his sense is evidently gathered from the proper place where St. Thomas treats expressly of this habit, inquiring whether it is natural, X x iij [p. 694] namely in 1-2, q. 1, a. 1; and he asserts that it is natural according to its inchoation, which the other habits do not have; and nevertheless that it is acquired, through the operation of the agent intellect and of the senses, presupposed to the assent of the passive intellect, through which it is proximately acquired. In which sense also Aristotle said that this habit is had from the senses and not from nature.

> 17 In eodem etiam sensu, intelligitur ad testimonium D. Th. de puero; quem dicit habere hunc habitum: sed non vti eo propter defectum ætatis. Intelligit autem eum habere secundùm inchoationem: quia hoc modo est naturalis: quem tamen non habet formaliter: quousque per primum assensum principiorum in eo generetur, & per sequentes perficiatur.

17 In the same sense, too, is understood the testimony of St. Thomas about the child, whom he says has this habit but does not use it on account of the defect of age. For he understands that he has it according to its inchoation, because in this manner it is natural; yet he does not have it formally, until it is generated in him through the first assent to principles and perfected through the subsequent ones.

> Circa solutionem primi argu. Asserunt moderni quidam: Non esse ponendum habitum: pro assensu principiorum vniuersalissimorum, quæ vocantur dignitates: quia cùm sint nobis notissima, absque vlla difficultate eis assentimus: & ideò per frequentem assensum eorum, non acquirimus habitum. Sed solùm esse ponendum: pro principiis particularibus scientiarum, quibus non facilè assentitur intellectus, cùm non sint adeò nobis nota: ideo facilitate acquisita pro iis indigemus: quæ vocatur habitus. Et hæc sententia videtur mihi satis probabilis: quamuis etiam sit probabile: *quòd in assentiendo his principiis, nõnihil difficultatis habeat intellectus: licèt minùs longè, quàm in assentiendo principiis particularibus*, & hoc satis est, vt indigeat habitu ad assentiendum, & vt nouam acquirat facilitatem per frequentem repetitionem assensuum.

Concerning the solution of the first argument, certain moderns assert that a habit is not to be posited for the assent to the most universal principles, which are called axioms: because, since they are most known to us, we assent to them without any difficulty; and therefore through frequent assent to them we do not acquire a habit. But they say it is to be posited only for the particular principles of the sciences, to which the intellect does not easily assent, since they are not so known to us; therefore we need for them an acquired facility, which is called a habit. And this opinion seems to me sufficiently probable; although it is also probable that in assenting to these principles the intellect has some difficulty, though far less than in assenting to particular principles; and this is enough for it to need a habit for assenting, and to acquire a new facility through frequent repetition of the assents.

> 18 Et ex hac doctrina respondetur ad arg. Concessa maiore, sed minori negata, quòd intellectus nullam habeat difficultatem in assensu primorum principiorum, & ideò nec vllam acquirat facilitatem, per repetitionem assensus. Nam experientia, docet oppositum: & quòd aliquam habeat intellectus difficultatem, quem per exercitationem vincit: & ex consequenti, quòd nouam acquirat facilitatem.

18 And from this doctrine the reply is given to the argument: the major being granted, the minor is denied, namely that the intellect has no difficulty in the assent to the first principles, and therefore acquires no facility through repetition of the assent. For experience teaches the opposite: both that the intellect has some difficulty, which it overcomes by exercise, and consequently that it acquires a new facility.

> Quid autem sit hæc facilitas: aut in quo consistat, diuersis modis explicatur ab auctoribus. Quibus omissis, dicendum est, *Facilitatem, non esse aliud, quàm modum quendam, per quem potentia efficitur expedita, atque prompta ad operandum, aptaque, vt cum delectatione operetur*, quod non habet ex se, vel à natura: & hunc modum tribuit ei habitus, tanto perfectiorem, quanto magis intenditur, atque perficitur, per repetitionem actuum.

But what this facility is, or in what it consists, is explained in diverse ways by the authors. Leaving these aside, it must be said that facility is nothing else than a certain mode by which the power is rendered ready and prompt for operating, and apt to operate with delight, which it does not have of itself or from nature; and the habit gives it this mode, the more perfect the more it is intensified and perfected through the repetition of acts.

[p. 695]

### An habitus principiorum sit idem secundum speciem pro omnibus principiis: vel diuersus pro diuersis — Whether the habit of principles is the same in species for all principles, or diverse for diverse ones.

> *An habitus principiorum sit idem secundùm speciem, pro omnibus principiis, vel diuersus pro diuersis.*

[…]

> DE distinctione specifica huius habitus nihil inuenitur apud auctores. Ideo sola ratione agendum nobis est. Videtur autem vnum esse ponendum pro omnibus, quod sic probo: *Habitus distinguuntur per diuersos actus*, vt sæpè diximus: sed habitus principiorum habet actum eiusdem speciei, circa omnia principia: ergo est idem secundùm speciem pro omnibus.

Concerning the specific distinction of this habit nothing is found in the authors; therefore we must proceed by reason alone. And it seems that one habit is to be posited for all, which I prove thus: Habits are distinguished through diverse acts, as we have often said; but the habit of principles has an act of the same species with respect to all principles: therefore it is the same in species for all.

> 19 Probatur minor, quia actus huius habitus, est assensus principiorum: & assensus sunt eiusdem, vel diuersæ speciei, per eandem, vel diuersam rationem assentiendi: quæ est quasi formale obiectum eorum: sed eadem est ratio formalis assentiendi semper primis principiis: ergo omnes assensus sunt eiusdem speciei, & ideo idem quoque erit habitus, secundùm speciem. Probatur minor: quia semper assentitur intellectus primis principiis, sine medio, habita solùm significatione terminorum: ergo semper eodem modo.

19 The minor is proved: because the act of this habit is the assent to principles; and assents are of the same or of diverse species through the same or a diverse ratio of assenting, which is as it were their formal object; but the formal ratio of assenting to the first principles is always the same: therefore all the assents are of the same species, and therefore the habit too will be the same in species. The minor is proved: because the intellect always assents to the first principles without a middle, having only the signification of the terms: therefore always in the same manner.

> Nostra tamen sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur, hoc modo. Prima est, *Habitus principiorum practicorum, & speculatiuorum, specie distinguuntur*: quam tenet D. Tho 1. p. quęst. 79. art. 12. Et probat euidens ratio: Quia actus, & habitus distinguuntur specie, per diuersa obiecta: sed veritas practica, quam continent principia practica, & circa quam versatur habitus, tanquam circa proprium obiectum, est diuersa specie à veritate speculatiua: cùm illa ex propria natura ordinetur ad operandum, hæc verò non: ergo distinguuntur habitus isti specie. Principia practica sunt hæc, & similia: Bonum est prosequendum, & Malum fugiendum. Virtus est amplectenda, & Vitium est repudiandum. Quæ per se patet ordinari ad operandum. Speculatiua sunt: Totum est maius sua parte. Homo est animal rationale: & similia, de quibus manifestum est nullum ordinem dicere ad operandum.

Our view, however, is explained by two conclusions, in this manner. The first is: The habits of practical and of speculative principles are distinguished in species. Which St. Thomas holds, 1 p., q. 79, a. 12. And an evident reason proves it: because acts and habits are distinguished in species through diverse objects; but practical truth, which practical principles contain, and with which the habit is concerned as with its proper object, is diverse in species from speculative truth, since the former by its own nature is ordered to operating, but the latter is not: therefore these habits are distinguished in species. Practical principles are these and the like: Good is to be pursued, and Evil is to be fled; Virtue is to be embraced, and Vice is to be rejected; which, it is plain per se, are ordered to operating. Speculative ones are: The whole is greater than its part; Man is a rational animal; and the like, of which it is manifest that they say no order to operating.

> 20 Secunda conclusio: *Habitus etiam principiorum speculatiuorum, distinguuntur specie, secundùm quòd in diuersis materiis inueniuntur*: hoc modo, vt habitus principiorum vnius scientiæ, distinguatur specie ab habitu principiorum alterius. Et si pro principiis vniuersalissimis, ponendus est habitus, pro diuersis etiam ponendus est habitus distinctus specie. Ita, vt alius sit habitus, per quem assentimus huic principio, Quodlibet est, vel non est, ab eo per quem assentimur illi, Totum est maius sua parte. Hanc conclusionem sic probo: Habitus distinguuntur per diuersos actus, & actus sunt [p. 696] diuersi per diuersa obiecta: sed assensus principiorum vnius scientiæ, specie distinguitur ab assensu principiorum alterius: & assensus vnius principij vniuersalissimi, distinguitur etiam specie, ab assensu alterius: ergo habitus etiam erunt distincti specie. Probatur minor: quia diuersa principia, continent diuersam veritatem, quam respiciunt assensus, tanquam proprium obiectum: vt diuersam veritatem specie continet, hoc principium, Homo est animal rationale, ab illo, Natura est principium motus, & quietis, eius in quo est: ergo efficiunt assensus specie distinctos, in intellectu, & diuersi assensus, efficient habitus etiam diuersos. Et idem exemplum adduci potest, in diuersis principiis vniuersalissimis.

20 The second conclusion: The habits of speculative principles, too, are distinguished in species, according as they are found in diverse matters; in this manner, that the habit of the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the habit of the principles of another. And if a habit is to be posited for the most universal principles, for diverse ones too a habit distinct in species is to be posited; so that the habit through which we assent to this principle, Anything whatever either is or is not, is another from that through which we assent to that one, The whole is greater than its part. This conclusion I prove thus: habits are distinguished through diverse acts, and acts are XX iiij [p. 696] diverse through diverse objects; but the assent to the principles of one science is distinguished in species from the assent to the principles of another; and the assent to one most universal principle is also distinguished in species from the assent to another: therefore the habits too will be distinct in species. The minor is proved: because diverse principles contain diverse truth, which the assents regard as their proper object; as this principle, Man is a rational animal, contains a truth diverse in species from that one, Nature is the principle of motion and of rest of that in which it is: therefore they produce assents distinct in species in the intellect, and diverse assents will produce diverse habits too. And the same example can be adduced in diverse most universal principles.

> 21 Et si dicas, Distingui specie assensus: sed tamen pertinere ad eundem habitum: quia sunt actus inadęquati respectu illius, ad omnia principia, & ad omnes assensus eorum se extendentis. In contrarium est, quòd si distinguuntur specie: licèt inadæquata, necesse est eos generare habitus partiales specie distinctos. Quia quælibet causa, producit effectum secundùm suam speciem, (licèt inadæquatum) ergo à causis specie distinctis, (licèt inadæquatis) necesse est effectus specie diuersos (licèt inadæquatos) procedere. Quare iam dabuntur diuersi habitus, saltem partiales, specie distincti. Verùm probatur, debere distingui specie totali: quia habitus principiorum, non habet tantam extensionem, ac intellectus: vt possit idem se extendere ad omnes veritates, nec habet maiorem extensionem: quàm habitus scientiæ, cui proportionatur, ac necessariò præsupponitur: sed habitus scientiæ, distinguuntur specie per diuersa obiecta formalia: ergo habitus principiorum, qui eis correspõdent, debent etiam distingui specie, per diuersas veritates principiorum, circa quas versantur, tanquam circa propria obiecta.

21 And if you say that the assents are distinguished in species, but nevertheless pertain to the same habit, because they are inadequate acts with respect to it, since it extends itself to all principles and to all the assents to them: against this is the fact that, if they are distinguished in species, though inadequate, they must necessarily generate partial habits distinct in species. Because any cause whatever produces an effect according to its own species (though an inadequate one): therefore from causes distinct in species (though inadequate) effects diverse in species (though inadequate) must proceed. Wherefore there will now be diverse habits, at least partial ones, distinct in species. But that they must be distinguished by a total species is proved: because the habit of principles does not have so great an extension as the intellect, so that one and the same habit can extend itself to all truths; nor does it have a greater extension than the habit of science, to which it is proportioned and by which it is necessarily presupposed. But the habits of science are distinguished in species through diverse formal objects: therefore the habits of principles, which correspond to them, must also be distinguished in species through the diverse truths of the principles with which they are concerned as with their proper objects.

> Ad arg. oppositę opinionis, neganda est minor; quòd habitus principiorum habeat assensum eiusdem speciei, circa omnia principia: nam licèt omnibus assentiatur, intellecta significatione terminorum sine medio, modus tamen iste assentiendi, & ratio formalis generica est: sicut etiam est generica in scientiis, assentire conclusionibus, per medium demonstratiuum. Sicut ergo in scientiis, specie distincta est ratio assentiendi, secundùm distinctam rationem principiorum per quæ assentitur intellectus conclusionibus, huius, aut illius scientiæ: & sicut per hanc distinctam rationem specificam: distinguuntur habitus scientiæ specie, ita in assensu principiorum distincta est ratio assentiendi specifica, secundùm distinctionem specificam diuersarum veritatum, quas diuersa principia continenti. Nam ratio [p. 697] assentiendi principiis, ipsamet veritas principiorum per semetipsam est, & non per aliud medium: diuersa igitur veritas immediata cùm sit, diuersa etiam ratio assentiendi erit, & diuersum assensum secundùm speciem efficiet: & diuersi assensus secundùm speciem, diuersos habitus principiorum generabunt.

To the argument of the opposite opinion: the minor must be denied, namely that the habit of principles has an assent of the same species with respect to all principles. For although the intellect assents to all of them without a middle, once the signification of the terms is understood, this mode of assenting and formal ratio is generic; just as in the sciences, too, to assent to conclusions through a demonstrative middle is generic. Just as, therefore, in the sciences the ratio of assenting is distinct in species according to the distinct ratio of the principles through which the intellect assents to the conclusions of this or that science, and just as the habits of science are distinguished in species through this distinct specific ratio, so in the assent to principles the specific ratio of assenting is distinct according to the specific distinction of the diverse truths which the diverse principles contain. For the ratio [p. 697] of assenting to a principle is the very truth of the principles, through itself and not through another middle; since, therefore, the immediate truth is diverse, the ratio of assenting will also be diverse, and will produce an assent diverse in species; and assents diverse in species will generate diverse habits of principles.

> TRACTATVS II.

T R E AT I S E I I .

> De habitu scientiæ,

On the Habit of Science.

> CIrca habitum scientiæ explicanda sunt, *An sit*, & *Qui sit*, & *An sit de singularibus, & contingentibus, atque entibus per accidens.*

oncerning the habit of science, these things are to be explained: C          whether it exists, and what it is, and whether it is of singulars and contingents, and of beings per accidens.

### An præter habitum principiorum, ponendus sit pro conclusionibus alter habitus distinctus, qui appellatur scientia — Whether, besides the habit of principles, another, distinct habit, which is called science, is to be posited for conclusions.

> *An præter habitum principiorum, ponendus sit pro conclusionibus alter habitus distinctus, qui appelletur scientia.*

[…]

> 23 PRima opinio est, quorundam modernorum, qui *cùm pro vniuersalissimis principiis non ponant habitum principiorum*: sed solùm pro particularibus huius aut illius scientiæ: asserunt nihilominus, talem habitum principiorum, postquam assensum eorum habet, habita notitia terminorum extendere se ad assensus omnium conclusionum eiusdem scientiæ: & ita præter habitum principiorum, non esse ponendum habitum scientiæ, ab eo distinctum.

23 The first opinion is that of certain moderns, who, although they do not posit a habit of principles for the most universal principles, but only for the particular principles of this or that science, nevertheless assert that such a habit of principles, after it has the assent to them, the cognition of the terms being had, extends itself to the assents to all the conclusions of the same science; and thus that, besides the habit of principles, no habit of science distinct from it is to be posited.

> Probant testimonio Aristot. 6. lib. Ethic. cap. 3. vbi enumerans habitus intellectuales, de sapientia, quæ est habitus vnus Intellectus, asserit, esse scientiam, & intellectum, simul eorum, quæ honorabilissima sunt: ergo sentit eundem habitum, sufficere pro principiis, & conclusionibus; quare non est necessarium multiplicare alterum.

They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 6, ch. 3, where, enumerating the intellectual habits, he asserts of wisdom, which is one habit of the intellect, that it is science and understanding together, of the things that are most honorable: therefore he thinks that the same habit suffices for principles and conclusions; wherefore it is not necessary to multiply another.

> 22 Probant deinde ratione: Quia assensus, quorum vnus dependet ab altero non possunt generare distinctos habitus: quia diuersi habitus independentes esse debent, sed assensus conclusionum, præsupponit assensum principiorum, à quo intrinsecam habet dependentiam, vt ex se patet: ergo non generat distinctum habitum ab eo, sed idemmet habitus, qui principiorum est, se extendit ad conclusiones. Maiorem probant, exemplo vniuersaliorum scientiarum, vt Dialecticæ, atque Philosophiæ, quæ licèt diuersas habeant conclusiones: non ideo tamen ponuntur in eis, pro singulis singuli, ac diuersi habitus, sed vnus qui se extendat ad omnes, propter intrinsecam dependentiam [p. 698] vnius conclusionis ab alia: cui præsupponitur necessariò, vel quam præsupponit: quod nos asseruimus, atque probauimus q. 3. Proœmiali: ergo cùm magis intrinsecam dependentiam habeant: conclusiones eiusdem scientiæ, à principiis eiusdem, quàm possint habere inter sese conclusiones ipsæ, sequitur non esse ponendum habitum distinctum pro conclusionibus, ab habitu principiorum: sed hunc se extendere ad omnes.

22 They prove it next by reason: because assents of which one depends on the other cannot generate distinct habits, because diverse habits must be independent; but the assent to conclusions presupposes the assent to principles, on which it has an intrinsic dependence, as is plain of itself: therefore it does not generate a habit distinct from it, but the very same habit which is of the principles extends itself to the conclusions. They prove the major by the example of the more universal sciences, such as Dialectic and Philosophy, which, although they have diverse conclusions, nevertheless do not on that account have posited in them a single and diverse habit for each conclusion, but one which extends itself to all, on account of the intrinsic dependence [p. 698] of one conclusion on another, by which it is necessarily presupposed, or which it presupposes, as we asserted and proved in Proemial q. 3: therefore, since the conclusions of the same science have a more intrinsic dependence on the principles of the same science than the conclusions themselves can have among themselves, it follows that no habit distinct from the habit of principles is to be posited for the conclusions, but that this one extends itself to all.

> Hæc tamen sententia manifestè contraria est eidem Arist. in eodem loco: cap. 6. vbi expressè docet: Non solùm habitum principiorum: quid dicitur intellectus, esse distinctũ ab habitu scientię, & aliis: sed neque posse cum aliquo eorum coincidere, his verbis: *Intellectus neque est scientia, nec ars, nec prudentia. Scientia: quia ipsum scibile demonstrabile est: ars, & prudentia: quia in his versantur, quæ sese aliter habere possunt. At nec sapientia est: est enim sapientis de quibusdam demonstrationem habere. Quod si ea quibus verum dicimus, & nunquam falsum, in his quæ possunt, aut non possunt aliter se habere, (& hæc sunt, scientia, prudentia, sapientia, intellectus: horum autem trium habituum, nullus esse potest, atque tres dico, prudentiam, scientiam, sapientiam) restat intellectum esse principiorum.*

This opinion, however, is manifestly contrary to the same Aristotle in the same place, ch. 6, where he teaches expressly that not only is the habit of principles, which is called understanding, distinct from the habit of science and from the others, but that it cannot coincide with any of them, in these words: Understanding is neither science, nor art, nor prudence. Not science, because the knowable itself is demonstrable; not art and prudence, because they are concerned with things that can be otherwise. But neither is it wisdom: for it belongs to the wise man to have demonstration of certain things. If, then, the things by which we speak the truth, and never falsehood, about things which either can or cannot be otherwise (and these are science, prudence, wisdom, understanding), and of these three habits none can be it (and I call the three prudence, science, wisdom), it remains that understanding is of principles.

> 25 Est etiam contra rationem. Quod sic probo: Habitus distinguuntur per actus: qui in intellectualibus, sunt ipsi assensus: sed assensus principiorum eiusdem scientiæ, & conclusionum eius distinguũtur specie: ergo ad habitus specie distinctos: quos generabũt, pertinere debent. Probatur minor: quia assensus distinguuntur specie, per diuersas rationes formales assentiendi: sed assensus conclusionum, habet diuersam rationẽ, ab assensu principiorum: vt ex se est manifestum, cùm assentiatur intellectus principiis sine medio, propter ipsam veritatem per se euidentem: conclusionibus verò, propter principia in demonstratione disposita: ergo assensus ipsi distinguentur specie. Et si dicas, distingui specie, tanquam actus inadæquatos eiusdẽ habitus: Contra hoc est: quòd si inadæquati sunt assensus, dabitur aliqua ratio assentiendi vniuersalior vtroque, sub qua comprehendantur: & quæ adęquata sit habitui, qui ponitur pro vtroque. Sed talis ratio est impossibilis: ergo impossibile est eundem esse habitum. Probo iterum minorem: quia talis ratio cõmunis vtrique assensui, esset assensus necessarij, aut euidentis, abstrahentis ab vtroque: quæ non potest esse vna, nisi vnitate generica, comprehendente sub se diuersos assensus secundùm speciem. Præterea: Etiam si inadæquatos esse daremus assensus principiorum, & conclusionum: cùm sint specie distincti necesse est, distinctos habitus, saltem partiales, & inadæquatos [p. 699] generare: & ita distinctus iam erit ponendus habitus pro conclusionibus, specie saltem partiali.

25 It is also contrary to reason, which I prove thus. Habits are distinguished through acts, which in intellectual matters are the assents themselves; but the assents to the principles of the same science and to its conclusions are distinguished in species: therefore they must pertain to habits distinct in species, which they generate. The minor is proved: because assents are distinguished in species through diverse formal ratios of assenting; but the assent to conclusions has a ratio diverse from the assent to principles, as is manifest of itself, since the intellect assents to principles without a middle, on account of the truth itself, evident per se, but to conclusions on account of the principles disposed in a demonstration: therefore the assents themselves will be distinguished in species. And if you say that they are distinguished in species as inadequate acts of the same habit: against this is the fact that, if the assents are inadequate, there will be given some ratio of assenting more universal than both, under which they are comprehended, and which is adequate to the habit that is posited for both. But such a ratio is impossible: therefore it is impossible that it be the same habit. I prove the minor again: because such a ratio, common to both assents, would be that of a necessary or evident assent, abstracting from both; which cannot be one except by a generic unity, comprehending under itself assents diverse in species. Moreover, even if we granted that the assents to principles and to conclusions are inadequate, since they are distinct in species it is necessary that distinct habits, at least partial and inadequate [p. 699] generate; and thus a distinct habit, at least by a partial species, will now have to be posited for the conclusions.

> Testimonium Arist. pro opposita sententia exposuit egregiè D. Th. non solùm in Commentariis eiusdem, sed etiam 1. 2. q. 57. art. 1. ad 2. vbi ait: *Sapientiam propriè sumptam*, de qua ibi loquitur Arist. *esse quendam habitum, verè quidem scientificum, sed vniuersalissimum*, qui circa conclusiones etiam vniuersalissimas, sibi proprias versatur: & simul de principiis, & conclusionibus scientiarum particularium, quodammodo iudicat, tanquam de inferioribus: Quia considerat altissimas causas, ad quas reducuntur inferiores, & à quibus dependent: atq; etiam vniuersalissimas rationes entis, vt essentiam, totum, partem, ac similes: à quibus particulares conclusiones, omnium scientiarum dependent; & quas aliquando demonstrat, per rationes vniuersales extrinsecas, vel ducentes ad impossibile.

The testimony of Aristotle for the opposite opinion St. Thomas explained excellently, not only in his Commentaries on the same passage, but also in 1- 2, q. 57, a. 1, ad 2, where he says that wisdom properly taken, of which Aristotle speaks there, is a certain habit, truly a scientific one, but the most universal, which is concerned with conclusions, also the most universal ones, proper to itself; and at the same time judges in a certain manner of the principles and conclusions of the particular sciences, as of inferiors: because it considers the highest causes, to which the inferior ones are reduced and on which they depend; and also the most universal rationes of being, such as essence, whole, part, and the like, on which the particular conclusions of all the sciences depend, and which it sometimes demonstrates through universal extrinsic reasons, or reasons leading to the impossible.

> 26 Et propter has excellentias, quodam modo se habet ad alias scientias, tanquam intellectus, qui est habitus principiorum, & simul est etiam habitus scientiæ, respectu suarum conclusionum, non tamen est idem habitus, cum eo, qui ponitur pro principiis eius: sed diuersus. Et eiusmodi vniuersalis scientia, non est alia, præter Metaphysicam, cui prædictæ excellentiæ conueniunt.

26 And on account of these excellences it is related in a certain manner to the other sciences as understanding, which is the habit of principles; and at the same time it is also the habit of science with respect to its own conclusions; yet it is not the same habit as that which is posited for its principles, but a diverse one. And a universal science of this kind is none other than Metaphysics, to which the aforesaid excellences belong.

> Ad arg. eiusdem sententiæ, Respondetur, Maiorem esse falsam, absolutè: quod probant scientia subalternans, & subalternata. Nam obiectum huius, continetur sub obiecto alterius: & conclusiones eius habent intrinsecam dependentiam, à conclusionibus alterius, per quas probantur, quasi per principia, & nihilominus, sunt habitus, & scientiæ specie distincti, apud Ar. & omnes. Et multò meliùs distinguentur, habitus scientiæ, & principiorum, licèt assensus conclusionum, habeat intrinsecam dependentiam, ab assensu principiorum: cùm habeant rationes formales diuersas: vt probatum est. In scientiis verò vniuersalioribus, alia est ratio: quia conclusiones, non solùm se præsupponunt, & intrinsecam habent dependentiam à principiis, eodem modo se præsupponentibus, ac dependentibus: sed omnes etiam conclusiones, habent eandem rationem formalem assentiendi, per medium demonstratiuum, & nihilominus etiam in his scientiis; distinctus ponitur habitus, pro principiis, & conclusionibus, apud Arist. & omnes.

To the argument of the same opinion the reply is that the major is false absolutely: which the subalternating and the subalternate science prove. For the object of the latter is contained under the object of the former, and its conclusions have an intrinsic dependence on the conclusions of the other, through which they are proved, as through principles; and nevertheless they are habits and sciences distinct in species, according to Aristotle and all. And much better will the habits of science and of principles be distinguished, although the assent to conclusions has an intrinsic dependence on the assent to principles, since they have diverse formal ratios, as has been proved. But in the more universal sciences the reasoning is different: because the conclusions not only presuppose one another and have an intrinsic dependence on the principles, which presuppose and depend in the same manner, but all the conclusions also have the same formal ratio of assenting, through a demonstrative middle; and nevertheless even in these sciences a distinct habit is posited for principles and for conclusions, according to Aristotle and all.

### An euidentia pertineat ad essentiam scientiæ — Whether evidence pertains to the essence of science.

> *An euidentia pertineat ad essentiam scientiæ.*

[…]

> 27 HOc est secundum explicandum de scientia, pertinens ad essentiã eius, *An videlicet euidentia sit ei essentialis*.
