Et [p. 700] quia prædicata essentialia cuiuscunque rei, & ex eius definitione: constat, necesse est definitionem scientiæ afferre, eamque explicare: vt ex eius explicatione, constare possit, an inter prædicata essentialia eius numerari debeat euidentia: quia si numeranda non sit, nec essentialis ei censebitur.

27 This is the second thing to be explained concerning science, pertaining to its essence: namely, whether evidence is essential to it. And [p. 700] because the essential predicates of anything whatever are established from its definition, it is necessary to bring forward the definition of science and to explain it, so that from its explanation it may be established whether evidence ought to be numbered among its essential predicates: because if it is not to be numbered among them, it will not be judged essential to it either.

> Arist. 2. cap. huius libri definiuit scientiam in concreto, dicens: *Scire, est rem per causam cognoscere, & quod illius est causa: & quod impossibile est, aliter se habere*: quam definitionẽ, si ad scientiam in abstracto applicemus, sub forma quidditatiuæ definitionis, hoc modo assignari potest: *Scientia, est cognitio vera & certa rei necessariæ, per propriam causam.* In qua *Cognitio*, habet rationem generis, quia in ea conuenit scientia cum cæteris actibus intellectus. Potest autem cognitio sumi, pro actuali, vel habituali, vel pro vtraque: & sic definietur vtraque scientia, actualis, & habitualis. *Actualis*, est assensus conclusionis. *Habitualis* verò, habitus per eam genitus. In communi autem modo loquendi, pro habituali potiùs sumitur. *Reliquæ* verò particulæ ponuntur pro differentia, vt per eas distinguatur à cæteris habitibus intellectus. Nam *Vera*, dicitur, cognitio vt distinguatur ab errore. *Certa*, vt distinguatur ab opinione, & cæteris cognitionibus, quibus nõ repugnat subesse falsum: per *Rem necessariam*, separatur à prudentia, & arte, quæ versantur circa contingentia. Particula denique *per causam* distinguit scientiã ab habitu principiorũ, qui non procedit per medium, sed immediatè assentitur veritati, habita notitia terminorum.

Aristotle, in ch. 2 of this book, defined science in the concrete, saying: To know is to know a thing through its cause, and that it is the cause of that thing, and that it is impossible for it to be otherwise. Which definition, if we apply it to science in the abstract, can be assigned under the form of a quidditative definition in this manner: Science is the true and certain cognition of a necessary thing through its proper cause. In which cognition has the ratio of genus, because in it science agrees with the other acts of the intellect. Now cognition can be taken for actual or habitual cognition, or for both; and in this way both sciences, actual and habitual, are defined. Actual science is the assent to the conclusion; habitual science the habit generated through it. But in the common manner of speaking it is taken rather for habitual science. The remaining particles are posited in place of the difference, so that through them it may be distinguished from the other habits of the intellect. For a cognition is called true so that it may be distinguished from error; certain, so that it may be distinguished from opinion and the other cognitions to which it is not repugnant that falsity underlie them; by of a necessary thing it is separated from prudence and art, which are concerned with contingent things. Finally, the particle through its cause distinguishes science from the habit of principles, which does not proceed through a middle, but assents immediately to the truth, once the cognition of the terms is had.

> 28 Distinguitur etiam à scientia, quæ habetur à posteriori, & per effectum: quam non comprehendit Arist. sub hac definitione: sed solam scientiam perfectam, quæ vocatur propter quid. Possumus autem definitionem vtrique communem, & quasi genericam designare, comprehendentem vtramque, mutata solùm vltima particula: *per causam*, & posita huius loco, particula, *per demonstrationem*: & erit hæc: *Scientia est cognitio vera, rei necessariæ, per demonstrationem.*

28 It is distinguished also from the science which is had a posteriori and through the effect, which Aristotle does not comprehend under this definition, but only perfect science, which is called propter quid. But we can designate a definition common to both, and as it were generic, comprehending both, by changing only the last particle, through its cause, and putting in its place the particle through demonstration; and it will be this: Science is the true cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

> Sed an completæ sint istæ definitiones, vel desit eis particula, euidens, saltem intelligenda: de hoc est præsens quæstio. Quæ vt meliùs intelligatur, explicandi, ac distinguendi sunt isti tres termini, *Certitudo, Necessitas, & Euidentia. Certitudo*, est firma adhæsio intellectus alicui obiecto, absque dubitatione, vel formidine. Ita eam definiunt Scholastici Doctores, in 3 d. 26. præsertim D. Th. quæst. 2. art. 4 Bonau. q. 4. Durand. in 4. d. 37. q. 8. Cæterùm firma adhæsio intellectus duplex est, *Apparens, & Vera. Apparens* est, quando intellectus, ex aliqua ratione probabili, atque ex efficaci applicatione voluntatis, tenaciter [p. 701] inhæret alicui obiecto: & de hac apparenti adhæsione, intelligitur illud axioma, positum ab Arist 7. lib. Ethi. c. 3. *Ita firmiter adhærent nonnulli suis opinionibus falsis, aut erroribus, sicut alij adhærent scientiis.* De hac verò firma adhæsione, non intelligitur definitio: sed de *Vera*, qua intellectus propter veritatem ipsam rei, aut solidam, ac firmam rationem, seu infallibililem auctoritatem, adhæret alicui obiecto. Certitudo autem sic explicata, habet illos tres gradus, quos superiùs explicuimus.

But whether these definitions are complete, or whether they lack the particle evident, which must at least be understood: of this is the present question. For its better understanding, these three terms must be explained and distinguished: Certitude, Necessity, and Evidence. Certitude is the firm adhesion of the intellect to some object, without doubt or fear. So the Scholastic Doctors define it, in 3, d. 26, especially St. Thomas, q. 2, a. 4; Bonaventure, q. 4; Durandus, in 4, d. 37, q. 8. But the firm adhesion of the intellect is twofold, Apparent and True. It is apparent when the intellect, from some probable reason and from an efficacious application of the will, tenaciously [p. 701] adheres to some object; and it is of this apparent adhesion that the axiom laid down by Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, is understood: Some adhere as firmly to their false opinions or errors as others adhere to the sciences. But the definition is not understood of this firm adhesion, but of the True one, by which the intellect, on account of the truth of the thing itself, or of a solid and firm reason, or of an infallible authority, adheres to some object. Certitude, then, explained in this way, has those three degrees which we explained above.

> *Necessitas* verò, in ordine ad propositionem sumpta, de qua non loquimur, est determinatio intellectus ad veritatem: & propositio necessaria erit, quæ ita est vera: vt repugnet esse falsam. quod explicuit Arist, illo verbo, *impossibile aliter se habere.* Habet autem necessitas eosdem gradus quos certitudo.

But Necessity, taken in order to a proposition (of which we are not speaking), is the determination of the intellect to truth; and a proposition will be necessary which is true in such a way that it is repugnant for it to be false; which Aristotle expressed by that phrase, impossible to be otherwise. And necessity has the same degrees as certitude.

> *Euidentia* denique, addit supra firmam adhæsionem manifestationem veritatis, sub claritate alicuius luminis: ita vt euidens dicatur obiectum, quasi clarum, ac perspicuum, seu manifestum. Hanc euidentiam seu claritatem habent principia ex se, scientia veró participatam à principiis. Et de certitudine, ac necessitate, nemo potest dubitare, quin sint essentiales sciẽtiæ, cùm vtraque sit expressè posita in definitione Arist. De sola igitur euidentia, cùm non sit expressa, quæstio esse potest: *An sit ei essentialis*? & ideo in definitione subintelligenda, aut declaranda.

Finally, Evidence adds over firm adhesion the manifestation of the truth under the clarity of some light, so that an object is called evident as being clear and perspicuous, or manifest. This evidence or clarity principles have of themselves, but science has it as participated from the principles. And of certitude and necessity no one can doubt that they are essential to science, since both are expressly set down in Aristotle’s definition. Concerning evidence alone, therefore, since it is not expressed, there can be a question: Whether it is essential to it? and therefore whether it must be understood, or declared, in the definition.

> Et prima opinio negat *essentialem esse*, ita Massius cap præsenti, q. 3. conclusione 1. & 2. Probat, primò: Quia scientia subalternata, est vera scientia, & tamen non est euidens: ergo euidentia, non est de ratione scientiæ. Minorem probat: quia potest contingere, quòd sit sine subalternante, & solùm habeat principia accepta, per testimonium eius, qui habet subalternantem: & tunc patet non esse euidentem. Et, etiamsi cum subalternante sit, intra tamen proprios limites, nescit reducere sua principia vsque ad prima & indemonstrabilia: ergo non habet euidentiam eorum, & ex consequenti neque conclusionum, quæ ex eis deducit. Nihilominus vtroque modo vera scientia est, cùm sit de re necessaria, per euidentem consequentiam.

And the first opinion denies that it is essential. So Diego Mas, on the present chapter, q. 3, conclusions 1 and 2. He proves it, first: Because subalternate science is true science, and yet it is not evident; therefore evidence is not of the ratio of science. He proves the minor: because it can happen that it exists without the subalternating science and has only principles accepted through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science; and then it is plain that it is not evident. And even if it is together with the subalternating science, still within its own limits it does not know how to reduce its principles all the way to the first and indemonstrable ones; therefore it does not have evidence of them, and consequently neither of the conclusions which it deduces from them. Nevertheless in both ways it is true science, since it is of a necessary thing through an evident consequence.

> Secundò probat: Quia Theologia, quæ deducitur ex principiis diuinæ fidei, per veras demonstrationes, non est euidens cùm ex principiis obscuris fidei, non possit colligi euidens cõclusio: & tamen est vera scientia, vt est manifestum: ergo euidentia non pertinet ad essentiam scientiæ.

Second, he proves it: Because Theology, which is deduced from the principles of divine faith through true demonstrations, is not evident, since from the obscure principles of faith an evident conclusion cannot be gathered; and yet it is true science, as is manifest; therefore evidence does not pertain to the essence of science.

> Hæc tamen sententia duo asserit falsa, Primum, *Quòd scientia subalternata, existens sine subalternante, & habens principia [p. 702] solùm accepta per testimonium eius, qui habet subalternantem, sit vera scientia.* Nam si principia solùm habentur, per testimonium illius, assensus eorum solùm erit fides humana, cui potest subesse falsum: ergo non possunt esse causa conclusionis certæ, aut scientificæ: alioqui effectus esset perfectior, quàm propria causa.

This opinion, however, asserts two false things. First, that subalternate science, existing without the subalternating science, and having principles [p. 702] accepted only through the testimony of him who has the subalternating science, is true science. For if the principles are held only through the testimony of that man, the assent to them will be only human faith, under which falsehood can lie; therefore they cannot be the cause of a certain or scientific conclusion; otherwise the effect would be more perfect than its proper cause.

> 31 Secundum quod asserit, est, *Scientiam subalternatam, etiam dum cum subalternante existit, in eodem homine, esse scientiã, intra proprios limites: sed non esse euidentem*: quia nescit reducere suas conclusiones, vsque ad principia indemonstrabilia. Hæc autem duo, manifestam continent repugnantiam: quia si nescit reducere principia: ergo non erit scientia. Probatur euidenter consequentia ex his verbis Aristotelis, quæ habentur cap. 2. huius libri: *Non scit, qui demonstrationem horum non habet*, &c. Hoc est, præmissarum, ex quibus constat demonstratio: quas si non scit reducere, non erunt sibi certæ: ergo nec certam cõclusionem ex eis deducere vllo modo poterit.

31 The second thing it asserts is that subalternate science, even when it exists together with the subalternating science in the same man, is science within its own limits, but is not evident, because it does not know how to reduce its conclusions all the way to the indemonstrable principles. But these two things contain a manifest repugnance: because if it does not know how to reduce its principles, then it will not be science. The consequence is evidently proved from these words of Aristotle, which are found in ch. 2 of this book: He does not know who does not have the demonstration of these, etc., that is, of the premises of which the demonstration consists; and if he does not know how to reduce them, they will not be certain to him; therefore neither will he be able in any way to deduce a certain conclusion from them.

> *Sulalterna igitur scientia*, simul cum subalternante existens duobus modis consideratur. Primo: *Intra proprios limites præcise*: hoc est, non considerando continuationem, aut vnionẽ, quam habet cum subalternante: & hoc modo, nec est scientia, vt probauimus capite 10. nec est euidens. Sed erit opinio quædam. Secundo consideratur, *vt continuata, vel vnita cum subalternante* in qua continuatione consistit formaliter subalternatio: & ideo solùm, vt sic sumpta, est formaliter subalternata: & hoc modo vera scientia est, & euidens: quia per talem continuationem auxilio subalternantis, reducit sua principia, vsque ad prima indemonstrabilia.

Subalternate science, then, existing together with the subalternating science, is considered in two ways. First, precisely within its own limits: that is, without considering the continuation or union which it has with the subalternating science; and in this way it is neither science, as we proved in chapter 10, nor is it evident, but it will be a kind of opinion. Second, it is considered as continued or united with the subalternating science, in which continuation subalternation formally consists; and therefore only as taken in this way is it formally subalternate; and in this way it is true science, and evident, because through such a continuation, by the help of the subalternating science, it reduces its principles all the way to the first indemonstrable ones.

> 32 Et, si dicas. Ipsam non reducere sua principa: sed subalternantem. Respondeo, Subalternantem reducere, vt sibi continuantur subalternata: & non alio modo: & hoc idem est, ac subalternatam reducere, vt continuatur cum subalternante. Ita enim fit, qui habet vtramque, habeat euidentiam principiorum subalternatæ, ratione continuationis: & ideo subalternata sit in eo vera scientia, & euidens.

32 And if you say: It is not it that reduces its principles, but the subalternating science; I reply: the subalternating science reduces them as the subalternate science is continued with it, and in no other way; and this is the same as the subalternate science reducing them as it is continued with the subalternating science. For thus it comes about that he who has both has evidence of the principles of the subalternate science by reason of the continuation; and therefore the subalternate science is in him true science, and evident.

> Vt igitur nostram sententiam explicemus, notandum est, *Scientiam* duobus modis sumi posse. Primo, *In quantum per lumen naturale intellectus haberi potest*: & hanc tantùm definiuit Aristoteles quia hanc tantùm potuit cognoscere. Secundo modo, potest considerari vniuersalius, prout solùm dicit assensum conclusionis, habitum per demonstrationem ex præmissis, siue per lumen naturale, siue per aliud quodcunque cognitis: quarum tamen certum habeat assensum [p. 703], siue per reductionem ad prima indemonstrabilia, siue alio modo.

In order, then, to explain our view, it should be noted that Science can be taken in two ways. First, insofar as it can be had through the natural light of the intellect; and Aristotle defined only this, because only this could he know. In the second way it can be considered more universally, as it says only the assent to a conclusion had through demonstration from premises known whether by natural light or by any other whatever, of which, however, it has a certain assent, [p. 703] whether by reduction to the first indemonstrable principles, or in another way.

> 33 Quia distinctione supposita, duabus conclusionibus continetur nostra sententia. Prima est, *Ad essentiã scientiæ primo modo consideratæ, pertinet euidentia*. Probatur: Quia si quis demonstrat conclusionem, per causam, vel effectum, cognitum per lumen naturale intellectus, necesse est, habeat euidentiam præmissarum: cùm sibi sint manifestæ sub claritate luminis naturalis: & consequentia, etiam eodem modo est sibi euidens: ergo conclusio, ex eis deducta, etiam est euidens. Probatur consequentia: quia ex causa per se omni ex parte euidenti, euidens quoque effectus debet sequi: sed ex tali assensu conclusionis euidenti generatur habitus scientiæ: ergo erit etiam euidens essentialiter. Quamuis autem euidentia, sit prædicatum essentiale scientiæ, eam tamen non expressit Aristot. in definitione quia satis manifestum erat, in verbis eiusdem definitionis hanc contineri. Si autem quis velit eam exprimere, sic dicet: Scientia est, cognitio vera, certa, & euidens, rei necessariæ per causam. Et si velit definire omnem scientiam, quia, & propter quid, sic dicet: Scientia est cognitio vera, certa, & euidens, rei necessariæ, per demonstrationem.

33 This distinction supposed, our view is contained in two conclusions. The first is: To the essence of science considered in the first way evidence pertains. This is proved: Because if someone demonstrates a conclusion through a cause or an effect known by the natural light of the intellect, he must have evidence of the premises, since they are manifest to him under the clarity of the natural light; and the consequence also is evident there in the same way; therefore the conclusion deduced from them is also evident. The consequence is proved: because from a per se cause evident in every respect an evident effect too must follow; but from such an evident assent to the conclusion the habit of science is generated; therefore it too will be evident essentially. But although evidence is an essential predicate of science, Aristotle did not express it in the definition, because it was sufficiently manifest that it was contained in the words of that same definition. But if someone wishes to express it, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through its cause. And if he wishes to define all science, both quia and propter quid, he will say thus: Science is a true, certain, and evident cognition of a necessary thing through demonstration.

> Secunda conclusio: *Ad essentiam scientiæ sub vniuersaliori illa acceptione sumptæ, non pertinent euidentia*: sed ita potest definiri: Scientia est cognitio rei certa per demonstrationem. Probatur hæc: Quia Theologia, quæ habetur ex principiis diuinæ fidei, est cognitio rei certa, per veram demonstrationem: ergo aliquo modo est scientia Propter consequentiam, quia non est opinio, nec fides humana, cùm sit certa: nec est fides diuina, quia fides non innititur demonstrationi, nec alteri argumentationi, sed solùm testimonio diuino: conclusio verò Theologica, non innititur immediatè testimonio sed demonstrationi: licèt altera præmissarum, vel vtraque innitatur testimonio diuino, & sit assensus fidei.

Second conclusion: To the essence of science taken in that more universal acceptation evidence does not pertain; but it can be defined thus: Science is a certain cognition of a thing through demonstration. This is proved: Because Theology, which is had from the principles of divine faith, is a certain cognition of a thing through true demonstration; therefore in some way it is science. The consequence is proved: because it is not opinion, nor human faith, since it is certain; nor is it divine faith, because faith does not rest on demonstration nor on any other argumentation, but only on divine testimony; whereas a Theological conclusion does not rest immediately on testimony but on demonstration, although one of the premises, or both, rests on divine testimony, and so is an assent of faith.

> Sed nec eadem conclusio Theologica, pertinet ad intellectum, qui est habitus principiorum: cùm sit deducta per demõstrationem: ergo pertinet ad habitum scientiæ. Probo iterum consequentiam: quia nec datur, nec dari potest alius habitus ad quem possit pertinere. Si ergo Theologia est scientia, licèt imperfecta: quia non est euidens: aliquo modo conuenire debet, cum scientia primo modo accepta: & ideo aliqua ratio scientiæ communis vtrique, abstrahi potest, ad cuius essentiam non pertineat euidentia. Et hæc est: quæ sub hac ratione communi considerata, definita à nobis est.

But neither does the same Theological conclusion pertain to understanding, which is the habit of principles, since it is deduced through demonstration; therefore it pertains to the habit of science. I prove the consequence again: because there is not, nor can there be, any other habit to which it could pertain. If, then, Theology is science, though imperfect because it is not evident, it must agree in some way with science taken in the first way; and therefore some ratio of science common to both can be abstracted, to whose essence evidence does not pertain. And this is the one which, considered under this common ratio, has been defined by us.

[p. 704]

### An scientia sit de singularibus, & de contingentibus, & entibus per accidens — Whether there is science of singulars, of contingents, and of beings per accidens.

> *An scientia sit de singularibus, de contingentibus & entibus per accidens.*

[…]

> DE his tribus separatim breuissimè dicemus quid tenendum sit. Et primò *de singularibus*, distinguendum est: nam quædam sunt, singularia quæ simul sunt species, vel eminenter, ac perfectissimè cõtinent perfectionem specificam: vt Deus, & Angeli: & vt plures tenent, in Angelis, non distinguitur differentia specifica ab indiuiduali. Et de his singularibus: certum est apud omnes, perfectissimam scientiam haberi posse. Alia sunt singularia, in quibus distinguitur differentia indiuidualis ab specifica, & extra rationem illius est: vt sunt corruptibilia: & fortè etiam Angeli id habent: nam valdè probabile est: multiplicare eos posse, sub eadem specie: & de his, potest esse dubium, *An possint esse obiecta scientiæ?* vel, *An scientia solùm possit esse de vniuersalibus.*

oncerning these three we shall say very briefly and separately what is to C           be held. And first, concerning singulars, a distinction must be made: for some are singulars which are at the same time species, or contain the specific perfection eminently and most perfectly, as God and the angels; and, as many hold, in the angels the specific difference is not distinguished from the individual one. And concerning these singulars it is certain among all that the most perfect science can be had. Others are singulars in which the individual difference is distinguished from the specific one and is outside its ratio, as are corruptible things; and perhaps the angels too have this, for it is very probable that they can be multiplied under the same species; and concerning these there can be a doubt whether they can be objects of science, or whether science can be only of universals.

> 35 Deinde distinguenda est *scientia*: quia tribus modis sumi potest. Primò, pro *certa & euidenti cognitione rei per discursum habita*, aut sine illo, per simplicem intuitum: & de scientia hoc modo sumpta, certum est, quòd versetur circa singularia quæcunque. Nam Deus, & Angeli, per notitiam intuitiuam, sine discursu, perfectissimè cognoscunt singularia omnia: & talis eorũ notitia intuitiua, perfectissimam habet rationem scientię. Nos quoque de Deo, & Angelis possumus habere scientiam: & mediis sensibus, habemus intuitiuam cognitionem singularium sensibilium: quæ secundùm hanc acceptionem, vocari potest scientia. Secundo modo, sumitur scientia, *pro sola discursiua, habita euidentem consequentiam*, siue vera sit demonstratio, siue non. Tertiò sumitur *pro discursiua, habita tamen per veram demonstrationem.* Dubium igitur procedit de scientia his duobus modis sumpta, *An de singularibus corruptibilibus haberi possit.*

35 Next, science must be distinguished, because it can be taken in three ways. First, for a certain and evident cognition of a thing, had through discursive reasoning or without it, by simple intuition; and concerning science taken in this way it is certain that it is concerned with any singulars whatever. For God and the angels, through intuitive cognition, without discursive reasoning, know all singulars most perfectly; and such intuitive cognition of theirs has the most perfect ratio of science. We too can have science of God and the angels; and by means of the senses we have intuitive cognition of sensible singulars, which according to this acceptation can be called science. In the second way science is taken for that only which is discursive, had through an evident consequence, whether it be a true demonstration or not. In the third way it is taken for discursive science, but had through a true demonstration. The doubt, then, proceeds concerning science taken in these two ways: whether it can be had of corruptible singulars.

> Sed adhuc duobus considerantur *singularia* hæc. Primò, *Vt participant naturam specificam*, in qua conueniunt: nempe, humanam, vel aliam. Secundò, *Vt sunt distincta per proprias differentias indiuiduales*: & hoc est considerare ea, vt singularia sunt formaliter, & reduplicatiuè. Et si primo modo considerentur, certum est, etiam de illis posse esse aliquo modo scientiam. Nam cùm de specie possit esse, per se primò & immediatè scientia, erit etiam de singularibus per participationem, & applicationem eiusdem scientiæ de specie, ad illa: quia, si de homine probatur, per demonstrationem, quòd sit risibilis, etiam [p. 705] potest probari de Petro, aut Ioanne, applicando eandem demonstrationem ad illum, probandoque per eam quòd sit risibilis.

But these singulars are further considered in two ways. First, as they participate in the specific nature in which they agree, namely the human nature or another. Second, as they are distinct through their own individual differences; and this is to consider them as they are singulars formally and reduplicatively. And if they are considered in the first way, it is certain that there can also be science of them in some way. For since there can be science per se, primarily and immediately, of the species, there will also be science of the singulars through participation and application of that same science of the species to them: because, if it is proved of man through demonstration that he is risible, it [p. 705] can be proved of Peter or John, by applying the same demonstration to him and proving through it that he is risible.

> 36 Et hoc modo in scientia Theologica, demonstrantur aliqua de Christo Domino, vt homine: ex principiis fidei, & propositionibus simul euidentibus. Vt quòd sit risibilis: quia est homo, per hanc demonstrationem ei applicatam: Omnis homo est risibilis: Christus est homo: ergo Christus est risibilis.

36 And in this way, in the science of Theology, some things are demonstrated of Christ our Lord as man, from principles of faith and propositions that are at the same time evident: for instance, that he is risible because he is a man, through this demonstration applied to him: Every man is risible; Christ is a man; therefore Christ is risible.

> Tota ergo difficultas est, de eisdem singularibus, vt singularia sunt, & distincta, per proprias differentias indiuiduales, *An de illis possit esse scientia discursiua, secundo aut tertio modo sumpta.* Et quidam dicunt esse posse, alij verò omnino repugnare id, aiunt. Interim nostra sententia duabus conclusionibus explicatur. Prima est: *Scientia discursiua, per veram demonstrationem habita, non potest esse vllo modo, de singularibus sic acceptis.* Probatur euidenter: quia vera demonstratio, est verus syllogismus, dispositus in modo, & figura, & procedens ex principiis vniuersalibus indemonstralibus, cuius medium, est vera definitio, composita ex genere, & differentia: sed hæc non potest ex terminis singularibus fieri: ergo nec ptest de singularibus haberi.

The whole difficulty, then, concerns these same singulars as they are singulars and distinct through their own individual differences: whether there can be discursive science of them, taken in the second or the third way. And some say that there can, while others say that it is altogether repugnant. Meanwhile our view is explained in two conclusions. The first is: Discursive science had through true demonstration cannot in any way be of singulars taken in this way. This is proved evidently: because a true demonstration is a true syllogism, disposed in mood and figure, and proceeding from universal indemonstrable principles, whose middle is a true definition composed of genus and difference; but this cannot be made from singular terms; therefore neither can it be had of singulars.

> 37 Nam dispositio in modo, & figura, non potest reperiri in terminis impropriè syllogismus expositorius: qui nimis impropriè syllogismus est, per quandam similitudinem ad eum, qui fit in terminis vniuersalibus.

37 For disposition in mood and figure cannot be found in singular terms except improperly, as in the expository syllogism, which is a syllogism very improperly, through a certain likeness to the one that is made in universal terms.

> Secundò: Quia de singulari, vt singulare est, non potest probari, nisi proprietas singularis, sibi soli conueniens: sed per principia vniuersalia, non potest probari, nisi vniuersalis, aut communis proprietas: cùm æqualiter conueniat omnibus singularibus, hoc est, non magis vni quam alteri: ergo talis scientia non potest esse vllo modo de singularibus, vt singularia sunt. Et cùm scientia discursiua, de hac solùm dicatur propriè, & simpliciter; etiam est dicendum simpliciter, quòd de singularibus non possit esse scientia discursiua. Ideo Arist. pluribus suæ doctrinæ locis, expressè negat, & absque vlla distinctione, *quòd scientia possit esse de singularibus*, & communis modus loquendi, totius Scholæ ita sentit.

Second: Because of a singular, as it is singular, nothing can be proved except a singular property, belonging to it alone; but through universal principles nothing can be proved except a universal or common property, since it belongs equally to all the singulars, that is, no more to one than to another; therefore such science cannot in any way be of singulars as they are singulars. And since discursive science is said properly and absolutely only of this kind, it must also be said absolutely that there cannot be discursive science of singulars. Therefore Aristotle, in many places of his doctrine, expressly and without any distinction denies that there can be science of singulars, and the common manner of speaking of the whole School holds the same.

> 38 Secunda conclusio: *Naturaliter loquendò, non potest dari scientia de singularibus, vt singularia sunt etiam per euidentem consequentiam, quæ non sit demonstratio.* Probatur hac ratione: Dari scientiam de aliquo, est probare aliquam proprietatem de illo, per euidentem consequentiam: sed de singulari, vt tali, non possumus naturaliter probare aliquam proprietatem, per euidentem consequentiam: ergo nec habere veram scientiam [p. 706] de illo. Minorem probo: quia proprietas singularis, vt singularis est ea, quæ sequitur ex propria differentia indiuiduali: vel ex eo: vt per eam constituto: sed nullam differentiam indiuidualem determinatam, certò cognoscimus, neque vllam talem proprietatem: nec potest à nobis certò cognosci naturaliter, vt omnibus est manifestum: ergo nec possumus eam probare de singulari ipso per euidentem consequentiam: neque hoc modo habere scientiam adhuc impropriam, de illo.

38 Second conclusion: Speaking naturally, there cannot be science of singulars as they are singulars even through an evident consequence which is not a demonstration. This is proved by this argument: To have science of something is to prove some property of it through an evident consequence; but of a singular as such we cannot naturally prove any property through an evident consequence; therefore neither have true science Yy [p. 706] of it. I prove the minor: because the property of a singular as singular is that which follows from its own individual difference, or from the singular as constituted through it; but we know with certainty no determinate individual difference, nor any such property, nor can it be known with certainty by us naturally, as is manifest to all; therefore neither can we prove it of the singular itself through an evident consequence, nor in this way have science of it, even improper science.

### An de ente per accidens possit dari scientia — Whether there can be science of being per accidens.

> *An de ente per accidens possit dari scientia.*

[…]

> ENs *per accidens* vocatur illud, quod componitur ex pluribus entibus in actu: vt album, aut musicum: de quo dubitamus: *An possit dari scientia per veram demonstrationem habita?*

Being per accidens is the name given to that which is composed of several beings in act, as white or musician; concerning which we ask: Whether there can be science of it had through true demonstration?

> 39 Et quidam distingunt, duplex ens per accidens: Vnum, *quod resultat ex duobus entibus in actu, casu, aut fortuitò concurrentibus*: vt musicum, aut ædificator, vel etiam inuentio thesauri. Et de hoc negant scientiam dari posse, quia non solùm secundùm esse, est ens per accidens: sed neque per se cadere potest, sub consideratione intellectus: sed sicut casu coniunguntur ea, ex quibus constat: ita per accidens omnino se habent ad considerationem intellectus. Aliud est ens per accidens: *quod resultat, ex duobus naturaliter concurrentibus, & vnitis*: vt Album: Quantum, &c. & de hoc dicunt posse esse scientiam: quia licèt sit ens per accidens secundùm esse, tamen per se potest considerari ab intellectu, per se definiri, & per se possunt demonstrari passiones de illo. Nam album definimus: quòd sit disgregatiuũ visus: & quantũ: quod sit corpus habẽs partes extensas.

39 And some distinguish a twofold being per accidens. One, which results from two beings in act concurring by chance or fortuitously, as a musician or a builder, or also the finding of a treasure. And of this they deny that there can be science, because it is not only a being per accidens according to its being, but neither can it fall per se under the consideration of the intellect; but just as the things of which it consists are joined by chance, so they stand altogether per accidens in relation to the consideration of the intellect. The other is the being per accidens which results from two things concurring naturally and united, as White, Quantified, etc.; and of this they say there can be science, because although it is a being per accidens according to its being, yet it can be considered per se by the intellect, be defined per se, and attributes can be demonstrated per se of it. For we define white as that which is disgregative of sight; and quantified, as a body having extended parts.

> Nostra tamen sententia est, *Quòd de nullo ente per accidens, vt ens per accidens est, possit dari scientia*: & de ente per accidens, resultante ex duobus, casu, aut rarò concurrentibus, ita sentit expressè Arist. 6. lib. Met. text. 5. 6. & 7. Verùm vt de alio etiam quocumque id probemus: Notandum est, duobus modis posse considerari. Primò: *Vt componitur ex duobus entibus in actu, per modum aggregationis*, hoc est nullo ordine in eis considerato: talis est cumulus, tale album, & musicum: vt solùm in eis consideramus, vnum aggregatum ex multis actualibus. Secundò: Considerari potest, *vt duobus constat ordinatis*: nempe, vno vt determinabili, alio vt determinante. Et primo modo consideratum, dicitur *vnum per accidens omnibus modis*. Quare de illo non potest esse scientia.

Our view, however, is that there can be science of no being per accidens as it is a being per accidens; and concerning being per accidens resulting from two things concurring by chance or rarely, Aristotle expressly holds this, Metaph. bk. 6, texts 5, 6, and 7. But in order that we may prove it of any other also, it should be noted that it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is composed of two beings in act by way of aggregation, that is, with no order considered in them: such is a heap, such is white and musician, as we consider in them only one aggregate of many actual things. Second, it can be considered as consisting of two things ordered, namely one as determinable, the other as determining. And considered in the first way it is called one per accidens in every way. Wherefore there cannot be science of it.

> 40 Prob. hoc. Quia nec habet vllo modo vnã naturam, nec vnam rationem: quare non potest vna definitione explicari: [p. 707] nec habere determinatas passiones: quæ de illo demonstrari possint. Ideo doctrina Arist. loco citato, ad omne ens per accidens se extendit: Si verò consideretur secundo modo: licèt sit vnum per accidens entitate, est tamen vnum per se ordine: & ideo potest definiri vna definitione, quo pacto definitur album, & quantum, illis definitionibus, quas adduximus. Potest etiam habere determinatas passiones, quę de illo probentur. Et de *numero sonoro*, hoc modo sumpto, ac de *linea, visuali*, tanquam de propriis obiectis, agunt musica, & perspectiua, vt vidimus c. 10. quæ sunt veræ scientiæ.

40 This is proved: Because it has in no way one nature, nor one ratio; wherefore it cannot be explained by one definition, [p. 707] nor have determinate attributes which can be demonstrated of it. Therefore Aristotle’s doctrine, in the place cited, extends to every being per accidens. But if it is considered in the second way, although it is one per accidens in entity, it is nevertheless one per se in order; and therefore it can be defined by one definition, in the way in which white and quantified are defined by those definitions which we adduced. It can also have determinate attributes which are proved of it. And music and perspective treat of sonorous number, taken in this way, and of the visual line, as of their proper objects, as we saw in ch. 10, and these are true sciences.

### An de casualibus, & fortuitis detur scientia — Whether there is science of things by chance and by fortune.

> *An de casualibus & fortuitis detur scientia.*

[…]

> 41 CAsuale vocatur illud: quod ex duobus casu concurrentibus constat: vt quòd æstiuum tempus, frigidum sit, ac pluuiosum. *Fortuitum* verò: quod fit ex duobus, à fortuna (vt dicitur) concurrentibus: vt inuentio thesauri, cum effusione terræ. Hęc autem duobus modis considerari possunt. Primo, *in communi*, vt dicuntur casualia, aut fortuita. Alio modo *in particulari*, vt est hoc vel illud. Et de eis primo modo consideratis, potest esse scientia: quia ratio casualis, aut fortuiti in communi considerati, per se vna est, & per se considerabilis. Ideo Aristo. de casu, & fortuna, sic consideratis, agit 2. lib. Physicorum. Sed de eisdem consideratis in particulari, nulla scientia dari potest: quia nullam rationem habent per se considerabilem, sed prorsus contingentia sunt, & per accidens. Quare nec definiri per se possunt, nec vllam habere passionem, de se demonstrabilem.

41 That is called Chance which consists of two things concurring by chance: as that summertime is cold and rainy. But Fortuitous, that which comes about from two things concurring by fortune (as it is said): as the finding of a treasure with the digging of the earth. Now these can be considered in two ways. First, in common, as they are called chance or fortuitous things. In another way, in particular, as it is this one or that. And of them considered in the first way there can be science, because the ratio of the chance or fortuitous, considered in common, is per se one and per se considerable. Therefore Aristotle treats of chance and fortune, so considered, in Phys. bk. 2. But of the same considered in particular no science can be had, because they have no ratio per se considerable, but are utterly contingent and per accidens. Wherefore they can neither be defined per se, nor have any attribute demonstrable of them.

> TRACTATVS III.

T R E AT I S E I I I .

> De opinione, & fide humana.

On Opinion and Human Faith.

### Quidnam sit opinio, & quid fides humana — What opinion is, and what human faith is.

> *Quidnam sit opinio, & quid fides humana.*

[…]

> 42 TRia sunt explicanda, *de opinione, & fide humana*: Primum: *Quid vtraque sit*. Secundum: *Quomodo distinguatur*. Tertium: *An opinio, & consequenter fides humana possit esse simul cum scientia?* Opinionem sic definire possumus: *Opinio est assensus alicuius propositionis, non necessariæ, per medium probabile, aut sine illo. In assensu*, cõuenit cũ scientia, & aliis notitiis intellectualib. & per eandẽ particulã, censetur exclusa à ratione opinionis, quæcunq; cogitatio, aut existimatio, seu suspicio, vel dubium, per quod intellectus non determinatur [p. 708] ad aliquam partem contradictionis, nec assentitur ei: sed vel leuiter cogitat, vel quasi hæret, aut pendet, inter vtramque partem. Assensus enim, determinationem eius dicit ad vnam partem, vel alteram, quam veram reputat, vel saltem probabilem. Dicitur autem *Probabilis*, vt distinguatur à scientia, & intellectu, qui sunt assensus euidentes. A fide autem humana distinguitur, per illas particulas; *Per medium probabile: aut sine illo*: quia fides humana non habetur per medium probabile, nec sine illo: sed per testimonium fide digni.

hree things are to be explained concerning opinion and human faith. 42 T           First: What each is. Second: How they are distinguished. Third: Whether opinion, and consequently human faith, can exist together with science. Opinion we can define thus: Opinion is the assent to some non-necessary proposition, through a probable middle, or without one. In assent it agrees with science and the other intellectual cognitions; and by the same particle there is understood to be excluded from the ratio of opinion any thought whatever, or estimation, or suspicion, or doubt, by which the intellect, not determined Y y ij [p. 708] to either part of a contradiction, does not assent to it, but either thinks lightly, or as it were hesitates or hangs between the two parts. For assent says its determination to one part or the other, which it reckons true, or at least probable. And it is called Probable in order that it may be distinguished from science and understanding, which are evident assents. But it is distinguished from human faith by those particles, Through a probable middle, or without one: because human faith is not had through a probable middle, nor without one, but through the testimony of one worthy of belief.

> *Per medium etiam probabile, aut sine illo*, dicitur, vt intelligamus duplicem esse opinionem, Vnam quæ habetur sine medio per solum simplicem intuitum ipsius veritatis probabilis, quã sic definiuit Aristoteles, cap. præsenti, dicens: *Opinio est acceptio immediatæ propositionis, & non necessariæ*. Alia est, *quæ habetur per medium probabile.* Nam vel colligitur ex immediata opinione, per consequentiam euidentem, aut probabilem: vel ex propositione euidenti, per consequentiam tantùm probabilem: & vtroque modo dicitur haberi per medium probabile. Quia vel ex parte propositionis, ex qua colligitur, solùm est probabile: vel ex parte consequentiæ. Itaque sicut assensus certus, & euidens, duplex est, nempe, aut per se euidens, quem intellectus habet cognita significatione terminorum; & dicitur *Intellectus*, aut euidens per medium demonstratiuum, & dicitur, *Scientia*: Eodem modo, duplex est assensus probabilis; Vnus, *qui habetur sine medio*, cognita significatione terminorum: vt dum intellectus, cognita significatione terminorum huius propositionis, omnis mater diligit filium suum, statim nulla expectata ratione, assentitur ei probabiliter, & potest vocari, *Intellectus opinionis*. Alter assensus probabilis est, *qui habetur per medium probabile*, vt expositum est. Et ita duplex est opinio, distincta absque dubio specie, per diuersum modum assentiendi, ex sola notitia terminorum, vel per medium: & vtramque comprehendit definitio assignata.

Through a probable middle, or without one, is said also so that we may understand that opinion is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, through simple intuition alone of the probable truth itself, which Aristotle defined thus in the present chapter, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition. The other is that which is had through a probable middle. For it is gathered either from an immediate opinion, through an evident or a probable consequence; or from an evident proposition, through a merely probable consequence; and in both ways it is said to be had through a probable middle, because it is merely probable either on the part of the proposition from which it is gathered, or on the part of the consequence. Thus, just as certain and evident assent is twofold, namely either evident per se, which the intellect has once the signification of the terms is known, and it is called Understanding; or evident through a demonstrative middle, and it is called Science: in the same way probable assent is twofold. One, which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms is known: as when the intellect, having known the signification of the terms of this proposition, Every mother loves her son, at once, awaiting no reason, assents to it probably; and it can be called Understanding of opinion. The other probable assent is the one which is had through a probable middle, as has been set out. And thus opinion is twofold, distinct without doubt in species through the diverse mode of assenting, from the cognition of the terms alone, or through a middle; and the definition assigned comprehends both.

> Fides autẽ humana, sic potest definiri: *Fides humana est assensus probabilis, propter testimoniũ fide digni habitus.* Ita vt per *Assensum probabilem*, conueniat cum opinione, & distinguatur à cæteris notitiis, aut assensibus intellectus: sicut de opinione diximus, per *Testimonium* verò, ab opinione; & hæc de primo.

Human faith, on the other hand, can be defined thus: Human faith is a probable assent had on account of the testimony of one worthy of belief. So that through Probable assent it agrees with opinion and is distinguished from the other cognitions or assents of the intellect, as we said of opinion; but through Testimony it is distinguished from opinion. And so much for the first point.

### An formido sit de intrinseca ratione opinionis & humanæ fidei — Whether fear is of the intrinsic ratio of opinion and of human faith.

> *An formido sit de intrinseca ratione opinionis, & humanæ fidei.*

[…]

> HOc etiam pertinet ad explicationem quidditatis opinionis & humanæ fidei. Quod vt intelligatur, explicandum [p. 709] imprimis est: Quidnam per formidinem significetur. Et nihil aliud est, quàm timor, ne falsa sit pars, cui assentitur intellectus, aut vera opposita. Opinio enim, vt diximus, est assensus probabilis, cui non repugnat subesse falsum: quod est esse assensum quendam debilem, de cuius veritate meritò timetur, aut timeri potest: quia sic ei adhæret intellectus: vt fundamentum propter quod ei adhæret: quod est veritas ipsa per se probabilis, aut ratio per quam deduxit conclusionem ex præmissis, non sit omnino solida, nec firma, sed quæ ex propria natura deficere potest, & aliter se habere. Dubium igitur est, *An timor iste, quem vocant formidinem, pertineat ad essentiam opinionis, vel humanæ fidei.*

This too pertains to the explanation of the quiddity of opinion and human faith. In order that it may be understood, it must be explained [p. 709] first of all: What is signified by fear. And it is nothing other than an apprehension lest the part to which the intellect assents be false, or the opposite true. For opinion, as we said, is a probable assent under which it is not repugnant that falsehood lie: that is, it is a certain weak assent, of whose truth one rightly fears, or can fear, because the intellect adheres to it in such a way that the foundation on account of which it adheres to it (which is the truth itself, probable per se, or the reason through which it deduced the conclusion from the premises) is not altogether solid nor firm, but such as can fail by its own nature, and be otherwise. The doubt, then, is whether this fear, which they call apprehension, pertains to the essence of opinion or of human faith.

> 44 Prima sententia, Distinguit duplicem opinionem, *Perfectam & Imperfectam. Perfectam* opinionem vocat eam: quæ innititur testimonio fide digni: *Imperfectam* verò: quæ innititur rationibus probabilibus. Et ad essentiam illius asserit, nullo modo pertinere formidinem: quia non solùm dicit assensum determinatum vnius partis, sed firmum, ac certum: non propter firmitatem testimonij, sed propter efficacem determinationem voluntatis, ratione cuius intellectus firmiter adhæret eidem parti: nec solùm firmiter, sed etiam tenaciter: vt superiùs ex Arist. adduximus. *Imperfecta* verò opinio, formidinem habet assentialiter annexam, sine qua, nec reperitur, nec reperiri vllo modo potest. Ita Durand. in 1 q. prologi, Masius cap. præsenti, qui, ita ait tenere Capreolum, & Caiet. quos ipse citat: & quod amplius est, D. Tho. pluribus suæ doctrinæ locis, præsertim 1. 2. q. 67. art. 3. vbi ita ait: *De ratione opinionis, est quòd accipiatur vnum, cum formidine alterius oppositi*, &c.

44 The first opinion distinguishes a twofold opinion, Perfect and Imperfect. It calls perfect opinion the one which rests on the testimony of one worthy of belief; but imperfect, the one which rests on probable reasons. And it asserts that fear in no way pertains to the essence of the former, because it says not only the determinate assent to one part, but a firm and certain one: not on account of the firmness of the testimony, but on account of the efficacious determination of the will, by reason of which the intellect adheres to the same part not only firmly but also tenaciously, as we adduced above from Aristotle. But imperfect opinion has fear essentially annexed, without which it neither is found nor can in any way be found. So Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue; Diego Mas, on the present chapter, who says that Capreolus and Cajetan, whom he himself cites, hold so; and, what is more, St. Thomas in many places of his doctrine, especially 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he says thus: It is of the ratio of opinion that one part is accepted with fear of the other opposite, etc.

> Probat etiam ratione. Nam qui opinatur, iudicat, opinionem, quam ipse sequitur, posse esse falsam: ergo ex propria ratione opinandi, tenet, ne falsa sit: quare timor iste aut formido, intrinseca est opinioni.

It proves it also by reason. For he who opines judges that the opinion which he follows can be false; therefore by the very ratio of opining he fears lest it be false; wherefore this fear or apprehension is intrinsic to opinion.

> Pro solutione huius quæ. distinguenda est duplex formido. Nam alia est, *Actualis*, quæ est actualis timor, Alia *Virtualis*, seu radicalis, quæ non consistit in aliquo actuali timore, aut dubitatione: sed in eo solùm, quòd est talem esse assensum opinionis, ex parte obiecti, aut medij assentiendi, cui non repugnat subesse falsum. Et ex hac radice, nascitur aliquando actualis timor aut formido, ne opposita pars vera sit, aut falsa illa, cui intellectus assentitur: & ideo dicitur virtualis, aut radicalis formido.

For the solution of this question a twofold fear must be distinguished. For one is Actual, which is an actual fear; the other Virtual, or radical, which does not consist in any actual fear or doubting, but only in this: that the assent of opinion is such, on the part of the object or of the middle of assenting, that it is not repugnant to it that falsehood lie under it. And from this root there is sometimes born an actual fear or apprehension lest the opposite part be true, or that part false to which the intellect assents; and therefore it is called virtual or radical fear.

> 45 Hac supposita distinctione, Nostra sententia est, *Virtualẽ aut radicalem formidinem, ad essentiam opinionis, aut humanæ fidei [p. 710] pertinere: Actualem verò, omnino esse ei accidentalem: ita vt sæpe reperiatur sine illa.* Hæc est communis sententia ferè omnium expositorum Arist. cap. præsenti. Et probatur expresso testimonio Aristotelis, 7. libro Ethicorum, cap. 3. vbi de opinione ita loquitur: *Nam si vera opinio, & non scientia sit, ex qua continenter agunt homines, nihil ad rationem id refert: cum nonnulli ex his qui opinantur, non ambigant, sed certò se scire existiment.*

45 This distinction supposed, our view is that virtual or radical fear pertains to the essence of opinion, or of human faith Y y iij [p. 710] but that actual fear is altogether accidental to it, so that it is often found without it. This is the common opinion of almost all the expositors of Aristotle on the present chapter. And it is proved by the express testimony of Aristotle, Ethics bk. 7, ch. 3, where he speaks thus of opinion: For whether it be true opinion and not science by which men act incontinently, it makes no difference to the argument, since some of those who opine do not doubt, but think they know with certainty.

> Et probatur euidenti experientia: Quia plures sunt opiniones, non solùm in Dialectica, sed etiam in Philosophia, & Theologia, communi ferè totius scholæ consensu approbatæ, & efficacibus argumentis confirmatæ: quas sequimur, absque vllo timore, vel formidine actuali. Et aliquando videmus, aliquos ex principiis euidentibus, deducere aliquam conclusionem, per syllogismum, quem putent euidentẽ verè non nisi probabilem, & tales, certam esse existimant talem, conclusionem, licèt vera sit in eis solùm opinio: ergo repugnat simul habere timorem, ne sit falsa, aut vera opposita: quare euidens est, actualem formidinem, non esse intrinsecam opinioni, cùm sæpe inueniatur sine illa. Virtualis tamen, aut radicalis formido, his etiam opinionibus intrinseca est: cùm ex parte medii assentiendi, non repugnet eis subesse falsum.

And it is proved by evident experience: Because there are many opinions, not only in Dialectic but also in Philosophy and Theology, approved by the common consent of almost the whole School and confirmed by efficacious arguments, which we follow without any actual fear or apprehension. And sometimes we see some men deduce from evident principles some conclusion through a syllogism which they think evident, but which is in truth only probable, and such men judge the conclusion to be certain, although in them it is truly only opinion; therefore it is repugnant that they should at the same time have fear lest it be false, or the opposite true. Wherefore it is evident that actual apprehension is not intrinsic to opinion, since it is often found without it. Virtual or radical fear, however, is intrinsic even to these opinions, since on the part of the middle of assenting it is not repugnant that falsehood lie under them.

> Testimonium autem D. Tho. de hac virtuali formidine, intelligitur, non de actuali.

The testimony of St. Thomas, moreover, is understood of this virtual fear, not of the actual.

> Ad arg. verò, Concesso antecedente cum consequentia, distinguendum est consequens. Nam si de actuali timore, aut formidine intelligatur, falsum est. Si verò de virtuali, aut radicali, verum: & ideo hanc solam esse opinioni intrinsecam probat arg. non illam.

To the argument: granting the antecedent with the consequence, the consequent must be distinguished. For if it is understood of actual fear or apprehension, it is false; but if of virtual or radical fear, true; and therefore the argument proves that only this is intrinsic to opinion, not the other.

### An opinio possit esse simul cum scientia de eadem propositione, & in eodem intellectu — Whether opinion can exist together with science concerning the same proposition and in the same intellect.

> *An opinio possit esse simul cum scientia, de eadem propositione & in eodem intellectu.*

[…]

> CErtum est *opinionem simul esse posse cum scientia, de eadem re.* Quia de linea, habet scientiam Geometra, & opinionem Dialecticus, aut Metaphysicus, *An distinguatur realiter à substantia.* Nec solùm est certum, quòd in diuersis hominibus, aut intellectibus, simul esse possint de eadem re, sed etiam in eodem intellectu. Nam idem geometra, habet scientiam de linea, & potest simul habere opinionem, de distinctione eius à substantia, Ideò, non quærit titulus quæst. An de eadem re simplici, possint esse simul in eodem intellectu, sed. *An de eadem propositione.* De qua certum est etiam, in diuersis [p. 711] intellectibus *posse esse scientiam, & opinionem,*

It is certain that opinion can exist together with science concerning the same thing. For of the line the Geometer has science, and the Dialectician or Metaphysician has opinion whether it is really distinguished from substance. Nor is it certain only that they can exist at the same time concerning the same thing in diverse men or intellects, but also in the same intellect. For the same geometer has science of the line, and can at the same time have opinion about its distinction from substance. Therefore the title of the question does not ask whether they can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same simple thing, but whether concerning the same proposition. Of which it is certain also that in diverse [p. 711] intellects there can be science and opinion.

> 47 Nam fieri potest, vt aliquis habeat assensum alicuius conclusionis per veram demonstrationem, quam alter deducat ex eisdem, vel aliis principiis, per syllogismum probabilem: & ideo solùm habeat opinionem. Difficultas igitur est, *An idem homo de eadem propositione, possit simul habere scientiam, & opinionem.*

47 For it can happen that someone has the assent to some conclusion through a true demonstration which another deduces from the same or other principles through a probable syllogism, and therefore has only opinion. The difficulty, then, is whether the same man can at the same time have science and opinion concerning the same proposition.

> Sed adhuc de scientia, & opinione est distinguendum: quia quatuor modis excogitari potest, quòd simul sint. Primò, *Secundum habitum:* ita vt idem homo simul habeat habitum scientiæ, & opinionis, de eadem conclusione. Secundò: *Ita vt simul habeat assensus vtriusque.* Tertiò, *Vt simul habeat habitum scientiæ, & assensum opinionis.* Quartò, *Vt simul habeat habitum opinionis, & assensum scientiæ.* & secundùm omnes comparationes, videtur procedere quemadmodum præsens.

But a further distinction must be made concerning science and opinion, because it can be conceived in four ways that they exist at the same time. First, according to habit: so that the same man has at the same time the habit of science and of opinion concerning the same conclusion. Second, so that he has at the same time the assent of each. Third, that he has at the same time the habit of science and the assent of opinion. Fourth, that he has at the same time the habit of opinion and the assent of science. And the present question seems to proceed according to all the comparisons.

> Circa quam est prima opinio negans, Scoti in 3. d. 24. q. vnica, §. contra hæc 1. Caiet. & Soti c. præsenti, & Masij, ibidem, q 5. Probant testimonio Arist. in hoc c. vbi eandem ferè q. proposuit, *An idem obiectum, possit esse scitum & opinatum, ab eodem.* Cui respondit, non posse. Prouitque hac ratione, *Scibile est, quod non potest aliter se habere, opinabile verò, quod potest aliter se habere, vt opinabile est.* Sed repugnat, eandem rem posse aliter se habere, & non posse aliter se habere: cùm sint contradictoria: ergo repugnabit, quòd aliquid simul sit scibile, & opinabile, aut scitum, & opinatum. Atqui hæc sunt propria obiecta scientiæ, & opinionis: ergo etiam repugnabit vtramque esse simul, in eodem intellectu, de eadem propositione, ex mente Arist.

On it the first opinion is the negative one, of Scotus, in 3, d. 24, single q., § Contra haec 1; of Cajetan and Soto on the present chapter; and of Diego Mas, in the same place, q. 5. They prove it by the testimony of Aristotle in this chapter, where he proposed almost the same question, whether the same object can be known and opined by the same man. To which he answered that it cannot. And he proves it by this argument: The knowable is that which cannot be otherwise; but the opinable, that which can be otherwise, as it is opinable. But it is repugnant that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictories; therefore it will be repugnant that something be at the same time knowable and opinable, or known and opined. But these are the proper objects of science and opinion; therefore it will also be repugnant, according to the mind of Aristotle, that both exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition.

> 48 Probatur deinde ratione. Primò, *de actibus, vel assensibus.* Deinde, *de habitibus. De actibus* quidem: Quia impossibile est, eundem hominem, iudicare simul, quòd res eadem potest aliter se habere: & non potest aliter se habere: cùm hæc sint iudicia contradictoria. Sed assensus scientiæ, est iudicium actuale de conclusione, quod non potest aliter se habere: & assensus opinionis, est iudicium de eadem, quòd potest aliter se habere: ergo actualem repugnantiam continent; quare non poterunt esse simul in eodem intellectu. Et quod amplius est, assensus isti repugnant, tanquam euidens, & ineuidens: quia de intrinseca ratione vnius, est euidentia, alter verò ex propria natura ineuidens est: cùm sit cõtingens, aut ex parte principij, ex quo deducitur: aut ex parte medij probabilis, per quod deducitur. Sed euidens, & ineuidẽs opponuntur priuatiuè, sicut lumen, & tenebræ: quia euidentia est manifestatio obiecti, sub claritate luminis: ergo repugnat esse simul in eodẽ intellectu: sicut repugnat [p. 712] simul esse lucem, & tenebras: in eadem parte aëris.

48 It is proved next by reason. First, concerning the acts or assents; then concerning the habits. Concerning the acts, indeed: Because it is impossible that the same man judge at the same time that the same thing can be otherwise and cannot be otherwise, since these are contradictory judgments. But the assent of science is an actual judgment concerning the conclusion, that it cannot be otherwise; and the assent of opinion is a judgment concerning the same, that it can be otherwise; therefore they contain an actual repugnance; wherefore they cannot exist at the same time in the same intellect. And, what is more, these assents are repugnant as the evident and the inevident: because evidence is of the intrinsic ratio of the one, while the other is inevident by its own nature, since it is contingent, either on the part of the principle from which it is deduced or on the part of the probable middle through which it is deduced. But the evident and the inevident are opposed privatively, like light and darkness, because evidence is the manifestation of an object under the clarity of a light; therefore it is repugnant that they exist at the same time in the same intellect, just as it is repugnant Y y iiij [p. 712] that light and darkness exist at the same time in the same part of the air.

> 49 De habitibus verò, probant secundò: Quia actus, & habitus, versantur circa idem obiectum, & per idem medium: & habitus, est inclinatio ad actum, circa tale obiectum, & per tale medium: ergo eandem prorsus repugnantiam habent cum actibus: quare nec simul esse poterunt.

49 Concerning the habits, they prove it second: Because acts and habits are concerned with the same object and through the same middle; and a habit is an inclination to an act concerning such an object and through such a middle; therefore they have altogether the same repugnance as the acts; wherefore neither can they exist at the same time.

> Secunda opinio est Durand. in 1. quæst. prologi, nu. 20. Vbi distinguit *opinionem:* quia duobus modis, inquit, haberi potest. Primo, *ex præmissis probabilibus,* aut euidentibus, per medium probabile: & vt tale cognitum ab opinante. Secundo, *ex præmissis necessariis,* atque euidentibus, & per medium, verè quidem probabile: sed euidens reputatum ab opinante. Et si primo modo habeatur, repugnat simul esse cum scientia: tam secundùm actum quàm secundùm habitum: vt asserit prima opinio: cum qua conuenit in hoc. Si verò habeatur secundo modo, simul esse possunt: tam secundùm actus, quàm secundùm habitus: in quo eidem opinioni contradicit.

The second opinion is that of Durandus, in 1, q. of the prologue, no. 20, where he distinguishes opinion: for, he says, it can be had in two ways. First, from probable premises, or from evident ones, through a probable middle, and one known as such by the one who opines. Second, from necessary premises, and evident ones, and through a middle that is truly probable, but reckoned evident by the one who opines. And if it is had in the first way, it is repugnant that it exist at the same time with science, both according to act and according to habit, as the first opinion asserts, with which it agrees in this. But if it is had in the second way, they can exist at the same time, both according to the acts and according to the habits; in which it contradicts the same opinion.

> Ideo probat hoc secundum tali arg. Tota repugnantia assensus opinionis, & scientiæ, prouenit ex eo, quòd per vnum iudicatur, conclusionem non posse aliter se habere, per aliud verò, posse aliter se habere: sed dum opinio habetur, per medium euidens existimatum, & ex præmissis euidentibus, iudicatur, conclusionem non posse aliter se habere: sicut per assensum scientiæ: ergo nulla restat in eis repugnãtia, vel oppositio, propter quam simul esse non possint. Quinimo conformantur omnino: quia per vtrumque iudicatur conclusio necessaria: & ideo, quòd non possit aliter se habere. Duæ autem causæ conformes, bene possunt ad eundem effectum concurrere: &, si assensus hoc modo non repugnant, euidens erit non repugnare habitus: qui propter assensus tantùm repugnare possunt.

Therefore he proves this second point by such an argument. The whole repugnance of the assent of opinion and of science comes from this: that by the one it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, but by the other that it can be otherwise. But when opinion is had through a middle thought to be evident, and from evident premises, it is judged that the conclusion cannot be otherwise, just as by the assent of science; therefore there remains in them no repugnance or opposition on account of which they could not exist at the same time. On the contrary, they are altogether in conformity, because by both the conclusion is judged necessary, and therefore such that it cannot be otherwise. But two conformable causes can well concur to the same effect; and if the assents are not repugnant in this way, it will be evident that the habits are not repugnant, which can be repugnant only on account of the assents.

> 50 Tertia opinio est, quorundam modernorum, omnino opposita his duabus: Quia affirmat, *scientiam, & opinionem simul esse posse, circa eandem propositionem, in eodem intellectu, tam secundùm actus, quàm secundùm habitus,* & siue opinio habeatur per medium probabile, vt tale reputatum ab opininante, siue reputatum necessarium. Solùm de propositione, de qua est vterque assensus, distinguit hoc modo: nam duabus modis considerari potest. Primò, *Vt propositio quædam est, circa quam versatur vterque habitus,* vel assensus. Secundò: *Vt est conclusio demonstrationis,* vel syllogismi probabilis, & prima consideratio, inquit, quasi materialis est: secunda, quasi formalis: Quia vna & eadem est propositio, circa quam versantur: sed illa eadem, est conclusio vtriusque syllogismi, qui cùm distinguantur specie [p. 713], propositio eadem, est quasi duplex conclusio formaliter, atque specie distincta: vnde fit, de eadem quidem propositione, esse vtrumque assensum, & habitum. Sed non de eadem conclusione, at de diuersis formaliter. Et hanc dicunt esse sententiam Alexandri Alensis 3. p. q. 79. memb. 3. D. Bonau. in 3. dist. 24. q. 2. art. 3. Durand. q. 1. prologi, & in 3. dist. 31. q. 4. Altisiodorensis lib. 3. Summæ, tit. 3. q. 4. & 5. Rich. in 3. dist. 15. qu. 1. & Villalpandei cap. præsenti, atque etiam D. Th. 1. 2. qu. 67. art. 3. vbi concedit eandem propositionem posse cognosci, per diuersa media: euidens, & probabile: tanquam per medium perfectum, & imperfectum, quæ non omnino repugnãt, quod repetit 3. p. q. 9. art. 3. ad 2. vbi P. Franciscus Suarius eandem sententiam sequitur.

50 The third opinion is that of certain moderns, altogether opposed to these two, because it affirms that science and opinion can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, in the same intellect, both according to act and according to habit, and whether the opinion is had through a probable middle reckoned as such by the one who opines, or reckoned necessary. Only concerning the proposition of which each assent is, does it distinguish in this way: for it can be considered in two ways. First, as it is a certain proposition about which each habit or assent is concerned. Second, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, or of a probable syllogism. And the first consideration, it says, is as it were material, the second as it were formal: because there is one and the same proposition about which they are concerned; but that same proposition is the conclusion of each syllogism, and since these are distinguished in species, [p. 713] the same proposition is as it were a twofold conclusion, formally and specifically distinct; whence it comes about that each assent and habit is indeed of the same proposition, but not of the same conclusion, rather of conclusions formally diverse. And they say this is the opinion of Alexander of Hales, 3 p., q. 79, memb. 3; St. Bonaventure, in 3, d. 24, q. 2, a. 3; Durandus, q. 1 of the prologue, and in 3, d. 31, q. 4; William of Auxerre, Summa bk. 3, tit. 3, q. 4 and 5; Richard of Middleton, in 3, d. 15, q. 1; and Villalpando on the present chapter; and also St. Thomas, 1-2, q. 67, a. 3, where he grants that the same proposition can be known through diverse middles, an evident and a probable one, as through a perfect and an imperfect middle, which are not altogether repugnant; which he repeats in 3 p., q. 9, a. 3, ad 2, where Father Francisco Suárez follows the same opinion.

> 51 Probant primò: Quia tota repugnantia, ob quam simul esse non possunt assensus opinionis & scientiæ, de eadem propositione est, qui repugnat, quod simul iudicetur, posse aliter se habere, & non posse: cùm duo hæc iudicia sint contradictoria: hoc autem ita esset, si per idem medium vtrumque esset iudicandum. Sed cùm id fiat, per diuersa media, nullam contineret repugnantiam, aut contradictionem: quia intellectum iudicare, propositionem non posse aliter se habere, vt est conclusio demonstrationis: & posse aliter se habere, vt est conclusio probabilis syllogismi, nullo modo repugnat: nec opponuntur contradictoriè, duo hæc iudicia, comparata ad diuersa media. Quod præsertim verum est, cùm actualis formido, non sit opinioni intrinseca: nec sit necessarium opinantem actu iudicare, quòd possit aliter se habere conclusio. Imò possit iudicare contrarium, vt notauit Durand.

51 They prove it first: Because the whole repugnance on account of which the assents of opinion and science concerning the same proposition cannot exist at the same time is that it is repugnant that it be judged at the same time that it can be otherwise and cannot, since these two judgments are contradictory. But this would be so if each were to be judged through the same middle. But since this is done through diverse middles, it would contain no repugnance or contradiction: because it is in no way repugnant that the intellect judge that a proposition cannot be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a demonstration, and that it can be otherwise, as it is the conclusion of a probable syllogism; nor are these two judgments, compared to diverse middles, opposed contradictorily. Which is especially true since actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, nor is it necessary that the one who opines actually judge that the conclusion can be otherwise; indeed he can judge the contrary, as Durandus noted.

> Secundò: Quia simul cum demonstratione, adduci potest & solet, probabilis ratio, ad probandum eandem conclusionem: sicut cum fide diuina, ad credendum eandem veritatem, ergo assentitur simul intellectus, propter vtrumque medium: & ideo vtrumque habebit suum effectum, qui est assensus probabilis, & scientificus, simulque erunt, alioqui frustra adduceretur vtrumque medium.

Second: Because together with a demonstration a probable reason can be, and usually is, adduced to prove the same conclusion, just as together with divine faith, for believing the same truth; therefore the intellect assents at the same time on account of both middles; and therefore each will have its own effect, which is the probable and the scientific assent, and they will exist at the same time; otherwise each middle would be adduced in vain.

> 52 Nostra sententia, quasi media est, & vna conclusione explicatur: *Scientia, & opinio secundùm habitus, possunt simul esse in eodem intellectu, de eadem propositione, non tamen secundùm assensus vel actus.* Per primam partem: Excluditur prima opinio, & ex parte secunda. Per secundam verò partem: Excluditur etiam ex parte secunda, & etiam ex parte tertia. Cæterùm nostram sententiam tenent authores illi, quos pro se citat vltima opinio: vt constabit eos legenti: videbit namque (nisi ego fallor [p. 714]) de solis habitibus concedere, quòd simul esse possint, non de assensibus. Et hic est sensus, D. Th. præsertim in vltimo loco si verba eius attentè considerentur.

52 Our view is as it were a middle one, and is explained in one conclusion: Science and opinion according to habit can exist at the same time in the same intellect concerning the same proposition, but not according to assent or act. By the first part the first opinion is excluded, and in part the second. By the second part, the second is also excluded in part, and the third as well. Moreover, those authors whom the last opinion cites for itself hold our view, as will be plain to one who reads them; for he will see (unless I am mistaken [p. 714] ) that they grant concerning the habits alone that they can exist at the same time, not concerning the assents. And this is the sense of St. Thomas, especially in the last place, if his words are attentively considered.

> Vt autem eam simul explicemus, & probemus, notandum est, *Scientiam, & opinionem, dum affirmant veritatem eiusdem propositionis, non esse oppositas contradictoriè, nec priuatiuè, imò, neque vllo genere oppositionis:* Quia contradictoriè non possunt opponi, ea quorum vtrumque affirmat: sed nec iudicia vtriusque necesse est contradictoriè opponi: ita vt per iudicium scientiæ, dicatur propositionem non posse aliter se habere, per iudicium verò opinatiuum, posse aliter se habere. Nam vt bene probant secunda & tertia sententia, necessarium non est, vt tale iudicium reperiatur in opinante: sed sæpè non reperitur, & aliquando reperitur contrarium. Porrò, nec opponuntur priuatiuè: quia assensus opinionis, non caret euidentia, nec ea propriè priuatur, sed quandam negationem eius dicit: sicut quælibet species, dicit negationem alterius: & tamen non propterea dicuntur priuatiuè, aut contradictoriè opponi: sed disparatæ esse. Et ita se habent scientia & opinio.

But in order that we may at once explain and prove it, it should be noted that science and opinion, while they affirm the truth of the same proposition, are not opposed contradictorily, nor privatively, indeed not by any kind of opposition: Because things of which each affirms cannot be opposed contradictorily; nor is it necessary that the judgments of the two be opposed contradictorily, so that by the judgment of science it is said that the proposition cannot be otherwise, but by the opinative judgment that it can be otherwise. For, as the second and third opinions prove well, it is not necessary that such a judgment be found in the one who opines; rather it is often not found, and sometimes the contrary is found. Further, neither are they opposed privatively: because the assent of opinion does not lack evidence, nor is it properly deprived of it, but it says a certain negation of it, just as any species says the negation of another; and yet they are not on that account said to be opposed privatively or contradictorily, but to be disparate. And so science and opinion stand.

> 53 Ac nec omnino disparatæ aut diuersæ sunt, sed valde similes: cùm in eundem finem ordinentur, qui est firmare veritatem in intellectu. Nisi quòd scientia id omnino efficit: opinio verò aliqua ex parte, non plenè, aut perfectè. Ideo solùm distinguuntur, tanquam perfectum, & imperfectum: vt egregiè D. Thomas ait in vltimo loco: quia scientia, est quasi forma perfecta, opinio verò quasi dispositio ad illam: & has rationes perfecti & imperfecti, habet ex propria natura, & essentia. Sed *perfectum,* & *imperfectum,* duobus modis repugnant, vel respectu duorum. Primò quidem, respectu eiusdem formæ: quia repugnat eandem formam esse, ex propria natura habitum, & dispositionem: & ita repugnat eandem qualitatem, vel habitum, simul esse scientiam, & opinionem. Secundò, repugnat in ordine ad idem subiectum: quia impossibile est, quòd idem corpus simul sit perfectè & imperfectè calidum: aut eadem pars aëris perfectè & imperfectè illuminata. Et hanc repugnantiam absque dubio habent scientia, & opinio respectu eiusdem subiecti, circa eandem propositionem. Quia opinio, non omnino, vel non plenè determinat intellectum, ad veritatem eius: nec firmum, aut stabilem efficit: sed determinat quidem infirmo quodam ac debili modo, & quasi indeterminatum aliqua ex parte relinquit: & hoc habet opinio quæcunque ex sua natura, & essentia, [p. 715] quomodocunque habeatur, etiam per medium probabile reputatum necessarium. Scientia verò, plenè, atque perfectè, & omnino determinat intellectum, ad veritatem propositionis demonstratæ, omnino etiam firmum, ac stabilem reddit.

53 And yet they are not altogether disparate or diverse, but very similar, since they are ordered to the same end, which is to make truth firm in the intellect; except that science effects this altogether, but opinion in some part, not fully or perfectly.
