Therefore they are distinguished only as the perfect and the imperfect, as St. Thomas says excellently in the last place: because science is as it were a perfect form, but opinion as it were a disposition to it; and they have these rationes of perfect and imperfect from their own nature and essence. But the perfect and the imperfect are repugnant in two ways, or in respect of two things. First, in respect of the same form: because it is repugnant that the same form be by its own nature a habit and a disposition; and thus it is repugnant that the same quality or habit be at the same time science and opinion. Second, it is repugnant in order to the same subject: because it is impossible that the same body be at the same time perfectly and imperfectly hot, or the same part of the air perfectly and imperfectly illuminated. And this repugnance science and opinion without doubt have in respect of the same subject, concerning the same proposition. Because opinion does not altogether, or not fully, determine the intellect to its truth, nor make it firm or stable; but it determines it indeed in a certain infirm and weak manner, and leaves it as it were undetermined in some part; and every opinion whatever has this from its nature and essence, [p. 715] however it is had, even through a probable middle reckoned necessary. But science fully, perfectly, and altogether determines the intellect to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and also renders it altogether firm and stable.

> 54 Ex quibus vtraque pars nostræ sententiæ efficaciter probari potest. Primò quidem, Quòd scientia, & opinio simul esse non possunt secundùm actus, vel assensus contra secundam & tertiam opinionem, hoc argumento: Impossibile est aliquid simul esse plenè, atque omnino determinatum, & non plenè, atque omnino determinatum circa eandem rem, cùm contradictoriè hæc opponantur. Sed per assensum scientificum, plenè atque omnino determinatur intellectus, ad veritatem propositionis demonstratæ, firmusque & stabilis in ea redditur: & per assensum opinionis, nec omnino determinatur, nec firmus, & stabilis efficitur: ergo repugnat simul esse hæc duo in intellectu, circa eandem veritatem. At dices pro tertia opinione concludere argum. hoc, respectu eiusdem medii, non verò ratione diuersorum repugnare, quod vtroque modo simul se habeat. Igitur probatur efficaciter, quod etiam per diuersa media repugnet: quia simul esse conuictum intellectum, & non esse conuictum, circa eandem veritatem: vndecunque id proueniat, siue per idem, aut diuersum medium, planè repugnat, cùm sint esse simul, & non esse respectu eiusdem: ergo non tollit difficultatem argumenti, quòd id fiat per diuersa media. Et si per diuersa media id fieri potest, sequitur assensum scientificum, & erroneum simul esse posse, circa eandem propositionem: ita, vt simul iudicet intellectus, veram esse, & falsam: veram quidem per demonstrationem, falsam verò per syllogismum probabilem. Tunc enim cessabit oppositio: quia solum esse dicitur respectu eiusdem, non verò respectu diuersorum mediorum: quæ tamen absurda sunt.

54 From which each part of our view can be efficaciously proved. First, indeed, that science and opinion cannot exist at the same time according to the acts or assents, against the second and third opinions, by this argument: It is impossible that something be at the same time fully and altogether determined, and not fully and altogether determined, concerning the same thing, since these are opposed contradictorily. But by the scientific assent the intellect is fully and altogether determined to the truth of the demonstrated proposition, and is rendered firm and stable in it; and by the assent of opinion it is neither altogether determined, nor made firm and stable; therefore it is repugnant that these two exist at the same time in the intellect concerning the same truth. But you will say, for the third opinion, that this argument concludes that it is repugnant for the intellect to be in both ways at the same time in respect of the same middle, but not by reason of diverse middles. It is therefore proved efficaciously that it is repugnant even through diverse middles: because for the intellect to be at the same time convinced and not convinced concerning the same truth, from whatever source this comes, whether through the same or a diverse middle, is plainly repugnant, since these are to be and not to be at the same time in respect of the same thing; therefore it does not remove the difficulty of the argument that this happens through diverse middles. And if it can happen through diverse middles, it follows that a scientific assent and an erroneous one can exist at the same time concerning the same proposition, so that the intellect judges at the same time that it is true and false: true indeed through demonstration, but false through a probable syllogism. For then the opposition will cease, because it is said to be only in respect of the same middle, not in respect of diverse middles; which things, however, are absurd.

> *De habitibus* verò, facilè probari potest quia non dicunt actualem determinationem intellectus, ad veritatem, sed quasi potentialem, & habitualem. Non repugnat autem, intellectum esse imperfectè determinatum actu, & posse plenè determinari, licèt plena determinatio actualis, repugnet non plenæ. Vnde diuersis temporibus, esse in eodem intellectu plenam, & non plenam determinationem, nullam continet repugnantiam. At eodem tempore id fieri, maximè repugnat.

Concerning the habits, however, it can easily be proved, because they do not say an actual determination of the intellect to the truth, but as it were a potential and habitual one. And it is not repugnant that the intellect be imperfectly determined in act and be able to be fully determined, although full actual determination is repugnant to the non-full. Whence that there be in the same intellect at diverse times a full and a non-full determination contains no repugnance; but that this should happen at the same time is supremely repugnant.

> 55 Ad arg. Scoti, quo probabat repugnãtiam habituum, Neganda est consequentia: quia licèt actus, & habitus versentur [p. 716] circa idem obiectum, & habeantur per idem medium, longè tamen diuersas rationes habent: quia habitus est, tanquam inclinatio, & quasi potentia ad actum, actus verò per actualem attingentiam fit obiecti, Sed non repugnat aliquem habere simul inclinationes ad actus repugnantes, quos potest exercere diuersis temporibus: licèt repugnet simul exercere vtrumque. Vnde licèt repugnet actus, aut assensus opinionis, & scientiæ esse simul, non repugnat tamen simul esse habitus.

55 To the argument of Scotus, by which he proved the repugnance of the habits, the consequence must be denied: because although act and habit are concerned [p. 716] with the same object and are had through the same middle, they nevertheless have far diverse rationes: because a habit is as it were an inclination, and as it were a potency to the act, whereas the act comes about through an actual attaining of the object. But it is not repugnant that someone have at the same time inclinations to repugnant acts, which he can exercise at diverse times, although it is repugnant to exercise both at the same time. Whence, although it is repugnant that the acts or assents of opinion and of science exist at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that the habits exist at the same time.

> 56 Ad arg. Durandi, Concessa maiore, & minore, neganda est consequentia. Quia repugnantia assensuum opinionis, & scientiæ, non consistit in oppositione iudiciorum: de quibus bene probatur, non esse necessarium, quòd simul habeantur. Sed in eo, quòd ratio opinionis essentialiter, est imperfecta, non omnino determinans intellectum ad veritatem, neque eum firmans in ea: ratio verò scientiæ essentialiter perfecta est, circa idem: cùm plenè atque omnino determinet intellectum, eumque in eadem veritate firmet. Firmum autem esse intellectum, & stabilem in eadem veritate: & infirmum simul ac debilem, repugnat: & pariter, simul esse omnino determinatum & indeterminatum. Et hoc sequitur, siue per idem, siue per diuersum medium id fiat: & ideo repugnat simul esse opinionem, & scientiam, circa eandem propositionem, in eodem intellectu. Itaque licèt actualis formido, non sit opinioni intrinseca: & licèt non possit haberi per medium verè probabile, sed existimatum necessarium, quæ concedenda sunt: Nihilominus, ex propria ratione intrinseca, habet assensus opinionis, non omnino determinare intellectum, nec firmare eundem in veritate. Et ideo non potest esse simul cum assensu scientiæ, plenè eum determinante ac firmante: sed adueniente hoc, & cum eo plena determinatione intellectus: cessat ille: quia cessat omnis indeterminatio, & aliqua pertinet ad eius essentiam: & ideo cessante omni cessat aliqua: & ex consequenti. cessat assensus: aliqua ex parte inderminatus, atque infirmus: sicut cessat debilitas membrorum, adueniente robore: & cessat ægritudo, adueniente sanitate. Et ex his constat soluta esse argumenta vltimæ opinionis. Et hæc de opere posterioris resolutionis adnotasse sufficiat.

56 To the argument of Durandus: granting the major and the minor, the consequence must be denied. Because the repugnance of the assents of opinion and of science does not consist in the opposition of the judgments, of which it is well proved that it is not necessary that they be had at the same time; but in this: that the ratio of opinion is essentially imperfect, not altogether determining the intellect to the truth, nor making it firm in it; whereas the ratio of science is essentially perfect concerning the same thing, since it fully and altogether determines the intellect and makes it firm in the same truth. But for the intellect to be firm and stable in the same truth, and at the same time infirm and weak, is repugnant; and likewise to be at the same time altogether determined and undetermined. And this follows whether it happens through the same or through a diverse middle; and therefore it is repugnant that opinion and science exist at the same time concerning the same proposition in the same intellect. Thus, although actual fear is not intrinsic to opinion, and although it can be had through a middle that is truly probable but thought necessary (which things are to be granted), nevertheless the assent of opinion has from its own intrinsic ratio that it does not altogether determine the intellect, nor make it firm in the truth. And therefore it cannot exist at the same time with the assent of science, which fully determines and makes it firm; but when this comes, and with it the full determination of the intellect, the former ceases: because all indetermination ceases, and some indetermination pertains to its essence; and therefore when all ceases, some ceases; and consequently there ceases the assent that is in some part undetermined and infirm: just as weakness of the limbs ceases when strength comes, and sickness ceases when health comes. And from these things it is plain that the arguments of the last opinion are solved. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the work of the Posterior Resolution.

> *Finis huius operis.*

The end of this work.

[p. 717]

### De fine, ac diuisione horum librorum — On the end and division of these books.

> *De fine, ac diuisione horum librorum.*

[…]

> 1 FInis, quem in his octo libris Topicorum intendit Aristoteles, est, *Methodum tradere probabiliter disputandi, de quocunque themate, seu oblato, problemate.* Et quia vniuersale, ac præcipuum instrumẽtum Topicæ disputationis, est ratiocinatio Dialectica, quam vocamus Topicum syllogismum, duo agit in toto opere; vt vniuersalem eius diuisionem proponamus. Primò, explicat naturam syllogismi dialectici: & partes, ex quibus componitur. Secundò: Quia syllogismus iste Topicus, hoc est localis dicitur: locos omnes, ex quibus argumentorum probabilium copiam deducere possimus copiosè tradit, & explicat, vt ita instructus Dialecticus, quamcunque disputationem, de rebus probabilibus instituere possit. Nos igitur breui quadam summa, tradere cupientes, ea, quæ necessaria sunt ad artem Topicam intelligendam, & liberalium artium studiosos instruendos; vt satisfacere possint consuetis interrogationibus subeundi examinis. Duo alia eodem ordine præstabimus. Primum: Quidnam Dialecticus syllogismus sit, explicabimus: quæ, & quot sint partes, ex quibus componi debeat: tam simplices, qualia sunt prædicata Topica, quam etiam compositæ: vt problema Dialecticum, & Dialectica propositio: de quibus Aristoteles agit, per octo priora capita primi lib. Deinde loca, ex quibus eruenda sunt probabilia argumenta, summatim colligemus, enumerabimus, atque explicabimus.

he end which Aristotle intends in these eight books of the Topics 1 T is to hand down a Method of disputing probably on any theme whatever, or proposed problem. And since the universal and principal instrument of Topical disputation is Dialectical reasoning, which we call the Topical syllogism, he does two things in the whole work, so that we may propose its universal division. First, he explains the nature of the dialectical syllogism, and the parts of which it is composed. Second, because this syllogism is called Topical, that is, local, he copiously hands down and explains all the places from which we can draw an abundance of probable arguments, so that the Dialectician, thus instructed, may be able to set up any disputation whatever concerning probable matters. We, therefore, desiring to hand down in a certain brief summary the things which are necessary for understanding the Topical art and for instructing students of the liberal arts, so that they may satisfy the customary questions of the examination to be undergone, shall carry out two other things in the same order. First, we shall explain what the Dialectical syllogism is, and what and how many are the parts of which it must be composed, both simple ones, such as the Topical predicates, and also composite ones, such as the Dialectical problem and the Dialectical proposition, of which Aristotle treats through the first eight chapters of book 1. Then we shall summarily collect, enumerate, and explain the places from which probable arguments are to be drawn.

### Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis, & ordo eius cum cæteris partibus Dialecticæ explicatur — What the object of this work is, and its order with the other parts of Dialectic, is explained.

> *Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis; & ordo eius, cum cæteris partibus Dialecticæ explicatur.*

[…]

> 2 EX his facilè potest intelligi; Quodnam sit obiectum huius operis. Nam si omnia, quæ in eo tractantur, vel sũt [p. 718] partes syllogismi Dialectici, vel loci, ex quibus argumentorum probabilium copia deduci possit, quæ etiam ad compositionem eiusdem syllogismi ordinantur: Scopus totius operis, cuius naturam, & proprietates intendit Arist. in eo explicare, idem syllogismus erit: & ex consequenti, subiectum, seu obiectum eius proprium. Nam præcipuæ conditiones obiecti istæ sunt. Ordinem etiam, quem Libri Topicorum seruent, inter cæteras partes Logicæ, & locum eis inter cæteras debitum, non erit difficile intelligere, sequuntur enim proximè libros de posteriori resolutione, nuper à nobis explanatos. Cuius ea est ratio: Quia inter species syllogismorum, post demonstrationem in posteriorum libris explicatam, dignior est syllogismus dialecticus cæteris: ideo tractatus iste de eo, tanquam de proprio obiecto agens, statim post eosdem libros debet collocari.

2 From these things it can easily be understood what the object of this work is. For if all the things which are treated in it are either [p. 718] parts of the Dialectical syllogism, or places from which an abundance of probable arguments can be drawn, which are also ordered to the composition of the same syllogism, then the aim of the whole work, whose nature and properties Aristotle intends to explain in it, will be that same syllogism, and consequently its proper subject or object. For these are the principal conditions of an object. Nor will it be difficult to understand the order which the books of the Topics keep among the other parts of Logic, and the place due to them among the others; for they follow immediately the books on the Posterior Resolution recently explained by us. The reason for this is: Because among the species of syllogisms, after demonstration, explained in the books of the Posterior Analytics, the dialectical syllogism is worthier than the others; therefore this treatise, dealing with it as with its proper object, must be placed immediately after those same books.

> *Quid sit prædicatum Dialecticum.*

What a Dialectical predicate is. 3

> 3 SImplicia, ex quibus proximè componuntur problema, ac propositio Dialectica, & remotè Dialecticus syllogismus, sunt *Prædicata Topica, seu Dialectica* (quòd idem est:) de quibus agit Arist. c. 4. primi libri, vbi ea enumerat, & singula propriis definitionibus explicat. *Prædicatum Topicum,* sic possumus in genere definire: *Est præcipua pars, ex qua componitur problema, ac propositio Dialectica. Præcipuam partem,* illud vocamus, ad distinctionem subiecti, ex quo eadem propositio Dialectica componitur. Nam copulam propositionis, non tam partem nunc vocare volumus, quàm nexum vtriusque partis, quo copulatæ propositionem componunt.

The simple things of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are proximately composed, and the Dialectical syllogism remotely, are the Topical or Dialectical predicates (which is the same thing), of which Aristotle treats in ch. 4 of the first book, where he enumerates them and explains each by its proper definition. The Topical predicate we can define in general thus: It is the principal part of which the Dialectical problem and proposition are composed. We call it the principal part to distinguish it from the subject, of which the same Dialectical proposition is composed. For we do not wish now to call the copula of the proposition a part so much as the connection of each part, by which, when coupled, they compose the proposition.

> *Quotuplex sit prædicatum Dialecticum.*

How manifold the Dialectical predicate is. 4

> 4 VIdentur ex vna parte *prædicata Dialectica esse quinque,* propter hoc arg. Quia prædicatum distinguitur prædicabili, tanquam actus à potentia: sed actus, & potentia, eodem modo numerari debent: quia potentia sumit vnitatem, ac distinctionem ab actu: ergo tot erunt prædicata, quot prædicabilia. Constat autem ex Porphyrio, prædicabilia esse quinque: ergo quinque etiam debent esse prædicata.

On the one hand the Dialectical predicates seem to be five, on account of this argument: Because a predicate is distinguished from a predicable as act from potency; but act and potency must be numbered in the same way, because potency takes its unity and distinction from act; therefore there will be as many predicates as predicables. But it is established from Porphyry that the predicables are five; therefore the predicates too must be five.

> Ex alia verò parte *videntur esse decem,* propter secundum argum. Quia prædicamentum non est aliud, quàm prædicatorum series, & ordinatio: ergo idem erit numerus prædicatorum & prædicamentorum. Constat autem decem esse prædicamenta [p. 719], ex Arist. ergo ponenda sunt decem prædicata.

But on the other hand they seem to be ten, on account of a second argument: Because a category is nothing other than a series and ordering of predicates; therefore the number of predicates and of categories will be the same. But it is established that there are ten categories [p. 719] from Aristotle; therefore ten predicates must be posited.

> 5 His tamen non obstantibus: Nostra sententia est, *Quatuor tantum esse prædicata Topica.* Vt Arist. expressè docet, 1. lib. c. 4. quæ sunt: *Definitio, Genus, Proprium, & Accidens,* ita, vt nec plura addenda sint, neque aliquod ex his auferendum. Tota autem difficultas huius rei, consistit in assignanda ratione, propter quam Arist. quatuor hæc prædicata posuit. Pro cuius explicatione, notandum est, Finem huius artis topicæ, vt diximus, esse *methodum tradere, probabiliter disputandi de quacunque re proposita.* Disputatio autem tribus partibus constat, ita ordinatis. Primò, *Quæstione,* seu interrogatione, quam titulum disputationis solemus vocare, sic dicentis: Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non? aut quid simile. Deinde *Locis,* ex quibus eruenda sunt argumenta probabilia, quibus mediis dubiam reddamus quæstionem: & tertio loco, *Argumentis ipsis,* quæ sunt syllogismi Dialectici, ex propositionibus Dialecticis compositi. Propositio autem Dialectica, (vt postmodum dicetur) est altera pars problematis. Problemata verò, & ex consequenti propositiones Dialecticæ, ex prædicatis fiunt: quia non est aliud problema, quàm quæstio, vel interrogatio, *An aliquod prædicatum conueniat tali subiecto:* vt dum dicimus, *An cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non?* idem est, ac si quæramus, An hoc prædicatum incorruptibile, conueniat cœlo, vel non. Vnde sequitur: prædicatum topicum non esse aliud, quàm id quod de re aliqua quæri potest. *Tot igitur erunt prædicata, quot quæstiones possunt de re aliqua fieri: & tot etiam quæstiones, quot prædicata.* Et cùm quæstio idem sit, ac problema: idem erit numerus prædicatorum, ac problematum. Et tandem cùm propositio, & problema, forma tantùm interrogationis differant, quia problema est interrogatio vtriusque partis contradictionis: vt si dicas, Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile, vel non, problema efficis. Propositio verò, interrogatio alterius partis, vt putásne cœlum est incorruptibile: tot sunt propositiones Dialecticæ, quot problemata. Et ita intelligitur, prædicatum Dialecticum esse primum, ex quo numerus problematum desumi debet. Deinde ex numero problematum, numerus propositionum Dialecticarum. Et ita, ex ordine ad problemata, & propositiones constituendas, desumitur numerus prædicatorum. Et discursus iste deducitur ex 4. cap. 1. lib.

5 These things notwithstanding, our view is that there are only four Topical predicates, as Aristotle expressly teaches, bk. 1, ch. 4, which are: Definition, Genus, Property, and Accident, so that neither are more to be added nor any of these to be taken away. But the whole difficulty of this matter consists in assigning the reason on account of which Aristotle posited these four predicates. For whose explanation it should be noted that the end of this topical art, as we said, is to hand down a method of disputing probably on any thing proposed. But a disputation consists of three parts, ordered thus. First, of the Question, or interrogation, which we usually call the title of the disputation, saying thus: Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? or something similar. Next, of the Places from which probable arguments are to be drawn, by which means we may render the question doubtful; and in the third place, of the Arguments themselves, which are Dialectical syllogisms composed of Dialectical propositions. Now the Dialectical proposition (as will be said afterward) is one part of the problem. And problems, and consequently Dialectical propositions, are made of predicates: because a problem is nothing other than a question or interrogation whether some predicate belongs to such a subject: as when we say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? it is the same as if we asked whether this predicate, incorruptible, belongs to the heavens, or not. Whence it follows that a topical predicate is nothing other than that which can be asked about some thing. There will therefore be as many predicates as there can be questions made about some thing, and as many questions as predicates. And since a question is the same as a problem, the number of predicates and of problems will be the same. And finally, since a proposition and a problem differ only in the form of the interrogation (because a problem is an interrogation of both parts of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible or not, you make a problem; whereas a proposition is an interrogation of one of the two parts, as Do you think the heavens are incorruptible?), there are as many Dialectical propositions as problems. And thus it is understood that the Dialectical predicate is the first thing from which the number of problems must be taken; then from the number of problems, the number of Dialectical propositions. And thus the number of predicates is taken from the order to the problems and propositions to be constituted. And this discourse is drawn from ch. 4 of bk. 1.

> 6 Quo supposito, hac ratione probatur ab Arist. *quatuor tantum esse prædicata. Prædicatum* est id, quod de re aliqua quæri potest, ad disputationem Dialecticam instituendã: sed quatuor [p. 720] tantùm quæri possunt: ergo quatuor tantùm sunt prædicata? Minorem probat: Nam vel quærimus de aliquo definitionem vt intelligamus naturam eius, vel genus: vt intelligamus, in quonam prædicamento sit: vel proprietates, aut communia accidentia: Et nihil aliud quæri potest, quod ad hæc non reducatur: ergo quatuor sunt prædicata: ita, vt nec plura, nec pauciora. Et hæc sunt, *definitio, genus, proprium, & accidens,* quæ suis definitionibus sic explicat cap. 4. 1. lib. *Definitio, est oratio, quid erat esse significans. Orationem* esse dicit: quia non est propositio, cùm nec verum contineat, nec falsum, vt animal rationale. Vocat etiam defintionem terminum, sumpta metaphora ex terminis agrorum. Nam ad quemlibet, solùm, & totum pertinet illud, quod intra terminos eius clauditur: ita vt nihil eius extrà sit, sed totum, quod habet, intra terminos comprehendatur. Sic definitio continet, quidquid pertinet ad essentiam rei: ita vt nihil eius sit extrà, nec aliquid sit eius, quod intra illam non comprehendatur: & ideo vocatur ab Arist. terminus. *Genus* verò, inquit, est, *quod prædicatur pluribus differentibus specie in quid:* Vt animal: *Proprium, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei, soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur:* Vt risibile, respectu hominis. *Accidens* est, *quod nec est definitio, nec genus, nec proprium, inest autem rei.* aut etiam, *Accidens est, quod inesse eidem potest:* vt albedo, respectu parietis.

6 This supposed, it is proved by Aristotle by this argument that there are only four predicates. A predicate is that which can be asked about some thing for setting up a Dialectical disputation; but four [p. 720] only can be asked; therefore there are only four predicates. He proves the minor: For either we ask about something its definition, in order that we may understand its nature; or its genus, in order that we may understand in which category it is; or its properties, or its common accidents. And nothing else can be asked which is not reduced to these; therefore there are four predicates, so that there are neither more nor fewer. And these are definition, genus, property, and accident, which he explains by their definitions thus in ch. 4 of bk. 1. Definition is an expression signifying what it was to be. He says it is an expression because it is not a proposition, since it contains neither truth nor falsehood, as rational animal. He also calls the definition a term, taking the metaphor from the boundaries of fields. For to any field there belongs alone and wholly that which is enclosed within its boundaries, so that nothing of it is outside, but the whole that it has is comprehended within its boundaries. So the definition contains whatever pertains to the essence of the thing, so that nothing of it is outside, nor is there anything of it that is not comprehended within it; and therefore it is called a term by Aristotle. Genus, he says, is that which is predicated of many things differing in species, in quid, as animal. Property, that which does not indicate what the being of the thing is, but belongs to it alone and is predicated convertibly, as risible in respect of man. Accident is that which is neither definition, nor genus, nor property, but belongs to the thing; or also: Accident is that which can belong to the same thing, as whiteness in respect of a wall.

> 7 Si autem dixeris: Vltra has quatuor quæst. aut interrogationes, seu problemata, quæ generalia esse videntur, plura possunt specialia quæri de re: vt, an sit homo: an sit leo: an sit substantia & innumera alia: ergo plura quàm quatuor, imò innumera prędicata debent concedi. Et præterea, generalia prædicata adhuc sunt plura: quia sicut quærimus de genere alicuius rei, vt, vtrùm Animal sit genus hominis, nec ne: ita possumus quærere de eius differentia, nempe, an Rationale sit differentia hominis: atque etiam de specie, vt an Homo sit species Petri, aut Ioannis: vel etiam an sit species animalis: ergo duo alia prædicata generalia sunt addenda, nempe, Species, & Differentia.

7 But if you say: Beyond these four questions, or interrogations, or problems, which seem to be general, many special ones can be asked about a thing: as whether it is a man, whether it is a lion, whether it is a substance, and innumerable others; therefore more than four, indeed innumerable predicates must be granted. And besides, the general predicates are still more: because just as we ask about the genus of some thing, as whether Animal is the genus of man or not, so we can ask about its difference, namely whether Rational is the difference of man; and also about the species, as whether Man is the species of Peter or John, or even whether it is a species of animal; therefore two other general predicates must be added, namely Species and Difference.

> 8 Circa primam partem arg. de interrogationibus specialibus asserit Rodolphus Agricola, lib. 1. de Inuentione Dialectica, cap. 3. errasse Arist. in assignando numero prędicatorum: quia sicut plura sunt genera problematum particularium, ita plura debent constitui prędicata, quàm quatuor. Sed plus mihi videtur errasse hic author reprehendendo Aristotelem: quia vera solutio ex doctrina eiusdem Arist. 1. lib. Topicorum, cap. 4. *& lib. 5. cap. vltimo, sub finem, colligenda est.* Quibus locis [p. 721] duo asserit. Primum, *Quòd cùm problemata ordinentur ad disputationem dialecticam,* cuius finis est determinatio eiusdem problematis circa quod disputatur: ita vt præiactis probabilibus argumentis pro vtraque parte, tandem decernatur: vtra earum sit probabilior: hinc sequitur, omnia problemata, quæ eisdem argumentis, & eodem modo determinantur, ad idem genus problematis pertinere: & omnia prædicata eorundem sub aliquo ex quatuor designatis comprehendi. Et ideo in hoc primo loco asserit, differentiam, si generalis sit, hoc est, si de pluribus speciebus prædicetur sicut genus, cum genere esse connumerandam, & non esse addendum pro ea aliud prædicatum. Secundum est, quod secundo loco docet, *Quæstionem accidentis finiri, aut determinari, ex eo solùm, quod quis probet conuenire subiecto.* Ex qua doctrina deducimus nos, omnia problemata specialia, quæcumque illa sint, reduci ad problema accidentis. Et omnia prædicata eorundem, ad prædicatum accidentis, Et ratio huius deductionis est: quia in omni problemate speciali quæritur: An hoc prædicatum conueniat tali subiecto, vel ei insit, necne, quod patet habere modum interrogationis, aut problematis accidentis, quo solùm quærimus, *An accidens conueniat, vel insit subiecto.* Et eisdem prorsus argumentis finiuntur, aut determinantur: quia si inquiras, an animal conueniat homini, necne, vel an homo conueniat Petro, necne, sufficienter determinatur, & disputatio eius finita erit: si probemus vtcumque ei inesse: quamuis nec probetur esse de essentia eius aut cum eo conuerti: nec alio modo speciali ei conuenire. Ergo ad formam problematis accidentalis reducuntur: & prædicata eorum sub prædicato accidentis comprehenduntur, nec opus est alia multiplicare.

8 Concerning the first part of the argument, about the special interrogations, Rudolph Agricola, On Dialectical Invention bk. 1, ch. 3, asserts that Aristotle erred in assigning the number of predicates: because, just as there are many kinds of particular problems, so more predicates than four must be established. But this author seems to me to have erred more in reproving Aristotle, because the true solution is to be gathered from the doctrine of the same Aristotle, Topics bk. 1, ch. 4, and bk. 5, last chapter, toward the end. In which places two [p. 721] he asserts two things. The first: Since problems are ordered to dialectical disputation, whose end is the determination of the same problem about which the dispute is held, so that, after probable arguments have been set out for each side, it may finally be decided which of them is the more probable, it follows that all problems which are determined by the same arguments and in the same way belong to the same genus of problem; and that all their predicates are comprised under one of the four designated. And therefore in this first place he asserts that difference, if it is general, that is, if it is predicated of several species as a genus is, must be counted together with genus, and that no other predicate is to be added for it. The second is what he teaches in the second place: that a question of accident is settled, or determined, solely from someone’s proving that it belongs to the subject. From this doctrine we deduce that all special problems, whatever they may be, are reduced to the problem of accident, and all their predicates to the predicate of accident. And the reason for this deduction is that in every special problem it is asked: Does this predicate belong to such a subject, or is it in it, or not? which plainly has the mode of interrogation, or of problem, of accident, in which we ask only whether an accident belongs to, or is in, the subject. And they are settled, or determined, by exactly the same arguments: because if you ask whether animal belongs to man or not, or whether man belongs to Peter or not, it is sufficiently determined, and the disputation about it will be finished, if we prove that it is in it in any way whatever, even though it is not proved to be of its essence, or to be convertible with it, or to belong to it in any other special way. Therefore they are reduced to the form of an accidental problem, and their predicates are comprised under the predicate of accident, and there is no need to multiply others.

> Ex eadem doctrina: Respondere possumus ad aliam partem eiusdem argumenti de specie, & differentia. Quòd si differentia sit subalterna, ad prædicatum generis reducitur: si verò infima, ad prædicatum definitionis. Species verò, ad prædicatum generis. Et ratio omnium est: quia iisdem argumentis definitur quæstio generis, & differentiæ subalternæ, cùm vtrumque prædicetur, de pluribus differentibus specie, in quid. Eisdem namque argumentis probamus animal esse genus hominis, & sensibile, differentiam subalternam eius: atque etiam, hominem esse speciem Petri, & Ioannis. Quia sicut genus prædicatur, in quid de speciebus, ita species, de indiuiduis. Iisdem etiam probamus: Animal rationale esse definitionem hominis, & rationale, esse differentiam atomam eius. Quod verò ad speciem attinet, satis etiam probabiliter respondent, Albertus [p. 722] Magnus, tract. 2. Topicorum ca. 8. in fine, & Sotus quæst. 5. vniuersalium ad primum: Non esse inter prædicata enumerandam: quia prædicata sumuntur per respectum ad subiectum commune, quòd non respicit species, sed singularia. Et ratio huius est: quia prædicata, vt dicebamus, ex propria ratione ordinantur ad constituenda problemata, & propositiones dialecticas: & vtrumque horum ad constituendum syllogismum dialecticum: qui non constituitur per se ex propositionibus singularibus, sed constantibus subiecto communi: in quibus solis reperiri potest forma syllogistica, ex modo, & figura constans, vt per se est manifestum.

From the same doctrine we can reply to the other part of the same argument, concerning species and difference: that if the difference is subaltern, it is reduced to the predicate of genus; but if it is lowest, to the predicate of definition. Species, however, is reduced to the predicate of genus. And the reason for all of these is that a question of genus and of subaltern difference is settled by the same arguments, since each is predicated of several things differing in species, in quid. For by the same arguments we prove that animal is the genus of man, and that sensible is its subaltern difference; and also that man is the species of Peter and John, because just as genus is predicated in quid of species, so species is predicated of individuals. By the same arguments we also prove that rational animal is the definition of man, and that rational is its atomic difference. As to what concerns species, a quite probable reply is also given by Albert Zz [p. 722] the Great, Topics tract. 2, ch. 8, at the end, and Soto, q. 5 on universals, ad 1: that it is not to be enumerated among the predicates: because predicates are taken by relation to a common subject, which species does not regard, but singulars. And the reason for this is that predicates, as we were saying, are ordered by their proper ratio to constituting problems and dialectical propositions, and each of these to constituting the dialectical syllogism, which is not constituted per se out of singular propositions, but out of those consisting of a common subject, in which alone the syllogistic form, consisting of mood and figure, can be found, as is manifest per se.

> 11 Ad primum argu. de prædicabilibus: Distinguendum est antecedens. Nam prædicatum vniuersaliter sumptum, distinguitur à prædicabili, sicut actus à potentia: & ideo eodem modo numeratur, ac prædicabile. Verùm prædicatum sumptam specialiter, pro Topico, non respicit prædicabile vt potentiam, sed solùm pro actuali sumitur: & modo quidem speciali, à generali prædicato distincto, hoc est, in ordine ad quæstionem, seu problema instituendum. Vnde alio etiam modo diuerso prædicata numerantur, diuersumque sortiuntur numerum à prædicabilibus, atque etiam à prædicamentis: quæ sunt ordinationis prædicatorum, vt sub ratione generali considerantur: non vt speciali, & Topica, ad specialem etiam finem iam explicatum ordinata. Quare non sequitur ex eo, quòd prędicamenta sint decem tot debere esse prædicata Topica. Et hæc est solutio secundi argumenti.

11 To the first argument, concerning the predicables: the antecedent must be distinguished. For predicate taken universally is distinguished from predicable as act from potency, and therefore it is numbered in the same way as predicable. But predicate taken specially, for the Topical one, does not regard the predicable as a potency, but is taken only for the actual one, and indeed in a special mode, distinct from the general predicate, that is, in order to setting up a question, or problem. Hence predicates are also numbered in another, different way, and are allotted a number different from the predicables, and also from the categories, which belong to the ordering of predicates as they are considered under a general ratio, not under a special and Topical one, ordered also to the special end already explained. Wherefore it does not follow from the fact that the categories are ten that the Topical predicates must be as many. And this is the solution of the second argument.

### Quid sit, & quotuplex problema Dialecticum — What a dialectical problem is, and how many kinds there are.

> *Quid sit, & quotuplex problema dialecticum.*

[…]

> 12 ARistoteles 1. libro, cap. 3. definit problema dialecticum, dicens: *Esse interrogationem,* seu *quæstionem vtriusque partis contradictionis:* vt si dicas: Vtrùm animal gressibile bipes, sit definitio hominis, necne? Quatuor autem sunt genera *problematum:* vt cap. 3. & 4. asserit idem Aristoteles: sicut quatuor sunt prædicata, Vt *Problema definitionis:* quale est illud, ex definitione hominis assignatum. *Problema Generis:* vt si dicas, Vtrùm animal sit genus hominis, necne? *Problema proprij,* vt dum dicimus, Vtrùm risibile sit proprium hominis, necne, & tandem, *Problema accidentis,* Vtrùm albedo sit accidens parietis, necne, cap. etiam 9. eiusdem lib. diuidit problema dialecticum vniuersaliter Aristot. dicens: Aliud esse *Practicum:* Quod pertinet ad electionem, vel fugam, vel aliquid de prosequendo [p. 723], aut fugiendo. Hoc enim, inquit, ad praxim, aut operationem ordinatur: & ideo dicitur practicum. Tale est hoc: Vtrùm voluptas sit eligenda, vel non. Aliud verò est *Speculatiuum:* Quod nihil de prosequendo, aut fugiendo continet, nec ad operationem ordinatur: sed solùm ad cognitionem veritatis: vt si dicas: Vtrùm cœlum sit incorruptibile: vel non? Alia etiam diuisione, potest diuidi problema, secundùm materias diuersarum scientiarum, in quibus reperitur: qua ratione dicimus: Aliud esse *problema Physicum,* vt, An principium motus, & quietis, eius, in quo est, sit definitio naturæ, necne? Aliud *Metaphysicum,* vt si dixeris: Vtrùm ens sit vniuocum respectu substantiæ, & accidentis, necne? Veruntamen formalis consideratio omnium problematum secundùm quam reducuntur ad quatuor illa, ex diuersis prędicatis desumpta, dialectici propria est: quia ad solum dialecticum pertinet, docere omnes, quonam modo disputatio sit instituenda, & quibus instrumentis in ea vtendum, ad consequendam notitiam veritatis, de qua disputatur.

12 Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 3, defines the dialectical problem, saying that it is an interrogation, or question, of either part of a contradiction: as if you say, Whether walking two-footed animal is the definition of man, or not? And there are four genera of problems, as the same Aristotle asserts in ch. 3 and 4, just as there are four predicates. Thus the Problem of definition, such as the one assigned from the definition of man. The Problem of genus, as if you say, Whether animal is the genus of man, or not? The Problem of property, as when we say, Whether risible is a property of man, or not? And finally the Problem of accident: Whether whiteness is an accident of the wall, or not? In ch. 9 of the same book, too, Aristotle divides the dialectical problem universally, saying that one is Practical: that which pertains to choice or avoidance, or to something to be pursued [p. 723] or avoided. For this, he says, is ordered to practice, or operation, and therefore it is called practical. Such is this: Whether pleasure is to be chosen, or not. Another, however, is Speculative: that which contains nothing about something to be pursued or avoided, nor is ordered to operation, but only to the cognition of truth: as if you say, Whether the heavens are incorruptible, or not? The problem can also be divided by another division, according to the matters of the diverse sciences in which it is found; for which reason we say that one is a Physical problem, as, Whether the principle of motion and rest of that in which it is, is the definition of nature, or not? Another Metaphysical, as if you should say, Whether being is univocal with respect to substance and accident, or not? Nevertheless, the formal consideration of all problems, according to which they are reduced to those four, taken from the diverse predicates, is proper to the dialectician: because it pertains to the dialectician alone to teach all how a disputation is to be set up, and what instruments are to be used in it for attaining cognition of the truth about which the dispute is held.

### Quidnam sit propositio Dialectica, & quotuplex, & quomodo distinguatur à problemate — What a dialectical proposition is, and how many kinds there are; and how it is distinguished from a problem.

> *Quidnam sit propositio dialectica, & quotuplex: & quomodo distinguatur à problemate.*

[…]

> 14 TRia hæc tradit Arist. li. 1. c. 3 in fine: sic in primis definiens propositionem dialecticam, quòd sit, quasi *propositio alterius partis contradictionis:* vt si dicas: Putásne animal rationale, esse definitionem hominis? Differre autem à problemate ait: non re, sed modo: quia *propositio,* vt vocabuli etymologia ostendit, proponit alteri aliquid: vt eidem rei propositæ respondeat, explicans, quidnam de illa iudicet, vel sentiat. *Problema* verò: Modum habet quæstio. & vtramque partem, per modum quæstionis agitandæ proponit: vt si dicas: Vtrùm animal rationale sit definitio hominis, necne? Itaque propositio dialectica, interrogat per modum simplicis propositionis: non per modum quæstionis: & assumit vnam tantùm partem: cùm problema vtramque, & per modum quæstionis interroget. Id duobus modis solet præferri, vel *formaliter* vtramque partem interrogando: vt in assignato fit exemplo: vel *formaliter* vnam, & *virtualiter* alteram: vt si solùm dixeris: Vtrùm animal rationale, sit definitio hominis? Et hoc modo proferuntur problemata in communi vsu scholarum, quoties quæstio aliqua disputanda proponitur: quod breuitatis studio, absque dubio fit, eo quòd iam ab omnibus intelligitur altera etiam pars interrogata, ex modo ipso problematicæ interrogationis.

14 Three things Aristotle delivers in bk. 1, ch. 3, at the end. In the first place he defines the dialectical proposition as being, as it were, the proposition of the other part of a contradiction: as if you say, Do you think that rational animal is the definition of man? And he says that it differs from the problem not in reality but in mode: because the Proposition, as the etymology of the word shows, proposes something to another, so that he may reply to the thing proposed, explaining what he judges or thinks about it. The Problem, however, has the mode of a question, and proposes both parts to be debated by way of a question: as if you say, Whether rational animal is the definition of man, or not? Thus the dialectical proposition interrogates by way of a simple proposition, not by way of a question, and takes up only one part; whereas the problem takes up both, and interrogates by way of a question. This is customarily put forward in two ways: either by interrogating both parts formally, as in the example assigned; or one formally and the other virtually, as if you should say only, Whether rational animal is the definition of man? And in this way problems are put forward in the common usage of the schools whenever some question to be disputed is proposed: which is done, no doubt, for the sake of brevity, because the other part too is now understood by all to be interrogated, from the very mode of the problematic interrogation. Z z ij

[p. 724]

> 15 Vbi aduertere debemus, quòd Arist. 1. lib. priorum, c. 1. non distinxit propositionem dialecticam à problemate: imò neque à propositione probabili: cùm dixerit *esse interrogationem contradictionis:* quod problemati proprium est, & rursus, propositionem dialecticam, per contanti esse interrogationem contradictionis: ratiocinanti verò, esse sumptionem apparentis, & probabilis. Ideo remisit distinctionem horum trium, ad cap. 3. lib. 1. Topic. quem citauit dicens: vt in Topicis dictum est. Ibi siquidem proprius erat locus distinguendi hæc: eo modo, quo à nobis distincta sunt. *Propositio dialectica* quadruplex est, sicut de problemate diximus: *Definitionis* est hæc: Putásne animal rationale est definitio hominis? *Proprij,* Putásne risibile est propria passio hominis? *Generis,* Putásne animal est genus hominis! *Accidentis,* Putásne albedo est accidens hominis?

15 Here we must notice that Aristotle, Prior Analytics 1, ch. 1, did not distinguish the dialectical proposition from the problem, nor indeed from the probable proposition: since he said that it is an interrogation of a contradiction, which is proper to the problem; and again, that the dialectical proposition is, for the one who questions, an interrogation of a contradiction, but for the one who reasons, the taking of something apparent and probable. Therefore he referred the distinction of these three to ch. 3 of Topics 1, which he cited, saying: as was said in the Topics. For there was the proper place to distinguish these things, in the way in which they have been distinguished by us. The dialectical proposition is fourfold, as we said of the problem. Of Definition is this: Do you think rational animal is the definition of man? Of Property: Do you think risible is a proper attribute of man? Of Genus: Do you think animal is the genus of man? Of Accident: Do you think whiteness is an accident of man?

> 16 Sed valde notandum est in hac parte, *Propositionem* sub hac generali ratione sumptam: solùm significare enunciationem, vt proponitur in syllogismo ad inferendam conclusionem. Quæ si proponatur primo loco, dicitur *Propositio simpliciter,* aut *Propositio,* seu *præmissa* maior, vel Prima pars antecedentis. Si secundo loco, dicitur *Assumptio:* quia sub propositione maiori: sub qua continetur, assumitur: dicitur etiam, *Minor propositio,* aut *Præmissa minor,* ac Secunda, vel posterior pars antecedentis. Et si in syllogismo demonstratiuo proponatur, dicitur *Principium:* si in syllogismo dialectico, *Propositio probabilis: & Propositio apparens:* si in syllogismo sophistico. *Propositio verò dialectica* præter enunciationem, addit modum propositionis, quasi per modum dubitantis: & problema, modum interrogantis, vt explicatum est.

16 But it should be carefully noted in this matter that Proposition, taken under this general ratio, signifies only an enunciation as it is proposed in a syllogism for inferring the conclusion. If it is proposed in the first place, it is called Proposition simply, or Proposition, or major premise, or the First part of the antecedent. If in the second place, it is called Assumption, because it is assumed under the major proposition, under which it is contained; it is also called Minor proposition, or Minor premise, and the Second, or posterior, part of the antecedent. And if it is proposed in a demonstrative syllogism, it is called a Principle; if in a dialectical syllogism, a Probable proposition; and an Apparent proposition, if in a sophistical syllogism. But the dialectical Proposition adds to the enunciation the mode of a proposition, as it were by way of one who doubts; and the problem the mode of one who interrogates, as has been explained.

> Ex quibus intelligitur, tam propositionem Dialecticam, quàm problema, atque etiam propositionem probabilem, deseruire ad disputationem instituendam: sed diuersa ratione: nam problema dialecticum deseruit per modum quæstionis propositæ ad disputandum: & ideo primum locum tenet, & quasi caput totius disputationis vocatur.

From which it is understood that the Dialectical proposition, as well as the problem, and also the probable proposition, serve for setting up a disputation, but in a different ratio: for the dialectical problem serves by way of a question proposed for disputing, and therefore it holds the first place and is called, as it were, the head of the whole disputation.

> 17 Propositio verò dialectica, deseruit, quasi pro interrogatione ad respondentem facta, vt per eam respondens proferat aliam: qua media, quid de re proposita sentiat, explicet: & ex data responsione, possit interrogans occasionem sumere, disputandi in vnam per alteram partem propositæ quæstionis. Propositio verò probabilis, deseruit iam ad constituendum syllogismum, quo possit intentum probari, & quæstio terminari, aut definiri. Itaque problema & propositio dialectica, sub [p. 725] propriis rationibus formalibus, ad instituendam disputationem pertinent, non tamen ad syllogismum dialecticum: nisi solùm antecedenter, & quasi præsuppositiuè. Sola autem propositio probabilis, pertinet ad eandem disputationem, tanquam pars syllogismi dialectici. Vbi aduertere debemus, quòd Arist. hoc loco distinguit propositionem à problemate, dicens problema partem interrogare.

17 The dialectical Proposition, however, serves as it were for an interrogation made to the respondent, so that by means of it the respondent may put forward another, through which he explains what he thinks of the thing proposed; and from the reply given the interrogator may take occasion to dispute for one or the other part of the proposed question. The probable proposition, in turn, serves now for constituting the syllogism by which what is intended may be proved, and the question terminated or settled. Thus the problem and the dialectical proposition, under [p. 725] their proper formal ratios, pertain to setting up a disputation, yet not to the dialectical syllogism, except only antecedently and as it were presuppositively. The probable proposition alone pertains to the same disputation as a part of the dialectical syllogism. Here we must notice that Aristotle in this place distinguishes the proposition from the problem, saying that the problem interrogates both parts.

### Quid sit, & quotuplex propositio probabilis — What a probable proposition is, and how many kinds there are.

> *Quid sit, & quotuplex propositio probabilis.*

[…]

> 18 PRobabile definit Arist. lib. 1. c. 1 his verbis: *Probabilia autẽ sunt, quæ videntur omnibus aut plurimis, aut sapientibus: & his vel omnibus, vel plurimis, vel maximè familiaribus, & probatis.* Quod intelligitur: aut propter rem ipsam, quæ ex se apparet vera: vel propter verisimilem aliquam rationem. Itaque probabile, non est idem, quod verum: nec etiam, quod necessarium, aut certum: sed quod apparet verum omnibus, aut pluribus, aut sapientibus. Sunt enim *propositiones in triplici differentia.* Nam quædam sunt euidenter veræ, & quarum veritas euidenter est cognita. Aliæ *euidenter falsæ,* & quarum etiam falsitas euidenter cognoscitur. Aliæ verò *medium tenent:* quia veræ sunt, aut falsæ, sed veritas, vel falsitas earum non est euidenter nota: quia causa earum, aut ignoratur, aut non plenè cognoscitur: & ideo pluribus apparent veræ, aliis verò etiam contingit apparere falsas, qui verisimilis ratio, pro vtraque parte esse solet. Et istæ dicuntur probabiles. Patet igitur, quo pacto probabilis propositio distinguatur à propositione, Vera, Certa, Necessaria, & falsa. Qui fieri potest, vt secundùm rem sit necessaria, veritatem habens necessariam: vel in re sit necessariò falsa, habens necessariam causam suæ falsitatis: & tamen probabilis videtur, propter verisimilitudinem, apparentiam veritatis, quam habet: vel propter verisimilem rationem, qua probari potest. Vt intelligatur, formalem rationem probabilis propositionis, nõ tam in re ipsa consistere, quàm in apparentia, vel apparenti ratione, respectu plurium, vel sapientum, vt docuit Arist.

18 Aristotle, bk. 1, ch. 1, defines the probable in these words: Probable things are those which seem so to all, or to most, or to the wise; and to these, either to all, or to most, or to the most familiar and approved. Which is understood either on account of the thing itself, which of itself appears true, or on account of some verisimilar reason. Thus the probable is not the same as the true, nor yet as the necessary or certain, but is that which appears true to all, or to most, or to the wise. For propositions are of three different kinds. For some are evidently true, and their truth is evidently known. Others evidently false, and their falsity too is evidently known. Others, however, hold the middle: because they are true or false, but their truth or falsity is not evidently known, because their cause is either unknown or not fully known; and therefore they appear true to many, while to others it happens that they appear false, since there is usually a verisimilar reason for each side. And these are called probable. It is plain, then, how the probable proposition is distinguished from the proposition that is True, Certain, Necessary, and false. For it can happen that in reality it is necessary, having necessary truth, or that in reality it is necessarily false, having a necessary cause of its falsity, and yet it seems probable on account of the verisimilitude, the appearance of truth, which it has, or on account of a verisimilar reason by which it can be proved. So that it may be understood that the formal ratio of the probable proposition consists not so much in the thing itself as in the appearance, or in an apparent reason, with respect to many, or to the wise, as Aristotle taught.

> Vnde sequitur, quòd quamuis repugnet, duas contradictorias esse simul veras, non tamen repugnat esse simul probabiles: quia sæpe contingit, vt vtraque habeat pro se viros doctos, quibus vera appareat, & etiam verisimiles rationes: quibus probetur. Verùm in ipsa re, necesse est alteram earum esse falsam. Non tamen est necessarium (vt aliqui decepti existimant) quòd si vna propositio est probabilis: eo ipso probabilis etiam sit eius contradictoria: cùm manifestum sit, posse contingere: [p. 726] quòd illa appareat viris doctis vera, & verisimiles rationes pro se habeat: hæc verò, nulli appareat vera, nec aliqua verisimilis ratio inuenta sit, per quam probetur.

From which it follows that, although it is repugnant that two contradictories be true at the same time, it is nevertheless not repugnant that they be probable at the same time: because it often happens that each has on its side learned men, to whom it appears true, and also verisimilar reasons by which it is proved. But in the thing itself one of them must be false. It is not, however, necessary (as some mistakenly think) that if one proposition is probable, by that very fact its contradictory is also probable, since it is manifest that it can happen Z z iij [p. 726] that the one appears true to learned men and has verisimilar reasons on its side, while the other appears true to no one, nor has any verisimilar reason been found by which it may be proved.

> *Propositio probabilis* duplex est: Quædam per se: Alia verò, *propter aliam:* ex qua deducitur. *Per se* probabilis, illa dicitur, cuius probabilitas ex sola notitia terminorum, absque alia ratiocinatione, per quam probetur, euidens est: ita vt intellectus non possit non iudicare, esse probabilem. Talis est hæc: Omnis mater diligit filium: aut omnis amicus diligendus est: & hanc propositionem per se probabilem, definiuit Arist. 1. lib. Posteriorum, dicens: *Opinio, est acceptio immediatæ propositionis, & non necessariæ:* Opinionis nomine, assensum talis propositionis immediatæ intelligens: hoc est, quæ sine medio iudicatur probabilis, ex sola notitia terminorum. Et assensus huius propositionis, per se probabilis, vocari potest intellectus, intra genus probabilis propositionis: sicut intra genus euidentis, vocatur intellectus assensus propositionis necessariæ, qui sine medio habetur, sola significatione terminorum cognita. Alia est *Propositio, non per se probabilis,* sed quæ ex alia per se probabili colligitur, per euidentem, aut probabilem consequentiam: aut ex euidenti alia, per consequentiam solùm probabilem. Et hęc est similis conclusioni scientificæ, quam ex euidentibus præmissis, & per euidentem syllogismum colligimus. Nihilominus ex vtraque propositione probabili, potest fieri syllogismus dialecticus, vt per se est manifestum.

The probable proposition is twofold: one per se, the other on account of another, from which it is deduced. That is called per se probable whose probability is evident from the cognition of the terms alone, without any other reasoning by which it is proved, so that the intellect cannot but judge that it is probable. Such is this: Every mother loves her son; or, Every friend is to be loved. And this per se probable proposition Aristotle defined in Posterior Analytics 1, saying: Opinion is the acceptance of an immediate and non-necessary proposition, understanding by the name of opinion the assent of such an immediate proposition, that is, of one which is judged probable without a middle, from the cognition of the terms alone. And the assent of this per se probable proposition can be called understanding within the genus of the probable proposition, just as within the genus of the evident the assent of a necessary proposition which is had without a middle, once the signification of the terms alone is known, is called understanding. The other is the Proposition not per se probable, but which is gathered from another that is per se probable through an evident or probable consequence, or from another evident one through a consequence that is only probable. And this is similar to a scientific conclusion, which we gather from evident premises and through an evident syllogism. Nevertheless, from either probable proposition a dialectical syllogism can be made, as is manifest per se.

### Quidnam sit syllogismus topicus, aut dialecticus — What a Topical or dialectical syllogism is.

> *Quidnam sit syllogismus Topicus, aut dialecticus.*

[…]

> EXplicatis singulis partibus, syllogismi dialectici: non erit difficile definitionem eius intelligere: quam assignauit Arist. c. 1. lib. 1. Topic. his verbis: *Dialecticus autem syllogismus est, qui ex probabilibus est collectus: id est, qui ex propositionibus probabilibus procedens, probabilem etiam conclusionem colligit.* Quæ sic intelligenda est, vt ex vtraque præmissa probabili, vel saltem ex altera, procedere debeat, nam sæpe contingit, vt ex vna euidenti, & altera probabili efficiatur. Talis est enim iste, Omne animal diligit sibi simile: Omnis homo est animal: ergo, Omnis homo diligit sibi simile. Conuenit autem cum syllogismo demõstratiuo, in communi: & generica ratione dispositionis, in Modo, & figura: distinguitur autem ab eo, specie, per modum concludendi: nam demonstratio concludit per medium necessarium: hoc est, per causam, vel effectum necessarium: probabilis verò: per medium probabile: quia nec reddit [p. 727] causam nec effectum conclusionis necessarium, sed solùm probabilem: hoc est, quæ talia apparent pluribus, aut sapientibus, vt explicatum est. Itaque non distinguuntur per solam materiam, vt probauimus in posterioribus, sed etiam per formam specialem, ex modo speciali concludendi desumptam: cùm in forma generica dispositionis syllogisticæ, conueniant. A syllogismo verò sophistico, distinguitur per formam veram, aut apparentem: atque etiam per probabiles, aut apparentes propositiones. Nam ex illis procedit dialecticus, sophisticus verò ex his. Sed diuersum quid est procedere, ex probabilibus, aut ex apparentibus: nam licèt probabilis propositio sit illa: quę apparet vera quamuis fortè vera non sit, non tamen cuicumque id apparet, sed tantùm sapientibus, idque propter fundamentum verisimilis rationis: vel propter verisimilitudinem eiusdem veritatis. Apparentia verò, ex quibus procedit syllogismus sophisticus, nec respectu sapientum dicuntur talia: nec etiam vera apparent, cum fundamento rationis probabilis, aut cum verisimilitudine eiusdem veritatis, sed cuicunque, & sine his fundamentis. Vnde solam, & nudam habent apparentiam veritatis, & ideo deceptoriæ propriè dicuntur: & syllogismus ipse, ex sic apparentibus procedens, vocatur etiam deceptorius.

Once the single parts of the dialectical syllogism have been explained, it will not be difficult to understand its definition, which Aristotle assigned in Topics 1, ch. 1, in these words: But the dialectical syllogism is one which is gathered from probable things; that is, one which, proceeding from probable propositions, gathers a conclusion that is also probable. This is to be understood thus: that it must proceed from both premises probable, or at least from one of them; for it often happens that it is made from one evident and the other probable. For such is this one: Every animal loves its like; Every man is an animal; therefore Every man loves his like. And it agrees with the demonstrative syllogism in the common and generic ratio of disposition in Mood and figure; but it is distinguished from it in species by the mode of concluding: for demonstration concludes through a necessary middle, that is, through a necessary cause or effect; whereas the probable syllogism concludes through a probable middle, because it neither renders [p. 727] a necessary cause nor a necessary effect of the conclusion, but only a probable one, that is, such as appear so to many or to the wise, as has been explained. Thus they are not distinguished by matter alone, as we proved in the Posterior Analytics, but also by a special form, taken from the special mode of concluding, since they agree in the generic form of syllogistic disposition. From the sophistical syllogism, however, it is distinguished by true or apparent form, and also by probable or apparent propositions. For the dialectical proceeds from the former, but the sophistical from the latter. But to proceed from probable things and from apparent ones is something different: for although a probable proposition is one which appears true, even though perhaps it is not true, yet it does not appear so to anyone whatever, but only to the wise, and this on account of the foundation of a verisimilar reason, or on account of the verisimilitude of that same truth. But the apparent things from which the sophistical syllogism proceeds are not called such with respect to the wise, nor do they appear true with the foundation of a probable reason, or with the verisimilitude of that same truth, but to anyone whatever, and without these foundations. Hence they have only the bare appearance of truth, and are therefore properly called deceptive; and the syllogism itself, proceeding from things so apparent, is also called deceptive.

### Enumeratio, atque explicatio locorum, ex quibus deducuntur argumenta probabilia, pro disputatione ineunda — Enumeration and explanation of the places from which probable arguments are deduced for entering upon a disputation.

> *Enumeratio, atque explicatio locorum, ex quibus deducuntur arg. probabilia, pro disputatione ineunda.*

[…]

> 22 HOc solùm restabat explicandum ex his, quæ pertinen ad disputationem dialecticam instituendam: nempe *Locus,* ex quo desumenda sint probabilia arg. vel syllogismi. Explicatis namque & cognitis huiusmodi locis, facile erit cuique argumenta probabilia inuenire, quibus in disputationibus vti possit. Et licèt vsus locorum, ad quamcumque scientiam pertineat, secundùm applicationem ad propriam materiam: eorum tamen explicatio, ad solam spectat dialecticam, cuius proprium munus est, methodum præbere omnibus scientiis, ac disciplinis, disputationem instituendam.

22 This alone remained to be explained among the things that pertain to setting up a dialectical disputation: namely the Places from which probable arguments, or syllogisms, are to be taken. For once places of this kind have been explained and known, it will be easy for anyone to find probable arguments which he can use in disputations. And although the use of the places pertains to any science whatever, according to their application to its proper matter, their explanation nevertheless belongs to Dialectic alone, whose proper office is to furnish all the sciences and disciplines with a method for setting up a disputation.

> 23 *Locus* autem, ex quo eruuntur argumenta, diuiditur in *Intrinsecum,* & *Extrinsecum. Locus Intrinsecus,* vocatur ille, qui ad substantiam rei pertinet, vel substantiam eius comitatur. Quæ ad substantiam pertinent, sunt hæc, Definitio, Genus, Differentia, aut Pars aliqua rei, vt Materia, & Forma: vel Partes integrantes, vt Caput, Manus, aut Brachium. Quod verò comitatur substantiam, aut est Totum: (quod ideo comitari dicitur substantiam rei: quia includit partes:) [p. 728] aut Descriptio ipsius rei, aut Proprium rei: aut Accidens: aut subiectum illius. *Vnde loci intrinseci, tantùm sunt nouem,* Definitio, Genus, Differentia, Partes, Totum, Descriptio, Proprium, Accidens, & Subiectum,

23 The Place, then, from which arguments are drawn out, is divided into the Intrinsic and the Extrinsic. The Intrinsic place is called that which pertains to the substance of the thing, or accompanies its substance. Those that pertain to the substance are these: Definition, Genus, Difference, or some Part of the thing, such as Matter and Form; or the integral Parts, such as the Head, the Hand, or the Arm. That which accompanies the substance, on the other hand, is either the Whole (which is said to accompany the substance of the thing because it includes the parts), Z z iiij [p. 728] or the Description of the thing itself, or the Property of the thing, or an Accident, or its subject. Hence there are only nine intrinsic places: Definition, Genus, Difference, Parts, Whole, Description, Property, Accident, and

> *Locus extrinsecus*, dicitur ille, qui non est in ipsa re, nec ab ea procedit, sed ex aliquo extrinseco desumitur. *Locus autem extrinsecus* diuiditur, in Eum, qui habet aliquam affinitatem cum ipsa re, & in Eum, qui habet aliquam repugnantiam cum ea. *Loci extrinseci habentes affinitatem*, sunt Coniugata, Similia, Causæ extrinsecæ, nempe Efficiens, & Finalis: Effectus extrinseci, Maius, Minus, Auctoritas Diuina, vel humana. *Loci verò extrinseci repugnantes*, sunt, Contraria, Disparata, & Dissimilia. Vnde loci extrinseci, vndecim sunt: quos si cum nouem extrinsecis coniungamus, inueniemus locos omnes, tam intrinsecos quàm extrinsecos, viginti tantùm esse: quos singillatim, breuissimè tamen explicabimus: Vt ratio singulorum intelligatur, & vsus eorum reddatur facilis.

Subject. The extrinsic place is said to be that which is not in the thing itself, nor proceeds from it, but is taken from something extrinsic. And the extrinsic place is divided into That which has some affinity with the thing itself, and That which has some repugnance to it. The extrinsic places having affinity are Conjugates, Similars, extrinsic Causes, namely the Efficient and the Final, extrinsic Effects, the Greater, the Lesser, Authority Divine or human. The repugnant extrinsic places, on the other hand, are Contraries, Disparates, and Dissimilars. Hence the extrinsic places are eleven; and if we join them with the nine intrinsic ones, we shall find that all the places, intrinsic as well as extrinsic, are only twenty. These we shall explain one by one, though very briefly, so that the ratio of each may be understood and their use made easy.

> *Locus primus à Definitione.*

The first place, from Definition. 24

> 24 Frequens vsus est huius loci *à Definitione*, in disputationibus, ex eo, quòd essentiam definiti continet, & cum eo conuertitur. Vnde fit: vt plures propositiones vniuersales deduci possint ex ea, quæ vocantur Maximæ, & quasi capita sub quibus plures particulares desumuntur, ad instituendos syllogismos dialecticos. Et si quæstio proposita, circa quam disputatur, sit Absoluta, possumus assumere in argumentatione, definitionem subiecti, aut prędicati, aut vtriusque: ex quibus deducuntur *Maximæ, Affirmatiuæ, & Negatiuæ. Affirmatiuæ* sunt, Quidquid conuenit definitioni, conuenit definito: & Quidquid potest conuenire definitioni potest conuenire definito, & aliæ similes. Negatiuæ, Quod non conuenit definitioni, non conuenire definito: & Quod non potest conuenire definitioni: non potest conuenire definito. Gratia exempli: Si proposita q. disputanda sit. *An dialectica sit necessaria ad alias scientias comparandas*, Subiectum huius quæstionis est *Dialectica*, *Prædicatum* verò necessarium: Possumus ergo vti definitione Dialecticæ, sic arguentes: Scientia docens argumenta conficere, necessaria est ad alias scientias comparandas: sed dialectica est scientia, docens argumenta conficere: ergo necessaria ad alias scientias comparandas. Et secundùm eandem proportionem, possumus vti definitione necessarij, quod est prædicatum quæstionis, atque etiam definitione, simul subiecti, & prædicati.

Frequent is the use of this place from Definition in disputations, because the definition contains the essence and is convertible with it. Hence it happens that several universal propositions can be deduced from it, which are called Maxims, and as it were heads under which several particular ones are taken for setting up dialectical syllogisms. And if the proposed question about which the dispute is held is Absolute, we can take up in the argumentation the definition of the subject, or of the predicate, or of both; from which are deduced Maxims, Affirmative and Negative. The affirmative are: Whatever belongs to the definition belongs to the defined; and Whatever can belong to the definition can belong to the defined; and others like them. The negative: What does not belong to the definition does not belong to the defined; and What cannot belong to the definition cannot belong to the defined. For example: if the proposed q. to be disputed is, Whether dialectic is necessary for acquiring the other sciences, the Subject of this question is Dialectic, and the Predicate is necessary. We can therefore use the definition of Dialectic, arguing thus: A science teaching how to construct arguments is necessary for acquiring the other sciences; but dialectic is a science teaching how to construct arguments; therefore it is necessary for acquiring the other sciences. And according to the same proportion we can use the definition of necessary, which is the predicate of the question, and also the definition of subject and predicate together.

[p. 729]

> Si verò quæstio sit Comparatiua, nempe, *An necessitas ad alias scientias, magis conueniat dialectica, quàm cæteris artibus*, vti possumus definitione subiecti, atque etiam prædicati, vel vtriusque deducendo ex eis Maximas quasdam, similes superioribus, cum his aduerbiis magis, & minus. Vt si dicamus, Cui magis conuenit definitio, magis conuenit definitum: & Cui minùs conuenit definitio: minùs conuenit definitum, & sic de cæteris.

But if the question is Comparative, namely, Whether necessity for acquiring the other sciences belongs more to dialectic than to the other arts, we can use the definition of the subject, and also of the predicate, or of both, deducing from them certain Maxims similar to the ones above, with these adverbs more and less. As if we say: To that to which the definition belongs more, the defined belongs more; and To that to which the definition belongs less, the defined belongs less; and so of the rest.

> *Secundus locus à Genere.*

The second place, from Genus. 25

> 25 Eisdem ferè modis vti possumus, *loco à genere*. Nam propter necessariam connexionem: quam habet cum speciebus, deducuntur ab hoc loco plures *Maximæ*. ex quibus instituere possumus argumenta: vt sunt istæ, *Quicquid essentialiter conuenit generi, etiam conuenit essentialiter speciebus*: &, *Quod repugnat generi, repugnat etiam speciebus*, sicque ad aliis, iuxta modos arguendi à definitione explicatos. Et ad hunc locum generis, reducitur locus Speciei: quia similem habet connexionem cum indiuiduis: & ideo non additur alter locus à specie, sed eædem ferè Maximæ deduci possunt, atque à genere: & eodem modo debent applicari, ad formanda argumenta à specie.

In almost the same ways we can use the place from genus. For on account of the necessary connection which it has with the species, several Maxims are deduced from this place, from which we can set up arguments: such as these, Whatever belongs essentially to the genus also belongs essentially to the species; and, What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species; and so of the others, according to the modes of arguing explained for definition. And to this place of genus is reduced the place of Species, because it has a similar connection with the individuals; and therefore no other place from species is added, but almost the same Maxims can be deduced as from genus, and they must be applied in the same way to forming arguments from species.

> *Tertius locus à Differenti,.*

The third place, from Difference.

> Valde similis est locus *à Differentia*, duobus præcedentibus à definitione & à genere. Nam duplex est differentia *Subalterna*, & *Atoma*. Et si *subalterna* sit, de eisdem speciebus prædicatur ac genus: & eandem habet connexionem intrinsecam cum eis. Quare eædem Maximæ, ex ea deduci possunt, ac ex genere, Si verò sit *Atoma*, cum definitione conuenit in duobus. Primò, In eo, quod intrinseca est speciei. Secũdò: Quia cum ea conuertitur. Vnde similes etiam Maximæ ex ea deduci possunt: ac deducuntur ex definitione, & eisdem modis applicari debent ad syllogismos dialecticos conficiendos.

Very similar to the two preceding places, from definition and from genus, is the place from Difference. For difference is twofold, Subaltern and Atomic. And if it is subaltern, it is predicated of the same species as the genus is, and has the same intrinsic connection with them. Wherefore the same Maxims can be deduced from it as from genus. But if it is Atomic, it agrees with definition in two things. First, in that it is intrinsic to the species. Second, because it is convertible with it. Hence similar Maxims too can be deduced from it as are deduced from definition, and they must be applied in the same ways to constructing dialectical syllogisms.

> *Quartus locus à partibus.*

The fourth place, from the parts.

> *Partes* sunt in triplici differentia, *Subiectiuæ*, vt species respectu generis, *Essentiales*, vt materia, & forma: aut genus, & differentia: & *Integrantes*, vt caput, manus, & brachium. Et ex his: Quædam sunt *necessariæ* ad consistentiam totius, sine quibus esse non potest: vt caput, cor, & similes. Aliæ *non sunt necessariæ*, sed sine illis esse potest: vt manus, digitus, pes, Et à primis potest deduci argum, à secundis deduci non potest: quia neque [p. 730] inferunt consistentiam totius, nec eam tollunt. A partibus plures Maximę deduci possunt, propter necessariam cõnexionem, quam habent cum toto, & cum eis totum: vt sunt ista: *Quod necessariò comitatur partem, necessariò etiam debet comitari totum*, &, *Quod repugnat parti, etiam repugnat toti*. Et hæc accipiuntur *ex parte subiecti* propositæ q. Aliæ verò possunt sumi, *ex parte prædicati* secundum proportionem.

Parts are of three different kinds: Subjective, as species with respect to genus; Essential, as matter and form, or genus and difference; and Integral, as head, hand, and arm. And of these, some are necessary for the consistence of the whole, without which it cannot be, such as the head, the heart, and the like. Others are not necessary, but it can be without them, such as the hand, the finger, the foot. And from the first an argument can be deduced; from the second it cannot be deduced, because neither [p. 730] do they infer the consistence of the whole, nor do they remove it. From the parts several Maxims can be deduced, on account of the necessary connection which they have with the whole, and the whole with them: such as these, What necessarily accompanies the part must necessarily also accompany the whole; and, What is repugnant to the part is also repugnant to the whole. And these are taken on the side of the subject of the proposed q. Others, however, can be taken on the side of the predicate, according to proportion.

> *Quintus locus à Toto.*

The fifth place, from the Whole. 27

> 27 *Totum* duplex est. Aliud *vniuersale*, quod est vniuersale prædicatum respectu inferiorum, quæ sunt partes eius subiectiuæ: vt genus respectu specierum: & terminus distributus signo vniuersali: vt omnis homo, respectu particularium, quæ sub eo continentur, Et ab hoc toto, ad eius partes, sumuntur omnia argumenta quæ fiunt à superiori ad inferius negatiuè: & in summulis sunt manifesta. Aliud est *totum Essentiale, aut integrale*, vt homo, equus, domus. Et ab hoc toto deduci possunt plures Maximæ, & ex eis confici plures syllogismi: vt, *Posito toto necesse est poni omnes pates necessarias*. Vnde valet arg. à positione totius, ad positionem cuiuscunque partis necessariæ, & etiam *Ablato toto, necesse est auferri aliquam partem necessariam*. Vnde valet argum. à negatione totius ad negationem alicuius partis necessariæ, sub distinctione: vt si deficit domus, aut non est fundamentum, aut non est tectum, aut non ex aliqua alia pars necessaria.

The Whole is twofold.
