One is universal, which is a universal predicate with respect to its inferiors, which are its subjective parts: as genus with respect to the species, and a term distributed by a universal sign, as every man, with respect to the particulars which are contained under it. And from this whole to its parts are taken all the arguments that are made from superior to inferior negatively; and these are manifest in the Summulae. The other is the Essential or integral whole, as man, horse, house. And from this whole several Maxims can be deduced, and from them several syllogisms constructed: as, When the whole is posited, all the necessary parts must be posited. Hence the argument holds from the positing of the whole to the positing of any necessary part whatever. And also, When the whole is taken away, some necessary part must be taken away. Hence the argument holds from the negation of the whole to the negation of some necessary part, under a disjunction: as, if the house is lacking, either the foundation does not exist, or the roof does not exist, or some other necessary part does not exist.

> *Locus sextus à Descriptione.*

The sixth place, from Description. 28

> 28 *Descriptio* est definitio, quam appellare solent *descriptiuam*: quia non explicat essentiam rei, nec per genus, & differentiam traditur, sed per propriam passionem, conuertibilem tamen cum re descripta: vt animal, aptum ad ridendum cũ homine: & ideo omnes Maximæ, quæ ex definitione deducuntur, ex descriptione deduci possunt, & eodem modo applicari ad syllogismos constituendos. Et quod de descriptione dicitur, de definitione, quid nominis intelligi debet: cùm conuertatur etiam cum re, non tamen de etymologia nominis: quia sæpe contingit, diuersa esse, id à quo nomen imponitur, & illud quod significat: quare non potest argumentum firmum duci ab etymologia ad rem significatam.

Description is a definition which they usually call descriptive, because it does not explain the essence of the thing, nor is it delivered through genus and difference, but through a proper attribute, which is nevertheless convertible with the thing described: as animal apt to laugh with man. And therefore all the Maxims which are deduced from definition can be deduced from description, and applied in the same way to constituting syllogisms. And what is said of description ought to be understood of the definition of what the name means, since it too is convertible with the thing; but not of the etymology of the name: because it often happens that that from which the name is imposed and that which it signifies are different; wherefore a firm argument cannot be drawn from the etymology to the thing signified.

> *Locus septimus à Proprio.*

The seventh place, from Property.

> *Proprium est, quod non indicat, quid est esse rei, soli autem inest, & conuersim prædicatur*: vt definit Aristot. cap. 4. 1. lib. quasi [p. 731] dicat propriam passionem, non pertinere ad quod quid est, seu rei essentiam, conuerti tamen cum ea, sicut definitio conuertitur cum definito. Et ideo iisdem ferè modis, eadem ferè argu. deduci possunt à proprio, atque à definitione: quia, *Cui conuenit definitio, conuenit propria passio*: &, *Cui non conuenit propria passio, nec definitio conuenit*. Et sicut bene colligitur, Rem esse perfectiorem, quo perfectiorem definitionem habet: Ita quò perfectiorem habet passionem; cùm hæc procedat ab essentia, tanquam à propria causa.

Property is that which does not indicate what it is to be for the thing, but is in it alone, and is predicated convertibly, as Aristotle defines it, ch. 4, bk. 1: as if [p. 731] to say that a proper attribute does not pertain to what the thing is, or to its essence, yet is convertible with it, just as the definition is convertible with the defined. And therefore in almost the same ways almost the same arguments can be deduced from property as from definition: because, To whatever the definition belongs, the proper attribute belongs; and, To whatever the proper attribute does not belong, neither does the definition belong. And just as it is rightly gathered that a thing is more perfect the more perfect the definition it has, so also the more perfect the attribute it has, since the latter proceeds from the essence as from its proper cause.

> *Locus 8. ab Accidente.*

The 8th place, from Accident. 29

> 29 *Accidens est, quod adest, & abest subiecto, præter corruptionẽ eius*. vt definit ibidem Arist. Sed hæc definitio, solùm videtur conuenire accidentibus verè inhærentibus, quæ ideo vocantur intrinseca: nihilominus etiam alia quæ solùm videtur extrinsecam denominationem significare, sub nomine accidentis hoc loco debet intelligi: vt dextrum esse, vel sinistrũ parietem: aut visum vel intellectum esse: quia in modo denominandi, similia sunt accidentibus intrinsecis. Ab accidente, deduci possunt plures Maximæ, & ab his plura arg. Vt, *Si accidentia prædicati, non conueniunt subiecto, non cohærebit prædicatum subiecto*: quo arg. vsus videtur beatus Petrus, Actor. 2. probans discipulos non fuisse ebrios: quia tempus illud tertiæ horæ diei, non erat conueniens ebrietati, & ideo, nec discipulis, cùm eadem hora eis imponeretur ebrietas. Et bene probatur, aliquem non occidisse alterum, si probatur eo tempore, quo occisus est, in eodem loco occisionis non fuisse, sed alibi.

An accident is that which is present to and absent from the subject without its corruption, as Aristotle defines it in the same place. But this definition seems to belong only to truly inhering accidents, which are therefore called intrinsic; nevertheless, the others too, which seem to signify only an extrinsic denomination, ought in this place to be understood under the name of accident: as for a wall to be right or left, or to be seen or understood; because in the mode of denominating they are similar to intrinsic accidents. From accident several Maxims can be deduced, and from these several arguments. As, If the accidents of the predicate do not belong to the subject, the predicate will not cohere with the subject: which argument blessed Peter seems to have used, Acts 2, proving that the disciples were not drunk because that time, the third hour of the day, was not suited to drunkenness, and therefore not to the disciples either, since drunkenness was imputed to them at that same hour. And it is well proved that someone did not kill another if it is proved that at the time when he was killed he was not in the same place as the killing, but elsewhere.

> *Locus 9. à Subiecto.*

Place 9, from the Subject.

> De *subiecto inhæsionis*, intelligitur locus iste, cui inhærent accidentia, non de subiecto prędicationis, cui potest prędicatum essentialiter conuenire: & ideo meritò numeratur inter locos intrinsecos. A subiecto possunt deduci Maximæ istæ & similes: *Cui repugnant accidentia, etiam repugnat subiectum*: vt si alicui repugnat intellectus, etiam anima, & si repugnant corporea accidentia, etiam repugnabit corpus. *Vbi subiectum est, ibi debent esse accidentia*: & *Vbi non sunt accidentia, nec est subiectum*: & *Motis nobis mouentur omnia, quæ sunt in nobis*: id est accidentia. Et ex his, & aliis Maximis, multa possunt effici arg. à loco subiecti: & isti sunt omnes loci intrinseci. Sequuntur extrinseci.

This place is understood of the subject of inherence, in which accidents inhere, not of the subject of predication, to which a predicate can belong essentially; and therefore it is rightly numbered among the intrinsic places. From the subject these Maxims and the like can be deduced: To whatever the accidents are repugnant, the subject too is repugnant: as, if intellect is repugnant to something, so also is the soul; and if corporeal accidents are repugnant to it, the body too will be repugnant to it. Where the subject is, there the accidents must be; and Where the accidents are not, neither is the subject; and All things move with our motion that are in us, that is, the accidents. And from these and other Maxims many arguments can be made from the place of the subject. And these are all the intrinsic places. The extrinsic ones follow.

[p. 732]

> *Locus decimus, & primus inter Extrinsecos, à Coniugatis.*

The tenth place, and the first among the Extrinsic ones, from Conjugates.

> 30 *Coniugata dicuntur voces, quæ sub diuersa terminatione, eandem formam significant, atque participant*: & propterea quasi idem iugum ducere videntur, vt Iustus, Iustitia, & Iustè; & omnes casus per quos variatur idem nomen: & verbum. Ad hæc reducuntur alia, quæ eandem formam significant, licèt diuersæ omnino sint voces: vt Iustus, & Studiosus: quæ ita se habent, quantùm ad rem significatam, sicut iustitia, & iustus. Ex his deducuntur istæ maximæ, & similes: *Quæ dicuntur de vno coniugatorum, suo etiam modo, & cum debita variatione, dicuntur de alio*: vt si Philosophus est sciens, Philosophia erit scientia: &, *de quo dicitur vnum coniugatorum, dicitur etiam suo modo alterum*. Et ex his, ac similibus propositionibus possunt fieri multa argumenta à coniugatis.

30 Conjugates are said to be words which under different endings signify and participate in the same form; and for this reason they seem as it were to draw the same yoke, as just, justice, and justly; and all the cases by which the same noun and verb are varied. To these are reduced others which signify the same form, although they are altogether different words: as just and virtuous, which are related, as regards the thing signified, as justice and just are. From these are deduced these maxims and the like: What is said of one of the conjugates is said also of the other in its own way, and with due variation: as, if the Philosopher is knowing, Philosophy will be knowledge; and, Of whatever one of the conjugates is said, the other too is said in its own way. And from these and similar propositions many arguments can be made from conjugates.

> *Locus 11. à Simili.*

Place 11, from the Similar.

> *Similia sunt, quæ participant eandem formam*: vt omnia alba. Ad quæ reducuntur, quæ habent eandem proportionem: vt auriga, & dux, quia similem curam ei, quam habet auriga in suo curru, debet habere dux in exercitu. Ad similia etiam reducuntur æqualia, & ab eis deducuntur Maximæ plures, pro argumentis instituendis, similes huic: *Cygnus disgregat visum: ergo etiam paries albus*. Sed semper debet fieri in his argumentum à ratione formali similitudinis, & non ab aliis materialibus, quæ habere possunt similia: non est enim bonum argu. si dicamus, *Cygnus est auis, ergo etiam paries albus est auis*.

Similar things are those which participate in the same form: as all white things. To these are reduced those which have the same proportion: as the charioteer and the general, because the general ought to have in the army a care similar to that which the charioteer has in his chariot. To similars are also reduced equals; and from them several Maxims are deduced for setting up arguments, similar to this: The swan disperses the sight; therefore the white wall does too. But in these the argument must always be made from the formal ratio of similitude, and not from other material features which similar things can have: for it is not a good argument if we say, The swan is a bird; therefore the white wall too is a bird.

> *Locus 12. à Causa.*

Place 12, from Cause. 31

> 31 *Quadruplex est causa, Finalis, Efficiens, Materialis, & Formalis*. Verùm locus iste, cùm sit extrinsecus, solam Finalem, & Efficientem complectitur: non Materialem, & Formalem, quæ cùm sint partes rei Intrinsecæ, potiùs ad locum partium pertinebunt. *Causa finalis est*, cuius gratia operatur efficiens & producit effectum: *Causa efficiens*, à qua effectus procedit Maximæ, quæ ex eis deduci possunt, similes sunt his: *Posita causa, necessariò ponitur effectus*: quæ intelligitur de causa actuali, & sufficienti, & *Non posito effectu, non ponitur causa*: quæ proprietatem harum causarum pertinent, in secundo lib. Phys. à nobis explicantur.

Cause is fourfold: Final, Efficient, Material, and Formal. But this place, since it is extrinsic, embraces only the Final and the Efficient, not the Material and the Formal, which, since they are intrinsic parts of the thing, will rather pertain to the place of the parts. The final cause is that for the sake of which the efficient operates and produces the effect; the efficient cause, that from which the effect proceeds. The Maxims which can be deduced from them are similar to these: When the cause is posited, the effect is necessarily posited, which is understood of an actual and sufficient cause; and When the effect is not posited, the cause is not posited. The things which pertain to the property of these causes are explained by us in Phys. bk. 2.

[p. 733]

> *Locus 13, ab Effectu.*

Place 13, from the Effect.

> Valde similis est locus iste præcedenti: quia eædem Maximæ, à causa, & effectu deducuntur: idem est modus arguendi in eis, vt à *Positione effectus, ad positionem causæ*: v.g. Si dies est, sol est in nostro hemisphærio. *Ablato effectu, aufertur causa*: vt, non est dies, ergo nec sol est in nostro hemisphærio. Sed intelliguntur istæ & aliæ similes, de causis necessariis, & sufficientibus.

Very similar to the preceding is this place, because the same Maxims are deduced from cause and from effect: the mode of arguing in them is the same, as from the positing of the effect to the positing of the cause: e.g., If it is day, the sun is in our hemisphere. When the effect is taken away, the cause is taken away: as, It is not day; therefore neither is the sun in our hemisphere. But these and others like them are understood of necessary and sufficient causes.

> *Locus 14. à Maiori, & 15. à Minori.*

Place 14, from the Greater, and 15, from the Lesser. 32

> 32 Similiores sunt duo isti loci, à maiori, & minori. & ideo de illis simul loquendum est. A maiori, sumitur hæc Maxima: *Quod potest efficere maius, potest efficere minus*. & à minori hæc, *Quod non potest efficere minus, nec potest efficere maius*. Sed vtraque debet intelligi, de maiori & minori, eiusdem conditionis. Nam si diuersæ rationis sint, non valebit argumentum. v.g. Angelus potest intelligere, quod est maius: ergo potest ambulare, quod est minus. Quia diuersæ conditionis sunt, intelligere, & ambulare. Item non potest ambulare, ergo nec intelligere.

Very similar are these two places, from the greater and the lesser, and therefore we must speak of them together. From the greater this Maxim is taken: What can effect the greater can effect the lesser; and from the lesser this one: What cannot effect the lesser cannot effect the greater either. But each must be understood of a greater and a lesser of the same condition. For if they are of a different ratio, the argument will not hold: e.g., An angel can understand, which is greater; therefore he can walk, which is lesser; because understanding and walking are of different conditions. Likewise, He cannot walk; therefore neither can he understand.

> *Locus 16. & 17. ab Authoritate Diuina, & humana.*

Place 16 and 17, from Authority, Divine and human.

> *Testimonium fide digni, cui fides innititur, valde extrinsecum est rebus testificatis vel creditis*: vt ex se est manifestũ. Vnde locus ab authoritate fide digni, maximè extrinsecus est. Sed si sit ab authoritate Diuina, infallibilem veritatem tribuit rei: quia cùm Deus sit summa, & prima veritas, non potest falli: & cùm sit summa bonitas, fallere non potest. Vnde quæ *DEVS* testificatur, ea infallibilem veritatem habent: & tales sunt res nostræ fidei, quas propter Diuinam authoritatem credimus, & argumenta Theologica, ab hoc præcipuè loco deducuntur.

The testimony of one worthy of belief, on which faith rests, is very extrinsic to the things testified or believed, as is manifest of itself. Hence the place from the authority of one worthy of belief is supremely extrinsic. But if it is from Divine authority, it attributes infallible truth to the thing: because, since God is the highest and first truth, he cannot be deceived; and since he is the highest goodness, he cannot deceive. Hence the things which G o d testifies have infallible truth; and such are the things of our faith, which we believe on account of the Divine authority; and Theological arguments are deduced chiefly from this place.

> 33 *Ab humana verò authoritate aut testimonio, non adeo firmum argum. deduci potest*. Sed valet plurimùm, ad explicandas res diuinæ fidei. Nam licèt sacri Doctores, homines fuerint, tamen expositio sacræ Scripturæ, quam omnes, vel plures eorum adferunt (etiam si dissentiat vnus, vel aliter) maximam facit fidem: quia non est credendum, permisisse Deum eos in hac re decipi, ad quos pertinet Scripturam exponere, & expositam aliis tradere. Valet etiam multùm in rebus, quæ dependent ex libera hominum voluntate: vt ad impositionem, & significationem nominum: quia nominibus vtendum est, vt plures [p. 734] vtuntur. Præterea in rebus quæ per sensus euidenter cognoscuntur: atque etiam in his, quæ ad historiam pertinent: quæ inniti debent euidentiæ alicuius, vt plurimùm, per assensus habita, ex qua ita contigisse, credunt alij. Sed non valet in his, quæ cognoscuntur per discursum, in quibus præcipuum locum ratio tenet, quanquam adhuc in his multùm valeat communis consensus omnium. Semper ergo ducitur arg. probabile, ab authoritate humana: & quo plures sunt, qui aliquid testificantur, eo efficacius arg. deducitur. Negatiuè tamen, non est ab authoritate humana arguendum, quasi probetur, rem non ita esse, quia à nemine narratur: quia non est necessarium scripta fuisse omnia.

33 From human authority or testimony, however, so firm an argument cannot be deduced. But it is of very great value for explaining the things of divine faith. For although the sacred Doctors were men, nevertheless an exposition of sacred Scripture which all, or most of them, put forward (even if one, or another, dissents) produces the greatest belief: because it is not to be believed that God has permitted those to be deceived in this matter to whom it pertains to expound Scripture and to hand it on, expounded, to others. It is also of great value in matters which depend on the free will of men, as for the imposition and signification of names: because names are to be used as most [p. 734] use them. Moreover, in things which are evidently known through the senses, and also in those which pertain to history, which must rest on some evidence, had for the most part through assents, from which others believe that things happened thus. But it is not of value in those things which are known through discursive reasoning, in which reason holds the chief place, although even in these the common consent of all is still of much value. A probable argument, therefore, is always drawn from human authority; and the more there are who testify to something, the more efficacious the argument that is deduced. Negatively, however, one must not argue from human authority, as if it were proved that a thing is not so because it is related by no one: because it is not necessary that all things have been written.

> *Locus 18. & 19. ab Oppositis, & Repugnantibus seu Disparatis.*

Place 18 and 19, from Opposites, and from Repugnants or Disparates.

> Non multum differunt duo isti loci, *ab Oppositis & Repugnantibus, seu Disparatis*. quia eadem ferè argumenta ab vtrisque deducuntur. *Oppositio quadruplex est*: vt in Postprędicamentis diximus. *Contraria*, quę est inter Album, & Nigrum. *Contradictoria*: Inter album, & Non album. *Priuatiua*: Inter cæcum, & videns; & *Relatiua*, Inter Patrem & Filium: Et in contradictoriè oppositis: Maxima hæc semper est vera: *Quod cui conuenit vni, non potest cõuenire alteri*. &, *Cui non conuenit vnũ necessariò conuenit alterum*: quia immediata est eorum oppositio. Et idem est in priuatiuè oppositis: non quidem absolutè, sed circa subiectum aptum: vt, *Cui conuenit cæcitas, non potest simul conuenire visus*: nec, *Cui conuenit visus, potest simul conuenire cæcitas. Et si visus non conuenit, necesse est conuenire cæcitatem*: &, *Si non conuenit cæcitas, necesse est visum conuenire*. In contrariis verò, valet arg. ab affirmatione vnius, ad negationem alterius: vt, est album: ergo non est nigrum. Sed non valet à negatione vnius ad negationem alterius: vt, non est album: ergo nigrum, quia oppositio contraria, non est immediata. Et similia argumenta deduci possunt, à repugnantibus, aut disparatis, quorum exempla satis sunt manifesta.

These two places, from Opposites and from Repugnants, or Disparates, do not differ much, because almost the same arguments are deduced from both. Opposition is fourfold, as we said in the Postpredicaments: Contrary, which is between White and Black; Contradictory, between white and Not-white; Privative, between blind and seeing; and Relative, between Father and Son. And in contradictory opposites this Maxim is always true: What belongs to one cannot belong to the other; and, To whatever one does not belong, the other necessarily belongs: because their opposition is immediate. And the same holds in privative opposites, not indeed absolutely, but concerning an apt subject: as, To whatever blindness belongs, sight cannot at the same time belong; nor, To whatever sight belongs can blindness at the same time belong. And if sight does not belong, blindness must belong; and, If blindness does not belong, sight must belong. In contraries, however, the argument holds from the affirmation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is white; therefore it is not black. But it does not hold from the negation of one to the negation of the other: as, It is not white; therefore it is black; because contrary opposition is not immediate. And similar arguments can be deduced from repugnants, or disparates, whose examples are manifest enough.

> *Locus 20. à Dissimili.*

Place 20, from the Dissimilar.

> *Dissimilia* appellantur, quæ diuersam habent formam, aut naturam: vt albedo, & dulcedo: album, & nigrum: homo & leo: ad quæ reducuntur ea, quæ licèt eandem formam habeant, non tamen in eodem gradu, sed diuerso: qualia sunt, calidum vt vnum, & calidum vt octo. Et ab vtrisque desumi possunt argumenta. Quia, *quæ vni conueniunt, non possunt conuenire alteri*. Sed semper sunt accipienda formaliter, hoc [p. 735] est, in quantum dissimilia in natura, vel gradu: & non secũdùm alias rationes materiales, in quibus, manifestum est, posse conuenire. Et hæc annotasse sufficiat, circa librum Topicorum.

Those things are called Dissimilar which have a different form or nature: as whiteness and sweetness, white and black, man and lion. To these are reduced those which, although they have the same form, yet have it not in the same degree but in a different one: such as hot as one and hot as eight. And from both, arguments can be taken: because what belongs to one cannot belong to the other. But they must always be taken formally, that [p. 735] is, inasmuch as they are dissimilar in nature or degree, and not according to other material ratios, in which it is manifest that they can agree. And let it suffice to have noted these things concerning the book of the Topics.

## Pro libris Elenchorum — F O R T H E B O O K S O F T H E S O P H I S T I C A L R E F U TAT I O N S . T R E AT I S E

## ON THE SOPHISTICAL SYLLOGISM

> PRO LIBRIS ELENCHORVM. TRACTATVS de syllogismo Sophistico.

[…]

> 1 Quo agit Arist. in duobus libris Elenchorum, vt vniuersali diuisione, totum hoc opus comprehendamus. *Explicat naturam syllogismi Sophistici, & partium eius*, ex quibus componitur: tanquam obiectum proprij. *Deinde locos omnes enumerat, ex quibus fallacia argumenta deducuntur*, aut occasionem sumunt: qui sunt Fallacię tam in Dictione, quàm extra Dictionem. Nos verò ea, quæ ad fallacias pertinent, ad summulas remittentes, in quibus copiosè explicantur, aliquid de natura, syllogismi sophistici dicemus: qua intellecta, quidquid in præsenti opere tradit de eo Aristoteles, aliqua saltem ratione percipi possit.

hat Aristotle does in the two books of the Sophistical Refutations we 1 W              comprehend, so as to embrace this whole work in a universal division. He explains the nature of the Sophistical syllogism, and of the parts of which it is composed, as of his proper object. Then he enumerates all the places from which fallacious arguments are deduced, or take their occasion: which are the Fallacies both in Speech and outside Speech. We, however, referring the things that pertain to the fallacies to the Summulae, in which they are copiously explained, shall say something about the nature of the sophistical syllogism; once this is understood, whatever Aristotle delivers about it in the present work can be grasped, at least in some measure.

### Quidnam sit syllogismus Sophisticus, & quotuplex: & an verus sit syllogismus, vel non — What a Sophistical syllogism is, and how many kinds there are; and whether it is a true syllogism, or not?

> *Quidnam sit syllogismus Sophisticus, & quotuplex: & an verus sit syllogismus, vel non?*

[…]

> 2 *Syllogismus sophisticus*, si etymologiam nominis sequamur, idem significat ac syllogismus sapientis, cùm σοφὸς sit sapiens: vsu tamen philosophicæ scholæ factum est, vt iam non syllogismus sapientis, sed decipientis, aut decipere volentis, per eum intelligatur. Quia per sophistam, non iam verum sapientem, sed eum, qui sapiens videri vult, omnes intelligunt. Definitionem, & Diuisionem *syllogismi sophistici* tradit Aristot. 1. lib. Topic. c. 1. Sed vt tria illa, quæ de eo considerari possunt, commodiùs explicentur, à diuisione incipiendum est.

2 The sophistical syllogism, if we follow the etymology of the name, signifies the same as the syllogism of a wise man, since σοφός [sophos] is “wise”; yet by the philosophical usage of the school it has come about that by it is now understood not the syllogism of a wise man, but of one who deceives, or wishes to deceive. Because by a sophist all now understand not a truly wise man, but one who wishes to seem wise. Aristotle delivers the definition and division of the sophistical syllogism in Topics 1, ch. 1. But in order that the three things which can be considered about it may be explained more conveniently, we must begin from the division.

> Diuidit autem Arist. syllogismum sophisticum, in tria membra, & primũ ita definit: *Litigiosus autem est syllogismus, ex his, quæ videntur probabilia, non sunt autem*. Secundum verò, his verbis, *Et qui ex probabilibus quidem, aut ex his quæ videntur probabilia est apparens*. Et paulo inferiùs, de vtroque in particulari loquens asserit, Primum esse verum syllogismum: Secundum, non verum, sed apparentem. Postremum mẽbrum, vocat paralogismum: & ait eum esse, quia assumit propositiones proprias alicuius scientiæ: quæ vt ab ea scientia assumuntur, necessariæ sunt: sed vt ab eo assumuntur, solùm apparent necessariæ, & sunt falsæ. Et talis est syllogismus iste: Lineæ ductæ ab eodem puncto, in idem punctum, sunt æquales: Chorda & arcus ducuntur ab eodem puncto: ergo sũt æquales. Syllogismus iste cõstitutus est in [p. 736] materia geometriæ, sed maiorem propositionem sic accipit geometria: Omnes lineæ rectæ, ductæ, ab eodem puncto, in idem punctum, sunt æquales. Et sic vera est, ac necessaria: sed cùm accipiatur in illo syllogismo, sine illa voce, recta, apparet quidem necessaria, quia apparet eadem: sed falsa est, & valde diuersa, vt constat, & ideo procedit ex propositionibus illius scientiæ apparentibus necessariis, non tamen verè necessariis, sed falsis.

Aristotle, then, divides the sophistical syllogism into three members, and defines the first thus: But the contentious is a syllogism from things which seem probable but are not. The second in these words: And that which is from probable things, or from things which seem probable, is apparent. And a little below, speaking of each in particular, he asserts that the First is a true syllogism, the Second not true but apparent. The last member he calls a paralogism; and he says that it is one because it takes up propositions proper to some science, which, as they are taken up by that science, are necessary, but as they are taken up by him, only appear necessary, and are false. And such is this syllogism: Lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal; the chord and the arc are drawn from the same point; therefore they are equal. This syllogism is constituted in matter [p. 736] of geometry, but geometry takes the major proposition thus: All straight lines drawn from the same point to the same point are equal. And thus it is true and necessary; but since it is taken in that syllogism without the word straight, it appears indeed necessary, because it appears the same, but it is false and very different, as is evident; and therefore it proceeds from propositions of that science which appear necessary, yet are not truly necessary, but false.

> 3 Ex his autem tribus syllogismis, primus, qui dicitur *Litigiosus*, & tertius qui dicitur *Paralogismus*, conueniunt in eo, quòd vterque seruat formam syllogisticam, cùm in Figura, & Modo constituatur: vnde ex hac parte non peccat: sed differunt in his ex quibus procedunt. Quia prior ille procedit ex his, quę apparent probabilia, sed probabilia non sunt: paralogismus verò, ex necessariis, ac propriis alicuius scientiæ, sed quę nec sunt necessaria, nec ad illam, scientiam pertinent, sed sunt falsa. Secundus verò, qui etiam litigiosus vocatur, in vtroque differt ab aliis duobus. Nam primò non seruat formam syllogismi, sed peccat in ea: & ideo dixit de eo Arg. esse litigiosum syllogismum. Nec verò esse syllogismum, hoc est, non habere veram formam syllogismi, sed solùm apparentem.

3 Of these three syllogisms, then, the first, which is called Contentious, and the third, which is called Paralogism, agree in this, that each preserves the syllogistic form, since it is constituted in Figure and Mood; hence on this side it does not sin; but they differ in the things from which they proceed. For the former proceeds from things which appear probable but are not probable; whereas the paralogism proceeds from things necessary and proper to some science, but which are neither necessary nor pertain to that science, but are false. The second, however, which is also called contentious, differs from the other two in both respects. For in the first place it does not preserve the form of the syllogism, but sins in it; and therefore Aristotle said of it that it is a contentious syllogism, but not truly a syllogism, that is, that it does not have the true form of a syllogism, but only an apparent one.

> Et ex his intelligitur, *Primum, & tertium, veram habere formam syllogismi*: & ideò veros esse syllogismos. Nam procedere ex apparentibus, aut etiam ex falsis, non tollit veram formam syllogismi. *Secundum verò non esse verum syllogismum, sed apparentem*: & tales sunt omnes, qui regulas syllogismorum non seruant: sed vel ex medio æquiuoco procedunt, vel non distributo, vel ex negatiuis præmissis: aut alios defectus patiuntur circa formam.

And from these things it is understood, first, that the First and the third have the true form of a syllogism, and are therefore true syllogisms. For to proceed from apparent, or even from false, things does not take away the true form of a syllogism. But the Second is not a true syllogism, but an apparent one; and such are all those which do not preserve the rules of syllogisms, but proceed either from an equivocal middle, or from one not distributed, or from negative premises, or suffer other defects concerning form.

> 4 Secundò intelligitur, *Hos tres syllogismos, essentialiter esse diuersos*: quia vel differunt ratione formæ syllogisticæ: vel ex parte præmissarum. Ex parte quidem formę, differt secundus à primo, & tertio: & cùm differentia ex parte formæ, sit essentialis, euidens est, differre essentialiter ab eis. Tandem primus, & tertius, licèt conueniant in forma syllogistica, & quasi generica, differunt tamen in forma speciali, ex modo concludendi desumpta.

4 It is understood, second, that these three syllogisms are essentially diverse: because they differ either by reason of the syllogistic form or on the side of the premises. On the side of form, the second differs from the first and the third; and since a difference on the side of form is essential, it is evident that it differs essentially from them. Finally, the first and the third, although they agree in the syllogistic and as it were generic form, nevertheless differ in the special form, taken from the mode of concluding.

> Nam primus procedit, & concludit ex his, quæ solùm apparent probabilia. Tertius verò, ex his quæ apparent necessaria. Ideo primus & tertius differunt tanquam veræ species syllogismi. Secundus verò, non differt ab eis, tanquam vera species quia cùm non habeat veram formam syllogismi, nec vera species eius esse potest: sed solùm secundùm apparentiam. Vnde [p. 737] duo illi, sunt syllogismi simpliciter, iste verò non, nisi secundùm quid: quia solam habet apparentiam syllogismi, eo modo quo homo pictus, solam habet apparentiam hominis: differt ergo ab eis analogicè.

For the first proceeds and concludes from things which only appear probable; the third, however, from things which appear necessary. Therefore the first and the third differ as true species of syllogism. The second, however, does not differ from them as a true species, because, since it does not have the true form of a syllogism, neither can it be a true species of it, but only according to appearance. Hence [p. 737] those two are syllogisms simply, but this one is not, except in a certain respect: because it has only the appearance of a syllogism, in the way in which a painted man has only the appearance of a man. It differs from them, therefore, analogically.

> Quocirca intelligitur tertia, *Diuisionem syllogismi sophistici in hæc tria membra, esse analogi in Analogata*. Verùm respectu duorum membrorum, nempe primi, & tertij, esse generis in suas species: & ideo Arist. non definiuit omnes vna definitione: sed diuersis: simul diuidens syllogismum sophisticum, in hæc tria membra: & singula definiens, propriis definitionibus.

Wherefore it is understood, third, that the division of the sophistical syllogism into these three members is a division of an analogous term into its Analogates; but with respect to two members, namely the first and the third, it is a division of a genus into its species. And therefore Aristotle did not define them all by one definition, but by different ones, at once dividing the sophistical syllogism into these three members and defining each by its proper definitions.

> Quartò intelligitur: *Generalem diuisionem syllogismi, in Demonstratiuum, Dialecticum, & Sophisticum, esse diuisionem generis in suas species*, si sophisticus solùm sumatur pro eo, qui non peccat in forma, quo pacto primum, & tertium solùm comprehendit. Nam solùm hoc modo sumptus, vera species syllogismi est: subalterna tamen, cùm in duas alias species diuidatur. Tertius verò syllogismus, non est species vera syllogismi, cùm forma careat: sed solùm secundùm apparentiam. Vnde si sophisticus sumatur, prout omnes tres comprehendit, eadem diuisio generalis ex parte eius, erit analoga: cùm vnum membrum comprehendat, quod non est syllogismus, nisi secundùm quid.

It is understood, fourth, that the general division of the syllogism into Demonstrative, Dialectical, and Sophistical is a division of a genus into its species, if sophistical is taken only for that which does not sin in form, in which way it comprehends only the first and the third. For taken in this way alone it is a true species of syllogism, though a subaltern one, since it is divided into two other species. The second syllogism, however, is not a true species of syllogism, since it lacks the form, but only according to appearance. Hence, if sophistical is taken as it comprehends all three, the same general division will, on its side, be analogous, since it comprehends one member which is not a syllogism except in a certain respect.

> 6 *Præter hanc diuisionem syllogismi* in tria illa membra, quæ essentialis est, diuiditur *diuisione accidentali*, in membra, secundùm duos diuersos effectus, vel fines, quos per eum intendere potest sophista. *Primus finis est*, ostentare scientiam, & aucupari gloriam: & tunc dicitur syllogismus *sophisticus* tantùm, *vel litigiosus*: quia sophista per eum, non tam intendit disputationem instituere, quàm litem, aut litigium, verbisque fallacibus conuincere respondentem, & ideo sapiens haberi, in opinione vulgi *Secundus finis est*, periculum facere: vel experimentum sumere de scientia alterius: & tunc dicitur *syllogismus Tentatiuus*.

6 Besides this division of the syllogism into those three members, which is essential, it is divided by an accidental division into members according to the two different effects, or ends, which the sophist can intend through it. The first end is to display knowledge and to hunt for glory; and then it is called a sophistical syllogism only, or contentious: because through it the sophist intends not so much to set up a disputation as a quarrel or strife, and to overcome the respondent with fallacious words, and thus to be held wise in the opinion of the crowd. The second end is to make trial, or to take a test, of the knowledge of another; and then it is called a Tentative syllogism.

> Deinde diuiditur etiam *accidentaliter, in quinque alia membra*, secundùm quinque inconuenientia, ad quæ sophista intendit deducere respondentem. *Et inconuenientia* hæc, solent vocari metæ, vel termini: quia quasi ad illa: tanquam ad metam, scopum, vel finem suæ disputationis, alium deducere intendit: Prima est, *meta Redargutionis*: Quando respondens cogitur, vi syllogismi apparentis negare: quòd priùs concesserat: vel concedere, quod negauerat.

Next it is also divided accidentally into five other members, according to the five absurdities to which the sophist intends to lead the respondent. And these absurdities are customarily called goals, or terms: because it is as it were to them, as to the goal, mark, or end of his disputation, that he intends to lead the other. The first is the goal of Refutation: when the respondent is compelled, by the force of an apparent syllogism, to deny what he had previously granted, or to grant what he had denied.

> 7 Secunda est *meta falsi*: Quando cogitur aliquid apertè falsum cõcedere, vt quòd ipsemet nõ sit homo, illo syllogismo: Quod ego sum, tu non es: Ego sum homo, ergo, Tu non es [p. 738] homo: *Tertia est meta inopinabilis*, seu *Paradoxa*: Quando cogitur concedere rem aliquam, opinabilem à sapientibus, vel opinione vulgi inauditam, quamuis fortè non sit falsa. Quarta *meta Solœcismi*: Quando aliquam incongruam locutionem compellitur concedere. Quinta dicitur *meta Negationis*: Quando cogitur ad inutilem minùs ornatam locutionem, per quam nugari videatur. Vt si cogatur dicere: Nasum, esse nasum curuum, aut simum: Et hæc syllogismo sophistico annotasse sufficiat: ex quibus cognoscemus naturam eius, atque etiam quot species, & membra habeat: & quotnam ex membris eius, sint veri syllogismi, quotque non veri, sed solùm apparentes. Fallaciæ verò omnes: quæ sunt quasi loca, ex quibus varij syllogismi fallaces deduci possunt, satis sunt in Summulis explicatæ: & ideo, non putamus, enumerationem & explicationem singulorum, in hac parte repetendam.

7 The second is the goal of the false: when he is compelled to grant something openly false, as that he himself is not a man, by this syllogism: What I am, you are not; I am a man; therefore, You are not AA a [p. 738] a man. The third is the goal of the unbelievable, or Paradox: when he is compelled to grant something unbelievable to the wise, or unheard of in the opinion of the crowd, although perhaps it is not false. The fourth, the goal of Solecism: when he is compelled to grant some incongruous expression. The fifth is called the goal of Babbling: when he is compelled to a useless and less ornate expression, by which he seems to babble. As if he is compelled to say that a nose is a curved or snub nose. And let it suffice to have noted these things on the sophistical syllogism: from which we shall know its nature, and also how many species and members it has, and how many of its members are true syllogisms, and how many not true, but only apparent. All the fallacies, however, which are as it were the places from which various fallacious syllogisms can be deduced, have been sufficiently explained in the Summulae; and therefore we do not think that the enumeration and explanation of each is to be repeated in this part.

> *Hæc tandem quæ circa vniuersam Logicam Aristotelis, annotauimus in nostris Commentationibus, dilucidam satis, reor, ac breuem eam efficient: vt facilè, & breui tempore possit liberalium Artium studiosis, huius florentissimæ Academiæ, à suis Magistris in Gymnasiis explicari, & ab eis percipi. Faxit DEVS Opt. Max. vt labor hic noster in gratiam eorum assumptus in gloriam eius, sacrissimæque Deiparæ, ac B. Thomæ, in maximámque eorum studiosorum vtilitatem (vti speramus) cedat.*

These things, finally, we have noted in our Commentaries concerning the whole Logic of Aristotle, rendering it, I think, clear enough and brief, so that it may easily, and in a short time, be explained to the students of the liberal Arts of this most flourishing Academy by their Masters in the Schools, and be grasped by them. May G o d , Best and Greatest, grant that this labor of ours, undertaken for their sake, may redound to his glory and that of the most holy Mother of God, and of St. Thomas, and to the greatest benefit of those same students (as we hope).

> FINIS TOTIVS LOGICÆ.

THE END OF THE WHOLE LOGIC.

Truth.

> Veritas ex parte adæquationis vna non potest esse maior altera, bene tamen ex parte fundamenti, & causarum. nu. 26. 636

On the part of the adequation one truth cannot be greater than another; but it can on the part of the foundation and of the causes. no. 26. 636

> FINIS.

T H E E N D.
